Preface
Although it is with some trepidation that I have
authored a new book on sugarcane technology, it
seems that it is an opportune time. Most practical
sugarcane technology texts are dated and develop-
ments in technology in the last 25 years have been
substantial. Undertaking the task of writing a book
was the suggestion of the publisher Dr. Jiirgen
Bmhns of Verlag Dr. Albert Bartens, who recog-
nized the need and persuaded me to produce a book
of practical usefulness. Many of the previous topics
have received a new treatment here and new mate-
rial is evidentparticularly in relation to cane quality
and payment, cane preparation, diffusion, clarifica-
tion and filtration, syrup clarification, continuous
pan boiling, molasses exhaustion, chemical control
of factories,boilers,steamgenerationand steamand
water balances.
The challenges have been to combine the new
technology with the old, to be critically selectivein
the materialpublished and to produce a book coher-
ent in form and content.It is importantalso to main-
tain a balanced perspectivebetween theoretical and
empiricalinformation.The practicingengineermust
use both to be effective, because in most cases a
theoretical background promotes a more productive
use of empiricalinformation.Where possible a con-
sistent structure has been followed in each chapter,
startingwith objectives,followedby theoretical and
fundamental issues, then design, equipment details,
operationand control, in roughly that order.
Whileattemptingtobe comprehensive,thetemp-
tation tobe totallyinclusivehashad to be resisted,in
order to meet the objectives of the book. The book
is designed to provide relevant and useful informa-
tion for the practicing engineer and technologist,as
well as for those involved in design and optimiza-
tion of processes and equipment.Further references
are provided for those needing to delve deeper. The
book covers most of the background material pre-
sented in courses on Sugq Processing Engineering
and Sugar Factory Design in the Louisiana State
University Collegeof Engineering.
A valuable foundation for sugarcane technol-
ogy has been laid by earlier authors, particularly
Tromp, Honig, Spencer, Meade, Hugot and Chen.
However, most of the information in this book has
been gleanedfrom theliteratureand from thosewith
whom I have worked over many years and from
whom I have learnedmost of what Iknow. I identify
with the quote of IsaacNewton: "If I have seen fur-
ther, it is by standingon the shouldersof giants".
I have been most fortunate in enlisting the aid
of outstanding collaborators, who authored roughly
a quarter of the book. They are all experts in their
fields and add immeasurablyto its value and useful-
ness. I am grateful too to those who have undertaken
to review the chapters, in particular Dr. Mike Ink-
son, Ian Smith, Dave Muzzell, Dr. Luis Bento, Dr.
Ed Richard, Jimmy Cargill, Dr. Regis Lima Verde
Leal andDr. DaveLove.Theircommentsandadvice
have been invaluable. John Dutton also contributed
thorough diligentediting and assistance.Ihave been
fortunate to have associated during my career with
these and other technologists in the international
sugar community.
In attemptingto produce a relevant text, SIunits
have been adopted.This will not be strangein most
of the sugar-producingareas. However, the IS0 set
of notation has been adopted, and the symbolsused
might appear unfamiliar to some readers. I believe
that familiarity with them will prove that they are in
fact easy to use and less subject to confusion.There
is a real need for standardizationin this area. In this
respect, the beet sugar industry has been more pro-
active, and the system used here brings cane and
beet sugar technology closer together.
I am indebted to the Louisiana State University
Agricultural Center for their support. Dr. Jiirgen
Bruhns proved to be far more than a publisher. His
many constructive suggestions have added value
and identified errors. He also helped to keep me
on the straight and narrow when I strayed on the
paths of inconsistency.Even so, in a work like this
it is difficult to ensure that no errors are present. I
trust they are few and far between and I take total
responsibility. I hope that readers will draw atten-
tion to them so that they can be corrected in future
editions.
Finally I wish to thank my wife Kath for her un-
failing supportand the fact that shenever begrudged
the long hours I spent on this task. I could not have
wished for a better companionthrough my sugarca-
reer.
Peter Rein
Baton Rouge
December 2006

Sugarcaneis a grass grown intropical and sub-
tropical countries. It is a complexhybrid of various
species, derived largely from Sacchmam? ofiina-
rum and other Saccharurn species. It is propagated
vegetatively by planting pieces of cane sf&. New
growth emanates from buds on the cane nodes,
ensuring uniform progeny. In the process of cane
breeding, new varieties areproduced and tested in a
constantsearchfornew andbetter varieties. Thishas
been a major factor in improvingproductivityin the
sugarcaneindustry.
Yields of canevary tremendously fromone area
to another, depending on cane variety, climaticfac-
tors, availability of water, m e growing pkctices
and tbe length of the growing season. The length
of the growing season may vary from 8 months in
Louisianato nearlywoyearsin Hawaii. Caneyields
may vary from 50 tlha in poor oonditiom to values
approaching 200 t/ha under exceptional conditions
with long growingperiods.Yield of sugar may vary
&om 5 tlha to 25 ma.
Cane is generally not replanted every time it is
harvested,but is allowed to regrow and produce an-
other crop,called a ratoonor stubble crop.The yield
declinesafter a number of ratoonsand at somepoint
the cane has to be ploughed out and replanted. Cane
is generally harvested in the winter and the length
of the crushing season is dictated by weather con-
ditions, principally rain. In some countries such as
Colombia,Peru and Hawaii,cane may be processed
virtually all year round.
The major reason for processing cane is to re-
cover sugar, which in its pure state is referred to
by its chemical name sucrose. It is formed in the
plant by a complex process but essentially consists
of a combination of the two monosaccharide sug-
ars, fructose and glucose. This is represented in
Figure 1.1. Sucrosehas the formula C,2H2,0,, and
is termed a disaccharidesinceit is comprised of two
monosaccharide units. The monosaccharide sugars
are six carbon sugars or hexoses, products of the
process of photosynthesis, which both have the for-
mula C6H,,06. They are termed monosaccharides
because they cannot be hydrolyzed to smaller car-
bohydrate molecules by the action of acids or en-
zymes.

The reverse of this reaction is termed inversion,
when under the right conditions, sucrose will be
hydrolyzed, and together with a molecule of water,
will lead to the formation of the two component
monosaccharide sugars. The sugars are in solution
in water together with other soluble components;
this liquid phase is referred to as juice. Other than
juice, the cane stalk contains about 13 g vegetable
fiber as a solid phase/100 g cane, giving the stalkits
structural rigidity. Fiber, juice and other terms are
defined in Section 1.1.3.

Most of the sugaris storedin these largesoft-walled

graduallytowardsthecenterof thestalkand thecells

filled with air.

Each cell is lined with a layer of protoplasm,
which is so thin as to be scarcely visible under a
microscope. The cell walls are composed mainly of
cellulose and hemicellulose. Cellulose is permeable
to water and solutes, while protoplasm is permeable
to water and some solutes only. Although sucrose
finds its way into the sugar storage cells by diffu-
sion, the rate of diffusion is very slow. Protoplasm
may be considered essentially impermeable to su-
crose molecules.
1.1.2 Locationof sucrose and
impurities
Thejuice contained in the parenchyma cells has
a higher concentration of sucrose and a lower con-
centration of nonsucrose than thejuice in the fibrous
schlerenchyma cells. Since the parenchyma cells
occupy roughly 70 % by volume of the cane, it is
apparent that most of the sucrose is contained in the
parenchyma cells. Similarly more sucrose is found
in the internodes than the nodes. The rind contains
relatively little juice, and is of high impurity con-
tent.
The cell walls are composed of long chains of
celluloseboundtogetherby hemicellulose andlignin.
Lignin is universally associated with hemicellulose
accompanying the cellulose in the fiber structure of
plants. It has an aromatic structure and is probably
deposited in the pores. Cellulose is insoluble, but a
small fraction of the other materials could dissolve
or may be dispersed in the juice as colloids during
processing, depending on conditions. The chemical
composition and the structure of the fiber vary ac-
cording to the part of the stalk from which it derives.
The fiber content of the parenchyma cells is much
lower than the rest of the stalk. Thus these cells are
easily ruptured in canepreparation.
Monosaccharides or reducing sugars are the
most abundant impurity in cane. Because they are
the building blocks for growth, a high reducing sug-
ar content is found in the immature top section of
the cane stalk. The reducing sugar content is lower
in the nodes, which are dormant regions.
Inorganic impurities constitute about 0.6 to
0.8 % of fresh cane stalks. Silica and calcium are
present in the cell walls, but otherwise more of the
inorganic impurities are associated with the vascular
bundles than the parenchyma. The inorganic content
of cane is higher in the tops and leaves.
The surface of the cane stalk is coated with a
thin layer of wax, often more concentrated in the
nodal regions. The external waxy deposit acts as a
protection against excessive evaporation of moisture
from the surface of the stem.
Starch is located in the nodes and not in the in-
ternodal areas (Clarke 1996)and there is more color
associated with the nodes than the internodes. The
rind contributes 50 % of the color in the cane, al-
though it constitutes only 30 % of the cane by mass
(Lionnet 1992).
1.1.3 Definitionsof components
Sugarcane is essentially a combination of juice
and fiber. Thejuice is an aqueous solution of sucrose
and other inorganic and organic substances. Fiber is
defined as all the insoluble material in cane and so
includes any dirt, soil or any other extraneous mat-
ter, as well as stalk fiber.
The most basic analysis of cane considers cane
to consist of water, dissolved solids or refractomet-
ric dry substance (RDS) and fiber. RDS is generally
measured using a refractometer and is often loosely
referred to as Brix.
In most cases the sucrose in the juice is mea-
sured using a polarimeter and so is not entirely accu-
rate, generally being lower than the sucrose content
by a few percent (see Section 25.1.2). Sometimes
therefore this is referred to as the polarization or pol,
which indicates the method by which it is measured.
Purity represents the ratio of sucrose to total soluble
material expressed as a percentage. Where pol and
Brix are used in the analysis, the resulting ratio is
termed apparent purity.
An accurate analysis for sucrose can be obtained
by chromatographic methods, outlined in Section
2.4.4. The total soluble impurity is estimated by
difference between RDS and sucrose and is termed
nonsucrose. Thus it is important in reporting or
considering the analysis of cane to be aware of the
method of analysis used.
Another component of the cane, namely the in-
organic material, is often reported in terms of the
method by which it is analyzed, involving combus-
tion of all organic material, namely ash.

1.2.3 Typical compositionof
deliveredcane
In practice the composition of cane received by
a mill depends not only on the composition of the
cane stalk,but also on other factorssuch as the cane
variety, the amount of tops and leaves, other extra-
neous matter, the time of season, the maturity of the
cane, the delay between burning and cutting and
delivery to the mill. The composition in each cane
growing area reflects the combination of all these
factors.Typical average figures for some of the ma-
jor cane growing areas aregiven inTable 1.2.
The variation in cane composition during the
season also depends on the conditions during the
crushing season.If climaticfactorsremain relatively
constant during the season e.g. in Colombia, Peru,
or Zambia, thereis minimal seasonalvariation inthe
canecomposition.Inotherareaswheretemperatures
change significantlyduringthe season,the variation
in compositioncan be quite marked.

1.2.5 Nonsucrose in cane
Monosaccharides. The most abundant nonsu-
crose components in cane are the monosaccharides
Figure1.6: Representationof cane
A Compositional; B With Brix-free wa-
ter shown.
Numbers represent mass fractions in
g/100 gcane.
glucose and fructose, otherwise known as reducing
sugars. They are generallypresent to the extent of a
few per cent of sucrose in mature cane up to almost
10per cent of sucrose in immaturecane. Monosac-
charides are most abundant near the top of the cane
stalk because they are associated with the growing
part of the cane. For the same reason, the contents
of these componentsaregenerallyhigherin canecut
duringthe high growth period. Incorporationof tops
with the cane significantly increases the monosac-
charide content of the cane (Legendre et al. 1999).
The action of ripeners reduces the monosaccharide
content by maturing the cane and so increasing the
sucrosecontent at the expenseof monosaccharides.
Ash. The ash content of cane is also higher in
the tops and the leaves and in additionis affected by
cane variety.This is an importantselection criterion
in cane cultivar development in places like Texas
where the ash content tends to be high (Legendreet
al. 1999).A significant proportion of the inorganic
material is silica. However potassium is the cation
in greatest abundance, followed by calcium, mag-
nesium and sodium; chloride is the main anion fol-
lowedby sulfateand phosphate.Their relativeabun-
dance varies with variety and soil conditions, and
there are traces of several other elements in smaller
quantities.
Polysaccharides. Polysaccharides are large
molecular mass carbohydrates present in the cane.
They include starch,cellulose, gums, cell wall poly-
saccharidesand dextran, and are composed of many
1.2.6 Extraneousmatter
monosaccharide units condensed together. They
vary in concentration from about 1500 to 3000 mg
per kg dissolved solids (Legendre et al. 1999), de-
pending on the cane variety. The concentration of
polysaccharides is generally higher in the tops and
leaves than in the stalk. Naidoo and Lionnet (2000)
reported that the content of gums, now more com-
monly referred to as total polysaccharides,is highly
dependenton locationand on the variety of the cane.
The variety effect is very pronounced, with a range
of valuesbetween 6500 and 12000 mg gumskg dis-
solved solids measured in different varieties. These
values are considerably higher than those given by
Legendre et al. (1999) because they include starch
and were obtainedby wet disintegrationof the sam-
ples, notjuice expression.
Starch. Starch is present in cane in the form of
small water-insolublegranules and constitutes a re-
servecarbohydratefood.It is formed by the conden-
sation of glucose and consists of a mixture of two
polysaccharides.The majorcomponentamylopectin
represents 75 to 85 % of the starch and has a highly
branched structure; the remainder, arnylose, is an
essentially unbranched polymer. The starch content
is very dependenton cane variety. Early varieties in
SouthAfrica were phased out and replaced by vari-
eties with much lower starch contents (Wood 1962).
In Louisiana it has been shown that the starch con-
tent can vary between 275 and 1500 mg/kg solids,
with an average of about700 (Legendre at al. 1999).
Thereis a higher concentrationof starchin the grow-
ing point and in the leaves. Mature cane also has a
slightly lower starch content.
Color. The color of thejuice in cane is largely a
function of the variety of cane (Lionnet 1992;Nai-
doo and Lionnet 2000),but varies considerablyfrom
one cane growing region to another. The color asso-
ciated with tops and leaves is much higher than that
in thecleanstalk.An additional 1% of topsor leaves
is estimated to increase the total color by 4 % or
15 % respectively (Lionnet 1992).Thus significant
amounts of tops and leaves can have an overriding
effect on color,greater than the effect of variety.
Organicacids. Some organic acids occur natu-
rally in the cane, the most abundant of which is aco-
nitic acid. These are largely responsible for the pH
of thejuice being around 5.3 to 5.5.
1.2.6 Extraneousmatter
Tops and leavesareregarded as extraneousmat-
ter, but so is everythingelse which may be delivered
with the cane including field soil, dirt, rocks and
tramp iron. These are all particularlydestructivebut
are not generally measured. However attemptshave
been made in a number of areas to measuretops and
leavesand to estimatefield soilby analyzingfor ash
in cane. Thesemeasurements have been made in an
effortto improvethe quality of cane delivered to the
mill. The analysisof tops and leavesis consideredin
Section 1.2.2.In Australia for a number of years the
dirt in cane was estimated visually by cane inspec-
tors at each mill.
The quantity of soilin cane is largely influenced
by the weather, as rainy weather inevitably leads to
higher ash in cane, but is also influenced by the har-
vesting and loading method. Mechanicalloading of
cane can lead to very high soilcontentsif the loaders
are of unsuitable design or are not operated prop-
erly. Mechanical loading is often a common reason
for rocks in cane. In SouthAfrica, ash in cane has
been measured routinely at a number of mills over
many years, using the measurement of ash as an in-
dicator of field soil (Lionnet 1996).Bearing in mind
that the base line ash contentis between 0.4 and 0.8
@I00 g clean cane, average values of about 1.5 to
2 @I00 g cane have been recorded. Generally cane
can be categorizedaccording to its ash content in %
as follows:
Ash content in %

1.2.7 Effect of cane delays
Once sugarcane is cut it is subject to deteriora-
tion, largely due to the activity of microorganisms.
This results in the loss of sugar and the formationof
undesirableimpurities.The extentof deteriorationis
determined by a number of factors, but in all cases
the effect on the recovery of sugar and the process-
ing of the cane is adverse. It therefore needs to be
kept to a minimum.
1 Sugarcane
Deterioration starts in burnt cane from the mo-
ment it is burnt, because the heat of the fire gener-
ally cracks the rind and exposes some juice. With
unburnt cane, deterioration starts when the cane is
cut. In green cane, this occurs only at the cut ends.
Deterioration occurs more rapidly in chopper har-
vested cane, because there are many more exposed
ends. The effect can be minimized by increasing the
billet length and by ensuring that the cutters on the
harvesters are sharp to get a clean cut; this ensures
that the amount of juice exposed to the atmosphere
is kept to a minimum.
In general the rate of deterioration is faster with
burnt cane than green cane.
Microorganisms in the soil or the air infect the
exposed juice. Depending on the organism which
predomihates, the products of their activity may be
some or all of dextran, ethanol, oligosaccharides,
and organic acids. All of the microorganisms use
sugar as a food. Apart from the direct loss of sugar
which occurs, the nonsucrose content of the cane is
increased, leading to a larger loss of sugar in molas-
ses and a lower recovery of sugar. The rate at which
these organisms metabolize sucrose is also largely
dependent on temperature, and their activity is great-
ly reduced in cold weather.
In Australia where chopper harvesters were first
widely used, systems of transport were developed to
keep the transport delay down to less than 16hours.
Above that time, dextran formation occurred to the
extent that the processing of cane was impaired.
Studies carried out in Louisiana when chopper har-
vesting was introduced showed similar results (Egg-
leston et al. 2001). In severe cases, dextran levels
can rise to above 1000 mgkg solids and the pH of
thejuice drops below 5.
With whole stalk cane, deterioration is not so
rapid and longer delays between burning or cutting
and harvesting can be tolerated. A number of stud-
ies were conducted in SouthAfrica to investigate the
changes occurring in the cane after harvesting. The
findings can be summarized as (Cox and Sahadeo
1992):
Ethanol is the most obvious degradation prod-
uct, not dextran.
Deterioration is much more rapid in burnt cane
than unburnt cane.
Loss of recoverable sugar in cane averaged
about 1 % per day, although some much larger
numbers have been reported.
The cane juice purity dropped about 0.6 units
each day. Lionnet (1986) showed reductions of
between 0.4 and 2.5 units depending on tem-
perature.
There is a loss in cane mass of 0.5-1.5 % per
day (this sometimes leads to an erroneous belief
that cane sucrose content increases after harvest-
ins).

1.2.8 Effect of cane variety
Cane is generally bred for a high yield of cane
per hectare and a high sucrose content. Equally im-
portanthowever is disease resistance or susceptibil-
ity. There are some significant differences between
varieties, which are generally chosen to suit the
growing conditions e.g. irrigated or rain-fed, early
mahuing, type of soil, length of growing period,
type of harvestingsystem.
Over time, the most popular varieties grown
in a particular area will change. Differences in the
composition of thejuice in differentvarietiesarenot
sufficiently large nor predictable to make process-

.

.
9 Changesdue to climatic condi-
tions and time of season
Where the cane is grown under irrigation and
the water supply is secure, there is generally little
change in cane composition from one season to
the next. However in rain fed areas, the yield and
the compositionmay be strongly affected by varia-
tions in rainfall. The effect on cane composition
can be clearly seen from the comparative figures
for drought seasons and normal seasons shown in
Table 1.6. The length of the internodeis generally a
functionof the rate of growth. In periodsof drought,
the internode length reduces and the fiber content
increases as a result. In extremecases the tops will
be left on the cane to facilitate the formationof cane
bundles where thatmethod of cane handling is used.
This results in sucrose content and the purity of the
juice reducing andjuice colorincreasing.
Conversely in areaswhere heavy rainis encoun-
tered in the courseof the season, extraneousmatter,
mainly in the form of increased field soil, is gener-
ally experienced.
Dependingon the climatic factors, there may be
a pronounced time of seasoneffect on the composi-
tionof thecane.If thecaneisimmatureatthestartof
a season,it can be expectedthat the sucrosecontent
and the purity of thejuice will be low and the invert
sugarcontenthigh.As the seasonprogressesand the
cane m a w , the sucrose content and the purity in-
crease. At this time the best sucrose recoveries are

It has been shown in Chapter 1that sugarcaneis
very variable in its composition. The value of sug-
arcane to a miller depends on the amount of sugar
thatcan be recovered fromit, and the costassociated
with processing the cane. It is desirable therefore to
have some means of evaluatingthe cane, so that the
processor can assess its value and adjust his plant
and equipment to be able to produce sugar from it
efficientlyand at minimal cost.
Ideally the processor should pay for cane what
it is worth in terms of its effect on recovery and
processing costs. A cane payment system which
achieves this gives an economic incentive to the
growers to produce a quality of cane which maxi-
mizes the production of sugar from the cane. This
is important in terms of its ability to minimize the
costs of production of the combined operation of
growing and processing cane. The average quality
of cane in a sugar industry is largely a consequence
of the incentives or absence of incentives for good
cane quality present in the cane payment system.h
this contextgood quality caneenableshigh sugarre-
coveries to be obtained while minimizing the costs
of processing.
To measure the quality of cane, systems for
sampling and analysis of cane are required. There
are a number of different ways in which this can be
achieved.
Evaluation of cane quality
21.1 Quality parameters
The most basic method of evaluating cane is
h m its overall analysis in terms of pol, fiber and
RDS or Brix. This gives an indication of how much
sugaris present in the cane deliveredto the mill, but
does not indicate how much of the sugar can be re-
covered. To estimate sugar recovery, a measure of
the total amount and nature of the impurities in the
caneis necessary.
Because of the adverse effect of tops and leaves
oncanequality andthe qualityof thejuice extracted,
the quantity of tops and leaves is sometimes mea-
sured. In addition the amount of extraneous matter,
particularly soil brought in from the field, is also
sometimesmeasured.
2.1.2 Effect on recoverablesugar
The quality of the cane influences the amount
of sugar which is extractedinjuice from the cane as
well as the quality or purity of thejuice. Clean fresh
cane is the ideal feed to a mill, because this facili-
tates extractionof sugarfrom the cane and yields the
highest purity juice for processing. This is seldom
achieved in practice.
The fiber content has the largest effect on ex-
traction. If the fiber content is higher, the quantity
of bagasse is greater and the loss of sucrose in the
bagasse is increased correspondingly.Various stud-
ies have looked at the effect that fiber content has
on extraction in a milling tandem. This has led to
the development of a series of "reduced extraction"
formulae, which attempt to account for the fiber
content. The sugar content of the cane has a posi-
tivebut smallereffectonextractionandit too should
be incorporatedinto a reduced extraction formula if
comparisonsaremadeof performancewith different
cane qualities.A number of correctedextractionfor-
mulaehave been published which correct extraction

a and b have not changed significantly.
2.1.3 Effect on mill capacity
Ln designing a sugar mill, there are three ele-
ments determined by cane quality to be taken into
account which determine the sizing of the plant:
1. The fiber content of the cane or the total amount
of fiber to be handled determines the extraction
plant size.
2. The total sucrose input determines the sizing of
the high grade pan station.
3. The nonsucrose input into themill sets the capac-
ity of the low grade pan and centrifugal station.
Changes in cane quality are generally reflected in
the changes in fiber and nonsucrose in the cane.
Canewith excessive tops and leaves for instance will
increase both these inputs significantly. Reductions
injuice purity due to cane delays or any other causes
also affect the input of nonsucrose. Deterioration of
one of these cane quality parameters can lead to a
situation where one part of the factory becomes a
bottleneck while there is surplus capacity elsewhere
in the factory.
Conversely improvements resulting from reduc-
tions in extraneous matter or higher juice purities
can lead to effective additional capacity, with no
capital expenditure.
It has been reported that a reduction of 1%
leaves in cane increases the crushing rate by 3%
(Scott 1977). Work reported by Reid and Lionnet
(1989) proved that excessive tops and leaves results
in a reduction in milling capacity. However the fiber
rate through the mlls remained reasonably constant
at the same mill speed; thus the reduction observed
is due directly to the additional fiber that has to be
processed. Similar findings are reported by Kent et
al. (2003), who showed that a reduction in tops and
leaves content of about 7 % led to an increase in
crushing rate of 15%. However in this case, too, the
fiber crushing rate was virtually constant.
A reduction in bulk density in the transport ve-
hicles is another capacity effect with excessively
trashy cane. Kent et al. (2003) found a reduction in
bin weights of 15 % with dirty cane. de Beer et al.
(1989) showed a reduction of 44 % in payload when
whole cane with all the tops and leaves is transport-
ed relative to transport of clean burnt cane.
Reid and Lionnet (1989) showed thatwith exces-
sivelytrashy cane, thenonsucrose inputinto afactory
can double compared with clean cane. This can have
a severe effect on the back end capacity required.

2 Cane evaluation and payment
2.1.4 Field soil and dirt
Soil in cane is not measured directly in most
sugar industries, because it is not easy to do. How-
ever, it has a very significanteffect on a sugarmill's
costs, and is therefore an important issuein the cost
of production of sugar.
The cane payment system in many industries is
based on the recoverability of product sugar from
the cane. Ideally, soil in cane also needs to be taken
into account in an effectivecane payment system.
All non-soluble solids in cane are defined as
fiber, and so soil in cane is regarded for analytical
purposes as cane fiber. The only analytical method
that can give a reliable measure of soil in cane is
ash analysis, using a suitable furnace (such as a
kiln designed for firing ceramic ware) to remove
by combustion all organic material from samplesof
prepared cane.
This is an indirect measure of soil in cane and
includes the natural ash of about 0.6 % in the cane
stalk.
The natural ash has to be subtracted from the
measurement to give the soil ash. Unfortunately it
is a lengthy analysis. In this respect the adoption in
the future of NIR analysis of cane could provide a
convenientmeans of quantifying soil in cane (Mad-
sen et al. 2003).
Excessive soilincaneincreases thecostof main-
tenance,leadsto increasedloss of sugar,reducesthe
capacityof the mill and the outputof the boilers and
leadstohigherusageof supplementaryfuels.InAus-
tralia it is estimated that annual maintenance costs
attributable to soil in cane average US$1.4 million
per year for each Australian factory (Purchase and
de Beer 1999).This represents on average 0.38 US
centsllb sugar.
An industry study undertaken in Australia (Mil-
ford 2002),among otherthings,makes thefollowing
statement:
"The biggest problems were seen to be t h e w
rateltonne cane charged by harvesters and the
narrow range of parameters that are measured
in cane. Both of these make it difjcult to adjust
rewards in relation to quality or performance.
Interviewees expressed the need for measure-
ment of new parameters in cane, as well as the
need to improve current analyses and set up
reward systems involving others currently mea-
sured."
2.1.5 Dextran
Nonsucrose components in cane extracted into
thejuice aregenerallyaccounted for in a measure of
the juice purity and these affect the loss of sugar in
molasses.There is one other nonsucrosecomponent
which needs to be consideredon its own, sinceit not
only affects the loss in molasses but also severely
affectstheprocessing of the canejuice. This compo-
nent is dextran,which as outlinedin Section 1.2.7,is
not a natural product in the cane, but a consequence
of microbialactioneither in cane(particularlychop-
per-harvested)subjectto long delays, or in the mill-
ing tandem itself.
Dextran only becomes a problem when the dex-
tran content of juice rises above about 2000 m a g
DS. In a number of countries it has never been of
real concern but in others it can almost bring a fac-
tory to a standstillwhen the infection is severe.This
generallyis theresult of long periodsof bad weather.
High dextran levels increase the viscosity of masse-
cuites to a point where sugar cannot be recovered
from them at all in severe cases, and in less severe
cases they slow down the pan boiling operationssig-
nificantly and increase the sugar loss in molasses.
Dextran is also generally penalized in raw sugar by
the refiner (see Section 20.5.2).
Dextran is strongly dextro-rotatoryand so influ-
ences sucrose determination by polarization. The
use of lead as a clarifying agent precipitatesdextran
so that its effecton the pol reading is negligible.The
use of lead has been stopped in most industries and
alternativeclarifying agents do not have this effect.
Thus the effect of high dextran on pol in cane is af-
fected by the clarifying agent used. In addition the
organism producing dextran from sucrose increases
fructose (which is levo-rotatory) relative to glucose
and in some casesmore than compensatesfortheef-
fect of dextran on pol in cane measurements.These
effects are described by Madsen and Day (2005).

.2 Cane paymentsystems
2 . Options for payment
In most industriesthe caneestates arenot owned
by the milling companies.This requires the use of a
system for payment for cane which is equitable to
both parties. The nature of the agreement between
millers and growers can have a significanteffect on
the efficiency of the industry, because it sets the in-
centives for both parties and affects how they con-
duct their operations. The features of a good pay-
ment system might include the following:
I. The system should promote the profitability of
the industryas a whole.
2. Growers and processors should split the pro-
ceeds from the sale of sugar on an agreed ba-
sis, so that they share the risk of variable sugar
prices.
3. The system should be simple and easy to under-
stand.
4. There should be adequatereward to both grow-
ers and processors for their efforts.
5. The systemshould be fair and equitable.
6. The grower should be rewarded for his perfor-
mance, good or bad, and should not be affected
by the performanceof the mill to which he sup-
plies his cane.
7. The processorshould be rewarded for his recov-
ery of sugar from cane, good or bad, and should
not be affected by the performance of the grower
supplyingthe cane.
8. Allowance must be made for adjustments to be
made to preserveequity between processorsand
growers following events outside the grower's
control, e.g. extreme adverse weather condi-
tions.

In most industries, the distribution is related to
the revenue obtained from the sugar produced. In
some cases this revenue pool may include proceeds
from molasses sales as well. Therefore growers and
millers share the risk or reward on sugar prices. In-
dia is an example where the price of cane is fixed
without being directlylinked to thevalue of the sug-
ar produced. The m

l
l then carries the risk of sugar
price fluctuations.
Generally the growers receive approximately
60 % of the proceeds and millers 40 %. These num-
bers differ from one country to another, depending
on local circumstances,including responsibility for
cane transport, whether molasses and otherby-prod-
ucts areincluded in thepool to be shared, and wheth-
er the revenues shared are from white or raw sugar.
The approaches adopted in different countries are
summarized by Todd and Forber (2005). There are
three di£ferentapproachesto sharingof the revenue:
(a) On an industrial basis. All proceeds are
pooled and, based on a pre-agreed split, a price per
tonne of recoverable sugar in cane is calculated.
This requires single c h a ~ e l
marketing, where all
sugar is sold by the industry or by individual mills

at a predeterminedprice. With this arrangement,all
growers in industryreceive the samepriceper tonne
of recoverablesugar,growers deliveringto a mill are
not materially affected by the mill's efficiency, and
an individual mill keeps most of the benefit of im-
proved mill performance
(b) On an individual mill basis. The mill pro-
ceeds are split on a pre-agreed basis. The result is
different cane prices at different mills and the pro-
ceedsreceived by the growerareaffectedby the mill
performance. This system tends to blunt the incen-
tive which either party may have to improve perfor-
mance, because the benefit will be shared with the
otherparty. It is a disincentiveforthe miller toinvest
for improved performanceanda disincentivefor the
growers to improve cane quality. Investment by the
miller tends to focus on reducing costs, for which
they retain the full benefit. However, it is easier to
negotiate changes to cane payment systems on an
individualmill basis.
(c) Processingfee paid to miller per tonne of
cane processed. The cost of milling cane is gener-
ally proportional to the tomes of cane crushed. To
overcome the disadvantagesin the previous two ap-
proaches, the miller is paid a processingfee for each
tonne crushed from the proceeds of the cane. This
is the basis of the Australian payment system. The

2.3 Cane sampling
A fundamentalrequirementfor cane payment is
a reliable and representativesampling system. This
is not a simple task, because cane is not a uniform
material.In somecasesthe analysisof caneconsign-
ments is used only to determine the distribution of
proceeds among growers and the absolute accuracy
of the data generated is not regarded as being im-
portant. However the amount of effort and expense
involved in a cane sampling and analysis system is
such that the generation of data which are also ac-
curate is worth strivingfor. Such data can have con-
siderablevalue in attaininga good factoryefficiency
control system.
In most industries, the cane is sampled,while in
others, samples of first expressedjuice are used to
infer the analysis of the cane.
To achieverepresentativesamplingfor payment
or massbalancepurposes,it is not necessaryto sarn-
ple every consignment. With a good representative
sampling system, sampling of only one-third of the
cane consignments will not lead to any loss in ac-
curacy.In sugarindustriessuch as thosein Indiaand
Kenya where thereare tens of thousandsof indepen-
dentgrowers,samplingof cane is impractical.Other
less sophisticatedschemesare therefore necessary.

.
1 Core samplingof cane
A core sampler is used to take a sample of cane
from a delivery vehicleprior to off-loading.It con-
sists of a rotating tube, 150 to 200 mm in diameter
with cutting teeth on the open end. The tube pen-
etratesthe cane in the vehicleeither from the top or
the side, cutting a core of cane which is discharged
from the tube once the tube is withdrawn. It is im-
portant that the corer is kept sharp to achieve a clean
cut of cane. A blunt corer will pull trash into it and
causejuice expressionerrors.
The top entry system, usually at an angle of
about 45" is preferred, since it tends to provide a
morerepresentativesample.I
f all thecaneis stacked
in the same direction, the whole cane stalk is likely
to be sampled,providingthe strokeof the sampleris
long enough. Side entry corers tend to samplepref-
erentially one part of the cane stalk. Fixed height
side-entry corers are not recommended since the

2 Hatchsampling
A good representative cane sample can be ob-
tained after the factory shredder because it is well
mixed and more homogeneous. However the sam-
pling hatchmust coverthefullwidth of the canecar-
rier and samplethe full height of cane on the carrier,
because there is usually some degree of classifica-
tion of particlesuesthroughthe canemat and across
the conveyor.The sample is taken from a full-width
hatch in the bottom steel deck of a slat conveyor,
opening against the direction of cane flow. This is
shownin Figure2.2.Wherea belt conveyoris in use,
a differentarrangementis used. Canecoming off the
headshaft of the conveyor is diverted into a sample
screw conveyoratpreset intervals.Againa fullwidth
sampleis taken. This is illustrated in Figure 2.3. An
alternativearrangementuses a full-widthswinggate
sampler situated below the headshaft of a belt con-
vey& at a transfer point. This is swung through the
stream of cane as it falls off the headshaft, catching
a full-width sample as it moves though the falling
stream of prepared cane.
Because the sample covers the full width of the
conveyor, the sample is necessarily quite large. In
South Africa a 20 t consignment will require that
eight samples each of 25 kg be taken, and correct
mixing and sub-sampling becomes important. This
is generallydone automaticallywith a seriesof sam-
pling conveyors, which also return surplus sample
to the main cane conveyor (Inman-Bamber 1989).
Details of the sampling systems in use are given in
the SouthAfrican LaboratoryManual (2005) and in
the ICUMSA MethodsBook (Anon. 2005), Method
GS5-5.
This system has the disadvantage that if cane
is stored in a cane yard, the identity of each cane
consignment needs to be maintained until the cane
is processed. It has been shown that a hatch sam-
pler is cheaper than a core sampler,both in terms of

2.3.3 Grab sampling
Grab sampling of cane for payment purposes is
not commonly used any more. It can only be used
with whole stalk cane. The sample is taken with a
mechanical grab oncethe cane is offloadedfrom the
vehicle. Since only the top surface can be sampled,
it is unlikely to result in a good estimate of extrane-
ous matter, particularly soil. The tines of the grab
shouldbe kept sharpand designedto achievea clean
"bite" so that trash from non-sampled stalks is not
included in the sample. The grab system is usually

2.3.4 First expressedjuice sampling
A number of sugar industries, such as Australia
and Florida, rely on a sample of the first juice ex-

of cane from the analysis of this juice. The advan-
tage of this systemis that it is easy to obtaina repre-
sentativesampleof the whole consignment.The dis-
advantage lies in the fact that the analysis depends
on the performance of the mill. Hugot (1974) states
that for this reason, primary juice from the first mill
rather than first expressedjuice from the feed roll is
a more reliable predictor of sucrose in cane.
Thejuice sample is collected from the pressure
feeder (if fitted) and the feed rolls of the first mill.
Inverted cones are used to screen out bagasse par-
ticles from thejuice sample (Milford 1989).In most
cases the juice is pumped directly to a mill labora-

allrequirea systemto trackaparticularconsignment
to the sampling point. This is easily achieved elec-
tronically, using tachometers on variable speed con-
veyors sothattheappearanceof eachconsignmentat
the samplingpoint can be accurately gauged. When
the new consignment reaches the sampling point a
calculatedperiod of time is allowed to elapsebefore
sampling is started, so that if there is any mixing of
adjacentconsignmentsit doesnot affectthe sample.
2.4 Methodsof analysis
2.4.1 Press method
This method uses a hydraulic press to express
juice from a prepared cane sample at a standard
pressure for a given time. The juice expressed is
analyzed for pol and RDS, and the plug of fiber is
weighed and analyzed for moisture.With a few as-
sumptions, the analysis of cane can then be calcu-
lated.
The system was introduced into Louisiana in
1976 and is now in use at all mills in this region.
Minor modifications to the procedure have been
made sinceits introduction.A prepared cane sample
of 1000gis pressedin a hydraulic press at a hydrau-
lic pressure set to give a pressure on the sample of
25.3MPa (3650psig)for2minutes. Juiceexpressed
from theperforatedbottom is collectedandanalyzed
for pol and RDS. A sample of the juice is centri-
fuged and a sediment volume is obtained. Roughly
30 % of the soil in cane is expressed in the juice
(Legendre 1992) and a factor is used to convert this
to a mass of solids which is then added back in the
calculationof the fiber content. The assumption was
made that thejuice expressedhas the samedissolved
solids content as thejuice remaining in the bagasse
plug. Initially no allowance was made for Brix-free
water and the procedure was found to give sucrose
content estimates which were too high by 3 to 5 %
of the sucrose value. In 1998a correction incorpo-
rating Brix-free water of 30 % (ratherthan the more
common 25 % value) was incorporated to give a pol
content in cane that agreed with analysis by direct
analysis. It is called a fibraque correction and leads
to more satisfactory results. However,Madsen et al.
(2003) showed that the pol content of canefromthe
press method was consistently slightly higher than
that obtained by direct analysisof cane.

of soil in the cane.

to achieve a better sample preparation and a stricter
control of sampling became necessary.
2.4.2 Wet disintegrationmethod
This method is generally regarded as the most
accurate, but has been deemed to be too costly to
run on a routine basis (Saranin 1986). This method
is used in South Africa and is referred to as the Di-
rect Analysis of Cane (DAC). It involves the disin-
tegration of a known amount of cane in a standard
quantity of water (generally 1000 g of cane and
2000 g water). Various designs of wet disintegrator
are available. Essentially the disintegrator consists
of a stainless steel bowl, which is preferably water
cooled, in which rotate some sharp hardened steel
blades at high speed. After 20 minutes, the sample is
thoroughly disintegrated and a mixture of juice and
finely disintegrated fiber is produced. A sample of
the extract is removed and screened prior to a de-
termination of pol and RDS. A sub-sample of the
prepared cane is dried in an oven to constant weight
to obtain the moisture content. The fiber content is
determined by difference.
Details are given in the SouthAfrican Laborato-
ry Manual (2005) and in ICUMSA Method GS517-1
(Anon. 2005). Calculations assume 25 g Brix-free
water per 100g fiber. Equations used are:
where: m, mass of cane and m, mass of water.
As an alternative the fiber content can be determined
directly. In Australia this was done by thoroughly
washing a sample of finely prepared cane in a cal-
ico bag. This method has now been superseded by
a different method (Loughran et al. 1988). This in-
volves pumping water through a sample of known
mass (500 g) of finely prepared cane in a stainless
steel cone with a 120mesh screen bottom. After the
samplehas been thoroughly washed, it is dried in the
same container by blowing air at 105O C through the
sample to constant mass. This is referred to as the
can fiber (not cane fiber) method.

2.4.4 Accuratemeasurement of
sucroseby chromatography
Both GC (gaschromatography)andHPLC (high
pressureliquid chromatography) can be used to give
an accurate measure of sucrose unaffected by the
presence of other optically active components(other
sugars and polysaccharides). This provides a more
accurate measure of sucrose unaffected by nonsu-
crose components, whose concentration changes
duringthe season and from oneseasonto thenext. It
also yields useful information on the concentration
of the monosaccharides.
Since 1981 weekly composite samples of raw
juice from South African mills have been analyzed
by GC to give an accuratemeasurement of sucrose,
fructose and glucose.
The pol/sucrose ratio so obtained is applied to
the mill's balance for the week to obtain a measure
of true sucrose in cane and in the raw juice. Apart
from providing more reliable data for cane payment
purposes, it alsoprovides more accurateinformation
for factory control and the estimationof losses (see
Section 25.2).
2.4.5 NIR Measurements
Near Infra-Red spectroscopy (commonly re-
ferred to as NIR) utilizes techniques to measure
the absorbance of wavelengths of light in the near
infrared region, either by measuring transmis-
sion through the sample or by reflectance from the
sample. The background to these measurements is
given in Section 25.1. It is a widely used technique
in many agro-industrial enterprises.
The technique is theoreticallycapable of moni-
toring multiple analytes quickly and conveniently.
It gives results rapidly, within a minute or two, and
requires little labor. It can supply more accuratean-
swers, more quickly, without chemicals and using
less labor than any other methods. However it is a
secondary measurement technique i.e. it relies on
W i g calibrated against other measurements. The
accuracy of the answers is no more accurate than
the primary analyses on which the calibrations are
based.
Two approaches to cane analysis have been in-
vestigated. The first measures the sucrose, dry sub-
stance, fiberandmoisturecontenton a well-prepared
sample of cane directly. The second measures the
sucroseand dry substancecontent in first expressed
juice for cane payment purposes.
NIR has been used routinely for cane variety as-
sessment over many years in Australia (Bmtherton
and Berding 1998),in Colombia (Larrahondoet al.
2001) and in South Africa (Meyer 1998). This has
led to theapplicationof NIR in these countriesto the
direct analysisof cane. NIR has also been shown to
provide a valid assessment of canequality;the meth-
od is far more precise and the error in the method is
reported to be much less than in the conventional
Louisiana cane analysis method (Edye and Clarke
1996).
Measurements on a solid substrateareinherent-
ly more difficult but potentially more advantageous.
Larger samples of prepared cane are used, so that
sub-samplingis less of a problem. Sampleprepara-
tion and presentation to the instrument are still im-
portant issues receiving attention.

3 SUPPLY
AND HANDLING OF SUGARCANE
3.1 Harvesting, transport and
storage of cane
3.1.1 Harvesting methods
Harvesting of cane is done manually or mechan-
ically. Roughly 80 %of the world's sugarcane is still
being harvested manually (Meyer et al. 2005), but
there are industries such as Australia and Florida,
Louisiana and Texas in the United States of Ameri-
ca, as well as smaller producers such as Papua New
Guinea, where the entire sugarcane crop is harvested
mechanically. In Argentina, Brazil, Colombia, Gua-
temala, Indonesia and the Sudan, the proportion of
sugarcane that is harvested mechanically is steadily
increasing. There are many reasons why sugar pro-
ducing countries have moved to mechanical harvest-
ing systems. These include a shortage of or unwill-
ingness by labor to harvest the cane, high labor costs
andlor poor labor performance.
Manual versus mechanical harvesting. In
many countries with low labor costs, it is still less
costly to harvest cane manually. In cases where the
topography includes sloping and hilly fields, me-
chanical harvesting is not an option because the ma-
chines cannot be used on such terrain. In most cases,
manual cutting leads to lower field losses and better
quality cane than mechanical harvesting. In manual
harvesting, the cane is cut and laid in rows. The tops
and leaves may be removed by the cane cutter be-
fore laying the cane down. In other cases the cane is
topped when lying on the ground. Manual harvesting
may include the use of mechanical loading. Manual
loading will always lead to better quality cane with
fewer limitations due to field conditions, but is be-
coming less common. With mechanical loading, the
way the grab loader is operated is important, be-
cause incorrect operation can result in large quanti-
ties of field soil and rocks being loaded with the cane
(Vignes 1980). This is particularly important when
the cane in windrows is push-piled. Alternatively
the cane cutters may build small stacks of cane in
the fields, thus minimizing the chance of picking up
excessive quantities of soil and rocks.
Whole stalk versus chopper harvesting. Me-
chanicalharvesting systems may be whole stalk har-
vesters or chopper harvesters. Whole stalk harvest-
ers generally lay the cane down on the ground for
collection by loading equipment after the stalks are
cut at the base and near the last mature internode
at the top. Chopper harvesters cut the cane into 150
to 300 mrn long billets that are deposited directly
into wagons or haul-out vehicles as the cane exits
the harvester. Whole stalk harvesters are most effi-
cient if cane is upright and tonnage is relatively low.
Both one- and two-row whole stalk harvesters are
available. Operating costs for whole stalk harvesters
are generally lower than for chopper harvesters, but
where cane tonnages are high and lodging of cane
occurs, chopper harvesters are the only option for
mechanical harvesting. Chopper harvesters are also
the only realistic option for green cane harvesting.
Losses are higher with chopper harvesters, not just
physical losses but also loss of juice and cane frag-
ments due to the numerous cuts. Sugar losses in har-
3 Supply and handling of sugarcane
vesting of 5 % to 15% are not uncommon in green
cane, but are usually lower with burnt cane (Sichter
et al. 2005, Whiteinget al. 2004).
There are many factors to be considered when
implementing a fully mechanized chopper harvest-
ing system (Ridgeet al. 1996,Meyer 1999).In terms
of field preparation and layout, the following need
attention:
Adequate headlands to turn the harvester at the
end of the rows.
Sufficientlyflat and rock-free fields for safe op-
eration of harvesters and haul-out equipment.
Compatible cultural operations, including
straightnessof rows (therow profile to allowthe
harvester to minimizepickup losses) and appro-
priate chamferingon cross-drains.
Adequate row lengths and optimal number and
capacity of haul-out units for efficient and cost-
effectiveharvester operation.
Compatiblerow spacingof thecaneand machin-
ery. With single row chopper harvesting, both
the harvester wheels and the haul-out wheels
traverse each interrow twice.
When operating in light and erect crops, modern
chopper harvesters have few problems with the
gathering and feeding of cane stalks into the har-
vester. As crop conditions become more sprawled
and lodged, the harvester must align and straighten
the cane along the direction of the row for it to feed
into the throat of the machine. When operating in
recumbent crops, efficient gathering and feeding of
the cropisthereforeincreasinglydifficultto achieve,
and feed through the machinebecomes more erratic
(DavisandNorris 2002).Machineperformance and
damage to the stool remain significantissues.These
effects are most pronounced in high yielding irri-
gated crops.
Losses and extraneousmatter.Billeting loss-
es in chopper harvesters are inversely related to bil-
let length. However, they are also directly related to
harvesting pour rate (mean material processing rate
of the harvester), the knife sharpness, the relation-
ship between chopper peripheral speed and feed-
train roller speed and the characteristics of the cane
(Hockings et al. 2000). Cleaning losses when har-
vesting unburntcrops are typically the largest single
source of loss with chopper harvesting. However,
losses can also be high in burnt crops if the extractor
fan speedis excessive.Higher fan speeds reduce ex-
traneousmatter, but also result in higher canelosses
(de Beer et al. 1996, Whiteing et al. 2004). Gener-
ally, cane loss will be low at fan speeds givingblade
tip speeds below 70 m/s; however,levelsof extrane-
ous matter (EM)removal may not be consideredad-
equate. Increasing fan tip speeds increases total ex-
traction,butreduces the selectivityof trash removal,
and tip speeds above 85 mls should be avoided as
cane loss will be very high (Meyeret al. 2005).
The efficiency of chopper harvesters in remov-
ing trash is dependent on cane variety, crop condi-
tion, crop yield, harvester pour rates and harvesting
conditions (Whiteing et al. 2001) and final E
M lev-
els are closely related to initial trash levels.Recum-
bent crops result in higher EM levels and cane loss
than erect crops of similar yield and variety (Whit-
eing et al. 2001) because of the less uniform feed
of these crops through the machine. Qpically, the

It is of interest to consider the effects of green
cane harvesting on the miller. The advantagesare:
Cane is fresher when it reaches the mill and has
a lower dextran and impuritycontent.
It degradesmore slowly in storage.

3 Supplyand handling of sugarcane
It leads to morefuel or more biomass, which can
be an advantage or disadvantage depending on
the situation of the mill.
There are a number of disadvantages,however:
There is more material to process.
The higher fiber content means that there is a
greater loss of sugar in bagasse.
More molasses is produced as a result of the
lowerjuice purity, and a higher loss of sugar in
molasses results.
The sugar color is affected adversely.
There is more starch in the juice because of the
higher starch content of the tops and leaves.
Milling costs depend on cane crushed, and rev-
enue depends on sugar produced; trash inflates
the formerand reduces the latter.
The bulk density of the cane in the transportve-
hicles is considerablylower.
Soil compaction. Harvesters and in-field trans-
port systems will cause some degree of soil com-
paction. Soil and climatic conditions may make this
an important consideration. Wheeled vehicles with
high flotation tires help to minimize field damage
and reduce this effect, but tracked vehicles have the
leasteffect on soilcompaction.Vehicles enteringthe
fields should be as light as possible. There is some
differenceof opinion on the magnitude of the effect
of soil compaction on cane yields. What is well-
proven is the fact that stool damage due to vehicle
traffic can have a substantialeffectand care needs to
be taken to keep wheels in the interrows.

2 Transportsystems
Cane is delivered in many different types of
loads and vehicles. These can include tractor and
trailer, with single or tandem trailers, various types
of trucks,largeroad vehicles,rail trucks and smaller
tramway systems.The optimum choice of transport
type depends on the distance from the mill. Direct
haul tractorltrailers are the usual choice for short
distances (< 10k
r
n
)
, while larger vehicles with
payloads over 20 t are better for longer distances;
this may require trans-loadingfrom infield haulage
equipmentinto largervehicles.
However there are examples of large vehicles
being used successfully for direct delivery. In the
northern cane areas of SouthAfrica and Swaziland,
rigid trucks with trailers or tractor and tandem trail-
ers with payloads of 24 to 30 t have been used for
many years with no adverse effects (van der Poel
et al. 1998:249).However field conditions are good
and the harvestingperiod is usually dry.
Usuallya mill will be set up tohandlejust one or
a limited number of types of transport.In most cases
cane is delivered only in daylight hours or perhaps
16hourslday. In somecasescaneis delivered around
the clock, which is the ideal because it minimizes
theneed to hold a stock of canein theyard. Schedul-
ing of cane transport vehicles to provide a continu-
ous supplyof cane to the mill and to optimizeuse of
the transport fleet is important. Use has been made
of GPS (Global Positioning System) systems in the
vehicles for many years, and is being extended to
use on harvesters (Crossleyand Dines 2004).
Cane may be deliveredin bundles held together
by chains, or in bulk deliveries of whole stalk or
billeted cane. The transport of cane is usually man-
aged and paid for by the grower, who runs his own
vehicles or employs a contractor to transport his
cane. In some places the harvesting and transport is
controlled by the miller. In this case, the harvesting
and transport can be considered to be the first part
of the cane processing operation; this has a number
of advantages,in particular minimizing the number
of harvesten and transport vehicles required and
enabling a minimum amount of cane in stock to be
held, thus improving the freshness of the cane at
crushing.
At most mills in Australia cane is delivered by
rail (predominantly 610 rnm gauge), with some
mills having a combined raiYroad delivery system.
These transport systems are highly efficient,requir-
ing a minimum of people since the system is highly
automated, making use of computerized scheduling
systemssometimesincorporatingGPS tools.
Road cane is delivered typically in 20-25 tonne
loads, with road ordinanceslimiting the sizeof load.
In some cases the load pulled by a single vehicle
may be increased by adding one or more trailers.
Depending on local restrictions, the load may be
limited either by total gross mass or by vehicle size
allowed. For long hauls, it is important to minimize
loading and unloading times and to minimize tare
mass. For this reason the loading and unloading
mechanisms should preferably not be included on

3.1.3 Bundle handling
In certain industries some cane is delivered in
the form of cane bundles secured with chains, usu-
ally three per bundle. They are usually associated
with winch loading or self-loading trailers. These
are cheap and flexible loading systems and are par-
ticularly suited to poor field conditions including
steep terrain. The loading systems are independent
of other field operations and deliverclean cane with
very low field losses. They are particularly suited to
smallcane growers.
The mill cane receiving system has to be able
to handle bundles in the cane yard. This requires
a gantry crane to unload the vehicles and load the
feed carriersand requires labor to hook and unhook
bundles and release chain locks when the bundled
cane is to be crushed. It also requires a system for
transporting chains back to the fields. Other disad-
vantages are the cost of purchasing, replacing and
maintainingthe chains,and the easewith which they
can find their way with the cane into the cane prepa-
ration system.
References p. 76
3 Supply and handling of sugarcane
3.1.4 Container systems
Containers or bins which hold from 10 to 20 t
cane may be a cost-effectiveoption, which minimiz-
es handling and transportcosts. Bins may be loaded
directly in the field and trans-loaded onto fixed bed
trucks for transport to the mill. They may then be
unloaded directly at the mill or stored in the cane
yard. A system for handling and unloading bins is
required at the mill, usually involving large fork lift
vehicles.
3.1.5 Cane weighing
Measuring the mass of cane delivered is an im-
portant operation because of cane payment implica-
tions. This is generally done on a weighbridge or
large platform scale at the mill, whether the cane is
deliveredby road or rail. The vehicle is usually also
weighed after discharging its load to establish the
net amount of cane delivered.If cane is delivered in
bundles, the same number of bundle chains must be
loaded onto the vehicleprior to taking the tare mass
of the empty vehicle. Most weighbridges now use
load cells, which makes them more reliable and less
in need of regular adjustment.Nonethelessa system
for routine checking and calibration of the scales is
required. Frequent checks are necessary to see that
the weigh platform is free of debris and that there
is always unchoked clearance between the platform
and the frame.
In somecases a weighing systemis incorporated
into a tippler,so that the weighing and tippingcan be
incorporated into a single automatedsystem.
3.1.6 Storagesystems
At most mills, cane is not delivered 24 h a day
and some cane has to be storedfor crushingthrough
thenight. Thestock of cane should be as low as pos-
sible to reduce the overall delay from cut to crush.
Various methods of storingcane areused and all
involve double-handlingand extra expense:
Cane may be stored in bundles and retrieved as
needed.
Canemay be storedon wheels,i.e. in vehicles or
trailers in the mill yard, and emptied as neces-
sary.
If a system of containers is used, cane will be
stored in containers.
Cane may be spilt loose onto the floor and re-
trieved by front-end loader or by gantry grab
crane. This is the least desirable option because
of the damage to the cane and the difficulty in
practicing a strict first-in first-out policy. Cane
density in the pile is around 300 kg/m3.
3.1.7 Damage and deterioration of
cane
InAustraliaall cane is harvested by chopperhar-
vesters and is delivered in billet form; cut-to-crush
times to minimize deterioration are critical and tar-
geted at less than 10hours. In other areas where the
control of harvesting and transport is not under the
control of the miller, cut-to-crush delays are longer.
Deteriorationof billeted cane can then become seri-
ous, particularly when the weather is warm and wet.
The effects on factory operation of cane delays are
outlinedin Section 1.2.7and the effects of excessive
dextranin Section2.1.5.
At mills where double handling of cane is prac-
ticed, damage to the cane occurs. This can hasten
deteriorationand increasesucroselossesby physical
and microbial means.
3.2 Unloading cane
Handling of chopper harvested cane at the mill
is considerably easier than handling whole stalk
cane. Billetedcane is usually well-containedin bins
or trailers and can be handled with less spillage. It
also flows more easily, with a lower propensity to
form large tangled bundles, common particularly
with unburnt whole stalk cane.

top. The wagon is secured to the tipping platform

3.2.4 Gantry cranes
Gantry cranes are used in cane yards which re-

The width of the cranesis usually of the order of

increases.Thus the area they covertends to be much

and lower the crane, for the traversing of the crane

Cane tables and cross car-
riers
3.3.1 Feeder tables
Mills that handle cane bundles will often have
one or more flat cane tables, onto which bundles
may be loaded. Once the bundle rests on the table,
the chain clasps need to be released (usually manu-
ally) before the cranepulls the chains free. Thus the
gantry cranehas to extend over the feedertables.
One or more feeder tables will feed onto cross
carriers or directly into the main cane carrier. Thus
it is possible to feed cane into the main cane car-
rier from a number of different feeder systems, to
ensure that different types of cane delivery can be
accommodated and still achieve a uniform feed into
the mill. This requires an operator to stop and start
and regulate the speed of the cross carriers to obtain
a uniform feed.
This arrangement becomes essential when the
identity of the cane needs to be maintained in the
cane conveying system for cane payment purposes,
so that the samples taken after the shredder can
be identified. Sufficient bundles from a particular
grower can be accumulated from storage or direct
delivery to accumulatea sufficientlylarge packet of
cane for a representativesample to be obtained.
These tables have solid decks, with chain sys-
tems that drag thecane to the discharge.In most cas-
es two or more different feed conveyors are needed
to feed enough cane into the systemat high crushing
rates.A kicker or tumbler is located at the headshaft
of each carrier. This consists of a slowly rotating
shaft, provided with radial arms or tynes, which en-
sure that the cane falls smoothly off the discharge
end, avoiding a heavy fall of a large mass of cane.

are as wide as the length of the truck or trailer. They
incorporate a system of chains dragging the cane

Cane cleaning
3.4.1 Dry cleaning
There are significant advantages to processing
clean cane. Dry cleaning of cane prior to processing
appears attractive relative to wet cleaning, because
the losses of sugar are lower. Systemsin use are de-
signed to remove some or all of the following: cane
leavesand tops, roots and stubble,sandor field soil,
clay mud balls, rocks and stones. The most cost-ef-
fective approach is probably to provide incentives
to the grower or harvester operator to deliver clean
cane. If this is not in the realm of the possible, dry
cleaning of cane could bring the following advan-
tages:
Costsavingsin terms of reduced wear and main-
tenance.
Increased factory capacity due to reduced quan-
tities of extraneousmatter.
Reduced energy consumption.
Higher calorificvalue of the bagasse.
Lower losses of sugarin filter cake, bagasse and
molasses.
Improvedsugar quality.
There are some disadvantagesas well:
Additional equipment has to be installed, with
associated capital, maintenance and operational
costs.
References p. 76
3 Supply and handling of sugarcane
A small quantity of cane may be lost in clean-
ing.
Provision needs to be made to dispose of the
waste material removed.
There may be implications for the particular
cane payment system.
Removal of tops and leaves. Given the obvi-
ous constraints on the performance of harvester
cleaning systems, a strong argument can be made
for additional secondary cleaning at the mill. Such
an approach allows the harvesting operation to be
optimized to minimize the cane loss, while ensur-
ing that clean cane is supplied to the milling train.
In a holistic analysis, the increased transport costs
associated with the mass of the trash and reductions
in load density are small compared with the gains in
mill performance, sugar quality and total cane re-
covery.
A pilot plant system for cleaning whole stalk
cane pneumatically was installed at St Aubin in
Mauritius (Rivalland 1999) and was run continu-
ously for a whole season (Anon. 1999).In this case
air was blown upwards through the falling s t a h
of whole cane, which entrained the trash and car-
ried it to a cyclone in which the solid material was
removed. A
i
r from the cyclone was recycled. The
trash was then chopped into smaller pieces before
being pneumatically transported to the bagasse car-
rier after the last mill. With the plant running at 60
to 90 tJh, 2 to 3 tmtrash was removed, representing
a removal of 50 to 66 %.
It has been shown that most of the trash can
be relatively easily removed from billeted cane at
the mill by blowing the trash out of the cane as it
drops from one conveyor onto another (Rein2005).
Roughly 80 % of the trash was removed by blowing
air at a velocity of about 30 m/s through a curtain of
falling cane. The interesting feature is that the sepa-
ration was achieved with virtually no loss of billets,
but the problem of disposing of the enormous bulk
of trash that rapidly built up at the mill was insolu-
ble. Higher air velocities were expected to remove
more extraneous matter, but CFD studies showed
that higher velocities in this geometry would lead
to recirculation of air in the separation area which
would reduce the efficiency of separation. A similar
system is in use at the Providencia mill in Colombia,
where the trash is blown out onto a large concrete
slab and managed with the use of a front-end loader.
Trash is reduced from 6 % to 1 % with whole stalk
cane and from 10 % to 3 % with billeted cane (Ridge
2001);similar plants are in use in Brazil.
Pneumatic cleaning of cane in Australia has
also shown that removal of trash from chopper har-
vested cane with a low level of billet loss is possible
(Sclzembri et al. 2002).The system was specifically
designed to process cane with no trash removal in
the field. The cane is directed into a 1.5 m wide air
stream. The cleaned cane falls onto a conveyor while
80 % of the trash (defined in this instance as dry and
green leaves) falls onto a separate conveyor. The re-
maining 20 % hash is collected in the a
i
r cyclone,
ensuring a clean plant without particulate emissions.
Results show that with less than 1 % loss of billets,
roughly 90 % of the leafy material was removed at
a cane rate of 100 t/h, reducing to 60 to 70 % in the
range of 200 to 300 t/h. A lower removal is evident
under wet conditions. This excludes tops, which are
not removed since they are aerodynamically similar
to cane billets. Removal is dependent on velocity but
no velocities are reported.Tests showed that in order
to reduce the trash particle sizes to approximate ba-
gasse, a relatively high power requirement to shred
the trash of 12 (kW .h)/t trash was required.
Other systems for mechanically stripping leaves
off cane are described by Bernhnrdt (1994).Where
leaves and tops are removed before crushing, the
only viable option is to bum the material in the boil-
ers. Some options for making use of tops and leaves
are given in Section 31.3,but in most cases these are
not attractive.
The difficulty with this approach is assessing
cane quality as delivered and rewarding it equitably
in a cane payment scheme. Analysis would have to
be done on a hand-cleaned sample or on the cane
after a mill dry cleaning system, if installed. This
may not be acceptable to all growers.
Removal of rocks and soil. If the cane is dry,
a high proportion of the soil in cane will separate
fairly easily. The use of perforated plate on a steel
deck, particularly where the cane tumbles onto the
deck, allows sand to fall through to be collected un-
der the carrier. Other approaches with whole stalk
cane include the use of carrier systems with gaps or
open slats that permit sand and small stones to fall
through the gaps while cane passes over them.
3.4.2 Cane washing
In countries where rocks are a problem, particu-
larly Hawaii, Mauritius and to a lesser extent South
Africa, various systems have been tried. McElhoe
and Lewis (1974) describe a dry cleaning plant
installed in Hawaii, aimed primarily at removing
rocks, but also removing cane trash.As whole stalk
cane falls off the end of a conveyor, an air stream is
directed at an angle of 45" through the cane. Rocks
fall almost vertically and cane is deflected over a
splitter and onto a conveyor to the mill. Leafy trash
is blown upward and onto a more distant conveyor.
Losses of cane are low, measured at 0.55 % and all
rocks less than 600 mm are removed. About 3 % of
the cane exits with the rocks, but most of this is re-
covered by a small salvager. An air velocity of 58
rnls was used which gave the minimum cane loss;
this required 26.4 m3/s air and absorbed 82 kW.
Higher velocities remove more trash but lead to
higher cane losses while lower velocities lead to
higher losses of cane with the rocks. Higher losses
areincurred with unburnt cane.The plant claimedto
remove 96 % of all rocks over a two-year period and
38 % of the trash.
Some ideas have been proposed by Rivalland,
which have not been tried on the full scale (Bern-
hardt 1994). Other systems in Reunion have in-
volved target plates on which cane falls, arranged
in such a way that large rocks can be heard if not
seen. The conveyor system is then stopped while
rocks aremanually removed. This is clearly an unat-
tractive option.
A successful system for removing rocks and
sand continuously has been described by du Plooy
(1994). A sketch is shown in Figure 3.8. An 11m
wide feed table feeds cane at a steady rate onto an
inclined plate. The cane stalks meet a revolving
tyned drum, which lifts the cane up and over the
drum. Sand and rocks fall down between the drum
and thecurved wiperplate between thetynesand are
removed at the bottom. Large rocks >350 mm are
combed to the sidesof the slopingplate by the tynes.
Divergentopeningsare incorporatedto preventjam-
ming. The diameter of the rotating drum is larger in
the center than the sides. The wiper plates can be
moved away from the drum by hydraulic cylinders
if anyjamming below therotating drum occurs.This
system has worked successfully in a few mills in
SouthAfrica, but can only be used with whole stalk
cane. However there is still some loss of cane with

3.4.2 Cane washing
The system of cane harvesting in Hawaii re-
quired an elaborate system for removing the exces-
sive amountsof soil, rocks and cane trash delivered
with the cane. This usually involved a bath for re-
movingrocks by floatingthe cane in a mud-in-water
suspensionof therequired density, followedby large
amountsof water washing and finally strippingrolls
to remove trash from the cane stalks. This plant is
elaborate and extremely expensive to operate and
maintain. Most mills using cane washing are some-
what simpler.
Most cane wash plants consist of one or two
cane tables inclined at an angle of 35" to 45", with
References p. 76
3 Supply and handlingof sugarcane
wash water sprayedontothe cane as it is transported
up the cane tables. The water is collectedunderneath
the cane tables, some of it is recirculated and some
bled off to a treatment system. Some arrangements
incorporate hydrocyclones in the circuit to remove
the bulk of the mud from the recirculatingwater.
Vignes(1980)reported on results of whole stalk
cane washing trials in Mauritius. Losses of sugar
measured in water leaving the washing plant were
estimatedtobebetween 1.4and 1.8% of the sucrose
in cane. Birkett and Stein (2004) did an extensive
study of cane washing in Louisiana and their results
may be summarized as follows:
Sugar loss measured in the water leaving the
wash system averaged 3.2 kg sugarlt cane when
washing billeted cane. Based on the average
recoverable sugar content of cane in Louisiana
over the same period, this represents 3 to 3.5 %
of recoverable sugar in cane.
Sugar losses are very variable, with measured
values ranging between 1and 7 kg sugarlt cane.
The loss when washing whole stalk cane is sub-
stantially lower, around 25 % of the losses with
billeted cane.
Ash removal isjust over 50 8 of ash in incom-
ing cane, with large variations.
Measured entrainment of wash water into the
extraction plant averaged 7.5 t1100t cane, vary-
ingbetween -1 1and 29 t/100 t cane.
Sugarloss is independent of the amount of wash
water used, with the wash waterquantityvarying
between 0.4 and 14m3/tcaneat differentmills.
The losses measured by Birkett and Stein (2004)are
considered to be underestimates because they take
no account of the microbial losses occurring in the
system. Because of the substantial entrainment of
wash water with the cane, the amount of imbibition
used in extraction has to be reduced corresponding-
ly. It is important to use the cleanest source of wash
water for the last wash, to minimize the entrainment
of breakdown products in the wash water, such as
organic acids and dextran, into the extractionplant.
Apart from the losses of sugar, cane washing
has other undesirable consequences. Eliminating
cane washing at Cora Texas mill gave the following
results (Monge and Schudmak 2002):
Less lime was requiredboth forjuice liming and
for control of the wash water pH.
Juice purity increasedby 0.7 units, leading to an
increasedrecovery of sugar.
Evaporators required less cleaning.
Extractionimproved by about 1 %.
Ash in bagasse increased and boiler efficiency
reduced.
Overallrecovery increasedby 10kg 96 pol sug-
ar per tonne cane (9.7 % additional sugar pro-
duced).
Lactic, formic and acetic acids have been measured
in wash water, sometimes at very high levels. In
somecases this has led to low pH values in evapora-
tor condensates,which have been reported to revert
to normal pH values on stopping cane washing.
3.4.3 Wash water handling and waste
disposal
The quantities of wash water circulatedover the
wash tables are large. On average, mills in Louisi-
ana circulate 3 m3/tc, although this varies widely
between 0.6 and 10m3/tc(Birkett and Sfein 2004).
The wash water rate at Cora Texas mill was 7 m3/tc
(Monge and Schudmak 2002). Baikow (1982) re-
ports that the minimum quantityof water required is
4.4 to 5.9 m3/tcand Vignes (1980) reported figures
between 2 and 2.6 m3/t,. In generalwash water isre-
circulated rather than used on a once-throughbasis.
Management of the wash water systemis complicat-
ed by the need to settle out the field soil and control
thepH and theodor,bothof which areaconsequence
of fermentationof sugarin the system.In Louisiana,
the mills practicing cane washing are able to store
all the water used in large holding ponds, because
of the short three month season.Natural degradation
over the remainingnine months of the year gets the
COD level down to the point where some of it can
be discharged.Ponds need to be emptied every year
to dredge the settled soil, which has to be trucked
away. Other sugarindustries require the solids to be
settledout and water treatmentforthe surplusthatis
discharged.This is an additionalcostrequiringextra
supervision.
Removal of soil, separated by whatever means,
is a costly operationwith no benefits. It allhas to be
loaded and transported to suitable solids dump sites.
