3.5.1 Apron carriers
3.5 Cane conveying
3.5.1 Apron carriers
The main cane carrier is often a steel slat con-
veyor, referred to as an apron carrier, although belts
are increasingly being used for this duty. The width
of the carrier is usually the same as the width of the
mill rolls and the steel slats are the width of the car-
rier and are bolted to bvo or more strands of con-
veyor chain, which has a pitch normally of 150mm
and a nominal strength of 36 to 45 t. In some cases
300 mm pitch chain is used with a higher ultimate
tensile strength.Thesteel slatsareoverlapping andso
are slightly wider than the chain pitch; some slightly
different designs of slat are available, as shown in
Figure 3.9. A roller chain is normally used to reduce
friction, because of heavy loads and relatively long
conveyors. The rollers may be replaced with blocks
of high density polyethylene, which slide easily on
the supporting runners and reduce wear and mainte-
nance. The return flight of the carrier is supported at
intervals on idlers.
Apron carriers normally run at a speed of 0.1
to 0.25 m/s but may be as high as 0.35 m/s and can
be inclined at an angle up to 23O to the horizontal.
These carriers have an arduous duty, since they have
to contend with acidic canejuice, sand, dirt and oc-
casional rocks and lumps of tramp iron. Because of
their robustness, one or more sets of cane knives
may also be run on these carriers. Maintenance and
the choice of correct materials are therefore of prime
importance. Stainless steel pins and bushes are rec-
ommended for the chain.
Certain measures need to be taken to ensure
that the area around the conveyor does not become
a cleaning problem. Adequate sealing between the
carrier side walls and the edge of the slats can be
achieved by welding an 80 x 80 rnm angle iron to
the carrier, running the full length of the carrier
above the slats. The use of 12 mm spacers between
slat attachment and the slat helps dirt to escape. The
intermittent cleaning of the chain using exhaust
steam or air jets directed onto the chain is also rec-
ommended.
Slats should not be too thick, preferably not
more than 6 mm, so that if fouling orjamming does
occur, the slat will bend out of the way rather than
break the chain or the attachment. Sprockets are of-
Figure3.9: Steelslat designsfor apron carriers
ten flamecut split-hub type and arranged to be easily
replaceable. At least 12 and preferably 15 teeth are
required on the sprocket,since a larger diameter will
improve performance and chain life.
Carriers need periodic close inspection, prefer-
ably weekly, to look for the following:
Chain wear (pins, rollers, bushes),
Sprocket wear,
Adequate chain tension,
Split pins or circlips broken or missing,
Loose nuts on attachments,
Incipient jamming or fouling of slats,
Cracked or broken Links or attachments,
Runner wear.

3.5.3 Chainand slat conveyors
Slatcarriers are considerablymore expensive to
install and maintain. These are used for conveying
shreddedcane where layoutsand elevationsexclude
the option of using belt conveyors. The design of
slatcarriers is fairly standardat most mills, the most
notable differencebeing the selection of chaintype,
and chain material specification. Generally two
types of steel chain are used, either standard roller
(25 t or 50 t) or block link chains. Heat treatment,
either through- or case-hardening is usually speci-
fied to reduce wear; hardening to between 32 and
36 Rockwell C is specified. If corrosion is a prob-
lem as well as wear, mass is more important then
hardness; then stainless steel pins and bushes are
recommended. However incorrect heat treatment
is one of the most common problems and needs to
be carefully specified and quality checked.Material
specificationsvary with applicationbut carbon steel
sideplates with stainlesssteel componentsare usual
for this application. The 400 series stainless steel
components are heat-treatable and can provide the
best combination of hardness and corrosion resis-
tance. Stainless steel side plates are preferred where
carriers are operating in hot moist conditions (e.g.
diffuser feed conveyors).InAustralia chain convey-
ors have typically 300 mm pitch Walkers type (cast
Referencesp. 76
3 Supply and handling of sugarcane
forklink)chain,also with hardened pins and bushes.
Some details of the chains used are given by Mc-
Culkin(1991);they generallyhave a higher nominal
strength of 70 to 80 t.
Slats and slat attachments vary with individual
mill preferences, and slats are generally spaced ev-
ery 6" or 7" link. Chain speeds are normally in the
range 0.4 to 0.7 mls and conveyors may be inclined
up to45". Steeldecksarebest madefrom3CR12for
long life. Furtherdetailson conveyorchain selection
aregiven in Section 7.1.3.
3.5.4 Magnets
It is common practice to install magnets on the
cane conveyingsystem,since it is almost impossible
to prevent the entry of tramp iron into the system.
Removal of tramp iron in this way pays for itself
very quickly,since the damagecaused to cane prep-
aration equipmentand mill rolls can be severe, lead-
ing to increased downtime and reduced recovery. If
hardened tips areused on shredderhammers,a good
tramp iron removal system is mandatory.
The most common system uses an electromag-
net suspended above a belt conveyor. In this case it
is desirable to run the belt slowly with a thin bed of
knifed or billeted cane, so that all tramp iron will
be pulled out of the cane. It is not easy to meet both
requirements at the same time. The belt should be
flat and well-supported under the magnet to avoid
sagging and achieve a uniform thickness under the
magnet. The magnet should be as close to the cane
as practicable and it is sometimes necessary to in-
stall a kicker ahead of a magnet if the control of the
cane height on the belt is erratic, or else chokeswill
occur at the magnet.Themagnetmay be installedon
a crawl beam,so that it can be pulled out of the way
and cleared of tramp iron attracted to it on a routine
basis without stopping production. Alternatively a
magnet can be made self-cleaning by providing
a thin continuous belt moving over the face of the
magnet, which moves the tramp iron to one side.
A more effective arrangement incorporates a
magnet at a transfer point, with the cane imping-
ing on the magnet. The cane must be presented to
the magnet as a free-falling loose stream; this has
a higher tramp iron removal efficiency. Letizia and
McDougall (1989) describe the use of a magnet
rated at 11kW on billeted cane at the top of a shred-
der chute at the belt discharge.It has a stepped face
plate so that the tramp iron lodges behind a wedge-
shaped projection on the face of the magnet. This
arrangementcan be used at any transferpoint, which
obviates the disadvantageof the extra height needed
for the shredder chute. With this arrangement, there
is the possibility that some tramp iron can be pulled
back into the cane.A further disadvantageis the fact
that the cane supply has to be stopped to remove the
tramp iron.
3.5.5 Conveyor drives and automatic
control
Variable speed conveyordrives. Variable speed
electric drives are most commonly used, with vari-
ablefrequencyAC drivesbecoming themost popular
choice.Hydraulicdrives are alsoused, sincethey are
well suited to changing speedsrequired by a control
system. Other variable speed systemsin use include
magnetic or hydraulic coupling systems. Magnetic
or eddycurrent couplings,typified by those supplied
by Heenan and Froude, are simple and reliable, but
larger drives require cooling water and the speed
characteristicson speedingup and slowing down are
not consistent, affected by the load at the time, and
so can affectthe quality of control achieved.
Conveyorspeed controls. Thereare somebasic
concepts incorporated in all conveyor control sys-
tems:
All conveyors operate in a linked cascade sys-
tem, so that they speed up and slow down to-
gether.
The speed of the shredder and all knife sets are
measured, and if any one of them slows down
due to overloading,the speedsof theconveyor(s)
ahead are reduced; below a minimum the up-
stream conveyors stop altogether.
The speed of each conveyoris measured by a ta-
chometer on the tail shaft;the speed of the drive
on the headshaft does not allow for events such
as breaking or slipping of drive belts.
All drivesincorporateinterlocks,which will pre-
vent them from running for reasons such as the
following:
o Conveyors ahead have tripped,
o A mill or diffuserhas tripped,
o Cane knives andor shredder not running.
Controls and relaying installed to fail-safe; de-
energized state stops the equipment.

Canethroughputcontrol.Thebasicthroughput
parameter to be controlledis the cane crushing rate.
This may be achieved in a number of differentways,
dependingon the plant and equipmentinstalled.
For a millingtandem, the speed of the first mill
is set and the control system maintains a constant
level in the first mill chute. The chute level controls
the speed of the conveyor feeding the first mill. If
a choked feed chute is installed on the shredder,
then the conveyors before the shredderareregulated
to maintain the shredder chute level and the speed
of the shredder feeder is regulated by the first mill
chute level control.
For a diffuser, a belt weigher on the conveyor
feeding the diffuser controls the speed of the con-
veyor feeding this conveyor. If a choked feed chute
is installedon the shredder, the belt weighercontrols
the speed of the shredders feeders as well. In some
cases the belt weigher is not installed and instead
the volumetric flow of cane is regulated by setting
the speed of the shredderfeeder, or in the absenceof
a shredder feeder, by measuring the height of cane
on the shredder conveyor and controlling the speed
of the conveyor to keep the product of height and
speed constant.
Loading the main cane conveyor. Even load-
ing of the cane conveyorgreatly facilitatesthejob of
the control systemand minimizesthe chance of any
chokes occurring. In this respect, processing chop-
per harvested cane makes the task much easier,since
thecane flows moreeasily. Particularlywith unburnt
whole stalk cane, the cane has the tendency to hang
together and lead to lumps on the conveyor.
With multiple cross carriers feeding the cane
conveyor, it is common to have an operator control
the feed of the cross carriers to give an even loading
on the cane conveyor.This is essential in the case of
a mill with multiple cross carriers that has to keep
different cane consignments separate so that they
can be identified and sampled after the shredder.
Even loading is best achieved under the follow-
ing conditions:
With a singlemethod of cane delivery,e.g. tram-
way wagons as in Australia, the mass flow rate
of cane is determined by the mass tipped and the
rate of tipping adjusted accordingly.
By installingload cellsunder the section of con-
veyor below each crosscarrier or washtable; the
speed of each cross carrier is controlled to give
a constantmass on that sectionof conveyor onto
which it discharges, and a very uniform flow of
cane is achieved.
Schematic control diagrams for controlling the
conveyors feeding a mill are shown in Figure 3.13
and Figure 3.14.Thesetwo schemesemploy slightly
different arrangements, but use the concepts de-
scribed above.The system is much simplified if bil-
leted cane is fed directly to a shredder without any
knives. A schematic diagram for feeding a diffuser
is shown in Figure 3.15; this has a fixed speed con-
veyor after the shredder.
A variety of different types of hardware can be
used to effect the control. Most are easily conEgu-
rable and easy to modify and adjust and generally
very reliable.A PLCis often used to handle the dis-
crete controls and interlocks and is integrated into
the overall control scheme. Having all the informa-
tion in a single system facilitates problem solving
and fault-finding.

4.1 Objectives and measure-
ment of cane preparation
The process of reducing the cane fed to the mill
into small pieces suitablefor the subsequentextrac-
tion process is referred to as cane preparation. The
size reduction is generally achieved through the use
of rotating knives in the cane conveying system and/
or passing the cane through a swing hammer shred-
der. The efficiency and throughput of the extraction
plant depend significantlyon the preparation of the
canepresented to it.
In addition, the cane preparation equipment can
use more than 25 % of total factory power require-
ments.The type of driveemployedand theefficiency
with which the power is utilized are therefore very
important.
A set of leveler knives is often installed on
whole stalk cane conveyors before any cane prepa-
ration equipment to achieve a more even feed to the
knives. With billeted cane this is often unnecessary
because the handling of billets makes it easier to get
a consistentlyuniform level on the feed conveyors.
4.1.1 Objectives
The objectivesof cane preparation are:
To reduce the sizeof the pieces of cane to a size
suitable for handling in the extractionprocess.
To rupture as many of the sugar bearing cells in
the cane aspossible to facilitatethe extractionof
sugar.
To produce a material that has the right charac-
teristics for milling and diffusion.
Generally the requirements for milling and dsu-
sion arenot dissimilar.The intentionis to reduce the
sticks of cane to small particles, which enables the
juice to be easily extracted, but which preserves the
characteristics required for feeding to a mill, or the
characteristics for an open non-compact bed if dif-
fusion is practiced. Pulverizingcane into "sawdust"
does not achieve these objectives. The optimum
preparation leads to a condition where most of the
sugar-containingcells are ruptured, yet long strands
of fiber are still present. This type of preparationfa-
cilitates the removal of juice, whether by milling or
diffusion.
Well-shredded cane has a higher bulk density
than knifed cane, thus assisting the feeding of the
mill. In addition, the long fibers produced by shred-
ding lead to a felting tendency in the prepared cane
whereby the particles become matted together with
a certain amount of tensile strength. This is highly
advantageous in terms of mill feeding. As the pre-
pared cane enters a mill, the interaction between
fibers pulls the mat of cane into the mill. It is widely
accepted therefore, that the degree of preparation
affects feeding of a mill and hence the capacity of
the mill. Thus attainment of the optimum prepara-
tion also has an advantage in terms of capacity of
the mill.
In practice it has been found that cane prepara-
tion with these characteristics is best achieved by
intensive shredding in heavy duty shredders with a
minimum of knifing, since intensiveknifing reduces
the averagefiber length.With whole stalk cane, it is
4 Cane preparation
necessary to have knivesaheadof the shredderto re-
duce the cane to pieces smallenoughto go down the
chute into the shredder.In the case of billeted cane,
it can be fed directly into a shredder without any
knifing at all. This is general practice in Australia.
In order to achieve maximum shredding and mini-
mal knifing, the concept of cutting whole stalkcane
into pieces resembling billets for feed to a shredder
has been used. This has achieved somesuccess after
modification (Reid 1994)but is unlikely to be used
again (Renton 1992).
With the trend to maximum shreddingand rnini-
mal knifing, Reid (1994)comments:
"The role of the cane knife has therefore be-
come that of a device to ensure that the shredder
is evenlyfed and that no conditionsexist that can
promote choking". Nonetheless a large number
of mills still utilize knives only as the method of
canepreparation.
4.1.2 Effect of cane preparation on
extraction
For both milling and diffusion, a greater break-
age of the sugar-containing cells results in higher
extraction and a lower final bagasse moisture. The
latter improves extraction and produces a material
that bums better in the boilers.
Hugot (1986) contends that knifing of whole
stalkcaneleadstogainsin throughputbut not extrac-
tion. It is oftenfelt that preparation is less important
in a millingtandem than for W s i o n becauseof the
additional size reduction achieved in the mills. This
is not true however, since the mills can reduce the
length of the pieces of cane but do not eliminate the
larger pieces. This was clearly shown by work done
by Moor (1974), who showed that the larger pieces
of cane in bagasse from a milling tandem without
a shredder persisted and that these larger pieces in
final bagassecontained3 times as much sugar as the
smallerpieces.
Following the installation of the first Tongaat
shredder in South Africa, tests reported by Moor
(1974) showed that for a 5 mill train, an increase
in preparation index (PI - see Section 4.1.3) from
77 to 91 gave an increase in extractionfrom 95.6 to
96.2 %, equivalent to 0.045 units of extraction per
unit PI change. This increased preparation resulted
in an increase in mill throughput of 4 %. Detailed
factory trials by SRI in Australia established that a
heavy duty shredder increased the extraction of a
&st mill by 2 % and the whole tandem overall ex-
perienced an increase of 0.05 to 0.06 units per unit
increase in preparation index. However Edwards
(1995) presented mill data showing an increase of
0.1 % in extraction for an increase in one unit POC
(pol in open cells). Payne (1982) reports that in-
creasingthe displaceabilityindex by fourunits leads
to a 1 % increase in extraction; this represents an
increase of 0.25 units extraction per unit change in
preparationindex.
Lafourche mill in Louisiana installed a Silver
Fiberizer,which was previously in operationin Tex-
as. At the same time, the feeder roll on number 1
mill was changed and a Donnelly chuteinstalled on
number 1mill; these affect feeding of the first mill
more than extraction.The turbinedrivedid not have
sufficient power (only 26 (kW.h)/$) to adjust the
shredder clearances to the optimum close settings;
distancebetween hammer and washboard was about
31 mm.Even so, thePIincreased from below 68 to
87, and extraction increased by 3.2%from 91.3 to
94.5 % (Rein 2002). This was achievedin spite of a
reduction in imbibition and an increase of 18 8 in
crushing rate, helped by the firstmill modifications.
The bulk of the extraction improvementis believed
to be due to the installation of the shredder. This
corresponds to an increase in extraction of 0.17 %
per unit increasein PI. It is likely that the effect of a
shredder is greater when the extraction in the mills
is at a lower level.
Cane preparation is the most important variable
affecting extraction in diffusers. If high extractions
are to be achieved,it is essential that the cane ispre-
pared in a heavy duty shredder so that most of the
sugar-containingcells of the cane stalk are ruptured.
Ideallythe type of preparationshould result in mate-
rial where all the cells are ruptured but where long
fibers are still evident, which will result in a cane
bed that is stable and open enough to allow high per-
colation rates to be achieved.
Hugot (1986)concludes:
"Finally,the shredder is particularly valuable
fromthemncial point of view: it provides sub-
stantial improvement in extraction,it constitutes
protection against stones and tramp iron which
have escaped the magnetic separator and it
costs only one-third the cost of a mill and re-
turns sometimes much more".
4.1.3 Measurementof cane preparation
4.1.3 Measurement of cane prepara-
tion
Since preparation is so importantfor extraction,
it is importantto be able to measure it routinely. Un-
fortunately the measurement of the degree of cane
preparation is difficultand existingmeasuresarenot
always reliable. Methods of measurement of cane 5
preparation include:
1. Bulk density;
2. Mean particle size;
3. Extent of breakageof cells.
In order to get a meaningful measurementof prepa-
ration, it is essential that a representativesample of
the prepared cane be obtained. This is not a simple
matterfor a number of reasons:
Samplingfrom the top layer on the belt or con-
veyor may give a biased sample, because often
some classification occurs on the exit from the
shredder e.g. more fines fall at the exit from the Preparedcane bulk density Inkghf
shredder.
, ~ ~ ~ - h ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~
of cane a consignment Figure 4.1: Relationship between fineness of prelpiol~ation
requires that a number of samples be taken, re- and the bulk densityof preparedcane (Crword 1970)
qusing mixing of the sub-samplesbeforetaking
the samplefor measurement.
It is not easy to mix and adequatelyobtain a reli-
able sub-sample.
If the sample is not finely prepared, biased
sampling omitting larger pieces often happens.
Because the sample required is generally small,
including or excluding a single chunk of cane
can seriously affectthe result,
A full-widthhatch samplefollowed by an automatic
sub-sampling system as used in cane payment sam-
pling systems is probably ideal. Murson (1980)re-
ported on an elaborate systemneeded to get a repre-
sentative sample of knifed cane from a rubber belt.
Bulk density.Bulk density is measured by com-
pressing a sample of prepared cane at a set pres-
sure for a given time. Cra$ord (1970)describes a
method for compressing a 6.8 kg sample for 5 rnin-
utes at a gauge pressure of 103 kPa. He showed
that the bulk density correlated with the fineness of
the prepared cane, with finer particle sizes giving a
higher bulk density (Figure 4.1). Bulk density has
alsobeen found to correlate with milling parameters
(Murry and Holt 1967). However bulk density is
also affected by fiber content. A refinement of this
approach corrects for composition of the cane and
the fiber content in particular and has been termed
the treatment number (Loughranand Murry 1989).
This requires a full analysis of the sample and so is
not used routinely.
Mean particle size. Size analysis of prepared
cane particles by sieving or screeningis highly tech-
nique dependent,particularlybecausethe material is
so sticky. However once a reliable technique is ob-
tained, size analysis by sieving cane can yield more
reliable and reproducible results (Marson 1980). It
has been shown that the specific surface or fineness
of prepared cane correlates best with the maximum
percolation rate through a bed of cane (Love and
Rein 1980),with finer preparations leading to lower
percolation rates. It was shown also that the mean
particle size obtained from sieving affects the den-
sity or compactness of the cane bed, which in turn
affectspercolationrate as well (Section6.1.3).How-
ever sizeanalysisof prepared cane on aroutinebasis
is not a practical proposition.
Measurement of cell breakage. The most com-
mon measure is the extentof cell breakage,obtained

4 Canepreparation
by tumbling cane and water in a container under
standard conditions and comparing the pol or Brix
of the extractwith that achieved in a disintegrator,in
which all cells are ruptured. These are generally the
only methods in routine use. Preparation Index (Pl)
is used in South Africa, the displaceabilityindex in
Hawaii (Payne 1962) and the "pol in open cells"
(POC) measurement in Australia. All these mea-
surements attempt to assess the degree of prepara-
tion by measuringhow much of the sugar in cane is
easily washed out of the prepared cane sample.This
is a useful approach since it assesses the prepara-
tion in terms of how readily extractable the sugar is.
Unfortunately it is not a reproducible measurement
sinceit is affected by cane variety and the amount of
extraneousmatter in cane. Nonetheless, if the mea-
sured values are averaged over a day or a week, a
good measure of preparation is achieved. In South
Africa it is considered that a PI of at least 92 is re-
quiredif an extractionof over98 %is to be achieved
in a diffuser. Payne (1968) in Hawaii suggestedthat
a displaceability index of at least 94 is required in
order to achievean extractionof 97 % or more.
Preparation Index (PI) has been adopted by
ICUMSA(Anon.2005) as an Official method (GS7-
3) and is described in the South African laboratory
manual (SASTA 2005). This involves tumbling a
sampleof 500g of prepared cane in 3000 g of water
for 30minutesand measuringthe Brix of theextract.

The displaceability index in Hawaii measures

PI and POC are the most commonly accepted
methods. It is importantto understand the differenc-
es between them, particularly at high levels around
90. There are a number of reasons for the different
numbers achieved in the two tests, some of which
are not obvious.These are:
1. PI uses refractometerBrix and POC uses polar-
ization.The purity of thejuice in the disintegra-
tor extract is lower than the purity of the juice
in the tumbling apparatus. Data given by Payne
(1962) shows that if Brix and not pol were used
in the test, in the range 91 to 95 displaceabil-
ity index, the number achieved would be lower
by an average factor of 0.97 (between 0.96 and
0.99). This factor is likely to be higher with a 30
minute tumbling time.Assuming afactorof 0.96,
POC should be higher than PI by 2 to 4 units.
2. Since the PI method tumbles the cane for a lon-
ger period of time, it may be expected to give a
higher number. It can be inferredfrom data given
by Rein (1972) that under these conditions, the
Brix of the extract after 30 minutes would be
about 1.1 times the Brix after 10 minutes. Thus
PI would be higher due to this effect by about 9
units.
3. Thecalculationmethod used in calculatingPOC
(equation4.2) is rigorously correct and the sim-
ple ratio used in the PI (equation 4.1) is an ap-
proximation.This results in calculatedvalues of
PI which are too high by about a factor of 1.01
i.e. one unit, rising to 3 units at low PI values
around 60.
Taken together, all these effects should result in PI
values higher than POC. Using the numbers given
above, an approximate estimate of the difference
gives a factor of about 0.96 x 1.1x 1.01= 1.07,or 6
units in the range of values around90PI. Data given
in Section4.3.7 indicatesthat thisdifferenceis prob-
ably closer to 5 units at a PI of 90.
In Louisiana the conditions of the standard PI
test have been changed to measure pol instead of
Brix overa 30 minuteperiod. Theresult so obtained
is expected to be higher than the standardPI method
by a factorof 110.96or about4 units.
Whether milling or diffusionis employed,sugar
mills in Australia and South Africa aim for a PI of

more than 90. This results in a type of material in
which individual fibers up to about 100 rnm long
are evident without any "chunks" of cane. Where
heavy duty shreddersare not employed,PIvalues of
around 70 to 80 are obtainedon average.
It is very important that the method used for
measuring cell breakage be specified when report-
ing an index of preparation.
Extraction rate. The rate at which sugar is
leached from cane, measured by conductivity,is the
basis for theDRI (diffusionrate index) measurement
(Kent et al. 2004). The method evaluates the time
constant of an exponential relationship describing
the change in conductivity as water is circulated
through a small packed bed of prepared cane. The
advantage of the method is the short measurement
time (10minutesper analysis)but the rate of extrac-
tion is not only affected by the degreeof cellrupture
but also by the liquid circulation rate and the pack-
ing density in the machine.Its usefulnesshas not yet
been established.
4.2 Cane knives
4.2.1 Leveler knives
Cane levelers are used on the main cane carrier
in an attempt to obtain a constant height of cane fed
to the knives or shredder. This steadies the load on
the subsequent preparation equipment and helps to
reduce the incidence of choking.These levelers op-
erate typically at fairly low speeds at a level 500 to
1500 mm above the camer. These knives do little
in the way of preparation and power requirements
are low. The motorgenerally has to be sized to cope
with the occasionallargebundle which would other-
wise cause a choke at the knives, but average power
consumed is low. Typical data aregivenin Table4.2
in Section4.2.3.
4.2.2 Cane knifing arrangements
Whole stalk cane knife arrangementsgenerally
consist of one or two knife sets preceded by a lev-
eler. Individual knife arrangementsnormally use a
straight knife, or less commonly a hoe type. Stan-
dard preparation arrangements in Australia in the
early to mid-1960s before the introduction of chop-
per harvesters consisted of two sets of knives fol-
lowed by a shredder. This is still common in many
areas that do not have billeted cane.
Where knifing only is employed,there are usu-
ally two sets of rotatingknives, often referred to as
primary and secondaryknives. Tip speedsof 60 m/
s are common,with a rangeof 30to 80m/s reported
in SouthAfrica (Reid1994).The first will cut about
200 mm or more off an apron carrier or anvil roll,
and the second with a clearance of about 50 mm
or even less. The primary knife carries out some
degree of additional levelingof the cane mat on the
carrier. Generally they are fixed hammers unless
there are large numbers of rocks or other extrane-
ous material in thecane, in which caseswingpalms
may be used to minimize damage.
In cases where the secondaryknives cut off the
main carrier,steel slats areessential,and it is neces-
sary to provide additional support below the camer
atthepoint of knifing.Withthetrend toagreateruse
of belts, different arrangements have been adopted.
Because the belt may get damaged at the point of
knifing, the knives are arranged to cut against the
headshaft of the conveyor or preferably an anvil
roller, which is placed just after the headshaft of a
belt conveyor. This is shown schematically in Fig-
ure 4.2. The cane leavingthe knives at high velocity
is made to impact a plate above the following belt
to prevent direct impact on the belt. Below the belt
a flat plate is generally installed (a "beater plate")
so that if a knife were to come off and hit the belt it
would not be able to penetrate through the belt and
cause seriousdamage.
Knifing on its own cannot give the degree of
preparation possible with a shredder. The action
of the knives is to cut the cane into small pieces,
leaving a high proportion of unruptured cells.
Moor (1974) reported PI values at Maidstone of
65 to 70 and Marson (1980) values between 62
and 83 at Amatikulu. Higher values are gener-
ally achieved with blunt knives, thus acting more
like a shredder. However, getting high through-
puts with blunt knives can be difficult. The use
of blunt knives and low clearances at Cora Texas
is able to achieve values in the mid 80s by the
Louisiana method, which gives a slightly higher
value. A PI in the low 80s is probably the limit
with conventional knifing.

Conventional rotation of knives means that the
knives rotate in a direction such that the knives at
the bottom are moving in the same direction as the
movement of cane on the conveyor. In some cases
reverse rotation is applied, in an attempt to achieve
finerpreparation with knives.
The old Empangeni mill in South Africa did
achieve a higher PIwith two sets of knives, with the
second set using heavy palmed swing knives rotat-
ing in areverse direction and with a grid plate above
the second knives.The swing knives were necessary
to minimizedamagefrom extraneousmatter.A feed
roll above the cane being fed to the knives was also
necessary to prevent cane being thrown up and back.
This was the result of efforts to improvepreparation
ahead of a bagasse diffuser and almost resembled
a shredder.Season average values of PI in the high
80's were reported in the last four seasonsbefore the
mill closed down.
This reverse rotation knife arrangement is also
shown schematically in Figure 4.2 C. The feeder
drum has a diameter similar to the swept diameter
of the knives, and turns at a speed roughly equiva-
lent to the speed of the carrier feeding the knives.
Typically it will have a 37 kW motor drive on a 2.1
m wide carrier. This system has been adopted more
widely since then because of its ability to achieve a
higherPI.
4.2.3 Knifespeedsandpowerrequire-
ments
Knives may be driven by electric motors or
steam turbines through gearboxes to achieve speeds
in the range of 400 to 700 min-I. Average speeds are
around 500 to 600min-l, and sometimesthe second-
ary knives are run faster than the primary knives.
Power absorbed should be related to the number of
knives, the swept diameter, knife pitch, clearance,
cutting depth and other factors such as friction etc.
In practice, only throughput and fiber content seem
to be important;Hugot (1986) suggests the power is
related to fiber throughput rather than cane through-
put.
In practice the power installed needs to be able
to handle occasional consignments of poor quality
trashy cane, which generally requiresfar more pow-
er than higher throughputsof clean cane.
Extensive testing of knifing configurations by
NickLin (1967) at four mills in Australia established
typical power requirements for installed power as
outlined in Table 4.1.
The installed power requirements are larger for
whole stalk cane because of greater power fluctua-
tions than those experienced when billeted cane is
processed.Motor sizing is dictated by the sizeof the
current surges. Couplingof the drives of both sets of

4.3 Shredders
Shredders act in a somewhat different way to
knives. Swing hammers rotate on a rotor at 1000to
1200m i d , with sweptdiameters in the range 1.4to
over 1.9 m, leading to tip speeds of about 100 mls,
with a range of 65 to 110rnls. The hammers are set
with a closeclearancebetween the hammer tips and
a grid plate or washboard of anvil grid bars at right
angles to the rotation of the hammers. High-speed
photography undertaken at Queensland University
shows that the impact of the hammer smashespieces
of cane while "falling" freely in the shredder (Cul-
len and McGinn 1974).The close clearancesare im-
portant in achieving a fine preparation of the type
required, i.e. long strands of shredded fibers. The
main actionof thegrid bars seemsto be to return the
particles into the path of the hammer so that further
"strikes" can occur.
Moor (1994) has described the development of
heavy duty shredders, to the point where PI values
higher than 90 are achieved. They generally have
massive hammers, each weighing 15 to 20 kg, ar-
ranged to give fullcoverage by the hammers across
the width of the shredder. Grid plates are adjustable
to give the close clearancesrequired.
Since the optimum type of preparation is more
easily achievedin a shredderthan by knifing, there is
a generaltrend tomore shreddingand lessknifing.A
singleheavy duty shredderon billeted cane achieves
the required degree of preparation and leads to a
simplified preparation stage. It also enables rubber
belts to be used as cane conveyers rather than expen-
siveand maintenance-intensiveapron caniers.
The observationof Hugot (1986)is interesting:
"The shredder fills a role which neither the
knives nor the mills canfu@ll. It establishes a
state of subdivision whichgreatlyfacilitates the
work of the mills."
4.3.1 Types of shredder
Prior to the mid-1960s there were basically two
types of swing-hammer shredders - the Searby and
the Gruendler. These were not dissimilar in con-
struction, with the Searby having relatively light
hammers (2 to 3 kg) and the Gruendler heavier
hammers (6 to 7 kg). Both machines typically ran
at 960 min-' on a diameter of 1520 mm, giving a
tip speed of 76 m/s. Hammer sizes gradually in-
creased to 6 kg on the Searbyunits, but considerable
wear on the hammers and the hammer bars due to
hammer swing was experienced. The hammers on
Gmendler shredders also increasedin mass to about
10kg over time. Provision was made to accommo-
dateflywheelson the shaft.
Interest in diffusion and the recognition of im-
proved performance due to fine preparation led
to the development of machines to achieve high
preparation levels. This was first evident in Hawaii
(Payne 1968),where swing hammer shredderswere
recommended as the most suitable cane preparation
equipment. However Payne introduced two stages
of shredding, following light knifing to achieve the
required degree of preparation. Concerns that fine
4.3.1 Types of shredder/ 4.3.2 Shredderfeeding
preparation would lead to mill feeding difficulties
were dispelled by the use of underfeed rolls, feed
chutes and roll surface roughening. Modem hard-
facing techniquesreduced hammer wear.
The types of shreddercan be categorized as fol-
lows:
Light duty shredders. These are represented
by the Searby and Gruendler shredders mentioned
above. There are still a number of them in use, but
they are not effective in achievingthe good prepara-
tion generally demanded for modem mills and dif-
fusers. No new shreddersof this type are installed.
Heavy duty shredders. The threemain types of
heavy duty shredderdesign are:
1. Silver shredders - the Buster and Fiberizer
-These swing hammer shredders developed in
Hawaii were run in series and achieved a dis-
placeability index consistentlyover 90, suitable
for diffusion or milling, with power consump-
tion up to 130 (kW. h)/$ Both had variable
speed feed rolls installed above the rotor. The
Buster had an open grid with anvils between
the hammers and the Fiberizer was more like
a conventional shredder. This arrangement was
based on the belief that two stages of shredding
were necessary to achieve the required level of
preparation. This is no longer the case and these
shredders are no longer seen in new installa-
tions.
2. Walkers Extra Heavy Duty shredder-This was
first introduced as a 1.53 m diameter machine
with 15kg hammers rotating at 1200min1
and
absorbing 75 to 80 (kW. h)/t, Later versions
have diametersincreased to 1.83m and are fit-
ted with feeder rolls with no preceding knives
and a larger angle of wrap on the grid plate. A
similar shredder is also supplied by Bundaberg
in Australia who have now absorbedWalkers.
3. Tongaatshredder-This was developedin South
Africa following the developments in Hawaii
and Australia. It is similar in dimensions and
speed to the Walkers unit but has a rotor of al-
ternately staggered profiled plates instead of
circular discs and spacers. A typical hammers
complement is 168 hammers of 20 kg each in
8 or 10rows. Sweptdiameterswere initially 1.5
m, but later shreddershave had 1.8m swept di-
ameters.Hammer width is dictated by the width
of the plates. Most shredders of this type are
2.13 m wide, although wider units have been
supplied.This design was licensed in Brazil and
elsewhere and is common in many sugar cane
areas. Details are illustratedin Figure4.4.
Hybrid types. A number of preparation devices
have been developedwhich are not clearly knives or
shredders. The Unigrator was developed to cut and
shred cane and was widely used for about 30 years.
In Brazil, a shredderwas developed which operated
on an inclined steel slat conveyor, and finds wide-
spread use in South America. From both of these,
a whole stalk shredder was developed, which has a
horizontal feed and a rotor arranged atthe end of the
conveyor. These have all found varying degrees of
success, depending on the local requirements. De-
tails aregiven in Section 4.3.5.
4.3.2 Shredderfeeding
It isnecessaryto achievea steadyfeed to ashred-
der if consistently good results are to be obtained
without unnecessary surges in power demand. Vari-
ous arrangements have been proposed for feeding
shredders, It is important to direct the flow of cane
into the nip wherethe hammersenterthe washboard
area. The cane hits the feed plate and slides into the
nip area. It is also important that the feed plate is
flush with the level of the first grid bar. The projec-
tion of the first grid bar causes surging and can lead
to choking (Greenwood 1971).
A number of installations in SouthAfrica have
a set of kicker knives propelling the cane into the
shredder.These knives have tip speedsroughly half
the tip speed of the shredderand do littlein the way
of preparation, as evidenced by minimal wear on
these knives. TWOdifferent feeding arrangements
areshowninFigure4.5. Thefirstarrangementrepre-
sentsthe original design forFelixton in SouthAfrica
(Renton 1992),which has not worked satisfactorily,
because the "billeted" cane does not slump in the
shredder chute as it would with chopper harvested
cane;intermittentslumpingwas found to make level
control difficult The preferred arrangement accord-
ing to Renton is shown in the second arrangement,
with a vertical feed chuteincludingfeeder rolls and
a knife "kicker" throwing the cane into the nip of
the shredder.

A simpler arrangement is sometimes employed,
which utilizes a set of knives cutting on the head-
shaft of the carrier feeding the shredder, directing
the cane towards the feed plate or into the nip of the
shredder.This is shownin Figure 4.6. A setof knives
acting as a kicker with a greater clearance from the
headshaft worksjust as well.
Crawford (1970) proposed an inclined chute at
60" to the horizontal with a set of feeder rolls being
the optimum arrangement. Letizia and McDougall
(1989) describe the development of a heavy duty
shredder fed by a chute at an angle of 60" and a pair
of feeder rolls. The contact angle on the bottom roll
was reduced to 55" in order to get the system to feed
reliably.
In the absence of kicker knives, a vertical chute
is normally employed. A vertical chute is now usu-
ally used above feeder rolls. The feeder rolls are pre-
sumed to give better performance, ensuring that the
shredder does not get overloaded,leading to a steadi-
er power consumption. They also provide significant
sound reduction. They may also be used as a method
of controlling cane throughput rate into the extrac-
tion plant, although Marson (1980) has shown that
unburnt cane rate is about 20 % less than burnt cane
rate at the same feeder roll speed i.e. the volumetric
throughput is affected by the presence of trash.
Australian experience suggests that a vertical
chute with feeder rolls and no kicker knives works
well. This is simpler than the installations shown
in Figures 4.5 and 4.6. Installation details for some
Australian shredders are given by Flanders et al.
(1992). The feeder rolls require very little power,
typically around 10kW, although the installed pow-
er is much higher. Some newer arrangements have a
variable speed flange-mounted motor and gearbox
on each feed roll.
According to Cullen (1986), feeder rolls en-
hance performance because of the large angle of
wrap possible.
4.3.3 Factors affecting the prepara-
tion achieved
A considerable amount of work was done in
Australia to identify the factors affecting the degree
of preparation achieved. The operating speed of the
hammers has been shown to have the most signifi-
cant effect. Operating a shredder at 1200minirath-
References p. 98
4 Cane preparation
er than 960 min-I was shown to increase POC by 6
units (Cullen 1986). These correspond to tip speeds
of 91 and 73 d s respectively.
The clearance between the hammers and the
grid bars in the washboard has little influence in the
range of 0 to 10 mm clearance. Above that however
the PI achieved can drop off quickly as the opening
is increased (Marson 1980; Cullen 1986).
Marson (1980) also showed that the speed of
the shredder had the greatest effect on preparation
and that throughput rate and the degree of knifing
prior to the shredder had no significant effect. Cul-
len (1986) confirmed that the degree of preparation
of cane entering the shredder had no effect on the
shredder PI achieved. This supports the theory that
knifing ahead of the shredder is unnecessary and
does not materially improvepreparation.
The number of rows of hammers and the mass
of the hammers are also not considered to affect the
preparation achieved. Cullen and McGinn (1974)
showed that there is no swing back of hammers with
15kg hammers. There can therefore be no justifica-
tion for using heavier hammers.
The angle of wrap of the grid bar is expected to
have a significant effect. Since the function of the
grid bars is assumed to be to propel the cane pieces
into the path of the hammers so that further strikes
can occur, a greater angle of wrap must facilitate a
larger number of strikes. Increasing the grid length
wrap from 90" to 160" increases the POC by 3 to 7
units, depending on configuration (Cullen 1986).
The degree of preparation achieved is reported
to vary at the same power input for different variet-
ies (Cullen 1986), indicating an effect of the hard-
ness of the cane.
4.3.4 Shredder size and throughput
The throughput of a shredder is proportional
to its width and operating capacities rarely exceed
250 tJh per m of width (Cullen and McKay 1993).
On this basis, a 2134 mm wide shredder should have
a maximum capacity of 534 tJh.
Extensive experimentation on a 2134 mm wide
heavy duty shredder at Amatikulu gave throughput
rates up to exactly 534 t$ and 76 t$ (Marson
1980). This confirms that the figure of 250 tdh per
m of width is achievable, although Marson made no
attempt to test the throughput limit.
Subsequent experience in Thailand has shown
that significantly higher throughputs, up to 350 tc/h
per m of width, are possible providing a feeder is
fitted. This still needs to be confirmed by further op-
erating experience.
Capacity is affected by the way the shredder is
fed. Steadyfeed and feed directed at the nip between
hammers and the top of the grid bars must yield
maximum throughput. If the power of the prime
mover is the limiting factor, high levels of trash in
cane will limit throughput because of the greater
power required to process trashy cane. Expressing
throughput in terms of fiber throughput partially ac-
counts for this effect.
4.3.5 Hybrid shredders
Unigrator. The Unigrator combines features of
knives and shredders (Ducasse 1974).It is located on
the top of the cane carrier. The blades cut upwards
through the bed of cane on the carrier. Cut pieces are
thrown upwards and these drop over a grid where
they are shredded against a grid by the knives. Clear-
ance on the grid is typically 10to 35 mm. The spring
loaded grid bar section allows the passage of stones
and tramp iron. One version has swing hammers for
greater protection.
The rotor runs at a speed of up to 1000 min-',
which with a swept diameter of 1.68 m leads to
tip speeds of 88 m/s. Installed power is about 15.5
(kW .h)/t, (approximately 2.3 (kW .h)/t,). It can
handle whole stalk cane, combining knifing and
shredding in one device, and up to 81 percent open
cells is claimed. However it does require a very even
flow of cane to the machine or else the operation is
erratic. A solution to this problem is to install a feed
roller mounted on top of the cane blanket unrnedi-
ately before the cane enters the machine.
Copersucar shredder. A horizontal shredder
was first installed in Brazil by Deon Hulett (Cross-
man 1994).This resembled the reverse rotation knife
arrangement in South Africa, with a grid plate above
the rotor and a feed drum just ahead of the rotor.
It ran with a hammer tip velocity of about 60 m/s
and the feeder drum had a peripheral velocity 15 to
20 % greater than that of the carrier. A close clear-
ance between the hammer tips and the cane carrier
was used.

These shredders have a number of advantages
and disadvantages, which will dictate whether it is
the device of choice in a particular circumstance.
The advantagesare:
It can do thejob of knifing and shreddingin one
ope&n, thus saving the cost of installing and
maintainingcane knives.
Less total power is required on average.
It is not damaged by rocks; this has been well
proven in Mauritius, where it is a major advan-
tage.
It requires less space and shorter conveyors,
since there is no need to gain height to feed a
conventional shredderchute.
The overall cost of the installation is lower
(Crossman 1994).
There are also some disadvantages:
Installed drive power has to be larger than for a
conventional shredder, because of larger power
surges experiencedin practice.
If an electric motor is used, the degree of slip
in the rotor circuit needs to be chosen with care
(Crossman 1994).
It is essential to have a good control system for
feeding cane. If the bed is too high, chokes can
occur and if too low, there is nothing to grip the
cane feeding to the shredder and its effective-
ness is lost.
Problemswith bearings and shaftmaterialshave
been reported by Crossman (1994).Adequately
designedshafts and bearings are necessary, with
suitably treated high alloy shafts.
It has to be fed by a slat carrier-a belt is not an
option.
4.3.6 Technical details of heavy duty
shredder design
Most heavy duty shreddersavailabletoday have
similar features. The grid plate is removable, to fa-
cilitate maintenance or replacement with a spare.
The grid plate is generally adjustable in two direc-
tions so that the clearance between hammers and
grid bars along the full length of the grid plate can
be adjusted. Individual grid bars are removable for
replacementor refurbishment.A safetydevicein the
form of shearpins or springsor hydraulically loaded
cylindersis provided on the grid plate to allow tramp
iron to pass through withoutexcessivedamage.
Greenwood (1971)studiedthe effectof different
grid bar arrangements.He found that the "pocketed"
type grid gave better results than the serrated wash-
board type and that a wider pocket is better than a
narrowerpocket. He suggestedthat thereis probably
a minimum pocket depth but not a maximum; the
bottom of the pocket fills with cane and protects the
retaining plates holding down the grid bars. Green-
wood proposed a mechanism for shredding involv-
ing the "flow" of cane through the compacted cane
in the pockets. Cane is shredded against the com-
pressed mat of cane in the pockets. This protects the
grid bars to some extent so that they wear less than
the hammers.
The angle of wrap on most grids is 90".A larger
wrap is desirableto improvepreparation,and angles
of wrap up to 120" are common on newer installa-
tions. Details of some heavy duty shredder installa-
tions are given in Table 4.4.
All heavy duty shredders operate with large
swing hammers weighing between 15 and 25 kg
each. The hammers are arranged in eight to twelve
rows, on rods passing through the rotor. Some de-
signs have bars which are fixed and some arefree to
rotate. Although the amount of swing back of these
hammers is considered to be negligible, some ham-
mershavebushedholes throughwhich the rodspass.
Wear of these holes is experienced,and bushes offer
the opportunity of re-bushing rather than discarding
the hammers when wear is experienced. However
in cases of excessivewear, the hammer may be dis-
carded before the hole wear becomes important.
With the disc and spacer arrangementprovided
in the Walkers shredder,club head hammers are re-
quired to give full coverage across the width of the
shredder. An advantage due to the construction of

very significant relationship between the degree of
preparation and thepower input. He studied the me-

work showed that the power required is dependent

4.3.8 Prime mover requirements
Nicklin (1967) observed that the current peaks
on knife and shredder drives play a large part in
detenninng the power of the motors required. He
considered the use of flywheels and the coupling of
knife drives to reduce peaks. The units he studied
had resistances fitted in the rotor circuits to give
about7.5 % slip.He suggests 15% slip as a suitable
figure, but this sounds very high.
Boshoff (1994) considered measurements of
power consumed in shredding and concluded that
in spite of large fluctuationsin reported data, an in-
stalled power of 45 (kW .h)/t, is adequate for good
preparation.Howeverhe reported largeload swings,
which are evident with a fairly steady feed to the
shredder. Some fluctuationin the speed of the drive
must be allowed to reduce peak loads on the prime
mover. This is easily achieved with a steam turbine
but not with an electricmotor. In the lattercasesome
external resistancein the rotor circuit shouldbe pro-
vided toprevent excessiveoverloads.Boshoff(1994)
gives examples of how this can effectively reduce
spikesin motor current and notes that externalresis-
tance to provide up to 7 % full load slip is used on
electric drives. This is especially important on hori-
zontal whole stalkshredders, where load swingsare
higherthan on conventional shredders.Howeverthis
leads to power losses,which on a 2 MW drivewould
be 140kW with 7 % slip.
To achievea speed in the normal range of 1000
to 1200 min-I, a turbine requires a gearbox. This
should be able to handle the surges experienced in
practice. With a 50 Hz supply, a 960 min-I motor
could be used but a gearbox is necessary to achieve
a higher speed. With a 60 Hz supply a 1200 min-I
motor is ideal.
The choice of a turbine or electric motor de-
pends on a number of factors, includingthe distance
from the steam supply and the steam or energy bal-
ance of the mill. The factors influencing the optimal
selectioncan be summarizedas:
Advantages of a turbiie drive
Good speedltorquecharacteristics;
Ability to handle load surges.
Disadvantagesof a turbiie drive
High capital cost of hubinelgearbox;
Cost of high pressure and exhaust steam reticu-
lation;
Higher maintenance costs;
Generallylowerefficiency;
More complex operating procedures,especially
start-up.
Advantages of an electricmotor drive
Lower capital cost, even accounting for extra
turbogeneratorcapacity;
Ease of operation.
Disadvantagesof electric motordrive
"Stiff' torquelspeed characteristics lead to ex-
cessivecurrents, unless large external slip resis-
tances are fitted;
Losses in externalresistances.
4.4 Operationand maintenance
Operation and mainte-
nance
When shredder hammers are refurbished, they
need to be individually weighed and matched prior
to installation, to preserve the machine balance.
These machines must be checked for balance on a
regular scheduleand balanced ifrequired. The lcnife
andshredderrotorsaresubjectedtoabrasivea
n
dcor-
rosive wear or buildup of foreign matter and should
be regularly checked using a vibration monitoring
systemduring normal operations.If a shredderham-
mer or knife is broken or lost during operation,it is
generallynecessary to stopandremove the opposing
element to keep therotor in balance.
The maintenance of knives and hammers be-
comes a significant production cost in those areas
where a significant amount of field soil comes in
with the cane. Knives generally need attention on a
less frequentbasis. If the knives or hammers are not
too badly worn, they will be built up by welding to
the original dimensionsand hard-facingis reapplied
as necessary. In somecases the worn ends of knives
are cut off and replacementends are welded on.
When the leading edges of the shredder ham-
mers get worn, preparation is not necessarily im-
paired, but feeding problems may arise. With sharp
edges, the hammer blows direct the cane towards
the grid entry.As the leading edge wears and the tip
edge edges steel overlay
Figure 4.13: Repair of shredderhammers
A Oneside worn; B Both sides worn;C Mild steel rebuilt;
D Hard-facing overlay to gauge
becomes rounded, the impact of the edge may give
some of the cane an upward component which can
retard cane entry into the nip of the shredder.
When shredder hammers are protected with a
hard-facing overlay, the end of the hammer can be
made to keep a sharp leadingedge as the softer met-
al below the overlay wears more rapidly. Depending
on hammer wear, hammers are removed and rotated
to use the opposite work face before removing for
repair or replacement.When both sides of the ham-
mer are worn, the hammer is removed for rebuild-
ing, replacing the mild steel lost and reapplying a
hard-facingoverlay.It is importantto ensurethat the
correct dimensions are achieved in the rebuilding
process, particularlyif closeclearancesareinvolved.
Wear in the bore of a hammer needs also tobe taken
intoaccount.If thebore wear is significant,the ham-
mer must be discarded or the bush replaced in the
case of a bushed hammer. The ideal way to check
the hammer length is through the use of a golno-go
gauge, with the hammer hanging from a pivot (to
take intoaccountbore wear)and being ableto swing
past a maximum length mark and not past a mini-
mum length mark.The process of wear and rebuild-
ing a shredderhammer is shown in Figure 4.13.
The use of hard metal inserts on knives and
shreddersis widespread in areaswheretheincidence
of rocks or tramp iron in the feed is minimal. On
knives,the hard metal piecesare welded to theknife,
and in shredders a block of hard metal is bolted to
the working face of the hammer.As wear occurs the
block can be turned to present a new edge on the
hammer. Indexing the hammer tips is far less time-
consuming than removing and replacing hammers.
These hard materials may also be used on the grid
bars to reduce wear.
It is sometimes necessary to replace or repair
grid bars in the washboard to ensure close clearanc-
es. In somecases a sparegrid plate is used toreplace
a worn one,enablingrepair to be done at leisure. It is
very important to ensurethat the grid is not warped
at all. If this is the case, the clearance will be close
in only one part of the grid and too wide elsewhere
so that inferior results will be achieved. This is fre-
quently overlooked and its importance cannot be
overemphasized.
The clearance between hammers and grid is
adjusted by moving the grid bar inwards while the
shredderis running but with no cane feed. The point
at which the hammers just touch the grid bars can

5.1 Extraction by mills
5.1.1 Extraction
The objective of milling is to separate the su-
crose-containing juice from the remainder of the
cane, which comprises mainly fiber. Extraction is
taken to mean the percentage of sucrose extracted
from cane in the mills, and equals sucrose in raw
juice as a percentageof sucrosein cane.
Cane can be assumed to comprise three compo-
nents, each with two sub-constituents:
1. Fiber, consisting of:
Vegetable fiber, and
Insoluble matter that is not fibrous but included
with "fiber" in caneand bagasseanalyses,some-
times measured as ash.
2. Dissolved solids, also referredto as Brix, con-
sisting of the water-soluble materialin cane:
Sucrose(usuallymeasured approximatelyas po-
larization or pol),
Nonsucrose (other soluble matter in solution)
-sometimesalso called nonsugar or non-pol.
3. Water, consistingof:
"Free" water (the solvent in which the sucrose
and nonsucrose are dissolved),
Brix-free water ("bound" water that forms part
of the cellulosic structure of the cane and is
therefore not available as a solvent for the su-
crose and nonsucrose and is not extracted in the
milling process).
In the mills, the cane is squeezed under high pres-
sure between successive pairs of rolls. These are
designedto express as much as possible of thejuice
(freewater +sucrose+nonsugar)fromthe insoluble
fiber. The residual cane from which juice has been
extractedis termed bagasse.
The percentage of the sucrose in the original
cane that is removed with therawjuice is termed the
"sucrose extraction", E, expressedas a percentage:
However, if clarifier mud recycling is practised, the
juice contains some recycled sucrose and the mea-
sureis more appropriatelydefined as:
whereliz,refers to the massflow rate of sucrose,and
the subscripts RJ, C and B refer to raw juice, cane
and bagasse respectively. "Pol extraction" and "Brix
extraction" are similarlydefined. In practice, extrac-
tion is most commonly expressed in terms of pol,
because pol is more readily measwed than sucrose.
The sucrose and pol extraction figures are numeri-
cally very close and can, for practical purposes, be
taken as equal. However, Brix extraction differs
quite significantly.
Someof the nonsucroseis lessreadilyextractedthan
sucrose. This is evidenced by the fact that the juice
extracted in the first milling stage (first expressed
juice) is always of higher purity than the raw juice
5 Milling
while that extracted towards the end of the milling
tandem (last expressedjuice) is always of lower pu-
rity. The residualjuice remaining in the final bagasse
is of even lower purity. Consequently,the extraction
measured on a Brix basis will be lessthan the sucrose
extraction.Illustrationsof the differencesbetween su-
crose and dissolved solids (Brix) extractions are seen
in Figure5.19 and in Table 5.6 in Section 5.8.1.
From reasonably well-prepared cane, it is usu-
ally possible to extract 60 % to 75 % of the sucrose
in one conventionalmill. If this cane is then passed
on to a second mill, very little more sucrosewill be
recovered since there is little free juice remaining
with the bagasse. To enable subsequent mills to ex-
tract more sucrose, additional water or imbibition is
therefore added to the bagasse. This mixes with the
remainingjuice in the cane, dilutes it and provides
more extractable material for the mills. The theory
and practice of adding imbibition is discussed fur-
ther in Section5.8.1.

mance

gasse. This can be expected to be proportional to
the mass of bagasse, which is in turn proportional
to the fiber content of the cane - a factor usually
beyond the control of the miller. To provide a better
measure of milling performancethat eliminates this

5.2 Theory of milling
The classic theories of mill feeding and extrac-
tion are perhaps most comprehensively set out in
the book of Murry andHolt (1967). Many other au-
thors have made significantcontributionsto aspects
of milling theory, including Crawford (1955, 1957,
1970), Murry (1960a, 1960b), Jenkins (1966), de
Boer (1969 and 1972), Cullen and McKay (1992)
and Wenese (1990 and 2003). The principles are
widely accepted and the description that follows
draws from a combination of inputs from the above
authors.
5.2.1 Basic volumetric model
Extraction in a mill is
achieved by squeezing prepared
cane between one or more pairs
of rolls. The model considers
millingasa seriesof singlestages
of squeezing between two rolls,
with the relevant feed widths and
work openingsfor each stage.
In practice,there is a wide va-
riety of mill conditions and con-
figurations. To permit a manage-
able model, the approach adopts
initially a number of simplifying
assumptions to create the model,
and thereafter examines the im-
plications of each assumption in
turn.
5.2.2 Assumptions for simple model
Milling is primarily a volumetric process. Con-
sider the mill feed diagram in Figure 5.1, in which
it is assumed:
a) A supply of prepared canelbagasse (hereafter
"cane") is presented in a slab of rectangular
cross-section1in m wide by h in m thick, to two
mill rolls (or rollers) each of length 1and diarn-,
eter din m.
b) The rolls are at a fixed distance apart, giving a
"work opening" h, in m.
c) The prepared cane comprises four components:
fiber, Brix-freewater,juice (=dissolved solids +
unbound water) and air. The insoluble ash con-
tent is normally small (1 % to 2 % of total) and
is included in the model as "fiber".
d) Extraction takes place sequentially,first air and
then juice. No insoluble solids (fiber) are ex-
tracted with thejuice.
e) The rolls are cylindricaland not grooved.
f) Both rolls rotate at a speed of n in s-l, to give a
roll surface circumferential speed of u in rnls,
i . e . u = ~ . d . n .
g) The feed is supplied symmetricallybetween the
rolls and in a direction normal (square) to their
centers.
h) There isjust sufficientpressure towards the rolls
to ensure contact onto the rolls (no additional
feedpressure).
i) The feed angle (angle subtended between the

point of first contact
with each roll and the
line between their cen-

j) There is no slip on the
roll surfaces and no
horizontal shearing of
the cane feed during
its passage through the
rolls.
k) There is no reabsorp-

5.2.5 Compaction ratio, compression
ratio and fiberfills
Authors are not universally consistent in the use
of the terms "compression" and "compaction" ra-
tios. The differences arise from the presence of air
or voids in the cane before it is squeezed in the mill.
The definitionsused here accord with what appears
to be the most common usage.
Compaction ratio. In this model, the cane is
compacted from its bulk density in the feed to its
density as it passes through the work opening. The
compaction ratio Cb is defined as the ratio of the
bulk volumetric ratev in m3/s at feed to the escribed
volume at the work opening.Thus:
Fiber fill. Fiber, Brix-free water and juice are
incompressible,so most or all of the air and someof
the juice may need to be expressed out of the cane
mat to achieve this compaction. However it is as-
sumed that the fiber flow remains constant through
the process and it is therefore convenient to use the
concept of "fiber fill" to describe the bulk density
or the degree of compaction at a particular point.
Fiber fill p, is defined as the kilograms of fiber per
unit timedivided by the escribedvolume V~ ,i.e. the
mass of fiber per unit volumein kg/m3. The fiberfill

Compression ratio. The compression ratio C,,
is defined as the ratio of the no-voidvolume of cane
at feed to the escribed volume at the work opening.
Without slip or reabsorption, this volume change is
entirely due tojuice removal. Clearly, the higher the
compressionratio, the higher the degree of juice ex-
traction.A physical limit is reached when reabsorp-
tion occurs (Section 5.2.10).

5.2.7 Non-cylindricalrolls
One of the assumptionswas that the rolls are cy-
lindrical and not grooved. For a number of reasons
discussed under Section 5.3.5, mill rolls are not of
plain cylindrical construction, but circumferentially
grooved.
This is easily accommodated in this theory.
With grooved rolls, the effectivesurface speeds,set-
tings and work openings are all calculated from the
mean diameter of the roll, i.e. (diameterover tips of
teeth +diameterover roots of teeth)/2.

5.2.9 Friction and feed opening

opening.

1 Reabsorption, shearing in the
cane and slip
In the simplified milling model above, no reab-
sorption is assumed. What is reabsorption?
In passing through the mill, the fist product
extracted is assumed to be the air. Juice extraction
actually commences before the last air is removed.
Once the last air has been removed (e.g. by the final
squeezeat the dischargeroll of a mill) the bagasse is
said to be in a "no-void" condition. The remaining
components then are only fiber and juice, both of
which are effectively incompressible.The densities
of these productscan be measured. That of dry fiber
p
, is about 1530 kg/m3 and that of juice p
, is be-
tween 1000and 1030kg/m3,depending on its Brix
and temperature.
Under carefully controlled experimental condi-
tions at the Sugar Research Institute and the Uni-
versity of Queensland,Australia, it was shown that
the no-void volume of the bagasse discharged from
a high-compressionmill is larger than the escribed
volumeat the final squeeze point. This phenomenon
is describedas reabsorption.
The ratio of the no-void volume of the bagasse
to the escribed volume is termed the reabsorption
factork.
In practice,reabsorptionfactorsin the orderof 1.2to
1.6are experiencedin well-operated mills.
Crawford (1957, 1959, 1970) postulated that
the pressure in the bagasse reaches a peak shortly
before the work opening (pinch point, at roll angle
0") between the two rolls. At this pressure, the free
juice can no longerpermeate backwards through the

densely compacted fiber to escape. From this point
therefore, the juice flows forward through the fiber
andor the entire mass of fiber and juice extrudes
forward through the work opening, traveling at a
velocity higher than the roll surface speed. Jenkins
(1966:106-107) has discussed the possible mecha-
nisms involved in this phenomenon.This peak pres-
sure is usually reached at a position between 3" and
7" before the pinch point. Thereafter the pressure
in the bagasse remains effectively constant until it
is released after the pinch point (Murry and Holt
1967:63). This was con6rmed by recordings of the
pressures as measured by pressure pins inserted in
test rolls (see Figure 5.3). Holt (1961) confirmed
that the whole bagasse mass does extrude under a
condition of sufficientpressure.
The neutral plane is defined as the position at
which the average forward velocity of the bagasse
equals the velocity of the roll surface at the axial
plane. After the neutral plane, the bagasse acceler-
ates to a speed faster than the roll surface (Murry
andHolt 1967:41).Themaximum pressureoccursat
the neutral plane (ibid:60) and there is no freejuice
or extractionbeyond this position (ibid:58).
In the model it was assumed that there is no slip
on the roll surfaces and no horizontal shearing of
the cane feed on its passage through the mill. Un-
der extrusion conditions this assumption cannot be
true, because there must be slip and/or shearing of
the cane blanket.
Reabsorption limits the amount of juice that
can be extractedat any particular milling stage.The
amount of reabsorptionis dependenton a number of
factors, and will generally be reduced by:

"Squirting" ofjuice is sometimes observed from

flowed forward through gaps in the roots of the roll

measures to counter squirting are generally the same
as those to reduce reabsorption listed above.

5.2.12 Mill load and torque
Because of the large differences in cane char-
acteristics, mill designs and milling practices, it is
not possible to construct a universal mathematical
model that will be applicable to all operating mills.
Between the isolated pair of rolls in the simple
model, the total radial force on each roll will be the
integral of the pressure over the working area of the
circumference. However, it will be seen from Figure
5.3 and Section 5.2.11 that, with reabsorption, the
distribution of this pressure is complex and some-
what unpredictable.
In real mills, there are many other forces to con-
sider. The top roll is the most highly loaded mill
component. Both the drive torque and the loading
of the hydraulics are applied through the top roll.
They work against reactions through the bagasse
from feeding devices, compression at two or more
rolls and at the trash plate, discharge scraper and
bearing friction, mill pinion torque and separating
forces, etc.
The static reaction forces from the feed and
discharge squeezes and the trash plate all pass
through the center of the top roll.
In operation,friction and feeding action result in
torque forces.
The net force from the discharge roll is far great-
er than that from the feed roll. The ratio of these
two forces varies widely. Hugot (1986:161-164)
quotes sources giving figures varying from 2 to
as much as 8. The ratio will depend on mill de-
sign (lower for pressure-fed mills than for 3-roll
mills), feeding arrangements, position of mill
along tandem, mill settings and other factors.
A figure of 4 5 is probably applicable to most
mills.
Absorbed power by conventional three-roll
mills, measured at the prime mover, is usually 8

to 12 (kW .h)/$. Allowing for gearing and cou-
pling losses of 20 %, this is 6.4 to 9.6kW/t fiber
per hour at the top roll input.

torque is thus 130to 190kN .m per t fiber&.

5.3 Mills and mill components
5.3.1 Conventional mills
"Conventional" here refers to mills with feed
and dischargerolls at a common level and vertically
floating top rolls, although some variations have
proved successful.Such alternativedesigns include:
Fives Cail's self-setting mills, with an articu-
lated frame supportingthe top roller.
Walkers hydraulics-in-line mills with hydrauli-
cally loaded dischargeroll.
Although many mills have been built with 5, 6 or
more rolls, these generally include pressure feeders
which may be considered as an "add on" feeding
device to a conventional mill. Pressure feeders are
therefore discussed under the topic of mill feeding
(Section5.9.5). Recent two-roll mills differ in many
respects from conventional mills and are therefore
accorded a separate Section (5.4).
Normal milling tandem plant is used for dewa-
tering diffuser bagasse, but the requirements are
generally more difficult because of the particular
conditions of high juice quantity and high tempera-
ture.This is covered in Section 6.5.

2 Headstocks
The purpose of the mill headstocks is to main-

5 Milling
Shaft. The forces acting on the mill rolls give
rise to shearing, bending, torsion and compressive
stresses (Cullen1968,Reid 1988).The top roll is the
most highly stressed, since it consumes about half
of the total mill torque (Kent and McKenzie 2001)
and is subject to bending against the reactions of the
feed roll, trash plate and discharge roll (Figure 5.4).
The stresses typically vary along the length of the
shaft as shown in Figure 5.8. The most important
stress is that from the combined torsion and bend-
ing (the vonMises stress). As shownin the diagram,
the highest von Mises stress is at the inner fillet
radius on the drive side journal. It is therefore not
surprising that most shaft failures occur at this po-
sition, followed by shaft-and-shell failures towards
the drive end of the roll.
Because the roll is rotating, the stresses are re-
peatedly reversed or fluctuating and the great major-
ity of failures are of the fatigue type. Under fatigue
conditions, failure occurs over time at an average
stress level well below that of the yield point of the
steel (the stress at which immediate static failure
will occur). Furthermore, in fatigue the local stress
is considerably increased above the average in some
areas by local stress raisers. Such a stress raiser is
the change of section at bearing fillet radii.
The extent to which the stress is raised by a
particular feature is termed the stress concentration
factor (SCF). The dimensions of mill roll shafts fall
outsideof the standard ranges quoted in most fatigue
design books, so that engineers such as Reid (1988)
and Smith (2005) have used finite element analysis
to determine the SCFs along mill roll shafts. This
has shown that the average stress is multiplied by an
SCF of 1.8to 2.0 for a smooth 30 mm fillet radius.
The SCFcan be reduced to about 1.3by using a 180
mm radius.
However, aspointed out by Reid, the surface fin-
ish of the fillet and adjacentjournal is of far greater
importance to stress concentration than is the size
of fillet radius. For example, a groove (caused by
poor machining, entrapped grit or welding inclu-
sions) with a root radius of 0.5 mm would have an
SCFof 14.5.Note that this SCF will amplify the al-
ready concentrated stress in the fillet. Such a feature
is highly likely to lead to failure.
To reduce failures, Simisain Brazil and Bunda-
berg in Australia have designed shafts with very
large fillets (150 to 200 mm radius) on the drive-

Correct specification, manufacture and mainte-

The key requirement forgood fatigue predicates
the usual specification of a ductile mild steel mate-

used in its normalized condition. Steels which fall
into this general category are SAE 1022 or the
BS 970 classification of 070M20 (formerly EN3).

35/40 tonne steel SAE 1045 or 080M40 (formerly
ENS). The shaft should be stress-relieved by hold-
ing for 6 to 7 hours at a temperature of between 580
"C and 620 "C before final machining when new
and again at each reshelling.

stress raisers. Reid (1988) details the following pre-
cautions for all rolls:

Shell. The favored specification for mill roll
shells used to be an "open-grained cast iron", since
this produced a rough finish to aid feeding. How-
ever, with higher loads and stresses and the devel-
opment of roll surfaceroughening techniques such
as carbon-arcing and subsequentlyhard welding, a
close grained, higher tensile material is now pre-
ferred. The material should be free from blowholes
and cracks. The shell should be cast in an upright
position to allow effective removal of slag inclu-
sions.
Care to avoid stress raisers, correct stress re-
lief treatment and magnetic and ultrasonic testing
of shafts for defects will minimize the chances of
mill roll failures. If availabIe,itis advisableto em-

see themanufacture,repair and re-shellingof mill

Flanges. Most top rolls are fitted with bolted
on steel flanges to contain the bagasse within the
pressure zone between the top roll and feed roll,
trash plate and discharge roll. These flanges need
to providea lateralclearance-usually about 5 mm
each side-for axial roll movement and tipping of
the top roll.
Some mills successfully use "fixed flanges".
These are strong, wear-resistant plates mounted
securely onto the headstocks. They are profiled to
cover the sides of the pressure zone.
Benefits of this system are lower cost and more
juice drainagearea than with conventional flanges.
A disadvantage is that bagasse buildup can cause
wear on the ends of the rolls if the flanges are not
correctlymounted.

5.3.4 Roll grooving
The milling model assumed simple cylindrical.
rollers. In practice, these would be extremely inef-
ficient devices. Until the mid-20"' century, milling
tandems were often preceded by a "crusher", whose
principal function was to break up the cane stalks,
Typical of these devices was the Krajewski crusher,
which comprised two rolls with coarse transverse
zigzag grooves cast into the shells. Better prepara-
tion equipment - particularly shredders - replaced
the function of such crushers.Now mill rolls are al-
most exclusivelycircumferentiallygrooved.
There areseveralreasonsfor theuse of grooving
on mill rolls;
The roller grooving assists in breaking up the
cane.This is a relatively unimportantfunction if
the cane has already been well prepared before
milling, e.g. to 90 PI by a heavy-duty shredder.
Grooved rolls present a larger surface area in
contact with the cane and hence better traction.
The canedoes not pack into the vee at thebottom
of the groove, thus providing a natural drainage
path for the expressedjuice.
The inclined faces of the roll teeth provide ad-
ditional extraction force on the cane without in-
creasing the hydraulic (or other) loading on the
rolls, i.e. without increasing the bending stresses
on the roll and its shaft as shown in Figure 5.9.
