The main disadvantagesof mill roll grooving are:
The roots of the grooves constitute "stress rais-
ers" that can lead to fatigue failure of the shell
and shaft.
For the same effective work opening between
two rolls, the free gap to pass any extraneous
solid objects such as eamp iron or rocks is re-
duced, increasing the likelihood of roll damage.
Common dimensionsof mill roll grooves are:
Pitch: From 25 mm (1") to 75 mm (3'3, with
50 mm (2")probably the most widely used.
Groove included angle:From 40" to 55".
In practice, mill roll grooves aregenerally machined
to a profile with a small flat (2-4 mm wide) across
the top of the teeth for strength purposes (as shown
in Figure 5.9).This also assists in applying welding
for surface roughening.The roots of grooves should
be sharp or rounded to a smallradius (say 1.5 mm)
to allow ajuice drainagepath.
Normal practice is to use the same grooving
profile on all rolls of a mill (e.g. 50 mm pitch, 45"
groove angle). In this case, the grooving of the top
roll of a 3-roll mill must be arranged to mesh with
that of the feed and discharge rolls. Thus, if the top
roll configuration has a tooth at the center or mid-
plane, then the feed and discharge rolls must have
grooves at the mid-plane.
Some engineers favor large pitch grooving on
the feed roll (to improvefeeding and mesh securely
with the trash plate), with smaller grooving on the
top and discharge rolls (to reduce mesh depth and
increase drainage channels at the final squeeze).
This can be accommodated by using double the
pitch on the feed roll (e.g. 50 mm on feed, 25 mm
on top and dischargerolls). In this case, the feed and
discharge roUs should both have a tooth at the mid-
plane, meshing with a groove at the mid-plane of
the top roll.
Hugor (1986:104)makes reference to "universal
rolls", where the grooves are arranged with themid-
dle of a tooth flank at the center of the roll. All rolls
then have identical grooving, but must be reversible
end for end. This requires a costly shaft design and
the concept is thereforerarely used. Simisa (J3razil)

5.3.6 Lotus rolls
Messchaert grooves cannot be used in top rolls
because there would be no easy outlet for the juice
except into the bagasse exiting the mill. They would
also seriously weaken the roll that is most highly
stressed and most frequently broken. Drainage from
the upper surface of the bagasse passing through the
mill is indeed a major problem, since the juice must
flow in the roots of the grooves all the way back
to before the first squeeze. This problem prompted
the "Lotus roll" concept of providing an alternative
drainage passage from the top roll.
The Lotus roll was invented and first installed in
Taiwan by Bouvet (1980). It comprises a roll with a
cast steel shell containing a number of radial drain-
age holes from the root of each groove, spaced at
regular intervals around the circumference. These
holes drain into axial channels running across the
width of the roll, out of contact with the cane being
milled, and discharging to the outside flanks of the
Lotus roll. Hardened plugs with small orifices are
inserted into the inlets of the radial drainage holes to
preclude large particles that might block the subse-
quent passages and to resist wear of the holes (main-
tain orifice profile).
The Lotus roll principle has been used success-
fully in a number of mills, including an application
for diffuser bagasse dewatering at Maidstone in
South Africa where final bagasse moisture was re-
duced by 2.0 to 2.5 percentage points while operat-
ing properly. The main problem is in keeping both
the radial and the axial passages clear of bagasse
particles. Once drainage is blocked, the rolls offer
no advantage. As a result, although they have been
tried in many factories and many countries, few are
in service.
5.3.7 Mill hydraulics and loadings
Early mills had all rolls mounted in fixed axes.
However, to gain the benefits of constant pressure, it
is necessary to allow at least one roll to "float". This
is usually the top roll. In order to apply the neces-
sary downward load, springs or weights operating
through levers have been used, but hydraulic loading
is now almost universal.
Most three- and four-roll mills have hydraulic
rams mounted in the headstocks or bearing caps, act-
ing vertically downwards onto the bearings of the top
roll (see Figure 5.6). The pressure on these rams is
provided by oil from a high-pressure pump. The oil
system needs to accommodate changes in volume as
the rams move with the float of the top roll. For this
purpose, an accumulator is generally incorporated.
The most common type is the Edwards gas-oil
accumulator, comprising a steel bottle enclosing a
synthetic rubber bladder inflated with an inert gas.
(nitrogen). The oil circuit is connected into the bot-
tle, filling the remaining void outside the bladder,
which expands or contracts to accommodate volume
changes.The accumulator should be located as close
as possible to the mill to minimize frictional flow
damping. This device operates at the full pressure
applied to the pistons of the mill hydraulics.
Other systems in use are designed to operate at
lower accumulator pressures. These systems there-
fore generally make use of different sized pistons
within the fluid circuits to amplify the final hydrau-
lic force:
In the dead weight system, a small diameter pis-
ton at the accumulator displaces oil that operates
on a large diameter piston at the mill.
In the air / oil system, the air operates on a large
diameter piston (or diaphragm) connected to a
small diameter piston pressurizing the oil that
operates on the large piston at the mill. (e.g. 0.6
MPa air pressure operating on a 400 rnm diame-
ter surface will produce a force of 75.4 kN. This
force on a 60 mm diameter piston will generate
26.7 MPa pressure in the oil circuit).
Typically, hydraulic systems operate at pressures
of 18 MPa up to 30 MPa. To overcome the separat-
ing forces generated by the mill pinions, the pinion
side hydraulic pressure should be maintained 0.9
to 2.0 MPa higher than the non-pinion side. (Some
mills use larger hydraulic pistons on the drive side to
counteract the pinion forces).
5.3.8 Mill bearings
For given performance, the total load required
from the hydraulics is proportional to the projected

8 Mill bearings
By far the majority of mill bearings are of hol-
low (ported) construction, either cast entirely of
bronze or comprising a steel housing with a bronze
lining.The bottom half of the top bearing is of solid
bronze. A typical alloy for mill bearings comprises
84 % copper, 10 % tin, 3 % lead and 3 % zinc, but
other alloys are also used.
Coolingwater is passed through the porting. The
water outlets areusually directedintoopen tun dish-
es where the temperaturecan be checked to warn of
any incipientproblems.
Various materials other than bronze have been
tried as bearing materials. White metal has a lower
coefficientof friction but a lower melting point and
lower mechanical strength. It is therefore more vul-
nerable to lubricant or cooling water failures or dirt
ingress.Plasticsand othernon-metallicmaterialshave
failed due to theirpoor heat conductingproperties.
Lubrication. The maximum permissible bear-
ing pressure for bronze bearings is usually 9.0 to
11.0MPa, dependingon the design and lubrication.
Because of this extremelyhigh pressureand the low
velocity, a lubricant with high viscosity yet good
flow characteristicsis required. Biturnastic-typeoils
and speciallyformulatedgreaseshave been success-
ful. "Extreme pressure" additivesare often incorpo-
rated, either in the standard formulation or added
specificallyto a bearing that is overheating.Certain
synthetic oils are able to cope with the duty, but are
high cost and an expensive option for this total loss
application.
Independentpositivedisplacementpumpsshould
be used for the lubricant supply to each bearing to
ensureproperdistribution.It should be introducedto

As the top roll floats, the top bearings have to
slide up and down in the headstocks. Because the
resultant of the forces on this roll is offset from
vertical, significantlateral forces are exerted on the
sliding faces in the headstocks. These are therefore
usually fitted with wear pads and should be lubri-
cated. The top bearing housings in some headstocks
areinclinedforward(towardsthefeed) to alignmore
directly with the expected resultant force.
Roller bearings.An alternativeto bronze bear-

Low friction;

No cooling water needed;

Tolerantof small misalignments;
Reduced roll length between centers (lower

Drive-side bearing landings must be larger than

High cost and not repairable.
5.3.9 Mill pinions
Thepinions used to drive the feed and discharge
rollsfrom the top roll need to be able to operate at a
relatively wide range of center distances, to accom-
modate differingroll sizesand settingsas well as ax-
ial misalignmentfrom the float of the top roll. This
presents unique problemsfor the pinion design and
conventionalinvolute tooth profiles and dimensions
are not appropriate. To meet the special require-
ments, the profile usually employed for mill pinions
is a compromise that has longer teeth with longer
addendum and dedendum, greater back clearance
and a more curved tooth face. As a consequence of
this compromise,transmissionefficiency is reduced
to 85% to 90 % (comparedto 96 % forpureinvolute
pinions under equivalent conditions).
With this profile, the tooth contact angle of pin-
ions operating at the optimum or "median" center
distance is approximately 25" from the circumfer-
ential tangent (i.e. 65" off radial). The contact angle
is less when closer in mesh and more when further
apart. This tooth contact angle generates a separat-
ing force that is related to the angleand is greaterfor
largerangles.
Most mill designs have all pinions on the drive
sideof the mill, but somehave doublepinions (extra
cost) or alternating, with one on the "tail" side in
order to balance the separationforces.
Some mills have been operated successfully
without any discharge roll pinion, the roll being
driven by the top roll via the bagasse. This practice
places excessive stresses on the top roll and is not
widely adopted.
As with mill bearings, the high pressures and
low rubbing velocitieson pinion teethrequire a high
viscosity lubricant. Lubrication is usually by oil
bath, often with the same lubricantused for the mill
bearings.
5.3.10 Trashplates and scrapers
The purpose of the trash plate (or "turnplate")
is to direct the cane from the feed opening (where
it has been compressed with somejuice extraction)
to the discharge opening for further compression
and extraction.To achieve this, it needs to intercept
the bagasse while still under some compressionand
transferit with theleastpossiblelossof compression
but minimum friction into the dischargeopening.
The trash plate settings (Section 5.7.6) are de-
signed to achieve this. At these settings, the bagasse
remains under considerablecompression, generating
both friction and wear and upward pressure against
the top roll. Indeed,the trash plate generally absorbs
approximately 20 % of the total hydraulic load ap-
plied to the top roll (Gomez and Echevern 2001).
Trash plate wearreflectsthe grooveprofileof the top
roll.
5.4 Two-roll mills
Trash plates may be cast in close-grained cast
iron, spheroidal graphite (SG) iron or equivalents,
semi-steel (cast iron plus scrap steel), cast steel or
stainless steel. The durability and cost tends to in-
crease in the orderlisted.With the precisionof mod-
em foundry technology, trashplates can be cast with
their teeth, saving significantmachiningcosts.
To prolong trash plate life, it is now common
practice to hard-face the upper surface of trash
plates (usuallywith a chrome carbide material). T
t is
important not to hard-face the area around roots of
the trash plate teeth, as this can machine off the tips
of the feed roll teeth and prevent good trash plate
seating along the flanks of the teeth .
The trash plates are mounted by bolts and spig-
ots on "dumbtumers". These are adjustable(by slid-
ing andlor rotating) to be able to pull the worn trash
plate into tightmesh with the front roll teeth.
Scrapes or "scraper plates" are used to peel
off the discharged bagasse from the top and dis-
charge rolls (see Figures 5.5 and 5.6). Scrapers are
not required to maintain any compression and are
therefore subject to lower forces than trash plates.
Consequently, lower grade materialscan be used for
their construction - usually cast iron or SG iron if
the scraperneeds a curvedprofile, or frommild steel
plate if not curved. Competentfoundries are able to
supply scrapers with cast teeth.

54.1 Stork-Werkspoordevelopment
To address the challenge of dewatering high-
-sture,high-temperaturediffuser bagasse, Stork-
-poor turned back to the simplicity and lower
mst of a two-roll mill (deBoer 1969).Further con-
sideration of the theoretical design requirements
led to the conclusion that a two-roil mili could of-
fer the same extraction and throughput capacity as
a three-roll mill. For this, the roll sizes of the two-
roll mill would need to be increased to the extent
that the combined mass (volume) of the two rolls is
nearly equal to that of the equivalent three-roll mill
(deBoer 1972). The two-roll mill would have con-
siderableadvantagesin simplicity,no trashplate and
power savings.
5.4.2 STG-FCB
Faced with the increasingcomplexity,power re-
quirements and cost of multi-roll mills, Australian
engineers also reverted to two-roll mills. The first
commercial design was at Ord River, using four
horizontally disposed two-roll mills, each fed by a
toothed feeder and linked by pressure chutes. This
proved somewhat problematic, particularly in rela-
tion to the applicationof imbibition (Batstoneet al.
2001). However, it promoted further development.
5.4.3 Bundaberg's high extraction
mill
Bundaberg Foundry Engineers built on the
theories of de Boer and SRI research into bagasse
"bridging" acrossthe roots of groovesand added the
concept of cocurrent, gravity-assisted drainage, to
developa new type of verticallyfed two-roll mill.
The principle of operation is fundamentallydif-
ferent from that of conventional milling in that the
milling takes place vertically and in the manner of
juice drainage.This is illustratedin Figure5.11. The
cane is fed vertically via a Donnelly chutebetween
two larger-than-usual diameter rolls. These rolls
have deep Messchaert-type grooves between every
tooth. In the extraction zone, the bagasse bridges
across these grooves and the extracted juice is ex-
pressed into the low-pressurezone in the grooves.
Shortly after through the maximum
compression area, specially designed nose plates
and scraper blades separate the bagasse and ex-
tractedjuice. Thejuice is removed cocurrentand led
away via the trays under each roll.
The recommended drive uses either hydraulic
motors or variable speed electric motors with high-
reduction epicyclic gears on each roll. In both op-
tions, the torque reaction is contained within the
mill itself by linking the torque arms of the two roll
drives.
Mill controlis achieved by varying the width of
the Donnelly-type feed chute to maintain a desired
torque on the mill drives: widening the chute in-
creasesthe compactionand torque, and vice versa.
This mill is reported to be able to provide
throughputs and extraction rates comparable with
multi-roll mills, while absorbing a total of about
1.4 (kW .h)/t, (equivalentto 9.5 (kW .h)/$). This

5.5 Mill drives
The effect of the reabsorption limiting device on
reabsorption is considered to be critical to the per-
formance. The forward extrusion of fiber through
the work opening still occurs as at the discharge of
conventional mills,but juiceis ableto drainfrom the
fiber into the grooves and be separated
by the reabsorption device.
As with Bundaberg's two-roll mill, it is claimed
that therolls can operateat up to 50% higherspeeds
due to theenhanced juice drainage.
Powerconsumptionis 20% to30% less thanfor
conventional mills. Capital and maintenance costs
are also significantly less, with fewer rolls and bear-
ings, no hydraulics and no trash plate.
5.5 drives
5.5.1 Mill drive power requirements
The power absorbed by a mill depends on many
factors.Among the most important are:
The crushing rate (power fiber throughput);
The mill speed(power speed torque);
The configuration (number, size and ar-
rangementof rolls);
The power lost in bearings, trash plate and pres-
sure feed chutefriction;
The mill feeding method;
The mill settings;
The hydraulicload on the toproll (power load
applied).
Given the above variability factors, the drive power
absorbed by most conventional mills operated to
their potential is of theorderof 8 to 12 for every
tonne of fiber processed per hour. Power for pres-
sure-fed is higher,for two-roll mills lower.
The first m
i
l
l is generally focused upon maxi-
mizing its extraction, sometimes for cane payment
reasons but mainly becausehighfirst mill extraction
is essential to good overall mill performance. The
final mill is alsoimportantas the"last gateway"and
is required to minimize bagasse losses and
tures. For these reasons, power for these mills usu-
ally tends towards the upper end (10-13 h)/

.
Note that all the above power absorbed values
are as measuredat the primemover (engine,turbine,
motor). Strain gauge measurements have shown
that, formost mills, close to 20 % of thedrive power
is dissipated in the reduction gearing.A further 5 to
8% of power can be lost in muff-type mill cou-
plings. The true absorbed power at the mill is thus
75-80 % of the above figures. With high efficiency
drives, such as high-reduction epicyclic gears, the
input power would be less.

Reciprocating steam engine drives. Most of
theearly mechanical mill drives were by singlecyl-
inder horizontal steam engines. these op-

pressures of between 700 and exhausting
at 200 They rotate at lowspeed (50-100
arefitted with largeflywheels and drive oneor more
mills via singleor double reduction spur gearing.
Internal steam leakage, mechanical friction,etc.
account for about 10-15 % power loss. The overall
energyefficiency of such enginesis generally a little

5 Milling
High-speed vertical steam engines are better
suitedto higherpowers. They aremore compact and
more efficientthan horizontal engines. In sugar ap-
plications, most are of the double acting twin cylin-
der type and run at 300 to 500min-'. They may use
simple or compound (above 1000 kPa) expansion.
They usually operate with higher pressure (1100
to 1700 kPa) superheated steam. Temperatures are
limited to about 260 "C because of lubrication and
mechanicaldistortionconstraints.This in turn limits
the overall efficiency of the engine. Nevertheless,
the efficiency of these engines is generally higher
than that of single stage turbines for powers up to
about500 kW.
Threeimportantdisadvantages of steam engines
relative to turbines for mill drives are:
Engineshave poor low-speedtorquecharacteris-
tics (startinga loaded mill);
Engines discharge oil into the exhaust range,
presenting various downstream problems (foul-
ing process and boiler heat transfer surfaces,
blocking steam traps, etc.);
Maintenance of engines is generally more de-
manding.
Steam turbine drives. Since their adventin the
1940s, steam turbines have been widely used for
mill drives.They are reliable and are easily adapted
to automatic speed control. They can be supplied
with auxiliary hand nozzles to be able to vary the
outputpower and efficiency -a useful feature when
planning for futureexpansions.
They have excellentlow-speed torquecharacter-
istics, generating starting/ stalling torques of up to
180% of full load torque. This needs to be allowed
for in the strength of gearing,mill couplingsand the
millitself.
For the typical powers of between 200 kW and
800 kW, most users select low cost single or two-
stage impulse type turbines. These are generally of
low overallefficiency -between 33 % and 47 % at
full load,dependingon steam conditionsand turbine
design. The no-load steam consumption for these
turbines is usually 12% to 20 % of full load, so ac-
tual efficiencies at operating powers are somewhat
lower than the full load efficiency figures quoted
by the suppliers. The turbines also usually operate
at well below their maximum (optimum efficiency)
speed.Actual efficienciesatoperatingconditionsare
therefore often only 20 % to 35 %. Failureto recog-
nize this often results in erroneous estimates of the
steam demand, with serious errors for the planned
mill steam balance.
In some factories where energy efficiency is a
consideration,higher efficiencymulti-stage turbines
areused. Thesemay have full load efficienciesof up
to 70-75 %. However, they are considerably more
costlyand have to competewith variable speedelec-
trical drives.
Mill driveturbines normally operateat speedsof
4 000to 7000m i d . High speedgearingistherefore
required, with a large overall speed reduction from
turbineto d.
Electrical drives. There is a greater variety of
electrical mill drives than of any of the other cat-
egories. Gradener (1964) detailed the comparative
features of nine types then available:
- AC slipring motor,
- AC squirrelcage motor with torque converter,
- AC commutator motor with series characteris-
tics,
- AC commutator motor with shunt characteris-
tics,
- DC system with mercury arc rectifiers,
- DC system with silicon rectifiers,
- AC-DC cascadesystem,
- AC-DC-AC cascadesystem,
- DC Ward Leonard system.
However,therehas been vast developmentin electri-
cal drives sincethen and none of the above would be
recommended for a new installation.
The preferred electrical drive is now the stan-
dard AC squirrel cage induction motor, supplied
from an appropriate electronic variable frequency
and voltage source.Totally enclosedmotors arepre-
ferred becauseof the dusty and humid mill environ-
ment. An auxiliary cooling fan is required because
of the need for adequatecoolingair flow at low mo-
tor speeds. Motorsmay haveto be slightlyoversized
because of the derating needed to accommodate the
additional heating caused by variable-frequency
supplies. Shoa duration torque overloads of about
140% of the motor rating can be accommodated by
the motors and the drive, for up to 60 seconds,even
at zero speed.
The variable frequency drives now available
generatean internalmodel of the motor to whichthe
drive is connected, enabling the drive to determine
the motor speed and torque at all times. Speed con-

trol with variation less than 0.5 % of the set speed is
attainablewithout a tachometerfeedbacksignal.
Because medium voltage variable frequency
drives are much more expensive than low volt-
age units, low voltage drives and motors are gen-
erally chosen. For drive powers of say 600 to 900
kW, 690V drives and motors are available, with a
substantial saving in cabling and 1or busbar costs.
However, the cost of medium voltage drives is re-
ducing with time, and coupled with the saving in
transformer cost, these may becomemore attractive
in future.
The main advantages of modern variable speed
electricaldrives for mills are:
Energy efficient (overall about 80 % with con-
ventional gearing, 90 % with epicyclic gear-
ing);
Easily controlled;
Low maintenance;
Torquecan be limited to protect gearing or allow
efficientepicyclicdrives;
Clean and cool -no steam pipes, etc.;
Well suited to use with compact (small foot-
print), energy-efficient epicyclicgearing;
Can be used cost-effectively for driving each
roll or a pressure feeder independently (no mill
pinions) i d in this application may be flange-
mounted directly onto the roll.
Disadvantages are:
Require larger power stationmachines (turboal-
ternators);
May need additionaltraining for electrical staff
unfamiliar with the electronics.
Hydraulicdrives.The developmentof efficient
high-torque, low-speed hydraulic drives has provid-
ed a furtheroption for mills.The drivescomprisean
electric motor driven hydraulic pump that provides
the driving fluid for ahydraulicmotor. The hydrau-
lic motor has radial pistons operating in a rotating
cylinder block mounted in bearings in a stationary
housing. Torque is provided by the action of the pis-
tons against a cam ring attached to the housing.
Speed is controlled by varying the flow of fluid
to the motor. This can be achieved by a variable
speed drive for the hydraulic pump, but is usually
by using a pump with a variable angle swashplate.
In the latteroption,overloadsare preventedby auto-
matically de-stroking thepump at a preset maximum
oil pressure.
Many hydraulic drives operate through con-
ventional final mill gears (indirectdrive). However,
modern hydraulic motors can operateat mill roll ro-
tational speeds and these may be direct coupled or
torqueam mounted on the mill roll shaft. They are
particularly well suited to driving individual rolls
or sets of rolls (e.g, pressure feeders) on multi-roll
mills. In such applications, the relative speeds of
the various drives on one mill need to be well con-
trolled. This control can be by speed (oil flow rate)
or by torque (oil pressure).
The drives are now well proven, with some 80
in Australia alone. Operation of well-engineered in-
stallationshas proven to be reliable,provided that:
The hydraulic oil is maintained in absolutely
clean condition;
Filters and oilsealsare regularly replaced;
The system is normally operated at not more
than 70 % of the allowable maximum hydraulic
pressure (e.g. at 24 MF'afor a 35 MF'a system).
Component wear does occur and the life of the
pumps and motors is not unlimited. Failures occur
most commonlydue to dirt in oil.
Vermaak (2001) has assessed the initial capital
costs as comparable with steam turbines or electric
motors with their associated gearing, tail bars and
couplings. Annual maintenance costs are higher
than forelectricbut lower than turbinedrives.
At full speed and in new condition, the overall
efficiency of hydraulic drives (from electric motor
to m
i
l
l roll) is high (80-85 %), but oil leakage at
low speeds and leakagefrom worn components can
reduce this considerably.
Advantagesof modem hydraulicdrivesfor mills

No speed reduction gearingis needed;
By using as individual roll drives, torque input
to top roll is limited;
Thispermits construction of larger, more power-
ful mills;
When shaft-mounted, tail bars, couplings and

Reduced cost of foundationsfor mill drives;
Reversible directionof rotation;
Easy torque and speed control possible;
Energy efficiency is good compared to many
other types of mill drive;
Can be used to provide additional power to a

5.5.3 Mill gearing
All prime movers except some hydraulic drives
operate at higher speeds than the mill rolls and
thereforerequire speedreduction gearing before the
final drive. Conventional large gearing is limited to
a reduction of about 8:l for a single stage. In most
cases, a combination of high- and low-speed gears
is needed.
High-speed gearing usually comprisesprecision
helical, double helical or parallel (spur) gears, nor-
mally with hardened teeth. These gears are usually
encased in sealed boxes with either splash or pres-
sure-fed lubrication. The relative action between
gear surfacesis a combinationof arolling and a slid-
ing motion.The contact areas are small and lubrica-
tion is thereforeessential.The grade and method of
application of the lubricant will depend on the gear
design and duty.
The final speed reduction normally comprises a
pinion driving a large "bull" gear. These are usually
parallel spurgears. High viscosity oil or light grease
is the usual lubricant for these gears.
Bearings supporting the low-speed gear shafts
used to be almost exclusively of the white metal
type, but modem designs increasinglyuse anti-fric-
tion (roller) bearings because of their lower mainte-
nance requirements.
In recentyears,high-reductionepicyclicand dif-
ferential planetary gears have been used for many
mill drives. These are high-precision boxes with
higher transmission efficiencies than conventional
gears (92 to 97 % vs. 80 %). They are also much
more compact. They do require diligent mainte-
nance, ideally including regular oil condition analy-
sis and vibrationmonitoring.
Figure 5.13 shows a modern compact, clean,
high-efficiencylow maintenancemill drive at Kom-
ati in South Africa. This drive comprises a variable
frequency electric motor, a high reduction Zollern
Dorstener planetary input with power-sharing he-
lical final gears and a Eurogear wire rope flexible
coupling (see Section 5.5.4). The transmission effi-
ciency (power input to top roll / power output from
prime mover) of this drive is 96 % (gearing) X 96 %
(coupling)= 92 %. This compares with about 72 %
for traditional gearing (80 %) and muff couplings
(90 %). The 630kW motor can thus deliver580kW
at the mill, which would have required a motor of
> 800kW with conventionalgearing.
The overall energy efficiency of this drive -
power station turboalternator(75 %), variable speed
electric motor (97 %) and transmission (92 %) - is
approximately67 %. This is three times better than
the 22 % of a single stageturbine (30 %) with tradi-
tionaltransmission (72 %). The benefits for factories
with cogeneration or bagasse by-product plants are
thereforeobvious.

5.5.4 Mill couplings and tail bars
5.5.4 Mill couplings and tail bars
Themillgearsareusuallymounted on fixed-axis
shafts to maintain accurate teeth alignment. As dis-
cussed in Section 5.7.2, the finalgearsdrive mill top
rolls that are designed to operate normally at about
10mm above their "at rest" position and to be able
to floatvertically upwardsby a further 15rnm under
abnormal conditions.This presents an inherent mis-
alignment problem.
To copewith this, the final connection between
the mill gearing and top roll is traditionally by
means of a 1.5m to 3.0 m long square-section"tail
bar", connected at each end by a loose-fitting muff
coupling as shown in Figure5.14. The couplingsare
usually of steel or of cast iron with steel hoops, and
the tail bars of ductile mild steel.The longer the tail
bar, the less the angular misalignment. However,
even with long tail bars, substantialseparatingforc-
es are generated by the contact angles between cou-
pling and tail bar. From the figures of Tosio (1992),
axialthrusts of the orderof 150kN can be generated
at 950 kN .m torque with 10mm misalignment of
a 2.0 m long tail bar. Other more complex tail bars
with concave-convex cross sections are sometimes
used, but sufferthe same problem.
The misalignment forces cause axial wear on
mill bearing fillets and wear of the couplings and
tail bars (seizure sometimes occurs). They also im-
pose reactions on the final mill gearing.In cases of
extreme misalignment, the couplingclearancescan-
not prevent bending forces on the top roll and final
gear shaft. Lubrication of the couplings
andlor wear pads can alleviate but not
eliminatethe wear damage.

costly connection from gearing to top

Multi-misalignment couplings. In 1987 a
radically novel type of sugar mill coupling was
introduced at the Umfolozi sugar factory in South
Africa by Eurogear (Tosio 1992). The principle of
operation is based on applying torquethrough steel-
wire ropes in tension between the arms of matching
yokes mounted on the gear shaft and the roll. These
Figure5.15: Eurogearlink mill coupling
5 Milling
flexible elements form balanced couples in a plane
normal to the couplingaxis. Thiseliminatesin a sin-
gle coupling the large bending moments and thrust-
generation that normally results from the axial and
radial misalignmentbetween gears and top roll.
These couplings have given excellent perfor-
mance, with low maintenance where primary gear-
to-mill alignment is good. However, where exces-
sive misalignment (greater than 25 rnrn) has to be
absorbed continuously, the life of the steel-wire
ropes is limited. To overcome this, the suppliers
have developed an alternative design utilizing end-
less polyester slings in place of the steel-wire ropes
(Figure 5.16). This design is constructed in such a
way that the slings do not have to flex in absorb-
ing misalignment, only twist slightly. Initial results
with this design are highly promising and it is now
preferred to the steel-wire type.The use of this cou-
pling is particularly advantageous when the space
between the gearbox and mill is limited.
Both link couplings and polyester sling cou-
plings provide major advantages over traditional
muff couplings in that they suffer negligible wear,
need little maintenance,transmit almostpure torque
with negligible axial and radial forces and absorb
very little transmissionpower.
Cane preparation
Themechanicsof canepreparationhave been re-
viewed in Chapter 4. Cane preparation has a strong
relationship with milling performance.
Sucrosein whole caneis containedasjuice with-
in thin-walled cells protected by the fibrousstructure
of the stalk. Extraction of this sucrose by milling
consists almost entirely of rupturing the cells and
then removing thejuice first by physically express-
ing it and then by diluting the remaining juice and
expressingthat.
The first part of this process -cell rupture- can
be performed by millpressurebursting cells or by at-
trition between roll surfaces traveling at differential
speeds. However,even mills specificallydesignedto
rupture cells, such as the Krajewski crusher, are ex-
tremely inefficient performers of this function. The
most efficientmanner toprepare cane for millingex-
traction is by first cutting the cane into short pieces
(ideally done by knives) and thereafter shredding it
very finely so that virtually all cells arebroken open.
Modem heavy-duty shredders operated well can
rupture over 90 % of the cells.
Such preparation enables mills to perform their
juice extraction function far more easily and much
more efficiently. It does so because:
Thejuice is made availablefor easy expression;
The cane density is increased and it is more ho-
mogenous, assisting feeding and throughput;
Lower mill feed / discharge ratios can be used,
reducing mill power requirement;
Reabsorptionis reduced by easier drainage.
ExperienceinBrazilindicatesthat,foran unchanged
throughput, the addition of a heavy-duty shredder
ahead of a milling train reduces the power absorbed
by the mills by an amountequivalentto the addition-
al power absorbed by the shredder,while extraction
is significantly increased. Moor (1974) described
the marked increases in both throughput and extrac-
tion on a milling tandem when a heavy-duty shred-
der replaced a light shredder.Throughput increased
by 7 %. Together with this, extraction improved by
an amount that, inserted into the formula of Hugot
(1986), was equivalentto:

5.7 Mill settings
It is necessary to ensure that the mills are set
up for optimal performance. The first key issue to
appreciate from the theory of milling is that "mill
setting" does not merely encompass the positioning
of the feed (front), top and discharge(back) rolls in
the appropriatepositions.Thereis an optimumcom-
paction ratio for the openings at each stage of the
passage of bagasse through the process, including
whichever of the followingare installed:
Donnelly chute to pressure feeder;
Pressure feeder to mill feed;
Donnelly chuteto underfeed roll;
Underfeed to mill feed;
Mill feed to trash plate centerheight;
Millfeed to discharge.
5.7.1 Mill roll settings
Settingup a milling tandem for a given through-
put usually starts with deciding the desired work
openings between the final three rolls of each mill,
i.e. that between top and dischargeldeliveryroll (the
discharge opening) and that between the top and
feed roll (thefeed opening).
Many different methods are used around the
sugar world, but virtually all effectively calculate
settings (openings)between rolls to givean escribed
volume sufficientto pass the required rate of fiber
at the desired compaction.This principle is applied
using densities and/ or ratios that havebeen empiri-
cally validated.
Various methods of calculating mill settings
have been reviewed by Upadhiaya (1988) and
Wienese(1990). Upadhiaya (1988) coversSouthAf-
rican (Natal),Australian,Farrel and Mauritiusmeth-
ods. Hugot (1986:201-213) details the Java method,
including values used for this method in Australia,
Louisiana and Cuba.The Brazil method is based on
the South African system with only a minor differ-
ence in the constant used and somewhat different
bagasse fiber contents.
Two widely used methods are discussed below:
the Australian"fiber fill" method and the SouthAf-
rican method (vanHengelandDowesDekker 1958).
Both are based on work openings being set in pro-
portion to the fiber throughput rate, but have been
selected to illustrate differentapproachesto this ob-
jective.

ber fills(massof fiberper unit area of roll surface)at

5.7.2 Adjustmentfor top roll float
Themill ratioR is mainly dependenton the posi-
tion and typeof mill.As with theAustralianmethod,
forpressure-fed mills,theratio isusually in the range
1.6to 2.0, whilefor simple three-roll mills, the ratio
may be in the range 1.8 to 2.8. For similar mills, the
ratios will usually reduce along the tandem from the
first (largestR) to the final mill (smallestR).
5.7.2 Adjustmentfor top roll float
The discharge and feed work openings calcu-
lated above are the actual openings required or ex-
pected in operation.Under these conditions, the top
roll should be lifted by the bagasse and "floating"
above its no-load position, being loaded downward
by theforcesof its own weight (a minor contributor)
and the mill hydraulics. TOallow for this, the rolls
in the empty mill must be set closer than the desired
work openings.
Theconfigurationof most three-roll millsis such
that the centers of both the feed and discharge rolls
are offset from the center of the top roll by an angle
of about 35" from the vertical. From this geometry,
the feed and discharge openings change by about
80 % of the vertical lift of the top roll. Thus, if the
setting calculations have assumed that the top roll
will lift 8 m
r
n above its no-load position, the feed
anddischargeopeningsshould be setat0.8 8 mm =
6.4 mm less than the calculatedwork openings.
It is strongly recommended that the mill rolls
and trash plate be drawn out in their empty and in
their full-scale working positions. Gibbon (1994)
has describedhow this can be done using a comput-
er-aided design and drafting package. His method
allowed for roll wear and established roll and trash
plate positions, trash plate profile,packers and an-
gles for setting up the mill,
However, this system requires fairly sophisti-
cated programming and most engineers still prefer
to perform this function manually on a "settings
board". This should be made up with moveable
pivot pins and trammels configured to represent the
centers of the three principal rolls of the mill. The
roll positions, settings and trash plate profile for
each mill can then be drawn on a sheet of paper and
retained. This enables the engineer to visualize the
working zone of the mill at full scale. The drawing
also produces a template for machining and check-
ing the trash plate profile.
Templates of mill pinions can also be rotated on
the pivot pins to ensure satisfactory meshing (con-
tinuous contact, sufficient engagement depth, no
bottoming,no reverse contact).
5.7.3 Pressurefeeder settings
With pressure feeders, the work opening is usu-
ally found to be optimized witli a compactionratio
(orfiberdensity)3.0to 3.5 timesthat atthedischarge
opening (Australian method). In the South African
method, this is equivalent to an opening ratio of 3.0
to 3.5 times the dischargework opening,afterallow-
ing for any differencesin roll peripheralspeeds.
5.7.4 Underfeedroll settings
With four-roll mills or mills with an underfeed
roll feeding either a pressure feeder or a mill, the
work opening between the underfeed and its oppos-
ing rollis usually such as togiveacompactionof the
order of 4 to 6 times less than that at the discharge
opening. The ratios decrease from the first mill to
the final mill.
5.7.5 Chuteopenings
Bagasseslipon the rolls at feed into the mill im-
pairs feeding and causes undue roll surfacewear. To
achieve maximum throughput without slip,equation
(5.12)in Section5.2.4 indicatesthat the width of the
feed into the mill should be half the sum of the feed
and top roll diameters plus the feed opening. Thus
the chute base width b is given by:
6 =h, +0.5. (d, 12+d,, 12) (5.36)
However, the assumption of no slip is unrealistic. In
practice,the best results can usually be expectedfrom
a chutewidth about 10% to 15% narrowerthan this.
Another method of setting chute width assumes
a ratio of the discharge work opening, h,. The opti-
mum for this ratio is usually of the order of 10to 12
times &for the first mill of a tandem, decreasing to
8 times h, for the final mill. In the absence of slip,
this implies a fiberdensityin the chuteof 1/12to 118
of the dischargefiber density.

5 Milling
Yet another method - or check against the set-
ting from the ratio method -is by the angle of nip,
defined as the angle, measured at the center of the
roll concerned,between the first contactpoint of the
feed and the line to the center of the opposite feed
roll (a
in Figure 5.1).The maximum angle of nip is
usually approximately50-55O, but should be less if
the roll surfaces are not rough.
It is important that the chute is positioned to
feed with equal "angles of nip" to both rolls. This
implies that the chute should be aligned centrally to
the gap betweenequal-sizedrolls, but offsettowards
the larger roll if they are of unequal diameters. The
chute may be set back slightly from this ideal feed-
ing position to facilitatejuice drainage away from
the top roll.
5.7.6 Trash plate settings
es. The profile and positioning of the trash plate is
thereforeextremelyimportant.
Whatever method is used to determine the trash
plate settings, it is strongly recommended that a
"settings board" (Section5.7.2) be used to draw and
visualize the trash plate in relation to the mill rolls.
The trash plate upper surface height may be set
by variousmeans,but most commonly by one of two
criteria:
1. The desired fiber fill over the center of the trash
plate (usually 55 % to 60 % of that at the feed
opening),or:
2. Setting the nose or "toe" (front top of the trash
plate profile) of the trash plate at the intersection
of a line drawn at angle 9 (usually 13' to 14")
from the centers of feed and top rolls and the
feed roll mid-diameter(i.e. half groovedepth).
Whichever method is used, the top of the trash plate
is then drawn with a radius r, equal to the distance
from the nose of the trash to the center of the
top roll. However,the fulcrum of thisradiusis offset
to provide a "sweep" that diverges by 4 % to 5 %
over the length of the trash plate. For example, if
the trash plate surface is 400 mrn long, the distance
of the trash plate surface below the top roll should
increase by 4.5 % of 400 = 18 rnrn from the nose
to the back end of the trash plate (Figure 5.17). The
nose profile is rounded "by eye" to provide strength
to the tips of the trash plate teeth.

5 Milling
Fiber exiting with the juice from each mill is
determined by the "separation efficiency" of the
mill, defined as the ratio of fiber in
into mill. For theseparationefficiencies,the average
valueof 0.895found by Wienese(1994)is used-see
Section5.8.2.
Distribution of imbibition. It is important that
theimbibitionisapplied asevenlyacrossthebagasse
flow as possible. Imbibition water can be distributed
by sprays, but these will block if solids are present.
Various fan and weir-type spreadersare available to
distributethe fiber-containingjuice from mills.
It is also important to distribute the liquid
through thedepth of the bagassebed. Somesystems
attempt to inject the imbibition into the bagasse as
it expands out of the mill discharge. Most apply the
imbibition before or after it tumbles from the dis-
charge scraper, hoping for some mixing of dry and
bagasse. Imbibition juiceis sometimesadded
directly into the mill feed chute, but this minimizes
the time available for mixing.
Whateverapplicationsystem is used, mixing is
incomplete and there is a nonuniform distribution
of dissolved solids in the juicecontained in thefeed
to the next mill. The more dilute imbibition juice,
having been added to the surface, is more easily
extracted than that which was already imbedded in
the cane. As a result, the Brix of juice extracted by
a mill is generally lower than the Brix of residual
freejuice remainingin the bagasseleavingthe mill,
although the Brix-free water in bagasse lowers the
analyzed total Brix in bagasse. This gives rise to
the concept of imbibition efficiency, which is de-
fined as extracted juice juice Brix.
For the reasons above,theimbibitionefficiencywill
normally be 100 However, with no imbibition
beforethefirstmill, theBrix of juice extracted from
this unit will be higher than that remaining in the
bagasse (due to the Brix-free water), giving an im-
bibitionefficiency 100 %. As an example,inTable
5.6 the first mill imbibition efficiency is 103.8 %,
the Brix of extracted juice is 19.5 % compared to
in cane, but if the Brix-free water is consid-
ered to bepart of fiber,the respectiveBrix valuesof
thefree juice are 19.8 % and 19.7 respectively.
and (1967) introduced an imbibi-
tion coefficient todescribethenon-idealmixing,
defined as the extraction achieved in a milling unit
as a of the extraction that would have been
achievedif thejuice in the bagassefeed to the
(bagasse and imbibition liquid)was uniformlymixed.
Study and characterization of imbibition coef-
ficients has proved difficult,even on the University
of Queensland's experimental mill. Practical values
were found to vary from about 1.05 in the first
reducingsteadily along the mill tandem to about 0.5
in the last mill. In the balance shown in Table 5.6,
the figures vary from 1.04 to 0.63.The main factors
influencing imbibitioncoefficientsappear to be (van
der et al.
Imbibitionlevel- higherimbibition,lowercoef-

cient;
Imbibition temperature - higher temperature,

Imbibition temperature. The best temperature
for imbibition water has been widely debated, without
reaching a unanimous conclusion. Advocates of cold
imbibition(ambientup to50 claim better feed-
ing.Certainwaxesincanemeltatabout60 andmake
the bagasseslippery. However, modem roll roughening
techniques able to overcomethisproblem.
Honig (1953) stated that "Hot imbibition has
definite advantagesin theefficiency of sugarextrac-
tion in themills".Probably mostengineerssubscribe
to this view, butthe improvementfrom hot 50
water is generally too small to be clearly measur-
able. However Honig also reported that experiments
in Java showed imbibition water at 85 to 95 did
not extractany more wax than water at 28 "C. Defi-
nite benefits (when sweet water is used) are the bet-
ter quality of the water (virtually zero impurities),
improved factory thermal efficiency and reduced
effluent temperature.
Imbibition pumping. Some installations use
perforatedbasecush cush conveyorstoremove fiber
from imbibition before pumping to next stage.
However,a simplersolutionis to usechokeless open
impeller pumps for this duty. These may be of the
inefficient but reliableinduced vortex type. Imbibi-
tion pumps usually run under "snore" conditions,
drawing in air with the liquid to prevent fiber ag-
glomeration by maintaining a low level in the suc-
tion tank.

Maceration is a of imbibition
that has been defined by (Anon. 1955:15) as
"the process in which the bagasse is steeped in an
excess of water or juice, generally at high tempera-
ture."This temperature is typically about 75-80'€.
In some industries, term macerationis incorrect-
ly used instead of imbibition.
An advance in the effective application of lim-
ited quantities of imbibition is the use of "mac-
eration carriers". The concept originated with the
Nobel maceration carrier in Java. Australia and Fiji
in particular have used these to good effect (Kerr
1954, 1970).
They comprise long, slow-traveling drag-type
in which some recycling is used to
providea flooded bath section in which the bagasse
is totally immersed and saturated.The liquid in the
bath is usually heated to a temperature of about
80 to make unbroken cell walls permeable and
promote sucrose extraction. The bagasse retention
time in the carrier is up to10 minutes.

5.9.1 surface preparation
5.9.1 Roll surfacepreparation
Mill roll surface roughnessis a critical factor in
achieving good feeding, minimizing slip and mini-
mizing reabsorption.
The traditional material specification for mill
rolls was "an open-grained cast iron", which re-
tained an inherently rough surface that assisted in
mill feeding.Subsequently,various surface welding
techniques have been developed and closer-grained,
tougher,more"weldable"materialsare preferred for
mill roll shells.
The first significant advance occurred with the
use of "carbon-arcing".This uses thick carbonelec-
trodes connected to a direct-current welding ma-
chineto"arc"onto the roll surface, thereby forming
hard ferro-carbide blisters.The blisterssurvivefor a
while, but eventually break away taking with them
small parts of the roll surface, thereby eroding the
tooth profile and increasing the rateof roll wear.
A much better technique has been the develop-
ment of high-chromium"arcingrods".Weldingwith
theserods depositsan austeniticmatrix of chromium
carbides on the roll. This has good roughness and
high wear- and impact-resistance, with a
C hardness of about 58. The chromium also resists
corrosion. This technique therefore maintains the
grooving profile and prolongsmill roll life.
Further advances have evolved techniques for
depositingeven harder, more durablematerialssuch
as tungsten carbide chips. A system widely used in
Southand CentralAmerica is theelaborate"pico"(=
beak or bill) system. Hard welding is applied along
the top of the teeth only, leavingsmooth flanks. The
welding is usually applied along about 25-50 mm
of the tooth top, with the leading edge built up to
6-10 above the tooth, the height tapering down
towards the back of the pico. The next starts
after a short gap (10-20 rnrn). The leading edge is
often built into a distinct hook. These are generally
expensive practices, but users justify their cost by
extended roll life and improved mill performance.
5.9.2 Chevrons
Chevronsarenotchescutinto thetopof mill roll
teeth to assist feeding the bagasse through the mill.
They are equally disposed around the periphery of
the roll, usually about 200 to 300 mm apart.
They are generally used on the feed roll and can
also be used on the top roll, but there is no point in
using them on the dischargeroll, where the bagasse
is effectively"pressuref e d from the feed roll.
The chevron is in the shape of an unequal vee,
with a radial (or even forward-hooked)face driving
the bagasse.They are usually cut to about one-third
of the tooth depthand about three times longer than
their depth. To avoid snaggingon the trash plateor
scraper, the chevrons are staggered in a single or
double helical pattern across the width of the roll,
inclinedat about10"from the roll axis.
With modern fine cane preparation and good
roller roughening, these large chevrons are of
doubtful value. An alternative that is as effective
withoutthelargelow-compressionarea and rollma-
terial wastage of chevrons, is to cut notches about
8 mm wide and 20 mm deep transversely across the
roll surface. They are cut in a similar helical pat-
tern to that used for chevrons, but closer together
-at150 to 200 mm apart. Donnelly (1961) rec-
ommended notches at 50 pitch around the roll
periphery, but this seems an excessivenumber with
modern roughening techniques.The notches can be
machined or manually cut with an anglegrinder.
5.9.3 Pusher feeders
"Pushers7' are mechanical devices designed to
force-feed bagasse into a mill. They are driven by
an eccentric and have a reciprocating action. Be-
cause of this, they introduce discontinuity into an
otherwise continuous process. They tend to have
high maintenancerequirements. Some pushers are
still in service, but, because of their obvious defi-
ciencies, the system has been largely abandoned in
favor of Donnelly chutes and continuous pressure
feeders.
5.9.4 Donnelly chutes

5.9.5 Pressure feeders
CSR in Australia developed the first continuous
pressure feeders during the 1930s.Thesecomprised
two smaller but conventionallygrooved rolls, posi-
tioned ahead of thenormal feed point into the open-
ing between the front and top rolls of a three-roll
mill. The discharge from the pressure feeder rolls
was peeled off while still under some compression,
by scraper-ornose-platesformingtheinlet of a short
divergingpressure chute.Thischute fed thepartially
compressed bagasse into the mill feed.
The pressure feeder rolls were driven from the
main mill drive by supplementary gears, at a higher
rotational speed so as to give a peripheral speed ap-
proximately equal to that of the mill rolls.
The device provided some juice extraction at
its roIls, improved extraction and moisture from the
fed mill (due to a denser feed and reduced drainage
requirement) and enabled higher throughputs. The
main problems lay in maintenance, with frequent
chute failures from various
causes such as:
Incorrect pressure feed-
er/mi~
openingratios;
I
Pressure feeder roll condi-
tion too rough in relation to
mill rolls;
Nose-plates not tightly
seated into pressure feeder
rollsor not well matched to
roll profile;
Inadequate chute mount-
ings or chute strength.
These remain problem areas,
although great progress has
been made by way of more ro-
bust designs, condition moni-
toring, alarms and automated
controls.
In later pressure feeder de-
the mill rolls, with the rolI speed accordingly lower.
Since the early 1980s, most pressure feeders sup-
plied have been independently driven by hydraulic
or variable speed electric drives. This enables the
pressure feeder speed to be controlled so as to limit
the torque on its rolls andlor to limit the pressure
generated in the chute. Various devices have been
developed to measure the pressure between or the
deflection of the pressure feeder chuteplates. These
can be used to control the pressure feeder speed but
are more commonly used only as alarm devices.
Direct torque measurements by strain gauges
fitted to tailbars or mill drives have also been used
to control either the speed of the pressure feeder or
to control the cane feed into the pressure feeder by
throttling the outlet of the cane feed chute into the
pressure feeder (Jacklinand Jenkins 1981, Paddock
and Farrell 1987).
Because it is designed to feed into the mouth
of a three-roll mill, the pressure feeder is usually
mounted with its axis at an angleof about 40' from
the horizontal. The usual feed mode is by a steep
Dopnelly chute. As with three-roll mills, this pres-
ents a problem with the feed angleand an additional
underfeed or "third'' roll is often used to turn the
feed. Figure 5.23 shows a typical configuration of

The power absorbed by a pressure feeder de-
pends on many factors, particularly setting ratios
and mill and pressure feeder roll surfaceconditions.
If anything is mechanically amiss (e.g. nose-plate
angle or adjustment, chute divergence), power ab-
sorbed can escalate dramatically. Wienese (1987)

South African mills of between 25 % and 40 % of
the combinedpower of the pressurefeeder plus mill.
These accord with the expected values quoted by
Walkersfor pressure feedersin normal good opera-
tion.
5.9.6 Toothedpressurefeeders
Toothedor"spikey" feedersarea variation of the
original pressure feeder concept - also introduced
by CSR, in the 1960s.The design was subsequently
licensed to Polymex and Fletcher Smith.The essen-
tial difference of the toothed pressure feeder lies in
the roll design.
b
Figure 5.24: Fletcher S
m
i
t
h - Polymex toothed pressure
feeder
In principle, the toothed feeder rolls are in the
formof smoothcylinders acrossthe length of which
are interspersed a series of circumferential rings
from which protrude large (about 80 mm tall) trian-
gular teeth or "spikes". (Alternatively,construction
can be by toothed discs and spacers). The sets of
rings are disposed alternately on the two rolls so
that they mesh between each other. The teeth on
each roll are staggered across the width of the roll
so that they do not all engage simultaneously (Fig-
ure 5.24).
The main advantages of this design over the
grooved roll design are:
The teeth provide a positive feed, so that roll
rougheningand tall feed chutes are not required
(the teeth are hard-faced for durability, not
"grip").
The pressure chute nose-plates engage tightly
against the smooth surface between rings of
teeth with gaps to allow the teeth to pass, thus
minimizing friction (power absorbed)and nose-
plate wear. Chute plate adjustment is less fre-
quent than with grooved pressure feeders.
They are reputed to require approximately 10%
less power than conventional pressure feeders
for the same performance.
The main disadvantageof the design is that it lacks
the juice drainage paths provided by conventional
roll grooving.
Mill capacity is a subjective parameter. With
largesettingsandor high speeds,higherthroughputs
are possible, but at lower extractions. Extraction in
turn is affected by many other factors-preparation,
imbibition, mill condition, etc. What is an accept-
ablelevelof extractionwill depend on many circum-
stances, such as:
Cost and affordabilityof additionalequipment;
Lengthof season-long seasonsprovidea great-
er return on the same investment;
Cane payment arrangements and sugar prices,
which determine the financial returns from ad-
ditional sugar.
The discussion on capacity should therefore be
read within the context of the particular mill con-
cerned.

following discussion assumes this type of arrange-

Within limits, the fiber throughput of a mill for
given settings is proportional to the mill speed. Pro-
vided the fiber content of cane is reasonably consis-
tent, the throughput of a milling tandem can there-
fore be controlledby:
Setting the speed of the first mill according to
the required fiber throughputrate;
Using the cane levelin the firstmill chuteto bias
upward or downwardthe speedsof allconveyors
prior to the first mill;
Using fixed speed intercarriers to feed all subse-
quent mills;
Controllingthe speed of eachsubsequentmill so
as to maintain a constant level in its feed chute.
This system is simple, effective and widely adopt-
ed.
Full d automation. The introduction since
the 1980sof independentmill roller drives and new
electronic control developments have opened pos-
sibilities for much more extensive mill automation.
Australian engineers have been in the forefront of
advancesin this field, particularlywith the previous-
ly difficult optimization of pressure fed mill opera-
tion. Authors such as Farrell et al. (1995) (concep-
tual control system), Weseneret al. (2002) (controls
at Proserpine, Queensland) and Kent et al. (2004)
(controls at various mills, including Harwood and
Rocky Point,NSW) have describeddevelopmentsin
mill controls. Their papers cover descriptions, mer-
its and problems of various control strategies, with
the most appropriatesystem being dependent on lo-
cal circumstances. Most of these papers deal with
pressurefed mills, but the principles can generally
be applied to four-roll mills with an independently
driven underfeed roll.
The process variables measured for the control
systemsmay typically include a selectionfrom:
Cane feed rate, measured by mass meters of an
appropriatetype;
Drive torques, measured by strain gauges, tur-
bine chest pressures,VSD electric motor torque
or hydraulic drive oil pressure;
Mill feed chute level,measured by conductivity,
capacitance or othermeans;
Top roll lift, measured by suitabledevices;
Roll speeds, measured directly or from the driv-
ing unit;
Imbibition flow rates.
To achievethe control objectives,these variablesare
used to make adjustmentsto:
Conveyor speeds (usually only before the first
mill);
Feed chute width or consmcting flap at its dis-
charge;
Speed of pressure feeder or of mill rolls;
Speed ratios of pressure feed to mill andlor of
underfeed roll to mill;
Imbibition flow control.
It is obvious that this array of variables and of con-
trollable parameters provides many and diverse
control options. Some general guidelines - perhaps
obvious, but often neglected - for the specification
of a workablesystem are:
Identify and focus on the key objectivesfor the
plant concerned (e.g. throughput or extraction?
Minimized water use? Constraints such as mill
power?);
Allow for sufficient flexibility (e.g. variations
in throughput to match seasonal cane supplies,
variation of imbibition depending on fuel bal-
ance);
Select control inputs that can be reliably mea-
sured (e.g. speeds, electric drive torques, feed
chute levels, rather than pressures in pressure
feederchutes or mill roll lifts);
Recognize the automationsupport requirements
-instrumentation skills, etc.
Do not over-complicate!
5.11.2 Routine mill tests
Consistently good extraction can only be
achieved by regularmonitoringof mill performance,
leading to adjustments as necessary.
Some factories calculate the extraction across
each individual mill,but this is fairly onerous. Suf-
ficientindicationof mill performanceis usually pos-
sible from monitoring individual bagasse moisture
trends.
Itis recommended that,asa minimum,sufficient
representative samples be taken of the discharge
from each mill to compile and graph weekly aver-
age bagasse moisture content figures for each mill.
5.11.2 Routinemill tests
For reliable data, the sampleshouldbe drawn across
the full width and depth of the discharge, and sub-
sampled for analysis. It may be necessary to tem-
porarily stop the following mill's imbibition while
sampling.
Recordingand plotting these exit bagasse mois-
tures will usually provide an early indication of any
problems. An exampleof the type of simpleplot that
may be used is given in Figure 5.26, covering the
first 14weeks of a season.
In the moistures plot shown, initial poor perfor-
mance of the final mill was rectified after week 3.A
problem developed in No. 3 mill in week 11-pos-
siblywith the trashplate,mill hydraulics,chutelevel
control or other cause. The moisture content of the
exit bagasse from this mill increased without com-
mensurate trends from the other mills. The problem
was corrected after week 12.
Conventional bagasse moisture analyses are
unfortunately tedious for the laboratory. Some e

5.11.3 Mill lift and hydraulic
pressures
As discussed in Section 5.3, a floating top roll
makes it possible to maintain pressure on the cane
at the maximum level permissible for the equip-
ment. If the top roll is not floating, it is probable that
the bagasse is not being optimally squeezed.
For this reason, various devices have been de-
veloped to indicate, and preferably also record, the
extent of mill roll lift. Because this lift is normally
only 5 to 12 mm, the devices usually provide for
signal amplification by mechanical or other means.
The most direct measurement is from a sen-
sor either on the mill roll shaft or on the roll flange
(provided it is truly concentric). However, these are
both moving surfaces in dirty areas. Many engi-
neers therefore measure the lift of the upper halves
of the mill bearings. In this case, care must be taken
to allow for the at-rest clearance between the mill
journals and the bearings.
The fact that the top roll is indeed floating does
not necessarily mean that the individual feed and
discharge squeezes are as intended. It might well
be that too much of the lift is being provided either
from the feed or from the discharge roll - or even
from the trash plate. These possibilities can only
be investigated by adjusting mill settings and noting
changes in performance.
The pressures of the individual mill hydraulics
should also be measured and recorded. The appro-
priate pressures will depend on the particular equip-
ment specifications, but note that for most mills the
gear-side hydraulic pressure should be maintained
at a higher level (usually by about 7-10 %) than the
pintle-side pressure. This is necessary to counter
the separating reaction forces of the mill pinions.
At least one mill manufacturer uses larger diameter
hydraulic rams on the gear side to allow for this, but
most prefer the benefit of commonality and rely on
different pressures.
5.11.4 Mill operation
Factors that affect mill performance include
physical issues such as cane quality, preparation,
number of mills, size and power of mills, mill set-
tings, imbibition, feeding and mill controls. One
of the most important factors of all is the caliber,
training, diligence and motivation of the staff in
the mill. This critical aspect of milling can have as
much effect on performance as the mill machinery.
It is only through people that the full potential of
equipment and technology can be realized.
Effective mill engineers spend time daily on
the mill platform, have dirty hands and "know the
music and lyrics of the mills". They touch, observe,
listen, feel and understand the mills. They patiently
optimize settings and they are also able to com-
municate with, train and motivate their operating
personnel.
5.12 Sucrose losses along the
milling train
5.12.1 Physical losses
Poor housekeeping and lax management can re-
sult in very significant sucrose losses along the mill-
ing tandem. Juice spillage, leaks in pipes, gutters
and pump glands, careless washing down and juice
mixing with roll lubrication or cooling systems are
obvious physical losses that need to be prevented
by careful observation and attention to detail. All
drains from the mill area should be regularly moni-
tored for sucrose content.
5.12.2 Sucrosedestructionlosses
Less obvious than the physical losses, but of-
ten greater, is the destruction of sucrose within the
milling process. Destruction occurs in three ways:
acid inversion, enzymatic inversion and microbial
infection. In a tandem that is poorly cleaned and
sanitized, losses may be 2 % of the total sucrose
in cane. In a well-managed plant, the losses should
be reduced to about half of this figure (Htigot
1986:326).
Acid inversion involves the chemical inversion
of sucrose into fructose and glucose and occurs un-
der acidic conditions, the inversion rate increasing
with lower pH and higher temperature levels. Even
at the natural pH of cane juice of the order of 5.5,
reference to Section 25.4 shows that the extent of
inversion is negligible at mill temperatures.
5.12.3 Measurementand control of sucrosedestruction
Enzymatic destruction results from proteins,
mainly invertase,that act as catalyststo promotesu-
croseinversion.Invertasemay be present in the cane
naturally or be produced by Saccharomycessp. and
isinactivated at temperaturesaboveabout65"C.The
productsarefructoseandglucosethat donot crystal-
lize and so arenot recoverableas sugar. Instead they
constitutemelassigenicnonsucrose,which increases
the quantity of molasses and therefore the sucrose
loss in molasses.
Microbial infection is caused by certain mi-
croorganisms, notably Leuconostoc species, which
destroy sucrose forming a variety of high molecu-
lar mass products, mainly dextrans, mannitol and
organic acids. These products are melassigenic and
some carry through the manufacturing process into
raw sugar. They increase viscosities and seriously
impair downstream processes such as crystalliza-
tion, filtrationand color removal, even when present
in small quantities.
lilbury et al. (1977) found that microbial in-
fection - particularly through Leuconostoc growth
- is usually the greatest cause of sucrose destruc-
tion (>60 % in their tests). In cases of severe infec-
tion, acrid odors can be smelled and slimy,rubbery
growths can be seen.
Other products of microbiological sucrose de-
struction in mills include ethanol (produced by
yeasts such as Saccharomyces sp.) and organic
acids, particularly formic, acetic and lactic, which
lower pH, require more lime for neutralization and
lead to increased molasses losses.
5.12.3 Measurement and control of
sucrosedestruction
Sucrose destruction causes a reduction in the
mass of sucrose and in purity, but the percentage
changes in these parameters are relatively small
and diicult to measure accurately.Their use as an
indicator of losses is also compromised by the fact
that the dextranproduced is stronglydextrorotatory,
which may mask the sucroseloss (Rein1995).
The microorganisms that are responsible for
most of the sucrose fermentation are mesophiles.
In addition lactic acid producing bacteria are active.
Mackrory et al. (1984) and others have established
that each part of lactic acid formed is equivalent to
roughly eight parts of sucrose lost in milling tan-
dems, the ratio being dependenton temperatureand
other factors.As an operating control measure, the
products of fermentationcan be measured. Depend-
ing on norms for the factory concerned, a lactic acid
level of more than 300 to 400 mgkg DS in mixed
juice will indicate that hygiene and sanitation is in-
adequateand correctiveaction is required.
To contain losses, the first essential is regular
and diligent washing. Prevent or clear up any stag-
nant pools ofjuice. Every shift, steamwith saturated
exhaust steam or vapor or wash with hot water, all
accessible areas of the mills that are in contact with
juice. Pay particular attentiontojuice screens,inside
the mill cheeks and juice gutters. On maintenance
stops, thoroughly clean these and other potential
contamination areas such as roll ends, juice trays,
dumbturnersand pump suctiontanks. Ideally, steam
cleaning should be for long enough to raise surface
temperaturesto >75O
C for at leasta minute or two.
Some mills use copper mill juice trays, juice gut-
ters and suction tanks, which inhibit Leuconostoc
growth.
Chemical sanitation by bactericides can be ef-
fective. Various commercial products are avail-
able, using compounds such as halogen derivatives
@leaches), formaldehyde, sulfur compounds, thio-
carbamates and quaternary ammonium compounds.
Each has advantages and disadvantages, and not
all are approved for use in a food plant. Results
from various countries show that efficacy can vary
widely with conditions and, where possible, alter-
native products should be tried. Results should be
measured by a competent independent organization
(sugar research institute or other). A full microbio-
logical assay would be the most reliable measure,
but careful monitoring of lactic acid in mixed juice
provides a simplerguide.
5.12.4 Cane payment implications
Most cane sugar industries apportiontotal sugar
revenues between cane (growers' share) and sugar
manufacturing (miller's share). Depending on the
cane measurement and payment system, losses
along the milling tandem may accrue to the growers
or to the miller:
If cane payment is by cane mass alone or by
mass plus analysis before the mill (e.g. core
References p. 146
5 Milling
sampling), the unmeasuredsucrose losses along
the tandem will accrue to the miller.
If canepayment is by "mass balance", where to-
tal sucroseismeasured as sucrosein mixedjuice
plus sucrosein bagasse(possiblycombined with
first expressed juice analysis), then the losses
will accrueto the growers.
Whatever the method of apportionment, if pro-
ceeds £tomsugar sales at a mill are shared, both
millers and growers are affected to the extent
that sugarproductionis reduced.

6.1 Theory
6.1.1 Mechanism of extraction
Extractionof sucrosefromsugarbeetwas always
carried out by means of diffusion.This is a process
in which dissolved molecules in solutions of differ-
ent concentrationwill diffuse due to a concentration
gradient until equilibrium is reached. In the case of
beet immersed in water, sucrosethat is containedin
the cells will diffuse across the cell walls, denatured
by heat, into the extracting liquid. To speed up the
process, beet is cut into thin slices a few mrnthick
and mixed with water or with ajuice whose sucrose
concentration is lower than that of the juice in the
beet cells.
Whenequilibriumis reached, the slices are sep-
arated and the treatment repeated until most of the
sucroseis extracted.The cumbersomebatch process
has been replaced by a continuous countercumnt
extraction process, which requires relatively simple
equipment and has a low power requirement.As ex-
traction proceeds, the concentrationgradient dimin-
ishes and the concentration of nonsugar substances
in the extractincreases.The beet diffusionjuice has
a purity higher than that contained originally in the
beet cells.
Differences between cane and beet extraction
hinge around the considerable differences in raw
material to be extracted. Because of the nature of
sugar beet, it can be convenientlycut into long thin
slices, but it was only once adequate preparation of
cane for diffusion was achieved that cane diffuser
installations were successful. Adequate preparation
implies that most of the juicebearing cells are rup-
tured, thus making the juice in the cane availableto
the extracting liquid.
References p. 173
6 Cane diffusion
The extraction process from cane can be mod-
eled as two mass transfer processes in parallel (Rein
1971). One is fast and represents the extraction of
sugar in broken cells from the surfaces of the parti-
cles. Therate of transfer is influenced mainly by the
velocity of liquid flow past the particles.The second
mass transfer process is much slower, representing
the rate of transfer of sugar from unbroken cells or
frombroken cellsin the interiorof the particles.The
rate of transfer is dependent on temperature which
affectsthe rate of diffusion.
It was found that in a fully mixed environment,
the ratio of rate coefficientsfor the two processes is
of the order of 100. In a packed bed environment,
the degree of solid-liquidcontact is not as good and
the ratio is somewhat lower and closer to 50 (Rein
1972). In a packed bed, a high juice velocity pro-
motes the rate of transfer and also improvescontact
with the particles, thus reducing the proportion of
juice which has to be extracted by the slower diffu-
sion process. Since the ratio is so large, increasing
the amount of sugar which can be extracted by the
faster process is very significant.
6.1.2 Variables affecting extraction
Laboratory and pilot plant work showed very
clearly that more intensive preparation of cane
makes more of the sucrose containingjuice readily
accessible to the extracting liquid, minimizing the
amount of sucrose which has to be extracted by the
much slower diffusional mechanism (Rein 1971). It
is not surprising that cane preparation is the most
important variable affecting extraction. The extrac-
tion plant should be designed in the firstinstance to
handle well-preparedcane.
The size of the diffuser in relation to the cane
throughput will have a big effect on extraction.The
longer the cane is in the diffuser, the greater is the
extractionachieved.Thesizeis measured in termsof
its screen area for a given bed height, or by the total
volume occupied by the cane bed. Relating this to
the cane throughput gives the cane residence time in
the diffuser, and this is the fundamental variable of
importance.The volumetric throughput is related
to the throughput in terms of fiber using the fiber
bulk density in the bed pC,F
as:
It is more convenient to consider throughput in
terms of the fiber rate m,, which is independent of
the amount of juice which may be associated with
it. The volumetric throughput is also related to the
screen areaA and bed height h:
From these two equations, the relationship between
throughput and residence time zcan be seen:
The quantity of imbibition water added to the sys-
tem in relation to the quantity of cane is also im-
portant. Because the mass transfer process involves
concentrationgradientsas the drivingforceformass
transfer, the use of a larger quantity of water will
result in generally larger concentration differences,
with a beneficial effect on the rate of extraction.The
velocity of liquid flowing past the cane particles
also affects the rate of mass transfer. It is necessary
therefore to attempt to improve the degree of con-
tact between liquid and solid, determined largely
by the percolation rate of liquid through the bed of
cane. The maximum percolation rate which can be
achieved is thereforealso an importantvariable.
Temperature has two effects on extraction.
Fitly it promotes the rate of mass transfer through
reducingthe viscosity and increasingthe rate of mo-
lecular diffusion. Secondly it denatures the protein
lining of the cell walls and therefore improves the
permeability of unbroken cells, making the extrac-
tion of sugar from these cells possible. Both these
effects however are somewhat less important than
the effect of the other variablesinvolved.
6.1.3 Fiber packing density
The density of the bed is measured in terms of
the amount of fiber per unit volume, otherwise re-
ferred to as the fiber packing density or fiber bulk
density. The amount of juice associated with the fi-
ber varies in the systemand the fiberpacking density
is the best representation of the degree of compac-
tion of the bed.
This quantity is important since it dictates the
volumerequiredfora givencaneresidence time (see
equation (6.3)) and also affects the percolation rate

is not lost. However thebagasse too is at an elevated
temperature and the heat in this is lost (although it
probably helps to reduce the moisture content of the
bagasse before reaching the boilers).
Measurementson vapor usage in a diffuserhave
yielded a figure of about 11t/100 t cane.

6.2 Plant and equipment
Thereareessentiallytwo variants of theprocess,
termed bagasse and cane diffusion. The former has
a single mill ahead of the diffuser and the latter ac-
cepts prepared cane directly into the diffuser. Early
installations favored bagasse diffusers, since they
representeda smaller step-changefrom milling, and
are still required in countries where payment for
cane is based on an analysis of first expressedjuice.
Cane diffusers have shown themselves to be
considerablymore cost-effectiveand are almost ex-
clusively favored in preference to bagasse diffusers
in new installations. Therefore, what follows is fo-
cused more on cane rather than bagasse diffusers,
although theprinciplesinvolved arelargely the same
in both cases.
6.2.1 Qpes of diffuser
A description of the different types of diffuser
which have been used over the years is given else-
where (Rein 1995).Thetypes of cane diffuserwhich
have been used can be categorizedas follows:
True countercurrent diffusers (e.g. DDS,
Saturne).
Moving bed diffusers (e.g. BMA, De Smet, Sil-
ver Ring,Tongaat-Hulett).
Other types (e.g.FS/van Hengel, Rotocel).
Experience with the different types of diffusers
over many years has resulted in the situation where
only moving bed dfisers are still used, with very
few exceptions.The DDS diffuser (Bruniche-Olsen
1966)was adoptedfromthebeet industrybut proved
unsuitable for large cane throughputs. Saturne dif-
fusers were based on the Miag wheel, and the long
liquid path length was impractical (D'Espaignet
and Rivalland 1974). The FS diffuser conceived
6.2.2 Moving bed diffusers
by van Hengel (Fitzgeraldet al. 1978) was a good
concept and achieved some good extraction values
but proved to be mechanicallyunreliable andexpen-
sive. Moving bed d i s e r s have proven to be low
in capital and operating cost and are the only type
consideredhere.
