6.2.3 Cane feed arrangements
Early diffusershad a maceration carrier that wet
the cane before depositing it in the diffuser, which
was not satisfactory(vanderRiet andRenton 1971).
Nowadays caneis fedinto the diffuser by a slatcon-
veyor running at right angles to the diffuser, gen-
erally over a miter plate, shaped so that cane falls
uniformly across the width of the diffuser.The miter
plate has adjustable sections to modify the distribu-
tion across the diffuser. Alternatively the distribu-
tion is changed by cutting or welding pieces onto
the miter plate. Oncea uniform distributionhas been
achieved, it is generaUy not necessary to modify it
again. A more sensitive adjustmentcan be achieved
by baffles at the point where the cane is transferred
onto the slat conveyor, which effect a changed dis-
tribution in the slat conveyor and thereby changes
the distributionacross the diffuser. It is importantto
have a uniform height bed across the width of the
diffuser.
In some diffusersjuice is sprayed onto the cane
as it enters the diffuser to compact the cane bed
below the feed conveyor. This is sometimes neces-
sary if insufficient head has been allowed for the
compaction of the cane below the feed conveyor.
It can lead to localized flooding and classification
of the cane particles at the feed end. It requires an
upturned screenarea outsidethe feed end of thedif-
fuser, so that liquid flowing out under the feed plate
does not overflow onto the ground. This is shown in
Figure6.6A.

6.2.4 Diffuserdriverequirements
A preferred arrangement employs dry feeding
of cane into the diffuser, with liquid applied to the
cane only after the bed has been formed. Experi-
ence with moving bed diffusershas shownthat more
stable liquid percolation conditions are achieved if
the prepared cane is fed to the diffuserdry, with liq-
uid applied only after the cane bed has been formed.
This requires a distance between the bottom of the
feed conveyor and the screendeck about three times
the final consolidated bed height. This approach
prevents classificationof fines and fibers which can
happen with a wet feed. In this case a vertical feed
plate is adopted and a flat screen behind the feed
plate can be used without any egress of liquid. The
canebed formedprovidesan adequateseal. Different
conveyorarrangementshave been used, as shown in
Figure 6.6 B to E. A slightly slewed conveyor such
as shownin Figure6.6 D enables a good distribution
to be achieved without any deflecting baffles.
It becomesmore difficultto get a uniformdistri-
bution with a wide diffuser.The 12m wide diffusers
at Felixton are chokefed across their widths, with a
surplusbeing continuouslycirculated.This achieves
the purpose of a uniform bed but is considered to
be unnecessarily complicated and would not be re-
peated.

6.2.5 Mechanical details
Chains. Depending on the size of the diffuser,
a fixed screen diffuser will have between 8 and 16
strands of chain, with slats between each pair of
chains, usually on each alternate chain l
i
n
k
.The
chain is a major cost component of a diffuser. The
cheapest chain incorporates alloy steel components
@ins and bushes) and generally lasts from 5 to 10
years before requiring replacement. It is important
that correction of pH with lime is used in the dif-
fuser, or else rapid corrosion of the pins may occur.
This situation is aggravatedby thejuice film trapped
between chain components in which much lower pH
values are possible as the trappedjuice degrades.
Stainless steel pins and bushes in the chain can
prolong the chain life to 25 years or more. Great care
needs to be taken in the heat treatment of the com-
ponents to get the hardness required without making
the pins brittle. A Rockwell C hardness of 46 to 48 is
generally specified. In this instance, the opportunity
to dispense with lime addition is a feasible option.
Generally, the type of material chosen involves a
trade-off between higher initial first cost and lower
maintenance/replacement costs.
Chain pitch varies between 250 rnm and 500
mm and the chains in use have a breaking load in
the range of about 150to 300 tonnes. Larger pin di-
ameters spread the bearing pressure and longerpitch
chain reduces the number of pins required. The opti-
mum chain design varies with the size and geometry
of the diffuser and affects not only chain, but also the
headshaft speed and therefore drive costs. Generally
the longer pitch chains are more cost-effective op-
tions in larger diffusers.
Screens. In a fixed screen diffuser, the screen
is made of perforated plate, either stainless steel or
3CR12, to resist the effects of corrosion and abra-
sion. Hole diameters vary from 6 to 12mrn with an
open area of 25 to 40 %. Although some diffusers
have used different hole sizes in different parts of
the diffuser,it has been established that the screen is
not the major resistance to flow and the hole size and
open area is not important. Moving screen diffusers
usually employ specially fabricated sections bolted
to the chains which transport them.
Headshaft and drive. Apart from the chain,
the headshaft and drive on a diffuser are major cost
items. Drive power requirements are low, usually
less than 100 kW, but drive torque values are very
high as illustrated in Section 6.2.4. A variable speed
drive is required, and AC variable speed motors are
usually used. Flange mounted motors with planetary
gearboxes have proved to be a neat and effective
drive system. Total diffuser electrical power require-
ments are low, with power absorbed of the order of
2 (kW .h)/t,. The major part of this is for the inter-
stagejuice pumps.
For relatively narrow diffusers, a solid shaft
with shrunk-on sprockets can be considered. For
wide diffusers, the required diameter of the shaft
becomes too great and a hollow shaft with cast-in
sprockets may be used. The drive must be equipped
with a torque limiting system to prevent damage in
the event of problems.
Aspectratio. Canediffuser widths vary between
4 m and 12 m, and have lengths of between 50 and
65 m. The choice of the lengthlbreadth ratio is made
purely on a capital cost basis; it has no effect on the
efficiency of extraction. Rearranging equation (6.2)
gives the following equation:
This shows that therequired residence time depends
on the bed height and the screen area A. The total
area is important and the ratio of length to breadth
does not affect the residence time. Generally a
length of 65 m is not exceeded because the chain
pull becomes too large. A longer and narrower dif-
fuser reduces the cost of the drive and headshaft due
to a faster bed speed. Since the screen area A is the
product of length 1and breadth b and the volumetric
flow rate is also given by the product h .b .uc, equa-
tion (6.21) can be written as:
Thus a longerdiffuser requires a faster bed speed for
the same residence time.
Bed screws. Press water clarification was prac-
ticed in early installations to remove fine solids
which otherwise plugged the top surface of the cane
bed when returned to the diffuser. van der Riet and
Renton (1971) showed that the clarifier could be dis-
pensed with if the bed were disturbed at the point at
6.2.6 Juice heating
which the press water was returned. This was done
with a number of helical screws installed vertically
in the cane bed, which rotate and lift the cane at the
point of press water return.
This is now common practice. The screws proj-
ect down to about 100mm from the screen and are
spaced about onemeter apart, with a flightpitch be-
tween 300 and 450 mm. They are commonly driven
by 7.5 k W motors. If the screws trip and stop rotat-
ing, the screws will be broken by the force of the
moving bagasse. Thus the installation generally in-
cludes a shearpin which will break in this eventual-
ity so that the screws can pivot upwards out of the
way of the moving cane bed.
Press roller. Diffusers generally have a large
press roller located before the discharge of the dif-
fuser, riding on the cane bed, with a diameter of
about3 m. Its purpose is to prevent floodingofjuice
and cane out of the diffuser and to reduce the mois-
ture content of the bagasse leaving the diffuser by
the weight of theroller squeezingthe bed.The roller
has to be free to move up and down with the bed as
the bed height changes.In amoving screen diffuser,
generally two lighter press rolls are used to reduce
the pressure on the screen.
Tray volumes. The tray volumes below the
screen should be large enough to hold all the juice
that will drain from a stagewhen a mill stopoccurs.
This depends on the dimensions of the stage, and
can be calculated assuming roughly 6 kg juice will
drain fromeach kg of fiber (roughly half thejuice in
the bed). This ensures that there will be no mixing
of juice from different stages if a mill stop occurs,
which would otherwise destroy the Brix gradient
and prolong the time before steady stateis achieved
after restarting.
6.2.6 Juice heating
At the feed end of the diffuser,juice is heated up
to about 90 O
C to heat the incoming cane to the re-
quired operating temperature as quickly as possible.
Scalding juice is circulated through the heaters at
the feed end of the diffuserat a rate of about 300 %
on cane. Flow meters on the lines to the heaters are
sometimes installed to monitor the amount of juice
recirculated.
Thetemperaturealongthe diffuser is maintained
by direct injection of vapor into some of the stage
trays. Direct contact heating of press water or stage
juice is possible using sub-atmosphericvapor (vapor
3 or 4) to achievebetter steam economy (Singhand
Allwright 2000).Further detailsare givenin Section
9.4.
6.2.7 Interstagejuice application
Juice pumped from each of the juice trays has
to be applied uniformly across the width of the dif-
fuser. This is achieved using an overflow weir or a
horizontal spray pipe. The spray system is able to
apply the juice more uniformly over the stage in
question,whereas the weir provides a curtainof liq-
uid, which results in localized liquid overloading of
the bed at that point.
A weir system has to be carefully leveled to
ensure that uniform distribution across the diffuser
is achieved. There is generally little bagasse in the
stagejuice to interfere with the distribution.None-
theless most weirs have drain plugs in the bottom of
the weir to purge any suspendedsolidsperiodically.
Spraypipesneed to be designed to achieveequal
flows through each nozzle. This requires that the
pressure drop down the pipe be small in relation to
the pressure drop through each nozzle. By the cri-
terion propounded by Knaebel(1981),the pipe di-

6.2.8 Instrumentationand control
Typical control loops found on a diffuser are
shown in Figure 6.7. All control systems are single
loops. The diffuser speed is set to correspond to
the particular set point on the cane throughput rate
controller.The speed is chosen to give the required
bed height. Level indicators at the feed end of the
diffuser indicate whether the desired level is being
achieved. If not, a minor correction to the diffuser
speed set point is required.
Controls on a 12-stage diffuser shown in Figure
6.7 are as follows:
Temperature controllers on the scalding juice
heaters regulate vapor flow to the heaters.
Two pH control loops measure the pH in stages
2 and 7 and control the speeds of the peristaltic
lime dosing pumps.
10 level control loops regulate liquid levels in
the bed by adjusting the interstagejuice sprays.
Percolation rate control may otherwise be car-
ried out manually.
The imbibition water controller admits water to
the diffuser at a set rate.
Two temperature controllers regulate vapor to
intermediate diffusertrays to maintain tempera-
tures along the diffuser.
High level alarmson the stagetrays give an indi-

cation of any trays full of juice.
Control of juice recirculation through the scalding
juice heaters is done manually, to achieve the de-
sired heat input at the feed end.
Electrical interlocks that will prevent the dif-
fuser from operating are typically:
Bed screw motor trip.
Diffuserdrive bearing lube pumps off.
Bagasse conveyors downstream of diffuser
tripped.
Diffuserkicker trip.
Chain tension detector activated(if fitted).

6.4.2 Cane residence time
The longer the time the prepared cane spends
in the diffuser the higher will be the extraction
achieved. Provision of adequate residence time is
probably one of the most important design specifi-
cations.
In practice the effect of residence time is not al-
ways evident in operating results. This is due to the
fact that as the cane throughput through the diffuser
is changed, it causes changes inthe percolation rates
in the difFuser,which may obscure the effect of fiber
residence time. These changes relate to the optimum
positioning of the interstagejuice flows as a function
of cane throughput rate (Section 6.6.3).
The relationship between fiber residence time T
and screen area of the diffuser A is given by equa-
tion (6.21). For a given volumetric throughput vCat
a fixed bed height h, the residence time is directly
related to the screen area of the diffuser. In practice,
bed heights in the diffuser range between 1.1 m and
1.8m. It is clearly of benefit from a residence time
point of view to operate with as high a bed height
as possible. In practice however percolation condi-
tions become less stable at the greater bed heights
and unless a system is installed to cope with changes
in percolation conditions, diffuser operators have
found it generally more satisfactory to operate with
lower bed heights.
As a rough guide, the values in Table 6.1 apply in
South Africa but can vary substantially depending on
imbibition rate, bed height and degree of preparation.
For a bagasse diffuser, Lamusse and Fitz-
gerald 1974) reported that a screen area of 5.5
(mZ.h)/t, would enable an extraction of over 96 %
to be achieved. In fact in its last season of operation
in 1982, the bagasse diffuser at Empangeni operat-
ing at a fiber loading of 6.0 (m2 h)/t, achieved an
e
extraction of 97.8 %.
The amount of juice held up in the saturated
cane bed of a diffuser is roughly 12 times the mass
of fiber (Love and Rein 1980). If the average fiber
content is 12 to 15 % in cane, the amount of juice
held up in the diffuser relative to incoming cane is
12x 0.12 = 1.44to 12x 0.15 = 1.8 kgjuicekg cane.
Sincetherawjuice offtakefromthe diffuser isrough-
ly equal to the tomes of cane entering the diffuser,
average juice residence time in the diffuser is 1.5 to
2 times theresidence time of fiber, higher if thejuice
trays below the diffuser are not kept empty.

6.4.3 Imbibitionrate
As with any solid liquid extraction process, the
more extractingliquor that is added, the easier is the
extraction. So it is with cane diffusion, where higher
imbibition rates will invariably result in higher ex-
tractions. The amount of imbibition water added is
generally related to the quantity of fiber being pro-
cessed, since it is the fiber which effectively forms
the cane bed and it is the fiber which removes with it
juice in final bagasse.
There is no maximum or minimum imbibition
rate for diffusion. Since high imbibition rates will
enable a smaller diffuser to be utilized to achieve
a given extraction, the reduction in the cost of the
diffuser would have to be balanced against the cost
of additional evaporator capacity and cost of steam.
The optimum imbibition rate for any extraction
plant therefore is dependent on the local factors at
that mill.

effect of imbibition level is greater in the case where
extraction is lower.

high imbibition rates of over 400 % on fiber can be

It should be emphasizedhowever thatit is not neces-

than on a milling tandem. Some diffusers operate

6.4.4 Number of stages
The use of a number of stages rather than a
single big mixed tank enables higher concentration
differences between sucrosein cane and sucrosein
percolating liquid to be achieved. As the number of
stages is increased, the case of true countercurrent
flow is approachedmore closely. However the ben-
efit drops off as the number of stages increases and
the marginal improvement becomes very small.
The earliest cane diffusers were installed with
about 18 stages. The trend has been in more recent
years to reduce the number of stages resulting in a
more cost-effectivedesign.High extractioncane dif-
fusers need have no more than 12stages.
From a mechanical structure point of view, a
lower limit on the number of stagesmay be imposed
by the length of an individual stage. If the length of
a stageis more than about4 m, an additionalbay per
stageis requiredas a consequenceof the mechanical
design of the structure.Theresulting costincreaseis
largerthan the saving in stagepumps and piping.
6.4.5 Percolation rate and flooding
Although preparation is the most important
variable affecting extraction in a cane diffuser, the
percolationrate is probably the next most important
variable. This is the rate at which liquid percolates
down through the bed of prepared cane. Laboratory
and pilot plant studies (Rein 1972)have shown that
an increase in percolation rate promotes the rate of
mass &ansfer and increases the proportion of the
juice in open cells that is accessible to the extract-
ing liquid.
The upper limit to the percolation rate is known
as the flooding rate. Flooding of the cane bed oc-
curs when more liquid than can actually percolate
downward between the cane particles is applied to
the top of the bed surface.This causes a number of
operationalproblems,includingwashing of caneout
of the feed or dischargeend of the diffuserin severe
cases, but in any event destroys concentration gra-
dients along the cane diffuser with a severely detri-
mental effect on extraction.
6.4.6 Temperature
Higher temperatures are advantageous in that
they increase the rate of extraction through higher
molecular diffusivity and reduced liquid viscosity.
However this effect is not as impoxtant as the effect
of preparation and liquid flow rate. Nonetheless it
was estimated that an increase in temperature of
5 "Cfrom 75 "C to 80 "Cwould lead to an increase
in extractionof about 0.2 % (Rein 1974).
The most importantreason for keeping the tem-
perature above 75 "Cis to controlmicrobialactivity.
This is discussed in Section 6.6.7. Generallydiffus-
ers are operated at round about 85 "C, allowinglow
quality steam bled from evaporators to be used for
heating purposes.

6.6 Control and operation of
diffusers
6.6.1 Monitoring of the efficiency of
extraction
Analysis of cane and bagasse is necessary in
order that extractioncan be monitored on a routine
basis. Measurement of the moisture content of the
bagasse from each dewatering mill is often also ad-
vantageous. Extraction in a diffuser is less depen-
dent on cane quality than in a milling tandem. Thus
the various forms of reduced extraction which have
been proposed are not really applicableto diffusers
(Rein 1975).
It is not possible to monitor the extraction
achievedin a diffuser on its ownbecause of thelarge
amount of juice associated with the wet bagasse
leaving the diffuser. An attempt has been made to
overcome this problem by washing off the attached
surplusjuice and measuring the amount of sucrose
left unextracted and not available by simple wash-
ing. This led to the concept of "difficult Brix" ex-
traction and the measurement of what was termed
specific extraction (Ferguson et al. 1972).This ap-
proach does allow the extraction achieved in the
diffuser only to be assessed, but the measurement
is technique-dependent and is not used on a routine
basis.
Because of the important effectof cane prepara-
tion on extraction,it is important that PI or POC be
measured on a routinebasis.Very often a drop in ex-
traction is associatedwith a deteriorationinprepara-
tion, which can be identified from routine analyses.
It is commonpracticeto takejuice samples from
eachstagein a diffuser on a regular basis, every hour
or once a shift. Dissolved solids (Brix),temperature
and pH of each sample aremeasured and a profile of
these variables throughthediffuser isplotted.An ex-
ampleis shown in Figure 6.10. These show whether
adequate temperature control is being achieved and
whether thejuice flow system is operating satisfac-
torily. Ideally, the Brix profile along the diffuser
should show a steeply descending slope at the feed
end of the diffuser, tailing off as the dischargeend is
approached.Any unevennessin this Brix curveis an
indicationof problems with the liquid flow system.
It is of vital importancethatthe bed height in the
diffuser be uniform acrossthe width of the diffuser.

2 Control of feed of cane and bed
speed
The cane feed to a diffuser involves the control
of the volumetric or mass feed rate into the diffuser.
This is generally done in one of three ways:
Control of the speed of a belt conveyor feeding
the diffuser,measuring the height of cane on the
belt and keeping constant the product of convey-
or speed and height.
Using the speed of feed rolls beneath a choked
feed chute feeding into a shredder ahead of the
diffuser, as the means of controlling the feed
rate.
Control of the mass flow rate of cane with a belt
weigher on a variable speed belt conveyor ahead
of the diffuser.
Once the volumetric flow rate of cane is approxi-
mately constant, the diffuser bed speed is selected to
give the required bed height. It is important to keep
the diffuser running at a constant speed if good re-
sults are to be achieved. The bed speed can be cal-
culated from a combination of equations (6.3) and
(6.22) which leads to:
Best performance is obtainedfroma diffuser running
under totally steady conditions. Attempts have been
made to vary the bed speed to keep a constant bed
height. Because of time lags involved, this has never
proved successful. Even if some short term varia-
tions in cane throughput rate occur, it is preferable to
run the bed at constant speed and the bed screws will
assist in leveling the bed. This policy greatly assists
the dewatering mills, which otherwise have to cope
with a fluctuating feed. The bed speed should only
be changed if a change in crushing rate is desired, or
if the bed height is to be changed. . . * $ I

6.6.3 Control of percolationin -
. .
diffusers
.
;
"
Flooding or percolation problems are often a
feature of diffuser operation if the diffuser is not set
up correctly. Anderson and Smith (1981) give a de-
scription of problems that can be experienced.
Ideal flow conditions in a diffuser as depicted in
Figure 6.1 are not usually achieved. There are two
sources of non-ideality:
1. Sideways dispersion leads tojuice entering trays
on either sideof thepreceding tray, as tracer tests
have shown (Love and Rein 1980).As Brix dif-
ferences between adjacent stages are not large,
other than in the fist few stages, such sideways
mixing does not have a significant adverseeffect
on extraction.
6.6.4 pH Control
2. Juice pumped from a stage tray does not all find
itsway to theprecedingtray, in a true stage-wise
system.There is always some degreeof recircu-
lation or bypassing occurring, dependingon the
operating conditions and the spray positioning.
This is illustrated in Figure 6.2. The results of
inappropriate conditions are either flooding or
percolationrates that are too low.
Relatively small changes in throughputrate through
the diffuser,or cane variety,or preparation,can have
a significanteffect on the optimum spray positions.
For this reason a systemhas been devised where the
point of application of interstagejuice can be auto-
matically controlled.This is done by measuring the
liquid level in the cane bed and adjusting the posi-
tion at which the liquid is applied to the top of the
bed to maintain the liquid level at the optimumlevel
(Rein and Ingham 1992). This gives better results
than merely settinginterstage sprays to handle aver-
age conditions.
The optimum spray advance can be calculated
from equations (6.10) to (6.12). This requires an
estimate of the percolation velocity in a diffuser,
which can be obtained from a fairly simple set of
measurements. This involves establishing steady
conditions in the diffuser with a liquid level in the
bed, but without any flooding, and then switching
off all the spray pumps. The rate at which the liquid
level drops, observed through the windows in the
sides of the diffuser, gives the percolation velocity.
This may be repeated a number of times to get an
estimate of the averageand range of percolation ve-
locities.
Ideally the point of applicationof thejuice from
each stage should be done automatically.Alterna-
tively manual adjustment is possible, advancing the
spray position if flooding occurs and retarding the
spray position if the bed is too dry i.e. a liquid level
is not visible in the bed.
It is common practice to back off the degree of
cane preparation when flooding occurs. This is an
inappropriateresponse and has a seriouslydetrimen-
tal effecton extraction.A better approachmakes use
of variable throw sprays to enablethe point of appli-
cation of juice to be adjustedinstead, and extraction
is maximized.
In the absence of adjustable sprays, the practice
of turning off one or more stage pumps where the
flooding occurs is less damaging to extraction effi-
ciency.
6.6.4 pH control
The pH of the juice in the diffuser is usually
controlled by adding lime into the diffuser. The pH
does not affect extraction and lime is added only as
a means of controllingcorrosion.The temperatureis
low enoughthat evenatthenormaljuice pH between
5 and 5.5,inversion of sucroseis not significant.
Adequate pH control can be achieved by add-
ing lime into two or three stages of the diffuser. It
is generally dosed into the trays, gets mixed in the
stagepump and thepH is measured on the discharge
pipe after the pump. Care must be taken to ensure
that over-liming does not occur in any one stage
(pH >7). This has been shown to affect percolation
adversely (Love and Rein 1980)and its effect is not
reversibleif thepH is subsequentlyreduced.Regular
inspection of data plotted as in Figure 6.10 helps to
assess whether the controls are working adequately
and whether the set points chosen are appropriate.
In addition,over-liming of juice in diffusers can
leadtothehydrolysisof acetylgroupsfromthehemi-
cellulose of the cane fiber leading to the production
of aceticacid.The acetic acid may then be volatilized
in the evaporators causing serious corrosion of pan
calandriasand vapor and condensate piping (Becken
and Graham 1989). In general, acetic acid levels in
cane from direct analysis, average around 200 mgl
kg DS. In a diffuser under good control, a value of
around 300 mgkg DS can be expected. Values mea-
sured at Felixton have, at times, been as high as 1000
m a g DS under poor conditions. In order to obvi-
ate these problems, lime is preferably added in more
than 1stage, and control is sometimes easier with a
dilute sluny of about 4 "Baum6. Ideally however the
diffusershouldbe madeof stainlessor non-corrosive
steel or have anticorrosion coatings applied, so that
the need for lime addition is obviated.
6.6.5 Corrosioncontrol in diffusers
The side walls and the screen of diffusers are
made of stainlessor corrosionresistant steel to over-
come the problems of combined corrosion~erosion.
Likewisethe pins and bushes of the chain are some-
times made of stainless steel, as the pH of thejuice
film between the chain componentscan easily drop
to a low level due to microbial action and is there-
fore very corrosive.
Referencesp. 173
6 Cane diffusion
The natural pH of cane juice is such that seri-
ous corrosion of the mild steel parts of a diffuser
can occur. For thisreason, lime is generally (butnot
always) added into one or more of the juice trays,
under automaticpH control.The objectiveis to keep
the pH at about 5.8 to 6.0 in all stages of the dif-
fuser.
The internal roof of the diffuser and the stage
trays need to be protected against corrosion, either
by regularpaintingor otherprotectivecoating, or by
using a corrosionresistant material such as 3CR12.
6.6.6 Maintenanceof diffusers
One of the major advantages of diffusion com-
pared with milling is the greatly reduced mainte-
nance cost. Very little routine weekly maintenance
is required, and only the followingitems need atten-
tion on an annual basis:
Chain runners wear and need to be replaced ev-
ery few years.
Lifting screw flightswear in spite of hard-facing
on the edges of the flights. They need periodic
attention.
Routinepump maintenanceis required.
A check on corrosion of trays and structural
steelwork is necessary, particularly at the feed
end of the diffuser where pH values are lower.
Chain pins and bushesneed to be replaced.They
have a life of between 5 and 25 or more years,
depending on the materials and the type and de-
sign of chain.
The diffuserdrive (variablespeed motor and re-
duction gears) needs routine maintenance.
Headshaftbearingsneed routine inspection.
6.6.7 Microbiologyof extraction
Low Brix raw juices degrade readily as a result
of microbial activity. At room temperatures a large
range of organismstermed mesophileswill ferment
sugarjuices. Perhaps the most evident microbialac-
tivity is shown by LRuconostoc sp,which are slime-
formingbacteria. Suchslime is commonly observed
in milling tandems where insufficient attention is
given to cleanlinessof the mills.Actionsrequired in
a millingtandem areoutlinedin Section 5.12.3.
In diffuserswheretemperaturesareconsiderably
higher, mesophilic organisms are rendered inactive,
but hyperthermophilesmay be active. They are gen-
erally lactic acid producing bacteria, and are active
at temperatures up to 70 OC. The pH range from 5
to 6.5 found in mills and diffusers does not have a
significanteffect on microbialactivity.
Control of microbial activity in diffuserssimply
requiresoperationat an averageof about 85 OC.This
ensuresthat the temperatureat no stagedropsbelow
75 OC, which is considered to be the minimum op-
erating temperature.Sufficientheater capacity must
be installed on scaldingjuice duty at the feed end of
the diffuser,in order to achievea bed temperatureof
atleast75 O
C within 1stage.Under theseconditions,
raw juice leaving the diffuser is at a temperature of
about 60 to 65 "C. No biocides are necessary if the
temperaturesare kept above the minimum required.
In diffusers, losses of sugar can be very high
if temperatures are not kept well above 70 "C. It is
not consideredfeasibleto operate diffusers at lower
temperatures, as losses under these conditions can
be severe.
The use of biocides in cane extraction plants is
expensive. In diffusers,theattainmentof satisfactory
levels of temperatureis a much simpler,cheaper and
more effectivemeans of microbiologicalcontrol.
The major degradationproduct of hyperthermo-
philes is lactic acid, which can be routinely mea-
sured. In addition, severe cases of microbiological
losses will be evident in an accompanyingdrop in
juice purity. The routine measurementof lactic acid
injuice is recommended as a control measure.Aver-
age values of 300 mgkg lactic acid on RDS repre-
sent a realistic target for both mills and diffusers.
In the beet sugar industry, pre-scalders are used,
in which the rawjuice is cooled down by heating up
the beet. The rationale is to produce a cooled raw
juice which can use last vapor or even condenser
water to transfer heat and improve steam economy.
This is likely tobevery dangerouswith cane in terms
of microbiologicallosses, because the temperatures
are ideal for the activity of a number of differentor-
ganisms. Biocides would have to be used heavily.
It is less appropriate for cane than beet because the
ambient and cane temperatures tend to be much
higher and microbiological flora are often well es-
tablished on cane, particularly if it is chopper har-
vested.

6.7.3 Effect on steam balance and
power requirements
Additional heat is required in the diffusion sys-
tem, generally obtained from vapor 1, 2 or 3 bled
from evaporators at an amount of about 11 % on
cane.Therawjuice leavingthe diffuseris at ahigher
temperature and so roughly half of this heat is re-
covered, but the rest of the energy is lost in the final
bagasse. If vapor 1is used for heating, the net effect
after evaporationis to increase the total amount of
steamrequiredin a conventionalsugarmillby about
3 %on cane. If vapor 2 or vapor 3 is used, a diffuser
mill will not require more steam than a conventional
mill.
A disadvantageof diffusionis the fact that more
of the sand coming in with the cane ends up in the
6nal bagasse and less in the mixed juice. Typically
for cane containing 2 % ash, ash % bagasse from a
milling tandem would be 3.3 by comparison with a
figure of 4.0 from a cane diffuser (Lamusse 1984).
By contrastAnderson and Smith (1981)report very
little increase in ash in bagasse from a bagasse dif-
fuser in Australia relative to milling. The effect of
increased ash is to reduce the calorific value of the
bagasse marginally (see equation (27.1)in Section
27.2.1).but a more severe disadvantage is the fact
that additional sand in bagasse may lead to more
wear in boilers. The effect of this can be minimized
in the design of the boiler generating tube banks.
Ensuringthat gas velocities through the boiler tubes
are less than 12 m/s will generally eliminate serious
erosion (Section 27.5.8).
van Hengel (1990) has shown that a diffuser
factory requires far less prime mover steam, so
that lower pressure boilers can be used. Alterna-
tively, diffusion is of considerable advantage to
a factory that exports power. Typically installed

ported from the diffuser factory.
If mud recycle from the clarifiers is practiced,
the bagasse to the filter station is saved and is avail-
able for fuel use.
6.7.4 Effect on rawjuice quality
The two most marked effects of diffusion on
juice quality are a higher color in juice and a much
clearerjuice, i.e. with lower suspended solids. Juice
color depends on the cleanliness of the cane and the
diffuser temperature, but can be an important issue
when attempts are made to produce a low color raw
sugar or a mill white sugar.

Comparison of juice quality from the milling
and diffuser tandems is shown in Table 6.5. This
shows clearly that the suspended solids content of
raw juice is considerably lower from a diffuser, and
that lactic acid, a good indicator of microbiological
activity,is significantly lower in diffuserjuice.
Juice from the diffuser has a slightly lower pu-
rity, but this is largely due to the higher extraction.
Suspendedsolids. In SouthAfrica the suspend-
ed solids in raw juice is accurately measured at all
mills, because it affects the payment for sucrose in
rawjuice. Thus it is easy to make valid comparisons
between juice from milling tandems and diffusers.
Table 6.6 shows average suspended solids levels
in raw juice for South African milling tandems and
cane diffusers for two high production years at a pe-
riod during the 1980s when roughly half the cane in
the industry was processed in diffusers. It is appar-
ent that suspended solids in milljuice arean order of
magnitude higher than in diffuserjuice. These mea-
surements are taken after thejuice screens. In most
cases,juice screensare notinstalled in diffuser mills,
as the solids levels in diffuserjuice are so low.
Data reported on South African mills indicates
that suspended solids values in juice from fixed
screen diffusers are lower than from moving screen
6.7.5 Juice screeningand filtration
diffusers. Typically, these values are 0.1 and 0.5
g1100 gjuice respectively.
Payne (1968)reports that juice clarificationcan
be undertaken in the diffuser itself because of the
filtering action of the cane bed. This involves heat-
ing the juice to about 90 "C and increasing the pH
to somewherein the range7 to 7.3. Thejuice is then
sent straight to the evaporators.However this is the
only reported case of clarifying in the diffuser itself
and the practice is not used elsewhere.
Juice and sugar color. On average,the color of
juice from a diffuseris about 10to 20 % higher than
mill juice, but is affected by a number of factors.
Rein (1999) showed how sugar color has varied in
SouthAfrica for a variety of reasons.The following
issues are of interest:
Processing the poor cane obtained in a drought-
affected season leads to an increase in color of
40-50 %, for both milling and diffusion.
When the change from processing half of its
cane supply by diffusion to full diffusion at
Maidstone mill took place in 1995, no signifi-
cant color change was evident as a result of the
second diffuser.
By contrast, the change from milling to diffu-
sion at Urnzimkulu in 1991 resulted in sugar
color moving from below industry average to
above industry average.
The juice from different varieties of cane in
South Africa can show very large differences
in color. The varieties giving the highest color
have juice colors more than twice the color of
the lowest color variety (Lionnet 1988).
There is a very large time-of-season effect on
cane and sugarcolor.The sugarcolorin the first
and last month of the season can be 50-100 %
higher than the color in the middle part of the
season.
The presence of tops and leaves has a signifi-
cant effect on the color of diffuser juice. Lion-
net (1988) found that average levels of tops and
leavesfoundin SouthAfricansugarmills would
increasecolorofjuice by about20 %.According
to Payne (1968), leaves either green or dry, are
the major cause of color development.
Higher temperatureslead to higherjuice colors.
Measurementsat Amatikulu mill showed that a
reductionin temperatureof about 10"Cresulted
in a dropof 25 % in color. Lionnet (1988),how-
ever, showed that a 10"C changein temperature
changes the color of juice by 12 %, but this ap-
plies to hand-cleanedcane.
From these observations, it is clear that, although
diffusion gives a higher color juice than milling,
other factors such as cane variety, cleanliness of the
cane, climatic conditions and time of season can
have a significantlygreater effect on color of juice
and sugar.
Other constituents. The starch content of dif-
fuser rawjuice is much lower thanjuice from a mill-
ing tandem. The higher temperatures in a diffuser
causegelatinizationof starchgranules,whichrender
the starchavailableto naturalenzymesthateliminate
starchin the cane (Boyes 1960).This has meant that
the use of amylaseto reduce starch in raw sugar has
generally been discontinuedin diffuserfactories.
Starch levels in sugar from diffuserfactories are
found to be 25 % lower and gums levels 12% lower
than those in sugar from conventionalmills (Koster
1995).
6.7.5 Juice screeningand filtration
Because of the lower suspended solids content
in the raw juice from a diffuser,juice screens are
often dispensed with entirely. Ln addition, the filter
area required is very much reduced because of the
reduced mud quantities.In SouthernAfrica the filter
screen area required has been found to be roughly
halved with a diffuser.If mud recyclingis practiced,
the filter station is eliminatedentirely.
6.7.6 Effect on overall sucrose
recovery
The effects of differencesin juice quality on re-
covery are both positive and negative. The amount
of filter cake produced is roughly half that in a dif-
fuser mill compared to a milling tandem and so the
loss in cake is halved. If clarifier muds are recycled
to the diffuser,cake loss is eliminated altogether.
Monosaccharide/ashratios in juice from diffus-
ers or mills appear to be the same, so that identical
finalmolassespurities can be expected.No effecton
h a 1molasses viscositiesisevident.Speculationthat
a diffuserleads to increased losses in molasses has
Referencesp. I73
6 Cane diffusion
been demolished by careful study of data covering
many years (Koster 1995).He showed conclusively
that there is no preferential extractionof nonsucrose
in a diffuser,and the lowerpurity is likely to be due
to the higherextraction. In fact, Koster believes that
a higher recovery is possible in a diffuser factory,
due to the lower cake losses.
Microbiological losses in milling tandems have
not received much attention, particularly as they
are very difficult to measure. Even when extensive
losses occur in the milling tandem, no significant
reduction in apparentjuice purity is evident.This is
partly due to the fact that dextran produced in large
quantitiesin mills by mesophiles is strongly dextro-
rotatory, artificially inflating the pol measurement.
In general the extent of losses in milling tandems is
unknown, since a means of measuring such losses
routinely is not available.
Experiments in the laboratory have established
an approximate conversion equivalence between
lactic acid fonned and sucroselost (Mackroryet al.
1984). Each part of lactic acid formed in a diffuser
corresponds to 2 parts of sucrose loss. A different
equivalencewas found at temperatures correspond-
ing to milling tandem operation; in this case, each
part of lactic acid formed means a loss of about 8
parts of sucrose. However this relationship is con-
sidered to be less reliable.
Datafrom Maidstonemill in Table 6.5show that
the lactic acid content in mill rawjuice can easily be
twicethat in diffuserjuice. Based on the equivalence
ratios between lactic acid and sucroseestablishedby
Mackrory et al. (1984), the loss in mills is probably
far more significantthan in diffusers.
6.7.7 Effecton operations
Because of the long residence time of cane in
the diffuser, start-up and liquidation operations are
somewhat more prolonged with a diiser. It is com-
mon practice to fill all the stages of the diffuserwith
water before starting up so an adequate supply of
water has to be available during &e maintenance
shutdown. Then there is a period of about an hour
before bagasse gets through to the boilers. This
means that an adequate bagasse store and system of
reclaiming bagasse to the boilers is necessary.
Likewise on shutting down, liquidation of the
diffuser takes a much longer time and the clarifiers
generally have to handle a reducing Brix juice dur-
ing liquidation.
In operation, diffusers are more flexible than
mills in coping with a wider range of throughput
rates. The diffuser speed can be run as slow as the
drive will allow, i.e. the turndown is very good, and
may be extended even further by changes in bed
height. Themaximum diffuser bed speed will be set
by the ability of the dewatering mills to handle the
quantity of diffuserbagasse.
If long stops are encountered due to mechani-
cal breakdowns, it is generally advisable to empty
the diffuser if the stop is to last more than about six
hours. If this is not done, significantdeteriorationof
the sugar in the diffuser can occur.
6.7.8 Expansion of mill and diffuser
capacity
Most diffusers have been installed as a result of
a required increase in crushing capacity. Small in-
creases in capacity can be obtained from a milling
tandem by fitting pressure feeders or by replacing
critical milling units, say the first and the last mill
with larger units, but the increase obtainable by this
means is limited. A cost-effectivemethod of expan-
sion involves installing a diffuser and utilizing the
best of the existingmilling units as dewateringmills
for a diffuser.Rivalland (1984)has confirmed theef-
fectivenessof this approachfrom a capital costpoint
of view.
Once the diffuser is installed and furtherexpan-
sion is required, the installation of a complete ad-
ditional diffuser can be expensive.Alternatively, a
reduction in extraction as a result of reduced cane
residence time is an option. However if it is envis-
aged that an expansion will be required at the time
that a new diffuser is being installed, it is probably
wise to pre-invest in incorporating headshaft and
chain designsthat can operatewith an expanded dif-
fuser.It is relativelycheapto increase the lengthof a
diffuser to obtain additionalcapacity in this way, by
extendingthe diffuser at the tailshaft (feed) end.
In Zimbabwe the capacity of a diffuser was in-
creased from 220 to 300 tonne canefh by increas-
ing the bed height from 1.3 to 1.8 m (Rein 1999).
This involved raising the top section of the diffuser,
including the press roller, and replacing and rear-
ranging the stage juice sprays to accommodate the
6.7.9 Maximumcapacity of a single extractionline I References
higher throughputand the more compactbed result-
ingfrom the increased bed height. It was necessary
first to check that the headshaft and drive were ca-
pable of handling the greater load. The modification
was successful,with the diffuserhandling thehigher
throughputwithout a drop in extraction.

7.1.3 Chain-and-slat scraper inter-

Chains.Thechains may be of many types. Sug-
ar industry conveyorchains used to be predominant-
ly of various cast malleable designs, but these have
been largelyreplaced by steel chains.Most suppliers
manufacture these to imperial (inch-based) dimen-
sions.Themost widely used chainsare 6"(150 mrn)
pitch crank-sidedroller chains (e.g. type 09060), 6"
(150 rnm) pitch parallel-sided roller chain, 6",8"or
12"(150,200 or 300 mm) block-type chains(Figure
7.4) and 200 or 300 mm Y-block chains.A type not
yet widely used but strongly recommended for this
applicationis 150mm cranked-link.rollerless chain.
This has similar servicecharacteristics to the roller
chains but is cheaper because it has no (unneces-
sary) rollers and permits short length adjustments
(Figure 7.5).
An important point to note with both cranked-
linked rollerless and Y-block chains is the direc-
tion of travel. To minimize wear of both chain and
sprocket, the driven surface on the chain should be
positioned on the sprocket periphery before engag-
ing with the driving sprocket tooth. For this, crank-
sided chain must operate wide sideforward (asindi-
catedinFigure7.5) andY-blockwith the yoke (wide
section)trailing (as indicated in Figure 7.6).

7.1.4 Belt-typeintercarriers
Rubber belt-type intercarriers are also used.
Where only moderate inclines are needed (c 20a),
flat surface belts can be used. However, for steep-
er inclinations (e.g. to feed into Donnelly chutes),
pocketbelt conveyorswith molded-on slatsor pock-
ets are quite widely used. The bagasse is conveyed
on the upper deck of the conveyor.
Compared with chain-types, the advantages of
belt-type intercarriersare:
They areusually relativelylowin initialcostand
in maintenancecost.
Their power requirements are low.
They are of light weight and can be easily re-
moved as a unit for mill maintenancepurposes.
Where height is limited due to the mill house
crane, a higher Donnelly chuteis possible.
Themain disadvantagesof belt intercarriersare:
It is more difficult to achieve clean operation
than with drag-typeintercarriers.
They are not conduciveto the efficient applica-
tion of imbibition. With flat belts, wetted ba-
gasse would slip on the belt and with pocketed
belts imbibition surges would result in messy
spillage. For these reasons, the imbibition is of-
ten applied afterthe belt, e.g. into the top of the
Donnelly chute. With this application, distribu-
tion into the bagasse is usually poor and there
is limited time for absorption and mixing with
the residual juice. (Note that imbibition mixing
is often poor even in drag-typecarriers).
Therepairof damagedbeltsmay requirespecial-
ized resources(e.g.forsplicing).For thisreason,
installations should be designed for relatively
simplebelt replacement.Holding sparebelts for
carriers of differinglengths may be costly.
A design of rubber belt intercarrier supplied by Tri-
con in Louisiana has found widespread use in this
region (Figure7.8). Belts 1.75to 2.2 m wide atincli-
nations up to 63' have been supplied.The cleats on
the belt are spaced between 350 and 600 r
n
m apart,
usually 500 mrn, and are 150to 225mm high. Drop-
ping of riddlings is prevented by the return belt run-
ning in a steel kough.The headshaft is rubber lined
with ceramic inserts to prevent slipping. The whole
unit is self-contained and can be removed as a unit
by the mill house crane. The disadvantagesare that
bagasse cannot be discharged from the mill into the
boot of the conveyor,and in most cases imbibitionis
added at the discharge of the conveyor into the fol-
lowing mill chute. Later intercarriers have used air
belt systems. Belts usually give 30 to 40 months of
service (morethan 10years in Louisiana).

7.1.5 Meinecke chute conveyors
A fourth method of inter-mill bagasse convey-
ing is by "fixed carriers" of the Meinecke chute
type. These are used between mills that are closely
spaced. The bagasse being dischargedfrom a mill
is kept under some compression by being con-
strained between noseplates or scraperplates on
the top and discharge rolls. These project the ba-
gasse upwards, usually at about 30' elevation, in a
slightly diverging chute of 1.5 to 2.0 m in length.
The width of this chute at its entrance needs to be
related to the discharge work opening of the mill,
and is usually between 5.5 and 8 times this open-
ing. From the top of this chute, the bagasse is dis-
charged onto a sloping (50" incline)feed plate
the next mill.
Although the Meinecke chute concept app
attractivedue to its having no moving parts, it
fers from severalinherentdisadvantages:
The maximum possible elevation is limited
this militates against good feeding of the
ceeding m
i
l
l
;
Sealing the upper noseplate against a flo:
top roll is problematic and can give severe
chanicalproblems;
It is not possible to inject imbibitionefficil
into the bagasse between mills.
For these reasons, their use is becoming less I
mon.

7.2.1 Bagassebelt conveyors
Belt specifications. The standard construction
for belts used for cane, bagasse and sugar convey-
ing has a carcass of several plies of square woven
cotton duck or syntheticfabric such as rayon, nylon
or polyester. These are cemented together with a
rubber compound and covered both top and bottom
withrubber orneopreneto sealagainstmoistureand
resist abrasion.Somerefineries specifyfood quality
PVC covers toprevent product contamination.
Suppliers' advice should be sought for detailed
specificationson very long or heavily loaded belts,
but for most bagasse and sugar belts (600 mm to
1500 mm wide) a four-ply construction with top
cover r 5 mrn and bottom cover 2 3 mm thick will
suffice. Some engineers specify both covers of the
same thickness (5 mm) so that the belt can be re-
versed (turned over) when worn.
General advice.
Maximum acceptable and recommended belt
speeds forbagasse are :
Widthof belt i
n mm 500-600 750-900 1000-1500
Maximum speed in mls 3.0 3.7 4.2
Recommendedspeed in m/s 1.2 1.5 1.7
Operation at the maximum speeds will curtail
belt life and generatedust. Good practicewould
normally be to operate at the recommended
speeds.
For accurate and reliable belt tracking, it is
essential that every idler be mounted exactly
square to the conveyor center-line.
Head- and tail-pulleys should be not less than
450 mm in diameter (preferably 600 mm).
Head-pulleys should be lagged with a 10 to
12mm rubber or neoprene cover for good trac-
tion.
A snub pulley should be installed immediately
behind the head (drive) pulley to increase the
angle of wrap and to steady the belt from cen-
trifugal "flapping" after the head pulley (Figure
7.10).
The load side (top) troughing idlers should be
spaced 5 1.5 m apart, with closer spacing to
support the belt in the loading zone. Return
idlers shouldbe spaced at 5 3.0 m centers.
Crowning (machiningwith a 5 to 10mm larger
diameterin the center) of head- and tail-pulleys
assists tracking but stresses the belt and should
be avoided if possible.
The tail-pulley should eitherbe of open (slatted
Figure 7.10: Bagassebelt scraperand riddlingstray
or spiral)constructionor be fittedwith a scraper
to preve t build-up of recirculatingbagasse.
For sh

t conveyors, screw-typetake-ups can be
used. For longer conveyors,a weighted gravity
take-up is recommended, in order to adjust for
temperature expansion/contraction of the belt,
belt stretchand possiblecutting and resplicing.
Spliced belts last longer, create less dust than
beltsjoined with clip-typefastenersand permit
the use of scraper-cleaners and ploughs.
Splices should extend in length by at least 1.5
and preferably 2 belt widths.
Long, wide (heavy) conveyors and conveyors
subject to frequent stops and starts should be
provided with either an electronicsoft starter or
a hydraulic clutch. This is necessary to reduce
stresseson both the drive and the belt.
On steeply inclined conveyors,a holdback may
be needed to prevent reversingwhen tripped un-
der load.
Most bagasse installations warrant the use of
fire-retardant belt materials and flame-proof
motors because of the dusty environment.
Dust management. Most of the dust creation
occurs at transfer points - at the feed onto or dis-
charge from a belt. Fine, dry bagasse dust can be
explosively flammable.To minimize dust:
Arrange for the feed to slide onto the belt, with
a component of momentum in the direction of
travel.
Avoid high drops; if not possible, try to arrange
for slidingchutes (at45' to 60' from vertical).

3 Magnets
Many factories have installed magnets on
the bagasse supplies to boilers in order to protect
againsttramp iron damage to boiler feedersor mov-
ing grates. Powerful electro-magnets are generally
preferred to more limited permanent magnets. Mag-
nets cannot preventalldamage-they donot remove
stainless steel, non-ferrous metal, timber or rocks.
Their effectivenessin removing magnetic material
is dependent on:
The power of the magpetic field generated;
The configuration of the installation.
The simplest type of installation is for the magnet
to be suspended over a bagasse conveyor belt. For
highest separation effectiveness,the magnet needs
to be as close to all parts of the bagasse as possible,
predicating a fast belt with thin bagasse layer. But
dwell time within the magnetic field is as important,
giving a conflicting need for a slow speed. A com-
promise is thereforeneeded and belt speeds of 1.3to
1.6rn/s can usually be used.
The overhead suspended magnets are fairly ef-
fective on well shredded cane and on bagasse, but
Mason and Reichard (1983) reported that they
did not provide satisfactory separation on coarse
(knifed)cane ahead of the shredder. Particularly on
this application,a much better alternativeconfigura-
tion is to capturethe trampout of theflow of bagasse
at a transfer point. This systemcan be very effective
on coarseor fineproduct, but:
It requires a magnet with a different shape of
magnetic field and a ledge under which the cap-
tured tramp is held until clearing;
Theposition andangle of the magnet arecritical
to its performance (for details, see Mason and
Reichard 1983).
Itisrecommendedthatreputablemagnetsuppliersbe
consulted for advice on anyparticular application.

8.1.1 'Qpes of screen
Cush cush screen. Before the advent of choke-
less pumps on milling tandems, it was common to
have a singlecush cush screen, sometimes referred
to as a cush cushconveyor,consisting of a long drag
slat carrier on top of a horizontalperforated screen
deck running alongside the mills. The juice from
each mill passed through the screen, and the drag
carrier conveyed all the bagasse strained out to a
cush cush return system. It is now general practice
to use chokelesspumps and this arrangementis not
often seen in practice. Details of this system and
also of vibrating screens, which also are no-longer
often used, can be found in Hugot (1986)
The remnants of the cush cush conveyor screen
system can still be seen in some mills that have in-
stalled chokeless pumps on the mills, where it has
been shortened and only strains out the bagasse
from primary and secondary mill juice on the drag
carrier scrapedscreen.The carrier also doesthejob
of elevating the cush cush to a return conveyor.The
chain operates in a very corrosive environment and
needs to be made of corrosion resistant steel; the
slats are generally wooden. Wedge wire screen is
the best material for the screen, because it is less
likely to clog, a common problem with these sys-
tems. Otherwise stainless steel screen is used, re-
placing copper and brass which was used in the
past.

DSM screens.These are sometimes referred to
as "ski jump" screensbecause of their shape. Juice
is carefully fed from a weir to the top surface of
the concave screen and the juice passes through
the curved static screen while the bagasse particles
are retained on the screen and slide down to be dis-
chargedat the bottom by gravity. The screenscome
in sections between 0.6 and 1.6m wide and the arc
of the screen on the frame generally encloses an
angle of 45". A sketch is shown in Figure 8.1. The
screen itself is made of hard stainless steel wedge
wires arranged at right angles to the juice flow.
The wedge wire design results in an opening in the
screen which is diverging so that it does not block
with pieces of bagasse. This concept is successful
in giving a non-clogging screen. Different profiles
of wedge wires are shownin Figure 8.2.
The gap sizebetween wires may be between 0.5
and 1.6 mm. When new, the leading edge of each
wire presents a sharp edge to the flowing stream,
but after prolonged operation the edge wears. It is
possible then to remove the screens and replace
them after turning them through 180" so that a new
edge is leading. The worn edge in the trailing posi-
tion is sharpenedagain in service.
The capacity of the screens is affected by the
size of the opening between screens. Brotherton
and Noble (1982) established maximumjuice load-
ings; relating liquid flow rates to screen area, these
f~creened

ranged from 34 t/(h m2) with the widest opening
of 1.6mm down to 21 t/(h .m2)with an opening of
0.65 mm. Manson andAmes (1982) presented simi-
lar maximum flow rates,varyingfrom42 t/(h .m2)
with the widest opening of 1.6 mm down to 24 t per
(h .m2)with an opening of 0.35 mm. In South Af-
rica, equivalent capacity based on installed equip-
ment on milling tandems is much lower at about
12t/(h .m2),with aperturesizesof 0.5 and0.75mm.

Rotating screens. These inclined rotating cy-
lindrical screens are becoming more common in
new installations.They differ from all the old de-
signsdescribed by Tromp(1936) in that wedge wire
screen is used and thejuice is introduced inside the
rotating screen, with the separated bagasse falling
out of the end of the sloping screen. A sketch of a
typical arrangement madepopular by Contra-Shear
is shown in Figure 8.4. Juice is introduced from
a head box, falling almost tangentially onto the
screen, but in a direction opposite to the direction
of rotation of the screen. This arrangementseems to
result in minimal blocking of the screen and gives
high throughputs and a high screeningefficiency.
Brotherton et al. (1981) found that the perfor-
mance is improvedif thejuice is addedin the same
direction as the rotation of the screen. A design
figure of 40 t/(h. m2) is recommended, signifi-
cantly higher than that achieved on DSM screens.
This loading was confirmed by Bickle and Webster
(1982), with feed addition in a directionopposite to
the direction of rotation. Screens were reported to
be free of blockage with fiber. Suppliers data tends
to be more conservative, recommending values
closer to 20 t/(h .m2).
These screen systems typically have a diam-

enough for a singlescreen to be used for high juice
rates, with the largest units having a diameter of

8.2.1 Batch scales
A batch scale system consists of a supply tank
above a weigh hopper, which accepts batches of
juice and records the mass before discharging.
The weigh hopper is tared before accepting a new
batch. Older systems incorporated mechanicalhy-
draulic mechanisms for weighing and conwlling
juice flows. Typical of this type are the Maxwell-
Boulogne and Servo-Balans scales, which were
the standard for many years. Servo-Balans scales
, incorporated test weights in theinstallation,so that
: theweighingsystemcouldbecheckedroutinely and
accurately.
Subsequently load cell systems have replaced
rhem.The weigh hopper is supported on three or
four load cells to record the mass. The electronic

Thesupplytankmust notbe allowedtooverflow

8 Rawjuice handling
The outlet pipe from either the supply tank or
the weigh hopper should not protrude into the
liquid in the tank below. This introduces a
weighing error.
The butterfly valves should be visible, so that
they can be readily checkedfor leaks.
The structure supporting the weigh hopper
should be rigid enough to ensure accurate mass
determinationsand preferably be free from vi-
bration.
8.2.2 Other meteringsystems
Magnetic flow meters are sometimesused in an
effort to measure juice flow. However they cannot
be expected to give an accurate enough measure-
ment. The installed accuracy is generally about 1
% and since it measures volume and not mass flow,
it is affected by juice density and by entrained air.
Even incorporatingan online density meter into the
system does not lead to acceptable accuracy.
Theonlyflowmeterwhichhastherequiredchar-
acteristicsis a Coriolis meter. It can measure flows
with an installed accuracy of 0.15 % and measures
mass not volume flow. Most meters can also give
a simultaneous output of density and temperature.
This type of meter can handle suspended solids in
the liquid,is insensitiveto variationsin temperature
and pressure, has a high turndown and is virtually
maintenance free. However the cost of these meters
risesexponentiallyas the sizeincreases.The80mm
meters cost of the order of $10 000, and more than
one meter would be required for flows above about
150tlh. Larger size meters are becoming available
but at a cost. Nevertheless installation is cheap and
easy and no lengths of straight piping are required
before or after the meter. It is expected that prices
will reduce in future as further improvements are
made to these meters.
8.3.1 Samplingsystems
It is common practice to collect a composite
rawjuice sampleovertheperiod of an hour. If batch
scalesare in use, a representative samplecan be ob-
tained by taking a small sample from each tip of
the scale. A sample tube projecting into the outlet
streamof the weigh hopper is adequate. The sample
tube needs to be carefully designed to ensure that
it does not clog with bagacillo. A sketch of a com-
monly used system is shown in Figure 8.6. It con-
sists of a 19 mm diameter pipe with 2.5 m m holes
drilled in it, located in the outlet from the batch
scales.The perforated end must cover the full width
of the flow and the angle of the holes is adjusted
so that the samplecontaineris about three-quarters
full at theend of the sampling period. The container
shouldbe fittedwith a lid, and if therawjuice is hot,
both the sampling tube and the containershould be
water cooled. The sample tube should be replaced
periodically (typically oncelshift) with another
tube that has been cleaned and dried.
It is important that a representative sample is
obtained, proportional to the juice flow. Thus tak-
ing a small amountfrom the dischargeof each scale a
tip achieves this. The holes in the sampler must not ,
be allowed to block or clog.
If batch scales are not in use, representative
samplingis somewhatmore difficult.Various meth-
ods of sampling juice automatically are described
by Chen (1993).
Sampling raw juice can be hazardous and can ,
easily give unreliable results if certain basic pre-
cautions are not taken. The most serious problem
is the potential for the sample to deteriorate, be-
cause conditions of temperature and concentration
are ideal for fermentation. This requires that all the

8.3.2 Suspended solidssampling
The analysis of juice samples is carried out on
filtered liquid and the presence of solid suspended
matter in the juice stream needs to be taken into
account. Since the suspended matter can constitute
between 0.1 and 1 gI100 g juice, its effect can be
very significant. The mass of suspended solids has
to be subtracted from the total mass recorded.
Samplingof juice to get arepresentative sample
that is not biasedin terms of particlesizeis difficult.
The swing sampler used in South African factories
has given adequate service (SASTA 2005). A cut
of the total juice stream is taken by swinging the
samplerquicklythrough thejuice stream. In this in-
stance a catch sampleonce per hour is adequate.
8.3.3 Pol vs. sucrose analysis
All routine mill laboratories use polarization,
commonly called pol, to estimate the sucrose con-
tent of juice. Although this is an excellent measure
for pure sucrose solutions,it becomes progressively
less reliable as the purity reduces. This is due to the
presenceof othercarbohydrates,particularly mono-
saccharides,which rotate plane polarized light and
this needs to be borne in mind in using the numbers
generated in calculations. The double polarization
method can be used to get around the major effect
of monosaccharides, but does not account for the
otherpolarizingmaterial (Section 25.1.1).
As noted in Section 2.4.4, HPLC or GC can be
used to get an accurateestimateof sucroseinjuice.
The ratio of pollsucrosehas been found to vary be-
tween 0.97 and 0.99 in South African raw juice but
is somewhatlower in Louisiana in therange 0.95 to
0.97. What this means is that using pol underesti-
mates the amountof sucroseenteringthe factoryby
between 2 and 4 gI100 g sucrose.Themagnitudeof
the error is such that accurateestimates of undeter-
mined loss can never be achieved without measur-
ing true sucrose.
The Brix of juice measured by a refractometer
has been shown to give an accurateestimate of dry
substancein the raw juice, so that no correctionfor
dissolved substanceis necessary.
8.4 Juice pumping
8.4.1 Pump duties
Raw juice contains some sand and fibrous ba-
gasse particles and is abrasive and corrosive. The
pump discharge pressure is fairly high, because
the juice is pumped through heaters and to a flash
tank at an elevatedheight and so pump wear can be
problematic.In some cases an intermediatepump is
used between primary and secondary heating, par-
ticularly if intermediate liming is practiced. Care-
ful design of the system is necessary to minimize
costs.
Tospecifythepumpduty,itisnecessarytoknow
the averageand maximum flow rates to be pumped,
including filtratereturn, as well as the head on the
pump under both conditions. This requires an esti-
mate of the pressure drop in the pipes and the heat-
ers, as well as the difference in elevation between
the suction and dischargeliquid elevations.
Liquid line sizing. Theoretically the problem
of line sizidg should be based upon economic con-
siderations. However,in the averagesugar mill, op-
timum economicline size is seldom realized owing
to unknown factors such as future flow rate allow-

of the flow rate squared. At the mean flow vrn
the
system head is less than that shown by the pump
characteristic.This head difference is absorbed by
the control valveregulatingthe flow.The maximum
flow obtains with the valve fully open where the
system curve intersectsthe pump curve. This is the
maximum power point and the motor must be sized
to deliverthe power required at this point.
In raw juice pumping applications, the liquid
contains abrasive solid particles, and has a lower
than neutral pH. This requires the use of hardened
materials of construction. If the quantity of sus-
pended solids is high, an open impeller is used to
provide a "chokeless" pump. Somepump efficiency
is sacrificed in this design.
If the discharge head is greater than about 100
rn of water, a multistage pump is required instead of
a singlestagepump. This is not usually the caseand
a single stage pump is usual in this duty. A lower
speed may also be specified,since wear due to ero-
sion is proportionalto speedto the fourth power.

underconsideration.This is covered by the range of

NPSH requirements. The pressure at the inlet
to the pump must be high enough to prevent cavita-
tion. This occurs when part of the liquid vaporizes
because the pressure has dropped below the vapor
pressure of the liquid. Net Positive Suction Head
(NPSH) is the pressure at the pump suction above
the vapor pressure of the liquid,expressedas a head
of liquid. The NPSH available in the suction sys-
tem must exceed the NPSH required by the pump,
which is a function of the design of the pump and
will be specifiedby the pump manufacturer.This is
not normally an issue in pumping rawjuice because
the temperature is relatively low. However it is ex-
tremely importantin pumping clarifiedjuice, which
is close to its boiling point.

I

10° 1

' 102 1O3
Capacity in m3/h
Figure 8.9: Efficienciesof centrifugalpumps
The available NPSH is calculated as the pres-
sure in the feed tank (generally atmospheric), plus
the differencein head between the minimum liquid
levelin the feedtank and the centerlineof the pump
(negativeif the level is below the pump centerline),
less the pressure drop in the suction piping to the
pump, less the vapor pressure of the liquid at that
temperature.
Some guidelines regarding NPSH and system
design are:
Actual NPSH requirements for a pump should
be furnished by the manufacturer by shop test
wherever possible.
The NPSH available must exceed NPSH re-
quiredfor the entire pump capacity range.
When system NPSH is limited, pump NPSH
requirements can be reduced by specifying a
lower shaft speed, a double suction impeller or
a differenttypeof pump;a combinationof these
measures may be required in extreme cases.
The suction pipe must be large enough, gener-
ally one size larger than the pump nozzle, with
a velocity less than 1.5 mls.
Long suction lines should be avoided, with a
minimum of bends and fittings.
8.4.2 Materials of construction
Raw juice generally has a pH between 5 and
5.5, but may be closer to 6 for raw juice from a dif-
fuser in which liming is practiced. In either case,
the juice is corrosive, and with the effect of sand
in juice, the net effect of corrosion combined with
abrasion is rapid deterioration of mild steel. Leaks
of juice around raw juice tanks are not uncommon.
It is generally worthwhile to use materials resistant
to these conditions. The most cost-effective mate-
rial for tanks and pipes is 3CR12,a high chrome
steel with propertiesclose to stainlesssteel.
Pumps and valves on raw juice duty are also
generally chosen to incorporate abrasion resistant
materials.

Juice leaving the extraction plant is closeto am-
bient temperature if a milling tandem is installed or
at about 60 "C in the case of a diffuser. Filtrate is
either returned to the raw juice tank, thus inflating
thejuice temperaturesomewhat,or to an intermedi-
ate tank after primaryjuice heating.The quantity of
filtratecanvary from5 %up to 25 %of therawjuice
quantity, depending largely on the suspended solids
content of thejuice and the consistencyof the mud
withdrawnfromthe clarifier.The objectiveis toheat
the juice up to a temperature a few degrees above
boiling point just before the clarifier. The juice is
then flashed in aflashtank, sothat thejuice tempera-
ture to the clarifier is always constant and dissolved
gas in thejuice is removed.
The juice is generally heated in two or more
stages, making use of lower pressure vapor in the
first stageto improve steam economy.Thus most of
the heat transfer considered here involves condens-
ing vapor to achieve the heating required, though in
the case of raw juice at lower temperature from a
milling tandem, the first stage could be heating the
cold juice with condensate from the evaporators.
This saves steam and is useful in cooling down con-
densate if cooled imbibition water is desired and in
providing cooled condensatefor flocculantprepara-
tion.
Juice heating is still mostly carried out using
shell and tube exchangers or tubular heaters. Plate
and frameheaters, generallyknown as plate heaters,
are finding increasinguse. Other types of heaters in
use areplatularheaters, supplied by the French com-
pany Barriquand, and direct contact heaters, where
the vapor is condensed in thejuice to be heated.

the definition that will be used here.

9 Juice heating
9.1.4 Use of evaporatorvapors
Mostjuice heaters are of the shelland tube type,
with the tubes held by tube sheetsat both ends.Juice
flows through the tubes and heating is accomplished
by steam or vapor condensingon the outside.
Generallyrawjuice is heated by vapor bled from
the evaporators.Exhaust steam may be used where
steameconomyis not an issue,but increasinglylow-
erpressurevapors are being used in order to achieve
better factory steam economy. Depending on the
degree of steam economy desired, vapor 1, vapor 2
and vapor 3 may be used. Thejuice is usually heated
in stages,with the lowestpressurevapor used for the
first stage, progressively increasing with each stage.
In most cases, two stages of heating are used, of-
ten with vapor 2 and vapor 1 being used. These are
referred to as primary and secondary heating
stages.
Vapor 3 and sometimes vapor 2 pressures may
be sub-atmospheric,requiring special arrangements
for the removal of condensate and incondensable
gases.The gases should be vented to the evaporator
body one or two stages below that supplying vapor
to the heater.

Resistance of scale. Scale deposits can build

needs to be considered. In round numbers, a con-
servative design value of 1.0 kW/(rnz . K) is often
chosen for secondaryheating using vapor 1,while a
slightly lower value of 0.9 kW/(m2.K) is used for
primary heating using vapor 2.
9.2.2 Liquid velocities
There is a limit on velocity imposed by the pressure
drop, and it is shown in Section 9.2.5 that the pres-
sure drop is proportional to velocity squared, with
implicationsfor the choice of pump and pump pow-
er. Thus it is not common to find velocities much
above 2 m/s. On the other hand if the velocity is '
much below 1.5 d s , heat transfer will be unduly
affected. Higher velocities can lead to enhanced
,
wear in tubes and headers and in pumps if higher

pressures result. Generally the choice of the correct ,
materialscan minimize theseeffects.Particularcon- :
ditions may dictate different optimal velocities, but ,
in generala velocity between 1.5 and 2.2 mls seems
'
to be ideal.
Juicevelocitiesdependon the flow rateof liquid,
and the diameterand number of tubes in each pass.

It is generally not economical to design for too
closean approachtemperature,i.e.the differencebe-
tweenjuice exit temperature and condensing steam
temperature. In the past the following guidelines
were used for the optimum approach temperature,
dependingon the vapor being condensed:
Exhaust steam 5to 8°C
Vapor 1 10to 12"C
Vapor 2 and 3 15to 20 O
C
In more recent times, lower approach temperatures
have often been used to improve thermal economy,
with about 7 "C being used on vapor heating. Since
the vapor 1 temperature is generally slightly above
110O C ,
it is generally adequate for heatingjuice to
be flashed and exhaust is not necessary, unless the
steambalance dictates that exhaust steam should be
used. Lower approachtemperaturesare also optimal
with more efficientheaters such as the various types
of plate heater.
In choosing the heat transfer coefficient to be
used in design, the value for a fouled heater just
prior to cleaningwould have to be used if just a sin-
gle heater were to be used. In most mills a number
of heaters are used on each stage. If the heaters are
taken off on rotation, the heaters on line all have a
different degree of fouling in the tubes. An average
coefficient for the set of heaters can then be used,
with care taken to ensure that at all stages of the
routine of cleaning the heating surface supplied is
adequate.
In overall terms, the installed heater capacity
in a factory varies between 3 and 9 m2 per tonne
caneth.
9.2.4 Tubular heaterdetails
Fixed tube sheet heaters are generally used for
heating sugar juice. Tubes are expanded into the
tube sheets, with best results obtained starting with
a 0.25 mm clearanceand a smoothcleanhole. Tubes
are normally arranged on a triangular pitch with a
pitch typically 1.25times the tube diameter. Square
pitch arrangementspermit fewer tubes to be used in
the same area and are not normally used.
'hbes. Tubes have a diameter in the range of
38 to 51 mm.Tube lengths may vary between 3 m
and 7.5 m. Longer tube designs lead to lower pres-
sure drops at the sameliquid velocity because of the
reduced number of passes. Copper and brass tubes
were often used, but generally stainless steel tubes
are chosen in new heaters, as they are harder, more
abrasion resistant, more cost-effectiveand need less
frequent replacement. Austenitic stainless steel,
typically gradeAISI 304, and ferriticstainless steels
such as AISI 430 and 439 are used. Type 304L is
often specified to minimize problems with deterio-
ration in the seam weld and is sufficiently ductile
for expansioninto the tube sheets.The high chrome
steel 3CR12 shows promise as a cheaper replace-
ment forAISI 430 tubes. Somecomparativedata on
heater tubes is given in Table 9.4.
As mentioned before, the thermal resistance of
the tube metal is not significant in the overall heat
transfer resistance. Using the example given in
Table 9.3, at a velocity of 1.5mls, the overall heat
transfercoefficientsin tubular heaters with stainless

Condensate and incondensable gases. Ar-

that these details are given adequate attention, as

properly designed. Condensateisgenerally removed

an easier arrangement for mechanical tube clean-

transfer coefficient, as mentioned in Section 9.2.2,
but this is insignificant in relation to the largeeffect
of scaling. In eitherdesign enough spaceneeds to be
allowed to enabletubes to be removed and replaced.
This is generally more easily achieved with vertical
than horizontalheaters.
Shell.The shell of the heater is usually made of
mild steel. It is designed to withstand exhaust pres-
sure and an allowanceis added for corrosion.No al-
lowance is made for differentialexpansion between
shelland tubes; it is safertouse 436 or 439 than 304
stainless steel or copper or brass if long tubes are
used, since 430 and 439 have thermal expansion co-
efficients closer to that of mild steel. Thejuice side
headers are designed for maximum liquid pressure
under closed outlet valve conditions.Pressurerelief
valves are generally attached to both shell and tube
sides to protect against over-pressurization.
In order to minimize heat losses and for person-
nel safety, heater shells are normally insulated with
a layerof glasswool or otherinsulation about 37-51
mm thick. An outer layer of aluminium gives a neat
outward appearanceand furtherreduces heat losses.
