9.3 Plate heaters
Theplate heater is a pack of thin plates arranged
in a frame so that the space between each alternate
plate is open to the same fluid. The plates are cor-
rugated, which gives them strength and helps pro-
mote turbulentflow.Theplatepackis assembled be-
tween a stationary frame plate and a pressure plate,
and compressed by tightening bolts fitted between
thesetwo plates.Thechannelplates and thepressure
plate are suspendedfrom an upper canying bar and
located by a lower guiding bar. The plates may be
arranged in a series of passes to achieve the correct
liquid velocity and an acceptablepressure drop.
The plates are sealed with gaskets, which direct
the two fluids into flow paths. The most common
gasket material used between the plates is EPDM
(ethylene propylene-diene monomer), which has a
temperaturelimit of 160"C.
Thusitis suitablefor all
juice heating duties. The plates are generally made
of 316 stainless steel, with a thickness between 0.3
and 0.6 mm.Type 316 is preferred to 304 because
of its lower susceptibilityto chloride induced stress
corrosioncracking.
High heat transfer coefficients above 3 kW per
(mZ.K) have been found with a herringbone plate
design, incorporating a maximum gap of 5.4 mm,
with the herringbones on the plates in contact with
eachother (Munsamy1982).Howevera "wide gap"
heaterwith agapof 6 to 16mm is normally used be-
cause of the propensity for small pieces of bagasse
fiber to block the inlet. This results in some of the
inherent advantage of a plate heater being lost and
a lowering of its heat transfer performance, reduc-
ing the heat transfer coefficientsto below 2 kW per
(m2- K). Nevertheless this is still almost twice that
expectedas a design value for conventionalheaters.
In the wide gap heaters,the steam-sideplatesre-
main in contact with each other, but there is no con-
tact between juice-side plates. For this reason, the
pressure on the juice-side needs to be higher than
the pressure on the steam-side, in order to support
the plates and prevent buckling and flexing (Currie
1986).Currie (1986)reportsanaverageheat transfer
coefficientof 1.8kW/(m2.K). Valdes et al. (1989)
report heat transfer coefficients in wide gap heat-
ers of over 3 kW/(m2.K) when the heater is clean,
droppingto a steady value of about 1.3kW/(mz.K)
when scaledafter72hours. Bubnik (1995)compares
coefficientsfor tubular and plate heaters used in the
beet sugarindustry. Dependingon the duty, theplate
heater coefficients are from 1.5 to 3 times those in
tubular heaters.
The advantages of plate heat exchangers over
shell and tube are reported to be as follows:
Heat transfer coefficientsare higher.
The area densityis much higher,givinga small-
er heater for the same duty.
It is lighterforthe sameduty andgenerallyleads
to lower installation costs.
Liquid holdup in the heater is lower.
The thermal inertia is lower, giving a quicker
response and facilitating close temperaturecon-
trol.
It is often possible to increase capacity by add-
ingadditionalplatesdependingonthe sizeof the
frame,
A closer approach temperaturethan that used in
,
shell and tube heaters is generally economically
feasible.
I
There are also somedrawbacks: I

It is not practicalto clean theseheatersmechani- ,
cally, because the gasketsare easily damaged.
Chemical cleaning is essential (Singh et al.
1997).
Gaskets need to be replaced occasionally and
this is an expensive maintenance item. It is im- I
portant that correct selection of gasket material
is made (Singhet al. 1997).
The small openings between plates are prone to
blocking with fibrous bagasse particles, and pe-
riodic reversing of flow is necessary.
In addition to the above, a further disadvantage is 1
the fact that sizing and calculation of pressure drop 1
is generally done by the suppliers of the plate units.
This is less satisfactory in some cases than being
able to do these calculationspersonally, particularly
to optimizethe installationwithintheparticularcon-
straints. Often the suppliers have no knowledge of #
the high scaling rates typical of sugarjuice heating
9.3 Plateheaters19.4 Direct contactheaters
and overestimate the value of the heat transfer co-
efficient for the required operating cycle. Pressure
drops between 20 and 100 kPa are normal, but a
pressure drop of at least 50 to 70 kPa is necessary
to generatesufficientwall stress to reduce the rate of
fouling. Because of the close spacing of the plates,
for the samepressure drop the shear stress is higher
in a plate heater than in a shell and tubeheater.
Juice velocities between the plates usually lie
between 0.6 and 0.8 mls. However high turbulence
is achieved which promotes heat transfer but also
increases pressure drops. Even though the multiple
returnpressure lossesare avoided,shortpath lengths
through the heaters are used to keep within reason-
ablepressure losses.
High foulingrates may be experiencedif bound-
ary layer shearing rates are not maintained at high
levels, and if bulk flow reversal on a time andor
pressure drop is not installed. With these provisos
plateheaters are thepreferred choiceof heater in the
beet sugar industry and are becoming so to a greater
extent in the cane sugarindustry as well.
Heat exchanger costs. Polley and Haslego
(2002) give equations for the cost of shell and tube
exchangers and plate heaters. The former are pro-
portional to area to the power 0.6 and the latter to
the power 0.69. For heaters of 500 m2,plate heaters
are shown to cost about 90 % of the cost of conven-
tional heaters. Once installation costs are taken into
accountthis drops to about 50 %, and could be even
lower if the higher heat transfer coefficients allow
a smaller plate heater to be used. Figures given by
de Viana and Coleman (1995) suggest an installed
cost of plate heaters about 75 % of shell and tube
heaters.
Maintenancecostsoveran appreciableperiod of
time should also be considered, taking into account
fouling, cleaning costs, repairing and regasketing
costs to arrive at the optimum installation.
Platular heaters. A type of plate heater of all-
welded stainless steel construction has been used
successfully in a number of sugar miIls. Different
arrangementsof the plates and channelsarepossible
(Martin 1993)and those onjuice heating use a con-
struction that gives a completely clear juice chan-
nel with no chance of solid hang up. The plates are
welded together at dimples in the plates protruding
into the steam space and no gaskets are necessary.
Heat transfer coefficient is claimed to be high be-
causeof thesmallhydraulicdiameter(equaltotwice
the gap between plates), which gives a higher coef-
ficient for the same velocity (from the Sieder Tate
equation 9.13). Access to the channels is easily ob-
tained by opening hinged lids on the ends of the ex-
changer. The lids are freeof piping orflanges.
Units have been installed as juice heaters in
which up to three stages of heating are done with
vapor 1, vapor 2 and vapor 3 all in the same unit.
This results in a very compact heating arrangement
with a minimum of piping and valves. Units used
at Komati mill in SouthAfrica have 322 m2heating
surfaceeach, with 1.5mrn 316stainless steelplates
arranged to give 20 mm gaps on thejuice side and 8
mm on the steam side, and have given good results
(Cargill 1995). However after 10 years in service
someleaks on the welds were experienced.
9.4 Direct contactheaters
Direct contact heaters are similar in design to
countercurrent direct contact condensers. In both
cases vapor is condensed and the liquid is heated
in the process. With juice heating however the liq-
uid to be heated is sugarjuice, and the vapor used
for heating is bled from the evaporatorand may be
above atmosphericpressure. Liquidvapor ratios are
lowerthan in a condenser,since a largertemperature
changein the liquid stream is generallyrequired.
They have a number of advantagesover indict
heaters:
A much closer approach (1 to 3 O C )
than the
values used with conventionalheaters given in
Section 9.2.4.
Because of the close approach, a lower quality
vapor can be used for heating.
Theheater body is much cheaper, with no tubes,
tube plates etc.
They are able to handle solidsin the juice with-
out blocking.
Less floor space is required.
There is no fouling or necessity to clean the
heater.
They are particularly advantageous where water
needs to be added as well as heating, as in melting
sugar;for this reason they have been used in refiner-
ies where they are termed vapor melters. Otherwise

Scale forms on the juice side inside the tubes
over time. It consists of both inorganic and organic
components, and varies in composition depending
Heated presswater out on the constituentsof the canejuice, its concentra-
. d=4M)mm
tion and the process conditions. This requires the
Figure 9.6: Direct contact vapor heater used for heating heaters to be taken off-line on a I=gUlarbasis, from

9.5.2 Formationof scale
In particular the composition of the scale is
affected by the point of application of lime. In
general with cold liming the degree of scaling is
more severe, because calcium salts are precipitated
as the temperatureincreases.In somecases a change
from cold to hot liming has enabled a mill to run for
a few months at a time without having to clean the
tubes.
In cases where hot Liming is used, the scale is
largely organic. It has a black color and often comes
away from the tubes in pieces resembling a bicycle
tube. It is most easily removed by baking the empty
heateri.e. leavingthe steamon with nojuice passing
through the heater. This dislodges it from the tube
surfacesand it can then be flushed out with water.
9.5.2 Formation of scale
Crawfordand Shann (1956)showedclearly that
apart from the effect of velocity, the degree of scal-
ing varies with time of season, reflectingchanges in
juice composition.They alsofound the scaleto have
a lower organiccontent atthejuice inlet and a higher
organic contenttowards the outlet. Silicashowed the
samebehavior and phosphate the inverse.
When heating sulfited juice, calcium sulfate is
precipitated as a scale, which is considered to be
more difficultto remove.
The strong influencewhich velocity in the tubes
has on the formation of scale within the tubes has
already been referred to in Sections 9.2.1 and 9.2.2.
Increasingthe velocity is the easiest way to prolong
the intervals between cleaning.
Valdes and Gomez (1983) showed that if the
juice is limed before heating, the degree of scaling
is higher the higher thejuice temperature,consistent
with the inverse solubility of calcium salts. They
confirmed the fact that scaling is less severe with
highjuice velocities.
9.5.3 'hbe cleaning
Tubes may be cleaned mechanically or chemi-
cally. Caustic soda is almost exclusively used for
chemical cleaning, pumping it through the heater at
varying concentrationsfor 4 to 12h. Heating vapor
is often left on the shellsideto keep the caustic tem-
perature at around 80 O
C to accelerate the cleaning.
The caustic solution in the heater is rinsed out with
water before the heater is put back in service.
Mechanical cleaning is generally done with ro-
tating brushes, chosen to suit the tube diameters.
In this case the heater headers are generally made
so that the headers can be opened and replaced as
quickly as possible.Variousarrangementsto handle
the heavy covers are in use including hinged cov-
ers, counterweighted covers or covers fitted with
hydraulic cylinders.It is importantto ensurethat the
heaters are empty and not under pressure before re-
moving the end covers. Drains are supplied for this
purpose.
If plate heaters are used, it is necessary to em-
ploy chemical cleaning. It is not practical to take a
plate heater apart on a routine basis, largely because
of the damag2thatcan be done to the gaskets (Singh
et al. 1997).
9.5.4 Vapor side fouling
Vapor side fouling is not generally a problem.
However if exhaust steam is used that is contami-
nated with oil from reciprocating steam engines,
periodic cleaning may be necessary. It is also pos-
sible to contaminatetheoutsideof thetubesif severe
entrainment is present in the vapor used for heating.
The sameproceduresused in cleaning the outside of
evaporatortubes may be used.
9.6 Juice flash tanks
9.6.1 Requirements of flashing
It is importantto heat thejuice to above theboil-
ing point and allow it to flash. This enables any air
in thejuice to be removed, and ensuresthat thejuice
runs at a constanttemperatureto the clarifiers.In the
process any air entrapped in particles of bagasse or
bagacillo also escapes, enabling these particles to
settle and not cany over with the clarifiedjuice.
The extent of superheating required does not
seem to be critical. It is generally thought that a
control set point 2-3 O
C above boiling point should
be used, so that even with some excursions around
the set point, thejuice will always be delivered su-
perheated to the flash tank. Temperaturesabove this
are deemed to be unnecessaryand only increasethe

9.6.4 Flow splittingto clarifiers
The SRI approach has been to provide a single
flash tank for each clarifier and to minimize tur-
bulence in the delivery line to the clarifier. This is
reasonable when only one or two large clarifiersare
in use, and the split of juice flow to different sized
clarifiershas to be done ahead of the flash tank.
In the case of a singleflash tank serving a num-
ber of different sized clarifiers,it is generallyneces-
sary to split the flow proportionately to these clari-
fiers in a subsequent distribution box. This is best
achieved with a number of overflowweirs,the width
of each weir being made proportional to the respec-
tive clarifiervolumes. In the case of the typeA flash
tank, the systemshouldnot at any time be ableto fill
the flash tank with liquid. It will inevitably lead to
liquid entrainmentand in the worst case to spouting
boilingjuice out the top of the clarifier,a very dan-
gerous circumstance.
9.6.5 Temperaturecontrol
It is important to control the temperature from
the heaters to within 1to 2 OC.This is not a difficult
task, and is generally done by regulating the steam
flow to the secondary or final heating stage using a
control valve. If vapor 2 is used in the primary heat-
ers, the supply is left uncontrolled to maximize the
extent of vapor 2 heating. Ensuring that flashing al-
ways occurs leads to a constant temperaturefeed to
the clarifiers and effective degassing. Ensuring that

9.7 Liquid-liquid heaters
Where the raw juice temperatureis close to am-
bient, as is the case with juice from most milling
tandems, the first stage of heating can be achieved
by heating the juice with condensate that has to be
cooledfor use as imbibition and for flocculantmake
up. Althougha shell and tube exchangercan be used
for this duty, with the condensate on the shell side,
the task is better accomplishedeither in a plate heat-
er or in a counter flow concentric pipe exchanger.
The latter consists of a number of sections of juice
tubes within an outer tube, an arrangement which
achieves higher condensate velocities and hence
heat transfer rates. A sketch of a typical unit, which
can be made up in many sugar mill workshops us-
ing standard mild steel pipes and fittings, is shown
in Figure 9.8. The heat transfer coefficienttypically
achieved in this liquid-liquidheat exchangeris about
1kW/(m2.K) atjuice velocities above 1.5mls.
For a mill using 40 % imbibition on cane, cool-
ing the condensatefor imbibition from 85 to 40 OC,
thejuice is heated from 30 to 50 OC. The steamsav-
ing is 3.4 % steam on cane, or 2.6 % steam on cane
if vapor 1from a 4-effect evaporatoris being saved.
In more general terms, the saving is 3.4 .(N- i)/N,
where vaporis bled fromthe ith effectof anevapora-
tor of N effects.
generallyboils at about 110OC, whilethejuice com-
ing from the clarifiersis slightly below 100OC. It is
common to heat thejuice to or above boiling point
in a heater ahead of the evaporators, since this is
generally considered to be cost-effective in respect
of evaporatorcapacity. If the juice entering the first
effect of the evaporatorsis below the boiling point,
part of the heating surface in the evaporatorhas to
be used to heat thejuice up to this temperature.This
is an inefficient use of the heating surface, and ad-
versely affects the rate of evaporation. Conversely,
juice entering the evaporator vessel above the boil-
ing point contributessome flash evaporation,assist-
ing circulation and promoting the rate of boiling
heat transfer. With some types of evaporator e.g.
Kestnerevaporators,it is consideredbad practice to
have the feed temperature too far below the boiling
temperature.
De Viana and Coleman (1995) have shown that
installing a heaterfor clarifiedjuice (alsoreferred to
as evaporator supply juice) ahead of an evaporator
set can be very beneficial. Installing a plate evapora-
tor ahead of the evaporators,the additional heating
surface equivalentto an increase in evaporatorheat-
ing surface of 2.4 % led to an average increase in
throughput of 6 %. The main effect was to increase
the heat transfer coefficientin the 6rst effect, where
the flashingof the feed was assumed to add signifi-
cantly to the circulation and performanceof the first
effect.
Rein and Love (1995)
report the results of two
tests with the clarified juice
heaters on and off ahead of
a Kestner evaporator. These
showed that heating the
clarified juice increased the
Kestner heat transfer coeffi-
cient by 15 % and 3 % in the
two tests.

9.8.2 Sizingheaters
Peacock and Love (2004)investigated the cost-
effectivenessof clarifiedjuice heatersby comparison
with the larger Kestner evaporator area that would
be requiredin the absenceof heaters.They conclude
that in fact the heaters are likely to be difficult to
justify. Their conclusions are however affected by
the assumptionof two tubular clarifiedjuice heaters
and a conservativeheat transfer coefficient; the as-
sumptionof a single large plate heater andthe use of
a Robert evaporatorcould lead to a differentconclu-
sion. The economics need to be looked at in each
specificcase. Cladiedjuice heatersdohoweverpro-
vide the option of achievinga marginal expansionin
evaporationcapacity at low cost.
Clarifiedjuice heaters using exhaust steam have
little effect on steam economy.The most steam effi-
cient optionwould beto use vapor 1heatingof clari-
fiedjuice, even though it would still deliverjuice to
the evaporators below the boiling point in the tirst
effect.
9.8.2 Sizingheaters
Generallyexhauststeamisused forclarifiedjuice
heating. In cases where steam economy is very im-
portant, the first stageof clarifiedjuice heating may
be done with vapor 1,but exhaust is still required
as second stageheating steam to get the temperature
abovethe boiling temperature in the firsteffect.
The considerations outlined for raw juice heat-
ing generally apply also to clarified juice heating.
In this applicationhowever thejuice is considerably
cleaner and if plate heaters are used there is less
chance of blocking the gaps between plates. Scaling
of clarifiedjuice heaters, whether shell and tube or
plate, is reduced in clarified juice heaters compared
with raw juice heating. The constant in the scaling
resistance expression (equation 9.17) is typically
0.001, a fraction of that of the primary and second-
ary heater stages.
The heat transfer coefficient in a clarifiedjuice
heater is generallytaken to be about0.1 kW/(m2.K)
higher than that on secondaryjuice heating.Thus in
a shell and tube heater, a conservative design heat
transfer coefficientof 1.1 kW/(m2.K) can be used.
This is considerablyhigherin plate heaters (Munsa-
my 1982).As for plate heaters on otherjuice heating
duties, extra valve and pipe arrangements for peri-
odic reversingof flow are necessary.

1 0 . Chemical and physical
processes
Only a few of the many processes that have been
tried for the purification of sugar cane juices have
retained any industrial importance. The 8" edition
of the "Cane SugarHandbook" (Spencer and Meade
1948) lists in Table 51 some 622 substances that
have been documented as being "used for purify-
ing, decolorizing, and clarifying sugar-containing
solutions". Treatment with lime in water or syrup
(saccharate) solution remains the basic method of
clarification, normally termed defecation. Lime
has been the universal chemical for neutralization
of the acidic juice, and the process varies in the
method and temperature of addition. Variations of
simple defecation have always the aim of lowering
the color and turbidity of the clarified juice. These
include:
Sulfitation.This combines treatments with sul-
furous acid (from SO, gas), and treatment with
lime solutions. Sulfitation may be carried out on
cold or warm juice, and, as well, on evaporator
syrup (double sulfitation).
Phosphatation.Small amounts of soluble phos-
phate may be added to juices to improve sirn-
ple defecation. Heavier additions would imply
"phosphatation" as a distinguishing term. Main-
ly, though, phosphatation techniques are applied
to the clarification of raw and refinery syrups.
Carbonatation. L i e d juice treatment with
carbon dioxide, followed by additional lime for
neutralization is termed "carbonatation". It is
now rarely used for the clarification of rawjuice,
but remains a core process for clarification and
decolorization of refinery syrups.
Another variation, often advocated as a means of
lowering the Caw content of clarified juice, and
hence of reducing problems with incrustations on
evaporator heating surfaces, is the substitution of
magnesia (MgO) for all or part of the lime (CaO)
in juice treatment. However this has not achieved
widespread use.
Industrial juice clarification can combine some
or all these treatments. The implementation of the
treatments uses a number of methods for the sepa-
ration of the precipitated impurities (sedimentation,
flotation and filtration), andhence a quite wide range
of process equipment technologies and designs.
10.1.1 Objectivesof juice clarification
The aims of juice clarification are:
Toform flocs to trap all suspendedmatter, which
canbe settled at a satisfactory rate;
To provide conditions of temperature, pH and
ion concentration which will maximize the pre-
cipitation of soluble impurities from thejuice;
To produce clarified juice of high quality, with
a minimum turbidity, color, and a low calcium
(Ca*) content;
To produce a settled mud which is amenable to
further processing (most commonly filtration);
Referencesp. 244
10 Clarification
To cany out the above at minimum cost, mini-
mum residence time, minimum loss of sucrose
(by inversion and other mechanisms)and mini-
mum formationof color in thejuice.
To obtain a clarifiedjuice pH that will minimize
inversion in the subsequent evaporation opera-
tion.
10.1.2 Analysis of rawjuice
The major componentsof raw canejuice that influ-
enceits clarification (Doherty and Edye 1999)are:
Sucrose,reducing sugars,monosaccharides;
Polysaccharides(dextran,gums, starch)and tri-
saccharide~;
Proteins,amino-nitrogencompounds;
Organic acids (aconitic, malic, citric), salts of
organicacids (e.g. calcium aconitate);
Salts of inorganicacids (e.g. KCl, CaSO,, phos-
phates);
Insoluble matter such as waxes, fats, bagacillo,
soil, sand, and clay particles. The size range
of these particles is 0.5 pto 2 mm,and their
nature and surface properties determine their
physico-chemical behavior in coagulation and
flocculation.
10.1.3 Effects of heating andlime
additiontojuice
Defecation clarification is usually carried out by a
combinationof:
The addition of lime Ca(OH), to raise the pH
value from 5.3 to 7.2-8.0. The Ca(OH), can be
in the form of milk of lime, lime-juice mixture,
or lime-syrupsaccharate.
Heating, in stages, to the boiling point, with
flashing to remove entrained or dissolved air.
The main precipitant is calcium phosphate,
which forms the basis of flocs that adsorb much
of the otherprecipitating materials. However, as
reviewedby Doherty and Edye (1999)thereare a
number of calciumphosphatephases (including.
mono- di- and tricalcium phosphates) formed
during liming. Tricalcium phosphate precipi-
tates at a relatively slow rate, and the organic
acids present inhibit the precipitation. The
physical elimination of impurities is not com-
plete, and, depending on the pH value of the
juice after the treatment, the residual Ca* con-
tent may be higher than its content in the origi-
naljuice.
Simple defecation methods of clarification are
cheap, yet very effective, except in the removal of
soluble impurities. In the process many of the or-
ganic acids are eliminated, since their lime salts are
insoluble and any albuminoid matter is coagulated.
Part of the pectin content and coloringmatter is ren-
dered insoluble,while othercomponents(starchand
polysaccharides)may be made soluble.
10.1.4 Chemical reactionsoccurring
in simplejuice clarification
A wide range of chemicaland physical reactions
takes place in thejuice. They can be classified as:
Thosedue to pH change;
Thosedue to changes in Ca* concentration;
Those due to the increase in temperature.
These reactionscan be subdividedinto chemicalre-
actions and physical reactions.
The major chemical reaction is that of the Ca++
cationwith thephosphate ion to form phosphate
intermediatesand toprecipitatetricalciumphos-
phate C%(PO,),;
Protein is denaturedby heating (denaturingtem-
perature is varied by pH). It then coats the solid
particles and thephosphate flocs, and impartsan
apparentnegative charge.Hot limingprocedures
usually result in the most completedenaturation,
as the isoelectric point for many proteins is be-
low pH =6;
Amino acids are not changedmuch by clarifica-
tion, though at high pH they can react with re-
ducing sugarsto give increasedcolor;
Reducing sugars are also usually stable, though
they can be destroyed at high pH and tempera-
tures in excessof 100"C.Therate isjust signifi-
cantat apH of 6 but increasesby a factorof 5for
eachpH unit increase;
Sucrose is inverted at low pH, high tempera-
ture;
Waxes, gums and pectins are denatured but oth-
erwise unchanged;

The major physical reactions for the formation of

Turbidity of clarified juice due to unscavenged
colloids and other particles is highly undesirable,
because it ultimately causes poorer sugar quality.

10.1.6 Practical proceduresfor
-
defecationclarification
Thedefecationproceduresmostused arethefol-
lowing:
Cold liming. The juice coming from the mills
is generally at a pH in the neighborhood of 5.5. It
is usually limed to a pH of 7.2, but may be taken
as high as 8.3. It is then pumped to the heaters in
order to bring thejuice tojust aboveitsboiling point
during itspassage,i.e., to 102"Cminimum.On leav-
ing the heater, thejuice passes into a flash tank and
returns to its corresponding boiling point with re-
lease of vapor. It passes immediately afterwardsto
the continuousclarifierwhereitspH dropsto a value
normally in the range 6.8-7.2. Cold liming is suf-
ficient for treatment of noble canes, and for manu-
facture of raw sugar. The clarifiers give a negligible
amountof scum.
Intermediate liming. Here the first lime addi-
tion is after the intermediatetank at -75 "C,
into the
'eye' of the secondaryjuice pump, as seen in Figure
Referencesp. 244
10 Clarification
10.2. The pH control setting is set about 0.2 to 0.3
units of pH higher than the desired clarified juice
pH. Flocculant is added in the feed launder of the
clarifiers.
In some intermediate liming installations the
tank provided as a buffer between the first and sec-
ond stage of the heating is deliberately designed
to approximate a "plug flow" characteristic with a
residence time of up to 40 minutes. This buffer en-
ables time for the natural amylase enzymes in the
juice, at its natural pH, to break down a substantial
fraction of the starch present in thejuice. Thejuice
temperature is controlled to a temperature (in the
range 70 to 80 "C) which is optimal for starch re-
duction, being a compromise between the higher
temperatures requires for rapid solubilization of
starch granules and the lower temperature which
avoids thermal destruction of the amylase. The
clarification is improved at the same time. There
would without doubt be some sucrose degradation
by heat and invertase activity in this process, but
this is difficult to quantify, and the advantages of
the modification are seen to overridethis disadvan-
tage.
Hot liming. Here the lime saccharate (or milk
of lime) is added just before the flash tank. The
pH control setting is set about 0.2 to 0.3 units of
pH higher than the desired clarifiedjuice pH. The
achievementof good pH control is technicallymore
difficultwith hot liming,but it is reported to achieve
the best quality clarified juice with the disadvan-
tage of more voluminous muds, particularly with
saccharateaddition.
Fractional liming with double heating. This
process is a variation of hot liming in which about
33 % of the total quantity of lime is made as a pre-
liming of the coldjuice, and 67 % at the second ad-
dition at the flash tank.
Compound clarification. This variation in-
volves the separation of the juice into two parts: a)
the primary juice, or juice from dry crushing, fur-
nished by the first mill, and b) the secondary juice,
consisting of the juice from wet crushing, and ex-
tracted generally by the second mill, in the case of
compoundimbibition.However the disadvantageof
having duplicate clarification systems led to a lack
of adoptionin factories.
10.1.7 Optimal pH of clarifiedjuice
The final pH of the clear juice going to the
evaporators is important. Hugot (1986: 404) states
that, when white sugar is required, an acid juice is
desirable and, the pH should be maintained in the
range 6.4-6.6. This reduces the sugar color at the
risk of significant inversion of sucrose. The lower
the pH of the product sugar the lower is its colorap-
pearance, and this is an advantage,though standard
color analytical methods should correct for this by
adjusting the pH to a constant value with NaOH so-
lutions. If only a good quality raw sugar is required,
Hugot (1986:404) maintains that the juice may be
left slightly alkaline,with a pH between 7.1 and 7.5.
This minimizessucroseloss by inversion,though he
cautions that alkalinejuice slows the pans, and that '
crystallizationis more difficult.
10.1.8 Role of phosphoricacid injuice
and additions of phosphate
Phosphoric acid occurs in the cane as both sol-
uble phosphates in thejuice, and in combination as
protein in the cell material. The latter compounds
being insoluble, only the soluble phosphates take
part in the defecation. They react with the lime and
form a precipitate that constitutesan importantpart
of the floc produced in the juice by the lime. The
organic phosphate is in the form of a complex with
organic compounds, containing about 10 % phos-
phate. Most of the organic phosphate material is in
the colloidal form, and is unavailablefor formation
of calcium phosphate precipitate flocs.
If the phosphate content is less than 200 to 300
mg P20,/kg juice, it is beneficial to make additions
of inorganicphosphate(phosphoricacid,superphos-
phate,etc.) toraisethejuice phosphatelevelto above
250-300 mglkg. Doherty and Edye (1999) quote a
rule that satisfactory clarification can be achieved
when the canejuice contains about300 mglkg phos-
phate (as P20,).
Julienne and Montocchio (1996) quote 200 mg
P,O&g juice as the minimum level of phosphate.
The benefits of maintaining an optimum level of
phosphateinjuice are listed as:
Greatercolloidal elimination;
Less calciumin clarifiedjuice;
10.2.1 The quality of Lime
-
Fastermud floc formation,with more rapid set-
tling;
* Better clarification with lighter coloredclarified
juice.
Disadvantages of too much phosphate addition can
be higher chemical costs, higher Lime consumption
and higher mud volume(and hencebigher filtermud
sugarloss).
The phosphoric acid will be added before lim-
ing. Some details of the addition procedures are
given in Section 10.5.3. Phosphoric acid is avail-
able comercially for use in the sugar factory in
liquid solution,and otherphosphatesina powder or
paste form. Sometimes ordinary superphosphate or
&calcium phosphate may be used. These materials
contain 30-60 % P,O,. They can be added using a
dry solids feeder, or are diluted to form a solution
of 12"or 1

' Barn6 beforeadditionas a liquid. Ni-
gum et al. (2001) claim that it is preferable to use
phosphoric acid as the additive, because of its ease
of handling, its high purity and its high content of
p,a, (-54 %I.
The phosphoic acid added to thejuice precipi-
tates part of the colloids and c o l o m matter that it
contains.Theprecipitateformedwith limeismainly
tticalciumphosphate.

10.3 pH control
Clarificationcontrol involves primarily the con-
trol of juice pH, which is affected by juice and lime
flow, and juice temperature.The basic type of con-
trol used in clarification is continuous closed loop
control of pH, assisted by other loops forjuice flow
smoothingand heater temperaturecontrol.
On-line measurement of pH used to be carried
out manually using colorimetrictestpapers, but now
sophisticated electronic methods using glass and
referenceelectrodeshave been developed sufficient-
ly to enable almost universal adoption forjuice pH
measurement. Previously it was necessary to cool
the sample before the pH meter, but new designs of
pH probe can work reliably at 100OC.
They are now relatively easy to maintain and
calibrate using standard pH buffer solutions, typi-
cally selectedforpH valuesof 4.0,7.0 and 9.2.Used
with automatic liming addition valves and regula-
tors, they have led to substantial improvements in
clarification.
Control of pH is almost universally carried out
using a standard control loop where lime addition
flow is controlledbased on thepH of thelimedjuice.
Signals from the pH probe are used to control the
flow of lime via a controller and actuator. The pH
probe has to be located at a point were the lime and
juice is properlymixed, not too closeor too far from
the lime additionpoint. This helps to prevent erratic
changesin juice pH and provides for better pH con-
trol (Meadows 1996).
Continuouscontrolis dividedintoopenloopand
closed loo^ control.
In open loop control the signal is derived de-
pendent on the variationsof the main disturbing
variables. In juice clarification the variation in
the juice flow rate and density of milk of lime
are used to determinethe flow rate of the milk of
lime.
However the rapid variations in the buffering
capacity of thejuices usually require that some
form of closedloop controlis used to top-off the
open loop addition.
In closed loop control, the system compares the
controlled signalto the setpoint (controldesired)
and generates a command signal to an actuator.
Injuice pH control a closedloopcontrollerdrives
have yet to be fully explored.
Referencesp. 244
10 Clarification
the lime (orlime-saccharate)additionvalve.The
juice pH sensor sends continuous signals to the
controller which in turn signals the actuator to
vary the addition dependingonthe signal.
The most important closed loop controller
is a PID (proportional, integral, differential)
controller. In a PID control the signal is equal
to the sum of the proportional, and an integral
and differentialterm of the controllederror (dif-
ference between the controlledvalue and the set
point).
Milk of lime addition has traditionally been carried
out through an automaticadjustedsplitterbox deliv-
eringinto ajuice mixing tank,
with the pH measure-
ment taken on thejuice outlet. With intermediate or
hot liming, and the use of lime saccharate,factories
are now moving towards using a static mixer in-
stalled in thejuice line. Saccharateliming solutions
have the advantage that they are easier to use with
conventional solids-tolerant commercial control
valves, such as the Clarkson 'C', Saunders 'A' or
Linatex types.
To minimize valve blockages it is good practice
to havea fully recirculating stream of lime mixture,
with the controlvalve insertedin a short stubbranch
to thejuice additionpoint.
Peristaltic (hose) pumps fitted with a variable
speed drive are widely used to pump the lime mix-
tureinto the stream,with the dosagerateproportion-
al to their speed. However, thesehavedisadvantages
of higher costs, and the fact that these drives have
operating limits and juice flow rates may vary re-
sulting in over-liming or under-liming of the juice
(Meadows 1996).
However they offer the ability to achieve far
more precise and reliable control than the use of
a splitter box, with very little operator attention.
They have thefurtheradvantagethat comparedwith
valves, the flow of lime dosed into the pipe is less
affected by the pressure in the pipe.
With good technology it is possible to reduce
pH variations in the clarifier feed to within a . 1 5
units. Control of pH is made much easier when the
lime density is constant and the juice flow rate is
steady.Much wider variationsin the pH of the limed
juice can cause problems with delayed reactions in
the clarifier,causing variableflocculation,increased
turbidity of the clarified juice and increased evapo-
rator fouling.
10.4 Types of clarifier
When the juice has undergone the desired treat-
ment it must be allowed to settle in order to sepa-
rate the clear juice from the precipitate formed in
the body of the juice. The settling or subsidation
is carried out in continuous settlers ("subsiders" or
"clarifiers").
10.4.1 Description of clarifiers
Multi-tray types. Before the use of flocculants
the most popular installationswere of the multi-tray
type e.g. Dorr, RapiDon; ATV, Bach, Graver, etc.
Multi-tray type clarifiers are generally divided into
several tiered compartments, so as to increase the
area for settling. Volumetric capacities of up to 4.5
m3per tJh wereused, withjuice residence times up
to 3 h, in an attempt to settle very light flocs. Up to
5 trays were used with Dorr designs feeding in at
the center and taking off circumferentially and oth-
ers with a circumferential feed and central take-off.
Flow patterns were complex and removal of mud
without mud re-entrainment difficult. Mud with-
drawal was from each tray separately (Don; ATV)
or from a deep cone at the bottom of the clarifier
(Bach,Graver).
The Dorr clarifier, which was the most widely
used, is a large cylindricaltank provided with a cen-
tral shaft rotating very slowly (12 h-I) and canying
scrapersof sheet metal that slowly brush the bottom
of each compartment.Thejuice to be clarifiedenters
tangentiallyat the top of thetankintoa "flocculation
chamber". Here, part of the mud rises to the surface
as a scum;and a special scraper that pushes it into a
smalllateraldischargeduct eliminatesthis.
As seen in Figure 10.7 a central tube connects
the upper parts of the various compartments. The
incomingjuice passes from the centraltube into the
several compartments by ducts that lead it across
the annular space in which the muds descend. The
mud that depositsin each is moved slowly towards
the center where it falls by an annular passage to
the bottom of the vessel, descending along the
length and on the exterior of the central tube. The
clarifiedjuice is drawn off from each compartment

offtakes.
Scott (1988) was able to enhance the perfor-
mance of a RapiDorr clarifier through relatively in-
expensivemodifications,including providing a mul-
tipoint clarifierjuice offtake in each compartment,
providing three 50 mm gas vent pipes in each of
the four compartments, and installing a semi-pres-
surized mud withdrawal system with only one mud
withdrawal control valve for the cladier. Modeling
has been used (Peacock et al. 2000) to investigate
the effects of simple structural changes on the per-
formance of the clarifier,leading to a recommenda-
tion for the placement of a simple baffle within the
vessel which could lead to enhanced clarificationio
the factory.

10.4.5 Capacitiesof clarifiers
10.4.5 Capacitiesof clarifiers
Multi-tray types. For multi-tray clarifiers Hu-
got (1986:445) has listed capacities from a number
of sugar producing regions. They vary from 2.1 to
3.8 m3/(t.h) cane (valueswhich approximateto the
juice residence time in h). Julienne and Montoc-
chi0 (1996) reported that the installed capacity of
clarifiers in South Africa dropped from 3.3 to 1.6
m3/(t.h) overthe period from 1975to 1995.
This is due to the introduction of SRI clarifiers
and better utilization of the capacity of multi-tray
clarifiers. Average installed capacity of multi-tray
units now averages 2, with a range of 1.4 to 2.3
m3/(t.h).
The type of multi-tray clarifier modifications
described by Scott (1988) enables the capacity re-
quired to be reduced further to below 1.5 m3/(t.h).
It is clear that the most important factor in clarifier
design for a lower residence time is the liquid flow
pattern,as the clarifiedjuice output is largely limited
by the re-entrainmentof flocsby localizedhighjuice
velocities.
However, the settling area of clarifiers is better
expressed in terms of the interior cross-sectional
area of the clarifier,multiplied, in the caseof multi-
tray types by the number of compartments.
he distinctionmade with referenceto the num-
ber of compartments allows for the space taken up
by mud, which is proportionallygreater with fewer
compartments. The quality of juice to be treated
plays an important part, as cane yielding refractory
juices require a greater settling surface. The Rapi-
Dorrdesignersin 1955assumed,before thewide use
of flocculants, a very slowjuice floc settlingvelocity
and a design clarifiedjuice residence time of 1.7 h.
Incremental improvements have allowed many
now to operateat orbelow 1.5hresidencetime, even
down to 1h residence time. If thejuice is refractory
(seeSection 10.5.3)or containsa largeproportionof
suspended matter it may be logical to hold thejuice
in the clarifierfor a longer period of time, although
times in excess of 3 h should be avoided because of
inversionproblems.
The retention time may vary according to the
type of liming technique utilized, because some
methods may result in a slower settlingjuice or the
reactions in the juice may be slower and require
more time than othermethods.

10.5 Operation of the clarifier
station
10.5.1 Clarifier operation
It is desirablethat thejuice be distributedamong
the severalclarifiersin proportion to their respective
capacities. For this, the juice is normally run into a
distributing tank having as many overllow weirs as
there are clarifiersin the battery.
During clarification in multi-tray clarifiers, the
pH of the juice falls by about half a unit. This drop
is more marked in the bottom compartment than in
the upper ones. The pH drop is smaller with short
residence time clarifiers.
Significantinversion losses do take place in the
clarifier, increasing with low pH and long residence
time. For 15 Brix juice at 100 OC, the formula of
Vukov (1965) predicts inversion losses as shown in
Table 10.3.The loss of sucrose in % on sucrose, in
the juice L, has been fitted by the equation 10.12,

by subtracting 0.009 for each 1 "C that the operat-
ing temperature exceeds the temperature of the pH
measurement:
where z is the residence time in the clarifier in min,
pH is the pH value at the clarifieroperatingtempera-
ture, t is the averagejuice temperaturein the clarifier
in OC.
The loss estimates for clarified juice given by
Sckfler (2001) are about 50 % higher than those in
Table 10.3, because a higher value of pH-tempera-
ture correction was used.
In addition, some decomposition of reducing
sugars occurs. Honig (1956) estimated this loss at
about 1 % perhour of the reducing sugars at 100OC,

when the pH is -7, reaching 3 % per hour if the pH
is increasedto -8.
One is tempted to increase tray area (and hence
capacity) in multi-tray clarifiers by increasing the
number of trays whilereducingthe height of the tray
compartments.This is limited,however,by theprac-
tical requirements for inspection and maintenance.
Generally the height per tray is made not less than
600 mm. The bottom mud compartmentis higher, 2
to 3 times the height of the intermediate compart-
ments.
At the end of the season, it is desirable to paint
the whole of the interior surface with a paint resis-
tant to the action of fermentedjuices. The surfaces
should be kept dry in the off-crop.
10.5.2 Mud level control,mud
consistency
It is difficult to control the mud level in a clari-
fierbecausethere is no distinctinterfacebetweenthe
mud and clearjuice. Insteadthere is atransitionzone
of significantthickness. Many SRI clarifiers have
conventionalsight glasses in the clarifier wall to en-
able a visual indication of the operating mud level
to be made. The operation of the mud withdrawal is
then regulated by the operator to keep the mud level
close to the desiredtarget. Various aids to the opera-
tors have been used. These involve draining off the
mud for timed periods, combined with maintaining
a constant level in a mud-receiving tank.
Light reflection or transmissionprobes have not
proven effective for the detection of the operating
mud level. Muller (1976) used ultrasonic level de-
tectors, sensitiveenough to detect the differencebe-
tween the densities of mud and juice, spanning the
likely operating level of the mud in the clarifier,and
used a gap-action control to operate the mud with-
drawalpump.
If mud should be pumped, the pumping action
should be as gentle as possible to prevent break-up
of the fragile floc particles. The high shear charac-
teristic of centrifugalpumps, as well as flow through
narrow pipes and valve orifices should be avoided.
Positive displacementplunger or diaphragm pumps
are more acceptable for this application. Many
multi-tray clarifier installations were supplied com-
plete with diaphragm-typeslurry pumps, but many
10.5.3 Phosphoricacid and other additives
of these have been phased out because of the short
life and high replacement cost of the diaphragms,
as well as the deleterious effects of clarified juice
quality when the diaphra,m ruptures. Conversions
of these to a non-diaphragm system have been re-
ported (Paddockand Quinan 1975).As well, Muller
(1976) reported success with a pneumatic-powered
blowcase device to lift the mud from the clarifier
mud outlet to a surge tank at the mud filters.
The consistency of the clarifier underflow mud
is dictated by the thickening characteristics of the
juice, the arrangements for stining and thickening
of the mud in the mud zone of the clarifier, the resi-
dencetime in the thickeningzone, and the operating
level of the mud-juice interface. Too low a level in
the latter will lead to thin mud. The clarifier under-
flow mud behaves as a Binghamplastic fluid whose
effectiveviscosity correlates with its total insoluble
solids (including bagacillo fiber). This is discussed
in Section 11.1.1.It is, however, normally analyzed
as themud solidscontentof the mud, independentof
fiber. Where, as an optionfor mud filter station op-
eration, factory juice screening is adjusted to leave
substantial amounts of bagacillo in the raw juice,
the fiber content has to be measured and added in
to estimate the total insoluble solids. For systems
where relatively little soil is present the mud solids
in the clarifier underflow (and filter feed) has been
recorded as averaging 6.1,5.05 and4.55 % for three
Australian factories (Noble and Brotherton 1978).
The higher loading of field soil in mixed juice
due to changed harvesting practices in recent years
increases the mud underflow fraction of the juice
but its effect on the mud consistency (mud solids
% underflow) has not been fully investigated. Mud
solids in the feed flashedjuice is relatively low (0.3
to 0.4 % for defecation factories, somewhat higher
for sulfitationfactories) in soil-freejuice, but values
five times higher have been recorded in an Austra-
lian factory (Steindl 1998), with dire consequences
with regard to increases in the mud underflow frac-
tion and in the mud filter loading.
10.5.3 Phosphoric acidand otheraddi-
tives
It has been shownthat, the greater the amountof
i phosphoric acid in thejuice, the easier is the clarifi-
cation. Unfortunately, certain varieties of cane give
a juice poor in phosphoric acid, which is difficultto
treat.Theseare thecanes termed "refractory". These
juices are improved by adding the quantityof phos-
phoric acid by which they aredeficient.
Phosphoric acid is available commercially for
use in the sugar factory in liquid solution, and other
phosphates in a powder or paste form. Sometimes
ordinary superphosphate or dicalcium phosphate
may be used. Thesematerials contain 30-60 g P,OJ
100g.They can be added using a dry solidsfeeder,
or as a dilutesolution of 12"-15" Baum6.
The phosphate added to the juice precipitates
part of the colloids and coloring matter. The pre-
cipitate formed with lime is mainly tricalciumphos-
phate. The quantity of phosphoric acid to be added
will vary depending on the variety of cane and the
circumstances. In general at least 200 mg P,O&
juice is required for good clarification. Any addi-
tionalphosphate should be added before liming.
The use of phosphoric acid additions improves
the clarification of refractory juices and thus is an
effective enhancementof the clarification.
10.5.4 Liquidation
At the time of short ( ~ 2 4
h) scheduled shut-
downs multi-tray clarifiersare generally left full. In
order to reduce the inversion losses in the hot juice,
it is good practice to raise the pH set point and to
lowerthe clarifiermud levelsfor somehours before
shutting down. Even so, the inversion losses are
quitesignificant(theestimatedloss at96 OC,7.2pH,
in 24 h storage time is 2.1 %) and the color of the
storedjuice increases appreciably(the estimated in-
creaseinjuice colorforthe abovestorageconditions
is 20 %). Full liquidations can only be carried out
several times in each season during extended stops.
During the liquidation periods a thorough internal
cleaning can be carried out and essential mainte-
nance of mud pumps and drives can be scheduled.
Because of the relatively low juice volumes
held in S N and SRT clarifiers, full liquidation of
these clarifier types can be made in shorter sched-
uled stopswith much less disruption to the process.
Maintenance and cleadiness can then be scheduled
more regularly, and sugar inversion losses and color
problems during storagecan largely be avoided.

10.6 Flocculants and dosing
systems
10.6.1 Types of flocculants
The most common flocculants used for juice
clarification as well as filter feed conditioning are
partially hydrolyzed polyacrylamide compounds,
which are anionic types.
Cationic types of flocculants have much more
limited use, mainly as decolorantsin syrup flotation
processes.These are discussedin Section 10.6.5.
Consideringthe anionic types, the partly hydro-
lyzed polymers of acrylamidehave a repeating unit
that forms a long chain of very high molecularmass
(viz.greater than lo7).
In the flocculant composition, occasional
-COOH or -COONa linkages occur instead of
-CONH2linkages in the chain. This is measured
as the 'degree of hydrolysis' of the flocculant viz.
hydrolysis = 100yl(x +y) in %, wherey is the frac-
tion of -COOH group (or-COONa) linkages,and x
the fraction of -CONH2linkages.
10.6.2 Physical reactionsof
flocculation
The formation of cane juice floc is based on
Ca&PO,), and protein. Its effectivedensity is varied
by surface chargeeffects (Zeta potential).
In one hypothesis for the mechanism of for-
mation of flocs, attributed to Ruehmtein and Ward
(1952), the chains in solution have a generally
negative charge and are unraveled, but also carry
occasional positively charged sites. These positive
charges attractnegatively charged floc particles and
then the flocculantmolecule bunches around them,
forming effective stabilizing agents for the flocs.
In another hypothesis (Whayrnan and Crees 1974,
1975),the presence of Ca++can also form a cation
bridgebetweennegativechargesonthe polymer and
the floc particles. This is shown in Figure 10.14.
The effectiveness of an anionic flocculant is
a function of its molecular mass and its degree of
hydrolysis, and varies with different juices. A de-
gree of hydrolysis of about 20 to 30 % is reason-
ably effective, and molecular mass range from 4 to
12. lo6.
Rocculants are active in juice at the 2 to 3
mglkg juice level. Higher dosages are given when
treating filter mud. Excessive flocculant usage can
causecarryoverand low sugar filterability.
Flocculation has been described by Crees et al.
(1977) as a two-stage reaction, the first step being
the scavenging of individual particles into micro-
flocs, and the second being the agglomeration of
these into macro-flocs that settle relatively rapidly.
Thehigher-hydrolysispolyacrylamidesare more ef-
ficient in the first stepbut less efficientin the second
agglomeration stage, leading to clearer juice with
slower settling flocs. There is an optimum hydro-
lysis level that applies depending on the juice and
operating conditions.
Turbidity due to un-scavenged colloids and
other particles is highly undesirable, as it ultimately
causes low filterabilityin sugars.Poor flocculant ad-
dition, bad clarifier design, and bad liming control
can contributeto high turbidity.
Provided the initial mixing is satisfactory, fur-
ther gentle agitation is not detrimental, but unduly
vigorousagitationcan causefloc damageand be det-
rimental to bothjuice clarity and floc settling rate.

10.6.4 Flocculanttesting
The simple batch settling test with a heated air
cabinetand 500rnL or 1000mL settling tubes (Sec-
tion 10.4.4),can be used forrapid evaluationof floc-
culant types and dosages.
A large sample of juice is taken from the flash
tank, poured into a beaker containing the flocculant
and then into the settlingtubes at the correctheight.
Comparisonsof the initial settling velocity (u,,) val-
ues, juice turbidity, and final mud volumes can be
used as a guideto the most effectivetypeanddosage
of flocculant.
10.6.5 Cationic flocculants
Cationic flocculants have not been widely uti-
lized for raw juice clarification, though they are in
wide use for reducing color in syrup phosphatation
processes. Somecolorbodies arenegatively charged
(i.e.anionic).Thecationicprecipitantattractsthean-
ionic color and forms a hydrophobic shield around
the colorant. More detail is given in section 14.6.
Recent reports on their use in conjunction with
anionicpolymers claim to reduce clarifiedjuice tur-
bidity (Olson and Zeller 1999, Gorjian et al. 2000,
Doherty et al. 2003). The latter found that addition
of commercial(andexperimental)cationicpolymers
were ineffectiveat dose rates below 10m a gjuice,
but noticeable at relatively high concentrations
(50-200 mglkg). Such high dose rates make the op-
eration quite expensivein chemical cost. In marked
contrast to the behavior with anionic flocculants,
clarification was found to be better if the cationic
polymers were added to the primary juice before
liming.

10.7 Sulfitation
SulEtation is the most widespread process en-
hancement of basic defecation clarification.The ac-
tion of sulfurdioxide(SO,) onjuice eliminatessome
of the colored matter (a property common to a
l
lac-
ids), and reduces to colorless compounds the ferric
salts that have been formed by contact with mills,

10.7.1 Preparation of sulfur dioxide
Sulfur dioxide is prepared from elemental sul-
fur, which is delivered in the form of powder or
smallsticksor cylinders.Sulfurforsugarfactoryuse
should meet the specifications:
Moisture below 10 g/kg
Ash below 1 gkg
Bituminoussubstances below 2.5 g/kg
Arsenic below 0.5 gkg
Sulfur dioxide is a gas resulting from the combus-
tion of sulfur:
Combustion takes place at a temperature of 363 "C.
Each part of sulfur requires one part of oxygen in
an exothermic reaction that releases 9280 kJkg of
sulfur.With the theoretical quantity of air(contain-
ing a m
a
s
sfraction of 23.15 % oxygen,volume frac-
tion 20.84 %) the mass of airrequired would be 4.3
times the mass of sulfur and the maximum content
of sulfur dioxide in the combustion gases is a vol-
ume fraction of 21 %. Normally about 60 % excess
air is used, and the gases contain a volume fraction
of 12-16 %, an averageof 148.
In the presence of water, sulfur bums to give
sulfuric anhydride SO, instead of sulfurous anhy-
dride SO,. On reacting with water, SO:, immediately
forms su-kuic acid, which can cause corrosion in
the piping. It also forms calcium sulfate(CaSO,) in
the juice, which leads to a rise of calcium content
in the juice, increasing the rate of scaling in heat
transfer equipment. The introduction of water into
the sulfur furnaceshould therefore be avoided, and
the airfor combustionof the sulfur should alwaysbe
dried. Often, for this purpose, the a
i
ris passed over
quicklime, which has a great affinity for water and
absorbs the moisturefrom the air.
10.7.2 Sulfurfurnaces
The older sulfur furnaces were of the tray type
where trays in the form of drawers slide in suitable
guides (Hugo? 1986:408). For optimum perfor-
mance, the tray area for a sulfur furnace should pro-
vide for a capacity of 19.5-24.5 kg/(m2.h) sulfur.
Where compressedair is used, air requirementsmay
be estimated at 6.2 m3/kg sulfur,assuming standard
air conditions.
A present trend is to replace the tray sulfur fur-
nace by a rotary furnace, which is more efficient.
Rotary sulfurbumen use induced draft. Mechanical
feed ensures continuous operation. Best results are
obtained with sulfurof high purity (99.6-99.9 g per
100 g). The sulfur melts by its own heat of com-
bustion in the rotating cylinder, presenting a large
surface for combustion as the sulfur drips through
the air.Air is drawn in at an adjustableneck ring and
anti-sublimation sleeve at the connection between
the rotating drum and combustion chamber, a cast-
iron or brick-lined compartmentwith baffles, where
the oxidationof the sulfurand mixingwith the dilut-
ing air are completed. An installation with manual
feeding is depicted in Figure 10.15.

10.7.5 Sulfitationapparatus
One sulfitationapparatusfor mixing the sulfita-
tion gases with the juice or syrup to be treated is
the Quarez. It consists of a rectangular tank divided
into two unequal and connected compartments.The
juice to be sulfited is fed into the smaller compart-
ment. A pump that takesit to the SO, aspiratorpicks
it up. This is designed in the form of a nozzle, on
the usual principle of an ejector. Thus it produces
an aspiration of the sulfurous gas, and the sullita-
tiontakes placeby contactand mixing in the vertical
descending column returning the juice to the tank.
The nitrogen and oxygen accompanyingthe SO, in
the furnace gases are released as bubbles at the bot-
tom of this column and are rejected to atmosphere
by a small vent pipe. The output of the recircula-
tion pump regulates the dose rate of sulfitation in
thejuice. It can be varied by regulating the speed of
this pump. Thepump shouldbe capableof an output
at least equal to 1.5 times the volume of juice to be
treated.
For some time there was a trend to replace the
Quarezby a sulfitationcolumn,which eliminatesthe
circulation pump. Generallythe mixed coldjuice is
sprayed into tall vertical cylindrical tanks, 1.2 m
or more in diameter and possibly 4.5 m high, fitted
for the upper two-thirds with a series of hardwood
grids made of 0.6 x 1.2m timbers set on edge. The
juice enters the top of the tower in a spray and falls
througb the wooden grillwork, where it encounters
the rising current of SO,. Either an air ejector in-
duces the flow of gas through the system or the SO,
is under pressure.
The sulfitatedjuices are drawn from the conical
bottom of the tower at a pH value of 3.8-4.0, limed
in a separate liming tank to pH 6.5-6.8, then heated
to boiling and settled.
According to Kulkami (1993) most juice lim-
ing-sulfitationdesigns in India use pressurized SO,
burner systems and two tanks with a total residence
time of 10-20 min. One of the tanks receives the
juice and lime and SO, continuouslywhile the other
serves for correction and completion of reaction.
Thus continuous sulfitation is carried out in cylin-
drical sulfitators holding a fixed volume of juice.
Heatedjuice (75O
C
) flowsthroughthe tank continu-
ously, while the milk of lime is added constantly to
the enteringjuice and a continuouspressurized flow
of SO, into the liquid near the bottom of the tank
supplies the needed circulation. The supply of gas
is kept constant, and a controller regulates the Lime
addition. In actualpractice,thejuice is pre-limed b e
fore entering the sulfitingtank, generally to neutral-
ity, and is maintained near the neutral point by the
sulfitation-limeaddition.
Good circulation and thorough mixing both of
the lime and of SO, are very important.A bent cir-
culation baffle gives the best results in cylindrical
sulfitators.Many designs have stirrers running at 50
to 100min-' to generate intense mixingbetween the
gas bubbles and the pre-limed juice. Biswas (2003)
modifiedthe stirreron thepopularN.S.1juice sulfitor
to have the entirelime flow added in thejuice entry
point and to have the limedjuice come in intimate
contactwith SO, gas after approximately5 seconds.
Avoidance of high alkalinities at high temperatures
or for extended periods is recommended for the
same reasons as in defecation control: such high al-
kalinities result in decompositionof reducing sugars
and in color formation.
Poor mixing of lime and juice may produce lo-
cal over-liming.Temperaturesabove75O
C aredetri-
mental and someprefer not to exceed70 "Cuntil the
final pH adjustmentis made, to givea clarifiedjuice
to the evaporatorsof pH 6.9-7.0.
10.7.6 Sulfitationprocedures
The standard sulfitation processes are the fol-
lowing:
Cold sulfitation. Sulfitationinvolves the formation
of calcium sulfite. The minimum solubility of cal-
cium sulflte is at about 75 OC. This salt thus is more
soluble cold than hot, and accordingly is deposited
in thetubes of theheatersin cold sulfitation.Starting
with the cold mixedjuice:
Sulfitationto pH of 3.8 to 4.5;
Lime to pH of 7.0;
Heat to boiling; settling.
Hot sulfitation.To avoid the disadvantage of ac-
celerated primary heater fouling, the standard sul-
fitationprocess is modified. Startingfromthemixed
juice, it undergoes:
Heating to 70-80 O
C
;
Sulfitation;
Liming; heatingto boiling; settling.
10.7.7 Advantagesand disadvantages of sulfitation
Hot sulfitation appreciably reduces the quantitiesof
lime and SO, required, but a disadvantage is that the
absorptionefficiency of SO, is reduced.
Sometimespart of the liming is done before the
initial heating step, and sometimes the part liming
is delayed till after the initial heating step. How-
ever, it is necessary that the same final pH should
be reached in thejuice going to the clarifiers. How-
ever, the rapidity of settlingand the volume of muds
depend on the reaction of the medium in which the
precipitateis formed. In practice, the following dif-
ferences between liming before sulfitation and l
i
m
-
ing afer sulfitationhavebeen noted:
Floc settlingis slower;
The volume of mudsis greater,it ismorehydrat-
ed, requiring a greater capacity in the filters;
* Hot pre-liming decreasesthese disadvantages;
-
In general, liming after sulfitation is preferable,
particularly when treating immaturecane.
Indian technologistsprefer the limingandsuffitation
operationsto be carried outas nearly simultaneously
LS possible, and in the one vessel. They claim bet-
ter results than those obtained either with sulfitation
k t or with liming first.

10.7.7 Advantages and disadvantages
of sulfitation
On comparing the practical results of sulfitation
with those of ordinary defecation the following ad-
vantages and disadvantages may be noted.
Advantages of sulfitation:
The mud settles more rapidly (hence improved
capacity of clarifiers).
The massecuites are less viscous and boil faster
(bettercrystallizationin consequence);
There is a marked improvement in color of the
sugar.
There is a slight gain in capacity of centrifu-
gals.
Disadvantages of sulfitation:
Therearemuch heavier foulingdepositsin heat-
ers. These may be avoided by suffiting hot, but
this involves an increase in the heating surface
required.
Greater expense(in sulfitation tanks, circulation
pump, sulfur, corrosion of vessels and pipes,
etc.).
Heavier use of lime in the process and in the re-
circulatingcooling water.
The residual sulfur in the sugar may exceed the
specification demandedby somecustomers.

11.1.2 Handlingof muds
Primary mud should be transferred from the
clarifierto the filters with a minimum of turbulence
to preserve the floc structure.This is aided by gravi-
tation of primary mud and good filterbootlevel con-
trol as both of these minimize the recycling of pri-
mary mud and ensurethat the mud flocis delivered
to the filters in prime condition. There is a need for
mud piping to be as short and direct as possiblewith
a continuous gradual fall and no inverted U-bends.
Sometimes mud removal is organized as sequential
fromeach tray frommulti-tray clarifiersusing timed
on-off valves. To be effective this system requires
some method of feedback on the consistencyof the
mud at each take-off.
Pumping of muds. Factories which pump pri-
mary mud and have poor or no ater boot level con- 1
trol are at a distinct &sadvantageand will have dif- 1
ficulty in optimizing the filter station. If it is neces- 1
sary to pump the primary mud, the pumping action
shouldbe asgentleas possibleto prevent breakupof
the fragile floc particles. The high shear character-
istic of centrifugal pumps, as well as flow through
narrow pipes and valve orifices should be avoided.
Positive displacementplunger or diaphragmpumps
are more acceptable for this application. Many of
the older multi-tray clarifier installations were sup-
plied complete with diaphragm type slurry pumps,
but many of these have been phased out because
of the short life and high replacement cost of the
diaphragms, as well as the deleterious effects on
clarified juice quality when the diaphragmruptures.
Successful conversions of these to non-diaphragm
systems have been reported (Padalockand Quinan
1975,Muller 1976).
The merits of Mono pumps and air blowcase
systems as possible means of mud transfer have
been assessed. Noble and Atherton (1978) found
both systems to be more effective in obtaining a
high mud solids output than the centrifugal pump
normally used for mud transfer. Blowcase systems
were inferior. However, there was no evidence of
any significantdifferencein thepol lossexperienced
with changes in the method of mud transfer.
A Discflo pump, from Discflo Corp. Lnc. USA,
has been foundto be an effectiveprimary mud pump
at a 12 000 tlday Australian factory. It uses multi-
disc impeller technology to deliver laminar, pulsa-
tion-free flow without close tolerance. The unit
pump has a 150rnm outlet and is powered by an 11
kW motor. It lifts the clarifier underflow mud ap-
proximately 80 m to deliver to the mud mixer at the
filterstationand efficientlyhandlestheprimary mud
without any filtratedilution.
Control is stdstop depending on the mud
tank level, with the start-stop cycle approxi-
mately every 20 s. In this case the doc damage
to the muds must have been minimized because
no flocculant addition has been used on the fil-
ters since converting from a centrifugal to the
Discflo pump.

Wtrate recycling. In addition to its advantage
in facilitating mud flow, filtrate from the filtrate
, pumps can be circulated back to the mud mixer in
order to condition the filter feed for improved filter
behavior.Agius et al. (1977) showed that dilutingfil-
ter feed with water could reduce the pol loss in filter
cake,but subsequentlychanged thediluentto filtrate
to reduce the evaporation loading.The filtrate recy-
clingwasfoundto halve thepol loss. Lionnet (1984)
found better performance with a solids content of
not more than -4 g per 100g filter feed.
Considerableexperienceis required to set up a
filter station to handlediluted filter feeds.Thin filter
feeds produce cakes with a high porosity enabling
high wash water rates to be applied effectively. Pro-
vided the bagacillo ratio qFMs0is kept at approxi-
mately 0.50, a filtraterecycle of 20 % can be toler-
ated. The higher the bagacillo ratio, the higher the
quantity of filtrate required to maintain an accept-
able cake. At high filtrate recyclerates, filter feed is
very mobile. This eliminatesany possibility of feed
pipe blockages, and allows an evenfeed distribution
across the full length of the filter. Itproduces cakes
which are very even and are not prone to erosion
from added water on top of the drum. This allows
most of the wash waterto be applied to thetop of the
drum, thereby floodingthis section. The excess then
runs evenly across the full face of the filter.
Having a separate filtrate recycle line for each
filterhas the addedadvantagethat if one filteris shut
down the filtrateto feed ratio is automaticallymain-
tained. The necessary recycle liltrate line cross-sec-
tional area in rnm2is -16.6 times the surfacearea of
the filterin m2.

It has been found beneficial to the filter rate to
add milk of lime or lime saccharate to the mud in
the mud mixer to reach a pH of just under 8.5. Floc-
culants are sometimesadded to improve the perme-
ability of the filter cake. Additions up to 1 mglkg
cane can be used to increase the mud removal rate
during times of difficulty in clarification. However,
the pol in cake can increaseas a result, unless extra
wash water is applied at these times.
The equipment for mud mixing usually consists
of an elongated open mixer vessel stirred with a he-
lical ribbon agitator (at -22 min-', or tip speed 0.7
to 0.9 m/s if paddle arms are used). Both the clari-
fier mud underflow and the added bagacillo (from
the bagacillo cycloneoutlet) enter at one end of the
vessel, and the outflow is taken from the bottom of
the other end to feed the filters, as shown in Figure
11.4. Normally the mud mixer is set horizontally,
but an effective variation has been to run a semi-
closed mixing vessel on an angle to the horizontal,
also shown in Figure 11.4.This eliminatesleakage
from the shaftseals, and lowers heat lossesfrom the
mixer. The mixer should be insulated.
Recently some mixers of the vertical tank type,
fitted with multiple paddles on the stirrer, have
been installed in systems that do not require added
bagacillo. The stirrer shaft carries a horizontal cross
bar -0.3 m from the floor and this has four 50 mm
wide plate fingers on each side extending to the
bottom. The stirrer speed is 22 min-' and the outer
tip speed is in the 5-6 mls range. The cross bar has
two support arms to form a triangle. The primary
mud feed to the mixer is via a 300 r

m vertical box

bottom.
11.1.3 Mud mixers
Mud mixers have the functionsof incorporating
any added bagacillo and conditioning the mud to a
satisfactory temperature and pH. Flocculant solu-
tions are sometimes added in the mud mixer, though
itispreferabletoaddthemseparatelyinsmallmixers
attached to each individual filter. Because the gums
and waxes present in filter mud tend to solidify at
temperatures below 75 "C and so reduce the perme
ability of the filter cake, it is an advantage to retain
a temperature above75 "C in the filter feed.Polonio
(2004) has recorded a reduction in the rate of cake
L i e or lime-saccharateaddition.Saccharate
addition to the filter feed at the mud mixer to con-
trol filtrate pH in the range 7.5-8.5, has proven to
increase retention and reduce pol loss. Consistent
retentions of 90 % to 95 % can be readily achieved
with saccharateaddition (Attard1993).At a 12000
tlday factory, syruphe saccharate is delivered
from the juice pH control circuit to the mud mixer
via a 20 mm PVC hose with a 12 mm manual ball
valve at the mud mixer for control. Saccharatehas
been used with successas long as it has a relatively
low syrup level in the mix.

The quantity of bagacillo usually provided is to

Bagacillo used as a filtering medium in mud
treatment should conform to two basic criteria:
It must be very fine, smaller than 0.85 mm in
diameter. The surface area of the filter aid is
most important(the smaller the size,the greater
the area per kg);
The bagacillopreferably shouldbe derivedfrom
short strands and pith, to give a satisfactorypar-

filtering capacityand, in fact, are detrimental.
Bagacillo collection from final bagasse. Ba-
gacillo extraction and transport from the bagasse
conveyorto the mud mixer is very importantfor fil-
ter operation.It is covered in detailin Section26.4.
Bagacillo from the juice screem. Bagacillo
which has passed through the juice screening pro-
cess conforms to these criteria and is generally su-
perior to that from dry collection systems. Attard
(1993) describes the rotary juice screen system at
Racecourse factory, equipped with 0.5,0.8 and 1.2
mm wedgewire screens.Fiberlevelsin the screened

screenedjuice to each section.
Thequantityof bagacillo in the unscreenedjuice

cane variety and shredder hammer wear. With new
shredder hammer tips, thejuice is screened through
Me 0.5 mm wedge wire. As the hammers wear, the
juice entry to the cush cush screen is varied to di-
rect the flow over the 0.8 and 1.2 mrn screens. Best
results have been achieved with the 0.5mm screens

11.2 Filter equipment details
11.2.1 Plateandframefilterpresstech-
nologies
The early equipmentused formud filtrationwas
the batch plate and frame filter press (Tromp 1936,
Jenkins 1966).The main advantage of the plate and
framesystemwas thathigh mud solidscontentcould
be achieved in the cake, even with a relatively low
bagacillo ratio.
Disadvantages were the high floor area require-
ment,high labor cost,high cloth screenmaintenance
cost, and unsatisfactory wash efficiencyin the water
wash cycle. The disadvantages forced the replace-
ment of the plate and framewith rotary drum filters
by the 1960s.
Since the demise of the filter presses for this ap-
plication, however, there have been great improve-
ments in the plate filter technology with the intro-
duction of chamber filter presses.Thesehave a plate
pack of uniform plates with a recess of 15to 50 mm
to receive the filter cake, but the chamber plates are
a combination of a filterplate and two frames in one
piece. The systems can be configuredfor fully auto-
matic batch operation.
A modification of the chamber system is the
membrane filter plate system. A special plate cov-
ered with imperviousmembraneis insertedbetween
each chamber plate. When the filter cake has been
fully formed the membrane is inflated with high
pressure liquid or air to compress the cake to a very
high concentration of solids.
The frame is then opened and the compressed
cake dropped off. Some technologists consider that
membrane filter systems have sufficient promise to
merit investigations as an alternative to the rotary
drum technology.
Allen and Wirnmler (1994) concluded after a
cane sugar factory trial that the Netzsch membrane
filterpress is a viable alternative to rotary vacuum
filtertechnology,citingadvantagesincluding double
the solids content in cake, reduced quantity of filter
cake for transport disposal, reduced sucrose losses
and reduced use of wash water. Disadvantages were
seen as its higher cost relative to the equivalent ca-
pacity rotary drum filter, and the possible need for
annual replacement of the filter cloth.

.

.
2 Rotary drum vacuum filters
The early rotary drum continuousvacuum filters
for cane mud filtration were pioneered by Oliver-
Campbell and describedby Tromp (1936),but much
larger and more efficientversions are now marketed
by a number of suppliers.A modem version manu-
factured by Jord Australia is shown in Figure 11.6,
and the flow scheme for its operation in a sugar
factory in Figure 11.7. The filter is composed of a
hollow large diameter stainless steel drum rotating
about a horizontal axis and partly submerged in the
liquidtobe filtered.Theperipheryof thednunserves
as the filteringsurfaceand it is typically divided into
24 independent sector decks, each occupying 15"
on the Acumference, and extending along the full
length of the drum. Each of these sections is con-
nected individuallyto an intemal vacuum system by
stainless steel pipes with large radius swept bends
terminating in three port high capacity distributing
valves situated at one end of the drum and carrying
three differentsectors.Thefirstis the cake discharge
sector which vents directly to atmosphere.The sec-
ond is the cake pickup sectionwhich connectseither
directly to a low vacuum tank system or to a high
vacuum tank system through a control valve which
maintains the sector at the desired lower vacuum.
The third sector connects to a chamber where a
higher vacuum is maintained, at about 25 to 40 kPa
absolute.Lionnet (1996)recommends80and40kPa
absolute for pickup and high vacuum. Note that a
slightly higher absolute pressure leads to a higher
filtratetemperature,whichis desirablefrom a degra-
dation point of view,
The exterior screening surface of the drum con-
sists of a sheet of stainless steel with fine perfora-
tions.Thesectordeckshavea backing of open lattice
polypropylene or steel grids. Wash assemblies are
installedto applyhot water tothe upper30°quadrant
of the drum. The cake removal is by means of ad-
justable, segmented scrapers typically formed from
high-density polythene sheet, and these are coun-
terweighted to ensure close contact with the drum
screening surface. To aid cake removal, the trueness
of the drumround can be less than 2 mm.The mud
pool of the filter is agitated by oscillating paddles
with adjustableposition and adjustable speed.
For reasons of minimizing floc damage, a mod-
em filter station should best have gravity flow from
clarifier to mixer to filters, and there should be no
pumping of mud at all with a minimum overflow to
the mud liquidating tank.

A recent study (Polonio2004)evaluated thirteen
different types of primary filter media for use in the
vacuum filtration of sugarcane mud by simulating
the cake formation and dewateringoperationsin the
rotary vacuum drum filtersemployed in sugar mills
in Brazil.
The primary filtering media tested included
screens with round bores, made by different proce-
dures, various open areas, superficial types of fin-
ish, thicknesses and chemical corrosion resistance.
He compared the filtering indices obtained in the
formation and cake dewatering steps, for variations
