perature was found to have a very important effect
on the cake formationrate.
Cleaning of screens. It is necessary to keep the
screen holes clean to minimizeblockage and loss of
filtrationcapacity. Blocked screens are indicated by
bright bare patches on the filter when operatingwith
thin cakes.
Normal procedure at many factories is to aqua-
jet blocked areas with a high pressure water blast.
However it is sometimes necessary to treat blocked
screens in situ with warm 5-10 % caustic soda so-
lution by placing the solution in the filter boot and
rotating the drum in the cleaning solutionfor several
hours prior to cleaning with the high pressure wa-
ter blast system. Some factories use 2 '

% sulfarnic
acid as thecleaning solution.Screensare chemically
cleaned when the opportunity arises, for example
during a maintenance stop after a three week con-
tinuousoperation period.
11.2.6 Capacity and sizing
Filter capacity. An accepted general standard
for the filter area rating, defined as the total filter
area per unit crushing rate, used to be 0.56 m2 per
tJh. In South Africa a common standard is 0.6 m2
per tJh for milling and 0.33 m2per tJh for diffuser
factories. The filter area rating for Australian mills
varies from 0.38 to 1.3 but mills which have the
highest ratings do not necessarily have the lowest
pol losses.A largefilter area will not guaranteea low
pol loss because many factors are involved. Sulfita-
tion factories in India have a atering area of 0.5 to
0.7 m2per t$ (Kulkurni 1993:170)
An improved standardis to provide amud solids
loading (excludingfiber) of 1t/h per 100m2of fdter
area. The maintenance of a reasonable ratio of ba-
gacillo to mud solids in the filter feed becomes very
important as the soillevels in cane fluctuate
Filtration theory is of limited use in estidting
filter capacity because the specific resistance of the
compressible cake varies widely with, among other
things, the bagacillo quantity and quality, the use of
lime in the feed, and the addition of flocculants.In a
typical modern filter with a pickup zone of 50" and
typicaldrum rotation in the range 1.5to 5 mintrevo-
lution, the pickup filtering time ranges from 13 to
42 s. Polonio(2004)estimatedfrombatch filter tests
that the cake formation time at a pressure of 50kPa
was around 25 s. Steindl (2001) tested the filtering
rate of factory feed mud using a small batch filter
test apparatus with 100 mm diameter of standard
filter screen surface. The filtrate draw through the
screen was over 80 % completed in 60 s. Steindl's
results show that:
Enhancedbagacilloquantityandqualitydoubled
the passage of filtrate;
Feed treated with -2.5 mglkg feed of floccu-
lantsA and B improved the passageof filtrateby
83 %and 154% respectively.
Feed treated with -2.5 mgkg feed of flocculant
C improved the passage of filtrateby 180%;
Feed treated with -2.5 mg/kg feed of flocculant
C as well as the addition of extra bagacillo im-
proved the passage of filtrateby 390 %.
A balance on typical solids indicates that the build
thickness of the cake would be approximately half
that of the filtrate passage value. Thus the cake
thicknessescorrespondingtothe valuesabovewould
range from 5.5 to 30.5 mm.

Atturd (1993) emphasizes the importance of
maintaining the correct mud level in the filter boot.
The filter boot level should be controlled automati-
cally to avoid overflow of filter feed and recircula-
tion of primary mud. Cake porosity will generally
increase with the lowering of the mud level due to
theactionof the agitator. Thepickup vacuumbridge
blocks need to be set at an angle of no greater than
18"h m the verticalto coincidewith 10% submer-
gence.Experiencehasshownthatthecakeformation
in the bootis very rapid and thereis no advantagein
setting the pickup block any earlier. At this setting
boot levelscan be ont trolled safely at 15% submer-
gence without sucking air,The agitator should pref-
erablybreakthesurfacetomix any waterwhich may
run into the boot.
The sole role of the agitator is to prevent the
build up of sandin the boot by providing gentleagi-
tation of the mud. Filter manufacturerstend to s
u
p
ply agitators with speeds far in excess of the mini-
mum required to keep the solidsin suspension.The
cake is very delicate while being formed in the boot
andis easilyerodedby the actionof theagitator.Ag-
itatorspeeds should be kept under 5cyclesper min-
ute. The larger filters seem to be more susceptible
to cake erosion and agitator speeds of 2 to 3 cycles
per minute are recommended. A check on the agita-
tor effecton the filtercan easily be made by switch-

cake thicknessand porosity. Any changes should be
evidentwithin 10minutes.
The effect of the agitator seems to be more no-
ticeable with dilute filter feeds when the bagacillo
ratio is low (under 0.45). Some filtershave been run
successfully with the agitator off for extended pe-
riods without any indication of a build up of sand
70 in the boot. The problem of sand buildingup in the

A successfulfilterboot levelcontrol systemuses

8 Filter cake washing
The pol in mud cake is reduced by applying
wash water to the face of the filter. The amount of
applied wash is typically in the range 1 to 2 kgkg
cake, or 6.5 to 13 kg wash waterkg mud solids in
cake. The total amount of water used is typically
around one quarter of the imbibition water flow to
the extraction trains.
Washingis usually applied afterthe cakepickup
section using several rows of atomizers that spray
hot water on the cake, as seen in Figure 11.12.The
ideais that the appliedwater movesthroughthecake
to displace thejuice.
Thewashingcan be continuednear thetopof the
drum by hot water applicationpipes and sheetmetal
distributors that allow water to drip on the cake, to
prevent over-drying of the cake. On the final arc of
the drumas it approachesthe scrapersthe cake is al-
lowed to dry without any water addition. With good
displacement washing, the quantity of wash water
that passes into the clear filtrate represents only a
minor fraction of the water applied.
The wash water is normally derived from hot
condensate and is preferably at a temperature ex-
ceeding 80 OC.This keeps waxes in the cake from
solidifying and helps avoid problems with bacterial
growth. It should be distributed evenly across the
length of the drum and is most effective when ap-
plied to the rising side of the drum. A fine film of
water should also 5ow down the side, almost into
the boot, enabling an effectiveseal over the cake as
it emergesfrom the boot.
The pol of the cake is lowered by having more
wash application. However, the rate of reduction in
the pol loss with increased wash has to be balanced
by:
The ability of the cake to absorb the extra water
withoutchannelingand inefficiencies;
The reduction which could have been achieved
by the same water if applied as extra imbibition
in the extractionprocess;
The extra demand for process steam for evapo-
ration of the extra water;
Thetendency for lowerpurity in the filtratewith
extra washing (some partly soluble impurities
are leached out during the wasJing, resulting
in a purity drop between filtrate and the clear
juice).

practice' values of poVmud solids ratio (qSmSo)

11.2.9 Operationalcontrol
The operation of the filter stage is complex re-
quiring the interaction of good equipment control
and conditioning of filter feed. The combinedinter-
action of wash water addition, saccharate addition,
filtrate recycle, filter and clarifier flocculant addi-
tion, maintaining the optimum fiber (bagacillo) ra-
tio, filter head setting, boot level, d
r
u
m speeds and
agitator speeds,as well as attentionto the trainingof
operators, has to be tuned for optimumresults with
regards to pol loss and filter operations.
The optimum conditions for operation depend
on the type and capacity of the filter installation
and its auxiliary services, on the mud solids loading
(varying with the soil loading in the juice), and on
the constraints on wash water addition.

Mud transfer preferably by gravity or by a low-
turbulence type of pump;
Continuous feed to the filter boot with no over-
flow;

11.2.10 Filter cake analyses and mud
solidsretention
Theestimation of the insoluble solidscontent in
a sampleof filtercake involves the determinationof
the fraction of total solids by drying, and a correc-
tion for the soluble solids. This is calculated from
the value of the water content in the sample and the
refractometer Brix of a filtered portion of the origi-
nal sample.
The fiber fraction of the insoluble solids is usu-
ally defined as that retained on a 100 mesh gauze
base sieve after extensivewashing with clear water.
The remainder is defined as the mud solids, and is
composed of clarification precipitates as well as
soil particles washed from the canein the extraction
train.
The fiberratio is the ratio of the fiber (or bagac-
illo) fraction to the mud solids fraction. It is usually
measured in filter feed as an operational control pa-
rameter, but can also be measured in filter cake to
assist in the calculation of filter retention.
Mud solids retention. Retention is defined as
thepercentage of thetotal mud solidsin filter feed
(excludingfiber) retained in the filter cake.
In filter evaluation the aim is generally to de-
termine whether retention is low (<70 %), medium
(70-85 %) or high (> 85 %). Methods which can be
used to detennineretention are:
Retention can be approximated from the rela-
tive fiber ratio in feed and cake. It is assumed
that allof the fiberin filterfeedisretained in the
cake.

11.2.11 Cake handling
Mud scrapers. The design of the mud scraper
that removes the cake from the drum is an important
factor in good filter operation. Imperfect scraping
can result in blinding of screens. Scraper operation
becomes especiallyimportantwith fast drumspeeds
and t
h
i
ncakes.
Most modem designs use segmented floating
scraperscounterweightedor sprungto follow irregu-
larities in the drum. It is important that the scraper
lightly bears on the drum with a wide uniform pro-
file curve face so as not to wedge any particulates
into the screen holes. In order to avoid snagging,
the width of the scrapertip should be wider than the
width of thecaulkingstripsbetween screensections.
Many materialshave been used in scraperblades but
the most common material presently used is high
density polyurethane. The blades gradually wear
and must be dressed occasionally to restore their
originalprofile.
Filter mud disposal. The simplest form of fil-
ter cake disposal is to have a sluice system which
washes the mud away to be disposedof in the fields.
Unfortunately, this systemis now largely prohibited
by environmental regulations. In any case it was
able to service only a limited area of field adjacent
to the factory. In Louisiana the mud is often sluiced
into large holding dams and dredged out in the off-
season; this is only practicable because of the short
three-month season.
If the mud filters are positioned at a high level
it can be arranged that mud falls through a chute di-
rectly into amud storagebin, arrangedto loadmotor
trucks. It is more usual, however, that the mud falls
from individual filters onto collection belts which
are then consolidatedontoa singlebelt that delivers
into an elevatedmud bin. Sometimes the filter mud
is combinedwith boiler ash obtained by settling and
filtration of the recirculated water from wet collec-
tors in the boiler flues. Themixture has an enhanced
value as a soilconditioner.
Itisimportantthat thewater contentof themudor
mud-ash mixture is regulated so that excessive spill-
age during truck loading and road transport is avoid-
ed, as this can lead to environmentalcomplaints.
Motor truck companies are often contracted to
remove the mud at their own cost, obtaining their
incomefrom sales of the mud to cane farmersfor its
value as a fertilizerand soil conditioner.Automatic
fillmechanismsallow therapid loading of the trucks
to be activated by the truck operator. Shrouds of
rubber matting can be used to minimizespillsPiom
loading. An injection water flushing system on the
concrete floor can be arranged to flush away mud
after each truck fill, with a sump pump transferring
the washings to the ash system and keeping the area
clean.
In an earlier system, the mud was dropped into
a trailer, which, as soon as it was filled, was taken
by tractor for spreading the filter cake on the fields,
and the trailerwas immediatelyreplaced to continue
the filling.
Where a mud belt systemis used there is theop-
portunityfor the fittingof a belt weigherto integrate
the total mud output from the station. The produc-
tion of the filtermud can be checked with the total
net mass of the loads in the motor trucks used to
remove the mud and deliverit to the cane fields.

11.3.5 Filtrate clarification
Filtrates are commonly returned to raw juice,
either to the raw juice tank prior to heating or to an
intermediatetank (if it exists).Thelatter systemhas
the advantage that the flow increase due to filtrate
return does not apply to the primary heating step.
To avoid the effects of filtrate return, it was a
commonpractice in the past to re-clarify the filtrates
in a special small clarifier, after reheating and l
i
m
-
ing.Avery clearjuice is thusobtained,togetherwith
thick mud, which is returned to the rotary filter.
Suviron Ltd., India, market a trayless clarifier
system and equipment for the treatment of filtrate
which they claim to provide consistently assured
performanceresults. Apart from the obviousgain in
the capacityof themain clarifierby avoidingrecycle,
it is possible that the more compact nature of mud
in the filtrate clarifier offers improved performance
at the vacuum filter station by increasing the thick-
ness and porosity of filter cake (Hugot1986:272),
as well as other advantages(lower color, lowerCaO
content, less deterioration). The disadvantages are
the extra complexity, the need for an extra heater,
reaction tank, and clarifier, and for extra addition
controls (lime or lime-saccharate, phosphate and
flocculant).
The filtratesmay alsobe treated by phospho-flo-
tation,aspioneered by Tateand Lyle(TaloFiltration)
for the clarification of cane juice. A scheme mar-
keted by ChemicalSystemsTechnologists(India)is

11.4 Microbiological losses
11.4.1 Effeet ~f temperature
The opportunity for microbiological losses in
the filter is relatively high, especially if the mud
temperature is allowed to fall below 75 O C . During
shutdownor stoppages,the filter must be thoroughly
drained and cleaned, and the surface steamed to dis-
infect the internal filtrate pipes and the drum sur-
face.
It is important to keep the filter feed and wash
watertemperatureshigh tominimizemicrobiological
losses in and around the mud filters. The wash wa-
ter would preferably be condensatewater at -80 OC.
Formaldehyde dosing is one effective method of

Evaporation is a key unit operation in a sugar
mill and is the principal factor that determines its
energy efficiency. It is the major user of steam in
concentrating clarified juice to a dissolved solids
content of about 65 to 68 %. The way the evapo-
rator station is configured determines the amount
of steam that the factory requires and so the ar-
rangement of the evaporators is a most important
consideration. Multiple effect evaporation enables
the steam requirement to be reduced and the bulk
of evaporation of water is done by this means. The
limiton syrupconcentrationis the approachto satu-
ration atwhichpointcrystallizationstarts. In theory
this would limit the RDS to about72 8,but in prac-
tice a safety margin of at least two units is chosen,
to allow some leeway in control and to allow for
same cooling of syrup in storage without crystal-
lization occurring.
This chapter starts with the fundamentals of
boiling heat transfer. The calculations for multiple
effect evaporationare coveredin detail,before con-
sidering the types of evaporator available and the
design of evaporators.The operation of evaporators
and the scaling and cleaning of evaporators follow
this.
1 Boiling heat transfer
L
12.1.1 Range of temperatures and
pressures
The steam suppIy to the evaporators is usually
b8exhaust steam, which may be ata pressure between
about 180 and 250 kPa. The correspondingvapor
saturation temperatures are 117 "C and 127 "C. In
this Chapter all pressures will be expressed in kPa
absolute values. It should be remembered that 100
kPa is equivalent to 1bar or 14.5lb/in2.
The lastvesselin the set of evaporatorsnormal-
ly runs at a pressure between 12and 17kPa, corre-
sponding to saturated vapor temperatures of 49 "C
and 57 "C.This pressurerangeroughly corresponds
to a vacuum of between 26.5" and 25" mercury in
most sugar mills, which tend to be located close to
sea level. The same vacuum at different elevations
or atmospheric pressures gives different absolute
pressures and saturationtemperatures.
This is a good reason to prefer the use of abso-
lute pressure to vacuum in all cases. The optimum
finaleffectabsolutepressureis discussedin Section
12.5.3.
Pressure evaporation, where most or all of the
vessels operate above atmospheric pressure, as
practiced in the beet sugarindustry, is avoided for a
number of reasons:
There is not the sameneed to reduce steam us-
age, since the fuel provided by bagasse is usu-
ally sufficient without extreme fuel economy
measures.
Cane sugarjuice is much higher in invert sug-
ars, so that increased color formation that re-
sults from the reaction of these reducing sugars
at higher temperatures is a bigger issue.
Sucrose losses and color formation are mini-
mized by lowering the temperature profile
through evaporation.
The lower temperature profile makes the use
of simple Robert type evaporators with longer
juice residence times feasible without excessive
inversion losses.

12.2.1 Rillieux's principles
It is also important to note the method used to

all the liquid in the vessel is fully mixed. However
in a falling film evaporator, this would clearly not
be true and the boiling point elevation should be
evaluatedat the valueof RDSrepresentingthe aver-
age of liquid inlet and outlet values (the inlet RDS
value is the averageof feedfrom the previouseffect
and recirculated liquid). This is not important with
low RDS juices, but can become very significant
when the liquid is more concentrated.
In comparing heat transfer coefficients, it is
important to understand how they have been calcu-
lated. In this text, forRobert and rising film evapo-
rators, the heat transfer coefficientis calculated as-
suming:
The liquid boiling temperature is higher than
the vapor saturationtemperatureby the boiling
point elevationsdue both to the dissolvedsolids
and the hydrostatichead.
The boiling point elevationdue to the dissolved
solidsis computed at the outlet Brix.
The heat transfer area is calculated using the
outside area of the tubes and the length of tube
between tube plates.
For falling filmevaporators, the boiling point eleva-
tion should be calculated at the average Brix and no
allowanceis necessary forhydrostatichead. Area is
calculatedthe sameway irrespectiveof whetherit is
a rising or falling film'evaporator.
12.2 Principles of multipleeffect
evaporation
12.2.1 Rillieux's principles
Multiple effect evaporation was developed by
Norbert Rillieux in Louisiana and was patented in
the 1840s.It has had far-reaching consequences for
sugar and many other process industries. From his
investigations in the cane sugar industry, he devel-
oped generalized rules or principles for evaporator
design and performance:
1. In a multiple-effectevaporator of N effects, one
kg of steam will evaporateNkg of water. Thus,
in a doubleeffectevaporator,one kg steamwill
evaporate two kg of water, in a triple effect,
three kg, and so on.
2. If vapor is withdrawn from the ith effect of a
multiple-effect evaporatorof Neffectsand used
outsidethe evaporatorsystemin place of steam,
the steam saving will be i/N times the quantity
of steam used in this duty. Thus, one kg of va-
por withdrawn from the second effect of a four
effect evaporator would save 2/4 x 1 = 0.5 kg
steam. Similarly, one kg of vapor withdrawn
from the third effect of the same evaporator
would save 314 x 1=0.75 kg steam.
Chen and Chou (1993) give a third principle, al-
though only the first two were the subject of Rill-
ieux's patents. This is:
3. Wherever steam or vapor is condensed, provi-
sion must be made to withdraw incondensable
gases continuously.
The first two principles are used to configure the
evaporatorarrangement tousejust the right amount
of steam for evaporation, consistent with the avail-
ability of bagasse and steam. Nearly all cane sugar
mills have an evaporator system comprising be-
tween 3 and 5 effects. It is also general practice to
bleed vapor from at least the first effect, and often
from the second or third effects, for heating duties
in the heater and pan boilingstations.
The steam economy achieved does not come
without cost however. The available temperature
difference between exhaust steam and final vessel
conditionshas to be sharedamong a greaternumber
of vessels as the number of effects increases. This
means that the surface area in total has to increase
correspondingly, and the larger number of effects
also adds additional cost in terms of extra piping,
control and complexity. Nonetheless it is gener-
ally always worthwhile to accept some extra cost
in view of the very much larger benefit in terms of
energy efficiency that accrues. This is covered in
more detail in Section 12.5.
12.2.2 Vapor bleeding
The further down the evaporator system that a
vapor bleed is taken, the lower is its temperature.
Thus to gain steam economy (and often capacity),
the bleed would be chosen to come from the lat-
est effect possible; this is normally constrained by
the duty for which it is to be used. Thus vapor 1
Referencesp. 316
Evaporation
is normally used for pan boiling andjuice heating,
although the first stage of juice heating and con-
tinuous pan boiling is often done with vapor 2. Va-
por 3 is only used in cases where abnormally high
steam economy is required, generally as a result
of a downstream activity that requires more steam
and/or bagasse, thus limiting its availability to the
factory.
12.2.3 Cocurrent vs. countercurrent
vs. mixedflow systems
It is normal practiceto configurethe evaporator
to operatein cocurrentmode i.e. with the liquid and
vapor flows in the same direction,as shown in Fig-
ure 12.3A. In other industries,it is not uncommon
to see evaporators operating in countercurrentor a
mixed flow arrangement, as shownin Figure 12.3B
and 12.3C. There is a case to be made for counter-
currentflow, because this resultsin the highest con-
centration and hence the most viscous liquid being
evaporated in the hottest effect. However cocurrent
operation is chosen in sugar processing for the fol-
lowingreasons:
Color formationdepends on concentration and
temperature. To minimize color formation,the
most concentrated stream is processed at the
lowest temperature.
Sucrosedegradationlossesaretime and temper-
I
ature dependent. The dissolvedsolidsresidence
times in the early effectsare lower in cocurrent
flow, limiting the sucrose losses.
The juice leaving an effect in cocurrent flow

Conversely in countercurrent flow, the liquid
entering an effect is sub-cooled, so that a pro-

transfer.
* In countercurrentflow, the flash in the hot clari-

The pressure profile in cocurrent flow is such

a simpler arrangement.
The major proportion of evaporator scale com-

Amixed flowsystemissometimesencountered.This

last effect, gaining some of the advantages of both
modes of operation. If evaporators are used which
incorporate circulating pumps anyway e.g. falling
film evaporators,pumping to any effect is possible.
12.2.4 Heat transfer rates
The rate of heat transfer is best expressed as a
heat transfer coefficient, representing the heat flux
per unit temperaturedifference,as defined in equa-
tion (12.11). The rate of heat transfer is sometimes
expressed as an evaporation coefficient, expressed
as kg water evaporatedper hour per squaremeter of
heating surface.This does not take into account the
temperature difference,which is the major driving
force for heat transfer. It is largely affected by the
aumber of effects in use, as well as by the distribu-
tion of heating surfaces, and so is inherently less
useful.
Heat transfer coefficients represent important
data in the design of evaporators.The same factors
influencingheat transfer injuice heating outlinedin
Section 9.1.3 apply in evaporation. Thus there are
a number of resistances to heat transfer in series,
a resistancedue to a liquid film inside the tube, an
effect of scale inside the tube, the resistance of the
metal tube, a scale layer on the outside of the tube
(uncommon) and a resistance to transfer through
the condensingvapor on the outside of the tubes.
However the case of evaporation is far more
complicated, since the heat transfer to the liquid
boiling inside the tube is more difficult to predict
from first principles. It is affected by the rate at
which the liquid flows through the tube, which is
an unknown, and by the level of liquid boiling in
the tubes, which can also vary significantly. Thus
a much greater relianceis placed on measured heat
transfer coefficientsin evaporators,choosingvalues
for design based on experience in similar applica-
tions.
As with juice heating, the degree of scaling in-
side the tubes is almost the overriding factor. Scal-
ing is more severe in evaporation than heating be-
cause more species of compounds will precipitate
as their solubility limits arereached in the courseof
concentratingthe liquid.
Heat transfer coefficients decrease along the
length of the evaporator train, because of the in-
creasein dissolvedsolidsconcentrationand thepro-
gressive reduction in temperature from one effect
to the next. Both these factors lead to an increase
in liquid viscosity, which reduces the rate of heat
transfer.
The heat transfer coefficients are different for
different types of evaporator. A comparison be-
tween those achieved in different types is given in
Section 12.6.2.The great majority of evaporators in
canesugarmills are still of the conventionalRobert
design. The performance of long tube rising-film
evaporators, also known as Kestner evaporators,
seems to be similar to that of Robert evaporators.
This discussion will therefore be restricted to these
types of evaporator.Reliable data for other types of
evaporatorare in any eventscarce,as Section 12.6.2
shows.
The heat transfer coefficients are considerably
higher when the tubes are clean than when they are
in a scaled condition. From a design point of view,
the heat transfer coefficient when the vessels are

5 Heat losses
No comprehensivemeasurementsof heat losses
in practice are reported.They are of course depen-
dent on the degree of insulation of the vessels and
piping. Fives Cail recommend a figure of 1.5 % of
the heat exchanged in the calandria for each effect
(Journet 2005). This seems to be a reasonable as-
sumption.The total heat losswill thereforebe high-
er with a larger number of effects.
The heat loss is higher from the first effects,
as the loss is dependent on the vessel temperature
relative to ambient temperature. Heat losses have
more significancein the firsteffectsince the loss in
evaporation will affect all subsequent vessels. It is
important to ensure that the early effects are well-
insulated. Conversely there is little need to insulate
the vapor line from the last effect.
12.2.6 Quantity of incondensable gases
A small quantity of incondensablegas is always
presentin steamand vapor. As thesteamcondenses,
the quantity of incondensablegas builds up and will
ultimately blanket the heating surfaceand stop heat
transferunless theincondensablesare removed.
There is relatively little incondensable gas,
mainly air, in exhaust steam. In evaporation, some
of the volatiles in the juice are evaporated, not all
of which condense, so that evaporator vapors will
have a slightlyhigher contentof incondensables.In
addition,for those vesselswhich are under vacuum,
higher quantities of air may be introduced through
leaks in the vessel or the vapor piping. Honig
(1963:172) reports that the quantity of incondens-
able gases varies from 10 mgtkg water evaporated
in the first effect to 100-200 mg/kg water evapo-
rated in a final effect.
Honig (1963:166-168) recommends that the in-
condensables content in steam should never be al-
lowed to rise above 2 g/100 g at any time to ensure
that the heat transfer is not adversely affected.This
implies that the amount of vapor to be withdrawn
should be at least 50 times the amount of incon-
densable gases. Thus the quantity of incondens-
ables purged should be 50 times 100-200 mg/kg,
i.e. 5-10 g&g or 0.5-1.0 %. It is a reasonabletarget
therefore to aim to vent 1 % of the vapor entering
a calandria.
The incondensablesmay be purged to the next
effect, but some references recommend purging
calandrias above atmosphericpressure to the atmo-
sphere and all otherincondensablesto the last effect
vaporspace,topreventincondensablebuild-upinthe
later calandrias.Thereis littledifferencein terms of
steam economy. However if all incondensables are
bled to the last effect,they shouldbe piped separate-
ly, so that adjusting one bleed does not change the
back pressure on another bleed, thus affecting that
flow.Choked flow occurs in all incondensablelines
vented to the last effect, and careful sizing of lines
is necessary to take this into account.In this respect
it is easier to vent incondensables successively to
succeedingeffects, with shorter incondensablelines
and choked flow only in venting the last calandria.

Calculation for multiple effect evaporation can
be simplified significantly through the use of a few
assumptions, to give answers that are surprisingly
accuratefor cocurrentmultiple evaporator systems.
The assumptionsnecessary are:
Thespecificheatof evaporationdoesnotchange
with pressure.
All liquid enthalpies are constant, regardless of
temperatureand dissolved solids concentration.
There are no heat losses.
It is shown in Section 12.1.4 that these assumptions
lead to equation (12.10), which states that one kg
of steamcondensed in an evaporator will evaporate
one kg of water. These assumptions lead to errors
which tend to workin opposite directions,thus par-
tially and fortuitously cancelingeach otherout.
The disadvantage of this method is that it takes no
account of heat transferrates and areas,which must
be calculated using the ~igorous

evaporation. From a total solids balance over an

method
Equations (12.28) to (12.37) are sufficient for
the calculations to be undertaken. It generally re-
quiressometrial anderrorcalculation,which nowa-

age or on a spreadsheet using iterative calculations.
Convergenceisnormallyrapid. A solution of simul-
taneous equations may also be used, but this still
requires some iteration to update some of the coef-
ficients (Hoekstra 1981). Equations for enthalpy of
vapor and liquid and for the saturated steam tem-
perature-pressurerelationshipfacilitatethe calcula-
tions, as given for instance by Bubnik et al. (1995)
or by the simplified equations provided in Section
32.1. The relationshipfor boiling point elevation as
a function of Brix (equation 12.1)is suitable.
The starting assumptionswill vary, depending
on whether a design is being carried out for a new
or upgraded installation or if calculations are be-
ing undertaken to evaluate the heat transfer perfor-
mance of an existing evaporatorset.

12.5.1 Infiuence of number of effects
Rillieux's first principle describes clearly the
fundamental fact that the steam economy is very
closeto the number of effects, i.e. anNeffectevapo-
ratorrequires 11Nkg steamto evaporate 1kg of wa-
ter. The total heating surface goes up more or less
in proportion to N.
In fact it goes up at a faster rate, because of the
phenomenon of boiling point elevation in each ef-
fect which reduces the overall temperature differ-
ence available for heat transfer. This is illustrated
in Figure 12.7, which shows that the sum of the
temperaturedifferencesmiis 51.7 "Cwhereas the
total temperaturedifferencefrom exhaust steam to
last vessel vapor is 65.0 "C.

3 Effect of exhauststeam and last
vessel absolutepressmes
The greater the difference in pressure between
the exhaust steam and the last vessel pressure, the
greater is the availabletemperaturedifferenceand
therefore the greater the potential for evaporation.
In practice there areconstraintsand limits on both
pressures and optima for both depend on the par-
ticular millcondiriom.
Exhauststeampressure. Thechoiceof exhaust
steampressurerequires a compromisebetween dif-
ferent factots.
If the exhaust steam pressure is high, more
evaporation can be achieved in a given set of
evaporators.
A high exhaustseeam pressuregenerally means
higher vapor pressures, making vapor bleeding
from latereffects feasible.
However there are good reasons for keeping the
exhauststeampressure down, includingthe follow-
ing:
A high exhaust steam pressure increases the
amount of exhaust steam generated in the tur-
Referencesp. 316
Evaporation
bines. This affectstheoverall energy balance of
the mill.
High pressures lead to a generally increased
temperature profile through the evaporators,
which leads to increased sucrose losses (see
Section 12.8.8)and unwanted colorformation.
In practice, an exhaust steam pressure around
200kPa seems appropriate in most circumstances.
Exhaust steam superheat is considered in Section
12.8.3.
Lastvessel absolutepressure.As withexhaust
steam pressure, there are conflicting factors which
affect the choiceof the optimum pressure of the fi-
nal vessel. The lower the last vessel pressure, the
greateris the overall temperaturehop availablefor
evaporation.However there are other factorswhich
are relevant:
Low pressures lead to low vapor densities,
which in turn lead to high vapor velocities that
promote entrainment.
Low pressureslead to low temperatures, which
result in higher viscosities, materially affecting
the rate of heat transfer.
The syrup temperature should ideally be close
to 60 "C,hot enough for feed to the pans but
low enoughto obviate lossesin the syrup tank,
this corresponds to a pressure of about 17
kPa.
Smith and Taylor (1981) showed that an optimum
for maximum capacity exists, which is fairly flat
in the region of 16 to 20 kPa, corresponding to va-
por saturationtemperaturesbetween 55 and 60 "C.
These conclusionsare generally supportedby most
writers. For instance,Hugot (1986:541) advocates a
final vacuumbetween 24 and 26",corresponding to
absolute pressures between 13.3 and 20 kPa. Perk
(1973) recommends that the final effect pressure
should not be less than 15kPa.
On balance a last effectpressure of 16to 17kPa
(25" vacuum) seems to be optimal in most condi-
tions.

12.5.5 Use of condensateflash
+ 8
It is normally of advantageto flash condensate
from one calandria to the calandria of the succeed-

occurs. Condensate from subsequent calandrias is
flashed to eachfollowingcalandria, and then mixes
with condensate from the next calandria. Conden-
satesfrompans may be addedto the combinedcon-
densatestreamto augmentthe process.
This arrangement has the followingadvantages:
Steam economy is improved, because vapor is
added to the calandrias, each kg of vapor flash
from condensate from the ith effectevaporating
an additional(N-i) kg of water.
It eliminatesthe condensateloss incurred if the
condensateis simply taken to a condensatestor-
age tank where flash to the atmosphereoccurs.
Thecondensatenottakentotheboilersis flashed
down to the pressurein the last calandria. This
is normally at a temperature of about 80 O
C to
85 OC, ideal for use as imbibition or for use in
the factory.
The disadvantage of condensate flashing is that a
slight reduction in overall evaporation rate results,
of the orderof a few per cent, sincethe effectof the
extra vapor flows lower down the evaporator tail is
to reduce temperature differences in the early ef-
fects, where heat transfer coefficients are high, and
increase temperature differences in the last effect
where the heat transfer coefficientis lower. Both of
theseeffectsare evident in the set of evaporatorcal-
culationsin Table 12.4;comparing cases5 and 6 for
quadruple effect and cases 9 and 10 for quintuple
effect shows that without condensateflash the area
required is slightly lower, but that with flashing fol-
lowing the arrangement in Figure 12.8,the exhaust
steamrequirementis reduced.
12.5.6 Heatingsurfacedistribution
The need to maintain a required pressure of
vapor 1 (and perhaps also vapor 2 if substantial
bleeding is done) will generally set the area of the
firsteffect (andperhaps the secondeffect).The area
necessary in subsequent effects is chosen to give
the required degree of evaporation. The areas are
often chosen based on vessels of the same size, to
simplify manufacture and reduce costs- However
this does not result in the optimum use of heating
surface. This is a consequence of the fact that the
last effect k value is much lower than those of the
earliereffects.
The optimumchoice of areas for evaporator ef-
fects (after those involved with vapor bleeding) has
been discussed by Hoekstra (1981), who showed
thatforthe optimumdistribution of heatingsurface,
the ratio of heating surface to temperature differ-
ence should be constant for each effect. This may
be written as:
=constant

Since the k values decrease towards the last effect,
causingtemperaturedifferencestoincrease,the area
of each effectshouldincrease down the tail to opti-
mize the distributionof areas.Rein (2001) showed
that with vapor 1bleeding, the optimum choice of
area in the subsequenteffects in a quadrupleeffect
systemcan lead to areduction of 7.3 %in area or an
increase of 4.1 % in capacity if the optimum distri-
bution is used instead of equal sized vessels.

Evaporation
Falling 6lm tubular evaporators. These evap-
orators have some of the same advantages as the
Kesmer evaporator, namely the use of long tubes
and more compact vessels. However, they require
uniform and adequate wetting of the tubes and so
need the complication of juice recirculation and
a distribution system feeding equal quantities of
juice to every tube. An emergencywater feedto the
evaporator is also required, in case the juice sup-
ply fails; the absence of adequate feed even for a
shorttime can lead to severe fouling of the tubes. A
pump-around systemand levelcontrolsrepresent an
additional complication. Typical arrangements are
shown in Figure 12.11.
Risingfilm plate evaporators. These are simi-
lar in constructionto plate heaters, with a series of
plates contained in a frame. Latest designs consist
of two adjacent plates welded together to constitute
the steam passages, with the juice passages formed
between adjacentsteam plates separatedby gaskets.
Juiceis fed in at the bottom and starts to boil within
the plate pack as it rises. The mixture of liquid and
vapor exiting from the plate pack passes to a ves-
sel in which the liquid separatesfrom the vapor and
some form of entrainment separator is installed.
These evaporators are often used as add-on heating
surface to an existing evaporator effect, but there
are someinstancesof their use as stand-aloneevap-
orator effects(de Beer and Moult 1998).
Care needs to be given to the design to ensure
adequate liquid flow rates through the unit. Design
of the plates and the juice distribution system are
important if uniform flow is to be achieved in the
evaporators. de Beer and Moult (1998) and others
report seriousscalingof theplates if the systemsare
not operated with sufficient recirculation or if the
juice distributioninto the plates is not uniform.
These evaporators give high heat transfer rates,
have a low holdup of juice and provide a compact
installation. Another version of these plate heaters
incorporatinga platepack inside an evaporatorves-
sel has not found much utility.
Falling film plate evaporators. This is the
newest design of evaporator. It consists of a pack
of corrugated stainless steelplates welded together,
without the need for gaskets. It is designed in such
a way that the juice passages approximate a series
of vertical tubes, typically 9 mrn in diameter(Sich-
ter et al. 2003) down which the liquid flows (Figure
12.12). Like the rising film system, steam or vapor

high temperaturesof the firstfew effects. The other

Effect of suspended solids. Plate evaporators
are susceptible to blocking by solid particles or ba-
gasse fibers, because of the small gaps. It is gener-
ally necessary therefore to have in-line strainers to
remove these particles.Juice distributorson falling
film evaporators are also susceptible to blocking
with solid particles, but they are now carefully de-
signed to distribute liquid in more than one stage
and have largely overcome the problems. Because
of the propensity for scale formation in cane sugar
mills,in somedesignsthewholedistributionsystem
can be removed to access the tubes for mechanical
cleaningif necessary (Journet2005).
Size and heating surface density. With the
trend to larger factories, it becomes more impor-
tant to be able to install evaporators of larger size.
The rising film plate units are generally restricted
to unit sizes of less than 2000 m2.Robert evapora-
tors are generallyrestricted to about 3000 m2each,
as the diameter gets too large. However Quinan et
al. (1985) report on the construction of a 5100 m2
evaporator; the diameter of vessels of this size is
6.9 m. Falling film and Kestner units of 6000 m2
and more have been installed, with considerably
smallerdiameters.
In terms of heating surface density, the falling
film plate unit has the greatest value of 240 m2of
heating surfaceper m3of volume. Rising film plate
units have a density of 90 m2/m3and tubularevapo-
rators a value of 40 to 50 m2/m3(Ausrmeyeret al.
1995).
Hydrostatic head effect. The liquid has to be
heated to above the boiling point when submerged
under a head of liquid. This has the most signifi-
cant effect at low absolutepressures,in which case
it seriously reduces the temperature difference for
heat transfer. A significant advantage of the falling
filmunits is the absenceof a hydrostatic head effect
on evaporation. This phenomenon becomes more
important the greater the number of effects a d
the higher the RDS,and it is particularlyimportad
when very high thermaleconomiesare sought.

Cleaning options. Robert and Kestner evapo-
rators can be mechanically or chemically cleaned.
All other options require chemical cleaning. With
better wetting in plate and falling film units, t
h
e
tendency to scale should be reduced,but there is no
evidence to support this. In-place cleaning of place
evaporators is easily accomplished.
Costs. The plate units are generally more com-
pact and should result in lower installation costs
However Robert and Kestner evaporators generally
provide a much simpler installation, with simpler
piping, no pumps and minimal controls. In 2005the
newer types of evaporatordo not appear to result in
lower installed costs.

long tube evaporatorsare significantlycheaper thas
Robert evaporators (Rein and Love 1995).
Expansion options. Rising film plate evapora-
tors are flexiblein that oftenadditionalplatescan be
added to the pack in the existing frame to increase
capacity.They are also finding increasingutility as
an add-on to a particular evaporatoreffect that r e p
resents a bottleneck.
An interesting expansion option involves re-
moving a tubular calandria from a Robert evapo-
rator and installing a falling film plate pack inside
the existingvessel. With the greaterheating surface
density and the higher heat transfer coefficientsob-
tainable,an effective increase in capacity of 100%
can be achieved in the same vessel (Rivalland
2000). Piping and valving costs associated with t
h
e

In other cases when mills expand, a large size
long tube evaporator is often installed as a first ef-
fect, with existingRobert vessels rearranged in the
remaining effects, to run in parallel in some cases.
This isparticularlyadvantageousin achievinga low
residence time in the hottest first effect.

sure to the first effectcan be controlled without
affectingthe vapor bleed pressures.
There are also some disadvantages:
Unless the exhaust steam pressure is controlled
to give a steady vapor pressure, variations in
pan vapor pressure could be larger with a pre-
evaporator since there is no base load of vapor
to the next effect.
There is a need to pump juice to the first effect
after the pre-evaporator.
Because of the varying load in the pre-evapora-
tor (dependent on the pan draw off), the juice
Brix varies more, making overall evaporator
control more difficult.
Vapor cells (pre-evaporators) lead to greater
fluctuations, which are more likely to lead to
entrainment(Perk 1973).
If the pan draw off is low, the heating surfaceis
under-utilized.
An evaporator set with a pre-evaporator achieves
essentially the same steam economy as an evapora-
tor set without a pre-evaporator, provided that the
set without the pre-evaporator has a 1steffect heat-
ing surface equal to that of the pre-evaporator and
the 1st effect, and where the pre-evaporator load is
absorbedby the 1steffect. On balance thereis prob-
ably little justification for the use of pre-evapora-
tors, which add unnecessarycomplication.
12.6.4 Vapor line sizing
Vapor lines need to be large enough to ensure
that the pressure drop along them is negligibly
small relative to the total pressure drop available.
It can be shown by calculationthat a pressure drop
between vessels of 1 kPa will reduce capacity of a
quadrupleeffectevaporatorsetby lessthan 1%, but
that to achievethe same effect in a quintuple effect,
the pressure drop between effects should be below
about 0.5 kPa.
Given that each vapor line has on average
2 bends, perhaps a gate valve and an entrancelexit
loss, a total of around one velocity head loss is ex-
pected. One velocity head is u2.pv/2Pa; in orderto
keep below 0.5 kPa, u2 . pJ2 should be < 500, i.e.
u <(1000/pv)0.5.
Clearly ahighervelocity is accept-
ableat a lowerpressure correspondingto alower va-
por density. Using this relationship, the maximum
calculated vapor velocity is shown in Table 12.7.
Table 12.7: Vapor velocitiesto givea0.5kPa pressure
dropbetween effects

in kPa in kg/m3 in m/s
These values should be used as a guide in siz-
ing vapor lines. A pipe diameter should be chosen
to give a velocity lower than those in Table 12.7.
Where the temperaturedifferenceacross an evapo-
rator is low (say 4 to 5 'C on a large 1steffect with
vapor bleeding), a smallerpressure dropmay be de-
sirableand a lower velocity selected.
12.7 Design of tubular evapora- ,
tor vessels I
12.7.1 Calandriadesign
The calandriashouldbedesigned to getuniform
steam flow to all tubes and to positively vent incon-
densable gases to the vapor space. With normally
encountered spacirig of tubes, it can be shown that
the pressure drop through the tube bank is negligi-
bly small,leadingto amoreor lessuniform pressure
in all parts of the calandria. Some designers have
considered that vapor velocities on the steam side
need to be kept high at all points in the calandria.
In practicetheheat transfercoefficienton the steam
side is so much higher than on thejuice side that it
is considered to have a minor effect. Thus uniform
boiling should be achievable,providing condensate
and incondensablegases are adequately removed.
Various arrangementsof steam and incondens-
able outlets have been proposed to achieve the ob-
jectives of uniform steam distribution and positive
venting of incondensable gases. Over the years a
wide array of different design features have been
employed, including multiple steam entry points,
steam lanes, baffles and variable tube spacing.

4 Removal of condensate and in-

The location of the points from which incon-

In order to ensure that incondensablegases are

It is wasteful of steam to bleed more than is nec-
essary, although venting to the following calandria
doesnot represent a totalloss of steam.Variousap-
proachescanbe used to control the amount vented:
An orifice sized to pass the correct amount is
sometimes installed, in which case the bleed
valve is leftfull open.
The temperature at the bleed point is measured
and the bleed is adjusted to achieve a tempera-
ture 1-2 "C below the condensing steam tem-
perature.
If the incondensablesare vented to atmosphere,
a thermostatic steamtrap can be used, which is
activatedby temperature to ventno morethan is
necessary.
In sizing orifices to remove incondensable gases
with the gases vented to the last effect,it should be
recognized that choked flow will be experienced
because of the low downstream pressure. This
means that sonicvelocitiesoccur and the available
pressure drop is less than expected. If the down-
streampressure is lessthan 0.55 times theupstream
pressure, choked flow will occur and the available
pressure drop for sizing purposes should be taken
as 0.55 times the upstream pressure. Thus design
of systems that vent all incondensables to the last
effect should take this fact into account, requiring
larger diameter flow paths. This is a good reason,

5 Liquidfeed and offtakesystems
The juice feed from one effect to the next will
flash as it enters the succeeding vessel because of
the lower pressure. Someearly designs fed thejuice
above the calandria, but this loses the effect that
flash has in driving circulation. If the feed enters
at a single point below the calandria, all the flash
occurs inone place and severe spoutingcan occur,
which is often the cause of considerable entrain-
ment. The flash can be put to good effect in rising
film evaporatorsby distributingit evenly around the
vessel below the calandria.Thispromotes velocities
through the tubes and significantlyelevates the rate
of heat transfer.
There may be some advantage in trying to op-
erate the vessel with varying concentrations within
the vessel. In a pan, arequirementis tom
i
x the feed
as rapidly as possible with the bulk of the material
in the vessel to keep uniform crystallizationcondi-
tions throughout the pan. In an evaporator however
there is no such requirement to establish a uniform
dissolved solidsconcentration in the vessel. Wright
et al. (2003)in fact recommendlocating the feed at
the periphery of the vessel, and assuming a number
of circulations through the tubes, a Brix gradient
from the periphery of thevessel to the outlet located
in a center downtakewill be achieved.
In any design it is essentialto arrange the inlet
andoutletsystemssothat no short-circuitingoccurs.
It is also advantageousto ensurethat the feedenters
below the calandria to promote boiling and reduce
spouting due to flash. This semi-sealed downtake
arrangement minimizes the chanceof short-circuit-
ing from a peripheral feed and ensures that the level
does not drop below the outlet funnel level.
The design of a feed system to spread the flash
uniformly in a vessel is not without pitfalls. The
system must be arranged so that an equal amount
of flash vapor enterseach feed inlet. A systemused
with successinSouthAfricaandelsewhereincorpo-
rates an externalflangedfeedring, easily accessible
fordismantlingand cleaning should it be necessary.
Individual inlets from the feed ring are located not
on the top of the ring but come off the side (Figure
12.15).Top located inlets would lead to all flashva-
por enteringthrough those inletsclosest to thepoint
where the feed pipe entersthe feed ring.

12.8 Operation of evaporators
12.8.1 Optimumoperating conditions
Thebest performancefroman evaporatorsetis
obtainedwhen it isrun as steadilyas possible.This
is generally achieved through the use of automatic
controls. The exhaust steam must be supplied at a
steady pressure, which should be a prerequisiteof
any sugar mill steam snpply and distribution con-
trol system. However the operation of batch pans
supplied with vapor fed from the evaporators will
always constitute a disturbance,which needs to be
taken into account in the operation of the evapora-
tors.
Thereis considerableevidencein the literature
to show that there is an optimum liquid level in
the tubes, generally assumed to be at a level one-
quarter to onehalf of the height of the tubes from
the bottom of the calandria (e.g. Guo et al. 1983,
Jones and Pouetti 2000).Watson (1986) reported
a maximum at 25 %, and a slow drop off up to 50
%. Very low liquid levels mean that there is insuf-
ficient liquid to evaporate and fully utilize the sur-
facearea;high levels areassumed to reduceevapo-
ration because of a hydrostatic head effect. This
effect is reportedly independen)of liquor Brix. In
practice this dependency on liquid level is not al-
ways as obvious as some of the literature reports
indicate. Nonetheless the level in each vessel (as-
sumingRobert evaporators)should be controlledat
a steady value.
Evaporation
Theoretically the level should be kept as low
as possible consistent with efficient operation to
minimize both the holdup of liquid and the effectof
hydrostatic head on the liquid boiling temperature.
This is particularly important in the last effect at
the lowest absolute pressure. The optimum level is
expected to be about 33 % of the tube length from
the bottom in the first effect, with some literature
suggestingthat this should fall along the evaporator
set to about 20 % in the last vessel. However the
sharp drop offin performanceat levels lessthan the
optimum as reported by Guo et al. (1983) suggests
that it is better to err on the side of slightly higher
liquid levels.
Optimum values of exhaust steam and final ef-
fect pressures are discussed in Section 12.5.3.
12.8.2 Automatic control of evapora-
tors
It is common practice to control the last effect
pressure at a constant value by varying the flow of
water to the condenser. It is also common practice
to control the liquid level in each effect by regulat-
ing either the flow into the vessel or the flow out
of the vessel. This depends on the way the con-
centration of dissolved solids in the syrup leaving
the last effect is controlled. The different options
commonly used in evaporator control are shown in
Figure 12.16.
In Figure 12.16A, sometimes referred to as in-
letfeed controlor cascadeforward control, the level
is controlled on the inletand the syrupBrix controls
the final vessel outlet flow, either by throttling the
outlet as shown in the figure or by recycling some
of the syrup back to the vessel. The overall rate of
evaporationrequired, often determined by the level
in the clarifiedjuice tank, is regulated by throttling
vapor 1 flow to the second effect. Regulating the
exhaust steam flow to the first effect would change
the vapor 1pressure, which is acceptablein the ab-
sence of a vapor bleed, but which is not acceptable
where vapor bleeding is practiced (as is normally
the case). If vapor 2 bleed is practiced, throttling of
vapor 2 to the third effect would be recommended.
Figure 12.16B showsoutletfeed controlor cas-
cade back control, with level controlled by regulat-
ing the flow out of each vessel. Syrup Brix control
is achieved by throttling vapor 1flow to the second
effect calandria. In this case, the juice flow to the
first effect is determined by the clarifiedjuice tank
level.
Accurate evaporator automatic control is diffi-
cult, because of the time lags involved. This gener-
ally means that the syrup Brix oftencycles, but this
is usually acceptable because close control is not
required and significant mixing and equalization
occur in the syrup tank.
If a Kestner evaporator is used as a first effect,
the control system is somewhat different, since the
level in the vessel is not controlled. From a control
point of view, the Kestner canjust be considered as
asectionof pipe.Figure 12.16C showsthe schemeif
a Kestnerevaporatoris used,parallelingthe scheme
in Figure 12.16A.
If falling film evaporators areused, the controls
are somewhat more complicated, because of the
necessity to controlthe recirculation flow and to add
water orjuice if the levelsor flowsin individualves-
selsfall below preset levels. Otherwisethe concepts
of control of the evaporator set are similar.
12.8.3 Effect of steam superheat
It is normal for the exhaust steam to be slightly
superheated, because it originates from steam tur-
bines which do not run at 100 % efficiency or from
let-down from a higherpressurerange. If a desuper-
heater is installed on the exhaust steam supply, the
extent of superheatis negligibly small. The energy
due to any superheat is small relative to the specific
heat of condensationand the superheatis easily lost.
Thus it is usual to neglect superheatin the exhaust
steam in calculations.
If thesuperheatis excessive, it ispossibleforthe
heat transfer rate to be affected adversely. In this
case a significantproportion of the heat transfer has
to take place from the vapor phase to the tube sur-
face, rather than by the far more rapid form of heat
transfer in condensation. Beale and Stewart (1963)
reported some experiments in an Australian mill,
which showed that providing the superheat is less
than 45 "C,
the superheatdoes not have any effect
on the rate of heat transfer and the rate of drop off
after that is low; a reduction of 7.5 % was recorded
with 100O
C superheat.
It is considered to be good practice to desuper-
heat exhaust steam automatically, as the extent of

12.8.4 Testingfor leaks
Leakage of air into the vessels under vacuum
is always a possibility. This may be due to leaking
joints or valves, or to leaks as a result of the cor-
rosion that occurs in the hot moist conditions. The
consequenceis a reduction in capacity and a greater
load on the vacuum equipment.
Since the evaporator vessels are not always in-
dividually isolated, they are usually not as easily
tested forair leaks as pans. A vacuumtest generally
involves drawing a vacuum and noting the increase
in pressure with time. Providing the absolute pres-
sure in the vessel is less than 53 kPa, the rate of air
entering the vessel is independent of the absolute
pressure. A vacuum test on a vessel should indicate
a rise in pressure of less than about 10 kPa in 30
minutes.
It is alsonecessaryto pressure testthe calandria
regularly. This should be done routinely by pressur-
izing the calandria with water.
12.8.5 Arrangement of vessels in series
and parallel
In the course of expanding a sugar mill, in-
creasesin evaporatorcapacity areoften achievedby
installing an extra, large, vessel and grouping the
remainingvessels in such a way as to achievea rea-
sonable distribution of area in each effect. This in-
evitablyresultsin a singleeffectbeing comprised of
more than onevessel. The decisionthen needs to be
made as to whether the vessels should be arranged
in series or in parallel on thejuice side.
The advantage of juice flow in series lies in the
fact that the vesselsbefore the last in that effectop-
erate at a lower dissolved solidsconcentration, thus
achieving on averagea higher heat transferrate be-
cause of the effect of viscosity on heat transfer.The
limitation is the fact there is no longer a pressure
differenceto cause the liquid to flow from one ves-
sel to the next in the same effect, and the intercon-
necting pipinghas tobe carefullydesignedwith this
in mind.
On the other hand,juice flow in series loses the
advantageofjuice flashinpromotingcirculationand
evaporation in all but the first vessel in that effect.
Smithand Taylor(1981) showed that this phenome-
non is more important in last effect vessels,provid-
ing a strong case for running vessels in parallel. In
this case, it is necessaryto design the feed piping in
such a way as to ensureuniform flow into theparal-
lel vessels. Thisis not difficult to achieve,if the feed
rings in each vessel are designed carefully with the
major pressure drop across the feed nozzles; if the
vessels are different in size, the flow to each vessel
in proportion to its heating surface area is achieved
by having the number of feednozzles on each vessel
in proportion to the area.
12.8.6 Syruppumping
Becausesyrupis extractedfromthe lasteffect at
its boiling point, the NPSH available on the pumps
may be low. In addition it is common to install a
strainer on the pump suction, which, if it blocks,
introduces a suction line pressure drop that makes
the situation worse. Thisisnormally only a problem
if the evaporators are installed at a fairly low eleva-
tion, providing little statichead on the suction side.
In this situation the followingcan help:
Have two suction line strainers in parallel, so
that one can be cleaned on the run. Particularly
aftercleaning,lumpsof scalewillbe caughtand
may clog the strainer.
Choosea pump with a lower speed.
Use a pump with a low NSPH requirement.
Ensurethat a bleed line (typically 25 mm diam-
eter)from the eyeof thepumpback to the vessel
vapor spaceisinstalled.It shouldhave avalveat
thepump,which is closedwhen that pumpis not
in use.
The packing or shaft seals should be kept in
good conditiontoprevent air enteringthepump,
which will cause problems with pumping syr-
UP.
Ensure the gland water supply (if required) is
reliable for the samereason.

12.8.8 Sucroselosses in evaporators
Seriouslosses of sucrosecan occur in the evap-
orator station because of high temperatures. The
highest process temperature occurs in the first ef-
fect of the evaporator. Because inversion and other
degradation reactions are temperature dependent,
this is important;the dependenceon temperatureis
exponential and so average and localized tempera-
tures areof great importance.Lossesarehandled in
more detail in Section 25.4 and a Table of inversion
rates as a function of operatingconditions is given
in Table 25.2. Here it is important to point out that
the rate of inversiondoublesfor every 6.3 "C rise in
temperature.
These reactions are also dependent on time and
pH and it is important to try to minimize the time
that the process liquid is held at high temperature
by minimizingthe liquidholdup. From an inversion
point of view, it is important also to keep the pH
up, above 7 and preferably above 7.4 entering the
first effect. Howeverthe effect of temperatureis far
more significant. For this reason it is desirable to
keep the temperature profile through the evapora-
t rs as low as possible.
Particularly if the evaporators run with a high
ex
I
st steam pressure, serious consideration
shouldbe givento first and secondeffectevaporator
designs that minimizejuice holdup, such as falling
film or Kesmer evaporators. Rein and Love (1995)
measured thedifferencesin residence timeforRob-
ert and Kestner evaporators and demonstrated the
effect that residence time has on undetermined loss
of sugar. Desuperheating exhaust steam is recom-
mended to eliminate the possibility of localized
high temperature regions. Since the effect of tem-
perature is exponential, such high temperaturesare
more seriousin terms of promoting sucroselosses.
Loss of sugardue to entrainmentis anothertype
of loss experienced in evaporators. This is covered
in Section 12.9.
12.8.9 pH Change
It is common to experience a change in pH
along the length of the evaporatorset. Generally a
dropin pH is experienced, which is of littleconcern
if the change is less than 1 unit. A pH of 6 or above
in syrupmust be achievedto minimize lossesin the
boilinghouse.
The change in pH may be due to a number of
factors:
The gradual transition of calcium phosphate to
tricalcium phosphate and its precipitation.
The evaporation of ammonia compounds.
The formation of organic acids as degradation
products of invert sugars typically at higher
pH.
When sodium carbonate rather than lime is used
for neutralization, a negligiblepH drop is recorded.
A rise in pH has also been observed when the raw
juice has a very high organic acid content, due to
deteriorated cane or entrainment into the mill of
cane wash water with a high organic acid content.
Volatilization of formic and acetic acid occurs as
concentrationsrise andpressures reduce, noticeable
by the low pH condensateformed.
Evap
12.9 Entrainmentseparation
Entrainment refers to the carryover of liquid
with the vapor stream out of the vessel. This results
in a loss of sugar and so needs to be eliminated.
This is achieved through the use of entrainment
separators, sometimes also known as catchalls or
save-alls. Entrainmentis the result of five different
circumstances:
1) Splashing of boiling liquid.
2) Localizedspoutingof liquid due tonon-uniform
conditions such as a localized feed point or air
leaks or internal incondensablepipe leaks.
3) Carryover due to foamingor frothing, often as-
sociated with start-up or shutdown or unsteady
operation.
4) Operational issues, including sudden pres-
sure changes, too high or too low liquid levels,
blocked entrainment return pipes or erratic re-
moval of condensatecausing changes in boiling
rate.
5) Entrainment of small droplets whose terminal
velocity is less than the velocity of the vapor
streambeing produced.
The first can be overcome by ensuring sufficient
disengagement space exists, the second should be
eliminated by modification and/or repair and the
third and fourth are abnormal and can be mini-
mized by careful operation.
The concern here is the last item, the removal
of smalldroplets which are likely to be in the range
of droplet diameters of 1 to 100 pm. They are en-
trained with the vapor however high the disengage-
ment spaceis.
The choice of type of separatoris influenced by
the followingcriteria:
Size of droplets to be removed. In this respect,
the size of the smalles oplets is of interest.
Droplets may go down to 1 m in size,but most
are above 10pm and prob ly up to a few hun-
dred microns.
'"?r
Pressuredrop through theseparator.Thisshould
be as low as possible, particularly in evapora-
tors where any pressureloss reduces the overall
pressureand temperature differenceavailable.
Self-draining ability of the separator or pro-
pensity to choke up. Generally this refers to
the liquid handling ability of the separator and
whether it requires routine cleaning.
Way in which entrained liquid is returned to the
boiling liquid.
Total installed cost of the separator.
All entrainment separatorsare based on some kind
of interactionin the balancebetweendrag and grav-
itationalforces.Thisis accomplishedin anumberof
ways: overcoming drag forces by reducing the gas
velocity (gravity separators or settling chambers);
introducing additional forces (venturi scrubbers,
cyclones, electrostatic precipitators); and increas-
ing gravitationalforcesby boosting the droplet size
(impingementseparators).
Some of these options are not feasible in sugar
processing.
12.9.1 'Qpes of separator
These devices make use of one or more of the I
followingmechanisms of separation:
Gravity,
Centrifugalforce,
Change of direction,
Interceptionand coalescence,
Inertial impaction.
Separation by gravity is not a practical solution
as too large a settling chamber is necessary. Cen-
~
trifugal action is therefore sometimesemployed to
achieve a separationmore effectively.
A large number of different devices have been '
employed in the past, with differing degrees of
success. Descriptions of these are given by Hugor
(1986537-540) and by Chen and Chou (1993:186-
193).
A number have been discreditedand only those
types in common use are covered here. The separa-
tors are either incorporatedin the top of the vessel
or in the vapor line from one vessel to the next or to
the condenser; they are preferablypart of the top of
the vessel,because separatorsin the vapor lines are
more expensiveto install and maintain.
Flow-reversal separators. Some entrainment
separators rely entirely on a change of direction
of the vapor flow, which leads to droplets getting
removed by inertial impaction onto solid surfaces.
One or more changesin direction may be involved.
The flow area in these separators should be sized
so that at maximum vapor flow rate, the velocity at
which dropletre-entrainment occursis not exceed-

ed.Dropletsneed tobe collected andreturned tothe
boiling liquid.
The simplest type is sometimes referred to as
a "top hat''. This involves two changes in direction
of the vapor, with the separated droplets having to
drain back into the vessel. A sketch is shown in

between the entrainment separation compartment
and the body of the vessel. Since there is a small
pressure drop through the separator, the vapor will
tend to flow up the return pipe in the absence of a
seal, re-entraining the liquid carefully separated.
The liquid sealis preferably outsidethe vessel, with
a sightglassand drainableU-leg. The typeof J-tube
return shown in Figure 12.17A is a disaster. It has a
tendency to block, which cannotbe seen or cleaned
without gettinginto the vessel.

Wiremeshseparators. Wire mesh eliminators
areperhaps the most efficient.Thewire mesh elimi-
natorconsistsof a pad of knitted wire, 100-300 mm
thick. Thewire diameteris generally 0.10-0.28 mm
thick, and the pad has a high void fraction of 0.95
to 0.99. The pads are containedin a support frame
or grid, and then located on steel supports in the
vessel. They are normally installed horizontally for
vertical upflow.
They are able to remove droplets larger than 2
to 5 I.lm and the pressure drop is normally less than
25 mm water. The mesh pads have good turndown,
operatingbetween 30-1 10% of their design capac-
ity. The upper limit is set by the re-entrainment of
liquid droplets from the mesh pad.
However, these demistersclog up over time and
periodically need to be removed and cleaned. Al-
though water sprays may be installed to flush them
periodically, the pads generally collect carbonized
sugar, which needs to be cleaned off by soakingin
a bath of caustic soda. The pads need to fit together
snugly. If there are any gaps between adjacent sec-
tions, localizedhigh velocities occur, which can se-
riously increase entrainment. It is very important,
therefore, that they are reinstalled correctly after
removal. Likewise there should be no gaps adjacent
to the side walls.

take up a significant proportion of the flow area,
requiring large areas. A more useful development
was the Polybaffle separator developed by CSR in
Australia (Frew 1971),followed later by the use of
chevron plates at Cattle Creek mill in Australia,
where they were installed vertically for horizontal
flow. This design has been modified and optimized
in SouthAfricaand Australia, where they havebeen
incorporated into "packs", which can be installed
horizontally on a support in the vessel for vertical
upward flow.

Sizing of entrainment separators. Entrain-
ment separators generally work more efficiently
at high velocities. However there is a limit to the
maximum velocity imposed by the onset of re-en-
trainment of liquid in the separator. The maximum
velocity dictates the area required and so a way of
estimatingthe maximumvelocity is necessary.
In the case of upward gas flow, there are two
opposing forces acting on a droplet: a gravitational
forceactingdownwardto accelerate the droplet, and

and the Souders-Brown equation for entrainment,

The Souders-Brown coefficient C is chosen to be
some fraction of the value required for the terminal
velocity. It can be seen from comparing equations
(12.46) and (12.47) that smaller particle sizes re-

on the velocity and so some iteration is required to
calculate the terminal velocity. In practice the value

than the superficial velocity ahead of the separator,

the plate relative to the approach. The angle a var-

and 54".

to the velocity uo squared multiplied by the vapor
density p

This shows pressure loss is calculated as a number

Pressure drop isgenerallylowest with wiremesh
separators, below 25 mm water. However pressure
drop is normally low with chevron plate separators,
of the order of 100-250 Pa (10 to 25 mm water),
but can be run at higher velocities and higher pres-
sure drops up to about 600 Pa. Cyclone type separa-
tors generally run with a higher pressure drop. Perk
(1955) suggests that 850 Pa is an acceptable pres-
sure drop for a cyclonic type of separator.
12.10 Condensate removal and
flashing
12.10.1 Pipingsystems
It is important to design condensate piping sys-
tems correctly to enable condensate to be removed
adequately and safely from steam heated vessels.
Condensate systems are described in Section 29.2.
Condensate piping to tanks or pumps should be
sized for a low velocity since pressure losses must
be small and the prospect of flashing occurring as
the pressure reduces needs always to be kept in
mind. In general condensate piping should be sized
assuming a velocity under average conditions of
0.75 mls.
Condensate lines to pumps need special atten-
tion, designed with low pressure drop and short suc-
tion lines. NPSH under the worst conditions needs
to be established and the pumping system designed
to meet it. A pressure equalization line at the pump
suction is essential and special efforts are necessary
to eliminate leaks.
12.10.2Trapsand U-legs
A system for permitting water and not steam to
be removed from heaters, evaporators and pans re-
quires a steam trap, or a U-leg seal, or a condensate
pot or receiver in which a liquid level is maintained
automatically. The types of steam traps used are
thermodynamic (e.g. Gestra traps), which are well
suited to high and steady loads, ball float traps with

Scaling on the inside of the tubes occurs over
time, as components within thejuice, mainly inor-
ganic materials, become saturated and precipitate.
This high concentration of precipitants takes place
where boiling occurs, i.e. close to the tube surface,
with theresultthat someof theprecipitated material
attachesto the tube surface.
The scale increases the resistance to the flow
of heat from the condensing steam to the boiling
juice. Thus the rate of heat transfer is much higher
when the tubes are cleanthan when they are scaled.
The rate of scaling is the net effect of deposition
and removal and is influenced by a large number
of factors, including the composition of the juice,
the sucrose concentration, the temperatureand the
velocity of liquid through the tubes. It is generally
found that the scale layer is thicker at the bottom
of the tube than the top, a function of the differing
velocitiesin the two regions.
It has also been found that the relative geom-
etries of liquid inlet and outletpiping can affectthe
occurrenceof scaling. Poor distribution of feed can
lead to non-uniform concentrationsand regions of
localizedhigh concentration,whereprecipitation of
scale is enhanced.Patterns of scaling within a ves-
sel can sometimes be cured by modifying the inlet
geometry. It has also been shown in practice that
scaling is more severe in an oversized evaporator
systemthan one which runs continuously at full ca-
pacity.
Various models have been used to describescal-
ing in different industrial applications. Heat trans-
fer resistances are present on the condensing steam
side, due to the metal wall, in the form of scale in-
sidethe tubeandin thefluid layercloseto theinside
of the tube. Under reasonably steady conditions, all
these resistances are more or less constant, except
