12.11.2 Characterizationof scale
Many investigations into the nature and com-
position of evaporator scale have been undertaken.
These have produced much information but have
not helped significantly to minimize or eliminate
scaling. The major inorganic componentsare silica,
calcium, magnesium and phosphate. The composi-
tion of the scale is affected by the composition of
the cane processed, which itself is affected by the
soil and climatic factors, although Walthew and
Turner (1995) report that the composition of the
scaledoesnot change much duringthe courseof the
season. The extent of scaling is also considerably
influenced by the pH control at the clarifierstation,
both the value of the pH, which affects the com-
position of the juice, and the steadiness of control,
sincepH excursionscan have seriousshort-duration
scalingeffects.The major scaling occurs in the last
effect. Scaling is often worse in the first than the
second and third vessels.
The major scale components and their suscep-
tibility to chemical cleaning agents are shown in
Table 12.10.
It is apparent that calciumis a major ingredient
in the scale. Generally the scale in the first few ef-
fects consists of calcium and phosphate. It is some-
what softerthan the scalein the last few effects that
is characterizedby a much higher concentration of
silica,which is harder and more difficult to remove.
Oxalate also seems to be a major component of
scale and interacts with silica to form very intrac-
table scale.
Walthew and Turner (1995) suggest that cal-
cium silicate, silica and calcium phosphate are
formed as colloidal particles in suspension before
being deposited around the crystalline material
(oxalate). It has been observed that scale tends to
form in layers, suggestingthat particularconditions
in evaporators cause deposition of differentmateri-
als. Considerableinformation on the compositionof
scale is givenby Honig (1963:124-142).
Methods of removing scale are summarized in
Table 12.11.The optimummethod is determinedby
local cost structures and the nature of the scale.
Variouschemicaladditiveshave been proposed,
which when added to the juice, are supposed to
modify the crystal habit or precipitation charac-
teristics to prevent scale forming in the tubes. No
chemicals have been consistently successful in the
cane sugar industry. Some are reported to lead to
a softer scale, which is easier to remove, or enable
the time between tube cleanings to be extended.
However nothing has been found to prevent the for-
mation of silica scale, which is the most intractable
componentof the scale. Walthewand Turner(1995)
have observed that anti-scalantschangethe quantity
and form of components like oxalate but generally
do not have a significanteffect overall.
The modern chemical additives proposed are
generally of two types, namely polyacrylic and
polymaleic compounds. Reports of their effective-
ness areinconsistent andarelikely tobe significant-
ly influencedby the make up of thejuice.
12.11.4 Chemical cleaning
Causticsodais the most commonlyused chemi-
cal for cleaning, or a mixture of caustic soda and
soda ash. In some cases, particularly the early ef-
fects, it can be used on its own. A concentration of
>20 g1100 g solution is usually required, although
this can be reduced if a suitable wetting agent is
added. Caustic concentrations between 10 and
40 g1100 g solution have been reported. The solu-
bility of sodiumcarbonatein caustic reduces as the
caustic strength increases (Walthew et al. 1997b)
and the caustic concentration should not exceed
20 g1100 g solutionif the mixture is used.
High caustic concentrations also make boiling
more difficult because of the high boiling point el-
evation.Consumptionof causticis in the range of 10
to 30 kg1100 m2surface area.
12.11.4 Chemicalcleaning
It is often the case that cleaning with caustic
needs to be followed by an acid clean. The sys-
tem must be flushed as thoroughly as possible, or
else a high proportion of the acid is consumed in
the neutralization of residual alkali. Acid followed
by caustic is not effective (Walthew et al. 1997b).
Since stainless steel tubes are most commonly
used, hydrochloric acid (also called muriatic acid)
is not recommended, even if an inhibitor is added,
because of the possibility of catastrophicstresscor-
rosioncracking. In this casesulfamicacid is usually
used, or perhaps formic or glycolic or phosphoric
acid. "Alumina ferric" used in Australia is a buff-
ered acid solution, consisting of a mixture of alu-
minium and ferric sulfates.
In some instances weak acids are unable to
remove scale in the last effects. In this case some
mills asin Louisiana forinstance,use coppertubes,
to enable hydrochloric acid to be used, usually at a
concentration between 1 and 3 gllOO g solution. In
severecases, ammonium bifluorideis added to give
a particularly aggressive cleaning chemical. Dam-
age to the shell and tube plates is excessive.
In all cases, scale removal is promoted by high
temperature, high concentration of the cleaning
chemicals and agitation of the liquid contactingthe
scale.
EDTA, sometimes referred to as versene, has
been found to be an effective cleaning agent, but
is more expensive than other cleaning chemicals.
Jones and Pozzetti (2000) reported that EDTA was
more effective in cleaning last effect scale than
caustic soda either on its own or caustic followed
by sulfamic acid. Doherty (2000) gives a descrip-

tion of the chemistry of EDTA. It can also be re-
generated and reused to some extent, but is still an
expensive treatment and not widely used. It has a
big advantage in not generating a chemical disposal
problem.
Sichter et al. (2003) reported that with a falling
film plate evaporator, rising film boiling with caus-
tic soda was necessary, apparently the bubbles caus-
ing increased agitation in this mode of boiling. The
disadvantage of rising film boiling is the require-
ment for a greater quantity of caustic and a longer
time for boil-out. This had to be followed by sulfa-
mic acid cleaning to remove hydroxyapatite scale.
In general boiling is more effective than spray-
ing cleaning chemicals into the top of the tubes
(Walthew et al. 1997b). The agitation induced by
the boiling action helps dislodge the scale. It is im-
portant after cleaning to be able to flush out pieces
of dislodged scale which can otherwise lead to
blockages in pipes and orifices on start-up.
Suhr and Schulze (2003) draw atrention to prob-
lems that can be experienced with falling film plate
evaporators. These relate to the formation of local-
ized areas of foam and upward flow, leading to lo-
cal dry spots and carbon deposits, and also to some
of the scale removed from the heating surfaces re-
maining in the vessel, redissolving and leading to
quicker fouling of the heating surfaces. They rec-
ommend routine calculation of heat transfer coeffi-
cients on a time period that avoidsscaling, to prevent
uneven juice patterns in the plate pack. They have
shown that if severe blocking of a pack occurs, the
pack can be removed and pressure-washed, but this
should only be considered in extreme cases. EDTA
or thermal shocking by water boiling and drying out
are recommended cleaning processes, but the latter
may not be good for the long-term structural integ-
rity of the plate pack.
12.11.5 Mechanical cleaning
In a number of sugarproducing areas, mechani-
cal cleaning of tubes is still much cheaper than
chemical cleaning, particularly in those countries
where labor costs are low. It is labor intensive and
generally a hot and unpleasant task. It does have the
advantage of not having to dispose of an effluent,
as is required with chemical cleaning. However it
does lead to a shortening of the life of the tubes due
to mechanical damage over time; on the other hand
corrosion of the internals of the evaporator with
chemical cleaning is avoided. This is not an option
for plate or falling film evaporators.
The evaporators need to be taken off-line and
cooled before the job can begin. This usually in-
volves filling the vessel with water. The water level
is normally reduced to a level about 0.5 m below
the top tube plate before cleaning under flooded
conditions begins. The cleaning of a set of evapora-
tors can be done in about 8 h once the evaporators
are cooled. Lionnet and Blaikie (2003) report that
cleaning rates in South Africa vary from 25 to 70
m2/h per operator for Robert vessels and 70 to 110
m2/h per operator forKestner evaporators; however
some values up to 50 % higher than these have been
encountered.
It is essential to keep the rotating cutting and
brushing equipment in good condition if effective
results are to be achieved. High cutter speeds of
2 800 to 4 500 m i d are used; higher speeds lead
to better cleaning but care needs to be taken not to
damage the tubes. It is also essential to ensure that
the sizeof the cutters is exactly suited to the internal
diameter of the tubes to be cleaned. Otherwise the
scale can be polished by undersize cutters, giving a
visual impression of a clean metal surface.
A description of the equipment used is given by
Honig (1963); Lionnet and Blnikie (2003) give de-
tails of the flexible shafts and tool heads used. It is
generally advisable to clean on a routine frequency
and not to let the scale layer get too thick. Otherwise
cleaning mechanically can become very difficult. In
some cases a caustic boil may be employed prior to
mechanical cleaning to soften the scale.
12.11.6 Steamside cleaning
Fouling on the outside of the tubes is not gen-
erally a concern. In the days when steam engines
were in use, oil contamination of exhaust steam
sometimes occurred, which affected the tubes in
the first effect. With turbines having replaced most
steam engines, this is usually no longer an issue.
Sometimes a black deposit is found on the outside
of tubes in later effects that is assumed to be a con-
sequence of entrainment of sugar from a previous
effect carbonizing on the outside of the tubes.
In most cases a weak acid clean together with a
wetting agent is adequate to remove the scale.
12.12 Starch and dextran removal
12.12 Starch and dextran
removal
Starch and dextran are polysaccharides which
are undesirable impurities in the raw juice. Starch
is present in the cane (see Section 1.2.5) but dextran
is formed after burning or cutting the cane and this
is more rapid when conditions are moist and warm.
It may also be formed in the milling tandem if mill
sanitation is not adequate. Dextran is produced by
the Leuconostic sp. bacteria from sucrose and is
made up of large numbers of glucose molecules, so
the fructose concentration may increase as a result
of this fermentation.
It is usual to add amylase in the evaporators to
reduce the level of starch in the product sugar. In
diffuser mills the starch content is low enough so
that amylase can generally be dispensed with en-
tirely (see Section 6.7.4).
Dextran is undesirable because of the penalty
on high dextran imposed by refiners and because of
its effect on elevating the viscosity of massecuites
to the point that throughput and recovery of sugar
are affected. In these cases it is generally essential
to use dextranase. Dextranase is often added in the
evaporators when dextran levels are high, although
this is not necessarily the optimum point of addi-
tion. Nonetheless, the use of both these types of en-
zyme will be covered in this chapter.
12.12.1 Enzyme properties
Enzymes are heat sensitive and will be rendered
ineffective above a temperature threshold, depend-
ing on the enzyme. They also are more effective in
dilute solutions, with the rate of reduction of starch
or dextran dropping off significantly as the dis-
solved solids content increases. However the effect
of RDS on the enzymes is dependent on the com-
position of the solution; in general the enzymes are
more effective in sugar mill solutions than in pure
solution when the temperature is elevated. In gen-
eral dextranases are less tolerant of typical process-
ing conditions than amylases (Morel du Boil and
Wienese 2002).
Tho basic strains of amylase are available, one
being inoperative above about 60 "C and the other
temperature tolerant enzyme retaining its activity
up to temperatures of around 90 "C. The latter is
more effective when used in the evaporators, but in
some countries its use is discouraged since its ef-
fect carries through into the molasses and affects
the products made from molasses.
Amylase is relatively cheap, since it is produced
in large volumes for the corn sweetener industry.
However dextranase is considerably more expensive
and needs to be used with more care and concern. It
is produced from one of three bacterial species but
dextranases from Chaetomium sp. are most com-
mon. They have a slightly better thermal stability
with an optimum temperature of around 50 "C or
slightly below this. This temperature Limit increases
slightly at higher sugar concentrations. Time is also
important and if added in dilute juice is only effec-
tive up to the juice heating stage where it is dena-
tured by high temperature. For this reason it is often
added into the cooler effects of the evaporators.
12.12.2Optimal use of enzyme
Enzyme is not sold on the basis of concentra-
tion as a chemical might be. Enzymes from differ-
ent sources can have different activities, which are
not obvious from product specifications. It is often
worthwhile, particularly with dextranase, to com-
pare activities of enzymes from different sources
through laboratory tests, to be able to choose the
most cost-effective enzyme.
Amylase is not effective in raw juice from a
milling tandem. Only once the gelatinization tem-
perature above about 70 "C is reached are the starch
granules disrupted so that the starch is accessible to
the enzymes. Amylase is generally added into the
penultimate effect of the evaporators. This gives it
sufficient time under the conditions of temperature
and RDS to achieve the required starch reduction,
particularly if the temperature tolerant strain is
used. It seems that the enzyme retains some residu-
al activity even in the pan house.
Dextranase is more effective in raw juice than
in syrup. Generally dextranase is added in the mill-
ing tandem at the penultimate mill and into the first
mill juice. It is desirable for the dextranase to have
the longest possible retention time prior to thejuice
heaters. Some mills provide retention time at about
50 "C for the enzyme to work most efficiently, and
some enzyme may be added into the later effects
Referencesp. 316
316 Evaporation
of the evaporators as well. The enzyme is inacti-
vated above about 60 "Cand the activity is greatly
reduced as the Brix increases. Roughly 30 % of the
dextran in juice crystallizes with the sugar. Thus
in order to meet a dextran limit of 300 mg/kg raw
sugar,thedextranlevel in syrupneeds tobe reduced
to below 1000mglkg DS.
High molecular mass dextransare broken down
quickly and further breakdown to smaller molecu-
lar mass polysaccharides takes considerablylonger.
Geronimos and Greenfield (1978) reported that
degradation of high molecular mass dextran has the
most significant effect on viscosity and handling
properties of massecuites. Breaking down dextran
to lower molecular mass ranges (< 1x lo6)has neg-
ligibleeffecton viscosity.Henceonlysufficientdex-
tranase and retention time to break down the high
molecularmass dextran is required. In addition, the
Haze method usually used in sugar contractsis not
sensitiveto low molecular mass dextran.
It is important to store enzymeat as low a tem-
perature as possible to prevent loss of effectiveness
in storage. Refrigeration is unnecessary but in hot
climates it should be stored in an air-conditioned
area.

Condensers and vacuum equipment are com-
mon to evaporators and vacuum pans. Nearly all
these vessels use direct contact condensers, where
the cooling water comesinto direct contact with the
vapor to be condensed.A condenseris usually used
on the tiltrate vacuum system as well, although at a
lower vacuum (higherabsolutepressure).
The mainadvantagesof directcontactcondensa-
tion are the cheapconstructionof the condenserand
the ability to achieve a close approach temperature;
this is particularly important because the saturation
temperaturesof the vapor arerelatively low and the
coolingwater temperatureis relatively high in warm
cane-growing regions. Both these factors impact on
thequantityof coolingwater used. Quantitiesof wa-
ter used are large.
The cooling water systems generally use spray
pondsorcoolingtowerstoeffectthecoolingrequired
and reject heat to the atmosphere.The temperature
at which the water is returned to the condensers af-
fects the quantity of water to be pumped and affects
the temperature of the gases going to the vacuum
equipment after the condensers. Vacuum pumps or
ejectors areused to remove the incondensablegases
from the condensers.
The more steamefficientthe factory,the smaller
is the cooling system required, because less heat is
wasted. In cases where heat economy is paramount,
attemptsmightbe made to recover heat from the hot
water returning from the condensers, but this is not
common in cane sugarmills.

Perk (1973)givesfiguresforthe averageamount
of air to be removed from raw pans as 13-14 m3/h
and refinery pans 9 m3/h,per m3strike volume, and
from evaporatorsas 3.1 or 3.8 m3/hper m2heating
surface in the last vessel of a quadruple or a quin-
tuple effect evaporator respectively.
There does not appear to be any scientific ba-
sis for establishing this quantity for vacuum filters.
Variousmanufacturersstatethat the vacuum system
should be designed for between 0.7 and 1.7 cubic
feethinuteper squarefootof filterarea,correspond-
ing to 12.8 to 31 m3/h for each m2of filter area. In
practice a value for the vacuum pump capacity of
18m3/h for each m2 of filter area seems to be sat-
isfactory.
The air which has to be removed from the con-
denser originates from three sources, namely from
leaks in the pan or evaporatorsystem, from air dis-
solved or entrained in the juice, syrup or molasses
fed to the vessel, and from airdissolved in the con-
denser water that is releasedunder vacuum. Because
of good contact between the condenser water and
the gases being pulled off the condenser, it can be
assumed that the gas is saturated with water vapor,
and this too needs to be estimated as a function of
the temperature of the gas stream. The amount of
water vapor in this stream can be calculated using
Dalton's law of partial pressures. It is highly tem-
perature dependent; if the exiting gas stream is not
adequately cooled a large proportion of this stream
is water vapor.
The vacuumpumps and ejectors used to remove
the gases are volumetricdevices, and so it is the vol-
ume of the gas stream that is of importanceand not
its mass. The amount of air from the three sources
can be estimated as follows:
1. The dissolved air released from the condenser
water is assumed to be 35 mglkg water, based
on estimates by Perk (1973) and Hugot (1986)
of 30 to 40 mg/kg dissolved airin water from a
cooling pond or tower.
2. Air from leaks can be estimated from vacuum
tests, where a vacuum is drawn and the increase
in pressure is noted over a given time period.
Providing the pressure in the vessel is less than
53kPa, therate of airenteringthe vessel is inde-
pendent of its absolutepressure. It can be calcu-
lated that a 1 kPa rise in absolutepressuredueto
air ingressresults in an increasein air density of
0.0115kg/m3.A vacuum test on a vessel should
indicate a rise in pressure of less than about
10kPa in 30 minutes. For design purposes, as-
sumea rise of 15kPa in 30minutes;then therate
of air ingress is calculated as:

where Vis the volume of the vessel in m3.
3. The dissolved air content of syrup is 100mgkg
and of juice is 200 to 250 mgkg (Hugot 1986).
It is assumedthat all of this is released,although
this may not necessarilybe true. Howeverthis is
the smallest amount of the three sources of air
and the error in this assumption is negligible.

13.1.6 Heat recovery
It is generally not feasible to recover heat from
the condenser water in a cane sugar mill. This is
morecommon in beet sugarfactories,whichin most
cases have a higher condenser water temperature
and a lower ambient and hence raw juice tempera-
ture (van der Poel et al. 1998). Sometimes a two-
stage condensing system is used to make some of
the energy availableat a higher temperature.
13 Condensers and vacuum equipment
13.2 Condensers 13.2.2 Qpes of condenser
13.2.1 Condenser arrangements and
requirements
It is usual for each pan and evaporator to have its
own condenser. The absolute pressure in each ves-
sel is controlled by regulating the water flow to its
condenser, as shown in Figure 13.1. In some cases a
common condenser is used for all condensation du-
ties, but this is seldom found in cane sugar mills.
The common condenser system has the advantage
that the cooling water system is simpler, but requires
longer lengths of large bore vapor piping from in-
dividual vessels to the condenser and large expen-
sive valves to regulate the absolute pressure in each
vessel. It also means that the condenser runs at an
absolute pressure lower than the lowest pan pres-
sure, requiring more condenser water and returning
somewhat cooler water to the cooling tower. The
maindisadvantage however is the fact that even with
good control, stopping and starting a batch pan on a
common condenser system invariably induces some
degree of disturbance to the vacuum of all vessels
attached to the common system.
The requirements of a good condenser are two-fold:
a) It should condense all the vapor with m
i
n
i
m
u
m
usageofwater,i.e.theoutletwatertemperatureshould
be very close tothe vaporsaturationtemperature.
b) It should cool the incondensable gases down to
as low a temperature as possible, and close to the
temperature of the incoming cooling water, even
at low evaporation rates.
In practice if the incondensable gases are not cooled
adequately, the vacuum pump or steam ejector may
become overloaded and so be unable to remove all
the incondensable gases. Then the absolute pressure
must rise, and corrective action generally involves
admitting more cooling water, which affects the at-
tainment of condition (a), i.e. a high water outlet
temperature.
The design of condensers for batch vacuum pans is
difficult since it has to cope with a very high tum-
down. Evaporation rates of around 80kg/(h .mZ) can
be experienced at the start of seed boilings, and final
evaporation rates vary from about 8 kg/(h .mZ)in A
pans to about 4 kg/@ .m2)on C pans. The ability of
a condenser to satisfy both requirements (a) and (b)
under all evaporation rates needs special attention.
Condensers can be divided into three basic
types, namely countercurrent, cocurrent and spray
jet condensers. The first two describe the relative di-
rections of flow of vapor and water. Countercurrent
condensers have the vapor entry at the bottom of
the condenser with the water flowing down the con-
denser counter to the direction of the vapor and are
generally more efficient. Cocurrent condensers have
the water and vapor entering at the top of the con-
denser; they require more cooling water and a larger
volume of air to be removed at a higher temperature
(Perk 1973) and few cocurrent condensers are seen
nowadays in sugar mills. Hugot (1986) expounds in
detail on the advantages of countercurrent condens-
ers; cocurrent condensers will not be considered any
further here. Both these types of condenser require
that incondensable gases be removed by a vacuum
pump or ejector system. Some typical internal ar-
rangements of two types of countercurrent condens-
ers are shown in Figure 13.4.
The third type is the spray jet condenser, which
introduces the water into the condenser through high
velocityjets. This has the effect of entraining incon-
densable gases with the water down the tailpipe or
water outlet line, which eliminates the requirement
for a vacuum system, but requires the use of signifi-
cantly more water, particularly at low vapor rates.
Apart from the higher flow of water, a higher pres-
sure drop across the nozzles is required, so that the
pumping power is significantly higher. A multi-jet
condenser is illustrated in Fi,aure 13.5.
Most condensers are external to the vessel,
but some condensers are located in the top of the
vacuum vessel itself. Internal condensers have the
following advantages:
The condenser is supported within the vessel
and does not need a separate external support
structure.
The condenser is not a pressure vessel and can
therefore be a cheaper construction.
It eliminates the need for a large diameter vapor
connection, which is subject to corrosion and at
times implosion.
The disadvantage is that the condensermay be locat-
ed at a higher elevation than an external condenser,
requiring a larger cooling water pump static head.
It may also require that the vessel be taller or wider
at the top.

only a 5.5 "Cdifference in temperature between air

vapor will bypass the cooling water becomes more
likely. The consequence is a higher temperature
stream to the vacuum system. In fact, most of the
effort in improving condenser inte~nals

to improving the contact of the incondensable gases
with the cooling water.

Thus it is commonevenwith singletray condensers

This is conservativefor well-designed condensers.
The pressure drop through the condenser is
small enough to be ignored. Hugot (1986) suggests
this is about 3 mm, or 0.4 kPa. It can safely be as-
sumed that the pressure is constant within the con-
denser.
Height of the condensing section. Various
authors suggest different condenser heights. Hugot
(1986) suggests that the height required is a func-
tion of the internal design of the condenser, and
more specifically of the time the water spends in
the condenser and the surface area offered by the
water to achieve the required heat exchange. Thus,
he quotes figures from Deerr of 4.5 m for a con-
denser without baffles and 3.6 m for a condenser
with four baffles. Australian experience covers
heights between vapor inlet and water distribution
of 1.8 to 3 m, with 2.5 m recommended (Hutchin-
son and Wright 1982).However, condensers with a
height of 1.6 m have been used with good results.
Stewart (1971) reported that most of the condensa-
tion appears to occur within thefirst 600 mm above
the vaporinlet, which impliesthat the timerequired
for condensationto occuris very short.Thereseems
to be littlereason to have a distance between vapor
inlet and water tray of more than 1.6m.
Strauss (1966) suggests that the height should
be a function of diameter, with both dimensions
chosen to give a volume of 0.75 m3/t vapor con-
densed per hour. He suggeststheheightshould vary
from3.5 times the diameter at a vaporrateof 2.3 t/h
to twice the diameter at 22.7 t/h or higher.
Diameter of the condenser. Hutchinson and '
Wright (1982) report that the ratio of body contact
volume to water flow is remarkably constant, at
values between 0.006 and 0.01 (m3 h)/t of injec-
tion water. At 12 kPa with 30 O
C water, the water
quantity is 35 times the vapor amount. Thus these
figures become 0.21 to 0.35 (m3
.h)/t of vapor. At

13.2.6 Absolute pressure control
This requires the use of an absolute pressure
transmitterand not an ordinarypressure transmitter,
which is affected by changes in ambient pressure.
The ideal controlsystemkeeps the absolutepressure
constant in spite of variations in evaporation rate.
Control is normally effected by regulating the flow
of water to the condenser. This system works well
and reliably, with two provisos:
the controlvalve must be properly sized;
the vacuum system drawing off incondensable
gases must be adequatelysized andin good con-
dition.
Butterfly valves with stainless steel discs and rub-
ber lined bodies are generally the most effective
valves for this duty. However they must be sized
for choked flow because of the low absolute pres-
sure downstream of the valve. Generally also some
degree of cavitation occurs. This does not cause
serious damage if the valve is installed close to the
condenseritself, becauseof the low staticpressure at
that point. Cavitationcan be eliminated if the valve
is positioned at a much lower elevation so that the
staticpressureprevents vaporization. Howeverif the
valve is installedat an intermediatepoint wherecav-
itation still occurs, the damagecaused by cavitation
can be much more severe,because the higher water
pressure leads to more severe damage as the vapor
bubbles collapse.
The second problem often occurs if a vacuum
pump loses efficiencydue to wear, for instance. As
thepumpcan no longerremovethe required volume,
the incondensable gases build up in the condenser.
Thecontrolsystemrespondstotheabsolutepressure
rising by opening the control valve further.This can
sometimeshave an effectoppositetowhatis desired.
The additional load of incondensablegases entering
with the cooling water makes the situation worse.
A considerable drop in the tailpipe water tempera-
ture is experiencedas a result. This means that large
quantities of cool water are returned to the cooling
towers, overloading the injection water pumps and
affectingthe performance of the towers. To stop this
happening, a tailpipe temperature override is often
incorporated in the control system, preventing the
control valve from opening further once a specified
minimum tailpipetemperatureis reached.
This situation can sometimeslead to a "frozen"
condenser, wherethe condenseris cool but the abso-
lute pressureis too high and cannot be reduced.This
is explained by Love (2005) in terms of a model of
a combined condenser and vacuum pump. This pa-
per givesa good insightinto the interactionbetween
condenserand vacuum pump.
Control of tailpipe water temperature is some-
times used as an alternative to absolute pressure
control. It keeps conditions fairly steady but is not
as good, because it does not necessarily keep the
absolute pressure constant. Its advantage lies in the
fact that it results in optimum use of cooling water,
rehuning water at the highest temperature possible
to the cooling towers.
13.2.7 Identifying air leaks
Air leaks are inevitably a problem, particularly
as the plant ages. Weld areas are particularly sus-
ceptible and should be regularly inspected and re-
paired. Various approacheshave been used to iden-
tify leaks:
Inspectionfrom inside the ducting or condenser
may allow leaks to be identified by daylight
showingthrough.
Filling vessels with water where possible will
indicateleaks.
Ultrasonic detectors are very efficient at identi-
fying leaks in a vessel under vacuum.
Smokegeneratorsinsidethe vessel may be used,
preferably with colored smoke, which escapes
when the vesselis pressurized.
Pressurizing a system with steam, if available,
will alsoindicateleaks at thepointswheresteam
escapes.
Smallpits due to corrosion in the tailpipe at the wa-
ter line in the water seal well are often the cause of
problems and arenot easily noticed.For this reason,
this part or all of the tailpipe should be of stainless
steel or 3CR12.

13.4.1 Design and specificationof cool-
ing systems
Thequantitiesof waterto be cooled and the cal-
culation of the heat duty are discussed in Section
13.1.5. The water is cooled by contact with cooler
ambient air, either in conventional cooling towers
or in spray ponds. Most of the cooling occurs by
evaporation and only a small proportion is by sen-
sible heat transfer. Thus a significant proportion of
the condensed vapor is evaporated in the cooling
system, typically 80 to 85 %, with only 15 to 20
% of the total cooling occurring by sensible heat
transfer. Since the total quantity of water circulat-
ing through the cooling system is about 30 to 40
times the amount of vapor condensed, the propor-
tion of the circulating water evaporated is about 2
to 2.5 %.
Since the cooling is directly dependent on the
difference between the water temperature and the
wet bulb temperature, both these temperatures are
major factors affecting the size of the cooling sys-
tem. The wet bulb temperatureis a function of the
local conditions, and varies significantlyduring the
courseof the year. Fordesignpurposes itis common
to use the wet bulb temperature which is exceeded
foronly 5 %of the timeof the crushingseason.This
gives an adequatecompromise between having ac-
ceptable return water temperatures without an ex-
cessively large coolingsystem.
Equation (13.9) shows that the heat duty is pro-
portional to the product of water flow rate and cool-
ing range. A smaller quantity of water returning at
a higher temperaturemay have the same heat duty
to be removed as a system with a larger quantity
of water returning at a lower temperature. However
the higher temperaturesystem will require a small-
Referencesp. 338
13 Condensers and vacuum equipment
er cooling system because the difference between
water and wet bulb temperatures is higher. Thus it
is important to ensure that condensers have a close
approach, returning the smallest quantity of water
at the highest temperature possible.
The choice of cooled water temperature is an
important issue. Specification of too low a tem-
perature means that a very large cooling system is
required. Too high a temperature makes it difficult
to achieve low absolute pressures, and the injection
water pumps and vacuum pumps have to be larger.
The cooling efficiency is sometimes used as a guide
in choosing the cooled water temperature, defined
as the temperature drop in the cooling tower as a
fraction of the maximum theoretical drop, which
is achieved when the outlet temperature equals the
wet bulb temperature t,,. Thus:
Nugor (1986) suggests that values of q should lie
between 0.5 and 0.7, and average 0.6. In practice an
outlet temperature about 5 OC above the wet bulb
temperature is not uncommon, leading to a value of
11 greater than 0.7.
The choice of cooling towers or spray pond de-
pends on the particular circumstances. The issues to
be considered include the following:
1. Spray pond systems are cheaper to construct,
consisting only of a set of pipes and sprays
spraying water into the air.
2. Cooling towers are more compact, taking up
less space. Spray ponds generally require a
large area to achieve the cooling required.
3. Operating costs for a spray pond system are
lower, because there are no fans to maintain,
and because the large volume of water held up
in the spray pond system generally does not re-
quire any chemical dosing.
4. Chemical treatment costs are higher in a cool-
ing tower and control of corrosion and micro-
bial growth is necessary.
5. If a low approach to wet bulb temperature is re-
quired for energy economy reasons, a cooling
tower may be more cost-effective.
6. The drift loss is larger with a spray pond system
and can be a nuisance in windy conditions.
7. There is a greater chance that the water will
be contaminated with wind-borne debris (and
sometimes local wildlife!) in a spray pond.
13.4.2 Coolingtowers
A variety of designs of cooling tower are avail-
ablefromcoolingtower suppliers. Generally they are
mechanical draft cooling systems, although natural
draft towers have occasionally been used in sugar
mills. They are generally cIassified as countercur-
rent or crossflow towers, descriptive of the direction
of a
i
rflow relative to that of the water. Intrinsically
the countercurrent tower is expected to be more ef-
ficient, but the crossflow tower can operate with a
lower power requirement or higher vapor velocities.
Entrainment separators are required ahead of the
fans to limit losses of water. A sketch of the two dif-
ferent types is given in Figure 13.7.
Cooling towers are normally sized by the s u p
plier. For tender purposes, the wet bulb temperature
as well as the quantities and temperatures need to be
specified. Two basic types of fill are used: splash and
film. It is essential to specify an open splash pack;
cooling tower packing with close clearances found
in structured packings or f3.h type packings invari-
ably blocks up with the products of microbiological
activity. It is impossible to guarantee that no sugar
will get entrained into the system, and even con-
scientious treatment of a cooling tower will never
eliminate microbial activity entirely. Entrainment
separators likewise need to have generous gaps be-
tween separating elements for the same reason.
The performance of a cooling tower is gener-
ally ascertained by measuring the driving force
for cooling represented by the enthalpy difference
between the air stream and saturated a
i
r
,as pro-
posed by Merkel (Coulson and Richardson 1999).
A performance characteristic or evaporation number
(kg.a .hlh,) -a is the interfacial area per unit vol-
ume and h height of the packing -is determined for
the tower from enthalpy differences and tempera-
tures, which is generally dependent on the liquid to
gas mass flow ratio, proportional to (%lm,)", where
the exponent n is characteristic of the packing and
has a value in normal applications between 0.5 and
2.5. This is often the basis for an acceptance test on
a cooling tower, because it accounts for the fact that
the conditions ofthetestare generally different from
the original specification for the most arduous duty.
Factors to be taken into account in a performance
trial are given by Morgan (1977).
In routine operation, it is important to ensure
that there is a uniform distribution of water onto the
13.4.2 Coolingtowers / 13.4.3 Sprays ponds
packing. Non-uniform water distribution can easily
lead to tower outlet temperatures higher by 10 OC.
In multiple cell systems, there should be equal flow
to each cell. Within a cell the distribution must be
uniform and cover the full area of the cell. Any area
where there is no flow is obviously lost area, but in
addition the area with no water has less static head
and the air will take the path of least resistance rob-
bing air from adjacentareas.
It is also necessary to check the performance of
the fans. If a particular fan draws less power, it in-
dicates that the air flow must be lower, leading to
worse performance.The pitch of the blades and the
clearancebetween thefan tips and thefan casing are
often the cause of lower air flows. Routinesampling
and treatment of the water is also a necessity. It is
usual to rely on a reputable chemical supplier who
makes frequent visits to the plant with advice on
treatment.
The negative pressure at the air inlets causes
dust, paper, plastic materials etc. to be sucked into
the towers, and screens are necessary on the water
outlets before the pumps to prevent this materialbe-
ing drawn in. The screens should be located so that
they may be easily accessedfor cleaning.

The sprays should be chosen with openings

suspended solids. The internal design of the spray
should preferably be free of vanes; a centrifugal
"garden spray" type that uses centrifugal force to
disperse the water is suitable in this regard. Spray

the spray nozzles used. This could typically be in
the range of 30 to 60 kPa.

generally provide enough volume to fill seal wells
and flumeson start-up.Pump suctions need to have
adequate easily cleanable strainers, to prevent in-
gress of any floatingmaterial.
13.4.4 Entrainmentand drift losses
Entrainmentloss in cooling towers is low, typi-
cally 0.05 9
% of the circulating flow. This may be
neglected by comparison with the evaporative loss
of 2 to 2.5 %.
Spray ponds will generally lead to much larger
drift losses. In strong windy conditions, sigaficant
quantities of water may be blown out of the sys-
tem; water losses by windage range between 1 and
5 % of the recirculation rate. Spray ponds however
have a lower evaporation rate as less of the cool-
ing is effected by evaporation,typically 55 %of the
heat added as opposed to 85 % in a cooling tower.
With both cooling towers and spray ponds, there
is generally an overflow of water from the system,
as the quantity of water condensed into the system
exceeds the quantity of water lost by evaporation
and entrainmentor drift losses. This overflow from
the system constitutes a natural blowdown and also
means that make up with water is unnecessary.
13.4.5 Water qualityand treatment
Evenwith an opencoolingtower packing,chem-
ical treatment of the system is necessary to control
the pH and corrosivenessof the water, as well as the
growth of slime in the packing. Slime growth can
lead to maldistributionof both air and water, which
can significantly reduce the effectiveness of the
packing. It is essential to control the pH throughad-
dition of lime and chemicals which reduce the cor-
rosiveness of the water. I
f this is not done diligently,
the very large piping systems involved in injection
water reticulation corrode rapidly. Repairs and re-
placement, apart from causing reduced reliability,
cost far more than the cost of an effectivetreatment
(Scott 1985).
Slipstream filtration of the cooling water is
sometimes recommended as a way of reducing
chemical treatment costs, since a high suspended
solidscontent makes it more difficult to control mi-
crobial activity.
In large spray pond systems,the quantityof wa-
ter in the systemis much larger and can operateas a
fairly efficient sugar-consuming system. Any sugar
entrained in the water which causes these problems
is degradedby naturalorganisms in whatis generally
a stablebiologicalsystemif the water quantity in the
system is large enough. Suspended solids settle out
in the ponds and slipstreamfiltrationis unnecessary.

5 Vacuum pumps
It was normal atone rime for a common vacuum
pump system to be used, either for a common con-
densersystemor as a common systemfor individual
vacuum pumps. It is now more usual for each con-
denser to have its own vacuum pump. Sometimes
the vacuum pumps are interconnected, so that a
common spare pump can be used in the case of the
failureof a pump orjust to boost a pump runningin-
efficiently. Howeverthecommon pipingand valving
involved canbe the source of leaks and often causes
more trouble than it is worth.
There are essentially two types of pumps seen
in use, reciprocating vacuum pumps and liquid ring
pumps. The reciprocating (piston) pump has the
highest efficiency,requiring only 0.4 kW per kg of
13.5.1 Liquid ring pumps
air handled at 10 kPa per minute, compared with
correspondingfiguresforliquid ring pumps and wa-
ter jet ejector of 3.7 and 5.8 kW respectively. Re-
ciprocating pumps are no longer common and this
discussion will be limited to liquid ring pumps and
jet ejectors.
13.5.1 Liquid ring pumps
Thepump consists of an impeller, with multiple
radial vanes, rotating in a cylindrical drum. The di-
ameter of the vanes is less than the drum diameter
and the center of the shaft is located eccentrically
in the drum,as shown in Figure 13.8.There are a
number of different variations on this design, but
all operateon the same principle. The liquid ring is
formed by centrifugal force as the rotor rotates and
the vanes and liquid ring are arranged in relation to
the inlet and outlet in such a way that the space be-
tween vanes and liquid ring increases past the inlet,
suckingairin, and thenreduces, compressingtheair
and dischargingit at the outlet.
They are generally compact, reliable and easy
to install and maintain, providing they are supplied
with good quality water. The lowest pressure attain-
able is determinedby the onset of cavitation,which
depends onthe designof thepumpandthesealwater
temperature. Generally this limit is in the range of
10to IS P a , depending on the design of the pump
and the service water temperature. The absolute
pressuresencountered in evaporatorsandin pans in
particularare such that single stagepumps generally
cannot do the duty without cavitationand damageto
thepump; momsatisfactoryperformanceisobtained
with two-stage pumps. Singlestagepumps are quite
adequatehowever for vacuum filters.
If a pump is marginal in terms of achieving the
vacuum required, an air ejector operated by atmo-
spheric air on the suction side of the pump can be
effective. It inc~vases
the vacuum attainableand the
additional air generally stops any cavitation occur-
ring.

Apart from water quality, the correct amount of

Too much water will overload the pump and too lit-
tle leadsto a rise in water temperature.This require-

=turn it to the system.About 90 % of the power ab-

dueto heat of compression and energy losses. Thus
a part of the water is continuously bled from the
pump to maintain the seal water at a low tempera-
ture. Condensationof someof the vapor also occurs,
and in a closed system the water has to be sent to a
cooling tower or heat exchanger to cool the water
supply.The amountof water used is generally speci-

13.6 Ejector systems
As an alternative to liquid ring pumps,jet ejec-
tors may be used, with either steam or water as the
motivefluid,whichentrainairin aspeciallydesigned
nozzle. Steamejectors are more common than water
jet ejectors, and generally require steam at an inter-
mediatepressure, around 400 to 1000 kPa.
The major advantage of ejectors over vacuum
pumps is the fact that they have no moving parts
and are thus maintenance-free. They also require
very littlespaceand areeasily and cheaplyinstalled.
However an ejector has to be designed for specific
conditions of pressure both for the motive fluid and
the vacuum conditions, and its efficiency falls off
rapidly outside these conditions.Thisis a severedis-
advantageif leaks developin the vacuum vessels and
the volume to be removed increasessubstantially.
13.6.1 Steamjet ejectors
A steam ejector may be used as a single stage
system, discharging to atmosphere, in which case a
silencer is required on the outlet. However a single
stage can only achieve a compressionratio of about

and so it is close to the limit in most sugar mill ap-

14.1 Introduction
Syrupclarificationis not a standard operation in
allraw sugarmills. Itisbecomingmorewidelyused,
particularly in the production of direct consumption
sugars, either to remove suspended solids or color
or both. Becauseof the viscosity and greater density
of the syrup, it is not possible to settle out the fine
suspended solids. Flotation clarification does how-
everworkeffectivelywhen appliedto syrup,without
any sophisticatedprocessrequirements.The aerated
phase is stable and does not require the extensive
use of chemicals to form and stabilize the scum
layer as for instance flotation in mineral processing
requires.
Flotation clarification is a process which has
found extensive use in water treatment and in the
mineral processing industry. The process has also
been used for many years in sugar refining in the
form of phosphatation.Until recently flotationsepa-
ration has received little fundamental attention.
Schojeld (2001) remarked as follows:
"... the lack of fundamental design criteria in
1991 painted a rather depressing picture of
D M (dissolved air jltrafion) design expertise
and whilst DAF had existed as an artform for
over 30years, as a science it was much less de-
veloped':
It has sincebeen the subjectof moreintensive study
using CFD techniques.
Applicationof flotationclarificationinraw sugar
mills was pioneered by Tate and Lyle (Bennettet al.
1977). The process was substantially improved by
the development of efficientpolyacrylamidefioceu-
lants and a number of installations clarifying syrup
have been installed throughout the world. Systems
have been installed in Hawaii, Taiwan, Louisiana,
The Philippines, India, Colombia, South Africa,
China, Mauritius and ~nany
other countries. It is at-
tractive because it is a simple process carried out
in inexpensive equipment. Subsequently flotation
clarificationhas been applied to filtrate from rotary
vacuum flters as well (Section 11.3.5).
As an alternative to filtration, flotation clarifi-
cation can be considered as a simpler and cheaper
option. It can be augmented with either sulfitation
or phosphatation to achieve particular sugar quality
criteria.
In this process, very 6ne suspended matter is
agglomerated and floated to the surface by fine air
bubbles. Separationby flotation does not depend so
much on size and relative density of particles being
removed as it does on their surface properties. The
process can be considerably enhanced through the
use of appropriate chemicals. In the mining indus-
try selectiveflotationof particular types of particles
is possible through the addition of chemicals which
changethesurfaceproperties.Theuse of flocculants
in flotation has a substantial effect on the process,
leading to mechanical entrapment of air bubbles in
the floc particles and greatly assisting the separa-
tion.
The mechanisms involved in the formation and
flotation of floc particles are complex. Little work
has been donetoelucidatethemechanismsinvolved,
andthe processhas evolvedthroughempiricalinves-
tigationsto aviableprocess.Optimizationinvariably

to be treated. An important aspect therefore is the
method for a suitablelaboratory test to simulatethe
process in practice and optimize conditions which
may vary dependingon location.

14.2.3 Aerationof syrup
Separation of particles either in clarification by
settling or by flotationclarificationis determinedby
the terminalvelocity of the particle.This is obtained
by equating drag and buoyancy forces. Using the
Stokes law relationship for the drag coefficient for
spherical particles of diameter d at low Reynolds
numbers (C,,= 24/Re), the equation for terminal
velocity u, is:
where Ap is the differencein density. The viscosity
of syrupp, is considerablyhigherthan that of juice,
which means that separationby settlingis more dif-
ficult in syrup. The density is also higher, so that
the density difference between liquid and solid is
insufficient to achievesettling in practice. However
in flotation, the density of the aerated floc is low,
and the density differenceis large, making separa-
tion feasible.Work reported by Echeverri and Rein
(2006) suggeststhat the density differenceis of the
order of 800 kg/m3 and the average floc velocity
1.4mm/s (5mlh). From equation (14.1) the average
floc size is 183pm.
Considerablevariation around these averagevalues
was observed.In practicetheparticlesbeing floated
are not spherical and Haarhof and Edzwald (2001)
report that the constant in equation (14.1) is higher
play a wider size range.
Electrolysisisgenerallynot practicalona full scale.
Experience in water treatment and sugar refining
has indicated that dissolvedair flotationgivesbetter
resultsthan thesimpleraerationby dispersed air flo-
tation (Saranin 1972). In refining, Hon-Jun (1990)
claims that the air bubbles are occluded within
the calcium phosphate flocs as they form, and so
must be small and preferably c 30 pm. Thus cal-
cium phosphate formation and aeration should take
place simultaneously and not sequentially. In the
case of syrup clarification,larger bubbles are quite
adequate, sincethere may be a total absence of cal-
cium phosphate floc, and the attachment of bubbles
to particlesis clearly by a different mechanism.
When processing syrup, dissolved air flotation
shows no advantage and if anything, gives worse
performancethan dispersed air flotation(Reinet al.
1987). This is evidence of the stable foam formed
in this application.In the interestsof simplicity and
cost, dispersed air flotationis a better option.
Zeng SiXian et al. (1998) have shown that an
improvementin the turbidity of the clarified liquor
is possible by applying ultrasonic vibration to the
liquor after the addition of flocculant.

an air to solids ratio is not meaningful. Instead an

14.2.5 Application of syrup clarifica-
tion in the raw sugar mill
However good juice clarification may be, there
is a largeincrease in turbidity of about 80 % across
the evaporators (Scott 1988). This indicates that a
syrup clarification process should be more benefi-
cial than elaborate steps to improve primary juice
clarification.The syrupclarifier alsoacts asa safety
net, removing suspended material arising from pe-
riods of upset and mud carryover in juice clarifica-
tion.
Conditions for flotatiop clarification need to
The choice of floccu-
lant, whetheradditional
chemicals are worth-
while and the Brix at
which theprocessoper-
ates, all depend on the
particular characteris-
tics of the material to
be treated. The oppor-
tunitiesand advantages
of using the process are
dependent on the local circumstancesprevailing.
Tate and Lyle patented a syrup clarificationpro-
cess referred to as Talodura syrup clarification. It
resembles more closely phosphatation in a refinery,
involvingheating to 80 O C
and addition of lime and
phosphoricacid (300mgP,O$g DS) to thesyrupin
a reaction tank prior to aeration. A reaction time of
1to 1.5minutes is allowedand the pH is controlled
by regulatinglimeadditionto givea pH of about6.5.
The premise of the process is that a primary floc of
calciumphosphatehas to be formed, beforeaddition
of flocculant and aeration, after which a secondary
floc is formed.
TheTalodura process is the center of the Blanco
Directo process developed by Tare and Lyle to pro-
duce direct consumptionsugar of 100-200I
Ucolor
(>on 1988).A flow diagram of the process is given
in Figure 14.4.
A slightly different process flow scheme is il-
lustrated in Figure 14.5, the flow sheet for a sugar
mill in Zimbabwe.Theraw syrupis pumped through
a heater where the syrup is heated up to 85 "C with
vapor 1,then passes throughan aerationstagewhere
airis dispersedintothe liquid.Thisconsistseitherof
a high speed aeration pump, or a suitably designed
air sparger. The liquid then flows to a small feed
tank where undispersed air has a chance to disen-
gage before the aerated syrup enters the bottom of
the syrup clarifier. No phosphoric acid or lime is
added.Justbeforethe syrupclarifier,polyelectrolyte
is added ahead of an in-line mixer. The in-linemixer
is designed to disperse the flocculant adequately
within the liquor without high shear that might lead
to breakdown of the floc. Finally the syrup enters
through the central feed pipe, the diameter of which
increases as the syrup enters to reduce the inlet ve-
locity.

14.3.1 Sugar quality
This scheme shows direct contact heating with
evaporator vapor and subsequent cooling by flash-
ing to the last evaporator body. Flash cooling re-
stores the Brix almost to the level before the direct
contact heater. This is a low-cost solution but indi-
rect heating may also be used. It is advisableto cool
the syrup after clarification to reduce the potential
for subsequentdegradationand color formation.
Syrup clarification in conjunction with phos-
phatation has been used with success to replace
syrup sulfitation in factories producing plantation
white sugar (Steindl and Doherty 2005).It produces
a lower color sugar and also has the benefit of sig-
nificantly reducing the residual SO, content of the
sugar. Trials in Australian mills indicated that the
process realized reductionsin viscosity and increas-
es in the rate of crystallization.
Clarificationof B molasses instead of syrup has
the advantagethat the quantity to be treated is small
and so a smaller clarifier can be installed. It also
seems to have the potential to remove larger quanti-
ties of impurities, and will achieve benefits relating
to lower 6nal massecuite viscosities and improved
recovery. However, compared to syrup clarification,
it does not achieve the same improvementin sugar
quality, and requires more steam for re-evaporation
of the diluted molasses and a solid bowl centrifuge
or other systemfor desweeteningthe scum.
Clarification of final molasses is sometimes
advocated as a means of improving alcohol yields
and yeast quality,Flotation clarificationof this type
could well achieve this objective.
14.3 Benefits of syrup clarifica-
tion
Syrupclarificationis characterizedby the stable
scum which is obtained. The process is simple, re-
quires little supervision, and the operating cost is
low since it requires only the use of flocculant and
may not require any additional chemicals.A further
advantage is that the scum can be directed back to
raw juice or perhaps to clarifier muds. If the latter
optionis employed,caremust be taken to prevent an
increase in the pol of the filter cake, but this can be
minimized by optimizing the operation. The major
benefits to be obtained from syrup clarification are
an improvementin sugar quality and a reduction in
massecuite viscosities. The advantages of this ap-
plication are greater when the quality of cane being
processed is poor. From being in the position where
the mill was regularly unable to produceVHP sugar
in South Africa, Empangeni mill with syrup clarifi-
cationwas ableto produceconsistentlygood quality
sugar meeting VHP specifications and for the first
time was able to achieve good molasses exhaustion
(Reinet al. 1987).
Although these benefits should help to achieve
an improvementin overall sugar recovery, the small
improvements anticipatedhave never been proven in
the face of normal recovery variations. The best way
of assessing the efficiency of syrup clarification is
still from turbidity removal results. A large number
of syrup samples tested from many different mills
have always shown the potential to achievea reduc-
tion in turbidity of 80 to 95 %.
14.3.1 Sugar quality
The Talodura process is claimed to remove
80 % of the suspended solids and lead to a reduc-
tion in sugar color of 8 to 10 % (Trott 1988).The
same benefits are claimed from syrup clarification
without lime and phosphoric acid addition (Rein et
al. 1987).
Some significantimprovementsin sugar quality
have been reported. A significant decrease of 15%
was found in color and gums of affinated sugar,
similar to that reported by Bennett et al. (1977).Tri-
als in Australia showed raw sugar color reductions
between20 and40 % and ash reductionsup to47 %,
with phosphate addition. A 15 % reduction in the
ash of the afhated sugar was measured in South
Africa, but the differencewas not established statis-
tically (Rein et al. 1987). In practice, the effects of
the syrupclarifieroperationwere extremelymarked;
analysisof dataforA massecuiteexhaustionand the
purity rise on A centrifuging showed better results
with the syrup clarifier in operation, indicatingthat
less washing was necessary to achieve the required
VHP sugar pol.
Steindl and Doherty (2005) confirmed experi-
enceelsewherethat theeffecton sugarqualityis sig-
nificantly greater than the improvements measured
in syrup quality suggest.

14 Syrup clarification
Syrup clarification has been particularly effec-

Fine screening of the melt could be dispensed with

steameconomy.Suspendedsolidsin white sugarare

14.4 Equipment
14.4.1 Clarifiervessels
Thevesselsused fordissolvedah-flotationinwa-
ter treatment are traditionally rectangular in shape.
This is moreconvenient when a bankof D M cellsis
used. This was also the geometry first used in phos-
phatation in sugar refining. However syrupclarifiers
have usually been made as circular vessels, because
single circularvesselsarecheaper to constructand a
simpler scum scrapingmechanismis possible.
Surface loading. The area required is deter-
mined by the rise time of the aerated doc particles.
The terminal velocity of the floc particles is expect-
ed to be in the range of 2 to 10m/h, calculatedfrom
equation (14.1). In practice, liquid surface loadings,
determined by dividing the volumetric throughput
by the surfacearea,in the range2.5 to 15m3/(m2-h)
or m/h are used in DAF in treating water. Haarhoff
and Edzwald (2001) report that practical surface
loadingsgreaterthan calculatedrise rates arenot un-
common. This is ascribed to further agglomeration
of the aggregatesdue to differentialrise rates.
A syrup clarifieris usually sized to have a reten-
tion time of around 20 to 25 minutes (Bennert et al.
1977,Rein 1988).If the depth of the clarifieris 1m,
the surface loading based on these times is 2.4 to
3 m/h, whichis at thelowerend of theloadingsused
for DAE
A breakthroughin flotationwater treatmentwas
the introductionof lamellas, which prevent vortices
and reduce the Reynolds number, and consequently
the turbulence, leading to a more efficient separa-
tion and higher capacity. Flotation units on water
treatment provided with lamella plates can achieve
higher loadrates (30-40 mh). Numerical simulation
of the flow in a hypothetical syrup clarifier provid-
ed with lamellas suggests that a surface loading of
40 m/h appearsfeasible(Echeverri and Rein 2006).
This has notyet been tried in practice with syrupbut
appears to hold considerablepromise.
Syrup inlet and outlet.The feed syrup should
enter with minimum disturbance at the correct den-
sity level, with a minimum of inlet energy to avoid
turbulence. The depth of the clarifier is important
only in providing sufficient height to be able to
maintain separate froth and clear liquid zones. It is
generally chosen to be between 1.0 and 1.5 m, but
may be as low as 0.8 m (Hon-Jun 1990).The diam-
eter is then chosen to give the required syrup resi-
dence time. The syrup outlet is normally positioned
at thebottom of the clarifierin theform of a circular
offtakering.
The openings in the ring have to be sized to
achieve an equal flow through each opening to get
14.4.1 Clarifier vessels
a uniform offtake. This follows the sameprinciples
used in designingcircularjuice clarifier outlets and
evaporatorfeed rings (Section 12.7.5) using Knaeb-
el's criterion (Knaebel 1981).
It is importantto keep all velocitiesin the clari-
fier at a low level, particularly at the inlet and off-
take. The positioning of inlet and outlets needs to
be chosen with care to ensure that short-circuiting
does not occur.In theory, the advantageof a circu-
lar clarifier is the fact that velocities are decreased
towards the periphery. In practice, offtakes at the
periphery of the vessel led to short-circuitingof liq-
uid to the outletsand recirculation patternssetup in
the body of the vessel (Rein et al. 1987).
Schofield (2001)confirms that one of the major
factors in hydrauliccontrol is the way in which the
subnatant is withdrawn, and that recirculating cur-
rentsareexperiencedandcanbeproblematic.Tracer
tests confirm the better performance obtained with
a bottom circularoutlet (Rein et al. 1987).Schofield
(2001) confirms that end-wall outlets replaced by
higher resistance multi-distributed outlets or perfo-
rated pipe laterals alleviate problems of recirculat-
ing currents.

A sketch of a syrup clarifier of the type used in
Tongaat-Hulett mills is shown in Figure 14.6. The
diameter is 4.9 m and has an average syrup depth
of 1.3 m. The central feed pipe has an increas-
ing diameter to reduce inlet velocity to less than
1.2m/min (20mm/s). A rotating scumrake scrapes
the scum off into a launder around the periphery
of the clarifier and the scum flows back to the raw
juice tank.
Clarified syrup is drawn off from the bottom
of the clarifier through a variable height weir. The
scum level in the clarifier is controlled by regulat-
ing the heightof the outlet weir in the overflow box.
Either a cylindrical weir or a straight weir can be
used. The weir overflow must be wide enough to
ensure that a change in liquid flow rate through the
clarifier does not materially alter the head required
to overflow the weir and so change the liquid level
in the clarifier.The equation for the weir crest as a
function of volumetric flow rate V is:
where h is the crest height and b the width of the
weir, both in m. The equationis implicitin h requir-
ing an iterative solution.
A new developmentin DAFwhich may haveap-
plication in sugar processing is the use of lamella
plate modules in flotation clarification. They have
a number of benefits (Schofield2001),includingre-
ducingturbulenceand recirculation,improving sep-
aration of aggregatesfrom the liquid, and assisting
in the directingof separatedflowsto their respective
outlets.
14.4.2 Systemsof aeration
Three approachesto dispersingair in the syrup
have been used:
Bleeding air into a pump. Allowing air into
the Buction side of a pump running at m-pole
motor speedispossible, but admittingtoomuch
air leads to air bindingand cavitation.It is pref-
erable to utilize an aerator e
o aerate the liquid
Referencesp. 351
14 Syrupclarification
only and not expect it to pump as well. This is
designed with radial blades and fins to achieve
a high degree of shear. A tip speed of 30 m/s
is required. An approach reported by Hon-Jun
(1990) incorporates a high speed rotor with
sharp edges on both rotor and annulus, which
have a cutting effect on the bubbles, producing
bubbles in the range of 10to 30 pm.
Stirred aeration tank. A separate cylindri-
cal tank is provided with a centralized stirrer,
which entrains air through a vortex. Alterna-
tively an air passage is provided down through
the middle of the stirrer through which air is
sucked into the liquid and dispersed by the stir-
rer blades.
An air sparger. This consists of a tube with a
large number of small holes through which air
is introduced in the form of fine bubbles. A sin-
tered plastic tube is inserted after a bend in a
section of pipe with a larger diameter. The air
is fed into the tubeand is strippedfrom the sin-
tered surface by syrup flowing through the an-
nular section between the sparge tube and the
pipe wall (Smithet al. 2000). The velocity past
the tube affects the size of bubbles formed; a
high velocity past the surface strips off bubbles
before they have had time to grow leading to a
smalleraveragebubble size.
In practice the amount of air provided does not
appear to be important, although a value of 0.04
m3air/m3 syrup has been regarded as a mini-
mum. Based on a high value of insoluble solids
content in syrup of 200 mglkg, the air solids ra-
tio is 0.18, far above values quoted for dissolved
air flotation in water treatment of 0.02 to 0.04,
or for refinery phosflotation of 0.02 to 0.03 (Sa-
ranin 1972).
However dispersedair flotation does not utilize all
the air added since some escapes in the form of
large air bubbles. Above a certain size floc, Haar-
hoff and Edzwald (2001) report that the amount
of air and the bubble size is unimportant in water
treatment; this seems to be the case in syrup clari-
fication too.
Not all the air is adequately dispersed in the
liquid, and a disengagementlfeed tank is supplied
ahead of the clarifier to allow any large bubbles of
air to escape so that they do not disturb conditions
in the clarifier. This is shown in the flow diagram
in Figure 14.5.
14.4.3 Scumhandling
The scum quantity varies considerably,but rep-
resents about 5 % by volume (Reinet al. 1987).The
scumrakes may be driven by a drivesupportedcen-
trally above the clarifier vessel as shown in Figure
22.6 (Section 22.3.2), but a simpler arrangement in
Figure 14.6 consists of a horizontal ring supported
on three sets of rollers located around the periphery
and driven by one of the sets of rollers. The scrapers
rotate atabout0.5min-I, slow enoughso that they do
not causethe liquid to rotate with the scum. It is not
necessary to desweeten the scum, since it can be re-
turned to mix with the rawjuice. The scum does not
flow easily and sometimes a water flush or prefer-
ably a streamof filtrate is used to promoteits return.
It is feasible to return the scum to the rotary vacuum
filters directly, but when this was tried the sucrose
loss in filter cake increased (Reinet al. 1987).

arrangementmakes use of a number of half-baffles,
typically 12, with each baffle oriented at 90' to the
preceding baffle. The design parameters for this are
not well defined, but the use of a calculated power1

14.5.2 Laboratory testing and evalua-
tion
In general, it is found that the syrup clarifier is
always able to achieve the same degree of turbidity
removal as that obtainable in the laboratory, of the
order of 85 % removal. Comparisonwith theresults
obtainedin the laboratoryprovidesa usefulcheck as
to whether the plant syrup clarifieris performing as
well as it should.
Referencesp. 351
14 Syrupclarification
A useful laboratory test involves rapid stirring
of syrup for three minutes in a small beaker held in
a water bath at 85 "C (Rein et al. 1987).The stirring
arrangementis such that air is entrained into the liq-
uid and dispersed by the impeller to saturate it with
air. Polyelectrolyteis gently stirred into the contents
of the beaker for 30 seconds after aeration and the
liquid is left standingfor twenty minutes. After this
time the separationbetween scum and clearliquid is
complete and samples of clear liquid can be taken
off for analysis. Milk of lime and phosphoric acid,
when used, are added to the liquid before aeration.
An important analysis in evaluating flota-
tion clarification is the measurement of turbidity.
ICUMSA Method GS7-21 (Anon. 2005) for de-
termining the turbidity of clarified juice involves
measuring the absorbance at 900 nm,a procedure
also used by Steindl and Doherty (2005). Rein et
al. (1987) used a different procedure involving the
measurementof absorbanceat 720 nm on a 10Brix
solution before and after filtering. Turbidity may
also be measured by a turbidimeter. A value less
than 25 NTU (nephelometerturbidity units) would
be expectedon a 25 Brix solution.
14.5.3 Scum layer control
It is necessary to control the thickness of the
scum layer in the clarifier. This can be doneby rais-
ing or lowering the liquid level in the clarifier by
adjusting the outlet weir height. The scum layer
should be as thin as possible to minimize the resi-
dence time. It should have sufficient time to allow
the liquid to drain out of the scum but not too long
thatthe aggregatesbegin to breakup and allow solid
particles to escape fromthe scumlayerand exit with
the subnatant or underflow. It should also not be so
thin that a significant amount of syrup is recycled
with the scum. It is generally kept to a thickness of
about 80 mm.
Unfortunately a reliable transducer to measure
the thickness is not yet available. The scum layer
thickness is most easily seen by inserting a glass
tube (typically 80 mrn diameter) down through the
scumlayer, blocking the top by hand or with a bung,
and without pulling it right out of the liquid,pulling
it up far enough to see the scum layer thickness in
the tube.
In practice some entrainment of floc in the un-
derflow occurs if control of the whole process is not
adequate. An instrument to detect this and recycle
syrupwith entrained solids would be valuable to en-
sure optimumsyrupquality at all times.
14.6 Enhancement of color re-
moval
An additional improvement in this process can
be achieved through the use of lime and SO, sparg-
ing. Since the precipitate formed is floated off, no
downstream filtrationis required.
Combining sulfitation with syrup clarification
gives additional color removal. Laboratorywork in-
dicated that sulfitationcould give 20 to 25 % color
removal in syrup as opposed to 7 % without SIIE&~
tion (Rein 1988). Subsequentfull-scale trials, using
2 000mg SOJkg DS, showed only a 15% reduction
in syrupcolor, althoughthe differencein sugarcolor
was much larger at 24 % (Smith et al. 2000). This
substantiated previous evidence that the improve-
ment in sugarcoloris greater than the color removal
across syrup clarificationsuggests.
Sulfurusage is in the range 600 to 1400mg sul-
furlkg dissolvedsolids.Liquid SO, may be used, but
sulfurburners are generally a cheaper option.
The incorporation of carbonatation with melt
clarification, called carboflotation, has been intro-
duced in a white-end refinery in Zimbabwe (Smith
et al. 2000),with the scumreturned to theraw house
I
syrup clarifier. Carbflotationis also referred to as a
commercialrefining process by Hon-Jun (1990).It
is an attractive option in treating refinery melt, but
carbflotationshowsno advantageover normal syrup
clarificationin producing raw sugar (Rein 1988).
An alternative to syrup sullitation is the use of
colorprecipitants.Theseare longchainpolyamines,
which when metered into the untreated syrup, in-
creasethe color removal from the 8-10 % level to a
value of 25-30 % (Trott 1988).This has the advan-
tage of not increasingthe sulfur dioxide level in the
sugar.Theseprecipitantsarepositively charged,and
are sometimes referred to as cationic flocculants
Because colorants are mostly negatively charged.
they form an adduct with the precipitants.
The first color precipitant, dimethyl ditallor

15.1.1 Solubilityand supersaturation
Sucrose is highly soluble in water. A saturated
solution of sucrose, a solution in thermodynamic
equilibrium with a solid sucrose phase, contains
roughly two parts of sucrose to one part of water at
room temperature, and almost five parts sucrose to
one part of water at 100 OC.In order to crystallize
sucrose, it is necessary to raise the concentration of
sucrose above that of a saturated solution, and con-
ml it at just the right concentration to achieve the
crystallization required. Therefore it is important to
establish the sucrose concentration at saturation un-
der the operating conditions.

accepted as representing adequately the solubility

15.1.3 Effect of nonsucrose
The nonsucrose components in solution have
four major effects on crystallization:
They modify the solubility of sucrose.The solu-
bility coefficientis generally less than unity for
low values of the nonsucrose/water ratio (see
equation (18.3) in Section 18.1.1), but at high
values it exceeds one, indicating an enhanced
solubility of sucrose.
They reduce the crystallization rate by slowing
down the diffusionprocess dueto higherviscos-
ities or by interacting with certain faces of the
crystalsurface,thus inhibitinglattice incorpora-
tion.
They affectthe shapeor morphology of the crys-
tal. This is linked with the previous point, in that
certain impurities block the crystallization sites
on some surfaces, hindering growth on these
faces, thus changing the shape of the crystal.
Certain oligosaccharides are particularly well
known as a cause of elongated crystals (Morel
du Boil 1991).
They increasethe width of themetastableregion
shown in Figure 15.1, providing a larger safe
range of temperature and concentration condi-
tions for graining.
The effects of nonsucrosevary from one cane grow-
ing area to another and at different times of the
season. They are generally difficult to measure or
predict.
Values of the solubility coefficientare shown in
Figure 18.1.They are affected not only by the non-
sucroselwaterratio but also by the ratio of reducing
sugars/ash.Valuesdropbelow onetoa valuebetween
0.8 and 0.9 at a nonsucroselwaterratioof three.This
implies that the solubility of sucrosein water reduc-
es as the purity drops.As the nonsucrose/waterratio
increases above three, the solubility coefficient in-
creases, exceedingunity at a nonsucroselwaterratio
above about four.
Few attemptshave been madeto quantifythe ef-
fect of nonsucroseon the crystallizationrate. Incor-
porating the proposal of Wright and White (1974)
into equation (15.11)gives:
In this equation, q,,,, is the nonsucroselwater ra-
tio. Love (2002) analyzed the results of a number
of workers and showed that the constant 1.75 is too
low. He estimated that the constant should have a
value around 2.4. The form of equation (15.12) may
be functionally appropriate but there is little agree-
ment on the values to be used in this equation.
15.1.4 Crystallizationrates
Equations (15.8) and (15.12) can be used to
estimate crystallization rates with suitable assump-
tions about crystal surface area (mean size, size
distribution and shape factors). However there are
no proven values of the parameters available to be
able to do so with confidence.A different approach
is to use industrial as well as pilot plant and labora-

These results together with some recent Australian
data are shown in Table 15.1.
Thesenumbers only give an approximationto ac-
tual crystallization rates, for the following reasons:
Mother liquor purity may vary widely duringthe
course of a boiling.
For a part of the process, evaporation and not
crystallization may be limiting, and the crystal-
lizationrate could on average be higher than the
values shown. This is well illustrated by Lion-
net's data on refinery boilings in the Table; the
first number representsthe rate in the early stag-
es of the boiling when evaporation rate exceeds
the crystallizationrate, while the second number
is the rate when the process is evaporation rate
limited.
Control of the process and in particular the su-
persaturationcan have a largeeffect.Panswhich
boil fast because of good circulation will give
higher apparentcrystallizationrates.
There is a large and variable dispersion in crys-
tal sizes, which influences average values sig-
nificantly. This dispersionis due to variationsin
crystal growth rate, which can differ by an order
of magnitude(Whiteet al. 1998).
Ithas been proposed that therelative growth rates of
crystals in a suspensionare dependenton the history
of the crystals (White et al. 1998). The growth rate
of each individual crystal is an innate property of the

The fact that sucrose solutions boil at a higher
temperature than water is discussed in Section
12.1.2. The elevation of the boiling point is shown
as a function of sucrose content in Figure 12.1,
which indicates that the boiling point elevation is
lower at lower temperatures. This data is presented
in a slightly different way as a function of rnasse-
cuite temperaturein Figure 15.4,based on Holven's
interpretation of Thieme's data (Chen and Chou
1993:238).
Saska (2002) points out that different correla-
tion equations for boiling point elevation are avail-
able, but have all been derived from only two origi-
nal investigations,one by Spengler on beet and the
other by Thieme on cane products. Other data by
Batterham and Norgate (1975) has largely been
neglected, other than in Australia. Saska undertook
further work and compared his data with previous
correlations.He proposedthe followingrelationship

It is similar in form to the integrated Clausius-Cla-

The purity term added accounts for the effect of irn-

Following from this, a useful property of su-

evation is directly proportional to the concentration
when expressedas g dissolvedsucrosdg water.Thus
if a solutionhas aboiling pointelevationof 10"C at

for pure solutions are higher at temperatures above
about 65 "C; the data of Holven as published by
Chen and Chou (1993) show on averagean increase
in boiling point elevationof 1 "C fora 10unit purity
change; on average the data of Saska show about
