15.1.6 Crystal size and shape
15.1.6 Crystal size and shape
Crystal size is important in product sugar be-
cause it usually has to meet some consumer quality
specification.Directconsumptionsugarhas an aver-
age size between 0.2 mm and 2 mm,depending on
the market requirements,with the largestsizesbeing
produced in India. The most common size range is
0.4 to 0.8 mm. Raw sugar for refining normally has
to meet size specifications to facilitateefficient af-
fination in the refinery.
Larger crystal sizes have less surface area per
unit mass and are easier to processin centrifugation
because the quantity of surface film is less on larger
crystals. However the larger surface area of smaller
crystals enhances the rate of crystallization. This is
particularly important in low purity massecuites,
where the crystal size is kept smaller, typically at
around 0.2 mm in C massecuites. The centrifugal
screen aperture size is chosen according to the size
of crystal to be separated.
Crystal size distribution is also important. The
more uniform the crystal sizedistribution,the easier
the centrifugal separation. Fine grain in a masse
cuite has the propensity to fill the gaps between the
larger crystals, resulting in a layer of crystal in the
centrifugal which does not filter or purge easily. In
addition small crystals may pass throughthe screen
1 apertures,leading to lower molasses exhaustion.
Crystal size distribution is generally character-
I ized by the coefficientof variation CV,which is de-
fined as:
where dmis the mean crystalsize and othe standard
deviation of the distribution.As the crystal grows,
the mean size increases so CV can be expected to
decrease. Ln practice sizedispersion effects are evi-
dent,resultingin differentcrystalsgrowing at differ-
ent rates. This conAictswith the traditionalMcCabe
law, which predictsthattheincreasein crystallength
with timeisindependentofcrystalsize.TheMcCabe
law would lead to an improvementin CVwhenever
crystal growthoccurred. White et al. (1998)showed
; &at a variation in crystal growthrates occurs, large-
, ly dependent on the crystal history; a fast growing
uystal will continue to grow faster than average,
W i n g to the conclusion that larger crystalshave a
higher growth rate. In A massecuites, the net effect
is for the CV to improve (reduce) as crystal growth
occurs, but in low purity massecuites the size dis-
persion effects are much stronger, leading to worse
CV values as crystal growth progresses (Rein and
Msimanga 1999).
It is convenientto assumethat the distributionof
sugarsizes followsoneof the standard distributions.
The common method of determination of mean ap-
erture and CVby sievingassumesa normal distribu-
tion. This however is symmetrical about the mean
and so sometimes includes negative sizes. Hoekstra
(1985)usedanegativeexponentialdistributionin an-
alyzingtheresults of continuouspan trials.Rein and
Archibald (1989) used the log normal distribution,
which better handles the non-symmetrical distribu-
tion but still incorporates a mean value and a CV.
White et al. (1998) also showed that the log normal
distributionis appropriate.In the beet sugarindustry
the RRSB (Rosin-Rammler-Sperling-Bennett)dis-
tributionis acceptedas the bestrepresentation of the
size distribution (van der Poel et al. 1998:106).
Measurement of crystal size. Crystalsize may
be measured in a number of differentways:
Product sugar may be dried and screened in
a nest of sieves for a standard length of time.
ICUMSA method GS2-37 applies (Anon.
2005). In the Powers method the mean aperture
is an averagesizebased on mass and is obtained
as the 50 % point on a plot of cumulative mass
sugar retained against aperture size. The stan-
dard deviation is obtained from the difference
between the mean on a cumulative distribution
plot relative to the 16or 84 % points.
A specificgrain sizeis sometimesreported.This
uses the result of a sieving test to produce an
"average" size in terms of surface area (SASTA
2005).
@
Sometimes only the "fines" are measured as
that fraction of the sugar which passes through
a screen with a 0.6 rnm mesh opening (28 mesh
Tyler screen).
Digital imaging is becoming more widely used,
because it does not necessarily require that the
sugar be separated and dried before measure-
ment. It is thereforeparticularly suitablefor low
grademassecuites.Theimage may be processed
manually (counting and measuring individual

15.1.8 The crystallizationprocess
Crystallization in a factory takes place under
vacuum and involves the simultaneous processes
of mass transfer and evaporation.Vacuum is neces-
saryto keepthe temperatureata lowenoughlevel to
minimize color formation and the inversion or deg-
radation of sucrosein the process.
In starting a batch boiling, theliquoris concen-
trated until the metastable zone is reached (Figure
15.1). Crystallization is initiated by adding some
very fineseed in theform of a slurry,whichprovides
the nuclei to start crystallization. From then on, the
concentration of the mother liquor is controlled so
that crystallization occurs without dissolving any
crystal and without the formation af new nuclei
(falsegrain). This requires the establishmentof suf-
ficientcrystalsurfacearea andcontrolof the feed to
the pan to controlmother liquor concentration.
The process has been traditionally carried out
in batch vacuum pans, althoughmore recently con-
tinuous systemshave been introduced.However the
processof initiatingcrystallizationisstillcarried out
ona batch basis.In somecases, the processis started
on a magma or footing, i.e. a mixture of liquor and
crystal from a previous boiling, thus avoiding the
seedingprocess.
15.1.9 Objectivesof thepan house
Thecrystallizationstagein a raw sugarhousein-
volves crystallizing as much sugar as possible from
&aporator syrup. The sugar has to be produced at
the required quality and the sugar content in the fi-
nal molasseshas to be as low as possible, since any
sugar left in this stream is a loss to the operation.
Crystallization needs to be carried out in a number
of stages to reduce the sucrose content infinal mo-
lasses. Dierent crystallizationschemesmay be em-
ployed to achieve these objectives.
In meeting these objectives, the operations also
need to be conductedin a way to meet the produc-
tion rate targets. This requires meeting certain crys-
tallization efficiency targets, so that installedequip-
ment does not constitute a bottleneck At the same
time care has to be taken to ensurethat the quantity
of steam and vapor used in processing is not exces-
sive.Itgenerallyfollowsthat efficientcrystallization
minimizessteam usage.
Sugar quality is affected by the quality of the
syrup to be processed, specifically its pwjty, color
andclarity.Theboilingschemeis selectedtoachieve
therequiredquality given the syrupto be processed.
The optimum scheme yields the required quality
with minimum equipmentcapacity.
A highcrystallizationefficiencyimpliesproduc- .
ing the maximum amount of crystal sugar ineach
stage of crystallization. The importance of this as-
pect is illustratedin Section 15.2.6. High exhaustion
ineachstageminimizesthe amountof massecuiteto
be boiled, which in turn minimizes the steam used
and thepan and centrifugalcapacity.

15.2 Sugar boiling schemes
Maximum recovery of sucroseby crystallization
cannot be achievedin one step.A l i t to the crystal
content is met at the point where themassecuitewill
no longerflow out the pan. Crystallizationis stopped
before this point and the massecuite centrifuged to
separate the crystal from the molasseg. The molas-
ses produced still contains crystallizable sugar and
the process is repeated in one or usually two more
stages to achieve the optimal sucrose recovery.The
purity of the massecuite decreases with each suc-
cessive stage as more sucrose is removed. Various
crystallization schemes may be employed to suitthe
purity of the syrup and the quality of sugar to be
produced.
The following crystallization schemes are com-
monly used to produce raw sugar:
Two-boilingscheme,
Three-boilingscheme,
DoubleEinwurf scheme,
VHP scheme.
15.2.1 Description of boiling schemes
used
These schemes are shown schematically in
Figures 15.6 to 15.9.There are a number of pos-
sible variations that may be introduced within each
scheme to meet particular conditions.For example,
the double centrifugation (affination) of C and B
sugars may be required to produce sugar low in
color and ash when syruppurities are low; while re-
circulation of the runoff syrup (back-boiling) may
be used to reduce massecuite purities when syrup
purities arevery high.
The choice of boiling scheme affects both the
total massecuitemass Rows and the energy required
for crystallization. They have different advantages
and disadvantages and should only be compared
for a well-defined set of conditions. Comparisons
of massecuite mass and energy requirements for 3
different schemes have been published by Birkert
(1978).
The number of steps required to exhaust syrup
to finalmolassespurity will depend primarily on the
purity of the syrup. The crystallization stages and
their separation products are usually identified by
letters.The highest purity stage is theA stagewhich
yields A molasses and A sugar. The other stages are
labeled B and C, but, in the case of the two-boiling
scheme, the sequence is altered and only A and C
sugars are produced.
In practice, rigid adherence to a crystallization
scheme during a complete season is rarely possible
and crystallization stations are designed with some
flexibility to cope with variations in quality of the
input syrupand output sugar.
Two-boiling scheme. The main advantage of
two-stage crystallization systems (Figure 15.6)
compared with three-stage schemes is a simplifica-
tion of the equipment needed by eliminating the B
sugar stage. However, the scheme does not appre-
ciably change the total volume of massecuite to be
boiled and therefore the capacity of the sugar house
equipment.

cuite. C massecuite is centrifuged in continuous
centrifuges and the C sugar is made into a magma
of about 85 purity. The A sugar is crystallized from
syrup using the C magma as seed.TheA massecuite
must be thoroughly exhausted in the pan and cool-
ing crystallizersto obtain a purity drop of at least 20
points between massecuiteand runoff syrup.

15.2.2 Comparison of boilingschemes
In summary, a two-boiling scheme is best suited
to handle a low syrup purity ( 4 2 ) .The three-boiling
scheme is the most widely used to produce sugar in
the 98 to 99 O Z
range and requires the least amount
of plant, but careful control of purities is necessary
to achieve a sufficiently low C massecuite purity to
facilitate good exhaustion of molasses. The double
Einwurf system simplifies operations and produces a
higher sugar quality and good molasses exhaustion.
The VHP system is used when the highest quality
sugar is to be produced; it requires more equipment
but iseasyto operatetoachieveboth good sugarqual-
ity and low molasses purity. It requires more steam,
but in general terms better quality sugar always re-
quires more remelting and a greatersteamusage.

15.2.8 Capacity and steam require-
ments
The design capacity of the pans required can be
calculated from the massecuite quantities and the
expected pan boiling times. It is important to take
into account the expected variations in syrup purity
during the crop, because this can have a substan-
tial effect on massecuite quantities, as Figure 15.10
shows.
Once the quantities and dissolved solids con-
tents of the massecuites and syrup/molasses feeds
are established, it is a relatively easy matter to cal-
culate the theoretical amount of steam required. In
practice, a pan factor of between 1.15 and 1.3 is
applied to the calculated evaporationto account for
steam and heat losses, vapor addition to molasses
conditioning tanks, steaming out of pans and gut-
ters, and vapor addition in the centrifugals.A value
of 1.3 applied to the calculated steamquantity gives
a conservativeestimate.For high gradepans a lower
factorcouldbe used.
The stem requirements for the four different
boiling schemesshown in Table 15.3have been cal-
culatedusing a pan factor of l.25 on all boilings and
theresults are shown in Table 15.4.
Since the amount of steam or vapor required is
essentially proportional to the quantity of masse-
cuite being processed, all the factors discussed
above that affect massecuite quantities also affect
the steam requirement. The steam requirement can
be reduced by limiting the amount of water used in
the pan house, as movement water in the pans, on
centrifugalsand in dilutingmolasses.

15.3 Batch vacuum pans
15.3.1 Qpes of pan
Many types of batch pan have been used over
the years, from the original design introduced by
Howard in 1813. They have evolved over the years
through a mixture of experience,common sense and
science to a fairly standard geometry, in the form
of a vertical cylindrical vessel, using vertical tube
calandrias, with steam or vapor condensing on the
outsideof the tubes. Various geometriesand types of
pan used in the past are described by Tromp (1936)
and Hugot (1986). Pans used today are still catego-
rized in terms of their shape. The variations in use
in cane sugar mills are generally covered by the
sketchesshown in Figure 15.13.
The most distinguishing feature of a pan is the
calandria. The most common design incorporates
a horizontal flat plate calandria. A single central
downtake is normally surrounded with vertical
tubes, an efficientdesign of simpleconstructionand
low maintenance. The diameter of the downtake is
30 to 50 % of the calandriadiameter,usually around
40 % for natural circulation pans, while smaller
downtakescan be used when a stirrer is installed.
Someolderpans use an inclinedplate calandria.
The plates of the calandria are angled between 10'
and 25" to the horizontal. This is a more expensive
construction. The top plate is made horizontal in
some cases.
A floating calandria pan has the downtake lo-
cated in the outer annular region. Although it was
developed in an attempt to improve the circulation
characteristics,measurements involving the use of
a radioisotope tracer showed that the conventional
central downtakeperforms better (Wright 1966).
There has been a trend to design pans with a
low head of massecuite, to improvepan circulation.
Low-head pans have particular value when viscous
low grade massecuites are boiled.
Some designers adopted a conical enlarge-
ment of the body above the calandria, to increase
the capacity of the vessel without increasing the
strike height and also to give a lower ratio of grain-
ing volume to final strike volume. However, these
flared pans were largely discredited because of the
negative effect on circulation (van der Poel et al.
1998:783-784). This has been confirmed by com-
puter modeling (Reinet al. 2004). Tippens (1972)
showed that straight-sided pans perform better than
flared pans while still being able to achieve an ac-
ceptable graining volume/massecuite final volume
of less than 0.33.
The shapeof the pan bottom shouldpromote an
even distributionof massecuite to the underside of
the calandria, without restrictingcirculation or pro-
viding stagnant areas, and allow the discharge of
massecuite within an acceptable time. Pans with a
" W bottom shapehave become more popular, par-
ticularly with large pans. This keeps the graining
volume small while still allowing good circulation
and acceptable striking times.

15.3.3 Batch pan design
p . 2 Pan circulation
I The rate at which massecuite circulates in a
is of vital importance. Since most pans rely on
a1 circulation,circulationand heat transfer are
ly linked. The density differencebetween the
,waporphaseand themassecuiteprovides the driving
force for massecuite movement. High vapor gen-
eration increases the drivingforce, and the balance
decween buoyancy forces and frictional resistance
determines circulation. Low resistance to flow of
rnassecuite in the pan leads to higher velocities and
p
o
d heat transferrates, which promote good circu-
lation. Thus theheat transferis strongly interrelated
with the fluid velocity or circulation.
Good massecuite circulation helps to achieve
uniform conditions in the pan, a vital requbment
for good crystallization conditions within the pan.
The achievement of all three objectives, namely
,good circulation, high heat transfer rates and uni-
form conditions in the massecuite, can be malized
&rough good design and appropriatechoice of pan
Fometry. As with all design, some compromise is
squired to achieve satisfactory performance with-
ontexcessiveequipmentcost.In generalterms,good
&culation isfavoredby pan designsthatincorporate
@ o m tubes, of larger diameter, with a low strike
height and largedowntake diameter.
Gaod choices of design variables are discussed
in the next section. Some basic issues which affect
massecuitecirculationneed consideration:
Massecuite flow paths should be clean and un-
obstructed.Any unnecessary steelinsidethe pan
represents a resistance to circulation. Louvers,
other steel devices installed in the pan, and any
unnecessary ironware in the massecuite should
be removed.
Incondensable gases should be vented through
the outside of the calandria,and not up through
the massecuite.
Likewise, condensate outlets should be posi-
tioned at the periphery of t
h
epan, and should
notrunfromthe bottom tubeplatedownthrough
the massecuite.
The syrup or molasses feed system should also
constitute a minimum obstruction to the cir-
culfiting massecuite. The feed should be intro-
duced through the periphery of the pan below
thecalandriaor throughminimumsizedpipesor
channelson the floor of the pan.
I
f the feed is conditioned and is at a higher tem-
perature than the boiling massecuite, the feed
must be directed under the calandria so that the
flash will aid circulation.
Theconicalenlargement or flaring abovethe ca-
landria has a negative effect on pan circulation.
Old pans can be changed fromflared to straight-
sidedpansby increasingthecalandriadiameters.
Pan volume in one case was increased by 25 %
and the heating surface by 52 %, leading to a
sigdcant net improvementin pan performance
(Bergeronand Carline2004).
Circulationcan be assisted by installinga stirrer
in the downtake or using circulation steam (jig-
ger) to promote circulation (Section 15.3.6).

3 Batchpan design
The calandiia is essentially a shell and tube
heat exchanger. The exchange area, expressed per
unit massecuite volume, is normally around 5 to
6 mz/m3. ThiS may be as low as 4.5 for low grade
pans, but for high grade strikes, where evapora-
tion rates arehigher, it can be increased to 9 m2/m3.
Although some variations in calandria design are
shown in Figure 15.13, only the horizontal tubular
calandria with central downtake will be discussed
here, sinceit is considered to be the only viable op-
tion. Someof themore recent designs are illustrated
in Figure 15.14.

eter, installed on a 120mm triangular pitch. Some
designs have used a lower pitch, about 115mrn,in
an attempt to increasethe area density.Tube diame-

grade massecuites;however even with refinery boil-
ings, diameters < 100mm are considered to affect
circulation adversely (Tippens 1972). Tubes above
this size exhibit less resistance and promote circu-
lation, but the lower arealvolume ratio is unfavor-
ableand thegrainingvolumeconsequentlyincreases
(Rouillard 1985). Tubes with a length between 900
and 1500 mm have been used in the past, but cur-
rently pans are designed with tube lengths between
600 and 1200mm.Short tubes are selectedfor low-
gradepans, while longer tubes are chosen for high-
grade pans or when a stirrer is fitted. Short tubes
give the best heat transfercoefficients,and probably

15.3.3 Batch pan design
Strike height. The optimum strike height (the
level of massecuiteat strike)depends on the duty of
the pan. As the massecuite head above the top tube
plate increases,the hydrostatic pressureon the boil-
ingmassecuite increases,raisingthe boilingtemper-
ature. As a result, the available temperature differ-
ence between vapor in the calandriaand massecuite
becomes smaller, leading to a reduction in evapora-
tion rate and massecuite circulation.The situationis
particularly critical at the end of the strike,when the
highest level coincides with the maximum density
and viscosity of the massecuite, all factors that im-
pair circulation.
Tippens (1972) reported that t
h
e maximum
evaporationrate in a stirredrefined sugarpan occurs
h
amassecuite level of 1.4 m above the calandria.
TAchg~mko
account the fall-off in evaporation rate
above this level, he calculated that the maximum
production rate is achieved with a strike height be-
tween 1.5 and 2 m above the calandria, and is little
affected within this range.Tests performed by Aust-
meyer (1986) in stirred beet sugar pans suggested
that a maximum heat transfer coefficient in low
grade boilings is reached when the massecuite level
is 0.8 m abovethe top tube plate, afterwhich it starts
reducing progressively as the massecuite level in-
creases.Howeverhe showed that for white boilings,
the maximum heat transfercoefficient is achievedat
a level of 0.15 to 0.65 m abovethe tube plate.
Usually however the height for maximum heat
transfer is lower for low grade massecuites. Strike
heightsbetween 1.2mand 2 mcan be found in batch
pans. Perk (1973) considers 1.35 m above the ca-
landria to be the optimum strikeheight and 1.5m to
be the absolute maximum. The optimum height is
lower with high viscosity low grademassecuites and
higher with high grade or refined boilings. A final
height or strikeheight around 1.2-1.6 m usually pro-
vides the best balance between quality, performance
and capacity.
Graining volume. The graining volume is the
volume of the pan up to the level of the top tube
plate, the minimum volume at which the pan can
operate. This represents the starting volume for a
batch, made up of a footing pulled into the pan or
grain produced by seeding in the pan itself.
Sincea largeincreasein size of crystal is neces-
sary from seeding to final massecuite, a large pro-
portion of seed in the massecuite means that more
pan cuts will be required to achieve the required
crystalsize.The graining volume should be kept to a
minimum and should be not more than 40 % of pan
strikevolume.
Disengagement height. Sufficient disengage-
ment height above the massecuite surface must
be allowed, so that massecuite splashing does not
lead to the canyover and loss of sugar.The required
height is given variously as 2.4 to 3.6 m (Tippens
1972).Howeverthe major problemis often frothex-
plosion, which occurs when a new charge is drawn
into the pan. Australian advice recommends an al-
lowanceof two-thirds to l times the massecuite vol-
ume abovestrikeheight. Thiswill determinethedis-

a space 2 to 2.4m high between the strikelevel and
the entrainment separator.
Pan feedsystem.Thepan feed systemshouldbe
designed to mix the feedinto the bulk of the masse-

with massecuiteis important to ensurethat no areas
of undersaturated conditionsendure,which can lead
to partialcrystaldissolution.Thefeed shouldbe into
the downtakeif a stirreris fitted.Otherwise it should
be directed uniformly under the calandria, particu-
larly if the feed is hot and flashes on entry; this as-
sists circulation. Two feed arrangements that have
been used with success without blocking are shown
in Figure 15.15.

Steam distribution. The steam system should
be designed to ensure uniform distribution to all
parts of the calandria.In addition, a positivepurging
of incondensables to appropriately placed outlets
is required. The same requirements for evaporator
vessels (Section 12.7.1) apply to pan calandrias as
well.
Shape of the bottom section. The shapeof the
bottom sectionshouldbe such as to keep the grain-
ing volume to a minimum. The vertical section im-
mediately below the bottom tube plate should not
be more than 150 mm (Tippens 1972).The bottom
section normally includes a slope of anything be-
tween 14"and 24O, to allow the massecuiteto drain.
In order to keep the graining volume low while still
permitting good circulation under the calandria, a
slope of around 18" is recommended. The use of a
L ,

u i q
"W" shapedcross sectionis usefulin theserespects,
particularly with large diameterpans.
Pan discharge valve. The discharge valve is
located in the center of a conical bottom pan. In the
past hydraulically operated valves were common.
More recently rubber-lined butterfly valves have
been foundtobe cheaperandeasierto maintaia,they
seal well and require only a compressed air supply
instead of a hydraulic pack for activation. Typically
for an 85 m3pan, a valve size of 760 mm is required
for C massecuiteand 600 mm forA massecuite.The
rubber lining attachment to the steel body must be
such that the rubber lining can withstand vacuum
conditions without detaching from the steel body.
With a "W' shaped bottom, two smaller valves dia-
metricallyoppositeeach othermay be used.

erations that apply in the case of evaporators (Sec-
tion 12.7.4) apply in this case as well. Condensate
is generally removed from the lowest point of the
shell,frommore than oneoutlet. It is advisableto be
generousin sizingthese outlets, becausecondensate
build up in the calandria reduces heat transfer and

15.3.4 Pan capacity
The starting point in determining the required
pan capacityis a mass balancethat definesthequan-
tities of massecuite of each grade to be processed.
Thiswill dependon the type of boiling schemeused
and the expectedexhaustionin eachpan stage.Then
an estimate of the boiling times for each grade of
massecuite is required. Dividing the throughput of
massecuite by the boiling times gives the capacity
required, in t or m3,for eachboiling grade.
However some allowanceneeds to be made for
the idle time experiencedon pans. Even in well-de-
signed pan houses, idle time is unavoidablebecause
of changes in relative quantities of different grades
of massecuite, massecuite transfers, waiting times
and holdups due to miscellaneous production con-
straints.Theeffectivetime utilizationon a batchpan
floor is expected to be about 80 %, and can vary sig-
nificantly around this value.
Therefore experience with pan operation is
needed to define capacity requirements accurately.
In South Africa a pan time index (Archibald and
Smith 1975) has been used over many years with
success to estimate pan requirements for a VHP
three-boiling system. This is simply defined as pan
15 Crystallization
capacity in m3for a given massecuite grade divided
by the massecuite rate in m3/h for that grade. The
followingvalues of pan time index are used:
A massecuite: 4.5 h
B massecuite: 6.0h
C massecuite: 9.0 h
For a conventional three-boilingsystem,which does
not require graining of B boilings, and where puri-
ties are usually slightly higher than in SouthAfrica,
the following pan time indices are more appropri-
ate:
A massecuite: 3.75 h
B massecuite: 4.5 h
C massecuite: 9.0 h
Pan ratings are usually based on averagemassecuite
throughputrates. The relative quantities of different
massecuite grades may vary substantially during a
season. This variation can normally be accommo-
dated by reallocating pan duties; thus it is advisable
to design some flexibility into the pan floor so that
some pans are capable of being used on more than
one grade of massecuite.

(1985) identified that the evaporation rate is in-
creased as the heating steam pressure, the vacuum
and the massecuite purity are raised, Conversely,
longer tubes, higher strike levels and high concen-
trationsreduce the evaporation rate.

Steam iqjection. The installation of a sparge
pipe system under the calandria to inject low pres-
suresteamis anotheroption to assist the circulation,
by reducing the effectivemassecuite density in the
calandria, promoting buoyancy forces and improv-
ing circulation, particularly with a high hydrostatic
head towards the end of a strike.
The simplicity,low cost and absence of moving
parts of this alternativemake itparticularly straight-
forward to put into practice. It is often applied in
low grade pans, but is unnecessaryin well-designed
high grade pans.
It should be noted that the vapor admitted does
not condense,but passes straightthrough the masse-
cuite without causing any superheating or dissolu-
tion of crystal.The advantageof jigger steamis that
it can be shutoff at any time,unlikea stirrer,and can
be adjustedto givetherequireddegreeof circulation.
CFD studies indicate that the circulationrate can be
increased substantially (Rein et al. 2004). Thus the
effect of steam assistance, often called "steam jig-
ger" is to enableahigher strikeheightto be achieved
as well as a reduced boiling time.
Sizing of a circulation steam system should be
based on vapor injection at a maximum rate of 25
kglh per m3of pan massecuitevolume. The number
of holes in the sparge pipe system and their size is
determined by the required flow rate of vapor. The
size of the sparge pipe has to be such that the pres-
sure drop in the pipe itself is less than 10 % of the
pressure drop through each hole. This is the same
principle required in the design of evaporator feed
rings and the equations in Section 12.7.5 can be
used. This ensures that flows through every hole
are roughly equal. A single sparge pipe ring below
the calandria may not be satisfactoryin a large pan,
where a 'fferent sparging arrangement should be
used to give a uniform distribution of vapor under
the calandria.
Air iqjection. The injection of air instead of
vapor has been adopted in some Spanish factories.
Injection of compressed airat 750 kPa preheated to
65-70 "Cbeneath the calandria of A pans was re-
ported to be effective in reducing the boiling times
by 11 % and to increase recovery without an ap-
preciable effect on the pan vacuum (Stobie 1999).
However this option requires a much largervacuum
pump or ejectorto remove the additionalair.
15.3.7 Entrainmentseparation
The principles of entrainment separation ap-
plicable to evaporators also apply to pans. Of the
types described in Section 12.9, the flow reversal,
centrifugaland chevronplate separatorsarethe most
successful.
Under most conditions, entrainment from pans
is negligible. Serious entrainment mostly occurs
during starting and stopping the pan, when froth
expansion or sucking air into the pan may occur. Lf
theseoperationsareproperly controlled,entrainment
from pans is minimal. Entrainment separatorsmust
be designed to have a high turndown; the range of
evaporationrates duringa batch boilingis very high,
as the data inTable 15.5 show. Howeveratlow evap

15.4 Continuousvacuum pans
Although the first patent for a continuous vac-
uum pan was awarded in 1932 to Werkspoor, it is
' really only since the late 1970s that continuous
pan boiling became a practical proposition. Ease
of operation has been a feature, which first led to
acceptance of continuous pans on low-grade duty,
and has subsequently been extended to high-grade
boilingswith the developmentof suitable measuring
transducers. A feature of the continuous system is
the lower temperaturedifference between calandria
steam temperature and massecuite temperature,
whilestill maintaininggood circulationwith natural
convection.
It is still necessary to produce seed massecuite
on a batchbasis for feeding to a continuouspan. At-
tempts have been made to produce seed on a contin-
uous basis, butmost of these have been unsuccessful
(Broadfootand Wright 1992). It is expected that in
theforeseeablefuture,seed will stillbe producedon
a batch basis.
In somecases,seed productionin batch pans can
be eliminated by feeding a magma of sugar directly
to a continuouspan as seed. Continuouspans are in
theory well-suited to a Double Einwurf system. In
this case, seed only needs to be made in a batch pan
for C boilings. C sugar is used as the seed for the B
pan, andB sugar as the seed materialforA boilings.
However, as with any DoubleE i n W system, con-
trol of grain size is crucial.

Circulation and heat transfer. As with batch

tube length and diameter.

the preferred massecuitelevel for maximum circula-

the following:

and so depends on the seed and massecuite crystal
sizes. The volume may be estimatedby assuming a
crystal growth rate based on experience or measure-
ment of rates in similar applications. An example
of this approach is the work reported by Hoekstra
(1985), who modeled performance in an A continu-
ouspan to establish parameters tobe used for design
purposes.
Such calculations, assuming syrup/molasses
feed enterseach compartment, take into account the
flow rate variation through the pan, which increases
from the seed flow rate to the final massecuite out-
flow. The crystal residence time inthe pan is there-
fore longer than that calculated by dividing the pan
massecuite volume by the outletmassecuiteproduc-
tion rate (the nominal retention time). Tracer tests
have shown that the ratio of actual crystal residence
time to nominal residence time may vary between
1.4and 1.8.Theratiois larger when theratio of seed
to massecuite crystal sizes is larger, i.e. when the
massecuite/seed ratio is higher.
Nominal residence times typically average be-
tween 2.5and 3 h forA massecuites, 3.5 to 4 h for B
massecuites, and 6 to 6.5 h for C massecuites.
The rate of crystallization depends on purity and on
the supersaturationin the pan, and can therefore be
quite variable.In practice the values of CDR shown
in Table 15.8 are considered to be typical.
Broadfoot (2005) reported data which show a
value of CDR of 240 kg/(m3 . h) for an 89 purity
massecuite. The crystallizationrate is dependenton
thepurity of the mother liquor, which variesthrough
the course of the pan, rather than on the massecuite
purity. Nonetheless the strong effect of purity is
evident.Even though these values aregrossapproxi-
mations, they are useful for approximatepan sizing
purposes.
Heating surface/volume ratios. Continuous
pans havegenerally been installedwith conservative
(oversized) heating surface areas. Heating surface/
volume ratios of 8 to 12 m-I are evident. Most of
these pans run with calandria pressures at or below
atmospheric pressure. Based on the average heat
transfer coefficients for A pans and the values for
C pans shown in Table 15.7, it can be shown that
lower heating surface areas can be utilized with
highercalandriasteampressures. The results of cal-
culations are shown in Table 15.9,for A and for C
massecuites. If heating steam of over 100to 105O C
is utilized, heating surface/volume ratios similar to
those in batch pans can be utilized.

Massecuite flow characteristics. The two ex-
tremes of continuous flow systems are a single
mixed tank and plug flow (Levenspiel 1962). In
practice plug flow is the ideal, which implies that
all crystals stay in the system for the same length of
time. The types of pan discussed in Section 15.4.1
attempt to provide a long path length or utilize a
number of compartmentsin series to approximateto
a plug flow system. In fact a model assuming that
the pan is equivalentto a number of perfectly mixed
tanks co~ected
in series has been used widely to
represent the flow characteristics of continuous
pans. The equivalentnumber of tanks is established
from tracer test analyses.A closer approach to plug
flow can be achieved by increasing the number of
compartments, and by ensuring that the design of
the crossover ports from one compartment to the
next makes short-circuitingimpossible.
Another prime requirement of a continuouspan
is to ensure that no stagnant volume exists. This can
also be establishedfrom tracer tests.

tem ensures that all crystalshave the sameresidence
time, thus ensuring a uniform crystal size distribu-
tion in the product massecuite. Furthermore it pro-

There is little benefit to be gained (in terns of
CV)by increasing the number of tanks-in-series
above 12. From tracer tests, it has been found that
a 12-compartmentTongaat-Hulett pan can generally
be represented by about 18 tanks-in-series (Reinet
al. 1985),and that 10compartmentSRIpansbehave

compartmentpan should be equivalentto 12tanks-
in series.The data in Figure 15.28suggestthat there

series, and so 8 compartments should be adequate
in most cases.
The compartmentsare generallymade the same
volume, to simphfy construction and reduce costs.
Broadfoot (1992) has shown that the ideal arrange-
ment incorporates compartment sizes that increase
in size from feed to discharge.If the compartments
are sized to provide equal crystal residence time in
each compartment,the crystal size distribution will
be improved, giving a CV about 2 units lower than
in the case of equal sized compartments(Broadfoot
1992). In practice, unless a very large increase in
crystal size from seed to massecuite is sought, or a
small number of compartments is used, this effect
is small.
15.4.3 Comparison of batch and con-
tinuouspan systems
The general conditions favoring either batch or
continuoussystems are well summarized by Leven-
spiel (1962) in relation to chemicalreactors:
"The batch reactor has the advantage of small
instrumentation cost andfIexbility of operation
(maybe shut-daon easily and quickly). It has
the disadvantage of higher labor and handling
cost, oftenconsiderableshut downtime to empty,
clean out, and refill,and poorer quality control
of theproduct. Hence we rnay generalize to state
that the batch reactor is well suited to produce
References p. 400
15 Crystallization
small amounts of material or to produce many
werent productsfrom one piece of equipment.
On the other hand for the chemical treatment
of materials in large amounts, the continuous
process is nearly alwaysfound to be more eco-
nomical".
This analysis is true for batch and continuous pans
as well. As factories have generally become larger
and have been looking to improve operating effi-
ciencies, the continuous pan has proved to be more
cost-effective.
Steam economy. Continuous pans can use a
lower pressure calandria vapor than batch pans,
while still relying on natural circulation.This allows
steam economy to be significantly improved where
this is of advantage. Continuous pans usually oper-
ate with At values of 25to 40 "Cas per Figure 15.27.
Batch pans without stirrers have to operate with At
values of over 40 O
C to achieve reasonable boiling
times, particularly as the pan fills up. Continuous
pans areoperatedin somemills with vapor 2or even
vapor 3, with significantsteameconomy benefits.
In addition,batch pan steamingsare eliminated,
reducing the overallevaporationload.
Where exceptionally high steam economy is
sought, the BMA vertical tower continuouspan has
advantages. It can operate with a very low At be-
cause of the stirrersand can be used to advantage in
association with a mechanical vapor recompressor.
Because of the continuous operation, vapor can be
drawn off the pan and recompressed continuouslyto
provide the calandria steam.
Pan volumes. More efficient use is made of in-
stalled pan volume in a continuous system. The ra-
tio of actual/nominalcrystalresidence time is 1.4 to
1.8 (Section 15.4.2). In addition, since production
is continuous and the pan is always full, the down-
time associated with striking and steamingout pans
is saved. Overall therefore,thevolumetricefficiency
of the continuouspan is on average 1.8times that of
a batch pan. It is important in comparing prices of
batch and continuouspans to take this difference in
volumetricefficiency into account.
Process control. Control of batch pan boilings
is more complicated than that of continuous pans,
although the latter tend to have more control loops
per pan. Both types can be successfullyautomated.
Encrustation oninternal pan surfaces.This is
a problem that is not encountered in batch boilings
since batch pans are normally steamed out after ev-
ery strike. Neither is this a serious problem in con-
tinuousB or C massecuiteboilings, which can oper-
ate for long periods without having to be emptied.
However, on high-gradeboilings encrustationof the
internal surfacesof thepan can become severe,lead-
ing to the formationof lumps.
Capital cost of installations. Continuous pans
may be more expensive per unit volume, but not
when the differencein volumetric efficiency is taken
into account. A comparative capital cost estimate
for a new factory showed that a system employing
continuouspans isjust over 2/3rd of the cost of the
conventional system with batch pans (Rein 1992).
Capital cost savingsaccrue because ancillaryequip-
ment such as vacuum pumps and injection water
pumps do not have to be able to cope with the high
peak loads associated with batch pans; this means
smallerpumps can be used.
Panhouse Bexibiity. Batch systemshave more
flexibility.Dependingonthetime of season andcane
purities,relativequantitiesof A, B and C massecuite
change. With batch pans the duties of pans can be
interchanged to accommodate these variations. In
continuous systems this flexibility disappears and
the continuous pans need to be sized to cope with
peak throughputs.
Operating labor. Factories that have changed
from batch to continuous pans have-usually real-
ized a saving in operating labor requirements. Con-
tinuous pans run steadily with less supervisionthan
batch pans.
Sugar quality. A consequence of the low boil-
ing head in continuous systems is more uniform
crystallization conditions. The boiling hydrostatic
head is reduced,and with good circulation,tempera-
tures vary less within the pan. Comparative tests of
batch and continuous pan boiling have shown that
the color of sugar produced in an A continuouspan
was on average 16% lower than that produced from
batch pans (Rein 1987).
Batch pan systems have an advantage in terms
of grain size distribution since each crystal in the
system has exactly the same residence time. How-

15.5 Pan control and operation
15.5.1 Conductof a batchboiling
The conventional steps involved in a batch pan
cyclearedescribedbelow:
1. Thepan is closedup and a vacuumisraised.The
pan is usually full of vapor after steaming out
the pan, which is achieved by admitting steam
at the top of the pan until steam wcapes from
the discharge valve. Admitting water into the
condenserrapidly reducesthe absolutepressure.
The time required to remove the small amount
of remaining incondensablegases by the vacu-
umpump (or ejector)ismuchreducedcompared
to having to evacuate a pan filledwith air.
2. The pan is filled with feed syrup to a level just
above the calandria. Then the steam or vapor is
opened to thecalandriaand thegrainingchargeis
concentratedtothedesired levelforseeding.This
isatimeofhxghevaporationrateand caremustbe
taken toensurethat entrainmentdoesnot occur.
3. Once the correctconcentrationof dissolved sol-
ids has been reached, the pan is ready forseed-
ing. It is usually held at the desired concentra-
tion to stabilize before seeding. One of three
methods may be used.
a) The concentration may be talcen into the
labile region, where grain forms spontane-
ously; when the pan boiler considers that
sufficient has been formed, water is
added to reduce the concentration into the
metastableregion.
b) Thechargeisconcentrated until theinterme
diatezone is reached, when a small amount
of powderedsugaris added; thisinducesthe
formationof new nuclei in the liquid and is
called shockseeding.
c) The liquor is concentrated into the m a -
stableregion, when a sluny of finelyground
seed is admitted; the small crystals in the
sluny are the nuclei on which the sucrose
crystallizes.Thisis calledfullseedingand in
theory the number of crystals in the masse-
cuite is determined by the number of crys-
tals in the slurryadded.
4. Grainestablishmentrequiresthat the mother li-
quor concentration be closely controlled to en-
sure that the crystals grow and that no crystals
Referencesp. 400
dissolve.The crystalsurfaceareais smalland the
evaporation rate is potentially much faster than
the crystallizationrate; water has to be added to
reduce the net evaporation rate, or if a stirrer is
fitted to maintain circulation,the steamsupply to
thecalandriaisreduced.Syrupor molasses is not
added during this period, because it would have
the effect of spreading the grain and increasing
the distancebetween crystals. This continuesun-
til sufficient crystal surfacearea has been estab-
lished (thegrain has been "brought together").
5. If a magma is used as a footing, seeding is un-
necessary. It is still necessary to melt out small
unwanted crystals and get the massecuite to the
right condition or consistency before starting
feeding.
6. Feeding syrup/molassesbegins. The crystalsur-
face area at this stage is sufficient for crystal-
lizationto be fast enough that the dangerof false
grain formation is greatly reduced. The feed is
admittedat a rate that maintains the crystal con-
tent and the consistencyof the massecuite at the
optimum value.
7. When the pan level reaches the strike level, the
feed is closed off. The massecuiteis finally con-
centrated up to the desired solids concentration
to achievea good exhaustion.
8. The steamvalve is closed, the vacuumis broken
by admitting air into the pan and the discharge
valveis opened.Thecontentsdischargeby grav-
ity into a crystallizer or strikereceiver. Altema-
tively part of the contentsmay be cutover to an-
otherpan; in this casefeeding of molasses/syrup
is subsequently resumed to grow the crystal up
to a larger size.
9. When the pan is virtually empty, steam andlor
hot water is admitted to wash the pan. It is im-
portant to ensure that all massecuite is removed
from the pan before starting the next batch. The
dilute wash, referred to as steamings,is diverted
awayfromthecrystallizers,to theremelter(from
A pans) or to molasses tanks, so that the masse-
cuite which has been carefully concentrated is
not immediatelydiluted by the steamings.
It is importanttominimize non-productivepan time,
by careful pan scheduling.It alsohelpsto breakvac-
uum and raise vacuum with steam in the pan. Cut-
over and strike pipinglgutters should be adequately
sized and adequately sized discharge valves should
be used to minimizedowntime.
dization
15.5.2 Seeding
Nucleation is usually induced in the pan by ad-
mitting a slurry containingvery finely ground sugar
particles. Variousmethods of preparing the slurry are
used, but they usually involveball milling of refined
sugar in alcoholfor a period of time, typically 12h.
Ninela and Rajoo (2006) outline procedures used in
somemillsin SouthAfrica; the recommendedproce-
dure involves milling 800 g sugar in 2 L of alcohol/
methylated spirits in a ball mill 160mm in diameter
and200r
n
m long at 74&I. After millingthe slurry
is made up to 6 L. Patterson (1985) recommended
ball milliig two parts of isopropylalcohol with one
part granulated sugar for 24 h. The quantity of slur-
ry required is usually determined by experience. It
is not believed that full seeding takes place in most
cases, i.e. some additional nuclei may be formed
when the slurry is admitted. In general terms, add-
ing more slurryleads to more, smallercrystalsin the
massecuite. In this respect consistent preparation of
the slurry is important.Ninela and Rajoo (2006)rec-
ommend 20 rnL slurryper m3of C massecuite.
15.5.3 Meeting crystal size
For batch seedboilings, crystalsizeis affectedby
the quantity and quality of seed as mentioned above.
For batch or continuouspans, the sizeand quality of
the magma or seed used as a footinghas a significant
effect. A small ratio of grainingto strikevolume as-
sists in meeting the required product crystal size. If
this cannot be achieved in a single strike as is nor-
mally the case, the massecuitehas to be cut over one
or more times to achievethe required crystalsize.
15.5.4 Vacuum testing
It is necessary periodically to check a pan for
leaks. Because of the warm humid conditions, cor-
rosion is always a concern. A vacuum test involves
drawing a vacuum and noting the increase in pres-
sure with time. Providing the absolute pressure in
the vesselis less than 53kPa, the rate of airentering
the vessel is independent of the absolute pressure.
A vacuum test on a vessel should indicate a rise in
pressureof less than about 10kPain 60minutes on a
new pan and 10kPa in 30 minutes on an old pan.

15.5.6 Boiling temperatures and pres-
sures
A significant loss of sucrose can occur dur-
ing crystallization operations. For this reason it is
advantageous to reduce boiling temperatures to a
practicalminimum and minimize residence times in
crystallization. High massuite exhaustions which
reduce the total amount of massecuite to be boiled
help to keep the losses to a minimum.
The lower boiling temperatures also enable va-
por bled from the evaporatorsto be used as heating
steamin the calandria with an adequatetemperature
differencefor heat transfer. Most massecuiteboiling
occurs with massecuite temperatures in the range
of 63 to 70 "C.In particular C massecuite boilings
take longer and are more prone to Maillard type
reactions, and the lowest possible massecuite tem-
perature is desirable.It is important tohave a steady
15.5.7 Effect of pan conditions and operation on sugar quality
absolute pressure during the process; variations if
significant can lead to either dissolution of crystal
or the formation of false grain, both of which are
undesirable.
In refined boilings, the temperature is main-
tained somewhathigher to promote the rate of crys-

15.5.8 Continuouspan operation
The crystal content in the h t compcutment
should be high enough with sufficient crystal area
present to obtain a high crystallization rate without
falsegrainformation.Thereafteritis the crystalcon-
tent that is controlled by most measurement trans-
ducers. The crystalcontent shouldincrease progres-
sively throughthepan. Thisischeckedby laboratory
RDS measurements when settingup the pan and pe-
riodically as required.
The ideal RDS profile through the pan has not
been established. Two schools of thought exist: the
firstholds tothe belief that thecrystalcontentshould
be kepthigh allthe way through the pan; the second
that a slightlylower RDS in the compartmentsleads
to better circulation and faster and more uniform
crystallization. In both cases the crystal content in
product massecuite must be kept as high as possible
to achieve a high exhaustion.
It is impossibIe to match evaporation rate and
crystallization rate through the pan. Depending on
the conditions and the performance of the pan, one
or other will be limiting.In theearlystagesitis like
ly that crystallizationrate is limiting, whereasin the
i latter sections where the massecuite Brix is higher,
evaporationis likely to be limiting because the crys-
tal surface area is high.In comparing crystaUization
rates in pans, both crystallization rate and evapora-
tionrate influencethe numbers achieved.
Because of steady conditions, reduced pan en-
trainment is expected. The shutting down of a pan
floor with continuous pans is simple. For a 16-hour
maintenance shutdown,no particular measures are
needed with continuouspans, other than perhaps to
dropthe massecuitelevel somewhat. If there areex-
tended millstops, the steam to the pans can be shut
ofF and no other action is necessary. The pans are
easily brought on line itgain after a stop, as long as
care is talcen to get the pan circulating well before
startingto feed seed and syrupor molasses.
Emptying and cleaning. Continuous A pans
are emptied and cleaned out on a regular cycle, of
somewherebetween one and four weeks. Cleaning
schedulesareusually chosen if possibleto fitin with
scheduled maintenance shutdowns. The disruption
toproductioncan be rainimizedif attention is given
to detail. At Felixton the total downtime associated
with emptying out continuousA pans was reduced
from 6 1

4 to 3 112hours (Montocchio 1988).This
involved steaming with vapor rather than boiling
with water, and the use of seed and cutover vessels
to store massecuite from different parts of the pan.
At start-up, massecuites are cut back to the pan to
minimize the time to start producing acceptable
massecuite.Broadfoot et al. (2004)report downtime
correspondingto aperiod of only 3.6 h when thepan
is not taking syrup feed.
The BMA continuous pan system is installed
with the facility to bypass any one of the four pan
stages,so that onestagemay becleanedout ata time
with minimum disturbance to production. Eletcher
Smith pans are sometimes installed with a center
partition, so that one half of the pan can be operated
independentlyof the other.This provides the ability
to clean one half of the pan while the other half is
stillin operation.
B continuous pans are usually emptied and
cleaned at a frequency between 4 and 20 weeks de-
pending on the cane growing area.C pans often run
for a whole season of 40 weeks, but may be cleaned
on a more frequent basis.
Encmstation. The issue of encrustationof sug-
aroninternalpan surfaceshas been covered in some
15 Crystallization
detail (Rein1990).It is really only an issue in high
grade massecuites, and unlessit isdealt with, causes
the following problems:
Sugar, whkh builds up on internal surfaces,
breaks off in pieces which can block tubes or
outlets and causelumps in the product sugar.
Progressivescaling or encrustation on the heat-
ing surfaces reduces the rate of heat transfer,
which under extended operation, can lead to a
reduction in productionrate.
A distinctionbetweenencrustation abovethemasse-
cuite surface and below the boiling massecuite
needs to be drawn, as the mechanisms of encrusta-
tion are different. Most of the encrustation below
the massecuite level can be overcome by insulating
the external surfaces of the pan to eliminate cool-
ing of the surfaces. Sharp corners or discontinuities
have been found to promote localized encrustation
and should be avoided. Measurementprobes should
have well-rounded edges, and calandria tubes are
ideally recessed and welded into the tube sheets, as
protruding tubes often provide the starting point for
significant encrustation. If the crossover ports are
below massecuiteboiling level, they may be a point
at which encrustationstarts, and may require steam
spargersto keep them free of encrustation.
Encrustation on surfaces above the massecuite
level generallyoccurs at a fasterrate. Itis causedby
massecuitesplashingontotheexposed surfaces,and
crystallizing on the surfaces before it has a chance
to run back down into the massecuite. This process
is speeded up by over-exuberantboilingwith exces-
sive splashing and in cases where viscosity is high.
Encrustation is faster when the supersaturation in
themassecuiteis higher and the crystalsurfacearea
per unit volumeis lower.Thusitisnotuncommonto
seemore encrustationin the fist few compartments
of a pan where evaporation rate and crystallization
rate are higher. It is alsofoundthat encrustationoc-
curs more rapidly when a pan is pushed hard at a
h i production rate with a higher supersaturation
level.
Encrustation above the massecuite surface can
be minimizedor eliminatedin a number of ways:
* Minimize the exposed surfacessuch as baffles;
Periodically spray water or feed syrup onto the
exposed surfaces;
Run a cold water supply pipe above a baffle, so
that theresultingcondensationtrickles down the
baffle to keep it clean;
Periodically raise the massecuite boiling level
above the encrustedareas;
Enswegoodcontrolof supersaturationandcrys-
tal content;
Run the pan as steadily as possible.
In some cases it has been the practice to raise the
pan absolutepressureperiodicallyto melt off the en-
crustation.This procedure is not recommended as it
severelychangesmassecuiteconditionsand thehigh
massecuitetemperaturespromoteproblems with un-
der-massecuiteencrustation.
15.6 Pan instrumentation and
control
15.6.1 Measurementtransducers
Conventional methods of measurement of pres-
swe, flow and level provide no particular problems.
The absolute pressure control requires an absolute
pressure transmitter,rather than a vacuum transmit-
ter (a pressure transmitter measuring pressure rela-
tive to atmosphericpressure). This ensures that the
pan boiling temperatureis unaffected by changes in
atmospheric pressure. Measurements used in pan
control are sensitive to temperaturevariations and a
controlledtemperatureis thereforeimportant (Saska
andRein 2001).
The major challenge in pan control is the con-
trol of the dissolved solids concentration, the crys-
tal content and the consistency of the massecuite.
Thereare no commercialinstrumentsavailablethat
can do this directly, and secondary measurements
have to be used to infer the quantities of interest.
At the start of a boiling, and particularly when
graining, the supersaturation of the liquor needs
to be controlled. As the boiling progresses, control
of crystal content becomes more important, and ia
the overridingfactordictatingthe consistencyat the
end of a batch.
Boiling point elevation and online refracto-
meters can be used to measure mother liquor con-
centration (supersaturation).They are useful at the
start of a boiling, but only measure the state of the
mother liquor and cannot be used to control the
whole cycle. Boiling point measurements are also
affectedby changesin massecuitelevel.
15.6.1 Measurement transducers/ 15.6.2 Control valve sizing
Sometransducersareused whicharesensitiveto
both the concentrationat the startof the boiling and
throughoutthe cycle:
Electrical conductivityis a useful method. It ac-
tually measures the activity of the ionicspecies,
but depends on both mother liquor concentra-
tion and massecuite consistency as affected by
increasing crystal content. It is used almost uni-
versally on B and C rnassecuites where the ash
contentishigh andrelativelyconsistent.Itis less
reliable in high grade massecuites, where varia-
tions in the ionic content have a greater effect
on the absolutevalue. Conductivityis non-linear
with respect to dissolved solidsconcentration.
Viscosity transducersbehaveinamannersimilar
to conductivity, but can be used on all grades of
boiling. A Ziegler consistency meter was com-
monlyused in the past, but it and otherviscosity
transducersarenowadaysless in evidence.
Radio frequency conductivity measurements
measure electrical properties at radio frequen-
cies (Radford et al. 1988;Reichard et al. 1992).
The measurementsare affectedby both conduc-
tivity and dielectric constant. They have some
advantages over conventional conductivity, in
that they can operatein the absence of ionic im-
purities (in refined boilings for instance), they
can tolerate some encrustation of the probe
without affectingthe readings, and it is possible
to separateoutputsrepresentativeof theresistive
and capacitivecharacteristicsof the massecuite.
Nuclear density meters are sensitive to crystal
content but are relatively insensitive to changes
I in mother liquor concentration. However they
can stillbe used for graining control (Donovan
1988).
Microwaveabsorptionmeasurementsarelargely
responsiveto water content and so measure to-
tal solidsaccurately. They are sirpilarto nuclear
density measurements since they are more r e
sponsive to crystal content than mother liquor
concentration. Their big advantage is the fact
that the measurementis not affected by changes
in purity (SaskaandRein 2001).
B is important to give careful thought to the place-
aent of the measuring devices. They should be far
mugh away from the feed and from vapor bubbles
r, that these do not affect the measurement. The
b m e n t becomes most important when the pan
hnot circulating fast, particularly near the end of
a boiling. The best position for a conductivityelec-
trodein abatch pan is insidethe bottom of the down-
take; alternativelyit should be located in the bottom
of the pan in a region where the massecuiteis mov-
ing rapidly.

Correct control valve sizing is essential if good,
reliable control is to be obtained. The first require-

calculate values of Cv for these conditions, to es-
tablish from valve supplier's specificationsthe size
of control valverequired. For liquid flows, Cv is de-
fined as the number of US gallons of water which
the valve will pass with a pressure difference of
1lb/in2across the valve. The equation is:
where the flow is expressedin US gawmin,the pres-
sure dropin Ib/in2and SGrepresents the liquid spe-
cific gravity. The units are not standard but histori-
cally this is the way that most valve suppliers state
valve capacities. Using SI units, the value of Cv is
most easily calculatedfrom
wherethe flow is expressedin m3/band the pressure
difference Ap expressed in bars (= kPaI100). This
gives a numerical value close to the conventional
value. The valve chosen should have a Cv value
largeenough to pass the maximum flow but still op-
erate at a reasonable valve opening ( ~ 6 0
% open)
under averageconditions.
Corrections are required if the valve sizeis less

viscosity is very high. A viscosity correction may
be required for molasses flow with small valve size.
Manufacturers' literature should be consulted for
these corrections.

15.7.1 Molasses conditioning
It is common practice to condition A and B
molasses before feeding to the pans. This involves
reducing the dissolved solids concentration and
heating the molasses to a constant temperature. A
combinationof 70 "C and 70 Brix is often used; the
steadyvalues of theseparametershelpto control the
pan conditionsmore easily. Only the material about
20 be fed to the pan should be heated to minimize
sucrose degradation. Dilutionof the molassesin this
way leads to a higher pan steam demand, and may
bereduced if steameconomy is a high priority.
The conditioning (or "blow-up") tanks are de-
signedto achieve the required temperatureand con-
centration and provide sufficientresidence time for
any small crystal in the molassesto dissolve.This is
best achieved in a well-stirred compartment where
the molasses is heated and diluted.This is followed
hy a plug flow section leading to the ofFtake to the
pans, to provide the requiredresidence time.

ig maintained in thefeed tanks. Thismay be doneby

16.1 Theoretical
considerations
16.1.1 Objectives and requirements of
cooling crystallization
Crystallization in a vacuum pan continues un-
til the point is reached where further crystalbation
would result in amassecuite that stops circulatingor
&at cannot be dischargedfrom the pan. Massecuite
leaving a vacuum pan is supersaturated and hot, in
the range 63 to 70 O
C
. Crystal content is high, but
it is still possible to achieve additional exhaustion
; by cooling the massecuite prior to centrifuging. As
- the massecuiteis cooled, the crystallizationrate re-
duces, but sufficient retention time in the cooling
systallizers will achieve the additional crystalliza-
tion desired.
It should be noted that the crystallization
' achieved in cooling crystallization will never make
, np for poor work done in the vacuum pan. The
massecuite dry substance and nonsucrose/waterra-
m
tio is determined in the pan and no further evapo-
I nition occurs in cooling crystallization. In addition,
Uemassecuitecrystal content and crystal sizeis de-
iedmined by what is done in the pan.
As the massecuite cools and sugar crystallizes
barther, the viscosity or consistency of the masse-
smite increases significantly. The h a 1 condition of
Pie cooled massecuite should be determinedby the
mistency that the centrifbgals can handle in the
rebsequent processing step.This is differentfor dif-
ferent grades and purities of massecuites. Ideally
cooling crystallizers should be sufficientlyrobust to
handle these massecuite conditions; if not the full
value of cooling crystallization is not achieved. It is
also necessary to ensure that massecuite pipes, gut-
ters and pumps do not limit the flow and handling of
these high consistencymaterials.
Massecuites display non-Newtonian flow char-
acteristics, and so it is incorrect to refer to the vis-
cosity of a massecuite; consistency is the more ap-
propriate t m . Both temperatureand dry substance
content dictate the massecuite consistency. Prior to
centrifuging, C massecuitesmay be reheated some-
what without dissolving crystalbefore centrifuging,
because the mother liquor is supersaturated. In the
case of high gradernassecuites,reheating is not nor-
mal practice; instead the temperature is generally
not allowed to drop below the limit for good cen-
trifugalperformance.
In either case, processing of highly viscous
massecuites above the optimum consistency can
lead to an excessive purity rise across the cen-
trifugal~,
thus negating some of the work done in
the crystallizers. Alternatively,if the consistency is
much below the optimum,the additionalexhaustion
which should have been achieved in the crystallizers
will be lost.
Crystallizer design must take into account the
grade of massecuite to be processed and the consis-
tency of massecuiteexperiencedin the particular lo-
cation. In this sectionaverageconsistenciesarecon-
sidered, but local conditions can have an influence
over and above these average values, depending on
factors such as cane quality.

16 Cooling crystallizers
16.1.2 Residencetimes and tempera-
tures
Different criteria are used to determine capac-
ity and residence time in the crystallizersfor differ-
ent grades of massecuite. As shown in Chapter 15,
it is important to achieve a high A massecuite ex-
haustion; therefore some A massecuite crystallizer
capacity is often provided to ensure good exhaus-
tion, augmentingthework donein thepans. Cooling
crystallizercapacity is nearly alwaysprovided for C
massecuites in order to reduce final molasses puri-
ties to a minimum and therebycontain the sugarloss
in molasses to a minimum. Usuallyno B massecuite
crystallizercapacity needs to be provided, other than
strike receivers (Julienne 1991). The only situation
requiring the installationof B massecuite crystalliz-
ers is the case of a B molasses purity too high to
achieve the required C massecuite purity. This can
arise if the syrup purities are abnormally high as a
result of very good cane quality, or if the A masse-
cuite exhaustion is too low; in the latter case it is
better to pay attention to getting that right.
A temperature limit of about 50 "C is necessary
in coolingAmassecuite,because below this temper-
ature it becomesmore difficult to separatethemoth-
er liquor from the crystal and excessive washing is
required. Where continuoushigh grade centrifugals
are used, better centrifugalperformance is achieved
with higher massecuite temperatures. In this case,
cooling of A massecuites may be avoided entirely
and A crystallizers will be eliminated or will have
low residence time.
C massecuites are normally cooled down to
about 40 "C. Although Lionnet and Rein (1980)
haveshownthat a decreaseof 5 "Creduces the equi-
librium purity of C molasses by 1 unit of purity, at
temperatures around 40 "C the crystallizationrates
are so low that a drop of only about 0.4units can be
expected for a further 5 "C reduction (Rein 1980).
Thus it is normally of little value to cool down C
massecuite much below 40 O
C
.
It is sometimes surmised that the initial rate of
massecuite cooling should not be too high, or false
grain will form in the massecuite. However pilot
plant work on C massecuite showed that it was im-
possible to cool the massecuite fast enough to form
falsegrain. It is more likely that false grain formsin
themassecuitein thepan duringfinaltightening,and
only becomes visible in the crystallizer. The final
temperaturereached in the crystallizeris considered
to be far more important than the rate of cooling.
In SouthAfrica the residence time provided in
A crystallizersvaries from a few hours to 15hours.
Because of the benefits that a highA massecuite ex-
haustion provides, it is worthwhile providing 12 or
more hours of residence time forA massecuites. For
C massecuites, a residence time of about 45 hours
is often provided. The optimum value depends on
the local economics. Pilot plant work (Steindl et al.
2001)showeda significantdrop in mother liquorpu-
rity up to 30 hours, and a slower drop to 48 hours,
abovewhich there is virtually no reductionin purity.
Rein (1980)has shown that increasing the residence
time from 30 to 45 hours will reduce the mother li-
quor purity by 0.5units. This could be higher if the
increased residence time is accompanied by a lower
h a 1massecuite temperature as well.
16.1.3 Mixing/stirring

Coolingcrystalliirs arealwaysfittedwith some
form of stirring element. The primary purposes of
these elements are to promote heat transfer and, in
the case of high grade massecuite, prevent crystal
from settling out. They also play an importantrole
in achieving plug flow of the massecuite through a
continuous system, helping to reduce short-circuit-
ing and/or stagnantzones.
Where the cooling elements are stationary, the
rotating elementsneed to be positionedcloseenough
to provide some shear to strip away cooled masse-
cuite from the heat transfer surfaces. Heat transfer
is slow in viscous massecuites and the speed of the
rotating element per se does not aid the rate of heat
transfer.
Various attempts have been made to establish
whether the speed of stirringaffectstherate of crys-
tallization. Full scale plant trials have shown no ef-
fect at all on mother liquor purity. Pilot plant work
(Lion.netand Rein 1980)has shown that a very high
stirring rate will increase the rate of crystallization
in C massecuites. Work in Australia predicts that a
high shear rate can substantially improve exhaus-
tion, but has little effect for residence times above
24 hours.
It is generally accepted that at higher tempera-
tures, and in the less viscous A massecuites, diffu-
sion of sucrosemoleculesto thecrystalsurfaceis the
16.1.4 Rheologicalpropertiesof massecuites
rate controlling mechanism. However at the lower
temperatures generally seen in C crystallizers, the
lattice incorporation step is rate controlling. The
change from diffusion control to lattice incorpora-
tion rate control occurs at some temperature below
50 "C (van der Poel et al. 1998, VanHook 1980).
Thus stirring may improve heat transfer and help
promote plug flow, but is unlikely to have a signifi-
cant effect on the rate of crystallization in Cmasse
cuites.

cuites
Knowledge of the flow properties and the rhe-

understand the behavior of these materials in the

that they are generally highly viscous, they are non-
Newtonian.Newtonian fluids show a fixed relation-
ship between the shear stress and the rate of shear.
The proportionality constant in the relationship is
the viscosity. In non-Newtonian flow, this no longer
holds. The behavior is best described by the power
law model:

Batchcrystallizershavegraduallybeenreplaced
by continuoussystems.In batch systems,batch pans
would dischargemassecuiteintocrystallizerswhere
the massecuite would remain and be cooled down
over a period of time, depending on the number of
crystallizers.The disadvantage of this approach is
that some of the crystallizers would be empty or
only partially full and so crystallizercapacity was
not fully used. A further disadvantageis the cost of
either additional labor or automation to open and
closevalves accordingto crystallizerlevels.
With the advent of continuous pans and cen-
trifugal~,
it makes more sense to run the crystal-
lizer~
as a continuous system, so that the full ca-
pacity of the crystallizers is utilized at all times.
In many cases, continuous crystallizers have been
introduced purely by interconnecting all the batch
crystallizerstogether.
This conversion has not always been success-
ful, because if it is not done with care and with due
regard for the flow patterns through the crystal-
lizer~,
effective capacity can be seriously reduced
due to by-passing and/or stagnant zones in the flow
system. This is dealt with in more detail in Section
16.3.2.Ifthis is not given proper attention,continu-
ous crystallizers are less effective than batch crys-
tallizer~.
As with other continuous systems, continuous
crystallizers are more amenable to automatic con-
trol and require less supervision.
Where batch pans are in use, it is necessary to
have a strike receiver, which acts as a buffer be-
tween the batch and continuoussystems. The strike
receiver must be sized according to the size and
number of batch pans striking into it. It normally
closelyresembles ahorizontalbatch crystallizer,but
the stirring elements are not usually water cooled,
at leastnot on high grademassecuites. The rotating
elementsare usually designedto scrapethe internal
surfaces of the vessel to ensure that no caking oc-
curs on these surfaces.
In both cases (continuous or batch), required
crystallizercapacity can be computed from the re-
quired residencetime in the crystallizers.

16.2.2 Horizontal vs. vertical crystal-
Batch crystalhzers are generally all horizontal
stirred vessels. Normal batch processing practice
entailed gravity flow from pan, to crystallizer and
then to centrifugal. When continuous crystallizer
systems were introducedit became feasible to make
use of verticalcrystallizers-verticalcylindricalves-
sels with a vertical axis stirrer.Vertical crystallizers
have a number of advantages over horizontal crys-
tallizes:
They have a smallerfootprint.
They can be placed on the ground without the
need for any supportingsteel work.
They are suitablefor installationout of doors.
* There are no shaft glands that can leak masse-
cuite.
They can generally be made largerin size.
They are cheaper to install than the equivalent
capacity of horizontalcrystallizers.
Thereare also some disadvantages:
It is not easy to back blend molasses into the
massecuite.
Channelingor by-passingof massecuitecan oc-
cur more readily.
Liquidating pumps are necessary to empty the
crystallizers.
In general,verticalcrystallizersaremore cost-effec-
tive and so are favored ahead of horizontal units in
new installations.
16.2.3 Horizontalcrystallizers
Nearly all horizontal crystallizers have a U-
shaped cross section, and the only differenceslie in
the nature and speed of rotation of the stirring ele-
ment. Capacities of individual vessels vary usually
between about 20 and 90 m3.The width of the ves-
sels ranges from 2 to 3 m, and the length may be up
to 10m. If the vessel is very long, a central bearing
in the massecuite may be employed. The rotation-
al speed is somewherebetween 0.5 and 0.1 min-',
with the lower speeds found on the lower grades of
massecuite.
de Bruyn (1959) gives details of some of the
earlier types of crystallizer.The most common type
of horizontalcrystallizer presently in use is often re-
ferred to as a Blmchard crystallizer.This is shown
in Figure 16.2, but different designs of rotating ele-
ment may be used; they may consist of radial q
with or without a ribbon attached to the ends of the
arms to scrapethe internal surfaces, or a set of heli-
cal coils in which the coolingwater flows.
Another type of horizontal crystallizer com-
monly installed in the middle of the last century is a
Werkspoor crystallizer.Its distinguishing feature is
the use of largerotating discsin which coolingwater
is circulated.Eachdisc has a gapin the formof a45"
or 60' sector, the cut out parts of alternate discs set
180' apart.A sketch is shown in Figure 16.3.
In many sugar mills, batch horizontalcrystalliz-
ers have been converted into conhuous flow sys-
tems. They have been interconnected at adjacent
ends, either using gutters at the tops of the vessels
or pipe interconnections at the bottom. The inter-
connections are generally made in such a way as
to prevent short-circuiting and make use of the full
volume of all the crystallizers. It is also common
practice to install at least one set of baffles in the
middleof the vessels to ensurethat there is no short-
circuiting within any individual vessel. It is some-
times considered good practice to have the rotating
elements break the surface of the massecuitefor the
samereason.
When connected in a continuoussystem, a head
difference is required for the massecuite to flow
along what is sometimes a long and tortuous route.
Various methods of overcoming or reducing the
problem have been adopted:
Successive crystallizers may be installed at
slightly lower elevations. This is not easily
achievedin aretrofit.Hugot (1986)suggeststhat
each crystallizer should be 140mm lower than
the preceding crystallizer, while some Austra-
lian installations have about 700 mm difference
in elevation between successive crystallizers.
Thiscreates a problem when the operation stops
for whatever reason and the bank of crystalliz-
ers has to handle the change in levels associated
with a no-flow condition.
The direction of rotation can be judiciously
chosen to assist rnassecuiteflow in the required
direction.Thiscan resultin theheight of masse
cuite at the discharge connection being higher
than at the inlet.
The flow may be split into 2 or more parallel
paths. This is very effective, since using two
equal sized parallel paths results in halving the

16.2.4 Verticalcrystallizers
Based on this discussion, the requirements of a
good vertical crystallizer can be listed as:
A long narrow flow path, in which all masse-
cuite has the sameresidence time.
Sufficientstiningin a directionperpendicularto
the flow direction to ensure a uniform tempera-
ture distribution.
Stirring elements which cover the full diam-
eter of the vessel, and preferably come close to
scraping the internal cylindricalwalls.
Staticcoolingelementswhichprovidea uniform
flow resistance across the full cross section of
the vessel, to ensure that no short-circuitingoc-
curs.
No unstirred regions or sections where masse-
cuite can stagnate.
Sufficient surface area to achieve the required
cooling.
Cooling elements that are sheared by the mov-
ing massecuite and do not trap cold massecuite
(e.g. fins which are too close together).
Care should be taken to minimize the length of
interconnecting piping between adjacent crystalliz-
ers, to reduce pressure drop. These should also be
insulated,as the contentsof these crossoversections
are not stirred, and internal encrustation of these
ducts can reduce the effective diameter in the ab-
sence of insulation.
