16.2.8 Vacuum crystallizers
Cooling crystallization under vacuum has also
been proposed as a means of achieving additional
crystallization. Some flashing will also occur, con-
centrating the massecuite, so that some liquid feed
might be necessary. The system was developed by
Bbghin-Say in France and can be applied to high
grade massecuites. This has most potential benefit
in cases where massecuite is discharged hot from
the pan, since the degree of cooling is limited by
the vacuum that can be generated. To reach a final
temperature of 40"C, a specialhigh vacuum system
is necessary. It therefore has little advantage in C
massecuites, where pan temperatures at strike are
generally kept low, to minimize the Maillard reac-
tion, and massecuites are cooled to around 40"C. It
might have more utility on A massecuites, but even
soits advantages in that contextdo not seemappeal-
ing.Vacuumcrystallizationrequires more expensive
vessels and associated vacuum equipment.
The advantages of this approach would seem to
be limited to the beet sugar industry and perhaps in
certain instances to cane sugarrefining. Some units
installed in beet factories have subsequently been
decommissioned.
16.2.9 Massecuitepumps
Pumping of massecuite is somewhat different
from most other pumping duties,because of the na-
ture of the material. The consistency is often very
high because of the need for high dry substance
contents in massecuites and low speed positive dis-
placement pumps are utilized. In most factoriesit is
necessary to pump massecuite at some stage, even
if only during liquidation. In new installations, at-
tempts are made where possible to eliminate the
need for massecuite pumps, by having the pan floor
at a high enough elevation to use a gravity flow sys-
tem.
The most widely used massecuite pumps have a
slowly rotating lobe turning in a shaped body with
a sprung seal on the outlet side to minimize slip.
This is often referred to as a rota pump or simply
massecuite pump, and a sketch is shown in Figurn
16.5.
Thernassecuite isabrasive,and a hardmaterial
of construction,often cast iron is used. Efficiencies
need to be maintained by minimizing the clearance
between the rotor and the sides of the pump. Leak-
age of massecuite from the glands of the pump h
a commonly encountered problem, and an adequate
sealing arrangement is an important attribute of a
massecuite pump. They can normally discharge
against a head of 500 kPa or higher at flow rates up
to 100m3/h.

Another type of positive displacement pump,
the external gear pump, as typified by the Broquet
pump, is used on massecuite and particularly on
pumping seed to a continuous pan. It is a more ex-
pensive pump, but it is reliable and does no damage
to the crystal. It generally has a very good sealing
arrangementwith minimal massecuiteleakage from
the glands.Slidingvane pumps, which arecommon-
ly used for pumping molasses, are also sometimes
wed on massecuites, but are less robust on heavy
duty products. A lobe pump is also useful in cases
where damage to the crystal is to be avoided and an
exampleis illustrated in Figure 16.6.

16.3 Operationand control
16.3.1 Operation of continuous crys-
tallizer~
I
The requirementsfor operation of a set of con-
6auous crystallizers include achieving the targeted
Lmperatureon leavingthe crystallizer,ensuringthat
the massecuiteis in the system for the requiredresi-
dence time, and ensuringthat the system can handle
the high dry substance in the massecuite necessary
for good exhaustion.
The rate of cooling is not as important as the
final temperature of massecuite achieved. Steindl
et al. (2001) report that rapid cooling is effective
only if the massecuiteresidence time is less than 20
hours. Attaining the desired outlet temperature re-
quires the provision of the correct amount of water
to the elements at the right temperature.Generally a
flow of water countercurrent to the massecuite flow
is the most efficientmethod of cooling. Sometimes
the water is sent to each of the crystallizers in paral-
lel, which gives better control over the rate of cool-
inginthe6rstfew crystallizers,butuses more water.
The flow of water may be automaticallycontrolled,
accordingto temperaturesin the system. Oftenhow-
ever maximum coohg is applied particularly if the
cooling surface is not quiteadequate.
Accurate measurement of massecuite tempera-
ture is sometimes a difficult task. It is essential that
the measuring element projects sufficientlyfar into
the massecuite to obtain a reliable and representa-
tive measurement. If it does not project far enough
into the massecuite, particularly if the measuring
elementis thick, heat can be conducteddown the el-
ement,giving a falsely low measurement, and some-
timesleading to an accumlation of cold massecuite
aroundthe element.Howeverif the elementprojects
far enough into the flowingmassecuite, the force of
the moving mssecuite on the element is sometimes
enough to bend or break it.
To achieve maximum residence time, the level
in the last crystallizer must be kept at its maximum
level, preferably via an overflow weir. The natural
tendency of theoperatorsto"cure ahead", i.e. tocen-
trifuge massecuite faster than it is produced, needs
to be limited.An overflowweir fromthe last crystal-
lizer to limit the minimum level is recommended. It
is importantalso to ensure that the stirring elements
do not lead to aeration of the massecuite because
this leads to an increase in massecuiteviscosity.
The processing of high Brix massecuite often
leads to problems with the crystallizer drives, par-
ticularly if the massecuite is cooled down further
than normal. This could be due to mill breakdowns
or particularly cool weather, since a significantpart
of the cooling can occur through the vessel walls. If

16.3.2 Massecuiteflow characteristics
It is very important that there are no dead spots
or stagnantregions in the continuousflow system. It
is also important to obtain a close approach to plug
flow, with all massecuite spending the same time in
the system, without any by-passing or short-circuit-
ing. This has been investigated on occasions using
crystallizers
tracer tests to determine a distribution of residence
times.
Simple calculations and a visual analysis of a
residence time distribution curve can provide quick
indicationsof massecuiteflow performance.A good
approachto plug flowis indicatedby a singlenarrow
tracer peak. If the time taken for this peak to appear
is close to the theoretical residence time (i.e. vol-
ume divided by volumetric flow rate), then there is
minimal dead volume. Tracer appearing much ear-
lier than the theoretical residence time indicatesby-
passing and a long tail to the distribution indicates
semi-stagnantregions. A double peak indicates t
h
e
existence of alternative parallel flow paths through
the crystallizer.

vide quantitative measures of performance,
model options being either dispersed plug flo
fully mixed tanks in series. These use respechve
a "dispersion coefficient" or an "equivalent num
of tanks in series" as measures of non-ideality.
though not directly comparable,Rein (1980) de
oped a relationshipbetween thesetwo parameters.
large "number of tanks in series" or a small "dis
sion coefficient" indicates a close approach to
flow. Some typical examples are shown in Fi

16.3.3 Maillard reaction
What is referred to as the Maillurd reaction is
in reality a number of different reactions involv-
ing reducing sugars and amino nitrogen. It results
in the formation of color bodies and high molecu-
lar mass substanceswhich increase viscosity. Often
associated with Maillard reactions is the Strecker
degradation,which leads to the evolutionof carbon
dioxide. The bubbles formed are small and so are
generallyretainedin themassecuite.This aeratesthe
massecuite,significantlyincreasing viscosity (New-
ell 1979, White et al. 1983).This is also known as
the phenomenon that causes molasses swelling and
foaming in crystallizers and explosionsin molasses
tanks, since it is exothermic.The effects of these re-
actions can be readily recognized in C crystallizers,
because the reactionslead to theproductionof ared-
dish color in the massecuites,as opposed to a dark,
almost black color in unaffected massecuites.
Almost one-third of the amino nitrogen in syr-
up has been shown to be destroyed by measuring
what remains in final molasses (Morel du Boil and
Schafler 1978).The reactions also destroy reduc-
ing sugars,formingadditional impurity and thereby
increasing molasses losses. Glucose is consumed
preferentially in the reaction, which leads to values
of the ratio of fructose/glucosegreater than one, al-
though fructosealsoreacts.Themonosaccharide/ash
ratio is also reduced as a result of monosaccharide
destruction, affecting massecuite exhaustion. High
concentrations and high temperatures promote the
reaction, with a 5 O
C increase in temperature lead-
ing to a doubling of the reaction rate (Newel1 1979,
Whiteetal. 1983).Thereactioncan be minimized by
boiling pans at temperaturesas low as possible. Par-
ticularlywith C massecuites,temperaturesshouldbe
kept below 63 O
C at strike, and cooled as quickly as
possible in the qstallizers. Molasses back-blend-
ingmay help to reduce the reaction rate by lowering
the massecuiteBrix.
16.3.4 Cooling water circuits
The consequence of any leaks of crystallizer :
cooling water into the massecuite is severe and
can badly affect crystallization. For this reason, it

is highly desirable to use a supply of good quality
clean water forcooling to reducethe chancesof cor-
rosion in the coolingelements.This would normally
require a small cooling system dedicated to cooling

crystallizers.In round numbers,afactoryprocessing
10000 tld cane would have a cooling tower circuit
handling about 100 t/h water with a heat load of
about 1 MW. The water quantity is readily calcu-
lated from an energy balance; it is expected to be
about 1to 1.5 m3water per m3massecuite.
Often condenser cooling water is used for this
duty. However this water is always contaminated
with sugar and often contains suspended solids.
I
Bad quality water will always lead to corrosion and 1
leaks, which require that the water supply to the of-
I
fendingcrystallizersbe cutoff, and sometimeslea&
to expensive repairs. Pressure testing for leaks in I
the cooling elements during off-crop is an essential
maintenancetask.
On the other hand, a small dedicated system
requires very little chemical dosing because s u w
contamination is not an issue. The water tempera-
ture does not need to be much below 35"C, i.e. it b
not an onerous cooling tower duty. The tempera-
differencebetween water and massecuiteshould nau
be too high, or else "freezing" of massecuite onm
the elements can occur. This is particularly notics ,
able in A massecuites,where temperaturedifferem;
es greater than 10 O
C have been observed to c a m :
sucrose crystallization on the cooling elements, ef-
fectivelyinsulating them.
The idealarrangementincludesa facilityto
trol the temperatureof the cooling water particularly
to A massecuites, to be able to control the o u W
temperaturefrom theA crystallizers.This can easily
be achieved by by-passing aproportion of the re-
water from the crystallizersaround the cooling tow-
ers to raise the water return temperature.

After crystallization,the sugarcrystals are sepa-
rated from the massecuite by centrifuging.Because
of the nature of the mother liquor, particularly the
high dissolved solids content and high consistency,
centrifugal forces need to be high, requiring high
speed machines. The equipment used is usually
refenred to as centrifugals or centrifugal machines,
although in the general process industries centri-
fuges would be the accepted term. In Australia they
are commonly referred to by the shortened form
"fugals".
There areessentiallytwo formsof centrifugalin
use, namely batch and continuous machines. Con-
tinuous machines are cheaper, easier to operate and
have lower maintenance costs. However they lead
to breakage of the crystal on discharge from the
machine and so are not normally used on product
sugars requiring a specified grain size. Some new
developments have led to the use of continuouscen-
hifugals on high grade product sugar, but they still
have some disadvantagesassociatedwith them.
Theprocessof centrifugalseparationneedstobe
preceded by a step in which the massecuiteis condi-
tioned foroptimum separation.Lnhigh grade masse-
cuites this may consist only of ensuring that the
massecuiteis at the desired temperature. Becauseof
the very high consistency of the mother liquor with
C massecuites, it is normal to install some kind of
massecuiteheater ahead of the Ccentrifugals.At the
outlet from the cooling crystallizers, the supersatu-
ration in the mother liquoris high and somereheat-
ingof the massecuitecan be donewithoutdissolving
any of the crystal.
After centrifugingthe massecuite,product sugar
is generally sent to a drier (Section 19.2). Lower
grade sugar will either be melted or made into a
magma for return to the pans as a seed or footing.
Melting is the term used to refer to dissolvingof the
sugarin water or clarifiedjuice. Theequipmentused
is covered in this chapter.
17.1 Theory
17.1.1 Batch and continuous centrifu-
gals
Because of the fact that the densities of crystal
and mother liquor are similar, and because of the
high viscosity or consistency of the mother liquor,
centrifugal separation is the only practical option.
The size of crystal to be removed is in the range of
0.1 to 1 mm on average and a metal screen is used
to retain the crystal and permit the mother liquor to
escape.
Batch and continuous centrifugals are quite
different in geometry. Diagrammatic sketches are
shown in Figures 17.1 and 17.2. In the batch ma-
chine, a cake is formed from which the mother li-
quor drains under the high centrifugal force. There
still remainsa thin layer of mother liquor around the
crystals, particularly at the interstices between crys-
tals. Therefore a washing stage is always included,
where water andlorsteamareappliedin the centrifu-
gal basket to wash the mother liquor off the crystal.

17.1.3 Solid-liquidseparationtheory
In the centrifuging of the massecuite, two
phases can be identified. Initially the liquid flows
throughthe packed bed of sugar crystals, following
the Blake-Kozeny equation,which gives the veloc-
ity u at which the liquid flows through the packed
bed. This equationis (Bird et al. 2002):
This shows that the velocity is proportional to the
diameter of the crystals squared d2 and inversely
proportional to the viscosity p.The gravitational
accelerationg should be replaced by the centrifu-
gal acceleration, which means that the flow is di-
rectly proportional to the centrifugal acceleration.
The liquid flows faster if the crystals are larger, but
in fact the term e3/(1 - E ) ~
has a much larger ef-
fect. Grimwood et al. (2003) report that the void
fraction E in a cake of sugar crystals is about 0.42.
Bruhns (2004) reported that the crystal volume
fraction varies between 0.35 and 0.5, depending on
the amount of fine crystal. Increasing E from 0.4
to 0.5 increases this term in equation (17.9) from
0.18 to 0.5, and reducing E to 0.3 drops this term
to 0.055. This emphasizesthe fact that a high void-
age is highly advantageous;it is highest with a bed
of uniform sized particles and deteriorates as the
spread in crystal sizes increases. Tbis can be un-
derstood by thinking of the small particles filling
the gaps between the large particles. Thus it is b-
portant to aim for as uniform a size distributionas
possible.
The second phase of the process occurs once
drainage is almost complete. Liquid is retained in
the bed of crystals by the surface tension and capil-
lary action at the points where crystals touch. The
higher the spin speed, the lower will be the liquid
retained. This liquid is sometimesreferred to as the
residual saturation.
From the work of Dombrowski and Browmll
(1954), the amount of liquid remaining in a centri-
fuged cake at a high G force is determined by the
capillary number, which is directly proportional to
the permeability of the cake and the G force and in-
versely proportional to the surfacetenslon. Accord-
ing to their correlations, a change in any of these
variables will have a direct effect on the moisture
contentof the cake.
Wright et al. (1995) obtained an expression for
drainage of molasses from the cake without any
wash water added. They could correlate the data in
terms of nonsucrose/solids ratio of the sugar from
experiments at two mills using the time for which
the G force exceeded 250 (t,,), the time-averaged
force during this time G,, as well as the mother li-
quor viscosity y and the CVof the sugar:
This relationship indicates that better drainage will
be achievedwhen thesugarhas alow CVwith alow-
er viscosity and a greater G force at a longer time.

5 Crystalbreakage
Crystal breakage does not occur to any sign&
cant extentin a batch machine. Ploughing the sugar
from the basket is gentle enough not to cause dam-
ageto thecrystals.Thesituationisdifferenthowever
in continuousmachines,in which thecrystalfliesoff
the top of the basket and impacts the monitor cas-
ing.
Work done by Swindells and White (1980)
showed that larger crystals break more easily than
smallercrystals and that the velocity at which crys-
tals impact a solid surface must be less than about
10 mls to eliminate breakage of crystals. Since the
fangentid velocity off the top of the basket is of the
order of 100 d s , it is not surprising that crystals
k a k when impactingthemonitor casing.Effortsto
dimhate breakage haveinvolvedone of the follow-
' k gapproaches:
I. Pressurization of the air space in t
h
e machine,
I in thehope that the greater air density will slow
I down the crystalmore rapidly.
2 Using an air currentto blow air in a directionto
deflecttheflyingcrystalsand reducetheirveloc-
ity.

. Using a rotating ring with vertical vanes, run-
ning at a slightlyslowerspeed than the basket to
I slow thesugardown and deflect it.
CIncrease the size of the monitor casing to give
the crystals sufficient time to slow down before
impactto a velocity below 10d s .
d Adapt the shape of the plate which the crystals
'
impact so that they strike only a glancing blow
initially and then continue to travel down the
I
continuously slopingplate in a way that avoidsa
directimpact.
'Rnly the last ewo approaches have been successful.
bw gradesugar,whichhas asmallgrainsize.Larger
pystals slow down more slowly, which means that
mexcessivelylargecasingisrequiredformostlarge
owed in high gradecontinuouscentrifugals,and
has been substantially successful in eliminating
breakage.
Rein andArchibald (1989)showedconclusively
that virtually no breakage of crystal occurs as the
crystal rolls up the screen, but that breakage occurs
on impact with the monitor casing, This has been
conhned subsequently by the operation of high
gradecontinuouscentrifugals.
Swindells and White (1980) also showed that
crystal breakage can be vastly reduced if the sugar
impacts a liquid layer on the solid surface. This is
made use of in magma machines discussedlater.

17.2.2 Batch cycle
Programmable logic controllers (PLCs) are
universally used to control the batch sequence. The
PLC will control the following sequence, starting
with an empty machine:
1. At the required speed for feeding, usually be-
tween 150and 240
&', open the feed valve.
2. Close the feed valve when the massecuite layer
reaches the required thickness, as sensed by the
feed limiter.
3. Accelerate the basket to its set maximum speed.
The maximum speed is about 1200-1500 min-'
for a 1.2m basket and about 1000min-I for very
large baskets.
4. Start and stop water wash. The first wash will
be initiated during acceleration and one or two
subsequent washes are normal during the cycle,
depending on the sugar being centrifuged and
the desired purity.
5. Control the speed at the high speed spin setpoint
for the specified length of time.
6. Decelerate the basket, until the correct speed for
ploughing and discharging the sugar is reached.
7. Open the discharge valve at the bottom of the
machine and initiate ploughing of sugar. The
plough engages the sugar cake and moves down
the basket to the bottom, after which it is retract-
ed and returned to its parked position.
speed.
9. Wash the basket to clean the screen before ad-
mitting the feed. The basket wash is sometimes
omitted or else is done only after a pre-set num-
ber of cycles.
10. Repeat the cycle.
The PLC normally has a control panel at each ma-
chine, at which the operator can see the status of
each cycle and change some of the parameters such
as wash times. The sequences in the cycle are shown
in Figure 17.3.
The length of each cycle depends largely on the
size of the motor, since the maximum current de-
termines the times for acceleration and deceleration,
which take the major part of the cycle. A slightly
longer spin time and/or a longer washing time may
be necessary under some conditions to achieve the
sugar quality required. Most machine manufacturers
will guarantee from 18to 25 cyclesh.

Screens. The screen on which the sugar
is retained is usually made of stainless steel,
brass or copper. It may have circular perfora-
tions of about 0.5 rnm diameteror slots about
0.4 rnm wide and 5 mm long. The open area
is between 18and 25 %. The size of the per-
forations relative to the crystal size is not as
critical as on continuousmachines. The sugar
cake formed retains the bulk of the sugar and
very little sugar passes through the screen
holes. The screens are installed with a slight
overlap, with care being taken to ensure that
a smooth surface is presented as the plough
scrapes the screen. The backing screen may
be one or two woven wire 4 to 8 mesh brass
or stainless steel screens.Howeverthe screen
may take up the shape of the backing screen
and purpose-designed backing screens with
a flatter surface are preferred, since they im-
prove drainageandhence overallperformance
of the machine. An example is shown in Fig-
ure 17.5.
Ploughs. Earlier designs had plough
blades which retracted totally out of the bas-
ket when not in use. New models have the
plough insidethe basket throughoutthewhole
cycle,but rotated outof the way of thefeeding
and washing processes. This is a cleaner and
neaterarrangementand reduces the amountof
plough movement required. Ploughs are pro-
vided with tips which wear and need replac-
ing and one supplierprovides a plough which
traps sugarin the tip and uses thelayer of sug-
ar to plough the screen.The geometry of most
ploughs is such that if the plough does meet
an obstruction,it ispulled towards the screen.
Broadbent centrifugalsare designed with the
plough pivot point outside the basket, so that
it will kick out rather than get pulled in. The

plough can be set right up close to the screen in this
case. Someothermakes providea basket steadysys-

ploughing, reducing the likelihood of a plough dig-
ging in and enabling closer clearances to be used.
The ploughs have been made larger on new models

Basket suspension.All machines have baskets
supportedfrom the top in a flexiblesuspensionsys-
tem. Special design of the suspension and bearing
assembly is required to be able to handle out of bal-
ance loads. Most have a coupling connecting the
shaft to a standard motor. Broadbent engineer the
motors to suit the duty and the shaft extends fiom
the basket all the way throughthe motor. Becauseof
the suspended basketdesign,themachinehas a reso-
nant frequencyat a critical speed.The criticalspeed
is quitelow and dependsonthe length of the spindle
andthe strengthof the suspensionbuffer. The design
should ensure a low critical speed and the centrifu-
gal must be fed at a speed above this.
Centrifugal support structures. A
l
l centrifu-
gals are a source of vibration, and the support struc-
tures must be designedto be strong and stiff enough
to resist vibration. This will invariably mean that
the support structure has to be considerably more
substantial than is necessary simply to support the
weightof the equipment.Stiffnessmust be such that
the resonant frequencies of the structure are at least
33 % andpreferably 50%higher than themaximum
centrifugal speeds. Details are given by Grimwood
et al. (2003).
The support structure is often a corrosion prob-
lem area, because of the hot moist conditions. Ad-
equate protection is important. It is also highly de-
sirable to provide generous headroom between the
ground and the steelwork supporting the machines.
It is then so much easier to servicepumps and other
equipment and keep the area clean.
Feed and discharge arrangements.The sugar
is discharged through a door in the bottom of the
basket. It is kept closed for most of the cycle and
opens eitherupward or downward dependingon the
particular design. The massecuite feed arrangement
usually has a butterfly valve to control massecuite
flow into the basket, and has either a second valve
or drip tray arrangementto prevent massecuitefrom
drippingintothe basket and contaminatingthe sugar
layer during centrifuging.The massecuiteis usually
directed onto a conical sloping plate attached to the
shaft androtating with it.This directs the rnassecuite
into the middle of the basket from which it flows
upwards and downwards to form a uniform layer. A
thicknessdetector closes the massecuitevalve when
the desired volume of massecuitehas been added.

crystal.
A steamwash, which may be vapor 1or even va-
por 2, as well as a water wash may be used. This has
the advantage of heating the crystal, making drying
of the sugar easier. It has also been suggested that
the steam condenses on the whole crystal surface,
including the surfaces of crystal that wash water
may not contact.This may allow the amountof wa-
ter used to be reduced.

screen will block with solid material, particularly
finepieces of bagacillothat arenotremoved in clari-
fication or that contaminate the massecuite by fall-
out into open crystallizers. This can also seriously
affect washing efficiency. This is largely overcome
by the use of specially made backing screens of the
type shownin Figure 17.5.
The use on an in-line sugar color measurement
(Neltec ColouQ) can help maintain product qual-
ity at minimum cost. It can identify quickly any
problems with any particular machine by relating
the measurement to the dischargeof a particular ma-
chine. The instrument is expensive and needs cali-
bration against factory measurements, but in many
circumstances it can pay for itself (Suhr 2003), by
pinpointing such things as nonuniform spray pat-
terns, effectof varying head in thefeed mixer,effea
of timing of water washes, screenblinding and false
grain in massecuites. The use of the instrument on
a raw sugar scroll was also claimed to produce raw
sugar for a back-end refinery within tighter toler-
ances and also reduced total massecuite quantities
by 5 % throughimproved exhaustion (King2006).

17.2.7 Basketinspection
Routineinspectionof centrifugalbaskets isvital.
Tney are suijmeh'ro a veryhge nrrmbm rfi~uess
cycles and are therefore prone to fatigue failure. In-
spection of the baskets should be carried out at least
oncefyearby experiencedand qualified people. This
requires removal of the basket from the machinefor
inspection,and should comprise:
Comprehensive crack testing, by dye penetrant,
magneticparticle or ultrasonic inspection.
Assessment of the extent of corrosion and/or
erosion of the basket.
The tightnessof thehoops, if fitted.
Particular attention should be given to the highly
stressed areas such as changes in section, areas
around holes,comers,and the connection to the spin-
dle.If repairs arenecessaryto thebasket, caremust be
takentoensurethat theintegrityof thebasketdesignis
not compromisedby unsuitable procedures.Thehelp
of the suppliers should normally be sought. Cracks
require that the basket be taken out of service.

17.3 Continuous centrifugals
ly for processing C massecuites and B massecuites
in factories where B sugar is not a product sugar.
They arealso used in refineriesif the sugarproduced
is to be remelted.A more recent development is the
use of continuous machines on high grade sugars.
This is not yet widely acceptedand the machinesare
somewhat differentto the conventionalcentrifugals.
They are dealt with as a separate Section (17.3.6).
Continuous machines have many advantages
over batch machines on low grade duty:
Maintenancecosts are much lower;
Capacity per machine is higher;
Theelectrical load is steadyand a smaller motor
can be used;
Bad quality massecuites.with a wide crystal size
range can be processed;
Steelworkcan be designed to handle less weight
and lower out of balance forces;
Capital costsare lower;
The whole installation is much simpler.
Widespread adoption of continuouscentrifugalsbe-
gan in the 1960s.Some significantmodificationsto
early designs were necessary to achievehigh levels
of performance(Archibaldand McEvoy 1975,Kirby
and Atherton 1974).These modifications included
improving drainage of molasses by drilling more
holes in the basket, increasing the speed, improving
the bearing lubrication, improving the addition and
mixing of water with the massecuite and increasing
the feed lines and valve sizes.

Feeding and washing. The masse-
cuite flow is controlled by the position of
a feed valve. This is usually an iris valve,
a variable orifice valve which feeds a
steady "rope" of massecuite into the ma-
chine.The spacebetweenthe feed and the
centrifugal throat is normally enclosed,
to prevent air being sucked through the
machine. The air cools the rnassecuite
and may interfere with the discharge of
molasses. The centrifugal acts like a large
pump and has the potential to pump a
large amount of air at the high speeds of
rotation. This can have a detrimental ef-
fect on the temperature in the machine
(Julienne 1982).

susceptible to stress corrosion cracking. Unlike the
batch centrifugal, it is necessary to fix the screens in
firmly to avoid their being thrown out by centrifugal
force with the sugar. A clamp ring at the bottom of
the basket holds the screen in place.
Centrifugal suspension.Tlvo approaches have
been taken to the support of the machine. Most
centrifugals incorporate suspension mounts inside
the casing, supporting the rotating assembly. For a
given out-of-balanceforce,this has the advantageof
a smaller mass subject to vibration and enables the
monitor casingto be sealed to the floor, but increas-
es the amplitude of vibration at the basket. Another
approach suspends the whole casing and motor as
well. This minimizesdrivebelt problems.
Monitor casing size. Since it has been estab-
I
lished that crystal breakage occurs when the crystal
impacts the monitor casing, the option of a larger
monitor casing is available for machines which
produce sugar for a magma footing, a duty which
I requires a reasonable crystal size distribution.Thus
; in South Africa machines producing sugar for mag-
ma with an 850 mm basket which normally have a
1.75m diameter casing have been made with a 3 m
casing.Similarlymachineswith an 1100m m basket
have been installed with a 3.2 m casing instead of
the normal 1.9m diameter.
Electrical design. Continuous centrifugals use
a standard motor, of 30 up to 110 kW, depending
on basket size. Since these machines accelerate all
the massecuiteup to high speed without recovering
any of the energy expended and induceconsiderable
windage, the energy efficiency of the machines is
not particularly good compared to a modem batch
centrifugal. Becausehigh G forces are necessary on
low grade centrifugals, and because the massecuite
throughput through each machine is relatively low,
i the specific power usage is high and lies anywhere
in the range 3 to 10kWh/tM,.Thisdepends on the G
force and the massecuitepurity.
17.3.3 Centrifugalcapacities
It is difficult to define the capacity of a cen-
hifugal exactly, because there is a trade-off at some
point between capacity and performance. A higher
capacity is possible with a lower sugar purity. It is
also possible for a machine to handle a high rate
of massecuite by adding a great deal of steam and
water and sacrificingperformance,leading to a high
purity rise. The throughput should be looked at in
relation to aparticular performancespecificationfor
a massecuite of specified quality (consistency and
crystal content). This has not stopped manufactur-
ers stating machine capacities, which are usually
significantly higher than accepted in most indus-
tries. In practice,each industry tends to formits own
throughputstandardson thebasis of local conditions
and requirements.

4 Screens
The screens used in continuous machines are
very different to those used in batch machines, and
the correct choice of screen is far more important.
In the first instance, a secure way of attaching the
screensisrequired, ascentrifugalforcetriesto throw
them out.Secondly,the sizeof aperturein the screen
and the screen open area have a much greater influ-
ence on performance. Thirdly the cystals are mov-
ing continuously across the screen, which causes
wear and requires a more frequent check on their
condition.
Theusualtypeof screenused is madeby electro-

the interrelationshipbetween some of the variables,
namely screen width and slot opening size. As the
screen is made thicker, the open area reduces.

17 Centrifugal separation
17.3.5 Operation of continuous
centrifugals
Recommendations on the optimum operation of
theCstationoutlined in Section 18.3.2contain some
issues relating to the performance of C centrifugals.
These and other detailissues are covered here.
Performance monitoring. Payne (1992) has
said: "Nowhere in processing can so much sugar be
lost so quickly and with so little notice". He makes
a strong case for routine monitoring of temperature,
crystal size and the purity rise across each machine.
Mother liquor purity measurements using a Nutsch
filter should be taken of the massecuite before the
centrifugal so that the purity rise across each ma-
chine can be monitored. It is not possible to get the
most out of the operation if this important variableis
not measured. Centrifugal purity rise should be less
than 3 units, and preferably less than 2 units.
Washing. This is achieved by addition of water
and steam.Because of the short time in the machine,
crystal dissolution is low. The extent to which the
water and steam mix with the mother liquor to re-
duce its viscosity and the extent to which the water
and steam actually wash the molasses film off the
crystal is unknown.
On low grade massecuites, it is normal to apply
all the water at the feed throat, part in a "lube rod
concentric with the stream of massecuite entering
the machine (Figure 17.8).Water quantity should be
measured with a rotameter. Steam is usually added
through holes in the feed tube to the mixing cup,
but somemay be added into a modified acceleration
cone (Figure 17.9).More water and steam needs to
be added with more viscous massecuites. Typical
water rates are 20 to 50 kg waterlt B massecuite and
30 to 120kg waterlt C massecuite. Although some-
times exhaust steamis considered to be more effec-
tive than vapor 1,this is normallybecause the steam
line to the centrifugals is undersized and a greater
quantity of exhauststeam is available.Eithervapor 1
or vapor 2 can be equally acceptable.The limit on
steam usage is the temperature of themolassesfrom
the machine. Higher temperatures promote better
separation of crystal and mother liquor, but a limit
on molasses temperatureof around 60 "C is practi-
cal. A design maximum steam addition rate used in
SouthAfrica on C massecuite is 28 kglt massecuite.
I
Crystal size and regularity.The crystals move 1
in a thin layer up the screen and undersize crystals ,
have a much larger chance of passing through the
screen in a continuous than a batch machine. It is 1
therefore very important to control the size of the 1
crystalin the C massecuite.A system to monitorav-
erage crystal width is required, either a microscope
with a graduated scaleor a photographic or comput-
er system. However it is not only the averagecrystal
size that needs to be monitored, but also the spread
in crystal sizes, or the fraction below the screen slot
size.The percentage of finesin the sugaris the most
criticalparameter.
In SouthAfrica, the miUs aim to achieve an av-
erage crystalwidth not less than 0.12 mm and aver-
aging about 0.15 nun, assuming a centrifugal slot
width of 0.06 mm. Note the length may be 1.5 to
2.0 times the width on average, but it is the width
that determines whether a crystal will pass through
the centrifugalscreen slot. In SouthAfrica C masse-
cuite purities are in the low 50s, but in Australia
the C massecuite purity is about 65. This makes it
easier to obtain a larger crystal size of around 0.28
to 0.3 mm.
Massecuite throughputcontrol.The through-
put shouldbeas steadyas possible and all machines
shouldrun at the samerate. Thisrequiresaconstant
massecuite supply head feeding the centrifugals.
There are two options for controlling throughput
on the machines,either to set the massecuitevalve
position and adjust the water quantity to give the
right sugar purity (80 to 85)or to set the water flow
rate and adjustmassecuiterate to give the required
sugar purity. The steam setting is adjusted to give
a molasses outlet temperatureof not more than 60
"C. There has been on-going controversy about
whether better performance is achieved running
the machines at maximum capacity or under-load-
ed. Payne (1992) and Kirby and Atherton (1974)
maintain that a lower purity rise is achieved at
high massecuite rates, but Julienne (1982) showed
that running machines at high throughput led to a
higher molassespurity rise; he found that reducing
the throughput by 10to 20 % led to a reduction in
molassespurity of 0.5 units.
The current drawn by the motor is directly pro-
portional to the massecuite throughput. This is of-
ten used as a means of throughput control; the feed
valve is adjusted to maintain a set motor current.
17.3.6 Continuoushigh gradecentrifugals
Screen condition. The screens need to be in-
spected routinelytolook for damageand wear. If the
chromelayerislost,theunderlyingnickelwearsvery
quickly. Wear is seen mostly just above the clamp
ring as the massecuiteflows ontothe screen. Nutsch
purity rises across the centrifugals will give an indi-
cation of holes in the screen or when worn screens
need to be replaced.When screens are replaced, the
dimensionsof the slotsin the new screens should be
checked to see that they conform to specifications.
Because of the relationship between screen thick-
ness and slot size, the weight of the screen can be
used as a quick means of checking that the screens
meet requirements.
To achieve the best performance, Ninela and
Rajoo (2006) recommend a screen management
program involving dailyscreeninspections,removal
and caustic washing of dirty screens because of the
buildup of scale, and replacement if damage is evi-
dent. If a screenneeds to be replaced, a f
u
l
lset and
not just a single segment must be replaced to pre-
serve the balance. Ninela and Rajoo (2006)reported
an averagescreen life of 6 weeks.
Sugar purity control. If centrifugals are run
steadily at a constant throughput, there is little need
I to adjust the water and steam flows. In practice the
operators look at the color of the sugar to gauge the
purity. Attemptsto develop a meter which can auto-
matically measure the color at the top of the basket
and control the machineautomaticallyhave not met
with success.T
h
i
s stillremains an opportunity to be
abletoreducesupervisionand ensureoptimalopera-
tion at all times.
Julienne (1982) showed that an increase of 1
unit of sugarpurity led to an increase of 0.1 unitsof
molasses purity. It is important that the sugar purity
be run at the minimum required level and that it is
not allowed to drift out of control.
It is often instructive to look at what is hap-
pening on the screen using a stroboscope.This can
pinpoint problems with feeding massecuiteonto the
screen or problems with drainage or screen defects.
In some machines a distinct "color line" can be
seen in the basket. A higher throughputor less wash
water moves the line towards the top of the basket.
En other machines, "fingering" of massecuite is ob-
Sewed, with fingersmoving up and downthe basket.
These fingers can sometimesbe correlated with the
pins in the mixing cup. Any fingers reaching the top
of the basket represent massecuite going over with
the sugar.
Basket inspection. Continuouscentrifugal bas-
kets should be examined on a routine basis in the
same way as for batch machines. Continuous ma-
chine bask& are not subject to the same cyclical
stress asbatch machinebaskets,but rotate ata much
higher speed, almost double the speed of batch ma-
chines. In both cases basket failurewill destroy the
machine and do great damage in a factory and is a
major safety concern. The same techniques of in-
spection applicable to batch machine baskets apply
(Section 17.2.7).
17.3.6 Continuoushigh grade
centrifugals
Because of the advantages of continuous rela-
tive to batch centrifugals, attemptshave been made
over the years to develop a continuous machinethat
can be used to produce high grade product A or r e
fined sugars. Some of these attempts are described
by Goodacreet al. (1984). The majorchallenge was
to overcome the problem of sugar breakage. Some
continuousmachineswereinstalledonAmassecuite
with 5m diametercasings, but this approachhas not
been successful.
Effortsby two different teamsin Australiahave
resulted in the commercialization of continuous
high grade machines, marketed now by Broadbent
andFives Cail STG.Themaindifferencesrelativeto
low gradecontinuousmachinesare as follows:
Theincorporationof a crystal deflectorcarefully
shaped to deflectthe sugarcrystals as they leave
the spinning basket. The angle of incidence is
suchthat the crystalsstrike a glancingblow. The
deflector is shaped so that the crystals continue
to "slide" downthe deflector, graduallyreducing
speed in the process.
The basket angle is reduced to 25O, to give the
crystal a longer residence time on the screen in
which to effect the necessary washing. Thelon-
ger residence time is due to the lower speed of
the crystal up the basket and also because the
reduced anglegivesa longer screen forthe same
basket diameter (Grimwoodet al. 2000).
The speed is reduced to less than half the speed
in low grade machines, to a value between 700
Referencesp. 452
17 Centrifugalseparation
and 900 min-l. This is feasible because of the
less viscousnature of high grade runoff. The re-
duced speed also assists in reducing the crystal
damage and helps to achieve the longer crystal
residence time. This is offset by the lower G
force.
Details of the machinesavailableare given by Greig
and Belotti (1995) and Grimwood et al. (2000). A
sketch of a high grade continuousmachine is shown
in Figure 17.13.These machineshave been effective
in almost eliminating crystal breakage, but require
more wash water. The argument is proposed that
this does not necessarily increase the purity rise or
the amount of dissolution of sugar because of the
shortwashing time in the basket. The screenused is
similar to that used in low grade machines, but it is
possbile to use a screen with a larger slot (e.g. 0.15
mm) and a higheropenarea because of the generally
larger sizecrystal in high grade massecuites.
There are few cases where continuous machines
have totally replaced batch machines. The continu-
ous machines are less able to produce sugar con-
sistently at the target quality for high pol sugars in
particular (Broadfootet al. 2002).The performance
is more affected by the specific purging character-
istics of the massecuite than a batch machine. The
effect of both the characteristics of the massecuite
and the amount of water added is shown in Figure
17.14. It was established by Broadfoot et al. (2002)
that the amount of molasses retained as a film on
the crystal correspondingto the datain Figure 17.14
was 10g/100 g sugar at zero wash water, dropping
rapidly as water is applied and reaching an asymp-
totebetween2 and 4gmolasses/100g sugarat water
rates above 6 kg1100kg massecuite.
According to Broadfoot et al. (2002), purging
qualities can be improved by:
Producing massecuites with a uniform large
grain sizewith a minimum of fine crystals.
Producing well-exhausted massecuites, because
the mother liquor dissolved solids content is
lower as a result.
Processing the rnassecuite at high temperatures
with no cooling.
Conditioningthe massecuitesby carefuldiluting
or heating.

17.4 Massecuitereheating
Massecuite has to be at the optimum tempera-
ture and consistency to achieve the best results in
the centrifugal.Thisisparticularlyimportantfor low
grade massecuites, because of the very high consis-
tency. It is general practice to have reheaters at least
on the C massecuitesin a raw mill and on low grade
refinery recovery bodings.
17.4.1 Mother liquor supersaturation
The mother liquor in the C massecuite leaving
the last crystallizer is generally supersaturated. At
the low temperature achieved (about 40 OC), the
crystallization rate is very low. It is estimated that
of 1.2, the sucrosefwaterratio is 2.8. This implies
that 0.07 parts of water may be added for each part
of sucrose. Based on a 35 true purity mother liquor,
this implies that 2 kg water can be added to 100kg
mother liquor. Alternatively, the temperature can
be raised from 40 to 57.5 "C to reduce the mother
liquor supersaturation to zero. Payne (1959) advo-
cates reheating to 55 "C.
Both dilution and increasing the temperature
have theeffectof reducing the massecuiteconsisten-
cy. Howeverdilutionof the massecuiteis the lessfa-
vored option, because it is extremelydifficultto m
i
x
water and masseeuite and there is a substantial risk
of dissolving some of the crystal in the process. The
option of heating the massecuite is preferred and is
much easier to control with little risk. Reference to
Section 16.1.4 showsthat the massecuite consisten-
cy is halved for every 9 O
C increase in temperature.

17.4.4 Pressure dropintubular reheat-
ers
A large cross-section is normally allowed to
keep the pressure drop to reasonable levels. How-
ever the pressure drop through the elements is also
relied upon to achieve a uniform velocity through
the tube bank without short-circuiting. If it is nec-
essary to pump the massecuite as a consequence of
the layout of the plant, it is preferentially done after
the reheater where the massecuiteis hotter and less
viscous.
Rouillard (1977) has shown that the Hagen-
Pouiseuille equation for laminar flow of power
law fluids given in equation (16.13) can be used to
calculatethe pressuredrop in reheaters as well, but
with a constant 1.5 times higher, i.e. a value of the
constant of 48 not 32. This difference is ascribed
to the fact that the flow path is longer thanjust the
depth of the tube bank. This equation simplified to
show the head loss H dependency on the variables
is shown below:
In thisequation,d,,isthe hydraulicdiameter(4times
volume of channelslwetted surface) and n the flow
index. The actual velocity u through the void space
is higherthan the superficialvelocity by a factor I/&,
where the void fraction & has a value around 0.8 to
0.9. This showsthat the pressure dropis higher with
a longer reheater, a higher massecuite consistency
and a higher velocity, and with a lower equivalent
diameter (flow area).
With the design shown in Figure 17.17, it has
been found that a superficialvelocity below 0.9 mk
or a maximum velocity between tubes of 1.3m/h is
satisfactory,but higher values may be possible, de-
pendingon conditions.Australianexperienceallows
for a superficialvelocity of 2.4 to 3.6 m/h, although
Forzntti et al. (1987) report superficialvelocities of
1.4 to 2.1 m/h.
17.5 Remelters and minglers
17.5.1 Design of remelters
Dependingon the boilingsystem adopted,some
or all of the B and C sugar may be remelted. The
requirements of a remelter are to provide sufficient
residence time for dissolution to occur and stirring
of the contents to promote dissolution and ensure
that no solids settle out. The remelt has also to be
produced at constant specifieddissolved solidscon-
tent and temperature.
Therearetwo basic approachesto equipmentfor
meltingsugar.The most common approachhas been
to use a horizontalcylindricalvessel,with a rotating
stirrer concentric with the melter shell.As shownin
Figure 17.19, sugar and melting liquid, either wa-
ter or clarifiedjuice, are added in one end and the
melt liquor overfiows at the other. Accurate control
of dissolved solidsand temperatureis difficult.The
second approach is to use a number of smaller tanks
in series, which may be compartments in the same
vessel.A sketch of such an arrangementis shown in
Figure 17.20.The top entry stirrershave the advan-
tage of eliminating seal leaks and the maintenance
of seals.Controlof temperatureand solidscontentis
done in the firstcompartment, and subsequentcom-
partments provide the residence time for the disso-
lution to occur. The small square compartments in
Figure 17.20 make it possible to suit the geometry
of the centrifugal station by arranging the compart-
ments in a way to minimize cost and promote ease
of operation and maintenance.More details of both
these types of melter are given in the section on re-
finery remelters in Section22.1.
In order to size the melter, the rate at which
crystals dissolve needs to be known. It is generally
accepted that the rate of dissolution is somewhere
between 3 and 10times the rate of growth.The rate
of growth of sugar crystals in low grade boilings is
about 3 mmh. A simple test done in a Tongaat-Hu-
lett laboratory measured the time taken for 0.9 mm
crystals to dissolveat 70 "Cin an amountof water t
o
give ah a l dissolvedsolidscontentof 70g1100g s e
lution. Five tests gave an averageof 4.6 minutes,in-
dicating a dissolutionrate of 12rnmih, which seems
reasonablein the light of crystallizationrates.
B and C sugar sizes are usually smaller, par-
ticularly after crystal breakage in continuous cen-

BRITISH TECHNOLOGY FROM YOUR GLOBAL A N D LOCAL PARTNER
The loss of sugar in final molasses is generally
the largest sucrose loss suffered by a sugar mill.
Both the quantity and the purity of the final molas-
ses contribute to the sucrose loss in the molasses.
The quantity of nonsucrose entering the factory in
the raw juice and the production or elimination of
nonsucrose during processing will affect the quan-
tity of molassesproduced.The nature and composi-
tion of thenonsucrosewill influencethe solubilityof
sucrosein molassesand hence the purity.
At thelowpuritiesinvolved,pol andBrix arenot
reliable estimators of sucrose and dry substance in
solution. The normal measurementsused in a sugar
mill laboratory are not accurate enough at the low
final molasses purities to give a reliable estimate
of molasses exhaustion. For this reason, chromato-
,gaphic methodsof measurementof the sugars con-
tent in molasses are often used, because they give
accurateand reliable answers.
The spectrum of nonsucrose components in
cane molasses is differentfrom that in beet molasses
and the work done on exhaustion of beet molasses
is generally not applicable in a cane sugar mill. A
comprehensivesurveyof work done in both beet and
cane industriesis given by Decloux (2000).
18.1 Molassesexhaustibility
18.1.1 Solubility of sugar in molasses
The amount of sucrose in solution is largely
affected by the amount of water in the massecuite
or molasses. A higher dry substance or Brix of C
masseculte will always lead to a lower ha1 molas-
ses purity. The limiting factor is the viscosity of the
massecuite. The nonsucrose/water ratio is a useful
quantity in considering exhaustion. The advantage
of this measure is that it is the samefor the masse-
cuite and the mother liquor.
Temperatureis of courseafactor-the coolerthe
liquid, the lower the sucrose concentration and the
purity. Lionnet and Rein (1980) show that cooling
themassecuitefrom45 to 40 O C
leads to a reduction
of 1 unit in the final molasses equilibrium purity.
This solubility temperaturedependenceis consistent
with what might be expected from the temperature
dependenceof the solubility of a pure sucrose solu-
tion.
Besides temperature,the solubility of sucrose in
molasses depends on the other components in the
molasses.In general, the monosaccharidesor reduc-
ing sugars decrease the solubility of sucrose, while
the ash increases the solubility.The ash components
are regarded as being more melassigenic, i.e. they
have a greater tendency to increase the loss of sugar
in molasses, because they increase the equilibrium
purity. In beet and in cane factories, it has gener-
ally been accepted that potassium and sodium are
considerably more melassigenic than calcium and
magnesium.
However, Sahadeo (1998) found that sodium is
the most melassigenicelement,followedby calcium
and magnesium, with potassium being less melas-
sigenic.Sincepotassiumis the most abundantion in
molasses,this findingis important.
The equation of Charles (1960) is commonly
accepted as representingadequatelythe solubilityof
sucrose in pure solutions:

solubilityof sugarin the impure solutionto thesolu-
bility in pure sucrose solution. The coefficient has
been evaluatedfor low-grademassecuites by a num-
ber of investigators, but there is significant variation
between different published results. The solubility

18.1.2 Laboratory exhaustiontrials
A numberof investigationshavebeen canied out
to investigateto what extent the purity of final mo-
lasses can be reduced. These have involved the rate
at which crystallization occurs to reduce the purity
and the solubility limit which defines ultimately the
lowest purity possible. This is sometimes referred
to as the equilibriumpurity, i.e. the purity achieved
once sufficienttime has elapsed so that saturationis
reached and no more crystallizationoccurs.
The equilibrium purity can be achieved in two
ways; first, by adding an excess of fine sugar and
allowing crystallization to continue for an extended
period,orsecond,by heating asampleof massecuite
until the crystals start to dissolve.
Lionnet and Rein (1980) undertook a com-
prehensive investigation into the exhaustibility of
C massecuite.The tests involved changing the con-
ditions on a planned experimental basis, and the
crystallization process was modeled mathemati-
cally. These investigations involved measurement
of sucrose and monosaccharides in C massecuites
by GC (gas chromatography)for the fist time. The
solubility relationships established corresponded
with molasses exhaustiontestsreported by Rein and
Smith (1981),based on boiling down tests approach-
ing equilibrium over an extended period of time. It
is recognizedthat exhaustionis oftenlimited by the
inabilityof factoryequipmentto handlehigh viscos-
ity massecuites;Rein and Smith (1981) showed that
no improvement in molasses purity was achieved at
a mother liquor viscosity above about 300 Pa.s. A
very strong relationship between the nonsucrosd
water ratio and viscositywas established.
Work done in Australia used a different ap-
proach, by raising the temperature of C massecuite
in the laboratory until sucrose crystals were ob-
semed to start dissolving.Approachingequilibrium
from an under-saturatedconditionis claimedto give
a closerapproachto true equilibriumpurity than try-
ing to approachequilibriumby cooling at high Brix
when crystallizationrates are very slow (Millerand
Wright 1977). However the methods of measure-
ment seem to introduce more uncertainty than the
experimentalmethod used.
Miller et al. (1998) however measured exhaus-
tion by cooling. They found that at least48 hours is
required to achieve a virtual equilibrium condition.
Since their standard test was over 24 h, Miller et al.
(1998) established "expected purities" of molasses
that could be achieved at two differentmotherliquor
viscosities, namely 100 and 250 Pa.s at the end of
a period of cooling to 50 OC. They show that above
250 Pa.s there is little reduction in molasses purity
achieved and that this limiting condition approxi-
mates to a nonsucrose/waterratio of about 4.
Exhaustion trials undertaken at Audubon Sugar
Institute (Rein et al. 2002) emphasized the impor-
tanceof concentratingup themassecuiteto ashigh a
level as possible prior to the crystallizers to achieve
good exhaustion. These trials showed that the
SouthAfrican target purity is achieved at a value of
qNs,, =4, which agreeswellwith values obtained in
the work done by Rein and Smith (1981) and values
given by Miller et al. (1998).
It is emphasized in the next section that meth-
ods of analysis have a large effect on calculations,
because values of pol and Brix deviate from true
sucrose and dry substance values more strongly in
low purity products such as C massecuite and final
molasses.In consideringfinal molasses,qNs, must
be computed from true sucrose and dry substance
values, or unrealisticallyhigh values are calculated.
18.1.3 Target purity equationsfor
molasses exhaustion
To assess the degree of molasses exhaustion
achieved, a benchmark is necessary. This is gener-
ally available in the form of a "target purity" equa-
tion. A number of different target purity equations
have been proposed over the years. Essentially they
have been derived through laboratory trials on vari-
ous molasses samples under controlled conditions,
thus establishing in essence equilibrium purity un-
der specifiedconditions.
The laboratory trials have all shown the impor-
tance of the nonsucroseiwaterratio qNSm.
Work car-
ried out in Australia (Milleret al. 1998), Colombia

A target purity can be thought of in two ways,
either the lowest molasses purity achievable in a
laboratory(equilibriumpurity),or the target realisti-
callyachievablein afactory.Theformerispreferred,
since it is an objective standard related to what can
be achieved and is not dependenton a subjectiveas-
sessment of what is acceptable.The difference be-
tween actual molasses purity and the target purity
is referred to as the Target Purity Difference (TPD)
and gives an indicationof potential improvement. A
low TPD is an indication of good molasses exhaus-
tion.
The target purity is significantlyaffected by the
measurement methods used in the process of deriv-
ing the formula. The effect of analytical methods
therefore makes it essential to specify the methods
used for each target purity equation.Those that have
been proposed are listed in Table 18.1.

phy), HPLC (high performance liquid chromatog-

to as reducing sugars when measured by the Lane
& Eynon method (L & E), which measures all re-
ducing substances and not only monosaccharides.
Monosaccharides decrease the solubility of sucrose
in molasses, while most inorganic components,
which constitutethe ash, tend to increase the solu-
bility. All the target purity equationstake these two
effectsinto accountin the ratio of monosaccharides
to sulfated ash (qMSlA)
or reducing sugarsto sulfated

approach, leading to a simple form of target purity
equation. Highvalues of q,, or q,,, enable lower
molasses purities to be achieved.
The Australian work assumes that a practical
limit is imposed by the viscosity of the material,
which limits the attainment of equilibrium in the
equipment used in the mills. For this reason two
different equations at two different viscosities are
shown in Table 18.1 (Miller et al. 1998), which are
regarded as "expected purity" equations and not
equilibrium conditions. In practice it is possible to
build equipment that can handle higher massecuite
and molasses viscosities. The extra cost involved
needs to be weighed against the financial value of
the extra sugar recovered.

The original Audubon Sugar Institute equa-

its modified form, which is more accurate at very

followingreasons:
It is based on an extensive experimental pro-
gram.
It makes use of the most accurate and reliable
measurements(GC).
It has been used extensivelyin SouthernAfrica
for 20 years and has been found to be reliable
under all conditions
It has alsobeenfound to be appropriatein Loui-
sianaconditions
Subsequent laboratory exhaustion work on mo-
lasses fromothercane-producingareasinAfrica
has confirmed its general applicabilityto within
1 unit of purity (Sahadeo1998)
t A survey of molasses from around the world
shows TPD values in the range of 3 to 7 units,
i.e. in theexpectedrange, conlirmingthegeneral
applicabilityof the equation (SahadeoandLion-
net 1999)
Modeling of crystallization led to target puri-
ties which agree closely with this equation with
qNsl, =5 (Lionnetand Rein 1980)
I
Zn many cases direct comparison of results between
industriesis not possible because of differentmeth-
ods of analysis.Pol is thefavored methodof analysis
in most countries because it is quick, but pol only
represents an "apparent sucrose" value. The pol/su-
crose ratio in molasses varies considerably during
the season and between seasons (Rein et al. 2002).
This makes pol measurement an unsuitable method
for accurate molasses sugar analysis. Chromato-
graphic techniques for the measurement of sucrose
as well as monosaccharides give the most reliable
results. Accurate GC techniques were used to de-
rive the South African target purity equations and
measure the target purity of the molasses. HPLC is

18.1.5 Effect of high dextran
and starchcontents
In laboratory boiling-down tests, high levels
of dextran have been found to lead to higher final
molassespurities (Millerand Wright 1977;Sahadeo
1998). This is not ascribed to an intrinsic effect on
solubility,but rather to the significanteffectof dex-
tran on viscosity. Increased viscosity slows down
mass transfer and prevents the same degree of con-
centration from being achieved.With high levels of
dextran, it is more difficult to achieve high masse-
cuiteBrix values.
In cases of long cane delays, when dextran lev-
els increase, TPD values are expected to be higher.
From the data of Sahadeo, it is expected that above
levels of 10 000 mglkg dextran on solids, the tar-
get purity should be increased by 0.2 units for each
increasein dextran level of 1000mg/kg dry solids.
However this is only evident once dextran levels
exceed about 10 000 mg/kg dry solids, well above
normal levels. Miller and Wright (1977) indicate
a greater effect of dextran, and suggest that every
1000mg dextranlkgdry substanceincreasestheex-
pected molasses purity by one unit. The greater ef-
fect may be due to the shorterexhaustion time used
in their tests.
Starchlevelsseem to have virtuallyno effecton
molassesequilibriumpurity (Sahadeo 1998)and do
not affect viscosity in the same way as gums and
dextran (Sahadeo and Lionnet 1999).
18.1.6 Maillard reaction
The Maillard reaction is described in section
16.3.3 and is important because of its adverse ef-
fects on molasses exhaustion. It results in the for-
mation of color and aerates the massecuite, signifi-
cantly increasing viscosity (Newell 1979). Newel1
showed that the ratio of fructose/glucoseincreases
when the reactions occur and that the extent of the
reactionscan be gaugedfrom valuesof the fructose/
glucoseratio.
Theoretically fructose is more readily con-
sumed in the reactions involved, opposite to what
was observed. In practice, the ratio of fructose to
glucoseusually has a value of around 1.2-1.3 in fi-
nal molasses, but with the occurrence of Maillard
reaction the ratio can rise to well over 1.5. Particu-
larly with C massecuites, if Maillard reactions are
to be minimized,pan strike temperatures shouldbe
kept below 63 "Cand the massecuite from the pans
should be cooled as quickly as possible, because
temperature is the major factor influencing its oc-
currence.

18.3.2 Recommendedpracticefor
achievinggood molasses
exhaustion
The check list below outlines best practices to
get good exhaustion. However, many factories are
unable to achievegood exhaustionbecause of equip-
ment limitations and low grade equipment issues
also need to be considered.
Operationalcheck list.
The C massecuite Brix should be as high as pos-
siblewithout causingunduepurity rises in the re-
heaterand centrifugals.Cmassecuite refractome-
terBrixshouldbeatleast97andthisvalue should
be furtherincreased in smallsteps up to about 98
in a planned program to establish the optimum.
If batch pans arein use, pan steamingsshould be
directed to the A or B molasses tank and not to
the crystallizers.
Massecuite purity should be controlled to give
at least25 g crysta1/100g massecuiteat the out-
let of the pan, in order to have sufficient crystal
surface area. The required massecuite purity
is calculated back from expected molasses pu-
rities, using the equation for crystal content
given in equation (15.19). (This assumes that
the B molasses purity is low enough so that a
low C massecuitepurity can be achieved)
The massecuite purity should not be much
higher than this, because higher purities not
only lead to higher quantities of C massecuite,
but the higher crystal content resulting increases
the massecuite viscosity. Equations in section
16.1.4 imply that the consistency is exponen-
tially related to crystal content, and an increase
in crystal content from 27 to 35 g1100g is likely
to increasemassecuiteconsistencyby a factor of
about 1.8.
Ideally C seed should be grained on A molas-
ses only, in the purity range 64-68 %. When the
overall factory purity profile is low, a blend of
syrup and A molasses may be required to reach
this purity range. During high purity periods, B
molasses may have to be used after graining.
It is importantto achievetheright size and regu-
larity of crystal in the seed. Correctslurryprepa-
ration is important(Ninelaand Rajoo 2006).
If a continuous pan is in use, it should be run
as steadily as possible with the production rate
set by the required evaporation rate. Ideally a$
production requirements dictate an increase or
decrease in production rate, set point changes
should be made in small steps.
The absolute pressure control set point should
be chosen to give a massecuite outlet tempera-
ture of about 63 O
C or less, and at all times be-
low 65 "C.
Absolute pressure must be steady at
all times. (It is evident that significantlyhigher
temperaturesare the norm in some sugar indus-
tries.)
Themassecuite conductivity profile in a continu-
ous pan should be chosen to be approximately
linearfrom the first to thelast compartment.This
profile may be modified with experience,but the
lastcompartment setpoint must givetherequired
massecuite Brix or nonsucrose/water ratio.
A system to monitor average crystal width is
required, either a microscope with a graduated
scaleor a photographic or computer system.An
image of every C massecuite strike should be
taken to check crystal sizeand regularity.
Theaveragecrystalwidth shouldnot be less than
0.12 rnm and shouldaveragemorethan 0.15m
r
n
assuming a centrifugal slot width of 0.06 mm.
Note the crystal length may be 1.5to 2.0 times 1
the width on average,but it is the width that de-
terrnines whether a crystal will pass through the
centrifugal screen slot.

18.4.1 Chromatographic separations
Crystallizerlevels should always be kept ashigh
aspossible to maximizethe massecuiteretention
time. Ideally, an overflow weir on the last crys-
tallizer should be installed to prevent the levels
droppingbelow a chosenminimum level.
Theidealmassecuiteoutlettemperaturefrom the
crystallizer is around 40 "C.
This figure should
berecorded and coolingadjusted asnecessary to
achieveit.
The massecuite reheater temperature should be
kept as low as possible at all times. The choice
of outlet temperature depends on massecuite
viscosity, and may be as high as 60 "C, but nor-
mally would be lower than this. The reheater
temperature is set by what the centrifugals can
handle. The reheater should have sufficientsur-
faceareaforthemassecuiteoutlettemperatureto
be within 3 O
C of the massecuitereheater water
temperature. Purity change across the reheater
should be close to zero (and can sometimes be
negative).
Nutsch (mother liquor) purity measurements
should ideally be taken at strike, after the crys-
tallizer~and after the reheater. Purity change
across each stage can then be monitored and
the crystal content can also be calculated. Purity
changes across the C station should be reported
routinely.
Massecuite throughput through the centrifugals
shouldbe as steady as possible and allmachines
should run at the samerate.Throughputthrough
the centrifugalsshould be set to producea target
molasses productionrate, as read on a molasses
scale or flow meter. As a rough guide, a target
related to the hourly non-pol input in raw juice
should be set, since molasses productionis pro-
portional to nonsucroseinput, as equation(18.9)
indicates.Alternatively,the previous week's av-
erage can be used as a target.
There are two options for controlling through-
put on the centrifugals.Either set the massecuite
valve position and adjust the water quantity to
give the desired sugar purity (80 to 85 %), or
set the water flow rate and adjust the masse-
cuite rate to give the required sugar purity. The
steamsettingis adjusted to reduce themassecuite
viscosityenteringthecentrifugal,togiveamolas-
sesoutlet temperature of not more than 60 "C.
Centrifugal purity rise should be less than
3 units, and preferably less than 2 units. This is
achieved by the correct combination of crystal
size, reheater temperature and steady through-
puts. Final molasses W S should be above 82.
Nutsch purity risesacrossthecentrifugalsshould
be measured routinely, to ensure that they are
being operated correctly, that there are no holes
in the screens, that the screensare not d m , and
that there is no excessivescreen wear.
Low gradeplant andequipmentissues.To achieve
good low grade massecuite exhaustion, plant and
equipmentlimitationsneed to be addressed.Particu-
lar requirements are:
Pans that can processhigh Brix massecuites,ei-
ther continuous or low-head batch pans.
A supply of condenser injection water at a
low temperature (say <32 "C) to enable a high
enough vacuum to be achieved (to keep the
massecuitetemperaturedown).
Vacuum equipment (preferably liquid ring
pumps) to give reliable steady absolute pres-
sure.
Preferably a gravity flow systemwith well-sized
connections to eliminate the need for pumping
massecuite.
Crystallizer drives and massecuite flow paths
that can accommodate high Brix massecuites.
Sufficient crystallizer residence time and ad-
equate massecuitecooling facilities.
Generously sized finned-tube reheaters to heat
massecuitewith a low approachtemperature.
Sufficientcontinuous centrifugal capacity with
adequate feed and control facilities for masse-
cuite,steam and water.
18.4 Molasses desugarization
18.4.1 Chromatographicseparations
In contrast to the widespread use of chromato-
graphic separation for recovering sugar from beet
molasses, only two installations of plant to recover
sugar from cane molasses by this means are report-
ed, and oneof these is assumed to no longer be oper-
ational (Kearney and Kochergin 2001). The reasons
for this are as follows:
Referencesp. 465
18 Molassesexhaustion
Cane molasses has a high content of suspended
solids, which generally requires membrane fil-
tration ahead of the separation.
Cane molasses has to be softened by ion ex-
change before the chromatographiccolumns, to
remove all divalentcations.
The sucrose content of cane molasses is much
lower than that of beet molasses, so that the po-
tential revenue is considerablylower.
The process is expensiveto install and operate.
However, once the separationhas been effected, the
potential forthe recovery of smallamountsof poten-
tially valuable by-products from the cleanedstreams
is considerablyenhanced.
Because the size of the plant is largely related
to the nonsucrose loading, it is probably more ben-
eficial to apply the process to clarified juice rather
than to molasses. Benefitsof reduced scalingin the
evaporators, reduced massecuite viscosities, better
quality sugar, as well as increased sucroserecovery
would be realized.
18.4.2 Ethanol precipitation
Decloux et al. (2001) showed that addition of
ethanol reduces the solubility of sucrose in pure
sucrose solutions. Addition of ethanol to molasses
was found to reduce significantly the viscosity of
molasses, but no reduction in molasses purity could
be achieved. It was surmisedthat additionof ethanol
solubilizes some nonsucrose and releases the water
previously linked to the nonsucrose, so that the net
effect of ethanol addition in molasses is neutral as
regards the solubility of sucrose.
Robertson (1978) showed that if the molasses
was limed to pH =8before ethanol addition,consid-
erableprecipitationof impuritieswas achieved. This
led to an increase in the monosaccharide/ashratio
and the removal of impuritiesled to an increaseof 8
to 9 unitsin the purity of molasses,fromwhich addi-
tional sugar could then be crystallized.This prqcess
seemsto be too expensivetobe viable in practice.
18.4.3 Other chemical methods
The Steffen process is probably the best known
of thechemicalmethods, and has been applied more
widely in beet sugarprocessing.Itinvolvesthe addi-
tion of finely ground burnt lime to diluted molasses
at a reduced temperature (9 to 14"C).A precipitate
of calcium saccharate is formed, which is separated
from the molasses and washed. Sucroseis re-gener-
ated from the calcium saccharate by carbonatation,
or, alternativelythe saccharate can be used for lim-
ing in the clarificationprocess. In theory, over 90 %
of the sucrose can be recovered from the molasses
using this technique.Thisprocess is not known tobe
in use on cane molasses.

19.1 Theory of drying
19.1.1 Context and objective
Drying is the final unit operation in the produc-
tion of raw sugar. It involves the apparently simple
process in which excess moisture is removed from
the sugar crystals after centrifugation. However,
this apparent simplicity is deceptive - the process
of sugar drying combines simultaneous mass and
heat transfer with chemical and phase changes.
Crawford (1952) described sugar drying theory and
practice as "a reasonably confused conglomeration
of ideas and methods which suggest that the basic
facts about drying and cooling sugar are not clearly
understood." Some 45 years later, Pakowski and
Grochowski (1997) averred that "description of the
drying process is still based on questionablemodels
and no reliable sugar drying curve is available."
Drying of raw sugar is necessary in most cases
for two reasons:
To achieve the required handling characteristics
of the sugar, i.e. to ensure that it becomes and
remains free-flowing and has the physical and
aestheticqualities demanded by the market.
To reduce the likelihood of loss of sucrose or
color formationvia microbiologicalor chemical
degradation.
As a guideline in preventing deterioration, sugar
should be dried to below a threshold moisture as de-
termined by a ratio known as the Safety Factor SF:
where w
, is the water (moisture) content, w
, the
sucrosecontent determined by polarization and wNs
the nonsucrose content of the sugar, all expressed
in g/100 g sugar. Hugot (1986) asserts that if the SF
is greater than 0.3 the sugar will deteriorate rapidly
and suggeststhat sugar be kept below 0.25. Howev-
er, there is no generalagreementon the "safe" limit-
ing value of SF.In India, a value of 0.22 is used for
white or refined sugars while 0.20 is recommended
for raws. South African practice is to use 0.23 for
all grades.
An Australian modification of the SafetyFactor,
used in some countries, is known as the DilutionIn-
dicator (DI),where:
This is an expression of the moisture percent non-
sucrose, and it is considered that a DI value greater
than 50 (which corresponds to a safety factor of
0.33) indicatesconsiderablerisk of deterioration.

Rotary cascade. The "workhorse" of sugardry-

comprises a cylindrical dnun, rotating at a slight

cradles (Figure 19.4).The drum is driven by a gear
ring or chain sprocketon its outside.The rollers run
on twopath ringsfastenedto theoutsideof thedrum.
An alternativedrive systemdrives the drum directly
via rubber wheels on which the drumrests. h either
system, thrust rollers are provided to prevent axial
movement.
