A standard arrangementwould have an induced
draft fan after the drier, which has the advantageof
maintaining the drier slightly below atmospheric
pressure, so that sugar dust is not expelled through
any of the seals (an environmentalnuisance and ex-
plosion risk). Where the air is to be heated, a heater
may be installed in the duct supplyingair to the dri-
er, or in the stationaryhood at the end of the drum.
Designs of lifters or flights vary widely, from
individual scoops to axial plates several meters in
length, usually with saw-tooth edges. The flights
should be designed to carry all of the sugar held up
in the drier, preventing any sugar progressing by
rolling along the floor of the d
r
u
m without being
lifted, a motion known as kilning. In addition, the
spacing and design of the flightsshould be such that
the curtain of falling sugar across the drum cross-
sectionis as near-continuousas possible.
Control of the residence time of sugar in a cas-
cade drier is achieved by adjusting the rotational
speed or (if possible) the slope of the drum. Since
the slope dictates the number of times each sugar
crystal will be lifted and dropped through the air
stream before exiting the drum, this parameter de-
termines the effectiveresidence time (the period in
contact with the air). Somedriers are designed with
adjustableslopes,eitherby raisinflowering one end
or by mounting the whole drier on a see-saw frame.
Many modern drier installations make use of vari-
able speed drives, allowing the drum speed to be
adjusted at will. Changing this partmeter changes
only the period spent by the sugar in the flights or
lifters (not the period in contact with the air). This
changesthe sugarholdup for a given throughput,but
has littleeffect on dryingeffectiveness. In general:
1. The speed of a cascade drier should be adjusted
to alter physical capacity of the unit (quantityof
sugar that can be transported from feed to dis-
charge without kilning).
2. The slope of a cascade drier should be adjusted
to alter the achievable moisture removal, or the
final moistureof the product sugar.
The main disadvantageof cascadedriers is the dam-
age that may be done to crystals by the tumbling
motion. There is unavoidably some attrition, or at
least scratching,of the crystalsurfacesin thistypeof
drier, causing some loss of the "sparkle" or "luster"
of the crystals and a certain amount of dust forma-
tion. In countercurrentflow,any finedust corningoff
the sugar as it dries will be carried by the airstream
to the wetter sugar, where it may adhere to the wet
surfacesof the crystals.
Cascade driers may be used as sugar coolers by
eliminating the air heater or even employing an air 1
chiller. A common arrangementis to use two rotary
cascade units installedone above the other, with the
sugar passing in series through first the top and then
the bottom unit, the former acting as a drier (with
heated air) and the latter as a cooler. Some careful
optimizationis necessary, however,in setting the air
temperaturesand flow rates to obtain maximumdry-
ing and cooling across the two units.
A modification to the standard rotary cascade '
unit is available to allow operation as a combined
drier-cooler. This involves the use of a draft tube
along the axis of the drum, extending from the dis-
charge end to the interface between the drying and
coolingsections.Cool airis then suppliedto the dis-
charge end of the drum in the normal way, and this
air travels the full length of the drum before being
removed at the sugar feed end. Hot air is supplied
along the draft tube, and the drying section there-
foreoperatesat anairtemperatureresultingfromthe

mixing of the hot and cool air streams.This system ,
is energy-efficientin that it reuses the heat released
in the cooling stageto enhancedrying.
Multitube drier-cooler. A variation on the tra-
ditional cascade drier is the Multitube drier-cooler
(Figure 19.6),whichconsists of twelve mini-drums,
each with lifters and employing the cascade princi-
ple, arranged in two concentricrings of six each, set
19.2.1 Types of equipment
intoa "tube plate" at each end and rotating together.
The sugar passes along the inner drying drums and
then returns along the outer cooling drums before
exitingthe unit. Thesuppliersjustify the addedcom-
plexity on the basis of:
1. Reducedcrystal damage and dust formationdue
to very short falls of the crystals in the mini-
drums.
2. Low space requirement to achieve both drying
and cooling.

Rotary louver. The main competitor to the cas-
cade drier has been the rotary louver drier (Figure
19.7).This comprises a cylindrical drum, as for the
cascade unit, but containing an inner shell made up
of overlapping tangential louvers. Each louver is
connected to the outer drum by a radial baffle, thus
dividing the annulus between inner and outer shells
into individual air passages. Air entering these pas-
sagesmust pass outvia thegaps between thelouvers
into the inner shell.The diameterof the inner louver
shell gradually increases towards the dischargeend.
Thiscauses the bed of sugarwhichformson the lou-
vers to progress towards the dischargeas it slidesor
rolls down the louvers with the drum rotation.There
is thereforeno need to slopethe drum, and the outer
drum is perfectly horizontal. This type of drier has
most accurately been described as a "mechanically
assisted semi-fluidized bed". Figure 19.8 is a cross-
section demonstratingthe principle of operation.

serves to maximize air flow through the feed end of
the drier where the sugar is wettest and offers the
greatest resistance to air flow,while permitting low-

Air removal from the drier is from a station-
ary hood at the discharge end via an exhaust fan,
although someunits have air removal via a pipe exit-
ing the drier at the feed end, and in some cases, air
isdrawn from both ends. This type of drier therefore
requires multiple fans,having one ormore supplying
the air (usually passing first through a radiator-type
heater) in addition to the exhaustunit and these must
be balanced by setting dampers in the air ducting.
The main advantage of the louver drier is that it
handles the product more gently than does the cas-
cade drier, thereby reducing damage to the crystals.
These units may therefore be expected to produce
less dust and a more sparkling sugar.
The retention time of sugar in the drier is ad-
justed by altering the bed depth, achieved by adjust-
ing the weir arrangement at the discharge end of the
drier. The weir comprises either a series of remov-
able rings of varying inner diameter, or a series of
vanes, the angle of which is adjustable. The rotation-
al speed of the dnunmay also be varied. Careshould
be exercised in adjusting this parameter, as too high
a speed will result in thinning of the bed at the feed
end, causing insufficient air flow through the sugar
at the discharge, while too slow a speed will cause
the sugar to build up at the feed, preventing suffi-
cient air from passing through the bed at this point.
The rotary louver may be used as a sugar cooler
without modification, but in addition, its design fa-
cilitates ease of use as a combined drier-cooler.This
is because the drum may be divided into two sec-
tions along its length, with the air channels in the
two sections separated. Heated air may then be sup-
plied to the first section, to provide rapid drying,
while ambient or chilled air is supplied to the latter
section to cool the dried sugar.
Fluidizedbed.A device that has found more re-
cent acceptance for drying sugar is the fluidized bed
unit. The simplest designs consist of a vessel con-
taining a distributor plate above a plenum chamber
into which the air is blown. The sugar is introduced
at one end of the plate and formsa bed, which, being
fluidized, flows across the plate to exit at the other
end. Above the bed, the sides of the vessel may di-
verge to reduce the airvelocity and allow disengage-
ment of fines. Nevertheless, a dust collection system
is necessary downstream of the unit.
The key element in the design of fluidized bed
driers is the distributor plate, which ensures even
distribution of air across the bed and therefore even
fluidization. Designs of distributor plates vary from
fairly sophisticated "bubblecaps", which physi-
cally prevent weeping of sugar through the plate, to
simple perforated plates, which rely on the velocity
of the fluidizing air to prevent weeping. Someplates
have apertures which converge in the direction of air
flow, so that a crystal falling into an aperture will
encounter a diverging opening, which will prevent
blockage. A popular type of distributor in modem
designs is the "gill-plate" arrangement, where the
apertures are angled to direct the air towards the
drier exit, to assist with propulsion of the sugar.
These plates reportedly reduce the blower power re-
quirement and areless prone to clogging than perfo-
rated plates (Pakowskiand Gmchowski 1997).
A problemencountered with earlierfluidizedbed
units was that the minimum fluidization velocity for
wet sugaris about an order of magnitude higher than
that for dry sugar. This meant that the bed would
not fluidize evenly, with very poor fluidization at
the feed end. It has therefore become standard for
the suppliers of these driers to compartmentalize the
plenum chamber and sometimes the bed itself, using
adjustable weirs which allow the sugar to overflow
from one compartment to the next. This allows the
air supply to each section of the bed to be tailored
19.2 Sugar driers 119.2.1 Types of equipment
to the fluidization needs of the sugar in that section.
Figure 19.9 is an example of a unit with compart-
mentalized plenum chamber and bed.
Wet sugar remains difficult to fluidize, how-
ever, and even at ten times the minimum fluidiza-
tion velocity, wet sugar will tend to lump and form
channels. This problem is addressed in one of three
ways:
1. The h s t section, or even the whole bed, is large
and perfectly mixed, so that wet feed sugar is
mixed into a large mass of dry sugar.An alterna-
tive practice is to recycle a portion of the dry
sugar to the feed end.
2. The whole drier is vibrated, or the fluidizing
air is pulsed. Oscillations impart energy to the
crystals, assisting sugar flow, destroying chan-
nels and promoting fluidization. The disadvan-
tages are additional moving parts and increased
power input. Although not the intended mode of

Schematic

operation, it is possible to operate the unit sub-
fluidized, i.e. with insufficient air to fluidize the
sugar.
3. Mechanical means are employed to keep the
sugar in motion. Stork fluidized bed driers are
provided with a rake system in the first two com-
partments to keep the sugar in motion "when
fluidization of the sugar is not yet effective due
to its high moisture content" (Hoks and Elfrink
1993). Early BMA designs contained "fin-
ger-like" lump disintegrators, but more recent
designs contain within the 6rst compartment
paddle-type screw conveyors with apertures in
the screw trough to admit air (Krell and Schmitt
1997).
An advantage of fluidized bed driers is that, if the
sugar is properly fluidized in the drier, crystal dam-
age is minimized, as each crystal is protected by a
layer of air.However, this gentle treatment has a dis-
advantage in that lumps tend not to be broken up.
By the same reasoning, fluidized bed driers are less
able to cope with inadequately centrifuged sugar.
Krell and Schmitt (1997) recommend the use of a
calorimeter for monitoring purposes upstream of
the drier. They also suggest that, for proper opera-
tion, the sugar supply from batch centrifugals should
be smoothed and "homogenized" by ribbon-flight
screws or conveyors.

The compartmentalized fluidized bed design
lends itself very readily to use as a cooler or combi-
nation drierlcooler, as each of the plenum chamber
compartmentsmay be supplied with airat a different
temperature using separate fans or dedicated heat-
ers. Another possibility for cooling sugar in a fluid-
izedbed is theuse of cooling surfaceswithin the bed
(e.g. hollow plates or tubes). These are usually sup-
plied with cool or chilled water, both increasing the
temperature driving force and providing a heat sink.
Care should be taken to ensure that the water used
is not below the dew point temperature of the flu-
idizing air, as moisture could condense on the cold
surfaces and dampen the sugar.
Caspers et al. (2003) recommend as the ideal
arrangement, from an energy conservation point of
view, a rotary drierfollowedby a fluidizedbed cool-
er containingcooling coils (with water as the cool-
ingmedium). Air flow requirementis reduced dueto
the action of the coolingcoils, and the exit air from
thecooler is suppliedto therotary drier.Totalenergy
requirement is reported as 53 % of the same system
without cooling coils, and 57 % of an arrangement
in which a rotary drieris followed by a plate hopper
cooler (described below).

Fluidized bed driers. The distributor plate is
at the heart of a fluidized bed drier design. It must
provide sufficientpressuredrop to distribute the air
evenly withoutexcessiveenergy consumption-Pa-
kowski and Grochowski (1997)recommend 10 % to

Selection of a superficial air velocity involves
ensuringthat the sugaris fully fluidized,while stop-
ping short of pneumatically conveying the sugarout
of the bed. Clearly both the minimum fluidization
velocity and the transportvelocity are dependenton
a range of variables, most especially crystal size.
Pachowski and Gmchowski (1997) claim a figure
for minimum fluidization velocity of 0.16 d s for
white sugar, which is vastly different from the 0.5
to 0.6 m/s reported for white sugar by nYaite and
Randall (1987),based on aperformancecomparison
between fiveunits atBritishSugar.Krell andSchmirt
(1997)calculatea range from 0.1-0.4 d s for 0.3 to
1.2 mm crystals. The authors suggest that, for most
sugar applications, the acceptable range of superfi-
cial velocitiesis between 0.4 m/s and 1.8 m/s.

Minimize the temperature of the sugar prior to

a maximum temperatureof 38 "C.
Protect the bottom layer of bags from dampness
and temperaturegradient via the floor by means

tic sheeting.
Minimize the outer surfaceof the bags exposed
to the ambient a
i
rby the use of large, near-cubi-

Give the sides of the stack a batter or taper of
20' for hessian bags and 7.5' for paper bags.

19.3.2 Raw sugar warehousing
Sugar stored in bulk in a silo becomes compact-
ed, causing thebulk density to increase with depth.
Hugot (1986)reportsa bulk densityof 1000kg/m3at
a depth of 6 m, which leads him to suggest an aver-
age design densityfor deep silos of 900 kg/m3.
Feedand reclaimsystems. Sugaris suppliedto
bulk stores, almost universally, by a conveyor run-
ningin theapex of theroof.Dischargefromthiscon-
veyor is by a movingplow (not an ideal application),
a throw-off carriageor a moving conveyor.A throw-
off carriage is a frame running on rails along the
conveyor,so that it may be moved to the desired dis-
charge point. It contains two pulleys around which
the belt is looped, and the load is discharged down
chutes on either side of the belt. These devices are
commonly employed to distribute sugar in a large
storage bin or silo.A "moving conveyor" alternative
is a shuttleconveyor, which is half the length of the
silo,mounted on wheels and can be driven in either
direction.Theshuttleis positioned to cany the sugar
from the main belt discharge at the silo midpoint
to the desired discharge position. Where it is desir-
able to distribute the stream of falling sugar around
the silo, a "flinger" (a rotating disc, typically 750
mm rotating at 75 m i d , onto which the sugarfalls)
or a thrower may be used at the discharge point. A
"thrower" is a very short (about 1m) belt conveyor
comprisingahead anda tail drum and two troughing
wheels between them. The belt is driven very fast
(over 10m/s) and thesugardroppedontoit isthrown
up to 20 m in a fairly neat stream,which can be fur-
ther controlled by the use of a target plate. These
devicesare useful for distributing bulk sugar evenly
intostorage (such as in trimming the holds of ships),
but causeabrasion of the sugar.
Recovery of sugar is usually by means of an
underground belt, onto which the sugar discharges
through slide-gates in the floor. Sugar remaining
along the sides of the store must be pushed to the
center. For raw sugar, this is often done by means
of a vehicle fitted with a bucket or blade for moving
the sugar.
i Lossesin storage.Raw sugar sufFers a gradual
lossinpolarizationandincreasein color when stored
for longperiods. Of the two phenomena, the latteris
' usually the more problematic, unless the sugar was
of poor quality to begin with. Rates of deterioration
~ u y
widely, dependingon the following:
Moisture content (in conjunction with polariza-
tion): In general raw sugar should have a Safety
Factor below 0.25.
Temperature: Raws should be stored at as low
a temperature as possible. van der Poel et al.
(1998) suggest that raw sugar at a polarization
of 97 "Z enter bulk storage at a "maximum ac-
ceptable" temperature of 45 "C,but that higher
temperatures might be tolerable for higher po-
larization raws. However, they go on to say that
the "desirable" temperature on storage is less
than 30 "C.Temperature gradients in the silo or
warehouseshould alsobe avoidedbecause these
cause migration of moisture.
Crystalsizedistribution:Largecrystal size and a
narrow crystalsizedistribution(particularlylow
levels of fines) favor good storage characteris-
tics,as specificsurfacearea (and thereforesyrup
content) is minimized.
Profile of nonsugars: Deterioration is strongly
dependenton the constituents of the syrup film.
Invert sugar reacts with amino acids to form
colored compounds, while ash componentscan
catalyze this reaction, as well as invert forma-
tion.
Ambient relative humidity: Equilibrium ex-
ists between raw sugar and the surrounding air
at a relative humidity between 60 % and 65 %.
Above this, the sugar will absorb moisture, and
below this level, the sugar will release moisture.
Prediction of degradation rates in storage is diffi-
cult due to the interrelated influences of the above
factors. South African experience has been that raw
sugarof about99.3"2stored for six months showsa
color increaseof 5 to 20 %.

20 RAW SUGAR QUALITY
A.B. RAVNO
Formerly Director SMRI and Technical DirectorIllovo Sugar Group,SouthAfrica
20.1 Introduction
Polarizationhaslongbeen theprimaryparameter
in establishing the quality and value of raw sugar to
the refiner. However, the importanceof other physi-
cal and chemical characteristics has increasingly
been recognized over the past century. This chapter
is designedto identify the importantraw sugarqual-
ity parameters, point out how processing conditions
affect quality and how sugar quality affects the re-
finer and the value of the raw sugar to the refiner.
20.2 Grades of raw sugar
Unlike the beet sugar industry,which manufac-
tures white (refined) sugar directly at the beet pro-
cessing plant, the cane industry generally produces
a raw sugar, which is then refined, either in-situ at
an annexed refinery or at a remote stand-alone re-
finery. Many investigators have reported on the
potential application of various new separation
processes for the direct production of white sugar
from cane, although none are yet commercially vi-
able (Bekker and Stolz 2001, Fechter et al. 2001,
Kochergin et al. 2001, Saska et al. 1999, Steindl
2001).
In addition to these developments, there are a
number of intermediategrades of sugar,which have
been partially refined, such as Brazilian Cristal,
Australian VLC, Blanco-Directo and various other
typesof plantationor mill white sugar.Most of these
sugars have a polarization greater than 99.6 "Z and
color less than 200 IU.They are usually produced
by somevariant of a standardrefining unit operation
for the removal of color andlor turbidity, as outlined
below:
In Brazil and India, a number of factories oper-
ate a combination of juice and syrup sulfitation
to producea very low color"white unrefined" or
"plantation white" sugar. In Brazil this is some-
times "forced" into spontaneouscrystallization.
The remainingmother liquor is dispersedacross
the surface area of the resultant microcrystals
due to the high surface area-to-volume ratio of
the product, which is then referred to as "amor-
phous sugar".
In the so-called Blanco-Directo process (Ben-
nett and Ross 1988), the raw juice is subjected
to "low-level" sulfitation(forcolorremoval),fol-
lowed by syrup clarification (for both color and
turbidity removal). The scums from the phos-
phatation (syrup) clarifier are mixed with the
normal filtermuds and theresultant filtrate,when
subjected to an additional flotation clarification
step, can be sentforward to the evaporators.

without the addition of any chemical agents, fer-
tilizers, pesticides or herbicides, either during the
growing or processing of the cane (Devilb 1999).A
number of companiesare now offering one or more
gradesof organicsugarto the market.

20.3 Effect of raw house opera-

There are a number of criteria that can be used
to define raw sugar quality, many of which are of
considerableinterest to the refiner.The most impor-
tant of these are pol, color, ash, insoluble solids, fil-
terability, dextran, starch, reducing sugars and grain
sizeldistribution(or grist), as they a
l

on the ease and cost of refining. In addition, both
moisturecontent and temperaturearecriticalfactors
influencing the keeping quality of raw sugar (see
Section 19.3.2).
Themost importantsinglefactorinfluencingraw
sugar quality is arguably the quality and physicai
condition of the cane received by the miller. Much
has been written regarding the effect of cane quality
on milling performance, efficiency and sugar qual-
ity (Section 2.1). However good cane quality does
not guaranteethat the millerwill producegood qual-
ity raw sugar. Processing operations within the raw
house can alsohave a significanteffect on raw sugar

20.3.1 Cane transportand harvesting
Although the presence of dextran in the sugar
industry has been recognized for over a century,
it was only the advent of large-scale mechanical
(chopper) harvesting in the late 1950sthat initiated
a period of intensiveresearchintothe causes andef-
fects of dextran on the manufacturing process. The
number of comprehensive reviews on the topic of
polysaccharides in sugar cane shows the amount of
research which took place, particularly in the 1970s
and 1980s (Atkns and McCowage 1984,Imrie and
Zilbury 1972, Kitchen 1988).Once dextran is in a
factoryorrelinery, it isnot removedto anyextentby
the traditional processing technologies. Dextran in
cane is minimizedby control of harvesting to crush
delays. Best results areobtainedwhen thecane sup-
plyltransport system is the firstunit operation in the
factory production line (King 2005).
Because the content of colorants is higher in
bops and leaves, excessive amounts of extraneous
: matter lead to higher colored raw juice and hence
' higher colored raw sugar. The amount of color is
' also dependenton cane variety (Section 1.2.5).
20.3.2 Sucroseextraction
I
Juice extraction using a milling tandem is char-
acterizedby shortresidence times for both cane and
juice, as compared to a diffuser. Together with high
temperatures, some color formation occurs in a dif-
fuser (Section6.7.4).
Microbial activity can occur along the milling
train and the associatedjuice screens leading to the
formationof dextran,lactic acid and/orethanol.The
most effective means of preventingmicrobiological
activity in a diffuser is to maintain operating tem-
peratures above at least 75 "C.Current practice in
South Africa is to aim for a temperature of around
85 O C
throughoutthe diffuser.Lactic acid levels are
routinely measured at many factories and a concen-
lration of 400 mgkg DS in juice is targeted as the
upper Iimit (Ravnii2001). An' alternativemethod of
control, which is used fairly widely in the beet in-
dustry, is the application of bactericides, usually in
theform of a periodic shock dose.
The method of juice extraction also influences
the starchcontent of the sugarsproduced.It has been
suggested that the diffusion process introduces less
starch than conventionalmilling (Watson and Nicol
1975:112).Theresults from variousdiffusionfacto-
ries in South Africa certainly support this observa-
tion. Despite relatively high levels of cane starch in
South Africa, most diffusion factories can achieve
starch levels of less than 150 mgkg in raw sugar,
without the addition of bacterial amylases in the
process.
20.3.3 Juiceheating
This operation requires careful control of juice
temperatures, in order to ensure adequate flashing
and degassing of the juice prior to clarification.
Failure to achieve complete removal of dissolved
air in the limedjuice impairs s e w and results in
the carryover of suspended material to the boiling
house. This can impact on raw sugar quality, lead-
ing to hgh levels of insolublesolidsand poor filter-
ability.
20.3.4 Clarification
Poor clarificationcan be caused by a number of
factors, amongstwhich the most common are:
Incomplete flashing/ degassing for the removal
of dissolved air.
Handlingjuices that are deficientin phosphates.
It is fairly common practice to add phosphoric
acid to raw juice to maintain phosphate levels
expressedas P,O, of at least 200 mg/L juice.
Poor juice flow distribution within the clarifier
leading to localizedturbulenceand carryover.
Temperaturegradients within the clarifierdueto
inadequate thermal insulation or unsteady juice
temperaturecontrol.
Inadequate mixing and control on lime and / or
flocculantaddition.

20 Raw sugarquality
Poor flocculantselection and / or preparation.
Thepresenceof high levels of dextran in the raw
juice.
It is evident from the above list that careful control
of the clarification stage is a prerequisite for opti-
mum removal of insolublematerials, most of which
can have a deleteriouseffect on raw sugarquality.
20.3.5 Evaporation
Themostcommon processingproblems that can
ariseat the evaporationstage are:
Sucroselossesasaresult of inversion-theseare
enhanced by higher temperatures and increased
residence times.
Color formation due to the higher temperatures.
The increased levels of reducing sugars (from inver-
sion)and of color bodies (from heating)can have an
effect on raw sugar quality. However King (2005)
reports that laboratory andfactory trials in Australia
have shown that there is very little color formation
during evaporation, relative to the color increases
later in the process.
20.3.6 Pan boiling
In view of the propensity for color formation at
the pan stage, it is important for the producer to re-
duce boiling times and temperatures and reduce the
amountof recycle/ remelt to a minimum, consistent
with the constraintsimposedby operatingefficiency,
plant capacity and the required sugar quality. Con-
tinuous pans offer an intrinsic advantageover batch
pans in this regard, as they are capable of operating
at lowertemperaturesdueto rhereduced hydrostatic
head of massecuitein the pan.
Another importantfactor that can have a major
bearing on raw sugar quality is the production of an
even grain size with a minimum of agglomerates
and / or very fine grain. This aids molasses separa-
tion and drainage at the centrifugal station and the
subsequent drying of the sugar. Careful attention is
required at the pan boiling operation where there
are advantagesto be gained froma sound automatic
control system.
20.3.7 Centrifugaloperations
As the bulk of the impurities in raw sugar are
located within the molasses film adhering to the
outside of the crystal, it is evident that the process
of separating the sucrosecrystal from the surround-
ing liquor should be done efficiently. This requires
a centrifugal station that is well designed, operated
and maintained.It makes little sense to have boiled
a good crystal quality from a well prepared liquor,
only to throw much of the benefit away due to poor
separationefficiency at the centrifugal station.
The simplest way to improve raw sugar quality,
particularly polarization and color, is to apply addi-
tional wash water in the centrifugebasket. However
there is a l i t to the effectivenessof this technique
and,when doneto excess, it results in reduced sugar
recoveriesand increasedrecirculationwithinthepan
stage-and hencemore sucroselosses and colorfor-
mation.
20.4 Specificationsand
standards
From its inception, probably in the 1300s, the
international trade in raw sugar has evolved into a
highly sophisticated and structured market. It is not
clear just how the earliest sugar trades were con-
ducted, but certainly visual quality was part of the
transaction in the early 1800s. It soon became nec-
essary to developsome standard analytical methods
that could be applied by both buyer and seller. The
inaugural session of ICUMSA in June 1897focused
on the measurementof polarization (pol), which to-
day still remains the most important, and in many
cases the only quality parameter associatedwith the
world's trade in raw sugar. The evolutionof the raw
sugartrade and the associatedanalyticalstandardsis
well covered in a review by McCowage (1997).
Arguably themost interestingdevelopmentfrom
a quality perspective was the introduction of defini-
tive specifications into the United States domestic
raw sugar contract terms in the early 1960s. Refin-
ers in the United States led the way by imposing
quality standards in which penalties and premiums
were assessed for several parameters other than pol
20.4.1 Non-centrifugal sugars
(GulpandHageney 1967); these laterflowedintothe
New Y
o
r
k No. 10 Contract in 1968. By 1984 this
had evolved into the current New York No. 14Con-
tract, which in 2006 governs much of the trade in
raw sugar in the USA. In additionto pol, the No. 14
Contract contains detailed specifications for mois-
ture (expressed in terms of safety factor), ash, color
(forboth whole and affinated raw sugar)anddextran
content (Arias 1993,McCowage 1997).Thisis cov-
ered in more detailin section 20.5.2.
20.4.1 Non-centrifugalsugars
In some areas of the world, sugar cane juice is
merely evaporatedto producea cruderaw sugar.The
sugar crystals are not separated from the residual
motherliquor (syrup).Thejuice isevaporatedaImost
to drynessand then castinopenmoldstoformloaves
or cones. This sugar is generallyconsumed close to
where it is produced, and is known by a variety of
names in differentparts of the world, namely:
Piloncillo,Panela or Panocha in LatinAmerica;
Gur, Jaggery or Khandsari on the Indian sub-
continent.It shouldbe noted thatjaggery can also
be made from the extractedjuice of the palrnyra,
date or coconutpalm.
These are all essentially non-specification sugars,
which are not free-flowing. They vary from light to
darkbrown in colorand are used either in food pro-
cessing and baking or for direct consumption.Some
of these sugarshave limited shelf life.
20.4.2 Centrifugalsugars
Nowadays most cane sugar factories produce
raw sugarfrom a multiple stage boiling system.The
bulk of these sugars are traded for refining, whilst
some are packed and sold for direct consumptionas
"brown sugars".

20.6 Refining qualities
20.6 Refining qualities
Thevarious unitprocessesin a sugarrefinery are
designedtoremovethesoluble,insolubleandcolloi-
dalimpuritiesin a raw sugar, so as to produce a very
high purity refined sugar. It has long been recog-
nized that certain of the impurities present can have
a major bearing on the efficiency and performance
of the refinery or on the quality of the refined sugar
product (Chou and Lee 1996, Watson and Nicol
1975:70).The most importantof these arediscussed
in the followingsections.
20.6.1 Polarization
In essence, the higher the pol of a raw sugar,
the lower the impurity load on the refinery and the
higher the refined sugar output or yield per tonne
I of raw sugar processed. The benefits of higher pol
I on the process utility requirements and typical op-
erating costs of a refinery have been documented
, (Humm 1979).
In practice there area number of additionalfac-
i tors, which can influencethe optimumraw sugarpol
for any given refinery. The most important of these
1; is undoubtedly the ruling basis price in the market.
Howeverit is oftenclaimedthat the existingpol pre-
miumsin most raw sugarcontractsdonot adequately
compensatetheraw producerforthe additionalcosts
incurred to deliver a higher pol raw sugar (Arias
1993,Carreno 1980,Mpez-Oiia 1983).
A further factor is the makeup of the final prod-
act m
i
x fromtherefinery-thatis, therelativeoutput
crystal, liquid sugars and soft (specialty)
=gars. A certain amount of 'mpuriity in the r
a
w
C
sugar input is usually required for the manufacture
of these high-margin, specialty products (Chou and
Lee 1996).
20.6.2 Color
From the scale of penalties listed in Table 20.6,
it is evident that color is one of the most important
raw sugar quality parameters for the refiner. This
was confirmed in a survey undertaken by Clarke
(1993).Both the absolutequantity and the nature of
the coloring matter in a raw sugar are of the utmost
importance,togetherwith their distributionbetween
the molasses film and the crystal itself.
Over the years many investigators have studied
both the naturally occurring color bodies in sugar
cane and the subsequent chemical reactions which
takeplaceduringprocessingcausingcolorincreases.
Itisevidentthat thetopic isvery complexwith many
factors playing a role in the final colorof raw sugar.
A number of comprehensive reviews have been pre-
sented (Clarke et al. 1985, Rver 1988, Smith and
Paton 1985).This is covered in more detail in Sec-
tion 23.1.
20.6.3 Filterability
Liquor filtration is one of the major unit pro-
cesses at most refineries, either for the removal of
insolublematerialor asaliquor-polishingstep.Any-
thing that impedes the normal rate of filtration is of
major importanceto the refiner, primarilybecause it
reducesthroughputand hence refining capacity.The
typical operating response is to reduce liquor Brix,
to reduce filter cycles or to increase temperature,
which are all costly in terms of increased usage of
steam and filtration materials and potential sucrose
losses.
The overriding factors influencing filter perfor-
mance are still the characteristicsof the materialbe-
ing fed to the filter and these aredeterminedboth by
the nature and quantity of the filter-impeding hpu-
rities present and by the efficiency with which the
preceding defecation process has been carried out.
Polysaccharides in raw sugar can have a major ef-
fect onSltera\d\1'ky.
Themost'hymmtofhese are
starch and dextran, which are described in greater
detail in the next two sections. Filtration is also
adversely affected by the presence of measurable
quantities of silica (Watsonand Nicol 1975:Ql)and
other finely-divided insoluble matter (particle size
c 1 p),
such as the phosphates/silicates of Ca2+,
Mg2+,A13+,Fe3+and residual filteraid, perhaps floc-
culants and abraded resin particles (Morel du Boil
1997).The number of technical publicationson this
topic in the scientific literature bears ample testa-
ment to its importanceto the refiner.Amongst these,
the reviews by Kitchen (1988:225-228), Lee and

Donovan (1996),Morel du Boil (1997),Watsonand
Nicol(1975) and Winn (1979)provide an excellent
overview of this complextopic.
A significant problem facing the refiner is the
factthat no methodhas yet been devised, which can
satisfactorilyrelate laboratoryfiltrationtests to actu-
alrefinery perfonnance. Many filterabilitytestshave
been proposed over the years. Most display low re-
producibilityand none, as yet, havereceived univer-
sal acceptance (Watson and Nicol 1975114, Winn
1979).Someof the most widely used procedures are
variants of the original test developedby Nicholson
and Horsley (1956).which is relatively simple and
requires only small quantities of raw sugar.
20.6.4 Dextrans
Dextran is readily occluded in the sugar crystal
as shown by theresults of a study in Louisiana(Day
1984).He found that at low dextran concentrations
in syrup, about 10 % ends up in the sugar, whilst at
dextran concentrations above 5 000 mgilcg on Brix
in syrup,this percentageincreasesrapidly to around
30 %. In a more recent industry-wide study over a
period of five consecutive seasons, the dextran in-
clusion rate in VHP sugar was found to lie between
20 % and 25 % of the dextran content of raw juice
(Moreldu Boil 2005,Ravno and Purchase 2005).
Theeffectsofdextranonsugarprocessingarenu-
merous and varied. Many rehers consider 250 mgl
kg (ICUMSA "haze method" GS1-15,Anon. 2005)
as thethreshold level, above which processing prob-
lems are likely to be experienced. The main prob-
lems confronting the refiner, when dealing with raw
sugars containing significant quantities of dextran,
are outlined in the followingsections.
Polarimetry. Dextrans are highly dextro-ro-
tatory with specific rotation values at least three
times that of sucrose. Hence they have the potential
to falsely enhance polarization. The extent of the
increase should be proportional to the amount of
dextran present with the enhancement being about
0.3 "2 per 1000 mgkg dextran (Chou and Wnu-
kowski 1980,Hanson 1980).However, in practice it
was found that the increase was not consistent with
theoretical predictions, as some of the dextran was
removed by the standard lead sub-acetate clarifi
tion procedure (Atkinsand McCowage 1984,Kit
en 1988:223).As a consequence, this effect can
unnoticed at low to moderatedextran levels.
Viicosity. The impact on viscosity is probal
the most important of the dextran effects in su,
processing,becauseit directlyinfluences heat tra
fer (boiling) rates, molasses exhaustionand purg
efficiency (Geronimosand Greenfield 1978).Lal
ratory studies have shown that viscosity increa
with both the absoluteconcentrationand the avert
molecular mass of dextran. Greenfield and Gem
mos (1982) found that the effect of dextrans w
a molecular mass of 40 000 Da was so small t
they disregarded it when developing a generalii
expressionfor the effect of dexrrans onjuice visc

protective colloid and inhibits coagulation, thus

the sucrosecrystalcan beinfluencedby the presel

of impurities,which arepreferentiallyadsorbedon a
crystal face, causing that face to grow more slowly.
A number of studies have concluded that dextrans
I can causeboth a reduction in overall crystal growth
rate,togetherwithcrystalelongationalongthe c-axis
(Keniry et al. 1967, Sutherland and Paton 1969).
However the exact name of the dextran effect on

questioned the degree of influence that dextran,
certain oligosaccharides and other polysaccharides
have on crystal shape. This debateis well covered in

a review onthe topic(Kitchen 1988:228-230). More

with the dextrans.
It has been shown that approximatelyone-quar-
ter of the dextran in liquor will be occluded in the
refined sugar crystals.At high levels of dexti-an this
,can make the sugar more difficult to dry and wndi-
tion. Finally it has been reported that dextran in re-
Fined sugar can cause distortion when used to make
hard candy ( V t 1981)and that it can cause sticky
(gummy)soft sugars, which are difficult to package
(Chouand Wnrrkowski 1980, Fowler 1981,Hanson
1980).
1 20.6.5 Starch
I
Starch occurs naturally in cane as small gran-
ales (1-5 pm) and is readily removed by filtration.
Itis insolubleuntil heated,when the largergranules
readily gelatinize and increase viscosity. During
milling,the action of heat and lime solubilizesmost
of the granules. Approximately 80 % of the starch
in raw juice survives clarification and is readily
occluded in the crystal - about ten times more so
lhan for reducing sugars. About 30 % of the starch
, in juice ultimately appears in the raw sugar crys-
tal. This starch is then transferred to the refinery.
The smaller insoluble granules apparently persist
through to the raw sugar and can causeblocking of
filters. The proportion of this "insoluble" starch in
juice is quite variable.
Starch contains two components - amylose
and amylopectin. The former is a linear polymer,
whilst the latter is a much larger, branched polymer
-hence they have differentproperties.The ratio of
amylose to amylopectin varies with plant species
and also with plant age and maturity. Cane starch
contains about 15 % to 20 % amylose. Amylose
readily retrogrades(i.e. becomes insoluble), and, in
this form, also contributes to filtration difficulties.
These two components of starch behave differently
with typical refining processes such as carbonata-
tion and phosphatation.
With phosphatation refining, starch adversely
modifies the precipitation and coagulation of cal-
cium phosphate (Murray et al. 1976). This results
in high residual phosphatelevels in the clarified li-
quor. Amylopectin is the major factor in stabilizing
calcium phosphatecrystallitesin suspension, caus-
h
g the formation of large dense coagulates,which
are difficultto float at an adequateupward velocity.
In carbonatation,theamylosefraction acts as a
protectivecolloid, coating the surface of the grow-
ing calcium carbonatecrystals,thereby suppressing
agglomeration of the calcium carbonateprecipitate
(Murray 1972).This results in poor filterability af-
ter clarification, severely reducing throughput. It
is generally accepted that starch levels exceeding
250 mg/kg raw sugar tend to cause refinery prob-
lems, particularly in carbonatation (Donovan
1993).
Over the years, various processes have been put
forward for the control of starch in raw sugar. The
use of thermostable enzymes, which hydrolyze the
starchis now widespread. The enzymesin question
areeithernaturally present in sugarcaneor are add-
ed during processing. The application of bacterial
amylases for the removal of starch in the refinery
is also practised fairly widely. Besijn (1995) reports
improved filtration rates when dosing a thermosta-
bleenzymeintothe sweetwaterreturn to themelter.
More recently Vawda et al. (2005)concludedthat it
was preferable to dose the amylase directly into the
melter,owing to the fluctuatingflow rate and starch
contentof the sweet water returns.

20.6.6 Moisture 20.6.7 Ash
Themoisturecontentof raw sugarisprobably the
most important parameter determining its stability
and keeping quality during storage. Microorganisms
in the molasses film surrounding the crystal are the
usual cause of serious deterioration and these cannot
developin solutions of high density or concentration,
such as would be found surrounding a well-dried
sugarcrystal(Chenand Chou 1993:344,Spencer and
Meade 1963:289).
Variousnonsucrose solids,which may be present
in the molasses film - such as invert sugars, certain
inorganic compounds(calciumand magnesiumchlo-
rides) and some colloids -are hygroscopic in nature.
The most significantof thesearethe reducing sugars.
Under certain conditions, they can absorb moisture
from the surrounding atmosphere, thereby causing
serious increasesin moisture contentand subsequent
deterioration of the raw sugar. The relationship be-
tweenmoistureandnonsucrosein themolassesfilmis
normally expressed in terms of the "safety factor" or
the "dilution indicator". These indices are described
in greater detailin section 19.1,which alsodeals with
the effect of relative humidity on moisture levels in
stored sugars.
The New York No. 14 Contract specifies that a
raw sugar should have a safety factor of 0.30 maxi-
mum. To be on the safe side many refiners require it
to be 0.25 or less (Watsonand Nicol 1975:105).This
is depicted graphically in Figure 20.1. It should be
noted that a raw sugar with a particularlyhigh reduc-
ingsugarcontent willnot conformto thenormal safe-
ty factor guidelines (Spencer and Meade 1963:295,
Steele 1986).
Affination is the main ash removal process,
although both carbonatation and bone char can re-
move a smallamount of the residual ashin affinated
sugar (Donovan 1993,Tuson 1979).High ash levels
in raw sugar will ultimately manifest themselvesin
reduced performance andyield, lower product qual-
ity, higher fuel consumptionand hencehigher refin-
ing costs.
For the refiner, it is important to distinguish
between the ash content of the total raw sugar and
that of the affinated crystal, with the latter being of
greater importance. The amount of ash removed in
the affination process is dependent on a number of
factors; of these, the quantity and composition of
the impuritiesin the adheringmolasses film are the
most important. With good affination, it is likely
that the impurity level of the affinatedsugar will be
about 15% of that in the whole sugar (Watson and
Nicol 1975:87).
Several authors (Donovan 1993, Watson and
Nicol 1975:106) have specified 1000mglkg as the
maximum level for ash in affinated sugar, while
Tuson (1979) quotes a lower figure of 300 to 400
mglkg. Someof the ash inside the sugarcrystalmay
also originate from the insoluble nonsugars sus-
pended in juice and syrup.
Certain types of nonsugars get included in the
growingcrystals,especiallyfinelydividedinsoluble
impurities such as silica and the sesquioxides, and
particularly iron in the colloidal form (Chen and
Chou 1993:348).
Ash impacts on refinery processes and perfor-
mance in a variety of ways:
The accumulation of high levels of chloridesin
the lower grade syrups can lead to the problem
of stress corrosion cracking of centrifugal bas-
kets (Tuson 1979).
High sulfate values in affinated sugar can pro-
duceseriousscalingin pan and evaporatortubes
(SpencerandMeade 1963:297).Chenand Chou
(1993:347) quote 400 mglkg washed sugar as a
practical upper limit.
High levels of ash, particularly sulfateions, can
also have an effect on color removal. Levels in
excessof 400 mgkg areclaimed to decreasethe
effectiveness of bone char (Tuson 1979)and of
acrylic and styrene resins, although to a lesser
extent (Donovan 1993).
20.6.8 Reducingsugars
Chou (1986) reports that sulfite levels of 200
mg/kg washed raw sugar can seriously reduce
the efficiencyof bone char decolorization.
Certain cations have a definiteeffect on yield or
recovery in the refinery. In this regard sodium
and potassium are considered tobe more melas-
sigenic than calcium and magnesium (Donovan
1993).
A number of "rendement" formulae have been de-
veloped over the years to evaluateraw sugars and to
provide an indication of potentialyield. The bulk of
theseincorporatebothinvertand ash astheprimein-
dependentvariables(Section22.1). Finally the pres-
ence of sulfite can, at times, be a problem with re-
specttofinalproductquality.In theEuropeanUnion,
the specificationfor all three gradesof refined sugar
callsfor sullitelevels tobeless than 10mgtkg. In the
United States,the Food & Drug Administrationhas
a sulfitelabeling requirement;any foodproducts,in-
/
cluding sugars that containmore than 10mgkg sul-
fite must be labeled as such (Chou 1986).In South
I Africa, some beverage-canning plantsrequiresulfite
levels in sugar to be below 6 mg/kg, due to potential
corrosionproblems within the cans.
I 20.6.8 Reducingsugars
Judging by the paucity of information in the
open literature, the level of invertin raw sugarsdoes
not appear to be a very important quality criterion
for many refiners. Fawcett (1986) and De Chatal
(1986) both report that high invert levels can result
in color build-up in liquor streams, when these are
subjected to high temperature and strong alkaline
conditions, such as would occur during carbonata-
tion. In addition, it was observed that during the
cold winter months problems were sometimes ex-
perienced when processing high invert raws. These
sugarswere easily identifiableby their high angleof
repose, which caused the sugar to hang up in chutes
and elevators.In addition the final sugarmay be dif-
ficult to dry,ifthe invertlevel is too high.
Donovan (1993) states that Tharnes Refinery
would ideally like to receive raw sugar with total
invertless than 0.8 d l 0 0 g.After affination and car-
bonatation, they try to maintain the invert level in
fine liquorbelow 0.25 dl00 g.The reason for this is
that high invert levels in raw sugars lead to a loss of
sucrose in molasses. The effects of invert on recov-
ery operations are twofold, depending on the level
present; one effect is to improve the exhaustion of
molassesand the other to reduce the exhaustion.
The overall effect is often measured using
qmS, the ratio of reducing sugars to nonsugars(the
so-calledTate & Lyle "g" factor):
At low invert levels (or low qms values), the
sucrose level in the exhaustedmolasses will d e
pend on themelassigeniceffectof the individual
non-sugars that arepresent.
At intermediatevalues,more crystalline sucrose
will be extracted,givinga lowerlevel of sucrose
in molasses.
Above this level, the effects of crystallization
inhibition and the higher viscosities, due to the
higher level of invert, cause an increase in the
levelof sucrosein molasses-duetothe difficul-
ties in extracting more sucrosewith the existing
pan capacity.
Donovan (1993) indicates that the optimum (mini-
mum practical) level of sucrose in molasses will
vary from plant to plant, but probably occurs at val-
ues of q
,
,
, (or"g") in the region of 0.6.
In South Africa, most factories produce a
99.3 "Z VHP sugar, which is then coated with high
test molasses(invertedraw syrup)to meet individual
customerrequirements.Dueto the high invertlevels
in the coating material, SouthAfrican raws have a
correspondinglyhigher reducing sugar content than
of most otherexporters(seeTable20.2). For sales to
Japan, the reducing sugar content is usually above
1%, without any apparent adverse effects for tbe
reher.
20.6.9 Otherparameters
Grain size. One of the most important physical
requisites of a well-boiled raw sugar is uniformity
of grain size with a minimum of conglomerates.
Raw sugarswith arelatively largeand uniformgrain
size (0.6 to 0.8 mm)will store better and createless
dust problems during bulk handling. If there are a
lot of fine crystals present, these will tend to blind
the sugar wall in the affinationcentrifugals, leading
to ineffective washing and reduced throughput and
hence increased cost for the refiner (Watson and Ni-
col1975:88). High levelsof sugardustalso pose the
20 Raw sugarquality
risk of sugardustexplosionsin bulk handlinginstal-
lations(Scheys 1998).
Residues from crop chemicals and process-
ing additives. In a number of countries there are
strict regulations on the use of biocides, herbicides,
insecticidesor pesticides on food crops and the per-
missible levels of any residues. Severalrefiners now
require declarationsfromraw sugar suppliersdetail-
ing all the chemicalsand additives,which havebeen
utilized in the growing and processing of the sugar
cane crop.
Initial studiesindicatedthatthe levels of organo-
chloride6r organophosphatepesticideresidueswere
below the limits of detection or toxicity,even in re-
finery molasses (Watson and Nicol 197592). How-
ever at that stage it was not known whether these
agentswere likely to appearin theend product in the
sameform in which they were originallyused.Since
those earlier studies, a great deal of work has been
done. Chou (1986)reports that compoundscontain-
ing conjugated double bonds are probably removed
by bone char, and those with ionic groups, by ion
exchangeresin. Further details on the maximum al-
lowable residue limits are to be found in the FDA
regulationsforthe USA and the CodexAlimentarius
Commissionforthe EU -many othercountriesalign
themselveswith one or other of these systems.
Thee elements.Many countriesalsohaveregu-
lations governing the maximum allowable levels
for heavy metals such as lead, copper and arsenic
in food products. The Codex Alimentarius Com-
mission specifiesthe followingmaximum limits for
refined (white) sugar - arsenic 1 mgikg, copper 2
mgikg and lead 0.5 mglkg.
In addition, iron contamination in soft sugars
can adverselyaffectproductquality and colorstabil-
ity.Iron exerts a catalyticeffect on darkening,whilst
there is also considerable evidence for the involve-
ment of phenolic groups in the autoxidativedarken-
ing of soft sugars during storage (Riffer1984).Iron
is oftenpresent in raw sugar, but in the refinery,even
iron-free liquorscan readily pick up new iron, either
from corrosion or from some of the chemicals used
in refining (e.g. phosphoric acid, kieselguhr, and
diatomaceousearth).
It has been reported that with bone char, the
removal of trace toxic impurities is virtually com-
plete, whilst with granular carbon there is a gradual
increase in their concentration in the liquor effluent
as each run proceeds (Watsonand Nicol 197592).
Microbiological properties. Before the role of
adequate moisture control during raw sugar storage
and transportation was properly understood, micro-
organisms were often responsible for significant
losses of sucrose (Honig 1963,Spencer and Meade
1963:291). Most stand-alone refiners process raws
from a number of origins, with differing levels of
microbiologicalcontamination.Henceitisimportant
for therehertoknow themicrobiologicalqualityof
its feedstock, especially slime-forming mesophiles
and thermophiles(Balogh 1986).Periodic sanitation
within the refinery is sometimesrequired.

and composition
21.1.1 Calculation of quantities of mo-
lasses
The quantity of molasses produced is normally
in the range of 3 to 4.5 t1100 t cane.It is largely dic-
tated by the amount of nonsucrose in the raw juice
entering the factory.A smallpart of the nonsucrose
may be eliminated in clarification, and some addi-
tional nonsucrose may be formed by degradation
reactions in the process. All this impurity exits in
the molasses stream; the larger the amount of non-
sucrose, the greater is the quantity of molasses.
Thefateand formationof nonsucrosein thepro-
cess is therefore an important factor in determin-
ing the quantity of molasses and hence the amount
of sugar lost in molasses. If pol and refractometer
Brix are used for analyses, the estimate of nonsu-
crose recovery in molasses is inaccurate and vari-
able.Where chromatographicmeasurementsof true
sucrose are available, the recovery of nonsucrose
in molasses from nonsucrose from juice has been
found to average0.9, with a range of 0.8 to 0.95.
It is of interestto establishthe quantityof molas-
ses produced. This is often related to the amount of
cane processed, or to the quantity of nonsucrose in
thejuice. The latter in particularis used as a perfor-
mance parameter in assessing the performance of a
factory. The mass flow of nonsucrose in raw juice

and time of year of the harvest (which dictate the
nonsucrose components), and the conditions in the
factory that have resulted in the elimination or the
generation of nonsucrosecomponents. By compari-
son with beet, cane molasses has a higher reducing
sugarcontent and a lowersucrose content.

21.1.3 Physicalproperties
21.1.3 Physical properties
Viscosity. It is shown in Chapter 16 that mo-
lasses is a non-Newtonian fluid which follows the
power law relationshipgiven in equation (16.1). The
flow behavior index n is usually in the range 0.8 to
0.85 andtheeffectiveviscosity varies with the shear
rate, reducing as the shear rate increases.The con-
stantKin equation (16.1) is preferablyreferred to as
the consistency rather than viscosity. However the
term viscosity is usually (incorrectly) used instead
of consistency. It is highly dependent on both tem-
peratureand dissolvedsolidscontent,as the various
relationships in Section 16.1.4 show. The chart in
Figure 16.1 gives the usual range of molasses con-
sistencies experienced. These values are summa-
rized in Table 21.8.
It is generally good practice to design the mo-
lasses system to avoid the possibility of aeration,
because viscosity values are inflated by aeration of
the molasses. Black and White (1977) investigated
the effect of aerationon molasses viscosity and de-
veloped amethod of measuringthe amountof air in
molasses. This was done by measuring the increase
in volume of a molasses sample as it is subjected
to successivelyhigher vacuums. They reported that
molasses stored for 10 months contains a volume
fraction of 14% air, from air trapped in the molas-
ses during centrifugingand from gas generation in
warm molasses. In general they reportthat molasses
cancontainup to 10% air,which causes an increase
in viscosity of 20 %. Their work showed that vis-
cosity could be correlatedwith the volume fraction
of air by the relationship:
In this equation po represents molasses viscosity
with no air entrained. Broadfoot and Miller (1990)
found a considerably higher effect of entrained air,
with 13.5% air leadingto a40 % increase in viscos-
ity. Measurements on Louisiana molasses showed
on averagean air volumetricfractionof 11%, which
was shown to doublethe viscosity relative to unaer-
ated molasses; the volume fractionair was found to
be as high as 30 % in isolatedinstances. Black and
White (1977) found that it was difficult to deaerate
molassesand that it was necessary to boil molasses
under vacuum to remove all entrainedair.
Values are also affectedby the dextran content.
Mochtar and Sumarno (1992) reported the follow-
ing relationship between viscosity and dextran con-
tent:

DS (considerably more dilute than average final

molasses or other sugar containingproducts to zero

21.2 Molasses cooling
21.2.1 Requirements
Many reports of extensive Maillard related re-
actions occurring in molasses tanks exist. In order
to ensurethatnoproblemswith Maillard reactionin
storage occur, it is necessary to keep the molasses
temperaturebelow40 OC.It is alsodesirable to keep
the temperature down to reasonable levels to mini-
mize degradation of fermentable sugars in storage
(seeSection21.4).
Because it is necessary to raise the temperature
of C massecuite to achieve a reasonable separation
oldjuice heaters are available. It generally requires
that the number of passes be reduced to keep the
pressure drop within manageable proportions; the
fluid Reynoldsnumber in the tube is expected to be
around one and velocitiesin the tubes are expected
to be below 50 mmls. Pressure drop may be calcu-
lated using the equations for non-Newtonian flow
(equation 16.6) using the length of tubes multiplied
by the number of passes as the length dimension.
The pressure loss in the return headers is negligible
by comparison with frictionalloss in the tubes,very
different to the turbulentflow case. Although scal-
ing is not a serious problem, it is easy to keep the
insideof the tubes clean andfree of suspendedsolid
21.2.3 Heat transfer coefficients
material. Julienne and Munsarny (1981) report that
a brushing of the inside of the tubes once a year is
all that is necessary.
Plate coolers. Some successful applications
of plate exchangers on this duty are reported by
Quinan and de Viana (1991) and by Julienne and
Munsamy (1981). Heat transfer rates are high and
the coolers are compact and relatively inexpensive
to install. Heat transfer is very dependent on liquid
velocity,and if thisisreduced the heattransferrates
fall off rapidly. Moreover viscosityhas a substantial
effect on performance.
There is a concern that consistent and equal
flows through all the parallel channels, which
normally number between 50 and 100, cannot be
guaranteed.Over-coolingof some of these can eas-
ily lead to higher flows through other channels, a
phenomenon which is not self-correctingin prac-
tice. Quinan and de Viana(1991)reported evidence
of outlettemperaturefluctuationsat different points
along the plate pack. They also observed somescal-
ing of syngenite (co-precipitated double salt of po-
tassium and calcium sulfates),particularly near the
water inlet. Occasional blockagesrequired periodic
molasses flow reversal.
Scraped rotary drum cooler. Experiencewith
a scrapedsurfaceheatexchangerin theform of aro-
tating drum is describedby Broadfoot et al. (1990).
This approach uses heat exchange from a thin film
of molasses on a cooled surface, subsequently
scraped from the surface prior to the pick up of
Table21.9: Heat transfercoefficientsfor molassescoolers
more molasses. Cooling is rapid but the equipment
used is expensive and this only becomes a viable
option if a disused rotary vacuum filter is available
for conversionto a molasses cooler. This was done
at Mourilyan mill, utilizing a converted 2.44 m di-
ameter, 4.85 m long filter. A cooler of this size can
cool molassesfrom 60 "C down to 40 O
C
at rates up
to about 12 t/h. The advantage of this approach is
the abilityto process high Brix massecuites without
any concernsabout pressure drop.
Air cooling of molasses drops or films. Mo-
lasses has been cooled in a "cooling tower" in
which molasses cascades from one inclined plate to
another (Wong Sak Hoi and de Balyon 1996). The
extent of cooling possible is limited and the likeli-
hood of aeration of molassesincreasingviscosity is
a problem.

higher heat transfer coefficients are obtained when

21.3.2 Choiceof molassespump
Positive displacement pumps designed for high
viscosity fluidduty arerequired.They are generally
chosenin preference to centrifugalpumps when the
viscosity exceedsabout 0.25 Pa .s, which suggests
that positive displacement pumps should be used
to pump molasses, while centrifugal pumps should
be used for syrup. The pumps have to be chosen to
pump molasses under the worst conditions, experi-
enced for instance at start-up when the molasses is
cold. These conditions probably span the extreme
range of consistencies from 1 to 50 Pa .s (1000 to
50000cP). Positivedisplacementpumps areable to
operate with high dischargepressures, up to 3000
kPa or more. However leakage can increase with
high pressure differentials, leading to a slight de-
crease in capacity.Clearancesbetween the rotating
elements and the stationarycasing of the pump are
important, and are better maintained if the correct
materials for the duty are specified.
The issues considered in selecting a pump in-
clude price, materials, packingheal arrangements
and maintenance costs. Positive displacement
pumps require a relief valve or a safety system to
recirculatemolasses and avoid over-pressurization.
They should not be run dry or damage to thepumps
will result.
The types of pump used in this applicationare:
Progressive cavity, sold by trade name as Mono
or Moyno pumps, which have a rubber cavity
lining.
Sliding vane, which has proved very success-
ful pumping molasses. The rotor is situated ec-
centrically in the cylindrical pump chamber;
a sketch is shown in Figure 21.2. As the pump
rotor revolves, mechanical and centrifugal and
hydraulic forces move the sliding vanes out-
wards against the pump chamber. The pump
has the advantage that it is self-compensating
for wear of the vane tips. It may incorporate a
relief valveon the body. Dischargepressures up
to 1000kPa are possible.
Gear pumps, which may be external or inter-
nal gear pumps; the latteris often known by the
tradename Viking,incorporatinga relief valve.
These are shown in Figure 21.3. These pumps
have two gears that mesh, with one gear driv-
ing the other. The outer radial tips of the gears
and the sides of the gearsform part of t
h
emov-
ing sealbetween inlet andoutletports. External
gear pumps in particular can operate with high
discharge pressures above3000 kPa.
Rotary lobe pump, incorporating two parallel
rotors in the single pump chamber, specially
shapedfor the duty and usually suitablefor san-
itary applications. Unlike gear pumps, neither
the number of lobesnor their shapepermits one
rotor to drive the other. There are a number of
different lobe designs, an example of which is
shown in Figure21.4. Dischargepressures up to
1000kPa are possible.

Pump efficiencies are usually in the range of 0.5
to 0.8. They are affected by mechanical losses,
viscous friction and volumetric slip or leakage. In
most cases of very high viscosity,a lower efficiency
dependent on viscosity must be used.
The flow rate is determined by the pump speed
and is largely independent of pressure. However the
power requirement is directly proportional to the
differentialpressure acrossthe pump.
21.3.3 Mass flow measurement
It is important to obtain an accurateestimate of
molasses production in order to achieve a factory
mass balance of sufficient accuracy to be able to
pinpoint and control sucroseloss. One of the prob-
lems associated with molasses is aeration, which
is variable, depending on the way the molasses is
handled. This means that volumetric methods of
Figure 21.4: Typical single-lobe (left)
and multiple (right)rotary lobe pumps
measurement,by dipping tanks or using volumetric I
measuring devices such as magnetic flow meters,
are not sufficientlyaccurate.
The most accurate measure is obtained from
batch scales, of the same type used on raw juice
flow (Section8.2.1). Howeverthey are considerably
smaller, because the molasses quantityis roughly 3
to 5 %of therawjuice quantity.Batchscalesforthis
duty are thereforenot costlyand load cell weighing
by these scales is reliable and mainly trouble-free.
The only other meter which approaches this in ac-
curacy is a Coriolis meter, which gives an accurate
mass flow measurement. Meters are easy to install
and maintain, but some caution is advised (Reinet
al. 2005):
A meter must be chosen which can handlea vol-
ume fraction of more than 10 % entrained air,
because somemeters stall at higher air levels.
If the flow is intermittent, as for instance hap-
pens when the flow is regulated by an on-off
level switch in the supply tank, some Coriolis
meters will give an incorrect result; a Coriolis
meter designed for batching is then required.

21.4 Storageof molasses
Most mills operate for only part of the year and
need to have molasses storagecapacity to allow for
this. In most casesitis not necessary to have enough
storageforrateable off-takethroughoutthe year, but
it is not unusual to see one or more storagetanks of
about 10 000 t capacity each, particularly at larger
mills. The tanks should have adequate venting to
prevent a build-up of gas in the event of Maillard
reactionsoccurring.
In some instancesmolasses has been storedin a
"dam in the ground. Quim(1993)givesdetails of
a 16000 t molassesin-ground storagefacility. This
is considerably cheaper to construct than a tank. It
requires careful ground preparation and an imper-
meableliner, generallyplastic, to containthe molas-
ses.A cover of a roof or a plastic membraneis also
required to preventrain dilution.
In allstoragesystems,precautionsaredesirableto
preventcondensationof waterthatdropsontothe mo-
lasses. This dilutes the top layer of molasses, which
can leadtolocalizedfermentation.Otherwisethehigh
dissolved solids content is such that microbiological
losses arenot significantin stored molasses.
W.4.1 Degradationin storage
Losses of fermentable sugars can take place
over the period of a few months. Work done on
degradationof A and B molasses in storage(Smith
and Cazalet 1987) shows that some sucrose is in-
aerted to monosaccharidesbut that thereis a reduc-
Pion in total sugar content. This can be minimized
by storage temperatures in the range 35 to 45 O
C
.
Their work also showsthat the traditionalLane and
&ynon method for measuring fermentable sugars
auderestimates the losses incurred; HPLC or GC
measurements of sucrose and monosaccharides are
mecessary to measure losses accurately.

21.4.2 Preventionof the Maillard reac-
tion
Reports of molasses t
a
n
k explosions appear
regularly from different parts of the cane sugar
world. Olbrich (1963) gives details of such events
goingback to 1922.The cause of theseeventsis still
debated today, but it appears certain that the cause
of the problems is the occurrence of MailZurul-type
reactions in the storedmolassesandis not microbio-
logical in origin.
Newell (1979) reported the results of a compre-
hensive investigation into the factors promoting the
reactions.The most importantfactor is temperature,
witha doublingof therate of reactionwitha 5"C in-
crease in temperature; this was confirmedby White
et al. (1983).The reaction appeared to increase sub-
stantiallyabove 65 OC,but was measurableat 50 O
C
.
It was also found that high dissolvedsolids content
and low purity promote the reaction, so that high
Brix molasses is particularly susceptible to this re-
action occurring.
Apart from the loss of sugars and glucose in
particular, other changes occur. Carbon dioxide is
evolved, evident in the initial stages as a volumein-
crease (swellingof themolasses) and the formation
of foam (Honig 1965).The pH also drops as a con-
sequence, promoting inversion of sucrose. A con-
siderable increase in viscosity is evident (White et
al. 1983).The reaction is exothermic, so that when
it occurs the temperature increases, furtherpromot-
ing the reaction. Thus once it starts and gains mo-
mentum, it is difficult to stop and can rapidly lead
to explosions in a closed vessel, or to solid charred
material in the worst case in a tank at atmospheric
pressure.
The best way to prevent this happening is to
cool the molasses to below 40 "C before storage. If
necessary, the Brix could also be controlled at not
more than 80. Even so it is good practice to pump
molassesfrom one tank to anotheror recycle molas-
ses within a tank periodically. Somemolasses tanks
arealso fitted with an air injectionsystemthat blows
compressed air into the tanks a few centimeters
above the tank floor. The amount of airneed not be
high, just sufficientto cause movement and circula-
tion of molasses in the tank. The air has the ability
to break up any foam which may have formed, but
moreimportantlythecirculationpreventsthe forma-
Referencesp. 510
21 Molasseshandling and storage
tion of hot spots in the tank, where Maillard-type
reactions may be starting, and so disperse any heat
generated.
Incidentsof seriousMaillardreactionsinmolas-
ses tanks in Mauritius(WongSakHoi anddeBalyon
1996), and in Louisiana have resulted in a mass of
dark brown carbonaceous solid and a small amount
of residualliquid.In both cases, the solidhas proved
to be contain 80 g carbonJ100 g sample and the liq-
uid about 2 g sucrose/100 g liquid. In both cases
and in Venezuela (Cordovez 1983)and in Indonesia
(Mochtar and Sumarno 1992), the side walls of the
tank had to be cut away to get to the solid mass to
dispose of it. A comparison of deteriorated and un-
deteriorated molasses composition is given in Table
21.10.
Cordovez (1983) and Mochtar and Sumarno
(1992) reported that once the reaction takes on seri-
ousproportions,recirculatingthemolassesoradding
water to quench it is not effective. Cordovez (1983)
found it necessary to add a few tonnes of dry ice or
to blow liquid CO, into the mass to stop the reac-
tion. Cooling the molasses to below 40 O
C before
storage was reported to have prevented any further
incidents.

Although a small amountof direct consumption
brown sugar is produced in some raw cane sugar
mills,the bulk of it is refined toproduce thehighpu-
rity low color sugarrequired by the market.The ma-
jor task of the refiner is to remove color, and in the
process also reduce the quantityof nonsucrosecom-
ponents in the product.Refining also involves 6ltra-
tion to remove insoluble solids in the raw sugar.
Variousgradesof raw sugarareproduced,which
are detailed in Section 20.1. The refining process
employed has to be designed for the quality of raw
sugar that is to be processed. In some cases a high
quality raw sugar has been produced specifically to
facilitaterefining and reduce the cost of processing.
The bulk of the white sugarproduced has a purity of
>99.9 and an ICUMSA color of <45.
Refining is usually carried out throughout the
year, as opposed to raw sugar production, the dura-
tion and timing of which is dictated by local condi-
tions, mainly climate. This means that a substantial
part of the raw sugar produced has to be stored, ei-
ther at the mill or therefinery or both.It is morecon-
venient to store and transport raw sugar than white
sugar. Raw sugar can be stored and handled in bulk
in non-sterile conditions, which is not possible with
white sugar.

the product being processed is of a considerably

details slightly.Decolorizationis covered on its own
in Chapter 23, because the origins, formation and
characterization of color need to be considered to-
gether with systems for color removal. Drying and
handling of white sugaris covered in Chapter24.

22.1 White sugar yield
A refinery takesin raw sugarandproduceswhite
sugar and a small molasses stream, which contains
the impurities in the raw sugar. The amount of mo-
lasses produced and the sucrose concentration in
it are dependent on the nature of the impurities. In
addition, any impurities formed in processing will
increase the amount of molassesproduced.The ma-
jor impurities are invert sugars and ash, and affect
the exhaustion of molasses through their influence
on the solubility of sucrose in molasses, as outlined
in Section 18.1. However the other impurities in the
molasses inevitablylead to molasses purities higher
than those found in raw sugar mills, for reasons as
yet unknown. Lyle (1957:344-371) discusses the is-
suessurroundingmolassesloss in some detail.
It is not possible to calculate the yield of white
sugarfrom a given raw sugartheoretically.However
a number of semi-empirical equations have been
proposed, which give a useful indicationof the sugar
yield to be expected.The simplest of these is:

molasses purity o
