In practice, there are other losses which occur,
filter cake losses and undetermined physical and
chemical losses, of the same nature as those in a
raw sugar mill outlined in Section 25.2. These are
often of the order of 0.5 to 0.8 % of the raw sugar
melted in a well-run refinery. When low pol raws
were the norm, this could be overlooked, but with
high pol raw sugar,it is necessary to allow for these
losses. These should be subtracted from the calcu-
lated rendement in equations (22.1) and (22.2) to
give a more realistic expected overall yield. Other
raw sugar quality factors that affect the refinery
operations and the yield in practice are outlined in
Section 20.5.
A refinery which is able to sell sufficient spe-
cialty brown sugarsand syrupsto eliminateany final
molasses production of course eliminates the loss in
molasses. This is a most desirable situation. In this
case the filter cake and undetermined losses still re-
main.
It is a worthwhile exercise for a refinery to cal-
culate an ash balance as well as a sucrose balance
over the refinery.A significantincreasein ash across
a refinery (>10 %) is indicative of reactions occur-
ring in the plant that result in a loss of sugar.
Sugar yield from week to week is computed on
the basis of sugar weighed into process. In fact the
sugarinput to the enterpriseis that which is received
into storage from the raw mills. The loss in storage
should form part of the overall assessment of sugar
yield. In most cases this is only establishedonce per
year when stocks are melted out. Losses in storage
are covered in Section 19.3.2.
22.2 Affination and melting
The purpose of affination is to remove as much
of the molasses film surrounding the raw sugar
crystals as possible, prior to the sugar being dis-
solved for further processing. The process involve
mingling a saturated sugar syrup, called affination
syrup, with the sugar under controlled conditions,
prior to removing the liquid in centrifugals. This is
a very importantprocess in refiningraw sugar, since
it achieves a substantial improvement in the sugar
quality, typically removing 50 to 70 % of the color,
ash and nonsucrose sugars present in the raw sugar.
An improvement in sugar pol from 97 to 99 O Z
or
from 98 to 99.5 "Z can be expected.A growing trend
over the last few decades has been a change to VHP
(very high pol) or similar sugar, which allows af-
fination to be dispensed with. This leads to a large
savingin capital and operating costs.
The process of dissolving the washed sugar, us-
ing a high quality sweet water, isreferred to as melt-
22.2.1 Raw sugar handling
ing, a scientifically inaccurate term, and the vessel
in which this takes place is called a melter. A sugar
liquor of about 68 Brix is produced and sent to clari-
fication.
22.2.1 Raw sugarhandling
Methods of reclaiming and conveying sugar
from storage are covered in Section 19.3. A most
important part of conveying the sugar to process is
weighing the sugar. The adequacy or otherwise of
factory control depends on the accuracy and reliabil-
ity of the system for weighing sugar into process.
Since an average size refinery produces between
half and one million tonnes of sugar per year, even
a small percentage error represents a large amount
of money. For this reason the most accurate form
of sugar mass measurement is usually employed,
namely batch scales.
They can generally be expected to give an accu-
racy better than 0.1 %. In small refineries, a Coriolis
meter may prove to be adequate for measuring the
melt liquor mass flow, with an accuracy better than
0.15 %. However to estimate sugar melted, the other
sugar containing streams entering the melter need to
be measured as well and subtracted from the melt
flow.
Sugar scalesof the ServoBalans type were com-
monly used for many years. These used hydraulic
systems with knife edges, flexuresand linkages, and
were inherently troublesome. In some cases reher-
ies were known to install two scales in series, but
were then faced with establishing which scale was
inaccurate! Batch scales are nowadays supplied with
, load cell weighing systems, which are considerably
more reliable. Even so it is wise to have a method of
checking scale weights on a duplicate scale either
routinely or when problems occur.
Batch scales may have a weigh hopper capable
of weighing anything from 0.5 to 2 t sugar per tip.
Larger refineries require a larger weigh hopper. A
refinery processing 100t/h would need a weigh hop-
per of 1.5 t with a cycle time of 45 s.
Control of the flow of sugar may be achieved by
the rate of discharge of batch scales into pro-
a
,
or controlling the sugar input on a belt weigher,
a more often by controlling the melt liquor flow,
which sends a signal to a variable speed conveyor
feeding sugar to the refinery.
22.2.2 Mingling
Affination syrup, a recycled run-off syrup from
the affination centrifugals, is heated to about 67 "C
prior to mingling with the sugar. The magma pro-
duced should have a RDS content of 92 to 93 %,
which requires adding on average 36 kg affination
syrup at 72 RDS to 100kg sugar.Mingling iscarried
out in a mingler, which is usually a U-shaped trough
fitted with a horizontal stirrer with a ribbon screw
and paddles to achieve the mixing. The design is
similar to that described for magma minglers in Sec-
tion 17.5.2. Sufficient volume is required to soften
the external film around the raw sugar crystals. The
mingler feeds a mixer supplying the centrifugals,
which incorporates a rotating heating coil, to be able
to control the temperature of the magma going to
the machines at about 50 to 55 "C. A coarse screen
in the system is desirable to trap extraneous solid
material ahead of the centrifugals.
The magma level should be kept constant to
maintain a constant head on the affination centrifu-
gals. The consistency also needs to be controlled
This may be done by admitting a fixed amount of af-
fination syrup in relation to the sugar mass entering
the rningler, or by controlling the power absorbed by
the stirrer drive, or by direct measurement of magma
density. pH may also be adjusted by the addition of
lime.
The affination syrup has a purity around 80 to
85,but this varies depending on the sugar being pro-
cessed. A water wash is applied during centrifuging
and so the quantity of affination syrupincreases. The
surplus is sent to the recovery house or is used in the
manufacture of brown specialty sugar.
22.2.3 Affinationofsugar
Traditionally batch centrifugals have been used
for affination, but since the sugar is to be melted,
breakage and moisture content of the sugar are not
important and continuous centrifugals can be used.
However washing of the sugar can be done more ef-
ficiently in a batch machine and batch machines are
still preferred in spite of the advantages of continu-
ous machines.
Affination on batch centrifugals is a costly pro-
cess. The investment in the centrifugals is not insig-
nificant and results in on-going maintenance costs.
Referencesp. 534
22 Sugarrefining
The quality of the sugar has a large effect on affina-
tion. Large uniform-sized crystals are more easily
washed and will purge more quickly and more effi-
ciently. Small crystalsand a high fines content cause
problems. For this reason the proportion of fines in
raw sugar is often part of the specification or penalty
terms in a raw sugarsupplycontract.
A check on the efficiency of affination can be
made by comparing the color of the affinated sugar
with thecolorachieved in a laboratoryaffination.The
latter will always be lower, but the color of affinated
sugar should not be more than 10 to 15 % higher
than what can be achieved in the laboratory (Peurson
2000).Ash measurementsmay alsobe used to assess
the efficiencyof affination.A

the efficientoperationof centrifugals outlinedin Sec-

is more important to keep the amount of wash water
used to a minimum,sinceany water added represents

22.2.4 Design of melters
A pre-melter is often seen in practice, or some
pre-melting is done in the screw conveyor from the
affination centrifugals. The latter seems to be the
better option in terms of simplifying the process.
The objective of the melter is to produce a melt li-
quor at 68 Brix at 75 OC. A lower RDS value leads
to a higher steam requirement and the highest pos-
sible RDS value consistent with the subsequentop-
erations is desired. The temperaturemay be as high
as 85 "C, but some operators prefer to use a lower
melter temperature to minimize color formation; a
minimum of about 70 O
Cis prescribedby the poten-
tial for microbial activityat lowertemperatures.
The time required for dissolution of the sugar
depends on the temperature, concentration of dis-
solved solids and the size of the crystals to be dis-
solved. A retention time in the melter of 20 to 30
minutes is common, with the longer time required
when melting large crystals at a high RDS and low-
er temperature. Remelt from the recovery house is
generally returned to the melter, which increases
the flow rate through the melter and needs to be ac-
countedfor in the design.
The design of the melter needs to be such that
there is no short-circuiting of crystal through the
system,to ensurethat there is no undissolvedcrystal
in the melt liquor.This indicates the need for a plug
flow system, but accurate control is difficult in the
face of outside disturbances. For this reason older
designs incorporated a pre-melter, or had two melt-
ers in series,which helped to achieve the degree of
control required. A single melter is a cheaper and
better option.
A series of stirred tanks has proved to be a suit-
able approach, with the temperature and sugar con-
tent control being established in the well-mixed first
compartment.Densityis agood measurementmethod
forthecontrol of sweetwater addition;itregisters ac-
curatelyenoughthe total sugarcontent,even if not all
thecrystal sugaris dissolvedin the firstcompartment.
An arrangementof afour-compartmentmelter in a U-
shaped melter shown in Figure 22.2 has proved to be
a good solution. Each compartment contains a draft
tube with an axial flow impeller.The overAow from
one compartmentto the next is arranged to eliminate
thechanceof short-circuiting.Thecirculationin each
compartment needs to be just sufficient to keep all
crystals in suspension.The terminal settling velocity I
of a 0.6 mm crystal in a 70 RDS solutionat 70 O
C is
<0.1 mls, and so the circulationvelocity outside the
drafttube doesnot require a high circulation rate.
Heating is usually carried out by direct steam
injection or through the use of an external direct
contact heater, which in this duty is normally called I
a vapor melter. Where direct injection of steam or
vapor is prohibited for food safety reasons, indirect
I
heating is required. This normally requires a strain-
er on the pump to the heater which will otherwise I
clog with extraneous matter. The design of a vapor
melter follows the design of a direct contact heater I
given in Section 9.4. This is a good application for
a direct contact heater since there is no penalty for
the dilution associated with direct contact heating.
The close approachtemperatureachievableis also a
great advantagein a refinery, because a low quality
(low pressure) vapor can be used to good effect in
improvingsteameconomy. The advantagesof a sim-
ple, non-clogging, cheap installation are also valu-
able. The flow rate to the heater is generally about
three times the melt liquor flow rate.
It is usual to incorporate a screening operation
on the melt liquor before further processing. This
need only be a coarse screening in a carbonatation
refinery,but a finerscreeningusing vibratingscreens
is recommended in a phosphatation refinery (Riffer
2000);at least a 60 mesh screen should be used.

rator volume in the first stage is larger to achieve a
lowerpH at which carbonatecrystalsaregrown.The
last vessel is smaller, since the primary objective of
the last vessel is merely to get the pH down to 8.5
and most of the crystalgrowth occurs in the preced-
ing saturator(s). Some75-90 % of the carbonatation
is achieved at the higher pH in the fist stage of satu-
ration. Gas piping should be sized accordingly.
In some cases, some or all of the saturators are
fittedwith steamcalandrias to maintain the required
temperaturesin the vessels. In general, however, the
control of temperahre in the saturatorsis not critical
and it is more c o m o n to use a higher temperature
of melt liquor going into the first saturator and live
with the reduction in temperature through the sys-
tem, which occurs due to the cooling and evapora-
tion caused by the spargingof gas. In general, a final
temperature of liquor leaving the last saturator of
about 85 "C is desired.
Liquid height in the saturator vessel is limited
by the head which the gas pumps can accommodate.
This could be as high as7 m, but is generallylimited
to about 2.5 m. Gas piping is arranged to feed gas
from above the top of the saturator down to a dis-
tribution system at the bottom of the vessel, so that
there is no danger of liquor findingits way back into
the gas reticulation and pumping system.
Gas distribution in the vessels is via saw-tooth
launders or a system of gas nozzles designed to dis-
tribute gas as evenly as possible across the cross-
section of the vessel. However, scaling in saturators
can be severe, and the nozzle system is particularly
prone to scaling which can lead to a maldistribution
of gas. Richter tubes for gas distribution are now
used in some refineries. This system uses a set of
parallel tubes, with downward pointing slots. The
slots are kept free of encrustation by mechanical
means, and this arrangementis thereforemore com-
plicated.
A system for entrainment separation on each
saturator is necessary to ensure that droplets of liq-
uid are not carried out with the gas leaving the ves-
sel. This must be sized for the highest gas velocity
which will be expected;this requires that even at the
highestgas rate thevelocity through the entrainment
separatormust be low enough not to entraindroplets
from the surfaces of the separator (i.e. < 7.5 m/s at
maximum flow rate). Chapman (1967)suggeststhat
1.5 m is sufficient freeboard above the liquid level
before the entrainment separator.
Saturator operation, performance and con-
trol. Values of color removal over the range from
20 % to over 60 % have been reported, but are gen-
erally in the range of 40 % to 50 %. Colorbodies are
trapped in the calcium carbonate floc and very high
molecular mass colorants may be removed in filtra-
tion. Bennett (1974) has shown that the mechanism
whereby impurities are removed from the liquor
involves chemical inclusion of nonsucrose within
the growing calcium carbonate crystals, and simple
adsorption of impurities is unlikely. A higher lime
addition rate generally leads to improved color re-
moval, but the lime addition rate is generally set to
give sufficientcalcium carbonatefloc to achieve ad-
equate filtrationrates.
Roughly 10-20 % of the ash in feed liquor can
be removed, largely due to the precipitationof insol-
uble calciumsalts.In orderto minimize ash content:
it is important that the final pH of the material leav-
ing the last saturatoris below 8.7.Murray and Rung-
gas (1975) have shown very clearly that above 8.7
the conductivity ash of the carbonated liquor rises
very steeply. In practice it is advisable to aim for an
exit pH,, of 8.5.
While it is important to control the final pH of
the saturators, it is equally important to run at the
correct pH conditionsin the first saturator. Reaction
conditions within the first saturator generally deter-
mine the filterability of the final carbonated liquor.
Maximum filterabilityis achieved if gassing is done
at a pH of about 8.5. This is not feasible in practice
because of the very low CO, absorption which will
occur at this low pH, and so in general, the firststage
pH is lun at about 9.5.The observed increase in fil-
terability with drop in reaction pH is attributable to
the propensity of calcium carbonate to form better
and larger conglomerates at lower pH values (Mur-
ray and Runggas 1975).
It is possible to increase the amount of color
removedby theuse of colorprecipitationchemicals.
Cationic polyamines, for example Talocarb intro-
ducedby Tate & Lyle, have been shown to be able to
reduce brown liquor color by 30 % at a dosage rate
of 200 mgkg DS. However it has been shown that
same degree of decolorization is not achieved in the
final crystal color and since the cost of the chemi-
cals is fairly high, this is a measurethat is onIy used
when a boost to colorremoval is required.
Theefficiencyof absorptionof carbon dioxideis
quite low,in the range of 20 to 50 %. Higher absorp-
22.3.1 Carbonatation
tion efficienciescan easily be obtainedat higher pH,
but the requirement to run the saturators at as low a
pH as possiblereduces the absorptionefficiency.
In general, the amountof lime used is of the or-
der of 5 to 9 kg CaOlt melt. Because larger quanti-
ties of lime require more gas for neutralization, the
gas pump capacity may sometimes determine the
highest permissible lime addition rate. In practice,
the intention is always to add as little lime as pos-
sibleconsistentwith an adequatefiltrationrate. This
is done in order to reduce the cost of lime and also
to minimize the amountof cake, since a larger quan-
tity of cake leads to increasedsugar loss in the cake,
more sweetwater and a higher cost of disposal.
Lime is generally prepared at a concentrationof
about 10-15' Baum6. The quality of lime used can
have a large influence on scaling and a high purity
lime source is highly desirable. Slaked lime should
be conditioned by retaining it in a tank before us-
age. Laboratory trials (Murray and Runggas 1975)
have shown that an ageing time of two hours is suf-
ficient.
It is important to ensure good mixing between
the lime and liquor before it enters the saturators.
It is not advisable to have a mixing tank ahead of
the first saturator, since holding liquor at pH val-
ues around 11 is detrimental. High pH levels lead
to destruction of monosaccharides.The breakdown
products include organic acids, which require more
lime in neutralization and increase the ash in final
molasses, thereby increasingthe loss of sugarin mo-
lasses (Bervoetsand Cox 1992).The ideal is to have
a high efficiencyin-lie mixer,just upstream of the
first saturator.
Control of addition of lime is best achieved
through theuse of a variablespeedperistalticdosing
pump, with the speed adjusted in a set ratio to melt
flow rate. Some older installationsuse a lime wheel
with satisfactory results. This is a rotating wheel
with scoopsattached,andvarying the speedchanges
the number of scoops of lime added. pH control is
effected by controlling the gas flow rate to the last
saturator.
Liquor filterability. Filterabilityof the liquor is
a quality of prime importancein the performanceof
the carbonatation station. The ease of separation of
nonsucrosefrom carbonatated liquors is determined
by the filterability of the precipitated calcium car-
bonate. Apart from the quantity of material to be
removed, which is largely determined by the lime
addition rate, the filterabilitydepends on the condi-
tions of pH and temperature under which the cal-
cium carbonatecrystals have been grown.
For each liquor thereis a particularlimeaddition
rate at which the filterability will be greatest. This
optimum lime dose varies from 4 kg CaOIt DS in
someliquors to over 12kg CaO/tDS in others.
It has been foundthat both solubleand insoluble
solids affect filterability.The two main factors af-
fecting the filteringquality of raw sugar are insolu-
ble suspended matter and starch (Murray 1972). In
practice, it has been found that starch does not sig-
nificantly reducethecakeresistanceor filterabilityat
concentrationsin sugar of less than 150mglkg (Lee
and Donovan 1996).Lee and Donovan (1995) have
shown that in order to achieve satisfactory filtration
performance in a refinery, a sugar with a filterabil-
ity of at least 50 % (defined in Section 22.5.1) is
desired, which corresponds to a level of suspended
solids of 300 mg/kg. Other sugar quality factors af-
fecting filterabilityare coveredin Section20.6.3.
Filtration of carbonatated liquor is covered in
Section 22.5.
Flue gas production and handling. In general,
flue gas from boilers is used in the saturators. The
CO, content depends on the fuel being fired in the
boilers;with coal firing,a CO, contentof I0 to 12%
is expected and a slightly lower value would be ex-
pected from an oil-fired boiler. With gas-fired boil-
ers a CO, content of 7 to 9 % is expected.The quan-
tity of gas required depends on the amount of lime
added which has to be neutralized.The gas quantity
can be easily calculated if someassumptionis made
about the efficiencyof gas absorption.In the normal
range of lime additions, the quantity of gas required
is of the order of 60to 120m3gash melt. In practice,
a design figureof about 150m3at STPltmelt should
cope with lime dosed at up to 10kg CaOlt melt.
It is general practice to scrub flue gases, to
remove particulate matter and traces of sulfur diox-
ide. In the caseof gas-fired boilers, scrubberscan be
dispensedwith. In most casesa two-stage scrubbig
system is required. In the first stage, the flue gas is
washed with water to removeparticulate matter, and
in the second stage, the flue gas is washed with a
soda ash solution to remove the SO, down to a level
of about 5 mglkg. In practice, most of the SO, is
removed in the first scrubber,but the soda ash wash
Referencesp. 534
22 Sugarrefining
is necessary to protect thepipes andgas pumpsfrom
excessive corrosion. The scrubbers are themselves
simple scrubbing columns packed with ceramic or
other packings, or simply fitted with baffles and liq-
uid sprays (Larnusse 198kT).
In some cases Rootes blowers are used to pump
thegasinto the saturators,but more often liquid ring
pumps are used. The liquid ring pump seal gener-
ally consists of a mild soda ash solution to minimize
corrosion. Even with soda ash washing, corrosion
in piping and pumps can be significant. Corrosion
resistant steels or glass-lmed pipes and gas pumps
are advisable.

2 Phosphatation
The mechanism of separation in phosphatation
is fundamentally different from carbonatation. In
phosphatation the principal mechanism is floccula-
tion, whereas carbonatationactsmainlyby inclusion
of impurities within the calcium carbonate crystals.
Phosphatation relies on the formation of a floc
formed by the addition of lime and phosphoric acid,
which with the addition of flocculants,capturesfine
colloidal matter and is separated by flotation with
dissolved air.
The development and fundamentals of the pro-
cess are well-documented by Saranin (1972). He
termed the process phosflotation to distinguish it
from earlier processes which attempted to remove
tkecalcium phosphate fioc formed by subsiding or
by filtration.The importantissues in achieving good
performance are the method of aeration (with dis-
solved air better than dispersed a
i
r flotation), the
way in which liquor is fed into and removed from
the flotation vessel and careful formation of the
phosphate floc, avoidingdamagein aeration.
The process was developed by Williamson in
Louisiana around 1920 and was operated in a rect-
angular clarifier. A number of variations of the de-
sign were introduced and the process as realized
in practice by Jacobs is illustrated in Figure 22.4.
Jacobs divided the tank lengthwise into six U-
shaped troughs, about760 mm deep at the feed end
and 150rnm at the outlet end. The vessel contained
heating elements to promote further formation of
small air bubbles within the clarifier.A scum drag
running the length of the clarifierremovedthe scum
at the feed end. The disadvantages of this process
were thehigh temperatureup to 98 OC, the longresi-
dence time and the large area required. The devel-
opment of polyelectrolyte flocculants improved the
efficiency of separation considerably, enabling the
time of clarificationto be reduced from about 45 to
20 min and the temperatureto be reduced to 82 OC.
Saranin (1972) developed a multi-cell system
which proved to be more efficient. Most modern
phosphatation clarifiers are circular with a rotating
scum removal system, following the design pio-
neered by Tate & Lyle, which they termed the Talo-
flocprocess. In concept,the systemis almostidenti-
cal to that used for syrup clarification described in
Chapter 14.
Limeandphosphoricacidareaddedintoa stirred
reaction vessel as shown in Figure 22.5. Lime may
be in the form of lime saccharate or slaked lime.
Saccharatemay be preparedby adding meltliquorto
7' BaumB milk of lime in the ratio 7:1. Phosphoric
acid is added at a rate of between 0.1 and 0.5 kg
P,O,/t DS and the pH is controlledto givea value of
7.3. The liquor is heated to 85 O C before adding the
reagents. It then passes to an aeration tank where air

22.4 Sulfitation
22.4 Sulfitation
Sulfitation is not commonly used in refineries
and is more widely used in raw sugar mills for the
production of mill white sugar (Sections 10.7 and
14.3). It may be used instead of carbonatation or
phosphatation in a refinery, or sometimes as a pol-
ishing and pH-adjusting stage after carbonatation.
This can add an extra 10 % decolorization, but re-
quires another stageof filtration.
Sulfurdioxide is produced by burning sulfurun-
der controlled conditionsand the liquor is contacted
with the gas in a countercurrent flow packed tower,
which incorporates packing or simple splash plates
or slats, or in a Quarez sulfitator, details of which
can be found in Section 10.7.The temperaturein the
burner should not be allowed to exceed 300 "C to
prevent sublimationof sulfurandthe airused should
be dry, to prevent the formation of SO, which leads
to the formation of sulfuric acid.
Sulfitationis carried out at a temperature of 80
to 85 "C and to a pH of 7 orjust below. A lower pH
leads to sucrose inversion.
22.5 Filtration
Pressure filtration is required to remove turbid-
ity and suspendedsolids from the liquor.In the case
of carbonatation, filtration is a part of the process,
with the calcium carbonate cake providing the
filter aid for the process. In other cases, diatoma-
ceous earth or perlite is added as a filter aid to the
liquor to achievethe required filtrationrates. Where
powdered carbon is used for decolorization, the
carbon is removed in filtration together with added
filter aid. Various grades of filter aid are available,
which can be chosen for the application to give the
required filtration rates and the required tightness
of filtration.
22.5.1 Equationsfor filtration
In the case of an incompressible cake, the re-
sistance to flow of a given volume cake is not a p
preciably affected either by the pressure difference
across the cake or by the rate of depositionof mate-
rial. On the other hand, with a compressible cake
an increase in the pressure difference or of the rate
of flow causes the formation of a denser cake with a
higherresistance.
Two types of operationneed to be considered:
where the pressure difference Ap is maintained
constant, or
where the rate of filtration is maintained con-
stant.
Equations may be derived for incompressiblecakes
for these two cases (Rein2000). In the case of con-
stant flow:
F represents the total resistance to flow of filtrate
(Bennett 1967)referredto as the filterability(in m2).
A represents the filtration area and p the liquid vis-
cosity. In the case of constant flow, V/r is constant
and so equation (22.3) indicates that the pressure
drop Ap is directly proportional to the volume of
liquid filtered V.
For filtrationat constant pressuredifference:
Thusfor a constant pressure liltration, there is a lin-
ear relation between V 2and r and between zNand
V.A value for F can be determined by plotting rN
against V under constant presswe conditions, and
using the slope of the line to calculate F given the
filtration area, pressure difference and viscosity of
the liquid.
In this analysis, the resistance of the cloth has
been ignored. The resistance of the cloth plus ini-
tial layers of deposited particlesis important, since
the latter not only form the true filter medium but
also tend to block the pores of the cloth, thus in-
creasing its resistance. Cloths may have to be dis-
carded because of high resistance well before they
are mechanically worn. No accurateanalysisof the
build-up of resistance is possible because the resis-
tance will depend on the way in which the pressure
is developed and small variationsin support geom-
etry can have a big effect. It is therefore usual to
combine the resistanceof the cloth with that of the
firstfew layersofparticles and assume that this cor-
responds to a thickness of cake as deposited at a
later stage.

22.5.2 Laboratory filtration measure-
ments
Filterability of sugar in solution has been stud-
ied over many years and attempts have been made
to measure it in the laboratory through the use of
standard laboratory filtration tests. These have gen-
erally been based on the filtration test method and
the apparatus of Nicholson and Horsley (1956),
which compares the filtration characteristics, using
a kieselguhr filter aid,of pure sucroseand of the un-
known raw sugar, expressing the ratio of filtration
rate of the raw sugar solution as a percentageof that
of the pure sugar solution. The filterability so mea-
sured of most raw sugars lies in the range of 40-70
%. Details of a slightlymodifiedprocedurearegiven
by Lee and Donovan (1996).
A simpler filtration measure sometimes used
merely measures the volume of filtrate collected in
a given time from a laboratory filter run under stan-
dard conditions.
From laboratory tests, values of F can be calcu-
lated,using equation(22.4).In somecases,the value
of f i rather than F is reported, since flow rate is
proportional to f i (Bennett 1967). Measured val-
ues of f i lie in the range 2.5 to 7.5 . rn. Ben-
nett reports that refinery filter stations experience
problems when f i drops below 4 . m.

22.5.3 Types of filters
It has been common practice to filter carbon-
atated liquor in a set of pressure filters, and then to
sweeten off the cake in a second set of sludge fil-
ters, normally plate and frame filters. This is done
in two stages, as shown in Figure 22.3, with each
set of filters designed specificallyfor a single duty.
More recently, automatic plate and frame presses
incorporatingpressurizedmembranes have been in-
troduced, in which filtration and cake desweetening
can be carried out in the same unit.
Thepressurefiltercycleendswhen filtrationrate
has dropped to a low level or when the maximum
cake thickness has developed on the filter elements.
Then the mud is sluiced off and goes to the sludge
filtrationstep. A major feature of the pressure filters
isthat the proportionof time off formud sluicinglre-
filling is relatively low, giving them a higher online
factorthan plate and frame filters.The total time out
of service on a pressure leaf filter for draining, mud
sluicing and preparing for the next cycle can be as
littleas 15minutes.
The features of the most commonly used filters
are summarized in Table 22.2. The Sweetlandpres-
sureleaf filter was introducedin the early 1920sand
has been the best known and most widely used filter.

can be made with large surface areas. This type of
filter is preferable to candle filters in this duty be-
cause of the largequantityof caketo behandled and
the smaller filter volume per unit surface area.
22.5.4 Filter area required
The installed filter capacity needs to be sized
for the worst quality of sugar anticipated without
leading to a reduction in melt rate. In fhis respect, a
minimum sugar filterabilityof the raw sugar should
be defined. Once the filterability has been defined,
the areacan be computed using equations(22.3) and
(22.4).
In global terms, an installed filter area require-
ment of 15m2of filtering areaper tonne meltm isre-
quired for carbonatation.Expressed as a volumetric
rate, a filtrationrate of 0.1m3/(m2.h) will generally
be acceptable for carbonatation and 0.3 m3/(m2.h)
for filtration with filter aid. This should be adjusted
for the amountof downtime which will be expected
on each filter due to mud sluicing, refilling, and
cloth cleaning.
22.5.5 Filter operation
The effects of syrup Brix and temperature are
shownin the effectof viscosityon the arearequired.
Either a lower Brix or higher temperature will re-
Referencesp. 534
22 Sugarrefining
duce the area requirement. Linear regression of fil-
tration data showed that the required area reduced
by 2.5 % foreach unit reductionin Brix (Rein2000).
Calculationusing equation (22.3) suggeststhat Brix
reductions leading to viscosity reductions will re-
duce the area required by about 5 % for each unit
Brix reduction. However, lower Brix values lead to
higher steam usage, and so are avoided where pos-
sible. Usingequation (22.3), a reduction of 5 O
C can
be calculated to increase the area required by about
8 %. I .additionthe requirementsof the downstream
decolorization process could dictate limits to the
temperaturerangefor filtration.
When filter aid is added for polish filtration or
together with powdered carbon, a pre-coat of filter
aidis usually depositedon the filter cloth before any
liquor is filtered.Thereafter body feed to the liquor
is common, to provide a continuously new filtering
surfaceto the liquor.
If poor filtering raws are encountered, the
amount of filter aid added or the amount of lime in
the case of carbonatation may be increased. In bad
cases, the refinery has to reduce melt concentration
or slow down therefinery.Blendingof bad and good
raws has limited usefulness, sincethe filterabilityof
a blend is not the arithmetic mean of the individual
filterabilities(Lee and Donovan 1995).
At the start of the filter operation, the filtrate
is cloudy until a cake has been established. This
liquor is recycled until the liquor is clear. The
establishmentof the initialcake at the startof a cycle
is very important. The most important requirement
is for this to be done at reduced pressure, generally
achieved by gravity feed to the filter. This results in
a less compactlayer close to the cloth, which gives
better filtering characteristics. Once the cake is es-
tablished, a change to pumped feed is made.
As outlinedabove, there are two possible modes
of operation, constant pressure and constant flow.
The latter is preferred (Morton.1978), particularly
since the cake is only subjected to full pressure at
the end of the cycle, and the averagecake resistance
is lower.It also enables the optimumoperation to be
established, in terms of reducing the overall number
of filter cycles. In fact, a filter running at constant
rate can itself be used to monitor filterability. The
length of time a filter runs at constant rate can be
used to compute filterabilityfrom equation (22.3).
As filtration continues, the thickness of cake on
the filter leaves increases. The filter should not be
run long enoughfor the cakes on each leaf to touch,
or the cakebecomes very difficulttoremove. In gen-
eral however, the cycleis terminated because the fil-
trate flow has dropped too much before this occurs
Once the liquor is shut off, a valve at the bottom of
the filter is opened. The filter is drained, and then
the mud is sluiced off the filter elements,into a mud
tank ahead of desweetening.

it requires much labor, and is prone to leak. New@

22.5.7 Deep bed filtration
A deep bed filter of the type used for
water filtration is sometimes used in re-
fining.It is packed with layersof different
sized particles, decreasing in size from
the topto the bottom of the filter.Particles
in the liquor to be filtered are trapped in-
side the bed and removed. This filter is
suitable only for low concentrations of
solids, and is most commonly seen after
phosphatation clarifiers to trap any en-
trained floc prior to pressure filtration.
This significantly increases the capacity
of the subsequentpressurefilterstage and
reduces the amountof filter aid required.
22 Sugarrefining
The layers of filter medium arecarefully chosen
both in terms of particle size and density. The fil-
ters arebackwashed in an upflow direction, with the
largestparticleshaving thelowestdensity,sothat af-
ter backwashingthe gradation in filter medium size
is preserved. An advantage of this filter is the fact
that backwashing is done with filtered liquor and
no additional sweet water is generated. Details are
given by Alder et al. (1987). Cyclesin each filter last
between 3 and 8 h. The process is cheap and easy to
operate. It can be run under fully automatic control,
with backwashing initiated at a given pressure drop
across the filter.
22.6 Evaporation and crystalli-
zation
22.6.1 Evaporatorsystems
Liquor from decolorization has a Brix value
between 60 and 65, and should be evaporated up to
about 75 ahead of the pans, to improve steam econ-
omy. Evaporationis generally carried out in at least
doubleeffect, with use made of vapor bled from the
evaporatorsas appropriateto minimizesteamusage.
The equipment used is similar to that described
for raw sugar mills in Section 12.6.1. However the
liquorhasbeen filtered andis cleanerand morepure,
with amuch reducedtendency to scale.Robert evap-
orators areseldomused and the use of othertypes of
evaporator is much more attractive. Low residence
time evaporators are desirable to minimize sucrose
losses and color formation, particularly as tempera-
tures tend to be somewhat higher than in raw mills.
Falling film evaporatorsarealso more attractivebe-
cause of the lower temperature differencespossible
with this type of evaporator. In general a smallcolor
increase across evaporationis experienced.
Heat transfer coefficients are higher because
of the cleaner liquid and reduced scale, but lower
because of the high sucrose concentrations. Typi-
cal values vary between 1.3 to 1.4kW/(mz.K) for
first effects running on exhaust steam to 0.6 to 0.8
kW/(m2.K) for vessels operatingunder vacuum
In some refineries, sweet water evaporators are
installed, where sweet water generation is high, as
in char refineries. This helps to reduce the overall
steamusage of the refinery.
22.6.2 Crystallizationschemesand
yields for white sugar
In most refineries, four white strikes are pos-
sible. On average a crystal yield of around 50 %
is achieved. This results in the relative quantities
of sugar produced reducing roughly in the ratios
8 :4 : 2 : 1 from first to fourth boilings. The color of
each strike sugar also increases and the fourth boil-
ingmay have a color of 150I
Ubut stillbe able to be
blended into a product with an average color of 40
because of the relativequantities.
A different schemeused in some refineries pro-
ducesonly one grade of white sugar.This is doneby
recyclingthe runoff to m
i
x with the fineliquor feed.
Sugarcolor is controlled by controlling the color of
the feed mix, by bleeding off as much runoff liquor
as necessary. This may be an easier way to control
average sugar color closer to the color limit, but
otherwise neither system appears to be better than
the otherin terms of quality and efficiency.
The crystal yield obtained on each boiling is
very important, particularly from a steam economy
point of view.Yield is defined as kg crystalline su-
crose/ 100 kg massecuite dry solids. High yields
lead to significantly reduced massecuite quantities,
which alsoreducesteamconsumption.Thisrequires
boiling a clean conglomerate-free grain to a high
crystal content in the pan. Centrifuging must also
be carefully controlled to ensure that the minimum
amountof water is used to achievethe desired qual-
ity, and that the basket is ploughed clean without
leaving crystal in it to get redissolved in the basket
wash between cycles.

possible may be calculated from the bulk density
of sugar, assuming that the void space is filled with
liquor. The calculations are summarized in Table
15.2, The bulk density of sugar is about 900 kg/m3

implies a void fraction of 0.433. Assuming the void

3 White pan house operation
Pan boiling in a refinery is similar to that in the
raw house, with a few differences. Because of the
high liquor purity, boiling and crystallization are
much faster. This normally makes continuous.pans
an inappropriatechoice, as the seed stillneeds to be
produced in a batch pan, which cannot be done in a
time much shorterthan 90 minutes. Pandesigns are
similarto thosedescribedin Section 15.3,but with a
higherheating surface/volume ratio on average.B e
causeof the lowerviscosity and higherheat transfer
rate, tube lengths may be a littlelonger than in low
gradeboilings,without any penalty.
Vertical continuous pans are in use in a limited
number of new refineries (Hempelman 2005). The
main advantage is the steady steam load, which
makes the achievementof high steameconomyeasi-
er through process integrationand theuse of recom-
pressors on the steady load. They require a seed to
be fed to the pans, which comprisessugarproduced
in batchpansand made into theformof a magmafor
feeding to the continuouspans.
A problem experienced in white boilings that is
not often encountered in theraw house is the forma-
tion of conglomerates. This is a phenomenon that
canoccur soon after grainingand involvesthe grow-
ing together of several crystals. In the raw house
graining is carried out at a lower purity, at which
level conglomeratespractically never form. At high
purity however conglomeratesmay form if the su-
persaturation is not closely controlled. To avoid
conglomerateformation, circulationin the pan must
be good (preferably with a mechanical circulator),
supersaturationmustbe keptbelow 1.2and the crys-

22.6.4 Recovery house operations '-
'
The runoff from the last product white sugar
boiling is known as return syrup, which passes to
the recovery house, where additional sugar is re-
covered. The quality of the sugar is below product
quality specifications and is melted before being
returned to the process. Remelt may be returned to
the main melter or to a point just before clarifica-
tion. Excess affination syrup is also returned to the
recovery house, if not used for the production of
specialty brown sugars.

Boiling schemes. A recovery house operation
parallels closely the operation of a raw sugar boil-

called crop boilings, with the last massecuite sub-

Section 18.2 apply in the recovery house as well. In
white-end refineries, the return liquor passes to the
raw sugar boiling house. A double Einwurf boiling
schemeis often employed (Lyle 1957:338),with the
third boiling sugmbeing used in a magmafed to the
second boiling, and the second boiling sugar used
in a magma for the first boiling. First boiling sugar
is remelted.This process is economicalin steamus-
age. Continuous centrifugalsare normally used.
Molasses exhaustion. Exhaustion of molasses

house. This islargely a consequenceof the different
spectrum of impuritiesencounteredin the two cas-

impurities are preferentially included within sugar
crystals, having a greater propensity to co-crystal-
lize.This is mostevidentin refinerieswhichprocess
VHP sugar. These contain a higher proportion of

Pans. Although batch pans have traditionally

and second crop sugars in rotation. This arrange-
mentminimizes capitalexpenditurein that only one
pan and one set of centrifugals handles all recov-
ery boilings. Steady operation, elimination of pan
steamings, improved sugar quality and the use of
low quality steam in the continuous pan all offer
potential for steam savings.

22.8 Steam requirements
The cost of producing steam in a refinery
of the largest cost items and so is generally
detailed attention. Unless the refinery is aaac
a raw sugar mill as a white-end refinery, the fue
steamgenerationhas to be purchased at a signifi
cost.
It is commonpractice to generatesteamat a
enough pressure to enable power to be generat
22.8.1 Steam/melt ratios
a back pressure turbine, exhausting at a pressure
around 200 kPa for process usage. To minimize the
cost of bought-in fuel, the boilers should be oper-
ated as efficiently as possible. The options for ef-
ficient design and operation of boilers are outlined
in Chapter 27.
22.8.1 Steamlmeltratios
The amountof steamused is often relatedto the
quantityof sugarmelted in the form of a steadmelt
ratio. A common target is a ratio of unity, i.e. mass
of steam required equal to the mass of raw sugar
processed.In the refining process, assuming a melt
dissolved solids concentration of 65 kg sugar/100
kg melt, 35t water is used for 65 t sugar, or a ratio
of waterlmelt of 0.54. Since the quantity of mo-
lasses produced is small, essentially all the water
added needs to be evaporated. This ratio therefore
approximatesthe minimum theoreticallyobtainable
steadsugar melted ratio in single effect evapora-
tion.
In practice, additionalwater is used in washing
the sugar and in desweetening process vessels and
filter cake, and a higher ratio has to be expected.
Some improvement is obtained in reusing steam
and or vapor in multiple effect mode, to reduce the
quantity of steam. The quantity of steam required
is inflated by ancillary operations,such as specialty
product operations. Nonetheless a steamlmelt ratio
of unity still represents a good target, one which is
not achieved by a number of large and profitable re-
fineries.
Ideally, the specific energy used is a more ap-
propriate measure than the specific steam usage.
This takes account of the fact that the steam may
be generated at different pressures; in the case of
high pressure steam generation,the higher enthalpy
gives a lower steam usage even at the same energy
usage. Electrical energy used is often of the order
of 230 MJ/t melt, and the use of one tonne steam at
200kPa per tonne melt isequivalentto 2600MJIt.In
these terms a target of 2800 MJIt melt would there-
foreseem to be reasonable.
Al Khaleej rehery reports an energy usage
of 2250 MJlt melt for a year, and a best month of
1925MJlt (A1Ghurair and Singh 2000). This is ex-
tremely low and is achieved by substantialprocess
integration and the melting of high pol raws.
22.8.2 Reducingsteamconsumptionby
operationaland plant changes
In the first instance, it is important to measure
steam usage accurately.It isnot possible to control
steam usage without reliable measurements. It is
also often worthwhile to measure steam flows to
the major users of steam in the refinery.
Lyle (1957:441) covers great detail on heat
losses in a refinery and what steps may be taken
to deal with them. He categorizes the losses into
three groups:
1. Preventing the escape of heat;
2. Reducing the work to be done;
3. Using the heat over again.
Preventing the escape of heat. Excluding
boiler efficiencies in this Section, preventing heat
losses requires attention to radiation heat losses
and piping heat losses, steam leaks, losses from
faulty steam traps, loss of condensates and steam
blowoff or venting to atmosphere.
Reducing the work to be done. The major
user of steam in a refinery is the pan floor. Maxi-
mizing pan yields and minimizing water usage in
the pan house can pay dividends, both of which
are facilitated by the use of pan stirrers. Keeping
the sugar concentration(RDS) as high as possible
through clarification and decolorization also has
a major effect. Improving the quality of raws pro-
cessed reduces steam consumption significantly,
and a major step change can be achieved by pro-
cessing high quality raws that enable affination to
be eliminated. Good automatic process control
systems that keep the plant operating steadily and
minimize production and recycle of off-specifica-
tion product minimize energy usage.
Production of specialty brown sugars in the
recovery house saves remelting sugar and conse-
quent steam usage.
Electrical loads should be minimized, which
is greatly affected by the power usage of centrifu-
gals. In general, keeping process temperatures as
low as possible helps.
The amount of water imported into a refinery
should also be kept to a minimum, since it all has
to be heated up to process temperatures.A refinery
is also more efficient thermally when run at maxi-
mum melt rate.
Referencesp. 534
22 Sugarrefining
Using the heat over again.The use of multiple
effect evaporators and extensive vapor bleeding has
a significanteffect, as it does in a raw house. How-
ever the extent of evaporationin a refinery is lower
and the scopefor steameconomy through the evapo-
rators is not as great.
Recoveringand reusing condensateflash and re-
covering heat from pan and evaporator vapors can
save significant quantities of steam. This may be
achieved in the right applications by direct contact
vaporheating.Thermo-compressorscan servea use-
ful purpose, but require steady flows and pressures
(Section 28.5.2). Continuous pans in the recovery
house enablelowerqualityvapor tobe used and help
achieve steadier steamconditions.
22.8.3 Pinch technology studies
Pinch technology is a tool used in undertaking
a rigorous and comprehensiveenergy minimization
study, and has maximum effectivenesswhen applied
to the wholerefinery operation.
Descriptions of the application in a refinery
context are given by Rein (1997a) and Thompson
and Inkson (2003).The latter show that thehigh pan
evaporationload dominates the refinery energy sys-
tem and condensing pan vapor constitutes a pinch
and determinesthe pinch temperature (around 55 to
60 "C).
The fundamental principle involved is that hot
and cold utility requirements are minimized when
heat is not transferred across the pinch. Conversely
recompressionacross the pinch has a very beneficial
effect.
Best results are obtained when scientific prin-
ciples are combined with capital costbudgeting in a
techniquewhich enables the rigorous determination
of the most profitable energy-saving design. If the
whole plant is considered, a misguided local opti-
mum will be avoided.
The technique will not recommend changes
to Brix profiles, steam pressures, etc. and takes no
account of process conditions that cause losses of
sugar or color development. In addition, the tech-
nique assumes constant flows, so solutions must be
checked in the light of fluctuations, mainly batch
pan demands. Thus it is important that the analysis
should be used in conjunctionwith good sugar tech-
nology.
22.9 White-endrefineries
Refineries may be classified in two categories:
stand-aloneor autonomousrefineries,
white-end or back-end or attached refineries.
Refineries have traditionally been stand-alone re-
fineries, usually located close to substantial sugar
markets. However there are some real advantagesto
back-end refineries in terms of cost of production
and they have become more popular in recent years.
22.9.1 Advantagesof back-endrefiner-
ies
Todd (1997) has shown that the average cost of
production of refining in attached refineriesis about
55%of the costin stand-alonerefineries. In order to
compete, autonomousrefineries have to be larger to
achieve economies of scale to lower unit production
costs.The advantagesof white-endrefineriescan be
summarizedas:
Fuel is essentially"free" sinceuse is made of ba-
gasse to provide the fuel required. This requires
that the sugar factory be made to be fuel-effi-
cient, but the cost of this is smallby comparison
with the savingsin fuel.
Combining the operations of the refinery with
the raw house saves overhead costs.
Integration of the operation of the refinery and
raw house saves the cost of a recovery house
and equipment to desweeten other refinery loss
streams such as scums, which may be returned
to the raw house.
Utilities are shared and surplus condensate can
be used to satisfy the refinery water needs.
Raw sugar quality is optimized to maximize
the profitability of the combined raw house and
refining operations; this generally means that
very low raw sugar color (below 1000and oftea
closer to 500 IU) is produced, further reduce
the cost of refining.

23.1 Colorantsandcolor forma-
tion in processing
Puresucroseis colorless,but may appearcolored
because of the inclusionof smallamountsof colored
material in the sugar. Color is the generic term used
to cover a wide range of componentswhich contrib-
ute to the color of sugar. Most of these compounds
are complex and not easy to quantify and so color
is measured as the total effect of all colorants on
light absorbance.This is not altogether satisfactory,
because different colorant components behave dif-
ferently in the various processing and decolorizing
operations. It is difficult sometimes therefore to es-
tablish what is occurring in these processes without
some better forms of measurement.
Removal of color is the most important func-
tion of a refinery.The color of the raw sugar and the
color specification of the product white sugar gen-
erally dictate what processes are incorporated into
a cane sugar refinery. The origin, formation and
response of different color components to decolor-
izingprocessesare thereforeimportantissues.In the
final analysis, it is the colorant molecules which are
incorporated into the sugar product which are the
most important; those colorants which remain in
the mother liquor and do not find their way into the
product to any extent are of lesser consequence.
23.1.1 Nature and origin of colorants
Someof the color originatesfrom the sugarcane
and some is formed in processing the cane through
to raw sugar and then to white sugar. The chemis-
try of colorants is extremely complex and will not
be considered here. Someexcellent references give
more detail, such as Riffer (1988), Mersad et al.
(2003)and van der Poel et al. (1998).
Thecolorincaneis affectedconsiderablyby time
of season and canevariety. The colorin therind and
nodes is 4 to 5 times the color in the internodes and
the tops and trash have very high levels of colorants,
orders of magnitude higher than the color levels in
the stalk (Lionnet 1992).The condition of the cane
has a large effect on the color originating from the
sugarcane. Smith (1990) reported syrup colors for
some mills in South Africa, which are reproduced
in Figure 23.1.This shows a very distinct seasonal
trend, with the color lowestin the middle of the sea-
son when the cane quality is at its best. Significant
variationsbetween mills are also evident, indicating
a cane supply area effect as well. This confirms that
the color dueto the cane is a very significantpropor-
tion of the total colorin the mills.

23.1.2 Measurementof color
23.1.2. Measurement of color
Color is generally measured according to the
ICUMSA methods (Anon. 2005), which involves
measuringlight absorbanceat 420 nm andpH 7.0 or
with no pH adjustmentfor refined sugars,after filter-
ing through a 0.45 pcellulosenitrate filter.This is
adjusted accordingto the thicknessof the measuring
cell, and is expressed relative to the concentration
of dissolved solids in the liquid sample. ICUMSA
color is abbreviated to IU (ICUMSA units) and is
calculated as:

where 6 is the cell length in mm and c the dissolved
solids concentration in g/rnL. The membrane used
for filtrationin thismeasurementhas an effecton the
color measured. It is often acceptedthat the 0.45 pn
filter removes some high molecular mass colorant.
Membranes with a larger pore size lead to a higher
color value, up to a membrane pore size of 1.2 pm
(Bento2003), above which pore sizehas no effect.
The absorbance is also affected by the pH, be-
causesomeof the colorantsaremore sensitivetopH
than others. This is a consequence of the structure
of different color molecules and the pH sensitivity
is used as a means of differentiatingbetween types
of colorant.This is expressedin the IndicatorValue,

Godshall (1997) gives a comprehensive report
on the factors affecting sugar color measurement.
Various other methods of expressing the color mea-
sured by absorbance have been used, which are not
recognized by ICUMSA, some of them defined as
qualityspecificationsby the user. RBU is sometimes
quoted and measurements undertaken at SPRI have
shown that the correspondence between IU and
RBU is within 4 to 5 units on white sugarand within
17 units on raw sugar.
ICUMSA also recognizes two other methods of
color characterization of crystal sugar,namely reflec-
tance and visual appearance according to the Braun-
schweigcolortypes,but neitherof theseiscommonly
used in cane sugarprocessing other than in the EU.
23.1.3. Identificationof colorants
Colorants have been separated in terms of mo-
lecular mass by gel permeation chromatography,a
technique used by a number of researchers. Smith
et al. (1981) showed that the colorants show three
distinct peaks, corresponding to high, intermediate
and low molecular mass. Bento (2003) measured
the componentsof polymeric color by GPC. Broad-
hurst and Rein (2002)measured the molecularmass
of colorants formed in processing. They found that
most cane sugar colorants in the sugar mill have a
molecular mass of less than 10000, but other stud-
ies have identified colorants with larger molecular
masses, some over250 000 (Bento2003).
Bento (2003) also characterizedcolorants by an
indicator value measured in the ultra-violet region,
which he called UIV. He showed that cane raw sugar
and white sugar show different componentsmaking
up the UIV values.
23.1.4. Colorformationin the raw
sugar mill
The family of enzymes known as polyphenol-
oxidasescatalyzes the oxidationof phenolsfrom the
cane (mainly chlorogenic acid) to products that fur-
ther oxidize in the presence of air or react with ami-
no groups to form dark colored melanin pigments
(Gross and Coombs 1976). The enzyme is inacti-
vated by heat and so the reaction stops afterheating
and clarification.Melanins are high molecular mass
compounds which are insoluble at high pH values
and therefore are removed in beetjuice clarification.
However in canejuice very littleis removed in clari-
fication and this colorant constitutes about 60 % of
the color in cIarifiedjuice (Paton 1992).Color also
forms in raw juice when it comes into contact with
iron in the steel surroundsof the extractionplant.
Smith et al. (1981) studied changes in color in
the raw sugar mill.They showedthat the colorof the
rawjuice increased as the extractionincreased down
the milling tandem. A color reduction of 20 to 25 %
was achieved over clarificationand a small increase
of 3 to 6 % occurred across the evaporators. Signifi-
cant color increase occurred in the pan house, with
most color formation evident in C massecuite. This
corresponds with the observed greater incidence of
theMaillard reaction in low purity massecuites.

Because conditioning is not limited by the rate
of evaporation,it is independentof the air flow rate,
which should be determinedon thebasis of ensuring
a uniform distribution of air throughout the sugar,
without overloadingthe dust extraction system. Mi-
kus and Budicek (1986) list the silo air flows from
23 references and the figures range from 0.02 to 87
m3/(h.g).Theyrecommend that air velocity be kept
above a minimum of 1 mm/s, because, at this ve-
locity the diffusion velocity of moisture against the
direction of air flow becomes significant.Bruijn et
al. (1982) suggest a value of 3 m3/(h.f). Various
authors (Rodgers and Lewis 1963, Dowling 1966,
Schwer 1964)have reported insensitivity to the RH
of the air as well, although the process models re-
ferred to previously suggest that lower RH should
accelerate conditioning. McGimpsey (Symposium
SIT, 1960) found that conditioning with drier air
(20 %RHinsteadof about40 %) halved therequired
conditioningtime and produced a drier product.
Due to their larger surface area, smaller crystals
condition faster than larger ones, making the larger
crystals the determinantsof the overallconditioning
time (Chapman 1970,Lu et al. 1977).However, for
the same reason, smaller crystals cake more easily
thanlarge. Smallercrystalscontainagreaterpercent-
age of water (availablefor migration and caking) at
a given ERH. It is thereforenecessq forcondition-
ing to proceed to lower moistures for smaller crys-
tals. BressanandMathlouthi(1994)foundthat water
activitydependedon crystal sizeeven more strongly
than temperature. While neither large nor small
crystals are advocated, authors agree that improved
conditioningmay be obtained by increasing the uni-
formity (lowering the CV) of the grain. Sieving out
fines is also beneficial to conditioning and reduces
caking propensity -Mikus andBudicek(1986)men-
tion removal of the fraction smaller than 0.3mrn.
High levels of conglomerateshave a definitedelete-
rious effecton conditioning,dueto the moisturethat
is trapped between the constituentcrystals.
In view of the diversity of influenceson the con-
ditioningprocess, there is no single optimumcondi-
tioningtime for refined sugar. Estimates of the theo-
retical time requirement range from 36 to over 100
hours, while existing installations around the world
operateatbetween24and72hours.KavanandMikus
(1982)calculatea theoreticaltime requirement of 36
hours, but BudicekandMikus (1980)recommendus-
ing twice this for conditioningplant. Most research,
however, points to somewhere near 48 hours as a
reasonable practical compromise, given acceptable
sugar quality and operating conditions. Bruijn et al.
(1982)pointout,however,that"difficult" sugar(bigh
bound moisture content, high conglomerate count,
high CV)continuesreleasing appreciableamountsof
moistureafter7 days of conditioning.Thereis, how-
ever, agrowingconvictionthat"every littlebithelps"
in the conditioningof sugar -it is woah supplying
conditioningair to bins andhoppers even if the sugar
residencetime is low. This reasoning is based on the
fact that most of the moisture lost during condition-
ing is lost in the first 24 hours.

24.1.2 Refined sugar drying and cool-
ing
Other processes in the refining of sugar, in par-
ticular pan boiling, centrifuging and drying, have a
significanteffect on the efficiency of the condition-
ing process.
The processes of relined sugar drying and cool-
ing, the applicable theory and the equipment used
are all the same as for raw sugar, and the subject is
dealt with in detail in Section 19.2. The main area
whererefined sugardiffersas faras these unit opera-
tions are concerned is in their relationship with and
effect on conditioning.
The process of removal of free moisture from
the sugarcrystalsin driersis believed to be the main
determinant of the amount of bound moisture left
on the crystals. Sugar dried at high temperatureshas
been found to have a higher residual moisture con-
tent than sugar dried at lower temperatures.
This may be attributedto two mechanisms. Dry-
ing that is too rapid has been found to lead to s e
vere agglomeration of previously clean crystals. In
other words, conglomerates may be formed in the
drier rather than in the pan. The second mechanism
is the formation of a "shell" of low-permeability,
amorphous sucrose around the crystal when dry-
ing is too fast to allow the sucrose to crystallize on
the crystal surface.The moisture trapped under this
layer is then bound moisture, and must first diffuse
through the layer in order to be removed. Dowling
(1966) showed that sugar dried at higher tempera-
tures (110 "C) subsequently released greater quan-
tities of bound moisture than that dried at lower
temperatures (55 OC), suggesting that attempting to
acceleratedrying by increasing temperaturesshould
be done with great caution.
It should be noted that it is not possible to avoid
the formation of bound moisture completely using
conventionalequipment(Stachenkoet al. 1966),but
slowerdryingis advocated.Aninteresting (butasyet
unproven) approach to accelerating the rate of con-
ditioningis theuse of apre-conditioningstep,hinted
at by severalauthorsbut discussedin detailby none.
This involves holding the sugar in a bin for a period
of several hours after drying and before condition-
ing. The bin is not aerated,and the theory is that the
R
H of the interstitialairwill quicklyequilibratewith
the sugar.Thereafter,theamorphoussugarlayermay
experience partial redissolution in the saturated en-
vironment,allowingthe sucroseto crystallizeon the
crystal surfacerather than the filmsurface.Although
this description is not particularly convincing,some
refineries hold their sugar in "pre-conditioning",
"curing" or "maturing" bins for 2 to 3 hours before
conditioning. Also, Tait's batch conditioning model
(SymposiumSIT, 1996)describes a process where-
by, by the use of a "wave" of high humidity air,later
conditioningcan be acceleratedso substantiallythat
conditioning may be accomplishedin 4 hours! Tait
refers to this as "relaxing" the sugar, and, while the
claim of 4 h conditioning requires better substantia-
tion, this certainly appears to present an avenuefor
further investigation.
The negative consequences of too-rapid drying
are so well accepted by BMA, that they design their
fluidized-bed driers to prevent it. Krell and Schmitt
(1997) describe how a drier installed at the Offstein
factory was unable to meet targeted product mois-
ture, and produced lumps, until the consequencesof
"shock" drying in the &st stage were recognized.
The gentle sugar transport process in fluidized-bed
drying does not disturb the amorphous sugar shell
around the crystal, making this type of dryer most
susceptible to downstream conditioning problems,
if drying rate is not carefully controlled. BMA now
have "paddle-screws" in the &st compartment of
their driers, in part to provide additional motion to
the sugar and reduce the likelihood of this problem
developing.
A further important aspect of the drying of re-
fined sugar that is supplied to a direct-consumption
market is any effect on the appearance of the sugar.
In general, sugar that is handled gently during dry-
ing retains more of its surface sparkle or luster. In
this respect, fluidized-bed drying is superior to cas-
cade drying, which tends to cause some crystal at-
trition. Countercurrent operation of a cascade drier
also presents the possibility that sugar dust, carried
24.2.1 Qpes of bulk silo
back along the drier by the drying air,may stick to
the wet crystals and further impair surface appear-
ance.
Cooling of refined sugar at a temperature as
close as possible to ambient before silo storage or
packagingis desirable. Casperset al. (2003)recom-
mend no more than 5 O
C above ambient.
24.2 Refined sugarstorage
Sugar storage takesplace in one of four forms:
1. Bins and hoppers, for short duration "surge"
storage; capacityup to a few hundred tonnes.
2. Short-termbulk storagesilos, of tall cylindrical
construction, frequently used for conditioning;
typical capacity 1000to 3000 tomes.
3. Long-term bulk storage silos, of lower aspect
ratio; typical capacity 20 000 to 80 000 tonnes.
4. Bagged sugar warehouses.
Mikus and Budicek (1986) compiled a superb
overview of the entire subject of refined sugar stor-
age, incorporating a most useful section on condi-
tioning. This work is highly recommended to those
who wish to obtain a fuller understanding of the
subject.
Authors differ on a "safe" RH for sugar storage
-the most common rule-of-thumb used by most re-
hers is that an RH below 60 % is acceptable. The
situation is complicated, however, by the fact that
the ERH varies according to the moisture level of
the sugar itself. Since impurities are concentratedin
the surface film, drying of the crystal further con-
centrates these impurities and therefore lowers the
ERH.What is disturbingis the rate at which refined

24.2.1 m
e
sof bulk silo
Bulk refined sugar is generally stored in cylin-
drical silos of up to 80 000 tonnes capacity, because
vertical cylindrical silos are usually cost-effective,
occupy a relatively small footprint and can readily
be conditioned. Designs differ mainly in terms of
construction material, approach to insulation and
sugar feed and extractionmechanisms.
Materials of construction. Silos are usually
constructed of steel or reinforced concrete. Epoxy-
lined mild steelis sometimesused, as is epoxy-lined
concrete. Stainless steel is encountered, but the
benefit of self-passivating steels is reduced by the
fact that the moving sugar abrades the passive layer.
Mild steel can be used quite safely as a material of
construction, because the conditioned air protects it
against corrosion. Concentriccylindricalsilos (silos
within silos) are sometimes used where different
sugars are to be stored in the same silo. Sugar of
different temperatures or qualities should never be
stored in contact with one another.
The need to insulate bulk sugar storage equip-
ment depends on capacity, sugar quality (degree of
conditioning) and temperature, climatic conditions
and materials of construction. It is highly undesir-
able to allow temperature gradients to exist in bulk
sugar storage because this causes moisture migra-
tion, which may lead to widespread caking. Howev-
er, Kochergin and Johnson (2001) question whether
insulation is necessary, as long as the air flow is
adequate to carry away migrated moisture. One
system for ensuring high efficiency insulation is to
blow temperature-controlledair through an annulus
around the silo wall - this is quite commonly em-
ployed in colder climates. Most steel silos employ
insulation material and/or an annulus of air chan-
nels, while many concretesilosareinsulatedas well.
Thompson (1998) notes that the thermal properties
of a typical double-walled steel silo with suitable
insulationmaterial between the walls are better than
those of a silo with 200-300 mm thick reinforced
concrete walls.
Mikus and Budicek (1986) suggest four catego-
ries for sugar storageand comment on their opera-
tion as follows:
Non-ventilated silos with unheated walls must
be suppliedwith sugarthat is conditioned,hes-
free and cooled.
Non-ventilated siloswith heated walls must also
be supplied with conditioned sugar. The sugar
must be of uniform quality and at the storage
temperature and must not be allowed to dry out
in the silo (e.g. at the surface).
References p. 576
24 White sugarhandling and conditioning
Ventilated silos with unheated walls must have
sufficient air that it can be used for both mois-
ture removal and temperature gradient preven-
tion. The air must be of "conditioning quality"
and the quality of the sugar should not fluctu-
ate.
Ventilated silos with heated walls require only
that the air be sufficient to carry away excess
moisture.
Feed and dischargesystems.The simplest ap-
proach to sugar feeding is to feed the sugar at the
apex of the silo, which is fitted with a conical roof
at an angle that matches the angle of repose of the
sugar.This has many disadvantages.Itresultsin dust
formation and crystal damage when the sugar level
in the silo is low. Also, because sugar pouring onto
the top of a heap will classify as it rolls down, this
may lead to sugar of differing crystal size distribu-
tion and buk density at the center and the periphery
of the silo. This would have a deleterious effect on
conditioning, as well as possibly causing problems
with someof the sugarin meetingproduct specifica-
tions.
The use of velocity-based distribution systems
such as high-speed rotating discs or thrower belts

24.2.3 Ventilation 24.2.4 Packed sugar storage
Air passage through the sugar is strongly rec-
ommended for all bulk silos, whether their duty is
to conditionor merely to store.In additionto mini-
mizing the likelihood of caking by carrying away
excess moisture, air passage eliminates problems
that may be associated with localized moisture
concentration, such as yeast activity. However,
where the intention is not to condition the sugar, it
is quite common practice to keep the RH of the air
up, rather than down. It is felt that by keeping the
RH just below the ERH of the sugar, the sugar will
not giveup moisture in any significantamounts.An
RH of 60 % is typical - the high RH has a second-
ary benefitof reducing dustproblems andexplosion
risk.
It must be noted that the air conditions must be
controlled so that the RH of 60 % is reached at the
coldest point in the silo,or dew pointproblems may
result. Storage silo ventilation air is often recircu-
lated (after being filtered and reconditioned),to re-
duce air emission to atmosphereand save energy if
the air is heated.
The standard method of dehumified air produc-
tion is to chill the air to a required dew point (re-
quired moisture content at saturation) and reheat
it to the silo operating temperature, resulting in a
specific relative humidity. It is often not necessary
to reheat the air, as the rise in temperature across
the blowers may be sufficient to reach the required
temperature.
The alternative to chilling is chemical de-
humidification. A neat system is the "desiccant
wheel" concept (an example is the system supplied
by Munters). In these units, the process air is de-
humidified by being passed through a chemical
desiccant,which is held in a slowly rotating frame.
When the desiccant moves out of the process air
stream, it moves into a regeneration stream, where
the moisture is driven off by a stream of hot air. It
is then returned by the rotation of the wheel into
the process air.
Moisture exclusion from rail or road tankers
is also important in preventing caking of sugar in
transit. It is fairly common practice to blow condi-
tioned air into trucks to dry them completelybefore
filling. Some refiners use polyethlylene "bonnets"
under the lids of the trucks to prevent moisture in-
gress.
CIzen and Chou (1993)provide alistof "common
sense" guidelinesfor storageof sugarin packages:
1. Keep sugar temperaturebelow 38 "C.
2. Maintain relative humidity below 60 %.
3. Keep pile heights to a practical minimum.
4. Store sugar separately from other products to
avoid picking up moisture,odors,etc.
5. Maintain limited inventories with rapid turnover.
6. Pack as much as possible for direct shipment.
7. In humid areas, use heat or air conditioning
to control relative humidity and temperature
changes.
8. Pack only conditioned sugar in moisture-tight
packaging.
This lastpoint is certainlythe ideal,but is frequently
not an economicsolution.An additionalpoint to re-
member is to ensurethat pallets are dry. Thames re-
finery in London dry any wet pallets (or new pallets
- "green7' wood contains high levels of moisture)
before use. A moisture-barrier between the bottom
layer of bags and the pallet is sometimesused.
Bagged sugarwarehouses should be built of ma-
sonry with tight roofs (to exclude both the weather
and buds) and concreteor wood floors.For capacity
calculations, Hugot (1986) suggests a bulk density
of 800 kg sugar per m3 of stack (not allowing for
corridors around the stacks), while van der Poel
et al. (1998) estimate 500 kg sugar per m3of total
warehouse volume. Air conditioningsystemsarede-
sirable, but are not universally used. The condition-
ing system may be run intermittently (only during
periods of high ambient RH).Tight control of RH is
not necessary -the minimum requirementis to keep
the warehouse temperaturea few degrees above am-
bient, with a minimumof 16'C, and to ensure good
circulationor air around the stacks.
When stackingbagged refined sugar, it is advis-
able to give the sides of the stack a batter or taper of
20' for hessian bags and 7.5' for paper bags (Hugor
1986;Lyle 1970).For plastic (polyethyleneor woven
PVC),commonpractice is to stepback by half-a-bag
width per layer, and interlock asmuch aspossible.
Theuse of racking in palletizedsugarwarehous-
ing, while expensive,is highly desirable.It keeps the
product clean, greatly reduces damage(bags torn by
pallet nails or careless forklift operation), increases
safe stacking heights and improves flexibility in ac-
cessing and moving product.
24.2.5 Color formation
24.2.5 Colorformation
When stored for long periods, refined sugar will
experience a gradual increase in color. The rate at
which this occurs is strongly dependent on storage
temperature. Chapman (1970) collected color in-
creasedatafromfoursites,andobtainedarangefrom
5 % per month at 20 O
C to 80 % per month at 60 OC.
Experienceelsewhereindicates that Chapman's fig-
ures are on the high side. SouthAfrican studieshave
shown color increases of anywhere between 10%
and 100 % over the period of a year. van der Poel
et al. (1998) report increases of less than 4 IU in 9
months,but comment that aircooling shouldbe used
if ambient is higher than 30 OC. SouthAfrican work
has found color increaseto be more rapid during the
first month of storage, after which the rate reduces.
This may be a consequence of storing non- or irn-
properly conditionedsugar, which experiences high
rates of color increase while it conditions. Mum et
al. (1974)report a linearincreasein colorwith time.
de Mancilha (1987) found that color formation rate
increased logarithmicallywith temperature.
Chapman recommends storage below 20 O
C to
minimize colorformation,while Clarkeet al. (1992)
suggest storage below 30 OC, and recommend fur-
ther that sugar entering storage should be below
45 OC. de Mancilha carried out testsin which it was
found that "up to 35 O
C
, browning was negligible".
Sugarsdiffer in their susceptibility to color increase
and their sensitivity to temperature - Clarke et al.
and Chapman comment that beet and cane sugars
may behave differently. Cheng et al. (1983) found
that "color development was more marked in sugars
manufactured by a carbonatation process than by a
sulfitation process". van der Poel et al. (1998) assert
that color increasewill depend on the invertcontent
and pH of the syrup film and the SO, content of the
sugar.
Other factors that affect color development in
storage are ash and moisture. Moisture and air are
necessary for most color forming reactions. A test
carried out in South Africa measured colorincrease
in identical sugar samples stored under identical
conditions, except that half of the samples were
packed in plastic (moistureimpermeable) bags and
theotherhalf in paper bags. The plastic-packedsug-
ar increased in color from 32 to 44 IU over a period
of eleven months, while the sugar packed in paper
increasedfrom 32 to 68 IU in the sameperiod.
24.3 Sugar handling
24.3.1 Conveying
There is no better way to introduce this topic
than with Lyle's (1970) wry comment that "thereis
no satisfactory conveyorfor refined sugar". How-
ever, sugar must be conveyed, and there are many
ways to achievethis.
Screw conveyors. These devices comprise a
central shaft running along the axis of a U-shaped
trough, with a screw or helical ribbon attached to
the shaft. The greatest disadvantage of this type of
conveyor is that the sugar crystals may be ground
between the screw and the shell, although Spencer
and Meade (1963) claim experimental evidence to
show that little crystal breakage occursif the trough
is filled to less than one third of its capacity. In any
event, the sugar level in a screw conveyor should be
below the level of the shaft,particularly if the sugar
is wet. Another characteristicof the screw conveyor
is mixing, which may be used to advantagein min-
gling or coating operations, for which the helical-
ribbon type is particularly suited. Tromp (1936)
gives the capacity of a screw conveyor as:
where
