d outside diameter of screw or ribbon;
p
, bulk density of the sugar;
p pitch of screw or ribbon;
n rotational speed of the screw;
c' coefficientof fullnessand slip.
An average c' value for a screw filled to just below
the shaft is given as 0.2.
Induced-motion conveyors. Grasshopper con-
veyors are simple troughs supported from below on
a series of links or flat springs.The trough moves in
a reciprocating motion, forwardsand upwards on the
forward strokeand backwards and downwardson the
return stroke. Since this action is rapid, the sugar is
thrown forward with each stroke, to land at a posi-
tion further advanced along the trough. The support-
ing bands are inclined backwards (about 30' to the
vertical) and strokeis short (typically 20 to 30 mm).

24 White sugar handling and conditioning
Grasshopper conveyors are simple, easy to operate
and clean, may be quite long and can be loaded in
heaps (as is the case below batch centrifugals)as the
grasshopperaction quickly levels out the sugar. Dis-
advantagesarehighmaintenancedueto thevibration
that they generate and possible classificationof the
sugarin the conveyor.To determinethe capacity of a
grasshopperconveyor,it is necessary to estimate the
average travel of the sugar crystals per stroke, and
then multiply by the frequency and the filled cross-
sectional area of the trough. Tromp (1936) suggests
that the trough should not be filled to a depth greater
than 150mrn, and proposes also the use of a "coef-
ficient of slip" (suggested value 0.5) i i ~
calculating
conveyor capacity. The effect of this factor is to re-
ducethe capacityby half to account for slippage.
Variationsonthe grasshopperconveyor are:
Vibrator conveyors which operate on the same
principle, but using high frequency vibration.
These can be enclosed (dust-free) but consume
more power and certainly classify the sugar.
Twinconveyorsovercomethevibrationproblem
of a grasshopper by oscillating two identical
units 180' out of phase.
Slip-stickconveyors are a recent innovation, op-
erating by means of a slow forward stroke fol-
lowed by a rapid return stroke.They rely on the
sugar slipping on the return stroke to advance
the sugar along the conveyor.
Belt conveyors. Belt conveyors are continuous
belts consisting of several plies of fabric impreg-
nated, bonded and coated with rubber. These run on
idlers, spaced at intervalsof about 1to 1.5m for the
top, load-carrying strand and much larger spacings
forthe lower,emptystrand.Thetop idlersareusually
in sets of three or five, with the center one horizon-
tal and the outer ones inclined at about 20" to the
horizontal,thusforming a trough.Troughing the belt
substantially increases its capacity and minimizes
the likelihood of spillageover the edges. Troughing
idlers should be pitched closely or the load will be
disturbed asitpasses over a setof idlers,causingflat-
tening out of the load and reduction in belt capacity.
Return idlersmay be singletubes or multiplenarrow
wheels if thematerialis sticky.Thecapacityof a belt
conveyorvaries with the squareof the belt width.
Belt conveyors may be inclined, but Lyle (1970)
does not recommend more than 22.5' for Qy sugar.
Hugo#(1986)prefers a limit of 20' and recommends
16". Belt speeds of 1.2 to 1.6 d s are common, ex- )
cept for ship-loading conveyors, which can run at
around 2.9 d s . A problem with belt conveyors is I
ensuringthe return strand is clear of adhering sugar,
whichiscrushedby thereturnidlersand createsdust
and mess. Many installations use brushes or scrap
ers after the head pulley, but these are not always
100% effective and present a risk of product con-
tamination.Feed ontoa belt conveyorshouldalways
be doneonthe centerline of the belt, as asymmetric
loading will cause the belt to track to one side, re
sulting in spillage and belt wear
A variation on the conventionalbelt conveyor b
theair-supportedbelt, whichhasnoidlersandtravels
over a deck-plateof perforated steel,through whid
air is blown, supporting the belt on an air cushion.
The air-supportedbelt minimizesfriction, thus min-
imizing power consumption and belt wear, greatly,
reduces maintenance requirements and is clean and
neat. These belts are usually fully enclosed, which
helps to avoidproduct confamination.
Bucket elevators. Bucket elevators consist of
chains, or more usually a belt to which buckets or
scoops are attached. These run over sprockets op
pulleys at each end and may be inclined, but a

Elevator belts for refined sugar should be sub-

AU elevators or inclined conveyors must be
equipped with a mechanism to prevent their run-
ning backwards in the eventof motorfailureor shaft
breakage. Run-back at best will result in mess and
inconvenience; at worst it will lead to serious and
expensive damage (a large bucket elevator running
back may reach such speed that it destroys itself).
Modem bucket elevators have off-track and zero-
speed detectors to minimize the likelihoodof equip-
ment damage.
Other conveyors. Drag chain or drag cable el-
evatorsor conveyorsconsist of a chain or cable with
platesor washersat intervals,which dragthematerial
up a closely fitting casing, chute or pipe. The Redler
conveyoris probably the best known, consistingof a
singlechainof rake-like links,and ismost commonly
used for coal. The Floveyor is a cable-and-disc ver-
sion running in a pipe, and is best used on dry sugar.
A range of conveying mechanisms are available for
conveying bagged sugar, including cranes, slings,
grabs, swing tray elevators, slat conveyors, rubber
apron conveyorsand gravityroller conveyors.
Pneumatic conveying. A completely different
option for sugar conveying is pneumatic transport.
An effective option is dense phase pneumatic con-
veying in which the sugar is conveyed in batches at
much lower velocitiesthan dilutephase, using much
less air and consequently with little crystal break-
age. The successful use of these systems at Huletts
Refinery in South Africa was reported by Gelling
(1996). The advantages are that it is clean, sealed
(contamination-free), space-saving, low mainte-
nance, safe and quiet. Disadvantages are the need
for clean, dry, filtered air, the need for a pressure
vessel, the requirement for good dust collection and
: the fact that chokescan be difficultto clear.The sys-
knis cost-effectivefor long or complex routes, but
Bnnot compete over short, straight transfers.
24.3.2 Hoppers, chutes and transfer
points
Hoppers and transfers. The primary design
consideration in the design of hoppers is efficient
and complete emptying without bridging or rat-hol-
ing. To guarantee zero holdup of sugar, the sides of
an "inverted-pyramid shaped hopper should be be-
tween 75' (Lyle 1970)and 77" (Hugot 1986),which
will result in 70" to 72" in the comers or valleys.
An angle of 65" is acceptable for conical hoppers
(Hugot 1986). Sheehan and Schneider (2003) made
use of the "angle of slide" to design the hopper por-
tion of their spouted fluidizedbed. They determined
anglesof slidefor dry, fine-dryand wet raw sugar to
be 41°, 48' and 58' respectively, but still designed
their hopper at 70" to allow for the "worst-case sce-
nario".
Wherepractical constraintsmake theseidealan-
gles impossible,possible solutions includeintermit-
tent air sparginginto the hopper to loosen the sugar,
and the use of membrane walls which can be flexed
by a pulse of air behind the membrane, to dislodge
any build-up. Vibratory dischargers are available
that fit onto the bottom of a discharge cone and ac-
tivate the material by vibration energy, eliminating
hang-up.
Chutes feeding conveyors should be designed
along the followingguidelines:
The sugar must strike the conveyor vertically or
in the direction of conveyor movement.
The chute must be as shortas possible.
Valley angles in the chute must be kept above
60".
A system for dust removal must be provided at
the point of impact of the sugar.
If at allpossible, steps should be taken to minimize
the impact of the sugar on the conveyor (or bin or
sugar pile). Various "shoe-type" devices exist for
use at the bottom of the chute, to absorb or deflect
the momentum of the falling sugar. An example is
shown in Figure 24.10, where a plate with a profiled
cut-out at the bottom of the chute feeds the sugar
gently on to the conveyor, minimizing dust forma-
tion and belt wear. Another option is to choke-feed
the sugar from the chute on to the conveyor, using
plates with semicircular cut-outs or rubber flaps to
control the sugar flow.

24.3.3 Screeningor sieving
24.3.3 Screeningor sieving
Fundamentals. Particle size classification of
somesortis routinelyemployed in almostall refiner-
ies. In its simplestform, screeningis used to "scalp"
off the coarsest fraction (lumps or conglomerates),
which is often done by screens attached to the dis-
charge end of rotary driers.At the otherextreme,the
refined sugar may be de-dusted, typically partially
removing the fraction less than 0.2 m
r
n
,eitherby air
(as in a fluidized bed drier or cooler) or by screen-
ing. In the caseof screening, an initial cut is usually
made at about 0.35 mm,as liner screens are more
delicateand blind more easilythan those with larger
openings.As linesare a significantcontributorto the
caking propensity of sugar, many refiners screen all
product sugar for this reason. The part of the fines
fraction that is superfluous to the requirements of
the refinery for castor or other specialty sugar is re-
melted.
Beyond scalping and de-dusting, the product
may be fully classified intoarangeof specialtyprod-
ucts. It is often useful to operate two screens with
close apertures,to allow the intermediatefraction to
be directed to eitherthe coarseor finefraction as the
demand or feed material varies. A secondarybenefit
of screening is that it cools the sugar - often quite
significantly.Yonkers refinery in New York reported
a temperaturedrop across screeningof 11OC.
Screenoperation.Screeningefficiency q is de-
fined as the percentage of undersized particles (by
1 mass) that remain with the coarse fraction,based on
, laboratory analysis (Zversonand Munroe 1982):
where:
wU, mass percentage of undersized particles in the
feed;
w , , mass percentage of undersized particles in the
oversized product.
This efficiencyis a measure of the sharpness of the
cut, as in industrial screening, not all of the under-
sized particles reach the screen (unlikein laboratory
screening), and the mesh size is typically coarser
than the coarsest fraction desired in the underflow.
Efficiency figures can be used in conjunction with
crystal size distribution to predict the production
quantitiesexpectedfor the various fractions.
The most important aspects of a screening in-
stallation are:
Cleaning action,whichshouldeliminateblinding
without interferingwith screeningefficiency.
Agitation, which must be strong enough to pre-
vent oversized particles from plugging the aper-
tures, but not so strong that undersized particles
are kept away from the apertures.
Conveying action, via degree of inclination, to
ensure that the oversizefraction is conveyed off
the screen at the desired rate. Note, however,
that slope also affects the effective(horizontally
projected) sizeof the apertures.
Feed rate control (or bed thickness control),
as too high a rate floods the screen, preventing
some of the finer fraction from reaching the
screen.
Percentage open area of the screens. Note that
the finer the aperture, the lower the screen ca-
pacity in t/(h .m2).
BurRhardt (1995)provides a list of factors to be con-
sidered in specifying a screening installation:
Number of fractions to be obtained.
Crystal size distribution of the standard frac-
tions.
Productcontactcomponents,preferablyof stain-
less steel.
Transmission of vibration to support steelwork
and the building.
Noise emission.
Feed distributionover the screeningsurfaces.
, Time and equipment needed for screen mesh
changing.
Screensused forwhite sugar areall of the wire cloth
type. Perforated plates are not used because of their
weight, small open area and susceptibility to blind-
ing. The woven pattern of the wires may be either
square or rectangular. Rectangular patterns suit
the more steeply inclined screens, while shallower
slopesor horizontal vibrating screenstend to use the
square pattern.

Sugar dust and explosion. Sugar dust results

Apart from sugar loss, machine bearing
ear and plant hygiene considerations, ex-
st also poses an explosion risk. There is
commonality among authors on data pertain-
o the explosivebehavior of sugar dust,but the
wing is a summary of published data, derived
inainly from Morden (1994), Mikus and Budicek
(1986), Hugot(1986), Dale and Kmetze (1999) and
wm der Poel(1998):
* The lowest minimum explosible concentratioa.
of sugar dust reported is 6 g/m3 for the finest
dust, but valuesrange up to 60g/m3for 0.1 mm
particles. A value in the range 10 to 15 g/m3
appears to represent sugar dust normally
encountered. Dust Ievels in sugar rdberies are
typically well below these levels, but the limit
may be exceeded in the headspace of silos or
bins. In addition, dust-laden surfaces contribute
to any hazard, as an explosionwill propagateby
lifting dustfrom surfaces.
Estimates of minimum ignition temperature
vary from 330 O
C to 480 OC, with most authors
favoring the upper value, which means that ig-
nition is unlikely to come from ordinary equip-
mentsurfaces in a sugarrefinery.However,these
temperatures are not especially high compared
with those for other potentially explosivedusts,
which,makes precautionary measures all the
more important.
Sugar dust is categorized as explosion class
St 1 (K,,
< 200 (bar . m)/s, weak to moderate
explosion),with a presswe rise rate of between
59 and 172(bar .m)/s. (K, is a measure of the
violence of an explosion and is the maximum
rate of pressure rise times vessel volume to the
third.)
The risk of ignition through buildup of elec-
trostatic charge depends on two variables. The
powderresistivity of sugardustisnot well docu-
mented,butvalueshavebeen quotedintherange
lo9to 1012ohm .m, which puts it in the medium
to high risk range (high resistivity powders will
tend to build up charge due to their electrical
insulation properties). Most authors report the
minimum ignition energy of sugar dust in the
range 20 to 50 mJ, which represents moderate

to high risk, although Morden obtained values
between 400 and 700 mJ, which indicates low
sensitivityto ignition and low risk.
The maximum explosion pressure for sugar
is approximately 9 bar (a range of 7.6 to 9.4
bar is reported). However, in interconnected
vessels, the propagation of an explosion from
one to the other can causesomeprecompression
of the dust cloud and therefore enhancement of
the explosion pressure, to a value well above 9
bar.
Explosion prevention. Explosion prevention is
largely the application of measures that aim at
avoiding the creation of a dust cloud or an ignition
source (the "fuel" and "ignition" sides of the "fire
triangle") as it is normally accepted that the "oxi-
dant'', oxygen, cannot be excluded. Common mea-
sures are:
Conveyors should be enclosed and dust extrac-
tion systemsshould be provided at all conveying
transfer points.
The correct lighting and electrical installations
should be used for explosive environments in
dusty areas.
Overloading of electrical reticulation should be
avoided.
A
l
l equipment should be properly earthed and
pipinglducting should be of conductive materi-
als.
A practice of cleaning properly before welding
or cutting should be employed.
All effort should be made to ensure that a layer
of dust is not allowed to build up in ducts.
High explosion-risk equipment should be in-
stalled in a safe location, preferably at ground
level.
Bucket elevators.Dale andKnoetze (1999)reported

24.3.5 Dedustingequipment
24.3.5 Dedustingequipment
It is necessary to draw off sugar dust from con-
veyor transfer points and the filling points of bins
and silos. This is normally done by means of hoods
over the transfer points and ducting carrying the
dust pneumatically to central collection equipment.
The pneumatic systems should be designed to keep
the dust concentration below the explosive limit of
10 to 15 g l d . In addition, the air passing through
sugardrierscarries away a dust fraction which must
be collected (fluidizedbed driers are often used as a
primary dust removal device).
Fabric filters consist of a battery of textile
"socks" (made of antistatic fabric) through which
the air is blown. These usually have arrangements
to dislodge the dust at regular intervals, typically by
means of a short counter-flow pulse of compressed
air.Themain disadvantageof these unitsishighpres-
sure drop due to progressiveblinding, which causes
a gradual reduction in the air flow through the dust
removal systemand a loss in collectionefficiency. It
is also imperative that moisture (and vapor) be ex-
cluded from the systembecausethis causes the cloth
to blind. However, these units offer high collection
efficiencies,with 99.9 % achievable. Stillhigher ef-
ficiencies may be achieved with cartridge-type col-
lectors, for which manufacturers claim outlet dust
concentrationsbelow 1 mg/m3.
Electrostatic separators are highly efficient sep-
arators(above99 %) which use a very high DC volt-
age to carry the dust particles to the walls of narrow
flow channels. These are, however, expensive and
should not be used in a necessarily dusty environ-
ment, which poses an explosiverisk by providing a
source of ignition.
Other dry separators are available, such as
standard cyclones, axial-flow cyclones (axial en-
try and exit with vanes in the flow path to impart
spin), and baffle or louver-type devices.These offer
trouble-free operation, but do not provide the high
efficiencies usually required. Some suppliers have
combined technologies and offer dry cyclones with
fabric filtersin the cyclone at the outlet.
Wet separators include irrigated cyclones, irri-
gated fans, scrubbers and baffle or louver systems.
These systems usually achieve acceptable efficien-
cies -above95 %for a combinationof water sprays
with cyclonic separation. Installations in South Af-
rica have had success with banks of irrigated axial-
flow cyclones in parallel (each unit no more than
100 mm in diameter). A commonly encountered
deviceis the Rotocloneirrigated fan, in which water
is sprayed into the eye of the fan and is dispersed
into the path of the dust-laden air entering the fan
casing. Dust loads of up to 5 g/m3can be handled,
and Lyle (1970)reports efficienciesof 96 % for the
Rotoclone. The device also has the advantage of
combining the duties of a fan and a dust separation
system in a single unit that has approximately the
same dimensionsas an ordinarycentrifugalfan.
The type N Rotoclone is a static separator that
"washes" the airthrough a curtain of water. The cur-
tain is created by the air being forced at high veloc-
ity around a partially submerged baffle. The design
of adjacent baffles maintains a circulation of water,
and collectionefficiency may be adjustedby adjust-
ing the water level (at the expenseof pressuredrop).
The device is low maintenance and is not prone to
clogging, because all apertures are relatively large.
Venturi separators make use of a venturi (con-
striction)in the air duct prior to a cyclonicseparator.
Water is injected into the venturi, which optimizes
airlwater contacting-manufacturersclaim that that
the venturi shape offers the highest possible collec-
tion efficiency per unit power consumption.
Baird and Beatts (1989) experimented with a
dustcollectionsystemintegrated intotheheadboxof
a rotary cascadedrier and reported good results.The
unit comprised a pack of chevron plates (more typi-
cally used for entrainmentprevention in evaporators
or pans), providing a tortuous path through which
the air had to flow, combined with water sprays to
keep the surfacesof the plates wet.
The major disadvantage of all wet dust collec-
tion systems is that they result in a well-aerated,
dilute sugdr solution, which provides an ideal mi-
crobiological environment. Bacteria are washed
out of the air, so it is impossible to keep the system
sterile. In addition, efficientcooling of the water (or
sweet water) by the air in the separator eliminates
temperature as a reliable means of microbiological
control. The wet surfaces of a cyclonic separator,
for example, are ideal sites for the proliferation of
Leuconostoc mesentemides. Possible mechanisms
of control are:
Keep the temperatureas high as possible in any
collection sumps or tanks (use steam sparging
if necessary) to avoid degradation outside the
separatoritself.
Referencesp. 576
24 White sugar handling and conditioning
In a recirculating system, keep the pH up by
adding lime (if fine spray-nozzles are used, this
may not be possible due to the threat of block-
age).
Use a biocide either continuously or in shock-
doses.
Regularly wash out the separator unit with bio-
cide, lime or steam.
24.4 Bagging andpackaging
Sugar is packaged into sacks, bags and pack-
ages ranging in size from a few grams to 1000kg.
The most common retail packs arethe 1kg (or2 Ib)
and 2 kg (or 5 lb) paper packs, while bags for com-
mercial customers are usually 25 kg, 50 kg or 1
tonne.
The detail of equipment,materials and configu-
rations availableforamodernsugarpackagingoper-
ation is best obtained from a major packagingplant
supplier such as Bosch.What follows is a summary
of the major options.
24.4.1 Weighersand feeders
In all cases, it is necessary to weigh the sugar
into or in the bag or pack. The oldest and simplest
method employed is where the bag standson a scale
and is filled manually from a filling spout. The bag
may then be topped up to the correct mass by hand
using a scoop.This method is still used in some in-
stallationsfor thebaggingof sticky brown sugars,as
their stickiness make them unsuitablefor automatic
bagging. Oneof the fillingmethodsfor 1000kg bags
is analogous, as the bag rests on load cells during
filling.
Sugars that are less sticky but not entirely free-
flowing, such as certain brown sugars and finer re-
finedsugars,may be meteredout using an augerfill-
er. This comprises a vertical feeding tube contain-
ing a rotatingauger or screw feeder, which delivers
a particular volumeof sugarper revolution.Clearly,
variationsin bulk density of the sugar,or any build-
up of sugar on the feeder, will alter the volume de-
livered. For this reason, these feeders are usually
followedby a check-weigher,whichfeeds its output
back to the shaftencoderof the auger, to adjust the
number of revolutions per pack. For sticky sugars,
machine parts such as hoppers and pans are often
coated with PTFEto minimize hang-up.
The most appropriate weigher technology for
free-flowing sugars depends on the weighing re-
quirements.If the packs areto be controlledto a cor-
rect average weight, the requirements are less oner-
ous than if all packs are to be of a minimum stated
weight. In the latter case, any variation in weight
constitutes sugar "giveaway" and must clearly be
minimized.
For the average weight case, feeding may still
be doneon a volumetricbasis. Sugaris typically fed
into one of several '%upswon a rotating carousel,
with a scraper to level off the sugar in each cup and
a bottom dischargefrom the cup.
The signal from a check-weighercanbe used to
controlthe height of theverticalcupsides, orto con-
trol a top-up auger that adjusts the final weight. The
check-weigheroutputon most machinesis also used
to reject packs that are completely out of specifica-
tion, and is oftencapturedelectronicallyfor produc-
tion records.
If allpacksaretomeet aminimum statedweight,
it is typicaltofill thepacksby weightratherthanvoi-
urne. Thenormalarrangementis two weighing pans,
one above the other. The top counterbalanced pan
fills rapidly and dischargesto the second at a weigh
just below the stated weight. The second pan has a
trickle of sugar that makes up the weight accuratel~
This type of weigher is accurate but expensive,and
may achieve up to 30 weighings per minute.
24.4.2 Packagingmaterials
Sugar is bagged in a range of materials, inc
ing jute or hessian sacks, jute sacks with poly
lylene liners, single- and multi-ply paper, poly
ylene bags and woven polypropylene with poly
ylene liners. The most common material for s
retail packs is single-ply kraft paper (at 80
g/m2),because it is cost-effectiveand can be
into a free-standing brick shape that lends itse
baling and palletizing.
Polyethylene "pillow" packs
cheaper and offer the advantagesof
meability and product visibility, bu
24.4.3 Forming,fillingand scaling
as well on store shelves or bale / palletize as easily.
Gusseted packs are possible, where the pack has a
blockbottom to make it free-standing.It is now pos-
sible to produce brick-shaped polyethylene packs,
but these are not yet widely used.
Multi-ply paper sacks are sometimes used for
the largerpacks as they offer strengthwhile limiting
the cost of the high-quality printable outer ply. An
alternative is woven polypropylenewith a polyeth-
ylene liner. This is the material used for one-tonne
bags, a semi-bulkcontainerthat whenfull is roughly
cubic. The full bag is free-standing, and has web-
b i g loops at itsupper cornersto allowit to be lifted,
usually by a fork-lift truck. The top of the bag is
closed by a drawstring, with a tamper-proof seal on
the inner polyethylene bag. Discharge is via a sock
in the base.
An important consideration in selecting pack-
aging material is its ability to prevent moisture up-
take or excessive moisture loss by the sugar. This
is particularly the case when packed sugar is to be
warehoused for an extended period. Moisture con-
tainment and exclusion is achieved by the use of
moisture-impermeable baniers in packing materi-
als (bags, balers or overwraps). Materials with low
moisture vapor transmissioncharacteristics,such as
polyethylene, may be used in one of the following
ways:
As the main packaging material;
As an inner bag or liner;
As a laminate or coating on a paper substrate;
As a free film between paper plies.
Moistureexclusionis an expensive option,but is un-
avoidablein somecases (and climates), particularly
when packing unconditionedwhite sugar.
A
l
l packaging materials used for sugar should
be acceptable for food use, including the inks and
glues. Packing material stores should be cleaned
regularly to prevent contaminationof any kind.
A compromisebetween bulk and packaged sug-
ar transport is a container-sized, single-use plastic
bag, which is inflated inside a container and then
filled with bulk sugar.To empty, the bag is cut open,
releasinguncontaminatedsugarandleavingthe con-
tainer clean on removal of the bag.
With increased requirements for product trace-
ability,it is now commonforlot numbers tobe print-
ed on to packages and balers on the packaging line.
This is usually done by ink-jet.
24.4.3 Forming,filling andsealing
Smaller paper packs are typically produced on
one of the followingtwo machine types:
Machines that use premade bags, which are
taken from a magazine, opened, presented to a
weigher discharge,filled,folded and sealed.
Machines which use paper from a reel, fonn
the bag, present it to a weigher discharge, fill
it, fold and seal. These may use unprinted pa-
per and have an integratedprinting line, or may
use pre-printed reels with photo-registration to
synchronizethe print with the machine. The bag
is formed around steel mandrels and the seams
glued. Figure 24.16 is a schematic representa-
tion of the forming, filling and closurefunctions
in a typical packing machine.
Filling of these paper packs is often by multiple fill-
ing spouts to increase machine speed. The pack is
vibrated to settle the sugar before sealing, and then
the sides of the pack are brought together and the
excess paper cut off. The top is folded over and
sealedwith glue,and while the glue dries the pack is
held firmly by guides and bottom andtop conveyors.
Thesemachinestypically run at speedsbetween 100
and 140bagdmin, although speeds up to 240 bags/
min are reported.
Polyethylene pillow packs are produced from
preprinted rolls with optical registration. The film
is drawn down around a vertical tube and the edges
heat-sealed to form a tube. The bottom edge is then
heat-sealed to form a pouch and the sugar intro-
duced via the forming tube. Once the pouch is full,
the bag is heat-sealed above the sugar and the film
is cut. Speeds of 50 bagslmjn can be obtained for

sack is filled via the valve opening and once full,
the pressureof the sugarkeeps the valve closed.The
advantageof this type of sack is that the filling ma-
chine is relatively simple and no closure process is
required. However, valve sacksare more expensive,
slow to fill (machinespeedsof 6 to 7 bagslmin) and
the lack of a tight seal presents the risk of leakage.
24.4.4 Baling andpalletizing
Smaller retail packs are usually bundled into
larger units for ease of storage or transport. This
secondary pack may be a premade paper baler bag,
or may be a "parcel", createdby amechanized wrap-
ping process. An increasingly popular option is to
wrap the bundle in polyethylenefilm rather than pa-
per, and then pass the bundlethrougha heated tunnel
to create a shrink-wrappedunit.
Packaged and baled products are usually pal-
letized in pallet-loads of up to 1.5 tomes. Fully
automated palletizers are available that operate at
30 bags or balers per minute. These machines are
programmed to arrange successive layers of prod-
uct alternately so that the final load is fully bonded
and stable, obviatingthe need for wrapping. In some
cases, pallet-loads are stretch-wrapped or shrink-
wrapped in polyethylene film to protect the product
and keepit clean.Furtherprotectionmay be afforded
by placing a cardboardcap over the top of the load.
24.4.5 Specialtyproducts
n o of the more commonly encountered spe-
cialty formats are:
Sachets.These arepouchesproduced for the ca-
tering trade, usually for adding to beverages. They
range from 3 g to 10 g, and may be a single piece
of polyethylene-coated paper folded over and heat-
sealed on three edges, or two pieces heat-sealed on
all four edges. A variation on the sachet is the tube-
sachet, in which the paper is formed into a narrow
tube and heat-sealed at each end. Sachet machines
use reels of preprinted paper, and can achieve vary
high speeds, up to some 50 sachets per second! Sa-
chets are then packed by mass into cardboard car-
tons.
Cubes. Sugar cubes remain a popular option
for many consumers. The sugar is moistened and
compressed into shaped dies (a range of shapes are
now encountered), before being ejected and dried.
An option offered on Elba cubing machines is mi-
crowave drying, which the suppliers claim reduces
energy costs by 25 %. Productionrates from a single
machine are up to 2700 kgh. Cubes may then be
packed into cartons, or wrapped individually or in
pairs before boxing.

The purpose of a sugar factory is to produce
crystalline sugar from sucrose in the raw material,
sugarcane. Chemical control of a sugar mill is gen-
erally taken to mean the system of collecting labo-
ratory analytical measurements of selected process
streams and products to enable an estimate to be
made of the losses of sucrose and the efficiency of
the process of recovering sucrose. It also provides
process data to the operatorsto assistthem torun the
factoryoptimally.
The measurements necessary need to be estab-
lished to achieve the objectives. The appropriate
data on the performance of a mill is fundamental to
efficient operation. Lord Kelvin has said:
"Whenyou can measure what you are speak-
ing about and express if in numbers, you know
somethingabout it."
Not only are the numbers required but also they
must be accurate and reliable enough for the pur-
pose for which they will be used.An important issue
is thereforedecidingonwhat informationis required
for adequateprocess control and what the most ap-
propriatemeasurements are to achieve them.
Sucrose can be synthesized only by the sugar
cane plant. It is not possible to make it in the sugar
factory. Sucrosecan however be destroyed or other-
wiselostin thecourseof itsconversionin thefactory
to crystallinesugar.Good factory controlfocuseson
accurate estimationof losses of sucrose.The losses
that need to be quantified are as follows:
Loss in bagasse;
Loss in molasses;
Loss in filtercake;
Undetermined loss (allother effects).
25.1 Measurements and
analyses
This section is not intended to cover analytical
details comprehensively. Full details of analyti-
cal and measurement techniques are given in the
ICUMSAMethodsBook in its latest version (Anon.
2005), various industry laboratory analytical manu-
als (Anon. 1984, SASTA 2005), and certain texts
(Chen and Chou 1993).An outline of all important
measurements is given here, together with theprob-
lems and drawbacks of each method and an indica-
tion of the appropriatenessof each measurement.
25.1.1 Overview of commonlyused
analyses
Polarization.The polarization,the opticalrota-
tion of plane polarized light by a sugar-containing
sample,is used to measure the sucrosecontent of a
solution. It is simple, quick and highly reproducible.
It is defined as the concentration (in g1100 g solu-
tion) of a solution of pure sucrose in water having
the same optical rotation as the sample at the same
temperature. For solutions containing only sucrose
in water, polarization (pol) is a true measure of the
sucrose content; for solutions containing sucrose
and other opticallyactive substances,pol represents
thealgebraicsumof therotationsof the components
present.There is no accuratesimpledirectmeasure-
ment of sucrosein impure solutions.
25 Chemicalcontrol of factories
Unfortunatelycane factoryproducts contain the
monosaccharides glucose and fructose as well as
sucrose (which is a disaccharide). These monosac-
charides are also optically active but in a different
way, to the extentthat in combinationthey rotatethe
plane of polarized light in the opposite direction to
sucrose.This "inverted" optical activitygivesrise to
the terminvert sugars.Their presence means that di-
rect polarizationmethods, while simpleandprecise,
do not give an accurate measure of sucrose in cane
juices or molasses.
A scale has been established and ratified by
ICUMSA, the International Sugar Scale, which is
accurate for pure sucrose solutions. A solution of
26 g sucrose dissolvedin water to a finalvolume of
100 mL at 20 "C is referred to as the normal solu-
tion and represents the 100 "Z point, with pure wa-
ter representingthe 0 "2point. The numerical value
is generally referred to as pol, a shorrened version
of polarization, and is widely used as a measure of
sucrose in a sugar mill. This becomes inaccurate in
lower purity streams, and the use of more accurate
techniques to measure sugar in impure solutionsbe-
comes desirable.The measurementis dependent on
temperature and is evaluatedat 20 O
C
.
The effect of a variable reducing sugar content
on pol can be overcome by the use of the doublepo-
larizationmethod,referredto as the Clerget method,
ICUMSA Method GS417-1 (Anon. 2005). The po-
larization is read before and after the totalhydroly-
sis of sugars in the sample using hydrochloric acid.
The sucrose content is calculated from the change
in polarization. This procedure eliminates the effect
of substances which are optically active but are not
hydrolyzed in the procedure. This analysis is often
applied to molasses because of the high content of
reducing sugars. The presence of oligosaccharides
can lead to someunpredictableeffects, but will gen-
erally lead to an over-estimation of sucrose. The
result obtained is therefore referred to as "apparent
sucrose" (Anon.2005).
Dissolvedsolids.The total dissolvedsolids con-
tentof a processstreamismeasuredin amil1labora-
tory on a Brix scale,representingg soluteper 100g
solution;0" and 100"ontheBrix*scalerefer to pure
* In 1986 ICUMSA recommended that the use of thetern Brix be
discontinued.Nevertheless it continues to be used throughout the
sugarindustry.
water and pure sucrose respectively. This scale was
derived originallyfrom a measurementof densityof
pure sucrose solutions using a hydrometer,a simple
and reliable method. However this lacks accuracy,
it is substantially affected by impurities and in low
purity streamsbecomes totally unj-eliable.This mea-
surement has been largely replaced by a measure-
ment of refractiveindex,which is relatedto the pure
sucrose content and also reported as a Brix value.
This is accurate only for pure sucrose solutions;
however the nonsucrose components present influ-
ence the refractiveindexin a similarway to sucrose.
It is more correctlyreferred to as refractometricdis-
solved solids, or RDS. It is also temperaturedepen-
dent and measurementsshould be referred to 20 "C.
It is more accurate and reliable than hydrometer (or
spindle) Brix and gives a closer approximation to
total solids. It is still inaccurate however in impure
solutions, giving a higher value than true dissolved
solids.
Instruments. Modern polarimeters and refiac-
tometers are mainly all digital, automatic, easy to
use and have interfaces suitable for connection to
data acquisitionequipment.A review of instruments
available is published periodically (Anon. 2002).
Some polarimeters now offer wavelengths in the
NIRregionat 882nm,whichcan copewithhigh col-
or solutions and do not always require clarification
and filtrationbeforemeasurement, at least when raw
sugar is being analyzed. Most modem refractom-
eters measure the critical angle and do not need the
sample to be filtered before analysis. However only
a small sampleof juice is requiredforRDS analysis
andiseasilycentrifugedor filteredbefore analysisto
remove the suspended matter. It is common practice
to have the manufacturers check these instruments
once per year during ~e off-crop period. Periodic
checks with water and quartz plates (polarimeters)
or standard sucrose solutions are necessary.
Reducingsugars. Invert sugars are usually de-
termined as the reducing substances in the sample,
known as the Lane and Eynon method, which uses
a procedureinvolving a titrationto determinethe re-
duction of a Fehling's solution. It is from this meth-
od of measurementthat invert sugars have obtained
the name reducing sugars. This is also only an a p
proximateanalysis,since othersubstancesincluding
some oligosaccharideswill be determinedas reduc-
25.1.2 Limitations and accuracies
ing sugars. The Lane and Eynon methodology can
also be used to estimate sucrose through measure-
ment of reducing sugars before and after hydrolysis
of sugars in the sample, analogous to the Clerget
doublepolarizationdescribedabove (SASTA2005).
This procedure is often applied to final molasses
where polarizationmeasurementcan be problematic
due tohigh solution colors, but also tends to overes-
timatedue to oligosaccharidesregisteringas sucrose
(Morel du Boil and Schaffler 1978).
Further analyses. Other analytical instruments
seen in a mill laboratory are pH meters, conductiv-
ity meters and spectrophotometers.pH is defined as
the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion activity
in solution. In pure water at 22 "C, this is exactly
10q g ion& and therefore the midpoint of the scale
is the neutral pH of 7. Most meters availableincor-
porate a temperature adjustmentto be ableto report
pH measured at 25 "C, which adjusts for the effect
rflemperature on the Nernst equation, but does not
h
;
for changes in solution characteristics with
temperature.Conductivity isused as an approximate
measurement of ash or inorganic species, in sugar,
juice or molasses.It is also used in controllingwater
quality in boilers and cooling towers.A spectropho-
tometer is usually availableto measure color, using
absorbance of a solution at 420 nm. The details of
color measurementsare given in Section 23.1.2.
Mill laboratories will generally also have an
oven or moisture teller or similar instrument for
measuring themoisture contentof bagasseandcane,
and periodically also for filter cake and sugar.
Most mill laboratories will also have the ability
to measure sugar traces in condensates and cooling
waters. Other analyses which may be undertaken,
depending on the mill's priorities, may includesome
or all of starch, dextran, ash in cane, preparation in-
dex for cane preparation, pol or Brix of cane wash
water and COD of effluent streams.
Some laboratories have the ability to measure
sulfated ash, which requires a muffle furnace. Sul-
fated ash is normally used on molasses, because it
is an easier and more dependableanalysis and more
nearly measures actual ash content (Chen and ~ h o u
1993:868). Measurement of sample conductivity is
much simpler and faster, with a sulfated ash figure
then derived from predetermined ash/conductivity
relationships.Ashincaneas an indicatorof fieldsoil
can be determined by ignition in a furnace without
the addition of sulfuric acid (carbonate ash), some-
times using a larger furnace such as a kiln designed
for firing ceramic ware. This is done routinely in
somelaboratoriesfor cane quality control.
Mill laboratoriesin some countries such as Co-
lombia (Larrahondo et al. 2001) have introduced
NIR (near iufra-red) spectroscopy to analyze all
liquidproductsoranalyzejuice samplesforcanepay-
ment purposes (Johnson2000). These systemsbring
considerablesavingsin labor,chemicalsand provide
results quickly and conveniently. This approach is
likely to become more widely used in the future.
It is also becoming more common to see labo-
ratory instruments interfaced directly to computers
for automated analyses, data capture and data pro-
cessing.This has benefits in reducing manpower re-
quired and in improvingthe accuracy and reliability
of data by removing human error or manipulation.
In some cases the laboratorycomputer may be inte-
gratedinto a larger laboratoryinformationsystem.
25.1.2 Limitationsand accuracies
AU of the measurements referred to above are
indict measures of the property of interest and are
oftenverytechnique-dependent.It is thereforeof the
utmost importance that the procedures conform in
allrespectsto thestandardprocedures.Most of these
are covered by ICUMSA methods and described in
the ICUMSA MethodsBook (Anon. 2005). In some
cases variations from these procedures or analyses
notcoveredby ICUMSAaredetailedinotherlabora-
tory handbooks,such as those publishedby theAus-
tralian and South African industries (Anon. 1984,
SASTA 2005). Care must be exercised in making
comparisons of data that may have been generated
using differentprocedures; often the proceduraldif-
ference can make comparisonsmeaningless.
Accurate measuresof sucrose,fructose and glu-
cose are measured in a number of research labora-
tories by chromatography, either HPLC or GC.The
difference between the analysescarried out in a mill
laboratoryand the true sugars(i.e. sucrosemeasured
by HPLC or GC)increasesas the purity of theprod-
uctmeasureddrops.ThepoYsucroseratioforinstance
averages 0.99 in raw juice in South Africa and 0.97
in Louisiana.The differencemay be ascribed to the
use of lead sub-acetake as a clarifyingagent in South
Africa, which leads to a higher pol reading because

done using lead sub-acetate and is still practiced in
some sugar producing areas. In most countries the
use of lead has been stopped and other clarifying
agents are in use. However the clarifying agent used
also affects the reading obtained. Lead for instance
precipitates dextran and some fructose, thus affect-

the fructose content is increased as a result of the

the poVsucrose ratio increases (Madsen and Day

The true solids content of raw juice measured
by refractometer is generally accurate, but becomes

25.1.3 Determinationof massflow
rates
To determine process efficiencies it is neces-
sary to measure the quantities of importance, using
scales,or massmetersas they arereferred to in some
countries.Virtually all mills measure the amount of
caneentering the mill and sugarproduced on weigh-
bridges, which provide accurate measures. Unfortu-
nately in some mills, these are the only mass flows
measured, and assumptionsof doubtfulaccuracy are
necessary to evaluate efficiencies in the mill. The
met result is unreliable and inaccurate data, making
it extremely difficult to exercise tight production
control.A further problem lies in the fact that cane
is weighed asit enters the cane yard and may not be
crushed immediately. In storage before processing,
there can be a mass loss due to evaporation and a
compositionchange dueto degradationin storage.
In order to have any reasonable process per-
formance data, the minimum additional mass flow
measurement required is the quantity of raw juice
leaving the extraction plant and entering the fac-
tory. It is also highly desirable to get accurate mass
&HIS of molasses, to enable the undetermined loss
to be established with some degree of confidence.
Where cane washing is practiced, a further mass
flow of cane after washing, or of bagasse, is nec-
essary, since the composition of the incoming cane
is changed during washing and significant amounts
of wash water are entrained with the cane into the
extractionplant.
Methods of measurement of raw juice flow are
discussed in Section 8.2 and of molasses in Section
21.3.3. Automatic batch scalesare recommended for
raw juice and molasses.A belt weigher may be used
for bagasse but this is seldom considered necessary.
Sufficientlyaccurate estimates of bagasse mass can
be derived by a fiber balancefrom cane weights and
measured fiber contents of cane and bagasse.
25.1.4 Cane analysis
Various methods of sampling and analyzing
cane are discussed in Sections 2.3 and 2.4. A cane
sample may be taken by a core sampler as it enters
the cane yard; if the cane is stored in the cane yard
and is not crushed immediately, it is subject to deg-
radation and does not represent the composition of
cane actually crushed. In other cases the cane may
be sampled after thecanepreparationstage,inwhich
case it is representativeof the cane being processed.
Somemethods of estimating sucrose or recoverable
sugarin canearelessthan ideal in termsof accuracy.
However because they are usually an intrinsic part
of the cane payment system, it is not easy to make
changes to the methods used.
In some industries the analysis of cane will be
used in balance and recovery calculations.This may
be subjectto errors due to delaysbetweensampling/
analysis and crushing. If cane washing is practiced
the discrepancy between cane analysis and what is
actually processed becomes much larger. In some
industries the raw juice and bagasse analyses and
rawjuice mass areused to calculate the composition
of cane crushed. In South Africa the cane analysis
calculated in this way is estimated and compared
with the numbers by direct sampling and analysis.
Theratioof pol calculatedcomparedtopol by direct
analysis and cane mass is called the Pol Factor, and
its value is used to flag either measurement or su-
crosedegradationproblems:

25.2 Factory sucrose balances
Sugarmanufactureinvolves the recovery as sug-
ar product of as much of the sucrose in cane as pos-
sible. It is economicallyimportant that this recovery
ratio is maximized. A balance of sucrose in input
and output streams usually leads to a discrepancy;
the diierence is termed undetermined loss.
25.2.1 Recovery calculations
Sugar in cane that is not recovered in the raw
sugar is lost:
in the cane washing process,
in bagasse after the extractionplant,
in filter cake and
in molasses.
Additional sugar is lost in process due to chemical
and physical losses, and this undetermined loss is
calculated by mass balance. Unfortunately,the cal-
culated undetermined loss is the differencebetween
two large numbers, and slight inaccuracies in mea-
sured input and output values cause this number to
fluctuatewildly especially over shorterperiods such
as one week. Unless specialsteps are taken to obtain
really accurate measurements,this calculated loss is
meaningless.
Reliable data is needed for the following rea-
sons:
to estimatehow much sugar is being lost;
to establish where it is being lost;
to measure changesin these lossesin responseto
changes made to improve conditions.
Cane washing. In some industries, the cane is
put through a washing station to wash off adhering
sand and soil. This process leads to a considerable
amount of the sugar being leached out of the cane,
particularly if billeted cane is washed. Estimates
vary from a few per cent to over 10% of the sucrose
in the cane. Estimatesbased on the quantity of sugar
leaving the washing plant are very variable and take
no account of fermentation of sugar in the wash
system.
Since the losses are substantial, it is worthwhile
to estimate the losses in the cane wash plant, by
analyzing the outflow for sugars and fermentation
products and measuring the flow rate. If the loss
in the washing plant is not measured, it cannot be
controlled. Cane washing should be avoided where
possible, since apart from the loss of sucrose, the
cany-over of bad quality wash water into the pro-
cess with the cane means that imbibitionon the mills
has to be reduced, and the impurity in the wash wa-
ter increasesthe impurity loadingin the factory,thus
increasing the loss of sugarin molasses.

as a percentage,is termed the overallrecovery. This

may be expressed relative to cane and is called the
sugar yield:

25.2.2 Application of true sucrose ana-
lytical data
If chromatographic analyses for sucrose in the
raw juice and molasses are available, they should
be used to calculate more reliable data than can be
providedby the traditionalpol balances. This can be
done in different ways. A central laboratory could
provide sucrose analyses on raw juice and molas-

require special preservation techniques for the raw
juice samples), and the resultsused to adjustpol bal-
ances.Alternatively an HPLCinstrument,or anNIR

could be used at the factory. Determination of glu-
cose and fructoseis oftenpossible at little extfacost
and effort, and this provides further useful informa-
tion. In all cases sucrose data is required only for
raw juice and molasses, because pol is adequatefor
estimatingsucrosein bagasse and filtercake.
The sucrose balance data will differ from pol
balances to a varying extent, depending on the poll
sucrose ratios. These are determined largely by the
level of reducing sugars present which in turn is a
function of cane maturity, but are also affected by
the methods used for clarifyingjuice for pol analy-
sis. Somegeneraleffectsare summarizedbelow:

25.2.3 Calculation of stock of sugar in
process
There is a substantial holdup of material in the
factory, representing a stock of sucrose in process.
In order to undertake a balance, it is necessary to
estimatethe stock in process at the start of the time
period and again at the end of the period of review.
This is done by measuring or estimating the quan-
tity of material in every vessel in the factory, and
measuring or estimating its sucrose content. Since
the quantity of sucrose in stock is of the order of
three times the amount of sucrose processed in one
day, attempts to undertake a balance over one day
are generally inaccurate and unreliable. The m
i
n
i
-
mum time period over which a reliable balance can
be obtained is one week and then only if the change
in stock over the week is small.
Not only the quantity but also the purity of the
material in stock might change from the beginning
of one period to the next. For period balancepurpos-
es therefore, the proportion of the material in stock
which will be recoverable as sugar must be calculat-
ed fromtheSJMformula,equation (15.26), using the
purity of the sugar produced and an assumed molas-
sespurity. Theestimateof recoverable sugarin stock
may be added to the quantity of sugar produced, to
give a "made and estimated" sugar quantity. Like-
wise the proportion of the stock allocated to molas-
sescontributesto the "made and estimated"molasses
quantity,used in calculating the loss in molasses.
A stock take over a period corresponding to
scheduled maintenance stops will give more reli-
able answers, since the stock in process is reduced.
Stock taking is less accurateif a running stockis es-
timated. The estimate of change in stock is also less
accurate at the beginning or end of a season, when
the factory is either being filled or liquidated with a
correspondinglargechange in stock.

25.2.5 Mechanisms and causes of undetermined losses
25.2.5 Mechanisms and causes of un-
determinedlosses
The mechanisms whereby sugar can be lost dur-
ing processing are many and varied. Losses may be
real losses of sucrose, or apparent losses that are due
to analytical or estimation problems. Some types of
loss are very small and may not occur at all mills.
However, it is important to be aware of the possible
mechanisms of loss occurrence. The calculated un-
determined loss is affected by:
Errors inmeasurement and analysis. Typical ex-
amples include incorrect estimation of juice to
the factory or molasses to storage, incorrect or
non-representative sampling, stock errors, etc.
Physical losses. These may be due to inadequate
entrainment prevention, foaming carry-over,
spouting in vessels, tank overflows, leaks, liqui-
dation losses.
Microbiological losses. These may occur in low
Brix juices at ambient temperature, when the
main products are dextran or ethanol (e.g. in the
milling plant), or at elevated temperatures when
the main product is lactic acid (e.g. in clarifiers
and filters).
Chemical losses. The major loss is probably due
to inversion, either at low pH or high tempera-
ture, but thermal decomposition and Maillard-
type reactions also cause losses.
Some symptoms of high undetermined loss
causes. Once the process and the mechanisms are
understood, some of the numbers produced in an
analytical report can give an indication of possible
causes. Table 25.1 gives an idea of symptomsto look
for if an undetermined loss problem exists.
In important areas it is sometimes advisable or
desirable to have redundant measurements i.e. more
measurements than are theoretically needed to un-
dertake a factorybalance. An example is the extrac-
tion plant control in South Africa. Measurements
made enable a cane sucrose input estimation to be
carried out in two ways, to be sure that cane pay-
ment data is correct. The ratio of the estimatedquan-
tities of pol entering the mill is termed the Pol Factor
(equation 25.1), which usually has a value around

25.3 Evaluation of factory per-
formance
It is important to have some metrics for the per-
fonnance of a mill.These may be benchmarks for a
particular m
i
l
l
,or may be yardsticks against which
comparisons of a mill's performance with that of
othermills are made.The performanceis affectedby
the quality of cane being processed, the equipment
in the mill, and the skill and ability of the operating
staff. Variations in cane quality are usually outside
the controlof the miller, and a number of themetrics
are derived with the intention of taking account of
these variations, so that comparisons independent
of cane quality can be made. These modifications
may not all be accurate in the way they correct for
cane quality, but in most cases represent an honest
attempt to compensatefor the canequality effects.
25.3.1 Overallfactory
The broadest measureof mill performanceis the
canefsugar ratio, i.e. the mass of cane processed per
tonne of sugar produced. Both these quantities are
weighed fairly accurately and this number is nor-
mally reliable. It is however still affected by the pol
of the sugar produced, and may be given tel quel
(i.e. as produced using the actual pol) or converted
to a standardpol, often 96 pol for historical reasons.
The tel quel number is more common and on this
basis the canelsugar ratio may range fiom 7 in the
most efficient countries to 11 in the less productive
industries.
This number is however greatly affected by the
sucrose content of the cane. A more useful number
for mill control is the overall recovery (OR),repre-
senting the mass of sucrose in sugar produced per
100 t sucrose in cane. This is normally considered
to be the product of two other measures,namely ex-
tractionandboilinghouserecovery.Therelationship
is given in equation (25.4).Extractionis the mass of
sucrose extracted in the mills or diffuser per 100t
sucrose in cane; the boiling house recovery is the
mass of sucroserecovered in sugarper 100t sucrose
in rawjuice from the extractionplant.
In most industries pol is used as the measure of
sucrose and the overallrecovery is obtainedby apol
balance. In countries where the true sucroseis mea-
sured, the pol OR is multiplied by the pollsucrose
ratio for sugar in cane, to give a sucrose overall re-
covery, which is usually lower because the povsu-
croseratiois c1.

25.3.4 Other factory performance measurements
25.3.4 Other factory performance
measurements
Apart from providing recovery efficiencies,
chemical control needs to include analysis of vari-
ous process streamsto give informationto operators
for the efficient running of the plant, as well as to
provide data to measure performance and maintain
optimal control of different sectionsof the plant.
Routine measurement of the pH of raw juice
through to syrup is necessary to checkon factory pH
control. In the filter station, mud solids in clarifier
derflow may be measured, as well as suspended
LrYr in filtrate, from which fi1tet retention can be
calculated. Filter retention should ideally be above
85% and should not be lower than 70% at any time.
Purity measurement of all massecuites and
molasses streams is necessary. The pan attendant
needs these to be able to calculate quantities using
a Cobenze diagram (Section 15.2.3) to achieve de-
sired massecuite purities. The purities also allow
the crystalcontentin the different massecuites to be
calculated.The importanceof these numbers in run-
ning an efficient pan station is discussed in Section
15.1.7.Information on pan strikes must be collated
and expressed in a form to show the quantities of
massecuite boiled. This is usually expressed as the
volume (m3) of each grade of massecuite relative
to the tonnes of cane crushed or relative to the dis-
solved solids input into the factory.
The main sugar quality parameter is sugar pol.
Depending on the specifications of the consumer
purchasing the raw sugar, other parameters such as
ICUMSA color, affinated sugar color, starch and
dextran may be measured, to be ableto producesug-
ar that generates the maximum income cost-effec-
tively. It is also important to control the moisture of
sugar going to storageto minimizelosses in storage.
The safety factor or dilution indicator (see section
19.1.1)is used to assesswhethermoisturecontent is
in the right range.
Another area of importance is the quality of
boiler feed water. Measurements have to be made
in the laboratory of sugar traces in condensates,
by the phenol - sulfuric acid or resorcinol tests
(SASTA 2005) or by the less accurate a-naphthol
test. In addition,pH and boiler chemicalsin samples
from boiler drumsneed to be measured on a regular
basis. This is of utmost importanceto the operation
of a good boiler station.
25.3.5 Time account
The factory reporting function needs also to
report information on the operating efficiency of a
mill. This involves reporting the downtime and its
causes. It is generally divided into the followingcat-
egories:
Operational
Mechanical
No cane
Scheduledmaintenance
In concept this is simple. In practice what consti-
tutes downtime and what category applies need to
be comgrekensiuelydefined.Problems occur for in-
stance in handling downtime for one extraction line
while the other keeps operating, or when a sched-
uled stop takes longer than planned, or when the dif-
ference between an operationalor mechanical cause
is not clear.
It is important to have a system of record keep-
ing by plant item to identify and quantify chronic
problem areas, which lead to low operatingefficien-
cies.This is vital in indicating the areas of plant that
need more attention. This can be done as part of a
laboratory information or a planned maintenance
system.
25.4 Inversion losses
25.4.1 Measurementof inversion
losses
Inversion losses cannot be estimated in pro-
cess from purity changes, since these losses are of
the same order of magnitude as the analytical er-
rors (Schafjer 2001). The best approach is to use
chromatographic determination of glucose, which
is more stable than fructose under front-end condi-
tions, expressed relative to chloride, DS (dissolved
solids) or sucrose. Schiifjer et al. (1985) used the
followingrelationship to estimate the inversion loss
of sucroseAm, from raw juice to syrup:
Thefactorsof 342and 180accountforthe molecular
mass of sucrose and glucose, respectively. This ap-
Referencesp. 600
25 Chemicalcontrol of factories
proach assumes that there is no glucose destruction,
and so if anythinggives a low estimate of inversion.
Schdfler (2001) reports that the loss from clarified
juice to syrup is normally in the range of 2 to 3 kg/t
sucrose in rawjuice. This can be much higher if the
conditionsare such that inversionis promoted.
The preferential destruction of fructose rela-
tive to glucose inflates the pol and leads to a mea-
sured increase in apparent purity across evapora-
tors (Schafjer et al. 1985).This is normal in most
evaporationsystems.Honig (1963) provides a more
detailed account of the behavior of reducing sugars
under conditionsexperiencedin the evaporators.

25.5 Factory reporting
25.5 Factory reporting
25.5.1 Purpose
The purpose of factory chemical control and
factory reporting is to make available information to
managers and supervisors in such a way that they
can understand how well or badly the mill is running
and so be able to identlfy any problem areas.
Factory report sheets should be designed with a
purpose. The laboratory produces a large amount of
data each day, which is a useful record of factory op-
erations. However it produces far more information
than most supervisors and managers need. Thesein-
dividuals should be presented with reports contain-
ing only the information that is useful to them. It
should also be presented in a form that is easy to un-
derstand and contain only the information on which
they will take action. Too often mill personnel are
presented with pages of computer print out, which
is largely unintelligible and which often conceals by
its sprawl some of the important information.
25.5.2 Benchmarking and technical
auditing of factory figures
Comparison of factory performance between
mills in a particular sugar industry, or between mills
in different regions, can be highly productive. In the
right circumstances it can also be a powerful moti-
vating tool for the factory personnel. There are some
obstacles to the process of making comparisons:
There is a lack of standardization of analytical
procedures used; the prime example is the dif-
ferent methods of measuring and reporting su-
crose.
* The effects of cane quality; although various
performance yardsticks attempt to account for
cane quality, they are not entirely successful.
DBerences in plant and equipment, processes
used and sugar quality produced.
Variations in sampling, frequency of analyses
and other factors that make comparisons diffi-
cult.
However these should not limit effortsto make com-
parisons. These differences can be taken into con-
sideration in drawing conclusions. The most useful
comparisons are made if chromatographic sugars
analyses are available, but these are available in only
a few of the sugar producing areas. The value of the
conclusions is directly related to the quality of the
data; good data will enable useful conclusions to be
drawn. Wright (2005) has proposed a system useful
for auditing the performance of sugar mills, which
includes a number of benchmarks for different pro-
cess areas.
The ideal benchmarking process for overall re-
covery of sugar from sucrose in cane has three ele-
ments:
It divides the variances into controllable (e.g.
molasses target purity difference) and uncon-
trollable factors (largely cane quality).
It makes comparisonsof all the key performance
variables affecting recovery.
It calculates the effect of any variance from aver-
age or target and computes the effect on overall
sugar recovery, and if possible puts a monetary
value to this.
Both benchmarking and technical auditing need to
have the key variables affecting overall recovery as
the main focus. These are all identified in the equa-
tions shown below.
Overall mill performance. In overall terms,
the recovery or yield of sugar should be related to
the recoverable sugar in cane. In general terms, this
results in a Factory Performance Index, a ratio of
sugar produced to the estimated recoverable sugarin
the cane processed. In Australia recovery is related
to CCS and expressed as a Coefficient of Work or
Pool Sugar Index, which estimates a refined sugar
yield (Wright 2005). In Louisiana, a Commercial
Recoverable Sugar is computed as the ratio of sugar
produced relative to an estimated Theoretical Recov-
erable Sugar. In South Africa, sugar recovered may
be compared to the Estimated Recoverable Crystal
or the Recovered Value.
Individualsugarlosses.The starting point is the
basic equation (25.4) showing the overall recovery
(OR) as the product of extraction and boiling house
recovery. Alternatively the overall recovery can be
expressed in terms of the individual loss items:
The individual loss items in this equation are all ex-
pressed as kg sucrose/100 kg sucrose in cane. The
loss in bagasse is given by:

25.5.3 Format of factory reports
The ideal report format should contain the es-
sential elements which make up the following cat-
egories:
Production data. This should give the quanti-
ties of cane, sugar and molasses produced, both
for the reporting period and for the season to
date.
Throughput data. The rate at which the fac-
tory is being loaded.As shown in section 2.1.3,
the prime throughput data, apart from cane, are
fiber rate, which affects extraction, flow rate of
dissolved solids (Brix), which affects the front
end of the factory, and nonsucrose input, which
affectsthe factory low grade station.
Cane quality. This has a substantial effect on
all parts of the plant and should if possible also
include measurements of extraneousmatter.
Time account. The time efficiency and the
major reasons for any downtime are crucial to
achievingthe capacity required.
Extraction plant performance. Various met-
rics expressing the efficiency of extraction of
sucrose from cane and the major variables af-
fecting it shouldbe reported.
Factory performance. In an analogous way,
the important process and boiling house perfor-
mance factors need to be shown.
Mill balance. Losses of sucrose should be
shown in the differentloss categories.

25.5.3 Format of factory reports
A report format which includes all these elements
is shown in Table 25.4. Variations of this are to be

reported. Someanalyses may not be undertaken rou-
tinely; however it is considered that the cost of un-
dertaking all the analyses necessary to provide this
data will repay itself many times over in terms of
better plant performance.
If true sucrose and monosaccharides are avail-
able, the incorporation of additional data e.g.
pol/sucrose ratios, glucose recovery, fructose/glu-
cose ratios, can be included. This all provides extra
useful information.

26.1 Bagasse characteristics
Bagassecontains most of the fibrousmaterialin
the cane fed to the mill, from which a large propor-
tion of thejuice has been removed. It has a low bulk
density and being fibrous in nature, is difficult to
handle as a solid. Although it is free flowing, it has
the propensity to choke, bridge and pack tightly if
not correctlyhandled. It also produces dust, which
can representa seriousfirehazard and a healthhaz-
ard under certain conditions. It is not corrosive but
it containssand thatwas deliveredwith thecaneand
so can be abrasive. It may also choke quite readily
and any chutes used in transportingbagasse have to
be diverging to ensure that chokingdoes not occur.
As produced, bagasse has a moisture content of
about 50 g water1100 g bagasse but, depending on
conditions, that can vary between 47 and 55g1100 g
bagasse. Most of the bagasse produced is burned in
the boilers. Typical proximate and ultimate analy-
ses used in boiler calculations,as well as a typical
breakdown of inorganiccomponents in bagasse are
given in Tables 27.1 and 27.2. Characteristics of
bagasse important in by-product applications are
given in Section31.2.
The averageparticle size is normally between 1
and 5 mm as obtained from sieveanalysis. It varies
considerably,depending on the type and degree of
cane preparation and the number of mills. Where
cane preparation is poor, some particles larger than
25 mm are evident. Bagasse from a diffuser system
is usually more fibrousin appearancebecause it has
been subjected to less size reduction in milling. As
a result it is also more difficult to shear and needs
more careful handling. The density of bagasse var-
ies considerably, depending on conditions. The
physical properties of bagasse are covered in more
detail in Section 32.5.
The ash content of bagasse is very variable, be-
ing largely determined by the field soil or dirt in
the cane processed. It is also affectedby the extrac-
tion process. Ln milling Muller et al. (1982) have
determined that on average 36 % of the dirt in cane
is removed in the raw juice, a figure confirmed by
experience in Louisiana. In diffusion however the
proportion of ash in raw juice is much lower, with
only about 10% extracted. Typically, cane contain-
ing 1.5 g ash1100 g cane will lead to 2.5 or 3.3 g
ash1100g bagasse for milling and diffusionrespec-
tively. Because of the dirt in the bagasse, handling
of bagasse can lead to substantial wear on equip-
ment due to its abrasive nature.
Bagasse is not a homogeneous material. It
consists of a mixture of fiber and pith having very
different particle shapes and aspect ratios. In han-
dling, the pith tends to separate quite easily (and
is the source of the dust problem). Classificationin
handling needs to be recognized in any sampling
system; in sampling from a conveyor a full-width
hatch sample needs to be taken if a reliable and
representative sample is to be obtained. Methods of
sampling bagasse are described elsewhere (Anon.
1985).

26.2 Bagasse storage and re-
claim
In Section 28.1 it is shown that the amount of
bagasse produced is of the order of 30 t bagasse per
100t cane. Most mills attempt to be independentof
outside fuel sources, so a part of the bagasse pro-
duced, typically 5 to 10 %, is usually taken to a ba-
gasse store, from which it can be reclaimed at any
time, such as during start-up or shut-down or in the
event of a m
i
l
l stoppage. Some of the bagasse may
also be taken in the form of bagacillo (Section 26.4)
for use in the filter station.
The value of bagasseas a fuelis increasinglybe-
ing realized, so bulk storage of bagasse for reclaim
for out-of-season use, or for by-product use, is be-
coming more common. Likewise methods to reduce
the in-season usage of bagasse andlor improve the
fuel economy of a mill include in some instances
bagasse drying. By-product use sometimes requires
the de-pithingof bagasse used for the production of
pulp, paper and bagasse board.
26.2.1 Bagasse conveying
Bagasse is usually conveyed by a drag-type slat
conveyor or a rubber belt conveyor. Details of belt
and drag-type slat conveyors are given in Section
7.2. Belts are usually selected in preference to slat
conveyorswhereconditionsallowtheir use, because
they are cheaper to install and maintain. The belt
angle of inclination is limited to 23O, which means
that a longer distance is required if the bagasse has
to be elevated to a boiler, for instance. A slat con-
veyor can operate at an angle up to 50' or even 60'
and sois the only choice in many cases, particularly
when modifications aremade to existingplant. Belts
arenormally selectedin the caseof newinstallations
with no plant layout constraints.
The particular application of bagasse conveying
to boilers is covered in Section 7.2.3. The bagasse
needs to be transferred from the conveyor to the
chutes above the feeders of each boiler.
Various types of fixed and adjustable ploughs
have been used to achieve that from flat belts but
there still seems to be a preference for slat carriers
feeding throughholes cut into the lower deck (Moor
2000).
Calculations for the size and capacity of a belt
are given in Section 7.2.1. Belt conveyors are usu-
ally run on troughing idlers, to get the best capac-
ity. Howeverbelt widths are often chosen according
to the need to avoid spillage rather than to achieve
capacity. Belts may also be arranged to run inside
a pipe, which gives a clean and cheap installation.
Aero belts are becoming more popular. In this case
the belt runs on a flat deck, without idlers, above a
plenum chamber.There are a number of small holes
in the deck supporting the belt, through which air
is blown from the plenum and the belt effectively
runs on a thin layerof air. Thisreduces thepower re-
quired and the totally enclosedconstructionprovides
a clean solution.The directionof travel is reversible,
which is advantageous in some circumstances e.g.
transfer to storage in crop and reclaim in off-crop.
Use of 3CR12 steel for the trough and plenum en-
sures a long maintenance-freelife.
Slat carriers are generallyof the samewidth as a
belt conveyorforthe samecapacity, but run at about
half the speed. They are more costly to install, by a
factor of about two. Because of the abrasive nature
of bagasse, hardness of the chain used is more im-
portant than corrosion resistance. A good review of
the important issues in the design and selection of
conveyor chain is given by deJahn (1975).
26.2.2 Bagasse weighing
It is necessary to weigh bagasseif it is to be sold
or used forby-productactivities.It is sometimesalso
necessary to weigh bagasse to establish a mass bal-
ancefor an extractionplant. This may be doneusing
one of a number of different types of belt weigher.
This may involve using load cells to weigh a sec-
tion of belt and idlers, or may makeuse of a nuclear
device based on gamma ray absorption.The former
is now the favored type, particularly because of the
cost of final disposal of a nuclear device.
Bagasse weighing is not an easy task because
of the low bulk density of the bagasse. This means
that the weight of the belt sectionmay be more than
that of the bagasse and high sensitivity and low re-
sponse to external disturbances is required. A sys-
tem for checking the calibration and periodic zero
adjustment should be incorporated. This is particu-
larly importantif bagasse dust is ableto settle on the
weighed section and increase its weightover time.

3 Bagasse storesand reclaim

It is normal practice to have a store for bagasse,
fromwhich bagassemay be reclaimed when themill
stops or on startup or shut down. Since shut down
and boil-off may take up to six hours, and startup
with cool boilers may take 4 hours or more before
bagasse gets to the boilers, the size of the bagasse
store should be such that it can hold bagasse for
steaming at say 30 % MCR for 12hours. For a fac-
toryprocessing 100tJh, this impliesa bagasse store
holding about 150tbagasse. Basedon a bulk density
of 200 kg/m3, the volume required is considerable
e.g. 750m3for 150t. Jackson (1984) reported on an
increasein bagasse storesizeatAmatikulumillfrom
500 to 1000t; this is equivalent to an increase from
125to 250 t bagasse for a 100tJh mill.
TWObasic geometriesforbagassestoresareused,
a circular silo store in wide use in Australia, and a
rectilinear shed in use in many othercountries.
Ideally the storage and reclaim of bagasse
should be done totally automatically. Magasiner
(1974) suggests the following sound principles for
a successfulreclaim system:
Conveyors must be generously proportioned to
caterfor high, short duration surgeloads,which
can occur during reclaimoperations.
With manual or partly mechanized reclaim sys-
tems, the conveyor feeding the boilers must be
sized to handle at leasttwice as much bagasse as
the boilers require.
With mechanical reclaim systems,bagasse must
be recirculated continuously at a rate greater
than that required by the boilers.
Conveyor drives must be sized to start under
full load conditionsand must be sequence inter-
locked.
