26.2.4 Bulk pile storage of bagasse
A number of factories attemptto storethe maxi-
mum amount of surplus bagasse for off-crop use.
Because of the large areas involved, this usually
meansstorageinthe open air.A systemwillpossibly
incorporate a long belt conveyor across a concrete
slab, with the ability to tip bagasse from the belt at
any point, or to a boom stacker moving on rails. In
some cases bagasse is transportedin large trailers to
remote storage areas. Bulldozers or front end load-
ers arerequired to move the bagasse into large piles
to storethe maximumamountof bagasse on thehard
surface storage area. The bulk handling vehicles
travel up the piles and in so doing help to compact
the bagasse. These vehicles are essential too in re-
claiming bagasse fed back to the mill bagasse store.
When the piles are completelyformed and profiled,
they may be covered or partially covered with large
tarpaulins.
Bagasseshould be storedon speciallyconstruct-
ed pads with a hard surface and preferably profiled.
This is necessary to ensure that any rain water run-
off or leachate is contained and treated or stored.
The bagasse may be stored on a single storagearea
or on a number of separated storage pads. Separate
piles enablethem to be more easily covered, assists
in first in-first out handling and helps contain fires.
Apart from the large area required, the main
problems associated with outside storage are rain
wetting the bagasse and the dust nuisance resulting,
particularly when bagasse falls a long distance from
the conveyor down to ground level. The net effectof
average rainfall is not serious. The exterior surface
of an uncovered pile forms a relatively impermeable
skin up to 30 rnrn thick (Dixon 1988). A compact
pile usually resultsin most rainfall runningoff rather
than into the pile. Pile managementbecomes impor-
tant in maintaining sloping piles and ensuring that
no "dams" form which can catch and hold water.
Because of the potential dust nuisanceproblem,
storage sites are sometimes chosen some distance
away from the mill.The sitesare chosenwith regard
to prevailing wind directions and the proximity of
residential areas. A buffer area around the storage
piles is maintained, preferably planted with trees to
act as a screen.
Temperature in bagasse piles. Bagasse dries
out in storage, largely as a result of exothermic mi-
crobial reactionsoccurring in the pile, which lead to
increased temperatures. If the temperatures get too
high, this can lead to spontaneous combustion, but
the production of organic acids in the pile generally
limitsmicrobial activity. Briceiw and Torres (2001)
report temperatures up to 60 "C in bagasse piles,
with moisture content reducing to around 40 %
within a few weeks. No visible deterioration of the
bagassewas evident.Nonethelessit is good practice
to operate a first in-first out system to minimize po-
tential deterioration in storage.
Dimn (1988) measured temperatures in a num-
ber of bagasse storage piles and found a consistent
temperatureand decompositionpattern. He reported
maximum pile temperatures 1.5to 2 m below thetop
surface of a pile, irrespective of the size and shape
of the pile. The temperature was often found to rise
to about 67 "C and stabilize. Darkening of the ba-
gassein this region was evidenceof somedecompo-
sition. However the moisture content seemed to be
little changed from fresh bagasse and the calorific
value of the bagasse was unaffected. Spontaneous
combustion is not common but can occur if the ba-
gasse dries out with an accompanying temperature
rise above 94 OC. Factors which cause the bagasse
temperature to rise from the quasi-steady IeveI of
65 "C to the onset of dry bagasse combustionhave
not been established (Dixon 1988). Monitoring of
pile temperatures can give advance warning of im-
minent spontaneousbagasse combustion,
Bulk density of bagasse. The amount of ba-
gasse stored per unit area is a function of the height
of the pile and the moisturecontent.An averagefig-
ure of 200 kg/m3may be used for a rough estimate.
In order to eliminate the variable moisture content.

26.3.1 Effecton boiler efficiencyand capacity
Drying the bagasse is therefore beneficial to boiler
efficiency for several reasons: (a) the lower amount
of water reduces the excess air required, at least
down to a level of 40 % moisture,below which there
is no reduction in excess air required (Magasineret
al.2002);(b)itis possibletoreachahigher adiabatic
flame temperature;(c)a smallerflow of gasespasses
to the stack. The ways in which bagasse moisture
and gas exit temperature affect boiler efficiencyare
illustrated in Figure 27.4.
However, drying the bagasse with the flue gas
goes well beyond that as it effectively reduces the
final gas temperaturepassing up the stack,using re-
sidual energy to effect the drying. This equates to
returning some of the gas enthalpy to the boiler and
reducing losses accordingly. Drieis, mainly rotary
drum and flash types, have been installed in Arner-
ica, Brazil, Philippines,Australia, China, Cuba and
India, but consistent results and conclusions have
not always been obtained and the degree of success
varies widely.
26.3.1 Effect on boiler efficiency and
capacity
The use of boiler exhaust gas to dry bagasse re-
duces the stack temperature and hence from an ef-
ficiency point of view is equivalent to adding more
boiler heat recovery surface. An economizer does
not give an efficiencygain as high as a drier,but has
been usually the preferred option because of lower
initialcosts,betterreliability and lower maintenance
requirements. However bagasse driers can reduce
stack temperature to a lower figure than either an
air heater or economizer. The use of an economizer
enables a reliable and relatively cheap reduction in
gas temperatureto be obtained with simple heat ex-
changeequipmentwith no additionalfans, gas ducts
or conveyors. With no moving parts, operational
and maintenancecosts arelower. The limit on outlet
temperaturesmust be high enough to ensurethat the
corrosion will be unimportantunless very abnormal
conditions occur (Magasiner1996).
Drying of bagasse not only reduces the effec-
tive boiler gas exit temperature, but alsoreduces the
amount of boiler gas produced, thus improving the
efficiencysignificantlymore than additionalheatre-
covery equipment on a boiler can achieve.However
it never makes economicsense to pay for the energy
required to dry bagasse. This only makes sense if
waste heat in boiler flue gas is used for drying.
An economic comparison of the two options is
necessary to determinewhich is the most cost effec-
tive alternative between economizers and bagasse
driers in each case. Maranhao (1986) reported that
the cost of installationof a bagassedrier represented
around 12% of the value of the boilers, with a stack
temperatureof 135-140 OC,while Magasiner(1996)
suggests that the cost of an economizerrepresents 6
to 8 % of the cost of the boiler with a stacktempera-
ture of 150"C. Thus it appears that an economizer
costs between 50-65 % of a bagasse drier.
Using information obtained in a prototype in-
stalled at the Nunorco sugar mill, Argentina, Carde-
nas et al. (1994) performed an evaluation conclud-
ing that diverting 50 % of the stack gases to the ba-
gasse drier increases the boiler efficiency from 71.4
to 84.9%, largely by reducingstacklosses,and with
a smallerreduction in furnace loss.
Dixon et al. (1998)showthat reducing the mois-
turecontentof bagassehas a substantialeffecton the
capacity of the boiler. However they estimate that a
limit of 30 % moisture is necessary for safe condi-
tionsin conventionalspreaderfiring.Atthis moisture
contentan increasein steamoutputofjust over 10%
is expected.Narendranath andRao (2002) report an
increase in boiler capacity between 5 and 8 % fol-
lowing the installation of bagasse driers achieving
bagassemoistures in the 42-44 % range.
26.3.2 'Qpes of drier
Initially, most driers were of the rotary type.
Furines (1976) described some early installations
in Florida. These were not always satisfactory and
often gave considerable trouble. Subsequentlyflash
driers were developed, since it was established that
very quick dryiig of the order of seconds, could be
achieved, particularly with good cane preparation.
This type has now been widely adopted. A review
of some of the bagassedrying plants used in several
countries showingthe rotary drum and the pneumat-
ic suspension drier as the most popular alternatives
is given by van der Poel et al. (1998:458).Most of
them have achieved a drop in moisture content of
Referencesp. 616
26 Bagassehandling, storage and drying
bagasse from 50 % orjust over to somewherein the
range of 30 to 40 %.
The swirl burner developed by SRI in Australia
dries bagasse being fed to the boilers using furnace
gases. This falls into a somewhat different category
to the driers considered here, in that it is an integral
part of the boiler and does not benefit from using
residual flue gas energy which would otherwise be
lost.
Rotary drum driers. This type of equipment
has been widely used for various dryingduties, con-
sisting of a rotating cylindrical drum, provided with
internaldeflectorsand cocurrentflowof bagasse and
hot gases.Airlock systemsmust be used on the ends
of the cylinder feeding and discharging bagasse,
to avoid air ingress which may cause a fire. These
driers have often proved troublesome, they are me-
chanicallycumbersome,and the risk of firesis high.
A number of driers installed in the past have been
decommissionedand removed.

Pneumatic flash driers. Direct contact with

cyclone. The wet gases go to the stack, while the
bagasse separatedin the cycloneis dischargedvia a

the combustionchamber.

26.3.3 Operationalissues
The plant described by Maranhao (1986) in-
volves theuse of an auxiliaryfan to directpart of the
gases before or after the air preheater to the front of
the boiler through an underground pipe, to the drier
locatedjust before the bagasse feeding system (Fig-
ure 26.5). Bagasse is separated from the hot gases
in cyclones,from which it dischargesinto the boiler
furnace.The advantageof this systemis the absence
of additional conveyors. However wear on most of
the componentsin the system is significant,requir-
ing ongoing maintenance.
A limit is imposed on the temperature of the
gas leaving the drier, which is in contact with met-
al and therefore must be kept below the dew point
of the combustion gases to avoid the formation of
acids that cause corrosion. As bagasse has a low
sulfur content, the temperature is lower than in the
case of boilers which use fossil fuels. For conven-
tional bagasse boilers the dew point is below 90 "C
(Magasiner 1996).
After 7years of experiencewith threepneumatic
bagasse driers installed in the Santo Antonio sugar
mill, Maranhao (1986) described briefly the units
andresults observed, summarized in Table 26.1.
The initial boiler efficiency was low and so sig-
nificant gains were possible with only an airheater.
The comparison shows how much more the effi-
ciency can be improved with a drier, with the best
performanceobtained with a combinationof airpre-
heater + bagasse drier. The reduction in excess of
air from 93 % to 35 % has a considerable influence
on the efficiency, apart from the reduction in stack
temperature.
The main concerns with bagasse driers are the
maintenance,reliability and susceptibility to block-
ages. Careful design can minimize these problems.
Thisrequiresthat all particleimpactsoccur at a shal-
low angle to minimize erosion. Erosion is not an is-
sue on bends on vertical up-flow, but all other bends
Table 26.1: Results withbagassedriersin SanAntonio sugar
Brazil (Maranhao 1986)
need to be very long radius or have easily replace-
able wear plates at the bends. It is also importantto
have oversized rotary valves. It is reported that the
valves have a working life of four seasons.
A potential environmentaladvantageof bagasse
driers in a well-designed system is the retention
in the moist bagasse of small particles entrained
with the flue gas, reducing the particulate emission
throughthe stack (vanderPoelet al. 1998).In India
it is reported that the gas exiting the cyclones has a
particulate loading of <100 mg/m3 (Narendranath
and Rao 2002). This also means a smaller quantity
of sand in the gases, which together with lower ve-
locities (because excess air is reduced) has resulted
in a longer service life of exhaust fans and stacks
(Maranb 1986).
26.3.3 Operationalissues
Themain operationalissueis the maintenanceof
equipment,particularlyrelated to wear. Even though
the concept has been around for many years, so far
the technology has not proved reliable and drier
projects have not been consistently successful. Re-
portsof successfulinstallationsof bagasse driersex-
ist, but none of the seriouslyfailed experienceshave
been published.In Colombiafor example,a bagasse
drier was installed in the late 1980s,which led to a
smooth and efficient operation of the boiler, elimi-
nating supplementary fuel consumption. However,
serious wear of some elements and problems with
the rotary seal valves were so severe that the drier
became a maintenance problem andjeopardized the
reliability of the plant. Finally it was dismantled.
Popular opinion in places like Brazil and South
Africa suggests that an economizer is better than
a bagasse drier because of fewer problems, even
though the efficiency is inferior. Whilst ba-
.mi,,, gasse driers can reduce stack temperature
to a lower figure than either an air heater or

26.3.4 Other alternatives for bagasse
drying
Drying using superheated steam. A fluidized
bed drier for beet pulp has been described (Jensen
2003), which is in use in a number of Europeanbeet
sugar factories. Essentially, superheated steam (e.g.
2.8 MPa, 250 OC) is used to evaporate moisture,
yielding a stream of vapor leaving the drier with
enough energy to be used as the heating media in
the first effect of the evaporators (e.g. 370 kPa, 150
OC). The vapor generated in the drier is recovered
in the factory. In this way, almost all the energy and
water is recovered, but the energy level of the steam
is lowered.
The main complication with high pressures is
the feeding and sealing of the drier, which in the
case of beet pulp has been solved by employing
rotary valves used in the paper pulp industry. The
major change required within the factory is the split
of the b t effect evaporator into two bodies, or the
addition of a steam transformeror another effect,to

range of 15to 20 d s seems reasonable,with slight-
ly higher values used for whole bagasse and lower
values selected for fine bagacillo or drier material.
It is desirable to keep the velocities as low as
possible, to minimize the fan requirements but also
to minimize wear in the ducts,which can be consid-
erableif there is significant sand in the bagacillo. In
practice a bagacillo duct of about 500 rnm diameter
is common in an average sized factory.

what the limiting ratio is;in practice air/solidsratios
of 4:1to 6:1have proved to be satisfactory.

in this application. Theoretically the pressure drop

forair in a ductarecloseenough in practice. The fan
motor required on a bagacillo pneumatic transport
and cyclone system will be between 25 and 75 kW
depending on the sizeof the mill.
26.4.5 Screw conveyors
In cases where the mud mixer is not too far from
the bagacillo screens, a screw conveyor may be
used to transport bagacillo. In most cases however
pneumatic transport is preferred as the suction of air
through the screenis one of the major variables used
to adjust the quantity of bagacillo achieved.
26.4.6 Bagacillocyclones
Cyclones are inexpensive devices and with
proper design, cyclonescan do a good job of sepa-
rating bagacillo or pith from an air stream. Particles
>5 pncan usually be separated from a gas stream.
The main issues in the design are the pressure drop
through the cycloneand the particle cut size i.e. the
average or the smallest particle size which will be
separated. Unfortunately best efficiency is obtained
with a high pressure drop and a design compromise
is required. In general a smaller diameter cyclone
gives a higher pressure drop and a higher collection
efficiency.
The pressure drops throughout the cyclone ow-
ing to several factors: (1) gas expansion, (2) vortex
formation, (3) friction loss, and (4) changes in ki-
netic energy. The pressure drop depends on the inlet
velocity. More specifically, the pressure drop Ap is
expressed as a number of inlet velocity heads:
The number of velocity heads K is a function of the
geometry of the cyclone and can have a value be-
tween 1and 20. Using an acceptedgeometryenables
the pressure drop to be estimated fairly accurately.
In the case of a standard Lupple cyclone shown in
Figure 26.9, K has a value of 8 (Darby 2001).
Because of fanandpressuredropconsiderations,
the velocity in the inletduct is normally in the range
of 10to 25 d s . Perry and Green (1997)recommend
an inlet velocity of 15d s . Based on this velocity, a
typical pressuredrop in the cyclonewill be 1kPa or
100mm water.

particularly severe at the cyclone entrancewhere the

or hard steel sections are recommended. It is better
to use an induced draft fan located after the cyclone.
This minimizes wear on the fan blades and keeps the
system slightly below atmospheric pressure, so that
any slightleaks do not createa dust problem.
26.5 De-pithing of bagasse
Some of the uses for bagasse as by-products re-
quire that the bagasse be processed prior to use, in
applications such as pulp, paper and particle board
manufactureas outlinedin Section 31.2.
The process of separating the pith from the fi-
ber is usually carried out at the sugar mill. The de-
pithed fiber is sent to by-product use and the pith is
returned to the bagasse handling system and burnt
with bagasse in the boilers. Thereis little difference
in calorific value between pith and whole bagasse
and modem bagasseboilers have no problem bum-
ing pith.

.

.
1 Fiber/pith split
Bagasse is arbitrarily divided into two com-
ponents, pith and fiber, on the basis of its visual
appearance. Pith originates from the soft-walled
parenchyma cells of the cane stalk and comprises
mainly smaller particles. Fiber originates from
the fibro-vascular bundles and the fibrous rind tis-
sue, and comprises mostly fine fibers with a length
of anything up to 50 mm. The ratio of pith:fiber is
usually accepted to be in the range 40:60 or even
30:70. This varies somewhat dependingon the type
of cane and thecanepreparation andextractionplant
conditions.
Separationof pith fromfibergenerally makes use
of the difference in characteristicsof the two compo-
nents, particularly the differencesin shapefactor.
26.5.2 Pneumaticseparation 26.5.3 De-pithers
It is possible to effect a separationpneumatical-
ly,providing the cane preparation has been intensive
and very few "chunks" are visible in the bagasse. If
bagasse is allowed to cascade down a set of angled
horizontal louvers or a section of angled screenper-
forated with slots, the pith can get sucked through
and the fiber falls down the screen to be collected
at the bottom. The pith is removed and transported
pneumatically. The equipmentis similar to that used
for bagacillo shown in Figure 26.7, but may be set
at a smaller angle between 60" and 70'. to-acueve a
I higher pith rate through the screens.
.-' n
- '
[ This separation is cheap and easy b d iequires
I very little maintenance. However the efficiency of
separationis not high and sometimesmore than one
stageof separation is requiredtoupgrade the quality
of the fiber produced. Sand or grit will be separated
with the pith fraction.
In most cases it is necessaryto resort to mechan-
ical de-pithing, particularly if some additional size
reduction is required to free pith remaining attached
to fibrous pieces. The development of de-pithers
and details of the de-pithers used in the past are
cataloged by Atchison (1971). Most de-pithers are
shredders with either a vertical or horizontal shaft,
fitted with fixed or swing hammers, and shrouded
by a perforated screen. The pith is sucked through
the screen and conveyed pneumaticallyto a cyclone
and the fiber is collected separately. In most cases
the bagasse is fed either from the top or side along
the axis of the rotor, with the fiber discharge at the
oppositeend to the feed.
De-pithers are supplied by Peadco, SPM and
Pallman. The vertical rotor machines have gener-
ally proved to give best results. The largest machine
sold by Pallman has a screen 2 m high and 1.6 m

27.1 Introduction
Boiler design has changed radically over the de-
cades, driven by a demand for more cost-effective
and more easily operatedand maintained units, by a
better understanding of the principles involved and
by improved materialsof constructionandconstruc-
tion techniques. The main evolutionary trends can
be summarizedas follows:
Operating pressures and steam temperatures
have increased to allow more power to be co-
generated;
Suspension firing, which is more efficient and
lends itself more readily to mechanical de-ash-
ing, has replacedhearth furnaces;
Ibbe erosion has been minimized by replacing
multi-passconvection banks withlow gas veloc-
ity singlepass banks;
Larger steam drums have been incorporated to
help stabilize water level control;
Expensiverefractorieshavebeen virtually elimi-
nated in favor of easily maintained all-welded
gastight enclosures,and
Furnace stability has been enhanced and stack
emissionscontrolled and minimized by the use
of advancedoverfireair systemsand the installa-
tion of more sophisticatedcontrol and collecting
devices.
This chapterreviews thefundamentalprinciples that
underlie the design of a boiler. Rather than deal his-
torically with its evolution it illustrates how these
fundamentalsare used to design new plant and how
they can be applied to improve the performance of
existing plant. The chapter deals broadly with three
subjects; the first covers the fundamentals;the sec-
ond discusses typical operating and maintenance
problems and suggests ways in which they can be
addressed; and the third deals with the pre-boiler
system and the design of boiler house and factory
pipework including the letdown and desuperheating
station.

27.2.1 Fuel characteristics
From a combustion point of view, bagasse is
a relatively "benign" fuel. This is because most of
the alkali metals, which are the dominant ash con-
stituents that cause clinkering on the grate, furnace
slaggingand convection heating surfacefouling, are
leached out in the extraction process leaving an ash
rich in silica. The alkali metals, predominantly low
melting point sodium and potassium, end up in the
molasses, which is why molasses is so difficult to
use successfully as a fuel. Silica has a high melt-
ing point and hence rarely causes deposit problems.
Moir and Mason (1982) indicate that silica can be
very abrasive.
Calorific value. The general formula for bio-
mass fuel energy is a constant times the true fiber
content of the fuel. Don et al. (1977) have shown
that the grosscalorificvalue (GCV,or higher heating
value Ho)of bagasse can be calculated from:
Wienese (2001) has refined Don's net calorific
value (lower heating valueH,,)
formula to read:
The correction for RDS (Brix, wRDS)
is introduced
into equations (27.1) and (27.2) to take cognizance
of the fact that the calorific value of sucrose, which
replaces fiber, is less than that of fiber.
These formulae yield results that are within
about + 2 % of values measured in South Africa,
Mauritius, USA, Colombia and Ecuador. They are
only valid if the carbon in the fuel is oxi-
dized completely to carbon dioxide. If
combustion is incomplete and some of Prin
the carbon is oxidized to carbon mon-
oxide the loss in availableenergy can be
significant.

Carbon, when oxidized to carbon dioxide, re-

The moisture content of bagasse usually var-
ies from about 46 % to 56 %. Its ash content, on an
as-fired basis, varies from about 1.8 % to 11.0 % of
which 1.3 to 1.8 percentage points is ash that is an
inherentpart of the fiber sbuctureand the remainder
superficial or free ash, which adheres to the external
surfacesof the plant material. Moistureis frequently
the only parameter that is discussed when evaluating
combustibility.As the following example shows, this
is misleading. A fuel having a moisture content of
50 % and an ash content of 2 % will have an inert
to combustible material ratio of 52/48 = 1.08.If the
moisture is 50 % and the ash contentis 5 % the ratio
is 55/45= 1.22.This ratio is important when evaluat-
ingacceptablegrateheatreleaseratesand the amount
of excess air required for completecombustion.
A "standard" bagasse is used in this chapter to
evaluate these parameters. This is a bagasse having
a moisture content of 52 % and an ash content of
2 %.The excess air and grate heat releaserate charts
shown in Figures 27.1 and 27.7 are based on this
fuel. "Effective" moisture w

27.2.2 Combustion air requirements
Combustion takes place in three stages. Firstly,
the bagasse is dried, then the volatile constituents
are driven off and burned and finally the remaining
carbonis burned.Thecombustionchemistryis com-
plicated. Table 27.3 lists the most important reac-
tions that take place. The amount of airrequired for
combustion(thestoichiometricairrequirement)can
be calculated, in aggregate,from the ultimateanaly-
sis of the fuel.Table 27.4 showshow this is done for
the fuel in Table 27.1. In practice, because it is dif-
ficult to mix fuel and airhomogeneously, more airis
needed to completecombustionthanthis calculation
indicates.Theextra airrequired is referred to as "ex-
cess" air and is usually expressed as a percentageof
the stoichiometric air;e.g. 23.7 % excess air means
that 1.237 times as much air is used to complete
combustionthanis theoreticallyrequired.
The excess air actually being used in a boiler
is most easily determined by measuring either the
amount of oxygen or carbon dioxide in the exhaust
gas. The oxygen content is usually reported as a per-
centageof the total or "wet" exhaustgas.Thecarbon
dioxidecontentis usuallyreportedas apercentageof
theexhaustgas after the moisturehas been removed.
The latter figure is referred to as "dry" exhaust gas
and is reported in this way for historicalreasons.
I
f 0,, CO, and CO are all measured on a
dry basis (as obtained from an Orsat appara-
tus) their sum will equal a constant. This con-
stant is approximately equal to the stoichiomet-
ric CO, assuming complete combustion. In the
case of bagasse the number is typically between
20.3 and 20.9 %. Figure 27.2 plots CO, and 0,
against excess air for a typical bagasse, bituminous
coal, light fuel oil and natural gas. Each fuel has a
characteristicstoichiometricCO, contentin %. Each
fuel also needs a typical amount of air to complete
combustion per 10000 W of H,.These figures are
scheduledin Table 27.5. Table 27.5 also schedulesa
number of useful engineeringparametersthat can be
derived from this basic data.
The amount of excess air needed for a particu-
lar furnace and fuel is a function of the furnace de-
sign and the fuel's effective moisture content. Ex-
periments carried out in the late 1950sin Australia
showedthat a pile of bagassecannotbe dried rapidly
enough by radiation. It can only be dried by direct
contact with hot gas. For well-designed suspension
firedfurnaces,excessairrequirementsgenerallyfol-
lowtheempiricalcurvesshowninFigure27.1. High-

27.3 Boiler efficiency
27.3.1 Measuringefficiency
The efficiencyof aboiler q is defined asthe ratio
of the energy output to the energy input per unit of
time expressed as a percentage; i.e.
where:
m mass of flow of steamproduced;
~
n mass flow of fuel burned;
hs, specificenthalpy of steam produced;
h,, specificenthalpy of feed water.
Unfortunately,it is not a simple exercise to measure
efficiencyin this direct way, particularly in the case
of a bagasse fired boiler. The main difficulty lies in
accurately measuring the mass of fuel burned. Be-
cause of the nature of the fuel, there are no reliable
meters on the market to do this. Measuring steam
flow andHoare not as difficultbut also present prob-
lems on commercialinstallations.Obtaining an an-
swer to within & 2 % is virtually impossible.
27.3.2 Quantifyinglosses
Measuringlossesand subtractingthesefrom 100
is an easier and more accurateway of doing thejob.
This method is referred to as the "indirect" method.
In the direct method, measurement inaccuracies are
reflecteddirectly in the result.In the indirect method
they apply to only the individual losses and because
each is relatively small the effect of an erroris mini-
mized.
Typical losses calculated as a percentage of a
unitmass of fuel for bagasse, coal,fuel oil and natu-
ral gas are scheduled inTable27.6. Table27.7 shows
how the calculationsare carried out for bagasse. The
only measurements needed are fuel moisture, ash
and Brix and excess air (0, or CO,) and gas tem-
perature at the exit fromtheunit's heat recoverysec-
tion. These can all be measured relatively easily.
Note that about 95 % of the losses from a ba-
gasse fired boiler are stack losses and are therefore
related to the exhaust gas temperature. Figures 27.4
and 27.5 plot boiler efficiency vs. exhaust gas tem-
perature for a typical bagasse and a typical coal, fuel
oil and natural gas.
For bagasse, the moisture loss is the most sig-
nificant followed by the dry gas loss and then the
unburned loss. Squeezingmore moisture out of the

27.4.2 Bagasse feeding and metering
type furnaces in the cane sugar industry. Pinhole
grates areused in preferenceto dumpgratesbecause
they require less maintenance. A continuous ash
discharge (CAD) stoker is used when air pollution
regulations require NO,, CO and particulate emis-
sions to be controlled witbin limits that do not per-
mit the intermittent peaks associated with pinhole,
vibrating and dump grate de-ashing. They are also
used when high ash auxiliaryfuels, such as coal, are
burned. Vibrating grates are also used sometimesfor
these fuels.
27.4.2 Bagasse feeding andmetering
Because bagasse cannot be stored inconverging
hoppers,a livefuelhandlingsystemmustbeused in-
stead.This usually comprisesa slat or belt conveyor,
diverging chutes that seal out "tramp air" and offer
some, albeitsmall, storagecapacity,feedersand,for
suspensionfiring,distributorsto convey the fuelinto
the furnace. Screw and single d
r
u
m feeders have
beenused extensively as meteringdevices.Both rely
on using relativelyhigh-powered motors to squeeze
the fuel though a fixedorificeand both stallif they
are installed under tall, large volume inlet chutes.
Three drum feeders, which use two rolls to meter
and a third to scarify the bagasse and act as a "live"
orifice,overcometheseproblems.Figure 27.6 shows
a typical three-drum feederandillustratesitsmethod
of operation. These feeders can be installed under
9 m tall chutes. They absorb less than 1kW under
normal operating conditions and, when fitted with
variable frequency drives, have linear volumetric
meteringeharacteristics.
Hearth furnaces such as the Ward furnace are
usually equipped with single drum pocket feed-
ers. These operate at constant speed and are really
"air excluders" rather than feeders. If chute height
abovea pocket feeder is more than about 1m it will
frequently srall. Eisner furnaces have self-feeding
chutes. Einer furnace chutes are fed directly from
the slat conveyor. As the fuel in the furnace bu&s
away it is replaced with fuel stored in the chutes.
Theseare kept topped up by bagasse droppingfrom
the slat conveyor into them. For Eisner furnaces to
work successfully it is important for the chute vol-
ume to be largerthan what istermed thefurnace"in-
stabilityvolume". The instability volume is defined
as the volumeof bagassein the furnace abovea line
drawn from the upper edge of the chute inlet to a
point where therear wall intersectsthe furnacefloor.
Lf chute volume is less ihan this,any instability in
furnaceoperation will lead to chutes running empty
and excessive amounts of tramp air being drawn in
and quenchingcombustion.

and low emissions
Figure 27.9 shows a typical cane sugar indus-

CAD stoker installation designed to achieve a high

zoned grate at MCR (maximum continuous rating)
is usually between 50 and 500 Pa.

27.4.6 Furnace size
The size of the furnace is dictated by fuel and
ash quality. Sufficient heating surface must be in-
stalled to reduce the gas temperature leaving the
furnace to a level at which alkali metals in the ash
have a chance of condensing out as solid, micron-
sized, particles in the gas stream rather than onto
the convection heating surfaces. A larger furnace
is required for bagasse having a high Brix content
because the ash in these fuels has a high alkali
metal content. Alkali metal salts condensing onto
convection heating surfaces are difficultto remove
by soot blowing. Sulfur and chlorine in the pres-
ence of alkali metals can be extremely corrosive
when metal temperatures exceed 480 O
C such as
occur in superheatersproducing steam in excess of
about 440 OC.In cane sugarfactorieswhere Brix in
bagasse is less than about 4.0 8,abrasion of con-
vective heating surfaces by silica, rather than al-
kali fouling, is the biggest problem. In these cases
furnace leaving temperatures of 935 to 985 O
C are
acceptable.

27.5 Boiler design
27.5.1 Designoverview
Factory process and power requirementsdictate
boiler steam conditions. If these are not correctly
balanced either too much steam will have to be let
downthroughreducing valves toprocess pressureor
steamwill have to be vented to atmosphereto make
up the power requirement. The procedures to be
adopted to determine what pressure and tempera-
ture is needed are outlined in Chapter 30. Most
- conventional factories can balance their energy re-
quirements when operating at 20 bar 360 O C
or, at
most, 30 bar 400 "C.Where the electrical load is
high to meet irrigationand/or village requirements
30 bar 400 O
C or 43 bar 440 OC steam conditions
usually suffice.Where power is exported to the grid
it is usually necessary to use a 60 bar 480 OC or an
80bar 520OC cycle.Magasiner (1996)discusses the
effect that operating pressure and steam tempera-
ture have on the physical size of a boiler and how
changes in these parameters affect heating surface
disposition. In essence, he concludes that higher
pressures require larger furnaces and economizers
and higher steam temperatures result in the need
to introduce two-stage superheaters. He also con-
cludesthat, at pressuresin excessof around 60 to 80
bar, gaslair air heaters become redundant in favor
of steam air heaters. If such a machine is selected,
fins must be pitched wide enough to prevent fouling
of the heating surface.
Although kPa or Pa are used as units for pro-
cess and range pressures or pressure drops, and ex-
pressed as absolute pressures, it is more common
and less clumsy for boilers to use bar as the unit of
pressure. In this text also, the boiler operatingpres-
surewill beexpressedas a gaugepressuremeasured
in bars i.e. bar (g). Note that 1bar = 100kPa.
Under steady milling conditions, the load im-
posed on a cane sugar factory boiler stationis rela-
tively steady, provided that the pan station is prop-
erly managed and the feed water station is correctly
designed. If these conditions are not present severe
load swingscan occur resulting in large water level
surges.
The required boiler efficiency will depend upon
the amount of fiber available, the amount of imbi-
bition used, the process plant steam demand and
the amount of fuel needed to meet off-crop opera-
tions. If the cycle as a whole is not as efficient as it
should be, an auxiliary fuel will have to be burned
to balance the factory energy requirements. If it is
too efficient, money will have to be spent on dis-
posing of surplusbagasse. Of the factors that affect
boiler efficiency reviewed in Section 27.3, bagasse
moisture and exhaust gas temperatureare the most
important. Drying bagasse in the mill more effec-
tively improves boiler efficiencyand also improves
extraction efficiency. Reducing exhaust gas tem-
perature also improves boiler efficiencybut this re-
quiresinstallingadditional heating surfacethat will
have to operatenearer to the exhaust gas dew point.
It will have to be designed with this in mind and
may well requireadditional care and possibly main-
tenance. Reducing exhaust steam consumption by
changing the evaporator configuration to allow for
more vapor bleed is a third alternative. The choice
of which route to follow is an economicone.
As mentioned in Section 27.3.2 boiler efficien-
cy can be improved by passing the exhaust gases
through a bagasse drier rather than over additional
heating surface.In thiscase the exhaust gas temper-
ature can be reduced to about 85to 95 O
C compared
to about 135OC with additionalheating surfaceand
the bagasse moisture content to about 38 to 45 %.
The improvement in efficiency is a function of the
reductionin exhaust gas temperatureand the reduc-
tion in excess air required to bum the lower mois-
ture fuel. Because the amount of fuel moisture to be
evaporated is alwaysequal to the incomingbagasse
moisture, the moisture in gas loss is a function of
the exhaust gas temperatureonly.
Drying bagasse thermally is rarely cost-effec-
tive. The capital and maintenance cost of the ad-
ditional equipment and its associated additional
power consumptionusuallyoffset the potential gain
in efficiency. Burning drier bagasse can sometimes
lead to boiler fouling and operational problems.
Magasiner (1987) deals with the effect that fuel
moisture over the range 0 to 56 % has on a typical
boiler's performance.
27.5.2 Heat transfer
Heat is transferred in a boiler by all three heat
transfer modes; conduction, convection and radia-
27.5.2 Heat transfer
tion. The equations that are used to calculate heat
transfer are summarizedin Table 27.9.
Heat is transferred from the hot gas in the fur-
nace by luminous (glowing fuel particles) and non-
luminousradiation(radiationemittedby the diatom-
ic gases CO, and H,O). Both of these heat transfer
modes areproportionaltothe differencebetween the
fourth powers of the absolute temperatures of the
source and sink. They are, therefore, very powerful
at the temperaturesfound in a furnace.
Heat is transferred in the superheater largely by
luminous radiation if the elements are exposed to
furnace radiation and by non-luminous radiation
and convection if the elements are shielded from
furnaceradiation.
Convectionand non-luminousradiation transfer
heat to the convection bank. About half of the heat
in the bank is transferred by non-luminous radia-
tion. Convective heat transfer is proportional to the
log mean temperature difference between source
and sink. Further details are given in Section 9.1.2.
In a tubular air heater, where the gas normally
passesthrough the tubes,convectionisthedominant
heat transfer mode on both the gas and air sides.
Heat is transferred by convection and to a much
smaller extent by non-luminous radiation in a bare
tube economizer. In a finned tube economizercon-
vection is the dominantheat transfer mode.
Convective heat transfer plays the dominant
role on the water and steam sides of a boiler and in
all cases conduction is the mode that applies within
the metal and any scale.
A similar equation to that used in Section 9.1.3
can be used to determine the overall heat transfer
coefficientacrossany component.The overall coef-
ficient is the reciprocal of the sum of all the heat
transfer resistances to heat transfer by convection,
conduction and radiation. In this case the equation
is written:
where the k, values represent the coefficients for
each of the heat transfer mechanisms, with units of
W/(m2
- K).
Table 27.10 schedules the magnitude of theheat
transferrates typicallyfoundin a boiler.Thesemust
be used with discretion as they can vary over a fair-

Figure27.13 showsa typical temperatureprofile
acrossa boiler tube.
Because the water side and tube metal heat
transfer coefficients are so much larger than the
gas side coefficients, they offer relatively little
resistance to heat transfer in the furnace, con-
vection bank and economizer and hence can be
ignored. On the other hand, in a superheater, the
steam side coefficient is only about one twentieth
that of the gas side coefficient so it plays a mea-
surable role and as a consequence the superheater
metal temperature is biased towards the gas tem-
perature. In addition, because the steam is su-
perheated, the tubes inevitably operate at higher
temperatures and hence a more rigorous analysis
must be carried out when calculating their struc-
tural integrity than would be required for the other
components.

heat transfer coefficientsare about equal and hence
the tube metaltemperatureis abouthalfway between
the airand gas temperatures.

In the furnaceand convection bank, gas and wa-
ter temperatures follow the trends shown in Figure
27.14, Curve A. In the superheater, air heater and
economizer they can follow either Curves B or C
depending on which way the fluids flow over and
through the heat &ansfer surfaces. If they follow
CurveB, the heating surfacearrangementis referred
to as a parallel flow exchanger. If they follow Curve
C it is called a contra-flow exchanger. Because the
log mean temperaturedifferencein a contraflow ex-
changer is greater than in a parallel flowexchanger,
less heating surface is needed for contraflow ex-
change than is needed for parallel flow exchange.
Curve A Curve B Curve C
Parallel flow
Figure27.14: CurvesA, Band C-contraflow andparallel
flow temperature profiles
Contraflow
Frequently a contra-flow arrangementis selectedfor
this reason. Where metal temperatures need to be
controlled, either to prevent overheating such as in
a superheateror to prevent acid dew point corrosion
such as in an airheater, a parallel flow configuration
is usually better. A contra-flow economizer is ac-
ceptablebecause the feed water temperaturedictates
its metal temperature. Provided this is higher than
the dew point of the gas, condensation and hence
corrosion cannot occur.
Acids tend to have higher dew points than pure
water so it is the acid dew point which is usually
relevant in boilers.Acid dew point is mainly a func-
tion of the amountof sulfurin the fuel. For bagasse,
which usually has very little sulfur, the acid dew
point is normally less than 90 OC. For high sulfur
fuel oils and many coals the acid dew point is of-
ten over 125 O
C and can be as high as 140OC. Con-
densation will occur on metals operating below the
dew point even if the gas temperature in the region
is above the dew point. In all cases the condensate
is predominantly hot, concentrated sulfuric acid,
which is highly aggressive.

27.5.6 Circulation
Water circulating through the boiler prevents
heating surfaces from overheating. At cane sugar
factoryoperatingpressuresof 20 to 80bar the differ-
ence in density between the waterlsteammixture in
the "riser" tubes and the water in the "downcomer"
tubes and pipes creates the driving forces that pro-
duce circulation. This is called natural circulation.
Pressure losses through the circuits balance these
driving forces. The ratio of the mass of water to
steam in a circuit is called the circulatingratio. Cir-
culating ratios of 20:l are common. Whilst burnout
is unlikely to occ-at a circulatingratio of as little
as 5:1,ratios aslow as this lead tomorerapid scaling
and drum level instability. Table 27.11 shows that
at a circulating ratio of 20:1 the volume of water in
a circuit is only 19.9 % of the total volume of fluid
flowing for a boiler operating at 20 bar and 27.5 %
for oneoperating at 30 bar.
Steam is separatedfrom the circulating fluids in the
steam drum.Baffles are incorporated in this drum
to define flow circuits and provide a mechanism
for water and steam separation to occur efficiently.
If the steam drum is large enough, well designed
baffles can limit solids cany over to the superheater
to less than 1 mglkg. Ia smaller drums, cyclones
or mist eliminators are needed to achieve this. The
boilers shown in Figures 27.10.27.15 and 27.24 are
equipped with cyclones. The unit shown in Figure
27.9 is equippedwith mist eliminators.
27.5.7 Heat recovery
To obtain the efficiency normally required from
a cane sugarfactoryboiler, the exhaustgas tempera-
ture leaving the heat recovery surfaces must be be-
tween 160 and 280 "C.
The lower temperature can
only be achieved by installing both an airheater and
an economizer. The higher temperaturecan often be
reached with an airheater only.
As discussed in 27.5.2, to avoid heat recovery
surface corrosion, metal temperatures must be kept
above the acid dew point of the exhaust gas. This is
best done by placing the air heater, which, if well
designed, will have a metal temperature about half-
way between the gas and air temperatures,ahead of
the economizer, which has a minimum metal tem-
perature a few degrees above that of the feed water
temperature.
This arrangementdoesnot alwayslead to a least
capital cost installationbut in most cases eliminates
acid dew point corrosion as well as air heater tube
plugging, which is largely caused by condensates
trappingdust like "fly paper".
The type of combustionequipmentinstalled and
the material from which it is made limits the maxi-
mum primary airtemperaturethat can be employed.
For pinhole and vibrating grates made of a heat re-
sistant cast iron this is about 300 "C. For a CAD
stoker and dump grate the limit is about 260 "C.

27.5.8 Erosion
Moir and Mason (1982) show that tube erosion
is approximately proportional to (gas velo~ity)~.~.
Meuronen (2003) shows that for an "in-line" tube
bank the exponentis 3.44 and for a "staggered tube
bank it is 3.30. He also shows that quartz particles
will erode tubing about 8 to 9 times more rapidly
than will coal ash.
To minimize erosion of convective heating sur-
faces whilst still maintaining reasonable heat trans-
fer coefficients,recent experienceindicates that gas
flow velocities over the external surfaces of tubes
should not exceed 10to 12m/s (reviseddownwards
from 15 m/s used in the 1980s and 1990s) and 20
to 25 m/s through them. Economizerelement return
bends are best placed outside the gas stream. CFD
studies can help identify where baffles should be in-
stalledto minimizehigh local erosionrates on exist-
ing boilers.
27.5.9 Fans
For a boiler to operate successfullyit must have
enough grate area to allow the fuel to be burned ef-
ficiently and enough fan capacity to provide the air
required to complete combustion and exhaust the
products of combustionfrom the unit.
Modem boilers are usually equipped with three
or four fans. The primary a
i
rfan supplies hot air to
the underside of the grate. The overfire air (OFA)
fan supplies the additional airrequired to complete
combustion. The induced draft (ID) fan exhausts
the products of combustionfrom the boiler to atmo-
sphere. A fourth fan is used to convey the bagasse
into the furnace. It is called the distribution airfan.
In somecasestheOFA and distributionairfan duties
are combined. Whilst on the face of it this appears
to save cost it frequently leads to control complica-
tions.
The response of a boiler to a load increase or
a low pressure condition depends on the amount
of excess fan capacity that is installed to acceler-
ate combustionbeyond the unit's MCR combustion
rate. Typically if the fans have a design margin of
5 % it will take about 20 to 25 minutes for a boiler
operatingat MCR to recover fromoperatingat 80 %
of normal operating pressure. If the design margin
is 20 % this is reduced to about 2 to 4 minutes. For
the design margin to be effectiveit must be applied
directly to volume and to the square of those com-
ponents of the Ap equation that are velocity depen-
dent.
Table 27.12 schedules the fan laws. These are
very useful in predicting how a given fan will per-
form under various operating conditions. Backward
curved and aerofoil bladed impellers are best used
for primary air and OFA applications. They have
self-limiting power characteristics. Forward curved
radially tipped impellers have good self-cleaning
characteristicsthat make them more suited to ID fan
applications.They have rising power characteristics
with load. The efficiency of a backward or aerofoil
bladed impeller varies from 71 to 78 %. The effi-
ciency of a forward curved radial tipped impeller
varies from 63 to 68 %.
There are four ways of controlling the output of
a fan:
By dampers placed in the inlet or discharge
ducting. Counter-rotatingdamperblades should
be used to obtain approximately linear control
characteristics with damper rotation (95 % of
full flow is obtained through parallel rotating
dampers when they are about 45" open whereas
contra-rotating dampers pass 95 % of full flow
when they are about 85' open).The power con-
sumptionof a damper controlledfanfollows the
fan characteristic curve. Dampers are used for
both clean and dirty gas applications.
By inlet radial vanes. Closing these throttles
flow by increasingpre-swirl of the gas entering
the eye of the impeller. Pre-swirl depresses the
fan characteristiccurve and hence lowerspower
consumption atpart load.Inletvanes areused on
clean air applications.
By inlet box louvers. These are small linked
dampersplaced in a box bolted to the eye of the
fan which rotate in unison to pre-swirl the gas
entering the eye of the impeller.They operatein
a similar way to inlet radial vanes except that
they are more suited to dirty gas applications.
They also save power at reduced load.

level will change not only as a result of a change in
inventory but also as a result of the change in pres-
swe. Because the second effect is more pronounced
than the lirst, an increase in load is manifested by a
rise rather than a fall in water level. This is called
"swell". The opposite is also true; when load drops
the apparent water level drops. This effect is called
"sW'.
Any device that attempts to control boiler water
inventory using water level only as input, therefore,
will initially react the wrong way; i.e. when load
increases it will reduce feed flow and when load
reduces it will increase feed flow. In boilers, which
have a large inventory of water, this is acceptable.
In boilers which do not have a large inventory better
results are obtained by matching feed flow to steam
flow using water level only as a t

curacies. This latter control strategy is called three
element control, i.e. steam flow, feed flow and drum
level are all used as control inputs. In essence, the
primary loop controls the feed flow using the steam
flow as its set point. The water level signal is used to
trim the steam flow set point signal.
For a three element control loop to react satis-
factorilyin a canesugar factoryenvironment,where
suddenvery largeload changescan occur, the water
level must be measured over a large range, prefera-
bly from-250 rnm to+250 mm around normal water
level. For this large operating range to be effective,
the steamdrum diameteronboilers operating at less
than 45 bar (g) must be at least 1750rnm. On lugher
pressure units, wherethe "shrink" and "swell" char-
acteristicsareless severebecause there is less steam
in the system (seeTable 27.11) and that which is in
it has a lower specific volume, smaller drums with
a water level range of -200 mm to +200 mm can be
used.
Furnace pressure control. For a boiler to oper-
ate safely,its furnacemust at all times operate under
a slight vacuum. If allowed to operate at a positive
pressure,hot combustion gaseswill puff out into the
boiler house where they may harm personnel and
possibly cause boiler house tires.
Furnacepressurecan be balanced by controlling
the outputs of either the induceddraftor primary air
fans. The choice depends primarily on the type of
drive with which each fan i s equipped. The time it
takes for either gas to flow from the furnace to the
ID fan or for air to flow from the primary air fan to
the furnace plays a secondary role. If both fans are
equipped with fixed speed drives it is usually best
to use the ID fan to control furnace presswe. If this
fan is equipped with a variable speed drive, such as
a turbine,better results are oftenobtainedby using a
fixed speed primary air fan with modulating damp-
ers or vanes to control furnace pressure. This is be-
causeit takes too long to accelerateor deceleratethe
ID fan's high inertialsystem.
Pressure or load control. Steam is used in a
cane sugar factory at constant pressure. Heat input
must be regulatedtomaintainthatconstantpressure.
Whilst ideally this is done by varying fuel and air
mass flow rates in unison, equipment shortcomings
make this objectivedifficult to achieve. The outputs
of both bagasse feedersand fans are volumetrically
controlled so density correctionsmust be applied to
convert their outputs to mass flows. In most cases
trimming fuel feed to maintain a constant fuellair
ratio as measuredby an 0, analyzerwill circumvent
this problem. On larger units (>75 t/h) or where an
auxiliaryfuelis burned simultaneouslywith bagasse
it is frequently best to use mass corrected airflow
rates in the controlloop as well as 0, t

m

Fieldet al. (1992)report using a nuclear density
meter successfully to convertfeeder output to mass
flow on a boiler burning bagasse (p, = 125 kg/m3)
and furfural residue (p, = -375 kg/m3). This was
needed to overcome feed problems associated with
having to burn both fuels in any ratio at any time.
Only one master pressure controller should be
used to control boilers operating in parallel. In this
way load, and hence load swings, can be shared on
a percentage basis between boilers. Biasing stations
can be installed to allow one, or more, boilers to
carry more load than the others.

27.6.2 Control loops
Three major loops are needed to control a modem
boiler. These are:
Boiler water level control;
Furnace pressure control, and
Boiler pressureor load control.
The first two also help ensure safe operation of the
boiler.
Two additional loops are needed to minimize
maintenanceof the unit. These are:
Superheatermetal temperaturecontrol, and
Back-end metal temperaturecontrol.
The first protects the superheater tubes from over-
heating during start-up or if load is dropped sud-
denly. The second protects the air heater tube metal
temperature dropping below the acid dew point of
the gas.
A third additional loop is used to control steam
temperature if constant superheat is required over a
large turndownrange.Where two-stage superheaters
are installed, this loop sometimes has a subsidiary
loop incorporated to prevent the interstage steam
temperature dropping down to the saturation steam
temperature.

27.6.4 Control technologies
The extentand sophisticationof control systems
varies enormously from one sugar mill to the next.
The simplest form of control system consists of a
series of single loop, stand-alonePID (proportional,
integral and differential) controllers with analogue
strip chart recorders doing the data recording. As a
minimum the parametersrecorded should include:
RecorderNo. 1 RecorderNo. 2
Steamflow Steam temperature
Feed water flow Exhaustgas temperature
Drum level Excessoxygen
Steampressure
The next level of sophisticationis aprogramma-
ble logic controller based control system that uses a
personalcomputerand SCADA(supervisorycontrol
and data acquisition) package as a humanlmachine
interface.Data is logged and trended digitally.
The next level up is a distributedcontrol system.
Thistypeof systemisoftenused tocontrolthewhole
sugar mill. The boiler controls form part of this.
Field based systemsthat are digital communica-
tions networks using microprocessorbased field de-
vice intelligence to improve plant performance are
now beginning to enter the boiler market. Intelligent
field devices (smart transmitters)not only sharepro-
cess variable information but status, configuration,
calibrationdata etc and can be accessedanywherein
the plant. McMillian and Considine (1999) indicate
that they typicallyrequire:
74 % less field wiring;
93 % less controlroom space;
80 % less field devicecommissioningtime.
Unfortunately, most digital systems have limited
memory capacityfor datastorageand thereforesam-
pling rates are reduced to increase the period over
which trend information is stored. Because these
trends do not reflect a true continuous picture of the
instantaneous operating changes that occur, ana-
logue strip chart recorders should still be used for
critical parameters such as steam flow, water flow,
drum level and steam temperature.

Wear on ID fan impellerscan be contained by either
hard facing the impeller blades or equippingthe fan
with replaceablewear Liners.
Replaceable liners should be used with caution

Combustion air and distributor air fan noise
levels can be minimized by installing inlet silenc-
ers. These are usually designed to reduce the noise
emitted to 85 dB(A) at a distance of 1 m from the
source. Provided that noise level measurements be-
gin at a distance several times greater than the larg-
est dimension of the source, the free fieldnoise level
decreases by about 6 dB for each doubling of the
distance from the source.

27.7 Stack emissions and

27.7.1 Regulationsand units of
measurement
Regulationsgoverningstackemissions vary sig-
nificantly from country to country and even from
stateto statewithin a country. They are likely to be-
come more stringentin time. Only particulate emis-
sionsareregulatedin most sugargrowingregions.In
countries such as the USA and France, regulations
arein forcegoverningCO,NO,, SO,, volatileorgan-
ic compoundsand heavy metals emissions as well.
Stack emission concentrations are defined in
three ways; either in terms of volume or mass per
unit volume of flue gas or as a mass per unit energy
input to the boiler. The third has the advantagethat
it is an absolutemeasurement.For thefirst two to be
of value, they must be referred to a standard excess
air concentration.Unfortunately different standards
areused in differentparts of the world making it dif-
ficult to compare numbers. The problem is further
compounded by the fact that some concentrations
are referred to the wet gas analysis and some to the
dry gas analysis. European Union norms are used
in this chapter. Approximate conversion factors are
included in Table 27.15.

emissionrate is a function of:
Fuel ash content;
Fuel moisturecontent;
Fuel size grading;
The type andrating of the grate;
The type and design of the furnace, and the
Boiler load.

3 Dust collectors
There are four ways of removing particulates
from fluegases.These are:
Bag filters;
Cyclonecollectors;
Wet scrubbers,and
Electrostaticprecipitators (ESPs).
Bag filters are not normally used in the cane sugar
industry becausebagasse char is an activated carbon
that is easily ignited. These collectors are therefore
a firerisk.
Cyclonecollectors. Because the efficiency of a
cyclonecollector is inverselyproportionalto its cell
diameter(i.e, the smallerthe diameterthe higher the
efficiency)bestperformanceisobtainedby arranging
smalldiametercells (250to 300mm)in bankscalled
multi-cyclone collectors. The cells can be mounted
horizontally or vertically. Vertically mounted cells
are generallymore efficientthan horizontalones but
tend to be larger and more expensive. Large diam-
eter (>I000 mm)Ter Linden type cyclones similar
to those used to collect sawdustare sometimesused
in banlcs but these are not normally as efficient and
frequentlyrequire more maintenance.
The efficiency of a cyclone collector is propor-
tional to the Ap across it. Howeverbecause the Ap is
a function of u2 and wear is a function of u ~ . ~ ,
it fol-
lowsthat there is a very definitelimit to the efficien-
cy that can be achieved without incurring excessive
wear.Theproblemis further complicatedby thefact
that larger char particles break down into smaller
ones when passing through cyclonecollectors mak-
ing them evenmore difficultto collect.Typicalfrac-
tional efficienciesfor a cyclone collector and a wet
gas scrubberare shown in Figure 27.21.
Horizontal multi-cell collectors are relatively
inexpensive and have a low pressure drop (Ap 350
to 650 Pa). Vertical cell collectors are medium cost
units and have a Ap of about 650 to 800 Pa. There
is little to gain by increasingAp beyond 1000Pa be-
cause char breakdown becomes significantat higher
equivalentcellvelocities.Theefficiency of both hor-
izontal and vertical cell collectors can be improved
- see Figure 27.21 Curve B - by drawing a frac-
tion of the gas flow with the dust into their collect-
ing hoppers and then recycling the gas back into the
main circuit through secondarycollectors.
For cyclone collectors to work effectively their
dust discharges must be properly sealed against air
ingress. Larger diametercyclonesarrangedin banks,
must dischargeinto independentlysealed systemsto
preventgas recirculatingfrom one cell to another.

27.7.3 Dust collectors
Wet gas scrubbers. There are several types of
wet gas scrubber available.The most common are:
Impingement['bath' type] scrubbers;
Venturi scrubbers;
Fixed vane scrubbers;
Perforated(sieve) plate scrubbers, and
Constant Ap or 'variable throat' cyclonic scrub-
bers.
Of these, the fixed vane scrubber, perforated sieve
plate scrubber and the variable throat scrubber are
widely used in the sugar industry. The fixed vane
scrubber has a limited turndown range. Pennington
(1999) reports that turndown of a singleunit is lim-
ited to 75 % of MCR. Two or more units must there-
fore be installed if emission limits are to be main-
tained over a reasonable operating range. The sieve
plate unit is the least expensive but its turndown is
also limited to about 75 % of MCR unless the sieve
plate area is adjustable on line. On the other hand,
the variable throat scrubber is able to accommo-
date larger load swings. It is capable of operating
efficie:tly down to about 30 % MCR. Its nozzles,
which are about 15to 20 mm in diameter, are prone
to chokingif thereis a high percentageof suspended
solidsin the water supply.Sieveplate and fixed vane
scrubbershave largernozzles.
Fixed vane and variable throat scrubbers have
a Ap of about 1250 to 1800 Pa. A perforated plate
scrubber has a Ap of about 1000 to 1500Pa. In all
cases, to minimize mist carry over, efflux velocity
must be less than 2.5 to 3.0 m/s at MCR. For the
variable throat scrubber to work successfully the
centrifugal or separating force must exceed a value
between 80and 130g dependingon particlesizeand
density. A fixed vane scrubber does not need such
a high "g" force. It relies on additional internals to
achieve similar results. A variable throat scrubber's
efficiency can be enhanced by saturating the gas
before it enters the scrubber proper. It is not clear
whether this is true for the other two types as well.

each machine.

The temperature of the gas leaving a scrubber
will vary from about 68 to 72 O
C depending on the
moisture in the bagasse, the gas temperature, the
quantity of water used per unit volume of hot gas
entering the scrubberand the temperatureof the wa-
ter entering and leaving the scrubber. Between 0.7
and 0.9 L of water is used per m3of hot gas entering
a scrubber.The amountof water evaporatedis also a
function of these parameters.As a rule of thumb, if
the diierence between the inlet and outlet scrubber
water temperatureis 20 OC, the scrubberevaporation
rate will vary from about 2.0 % of boiler MCR for
the higher flow rate to 3.3 % forthe lower flow rate.
If the temperaturedifferenceis zero, the evaporation
rate will be about 7.5 % of MCR.
Electrostatic precipitators. Electrostatic pre-
cipitators (ESPs)are very bulky and costly pieces of
equipment.Thereareonly a limited number of them
operating in the cane sugar industry in 2006. They
are installed in areas where very stringent emission
limits are in place. Frequently these installationsare
subject to continuousemissions monitoringby state
authorities. ESPs use two sets of electrodes that are
insulated from each other to collect dust. The col-
lecting electrodesare grounded. The dischargeelec-
trodes operate at a high DC voltage (60 to 120kV).
Plate type collecting electrodes and tube type dis-
charge electrodes are commonly used. Sometimes
the discharge electrodes are equipped with studs or
spikes to enhance their performance.ESPs are usu-
ally equipped with 3,4 or 5 fields.
Precipitationof particulatematter in an ESP can
be defined approximatelyby the Deutsch equation.
In this equation q is the removal efficiency (ex-
pressed as a percentage) and the exponent k can be
described as the product of the specific collecting
area of the ESP and the migration velocity. The ef-
fective migration velocity takes account of all limit-
ing process variables. It must not be confused with
the actual velocity of a dust particle.
The actual behavior of an ESP depends on the
physical and chemical properties of the material to
be collected, on the characteristicsof the gas and on
the electrode geometry. A modified version of the
Deutsch equation that takes account of variations
in the effectivemigration velocity is used to size an
ESP. This equation includes an exponent applied to
the migration velocity that corrects for variations in
particle size downstream of the electrical field.
The performance of an ESP is sensitive to gas
velocity, particle resistivity (the higher the resistiv-
ity the lower the efficiency), gas humidity and gas
temperature. Efficiency increases with increasing
humidity and decreases with increasing gas veloc-
ity and gas temperature.When burning bagasse, the
low resistivity of the carbon dust causes current to
flow to ground before it can charge the particles.To
avoid emission spikes caused by the sudden release
from electrodes of collected carbon particles, either
a cyclone collector or a non-saturatinggas scrubber
must be installedin serieswith anESPto removethe
larger carbon and char particles.
As a rule of thumb, the efficiency, q,per field
of an ESP is about 85 %. For a two-field machine,
thereforethe efficiency can be calculatedas follows:
[(I00 - 85) - (851100
- IS)] = 2.25 % and hence
q =97.75 %
For a three-field machinethe efficiency is calcu-
lated as follows: [(lo0 -97.75)-(85f100 .2.25)] =
0.34 % and henceq = 99.66 %.
ESPs have a Ap of between 150to 250 Pa. The
Ap across the inlet and outlet gas distributiondevic-
es accountsfor most of this.
27.7.4 Choiceof collectorand collector
location
For the foreseeable future it is clear that wet
gas scrubbers will be the "collector of choice" for
most mills where fairly stringent particulate ernis-
sion control becomes necessary. Whether the ID fan
should be placed before or after the scrubber,how-
ever,is not so clear. If bagasse is the only fuel to be
burned, placing the fan after the scrubber has many
advantages,the most important of which are:
A "wet" fan has to handle only 75 to 80 % of the
volume that a "dry" fan has to handle.
There is no need to protect the ID fan from ero-
sion by installing a cyclone collector upstream
of it as would be the case with a dry fan.
A dry fan will, therefore, absorb about 25 to
35 % more power than a wet fan.
The main disadvantagesare:
A wet fan must be epoxy lined to minimizecor-
rosion. Present day epoxies can only withstand

a maximum operating temperatureof about 120
"C. If the scrubber water supply fails, the boiler
must be shut down to prevent damaging the ep-
oxy. Alternatively, a second emergency water
supply must be available to take over immedi-
ately from the main supply.
27.7.5 Gaseousemissions
NO, and CO. Nitrogen oxides and carbonmon-
oxide are the two most importantnoxiousgas emis-
sions. They are considered togetherbecause, as will
be seen shortly, there is an interaction between the
two. Of the six different nitrogen oxide (NO,) spe-
cies, only two, nitric oxide (NO) and nitrogen di-
oxide (NO,), are considered serious pollutants. The
others occur either in much lower concentrationsor
areunstableat ambientconditions.Nitrogen dioxide
reacts with hydrocarbonsto form smog. Nitric oxide
is primarilygeneratedin the furnace and is then oxi-
dized to nitrogen dioxide as it exits the stack.There
are two sources of nitric oxide in boilers: fuel NOx
formed from nitrogen in the fuel and thermal NO,
formed from nitrogen in the combustion air. The
furnace temperaturein a bagasse fired boiler is nor-
mally too low for air nitrogen to convert to NO, so
fuel nitrogen is the predominantsource of NO,.
About 15 to 25 % of fuel nitrogen is converted
to NO,. The conversion rate will depend on the fuel
moisture content (the lower the moisture the high-
er the conversion rate) and the furnace design. It
reports mainly as NO in the stack with about 3 to
5 % reporting as NO,. It is usually measured in
mL NO/m3of dry gas but the NO, concentration in
the exhaust gas is reported as NO,. With standard
fuel having a nitrogen content of 0.0015 kgkg this
translates into a NO, level of about 270 to 550 mg/
m3(STP) (- 135to 270 d m 3 )at 6 % 0, on a dry
gas basis (-0.19 to 0.38 lb/MMBTU).
Reducing flame temperature can reduce NO,
without using a catalyst.This can be done by usinga
largewater-cooled furnace or stagingcombustion or
recirculating inert gas or by injecting steam andlor
water into the furnace or any combination of these
technologies.A water-cooled furnace with some de-
gree of staged combustionis needed to achieve the
uncontrolled NO, level referred to above. Inert gas
recirculation and steamlwaterinjection are difficult
to use commercially.
SNCR process. Urea solution (which releases
ammoniaonheating)can alsobeused toreduceNO,
to N,:
4 NH, +2 NO, +0, -+ 3 N, +6 H20 (27.12)
If properly engineered, urea injection into the fur-
nace can reduce NO, levels by about 50 %. If too
much NH, is used, either because it is injected into
the wrong temperature zone or because CO levels
are too high or because of equipment or installation
deficiencies,a phenomenon called NH, slip occurs.
If sulfur is present, NH,slip causes ammonium bi-
sulfate to deposit in the heat recovery tower. This
salt can be corrosive and can choke the pass. Urea
should not be injected into the convection banks of
a boiler. Injectingurea to controlNO, is called a Se-
lective Non-CatalyticReductionProcess (SNCR).
Sun and Stamatakis (2004) advise that SNCR
reactions only work efficiently within relatively nar-
row CO and temperature bands. They also advise
that as CO concentration increases the temperature
foroptimumNO, reductiondecreases.Fromtheide-
alized curves shownin Figure 27.23, for which they
provided the data, it is clear that for low NH, slip
the optimum temperature band is between 925 and
950 "C at a CO concentrationof 125mg/m3(STP).
This reduces to 875 to 900 "Cat a concentrationof
315 mg/m3(STP) and 825 to 850 O
C at a concen-
tration of 560 mg/m3 (STP). These temperatures
are lower than the furnace gas exit temperaturesen-
countered in conventionalbagasse fired boilers (see
Section 27.4.6). For urea injection to work success-
fully, therefore,the furnace of a bagasse fired boiler
needs to have more heating surface than is usually
installed. Increasing furnace height is the most cost
effective way of adding this surface. It also has the
added bonus of increasing urea residence time. In
practice performance will fall short of the idealized
curves shown in Figure 27.23 due to mixing, distri-
bution and other inefficiencies.
Twoor eventhreeinjection levels aresometimes
needed to cater for furnace temperature profiles
varying with fuel quality and load. Whilst it should
be possible to achieve a NO, reduction of about
50 % at CO levels of less than 500 mg/m3(STP), at
a CO level of 1 250 mg/m3(STP) the reduction can
be as low as 15% for the sameM

nace. Between 2 and 4 % is converted to sulfur tri-
oxide. SO, combines with moisture to form H2S0,
that condenses, as discussed earlier, on metal sur-
faces operating at temperatures below the acid dew
point. The SO, concentration in the stack emission
is a function of the amount of sulfur in the fuel and
generally because there is little sulfur in bagasse it
does not present a problem. In some areas, where
cane is grown on volcanic soils or in swampland
such as in Florida, where ground waters contain hy-
drogen sulfide,problems can arise. Problems occur
when either heavy fuel oil or high sulfur coals are
burned as auxiliary fuels. It ought to be possible to
reduce SO, emissions in flue gas desulphurization
plants designedfor fossilfuelsbut sofar this has not
been demonstratednor has it been necessary.
Very small amounts of unburned hydrocarbons
in the form of volatile organic compounds form in
a bagasse fired boiler. The same methods that are
used to control CO can be used to minimize volatile
organiccompound levels.

27.7.6 Discards disposal
There are many ways of handling and dispos-
ing of discards(ash, grit and particulates).The most
successful all use water as a transport medium.
Pneumatic conveyors have been tried without suc-
cess. Mechanical conveyors such as screw or slat
conveyorsall sufferfromhighmaintenanceand they
are also difficult to seal properly. In general both
pneumatic and mechanical conveyors fail because
the activated carbon particles in the discards, when
exposedto air,igniteand burn to formlargeclinkers.
Hoppers are also distorteddue to these uncontrolled
fires.
About 15 to 25 % of the discards report as
trough.The boiler shown in Figure 27.10 in Section
27.4.4 is equipped with a submerged belt ash con-
veyor. Submerged slat conveyors have proven to be
maintenance intensive in this application. On boil-
ers fitted with pinhole and dump grates where large
quantities of ash are discharged in short intervalsof
time it is best to sluice the ash away. The boilers
shown in Figures 27.9 and 27.15 are equipped with
sluicesystems.
Gritscollectedin undergrateand boilerhoppers
and dust collected in mechanicalcollectors are best
sluicedas well. Hydraulicseals that allow water and
discards to flow to waste whilst preventing air infil-
tration into the hoppers should be used.
To minimize corrosion the quality of sluice
and scrubber water should be kept within the limits
scheduled in Table 27.16. They should be recycled
to maintain a high residual alkalibuffer.
There are a number of ways of treating sluice
and scrubber water. Of these the most successful
are:
* In larger settlingponds if land is available,alter-
natively;
In clarifiersand vacuum belt filters.
Munsamy (1989) and Vennuelen and Vawda (1989)
both report on successfully using settling ponds as
wet lands. Whilst Munsamy reports only on using
the ponds to collect boiler discards, Vennuelen and
Vawda report on using them to dispose of mill ef-
fluents as well. The area required depends on many
factors the most important of which is the cleaning
frequency. If this is to be an annual occurrence, the
area required will be determined by the volume of
discards to be stored. If it is intended to clean the
pond at say weekly intervalsits size will be dictated
by the area needed for the discards to settle. 'If.pi-
cally the hydraulicloadingwillvary f
