27.8 Boiler operation and main-
tenance
27.8.1 Manufacturer's manuals
Reference to manufacturer's manuals will usu-
ally provide solutionsto most general operating and
maintenance problems. From time to time specific
problems occur for which there are no ready-made
solutions. Frequently these are due to changes in
fuel quality or load profile. They should be tackled
from first principles. Keeping accurate detailed op-
erating records will help identify their causes and
pinpoint solutions.
Some of the lessons learned in earlier sections
of this chapter are drawn togetherunder thisheading
to provide a broad overview of how these can affect
reliability.
27.8.2 Start-upand shutdown
Lighting and bringing a boiler up to pressure
should follow a definite procedure to avoid placing
undue stress on its components-see Section 27.5.3.
Manufacturers place time constraints on pres-
sure-raising in order to achieve this. Figure 27.16
in Section 27.5.3 shows a typical curve for boilers
equipped with panel wall furnaces operating at be-
tween 20 and 80 bar. The curve is based on using
two different firing rates; an initial rate of about %
the normal rate to bring the water in the boiler up
to about 60 O C and the normal rate to allow water
temperatureand boiler pressure torise in accordance
with the curve.The curve for tube and tile construc-
tion boilers should be stretched out by about 20 to
40 %, dependingon the type of constructionused, to
give the refractories time to reach equilibrium tem-
peratures.
Air should be vented from the pressure parts
until pressure has reached at least 1.5 bar (g). The
superheater drain should be kept open until the unit
is operating at no less than 20 % of MCR or until
superheatermetal temperaturesare under control.
Shutting down and banking should also follow
definite procedures. A pile of bagasse left on the
grate will smolderresulting in a dangerous accumu-
lation of explosive gas in the furnace and/or boiler
passes.
27.8.3 Control systems
Water level and combustion controls should be
tuned to provide stable operating conditions. Let-
down stations to process should be tuned to avoid
large load swings being imposed on the boiler sta-
tion.
The lack of proper water level control is fre-
quently cited as a major problem in the cane sugar
industry. The most common causes of unstable wa-
ter level are:
Large, short cycle load swings;
Unstable combustiondue to cyclic fuel feed;
High boiler water alkalinity;
Oil in the boiler feed water;
Poorly tuned controlloop;
Oversized feed water pumps;
Oversized feed water control valve;
Undersized steam drum.
Where appropriate, older single element or two-el-
ement control loops should be replaced with three-
element controls. On three-element loops, the feed
water flow signalmust track the steamflow signalac-
curately without the water level signal dominating.
If the fuel feed across the width of the boiler is
not uniform, a standing wave can form in the steam
d
r
u
m opposite the point where fuel flow is highest.
Thisoftenmanifestsitself aswater carryovertothose
superheatertubes drawingsteam from this area.
The most common causes of combustion insta-
bility are:
Irregularfuel feed;
High fuel effectivemoisturelevels;
High excess air levels;
Inappropriate overfire air nozzle placing and/or
design.
27.8.4 Other operational concerns
Furnace slagging and boiler convection heat-
ing surface foulingproblems are not common in the
cane sugar industry when the dissolved solids con-
tent (Brix)in bagasse is less than about4 % although
they may occur at higher Brix levels and when tops
and trash and/or coal is burned as well. Reducing
Brix by improvingextraction is the best way of pre-
venting them. Minor reductionsin their severity can
be obtained by reducingthe primary air temperature,
and changing the excess air and overfire to primary
27.8.4 Other operationalconcerns
airratios.These, however, arepalliativesand may or
may not help.
Tube erosion is a common problem. It occurs
where sand in the gas stream impinges on heating
surfaces. This usually happens where gases change
direction on entering the superheater pass, around
comers in multi-pass convection banks and at the
endsof economizertube banks. Keeping gas veloci-
tieslow ( 4 2m/s) and,whereappropriate,baffletips
clearof tube surfaceshelps containtheproblem. Re-
arrangingtube geometry and using smallerdiameter
tubes at the expense of performance can sometimes
help alleviatesevereproblems.Meuronen (2003)re-
ports thathigher wearrates can be expected on tubes
located alongside boiler walls as opposed to those
located in the centre of a bank. He also reports that
for in-line banks higher wear rates can be expected
on tubes that are locateddeeperwithin the bank. His
Iindings are supported in practice. For staggered
tube arrangementshe reports that the secondrow of
tubes suffers the most erosion.
Furnacetubecracksfrequentlyoccurinpanelwalls
where tube fins aremore than 30 mm wide. They also
occur where weldmg is not carried around the ends of
fins exposed to fumace radiation such as might hap-
pen around spy holesor any otherfumacepenetration.
Tubecrackingis acceleratedby internalscale.
Metal surfaces will corrode during the crop if
they are allowedto operatebelow the acid dew point
temperature. Air heater andor economizer tubes
are particularly prone to attack. In both cases, as
discussed in Section 27.5.2,corrosion can be con-
tained by correct design. Thermocouplesshould be
attached to "at risk" surfacesso that correctivemea-
sures, such as bypassing the air flow around an air
heater to prevent over cooling of the tubing, can be
taken when appropriate. Bypass dampers should be
automated where possible. High airflow velocities
lower air heater tube temperatures. Baffles can be
fitted to ducting to distribute air flow evenly across
a tube bank and hence eliminate high velocity con-
centrations. CFD studies help with this analysis.To
prevent economizer corrosion the feed water tem-
perature should always be abovethe acid dew point.
High temperaturecorrosion can occur in superheat-
ers when steam temperatures exceed 440 "C. The
mechanism is complicated but is usually more pro-
nounced when burning high chlorine fuels that are
also high in alkali metals. If sulfur is present as well
severe corrosioncan occur in a matter of months.
Most external corrosion damage occurs during
the off-crop. Heating surfacesshould not be cleaned
by washing down unless they can be properly dried
before the boiler is "boxed"; i.e. closed up for stor-
age. Hot air can be blown through the air and gas
passes to prevent metal temperatures dropping be-
low the acid dew point.
Internal surfaces can be protected from corro-
sion during the off-crop by drying the unit out com-
pletely and putting trays of desiccant material such
as quicklime (CaO) or silica gel into headers and
drums before boxing up. Alternatively, units can be
filled up completely with water and dosed with an
oxygen scavenger. Engineershave their own prefer-
ences for their particular situation depending on the
type of unit, the length of off-crop and the ambient
conditions.
27.8.5 Upgrading boilers
Many of the older boilers in the industry, par-
ticularly thosethathave morethan two drumsandlor
multi-passconvectionbankswere designedat a time
when the combustion of bagasse was not as well
understood as it is today. As a result many of these
units have grates that are larger than required and
hence they lend themselves to having their capaci-
ties increased. It is not soeasy to increase operating
pressure as this normally requires expensive pres-
sure parts to be replaced. Steam temperature can
usually be increasedwithin reason.
Enhancing performanceof existingplant is often
a cost-effectiveway of incrementallyincreasingfac-
tory throughput. Unfortunately,there is no general
rule for establishing what steam output a particular
unit is capableof achieving.Whilststudiesshow that
capacitiesfrequentlycan be increasedby as much as
20 %, a full analysis of a unit must be undertakento
establish its potential and "pinch points". This must
cover as a minimum the following:
Fuel and ash quality;
Fuel feed, furnace design and overfire air de-
sign;
Superheater design and materials of construc-
tion;
Convectionpass designwith particularreference
to gas velocity profiles;
Heat recovery tower performance;
Fan capacities;

27.9.5 Feed water treatment
Chemicals are dosed into the boiler system to
maintain the correct boiler water chemistry. In the
classic treatment regime caustic soda is used to con-
trol pH. Dosing should takeplace as far upstream as
possible to protect the pre-boilersystemas well. So-
dium sulfiteis dosedas anoxygen scavengerintothe
deaerator storage vessel or immediately afterit. Tri-
sodium phosphate is dosed into the steam drum to
Captureany hardnessthat may have slippedthrough.
This chemicalshould not be dosed into the feed line
as it will precipitate hardness in the feed line and
economizer,if oneis installed.Newer regimes,often
using volatile reagents, are making their presence
felt. For them to be successfulthey must all mop up
residual oxygen and hardness and control pH. Hy-
drazine must not be used as an oxygen scavengerin
the food industry. It is poisonous.

27.10.1 Pipeworkdesign
calculations should be carried out on long, large
bore pipelines to confirm pipe diameter selections.
It is best to use conservativepressuredrops,bearing
in mind that they vary as the square of velocity, in
order to cater for unusual steamdemands.Frequent-
ly high pressure drops result in a significantloss of
power and can also become a production bottleneck
when trying to process a difficultcrop.
There are a number of different types of steam
traps on the market. Expert advice should be sought
before selecting the types of traps required.'signifi-
cant amounts of energy can be lost if traps are not
maintained.
Wedge gate or parallel slide valves should be
used forisolating purposes.These valves should not
be used as control valves. Globe or V-port parallel
slide valves should be used for this purpose. Where
double isolating valves are used, a small diameter
"telltale" valve should be installed between them to
enablethe shutoff effectivenessof each to be proven
and to depressurize the systemif maintenanceis re-
quired.
Water traps, such as Kelburn separators, are
used in steam lines to prevent massive slugs of car-
ryover entering steam turbines. They generally rely
on centrifugal force to separate the water from the
steam. They are "last resort" devices. If boilers are
correctlydesignedand operatedand water treatment
is kept within recommended limits, slug carry over
should not occur.

27.10.2 Pressure letdownsystems
When high pressure steam is let down to exhaust
pressure the enthaIpy remains virtually constant;
i.e. the process is adiabatic. Depending on inlet and
outlet conditions the outlet steam temperature is
about 15 to 30 O C
lower than the main steam tem-
perature. As exhaust is usually used in non-contact
heat exchangers where saturated steam is required
formaximumheat transfer,letdown steammust also
be desuperheated. For temperature control purpos-
es, letdown steam is desuperheated to about 10 O
C
above saturationtemperature.
The quantity of high pressure steam required to
produce 1 t of letdown desuperheatedsteam can be
calculatedfrom simultaneousequationsdefining the
mass and energybalances i.e.:
From equations27.18 and 27.19 the fraction of high
pressure steam needed is:
and the amountof spray water required is:
Table 27.25 schedules the amount of high pressure
steam needed to produce 1tonne of exhaust steam.
Where there is a possibility of the spray water
not being totally evaporated within the valve body a
stainless steel liner should be installed in the down-
stream pipeline to prevent pipeline thermal fatigue.
This occurs when relatively cold water impinges
cyclicallyon a hot pipeline.
Suspended or dissolved solids in spray water
will deposit in the system. Good quality, deaerated
exhaustcondensateis usually good enough to use as
spray water for the processpressure letdown station.
For superheater interstage desuperheating and for
desuperheaterslocated upstream of a turbine a high-
er quality water is required. As a rule of thumb this
should be equal in quality to or better than the qual-
ity of steam leaving the boiler steam drum.At boiler
pressures of up to 60 bar this translates into water
having a solids concentration of less than 1mgtkg.

Demineralized water or condensed saturated steam
taken from the steamdrumcan be used for this pur-
pose. In the latter case, feed water or combustion air
or a combinationof both can be used as a heat sink.
There are a number of different types of let
dowddesuperheating valves on the market. Those
that combine both functions within the same valve
body often do a good control job but sometimes
suffer from thermal fatigue. Where the Ap is large
it is sometimes better to break the pressure down
in two stages. Pressure and temperatwe tappings
should be located well downstream of the letdown/
desuperheating station. Each manufacturer has his
own recommendationsfor the correct positioning of
pressure and temperaturetapping points.
Safetyvalves shouldbe installedin thepipework
after a letdown station to protect the line and the
equipmentconnectedto it in case the controlsfail.
Whilst someletdown stations are relatively qui-
et, some can be very noisy. Attenuating noise suc-
cessfully is difficult. Noise generated in a letdown
station dissipates radially from the station as well
as axially down the piping. Enclosing the letdown
station in a sound muffler or special acoustically
lined building can absorb radial noise. Increasing
the thicknessof the thermal laggingcan help absorb
axial noise. Specialist help is often needed to solve
noise problems.

28.1 Steam availablefrom
bagasse
28.1.1 Quantity of bagasse
The quantity of bagasse is determined primar-
ily by the fiber content of the cane being processed.
Nearly all of it ends up in the bagasse, but some
finds its way into the raw juice going to the factory,
and some bagacillo is usually required for use on
the rotary vacuum filters. Both these leave the fac-
tory in the filter cake. In the absence of these losses,
the bagasse quantity m, could be calculated from
the cane mass riz,by the following equation:
This gives a range of typical values for the bagasse
quantity produced, based on average fiberand mois-
ture contents, of between 27 and 32 tI100 t cane.
The amount of bagasse lost in the raw juice and
the filters depends on whether milling or diffusion
is being practiced. Typical values are given inTable
28.1. These values assume that the quantity of raw
juice is roughly the same as the quantity of cane be-
ing crushed, and that the bagasse moisture content
is 50 %.
In round figures, the quantity of bagasse is re-
duced in milling by 2 and in diffusion by 0.75 t per
100t cane. If mud recycle is practiced in diffusion
factories, no fiber is lost in filter cake, and it all ends
up in the final bagasse.
There is also a seasonal effect in many sugar-
producing areas. The fiber content is sometimes
lowest in the peak of the season, when the Brix
loading, and hence factory steam load, is at its high-
est.
In practice a small proportion of the bagasse
should be put aside in a bagasse store for recovery
and use during start-up or shutdown, or for use dur-
ing mill stops. This should be somewhere between
5 and 10% of the total amount of bagasse produced.
This amount is dependent on the time efficiency of
the mill.
Given all the issues which affect the amount of
bagasse available for steam production on a con-
tinuous basis, the amount of bagasse available may
be anywhere between 22 and 35 tI100 t cane, but is
more usually in the range 25 to 30 t/100 t cane.

28.2 Sugar mill steam require-
ments
28.2.1 Prime mover energy require-
ments
The major high pressure steam requirement is
for prime movers and is largely determined by the
split between electric motors and steam turbines.
Where high energy efficiency is sought, it is gen-
eral practice to use electric motors; electric power
is generated on high efficiency turbo-alternators
and the overall high pressure steam requirement is
reduced. If steam turbines are used as prime mov-
ers for mills, shredders, knives, pumps etc. the ef-
ficiency of the turbines is generally much lower and
morehigh pressuresteamis necessary.
The starting point is an estimate of the power
required by the prime movers. This is generally in
the range of 25 to 35 kWhIt,. It depends on how
many mills are used, how much power is required
for cane preparation and the other power require-
ments of the mill. A typicalbreakdown of this pow-
errequirementis shown in Table 28.2.
Table 28.2: Sugarmill absorbed power requirement
Canepreparation 8 5 6.4
Milling 10 12 10.5
Powerhouseturbines 10 18 15.0
Boiler auxiliaries 2 - -
Total 30 35 31.9
28.2.2 Balancebetween high pressure and exhaust steamrequirements
The values given by Hugot (1986) show that
variations can be quite large depending on circum-
stances; in general Hugot's numbers are high by
present standards. Advances in energy efficiency
have brought these numbers down. The use of vari-
able speed drives on pumps, fans and centrifugals,
particularly with regenerative braking, have helped
to reduce these power requirements. The use of dif-
fusion instead of milling reduces this requirement
by about 5 kWhIt,.
A value of 30 kWh/tc seems a reasonableaver-
age in most cases. Installed power may be some-
what higher.
The amount of steamrequired is determinedby
the HP steampressure, the exhaustpressureand the
efficiency of the turbines. A number of combina-
tions of boiler pressure and turbine efficiency can
be chosen to give the required specific steam con-
sumption.The steamrequired for the options avail-
ableis discussed in more detail in Chapter 30.
28.2.2 Balance between high pressure
and exhaust steam require-
ments
If the exhaust steam produced by steam tur-
bines is greater than that required in the factory,
surplus exhaust steam will need to be blown off to
atmosphere.This is not a sustainable situation, and
generallyoccursif thehigh pressure steamis gener-
ated at a lower than averagepressure, or if the steam
turbines in use are inefficient. The situation can be
improved by reducing theexhaust steampressure.If
raising the HP steam pressure is not an option, the
situationcan be rectified by makinguse of more ef-
ficient prime movers,eithersteamor electric.
If it is essential to vent steam,it is betterto blow
off vapor 1 than exhaust steam. This ensures that
all good quality exhaust steam condensate can be
recovered for boiler feed water, and allows a some-
what greater evaporation rate to be achieved on the
evaporators.This can be achievedby settingthe va-
por 1 relief valve to blow off at a pressure closer to
its normal operatingpressure so that in most cases
it will blow off before the exhaust steam blowoff
operates.
If there is a surplus of exhaust steam, there
is no point in reducing the steam used in the pro-
cess house, as it will merely result in more exhaust
steambeing blown to atmosphere.Oncethe process
steamrequirementis established,the specificsteam
consumption of the prime movers must be chosen
such that the steamrequired is less than the process
steamusage.
28.2.3 Steam losses
There will always be some energy losses which
translateintoadditional steamusage. At start-upthe
ranges need to be heated up and so losses are ex-
perienced. Under normal operation, there are heat
losses to the ambient, leaks (hopefully minor) and
occasional venting, due largely to unsteady opera-
tion. Losses occur in all steam ranges and an aver-
age loss of about 3 % seems reasonable.
Ithas also been proposed that the lossis not lin-
early related to the size of the mill. An empirical
equation is sometimes used, based on the crushing
rate mc in tlh, such as:
where n and c are constants. The value of n may be
taken as 0.67 and c typically has a value of about
0.1.
28.3 Process steam usage
Process steam refers to all exhaust steam used
in evaporation, in the pan station and in juice heat-
ing. This will also includethe effectof any diffuser
heating requirements.
In most casesthisrepresentssomethingbetween
40 and 60 t steam1100 t cane. The most steam-
efficient mills that operate electrical cogeneration
plants forexportof power achievethe lowest figure,
while the higher number is found in factories with
higher than averagecane fibercontentin an attempt
to avoid a bagasse surplus,or if otheractivities such
as a white end refinery are supported. In the ab-
sence of condensingturbines, all the exhaust steam
produced should be used in the process house. In a
diffusionmill the minimum exhaust steamproduc-
tion is estimated to be 37 t steam1t cane (Reidand
Rein 1983) with full electrification. This figure is
Referencesp. 678
670 28 Factory steam balance
higher with milling, but exhaust steam production
ceases to be a constraintif condensingturbines are
used.
Minimum process steam usage using present
technology is estimated variously to be 35 t/100 t
cane (Reid and Rein 1983), 33 tI100 t cane (Broad-
foot 2001) and 34 t/100 t cane (Kong Win Chang et
al. 2001). These values can only be achieved with
extensive process integration, which has adverse
implications for operability unless the plant is al-
ways run very steadily.
28.3.1 Evaporatorconfiguration
The number of evaporator effects and the ex-
tent of vapor bleeding have the greatest effect on
the process steam required. The effect of different
arrangementsis shown in Table 12.4. It is usual to
adjust the number of effects and the vapor bleed ar-
rangements to obtain the appropriateexhaust steam
usage that is consistent with the desired steam and
bagasse usage.
28.3.2 Pan requirement
This depends largely on the type of boiling
schemein operation.Those schemesthat use a min-
imum number of boilings and minimize the recycle
of low-grade sugar use less steam. It is shown in
Chapter 15 that high exhaustions in the pans lead
to lower steam requirements. For a given type of
boiling scheme, the steam usage is determined by
the dissolved solids or Brix rate to the pan floor. In
addition, the purity of the syrup has an effect, with
lower purity generally requiring more recycling
of sugar and a higher steam usage. The amount of
steam required in the pan house varies widely. In
Australia it is estimated that steam or vapor usage
is in the range of 0.9 to 1.1t/t DS in syrup to the
pan floor (Broadfoot 2001) for the Australian boil-
ing scheme.The VHPandDoubleEinwurf schemes
use somewhat more steam but therange of 0.9 to 1.2
t steam/t DS in syrupcovers all systems.
T
t is possible to calculate the amount of wa-
ter evaporated in the pans from a pan house mass
balance. However, water is added to centrifugals,
blow-up tanks and the remelter, all of which needs
to be evaporated. Some steam will also be used on
the centrifugals, the sugar drier and in heating the
water of the reheater calorifier. It is common prac-
tice to apply a "pan factor" to the calculated pan
evaporation to take account of this extra evapora-
tion requirement. A factor of 1.3 is conservative.
and a value of 1.15 to 1.25 may be more appropri-
ate.
The choice of a lower pressure steam from a
later evaporator effect has a marked influence on
steam usage. It is not uncommon to see continuous
pans operating on vapor 2 and in some cases batch
pans as well (Reidand Rein 1983). Vapor recom-
pression on continuous pans is also a feasible op-
tion because of the steadyevaporationrate.This has
been occasionally used in the beet sugar industry
but not in cane sugar factories.
28.3.3 Juice heatingrequirements
It is still usual to use exhaust steam on heating
clarified juice prior to the evaporators in order to
achieveatemperatureabovethe boiling point in the
firsteffect. Otherwiserawjuice heatingis generally
done using vapor 1 and sometimes vapor 2 on pri-
mary heating. Calculation of the quantitiesinvolved
is outlinedin section 9.1.
28.3.4 Options for reducing process
steam usage
If it is necessary to reduce the process steamus-
age to get a factory into balance, or to be able to
generatea surplusof bagassefor cogenerationor by-
product opportunities, a number of options can be
considered.Theseare listed as follows:
Do maximum evaporation in multiple effect in
the evaporators, not the pans. This means the
syrup Brix from the evaporators should be as
high as possible.
Increase the number of evaporatoreffects.
Make good use of condensate flash.
Use vapor 1
,vapor 2 or even vapor 3 on the pan
floor.This may require upgrading of pans to im-
prove circulation with a lower pressure heating
steam.
Improve the exhaustionsin the pan station, par-
ticularly in A massecuite boiling and centrifug-
ing.
28.4.1 High presure steam
Minimize the amount of water used in the pans
and centrifigals. In order to do this, it is gen-
erally necessary to measure and control this
amountof water.
Use clarified juice instead of water for duties
such as melting sugar.
Usea liquidlliquidheater to do the first stageof
heating of raw juice with condensate. This also
servesthe purpose of cooling down condensate
for use as imbibition on the mills. It is not an
option with diffusion, where the raw juice is al-
ready at a temperatureof 60 "Cor higher.
Use vapor 1 and vapor 2, and perhaps even va-
por 3, for juice heating. This may require ad-
ditionalheater surface area.
Reduce the amount of imbibition on the mills;
this will affect extraction adversely.
Reduce filter wash water; this will increase the
loss of sugarin filtercake, or practicemud recy-
cling.
Increase the bleed vapor temperatures to gain
more from bleeding vapor. This generally re-
quiresmore evaporatorheatingsurface.
Ensurethatany valveswhich canletdownsteam
from exhaust to vapor 1 or vapor 2 are sealing
completely.Theseletdownsshouldbe used only
on start-up or shutdown, and ideally should in-
corporatea doublevalve andbleed arrangement
to eliminate the possibility of unwanted and un-
noticed bypassing.
28.4 Overall steam balance
A factory steam balance is best planned and
designed using a diagram similar to that shown in
Figure 28.1. The data on this diagram are for a mill
crushing 10 000 t,ld with a fiber content of 14.0
kg1100 kg cane, producing bagasse with a moisture
content of 51 kg1100 kg bagasse. The process steam
data come from the evaporator data in Table 12.4
for a quintuple effect evaporator (case 9). This is
a fairly efficient factory and can send 12% of its
bagasse to a by-product use; or otherwise reduce
the boiler efficiency to consume more bagasse. Fig-
ure 28.2 shows the situation for a factory which is
less steam-efficient,making very little use of vapor
bleeding.Lessefficientturbines are used and a boil-
er efficiencyof 65 % keeps the factory in balance.
The starting point must always be the amount
of bagasse available. After making allowance for
storage of some bagasse for subsequent reclaim,
the boiler capacity and pressure must be chosen to
bum the required amount of bagasse. At the same
time a knowledge of the amount of steam required
is necessary in order to choose the combination of
boiler pressure and boiler efficiencywhich will pro-
vide this.
Generally some flexibilityin the boiler efficien-
cy is desirable to cope with variations in bagasse
production rate during the season. This may vary
with cane crushing rate and with the fibercontent of
the cane,as equation (28.1) shows.
28.4.1 High pressure steam
Thecorrectplaceto startin definingtheHP steam
pressure and the turbine requirements is the exhaust
steam pressure and temperature (Inkson and Misplon
2005).From there the next stepis tochoosetheupper
end of the steam cycle, in close cooperation with the
turbine supplier.
The power required for all the prime movers in
thefactoryneedstobeestablished.Thesteamrequired
dependson the choice of boiler pressure andefficien-
ciesof turbo-alternatorsand mill turbines.Thechoice
of prime movers should lead to a steam requirement
somewhat less than is available from the boilers and
lessthanthe process steamrequirements.Thebalance
should be let down to the exhaust range. The regu-
lation of the letdown steam is the way of achieving
control of the exhaust steam pressure. The choice of
exhaustpressureneeds to be made before the turbine
requirementscan be fixed (Section 12.5.3).
Ideally there should always be some letdown of
steam at all times, so that the exhaust pressure can
be controlled at a steady value. Bearing in mind the
variations in steam demand in different parts of the
plant at different times, it has been suggested that on
average the exhaust letdown should be between 5 %
and 25 % of the exhaust requirement, and preferably
closer to the upper end of the range under average
conditions.
In someoldermills,highpressuresteammay also
be used for steam ejectors removing incondensable
gases from evaporatorsandpans.

28.4.3 Otherfactors affectingthe steambalance
28.4.3 Otherfactorsaffectingthesteam
balance
Instantaneous vs. overall balance. The differ-
ence between the instantaneous and overall steam
balance needs to be recognized. The overall bal-
ance needs to take account of the effect of inter-
mittent or unsteady operations due to mill start-up,
shutdown and unscheduled mill stops. The effectis
that the steadcane ratio will be somewhat higher
on an overall basis than might be expected from
looking at instantaneous steady state values. This
differenceis of the order of 3 t steam1100 t cane in
a well-run factory.
Effect of crushing rate. It is inevitable that at
times the mill will run at lower crushing rates, due
to cane supply or operationalproblems, and that at
times there will be a desireto crush at a higher than
average rate for various reasons. Both these situa-
tions can have a significant effect on the steam bal-
ance. Most noticeable is the effect on the bagasse
surplus/deficitsituation. Above or below the opti-
mum break even point, a surpluscan be produced or
a deficit situation can be realized very quickly. Op-
erational responses may include altering the boiler
efficiency by bypassing some of the heat recovery
equipment, changing the imbibition rate and some-
times burning supplementary fuel, which however
is costly and to be avoided if possible.
Effectof cane and bagasse quality. Changesin
cane fiber content and ash content can significantly
affectthe quantity and quality of bagasse available,
due to seasonal and climatic factors. This affects
the quantity of bagassenecessary tobeburned, with
a significant effect on the bagasse balance.
Changes in the composition of the cane also
affect the juice quality and quantity and hence the
load on the evaporators and the pan floor, changing
the steamrequirement.
Comparison of milling vs. diffusion. The dif-
ferencebetween milling and diffusion is covered in
some detail in Section 6.7.3. The most significant
differenceis the vastly reduced power required for
the diffusion extraction plant. High pressure steam
to a diffusion extraction plant is roughly one-third
of that required in milling and the amountof steam
letdown to the exhaust range is increased corre-
spondingly (Rein and Hoekstra 1994). The other
major difference is that the quantity of bagasse
available for the boilers is higher with diffusion
because less leaves the site in filter cake, and may
be eliminated entirely if clarifier mud recycle is
practiced. The overall quantity of steamrequired is
little changed and is affected largely by the vapor
bleeds chosen for heating on the diffuser.van Hen-
gel (1990) pointed out that the alternativeto a high
steam letdown is to choose lower pressure boilers,
reducing the cost of the boiler plant.
Effect of electrification. High efficiency and
minimum steam usage can be achievedwith exten-
siveuse of electricdrives. This doesnot necessarily
reduce the overall prime mover power requirement
-the plan for high efficiencyat Pioneer in Australia
still requires 30 kWh/tc (Lavaracket al. 2004) and
estimates in Mauritius assume 28 kWhIt, (Kong
W
i
n C h q et al. 2001) - but the amount of high
pressure steam required for the sugar mill complex
is greatly reduced.
Effect of bagasse moisture content. Lower
bagasse moisture significantly affects the steam1
bagasse ratio shown in Table 27.8. The amount of
bagasse produced is slightly reduced becauseof the
lower moisture content, but the overall effect is a
very much improved ability to generatesteam with
drier bagasse.It is always beneficialto strivefor the
lowest possible bagasse moisture content for this
reason. There is an added benefit in the increased
extraction obtained. This is one of the key opera-
tional performanceparameters to be monitored.
28.4.4 Power availablefor export
Cogeneration of power is mistakenly taken to
mean the generation of power surplus to the mill's
needs, which is available for sale to third parties.
Inkson and Misplon (2005) suggest that cogenera-
tion couples a user of low grade heat, in this case
the process house, to the power generation station.
Surplus power may be exported during cogenera-
tion when the mill is running or burning stored ba-
gasse when the mill is stopped.
Practical implications of power export are cov-
ered in Section30.6. The potential for cogeneration
lies in utilizing whatever high pressure steam can
Referencesp. 678
28 Factory steam balance
be produced to maximize the generation of power
in efficient turboalternators. Ideally all steam let-
down to exhaustis throughgeneratingturbines, and
if a surplus relative to the factory's needs is gener-
ated, use of a condensing turbine may be made to
maximizepower production. The controlof exhaust
pressure is achieved by controlling the flow to the
generating turbines to keep the exhaust range pres-
sureconstant, or in the caseof condensingturbines,
controlling the pass-out to the exhaustrange.
The steam balance diagram then looks some-
what different as shown in Figure 28.5.
Themosteffectiveway of increasingthe amount
of power available is through the use of high pres-
sure boilers. The amount of surplus that can be ex-
ported dependson a range of factors and is summa-
rized in Table28.3.
If condensing turbines are used, then power
available for export is also affected by the process
steamusage. In the extremecase of 8.1 MPa (80bar
(g))boilers,process steamusage of below 40 ti100 t
cane must be achieved. Wright (2000) has shown
that mechanical vapor recompression (MVR) is
not useful in increasing power available for sale,
since the power required by the compressoris more
than the additional power which can be generated
thereby.
For a conventional 300 tJh factory, Rein and
Hoekstra (1994)calculatedthatwith 3.2MPa(31bar
(g))boilers, a surplusof 1.9MW would be available
for sale from a mill and 6.4 MW from an equivalent
diffuser mill. Thisillustratesthe potential advantage
which diffusion has in a cogenerationmill.
28.5 Vapor recompression
28.5.1 Situations conducive to recom-
pression
Recompression of vapor can help improve the
steamefficiency of a sugar mill substantially in the
right conditions. This may be achieved either by
vapor recompression, using high pressure steam
through a steam nozzle (thermo-compressor) to
compressa lowerpressurevapor to an intermediate
pressure, or through mechanical vapor recompres-
sion (MVR) using a centrifugal compressor to do
the recompression.
The requirement for thermo-compressionis the
availabilityof surplus high pressure steam to do the
recompression.This makes use of steam that would
otherwise be let down to the exhaustrange through
a controlvalve.
For mechanical vapor recompression to be ad-
vantageous there must be surplus power available
and a prime mover to drive the compressor. In some
caseswhere electricalpower is cheap, it may be op-
portune to purchase power for this purpose.
In both cases, the benefitis maximized when all
conditions are steady within the mill. Fluctuating
conditionsmake it difficultto extract the maximum
advantagefrom vapor recompression.
Thermo-compression has been practiced in
various industries for many years. Its big advantage
lies in its simplicity and low cost. The main prob-
lem associatedwith these deviceslies in the need to
keep very close to design pressures and flow rates,
because efficiency falls off very rapidly as devia-
tions fromthese conditionsoccur,particularly if the
motive steampressure drops.The entrainment ratio
(ratio of entrained vapor to motive steam) is cru-
cial and there is little information in the literature
that enablesit to be calculated. Resultsof test work
undertaken on compressingevaporatorvapor using
a thermo-compressor were compared against an
empiricalformula given by Hugot (1986:558).This
gave values of entrainment ratio that were lower
than empirical formulae suggest (Reid and Rein
1983).
The turndown on a thermo-compressoris poor
and deviations from design conditions should be
lessthan 10%. In orderto achievesomevasiation in
capacity without changing the pressure conditions,
a setof different sizedthermo-compressorsmust be
installed,which are individually switchedon or off
such that the combination gives the required flow
rate.
The efficiency drops off rapidly as the pres-
sure ratio (ratio of pressure of compressed vapor
to aspirated vapor) increases. This limits its use to
compressing vapor across just one stage or at the
most two stages of an evaporator.This device has
a further disadvantage when recompressing vapor
1 to exhaust in that it results in mixing sometimes

28.5.3 Mechanical vapor recompres-
sion
This has been used with successin the beet and
cane industry to improve thermal efficiency. The
MVR can be driven-by a steam turbine, in which
case pressure control can be achieved by varying
the turbine speed, or by an electric motor, in which
case adjustableinlet vanes are normally employed.
It is capable of a much higher entrainment ratio, up
to about 5, compared to a thermo-compressor that
is limited to values of less than 2.5. Nonetheless the
MVR is also better suited to applicationswhere the
pressureincrease is not too large, or else the sizeof
the compressorrises rapidly and may require more
than onestage.
In order to get any kind of significanteffect, the
compressor and its drive need to be of fairly large
size. Allan et al. (1983) describe experiences with
an MVR driven by a 690 kW steam turbine com-
pressing vapor 1 to exhaust steam. This adds 2.7
kWh/tc to the prime mover power requirement and
representsa power usageof 23 kWh/t of vaporcom-

29 Water and condensatesystems
29.1.2 Evaporation losses
Evaporationoccursfromcertain process streams
andduringjuice flashing.Partof thewater condensed
in direct contact condensers will evaporate in cool-
ing towers or spray ponds, to provide the evapora-
tive coolingrequired. As much as 85 % of the vapor
condensed evaporates to provide the cooling.There
is also a driftlossfrom the coolingsystem (typically
5 % of the water flow in the coolingsystem),but this
is aphysical and not an evaporation loss.In addition
some evaporation of scrubber water occurs in wet
scrubbers.The latter is around 10 % of the amount
of HP steam generated.

29.2 Boiler feed water
29.2.1 Condensaterecovery
--- r
Condensatewill always be used'as water of first
choice for boiler feed. The quantity of condensate
produced is much larger than the amount required
in the boilersand the surplus should be used for pro-
cess water duties in themill.The amountsof various
grades of condensate are dependent on the config-
uration of the evaporators and the extent of vapor
bleeding. A steam balance is necessary to calculate
the condensate flows from heaters, evaporators and
pans.
29.2.2 Condensate quality
Selecting the best quality condensate for boiler
feed generally means using exhaust steam conden-
sate to the maximum extent, since it is the clean-
est. Vapor 1 and later condensates are sometimes
contaminated with volatile components, which are
evaporated with water in the evaporators and pans,
and in addition these condensates can potentially
be contaminated by carryover of sugar juice dur-
ing boiling. Apart from sugar, these condensates
can also contain smallquantities of ethanol, volatile
organic acids such as formic and acetic acid, and
ammonia. Ethanol and organic acids enter the fac-
tory in the raw juice and are generally formed by
degradationreactions in cane before milling andlor
in the milling plant. They may be volatilized in the
evaporatorsand in severe cases the acid vapors can
causecorrosionof calandriasand condensatepiping.
High levels of acetic acid in condensate were found
at a diffuser mill where over-liming in the diffuser
lead to high levels of acetic acid in juice (Schaffler
et al. 1988).In Louisiana high levels of organic acids

responsible for high levels of acid in condensates,

Ethanolin cane has been used as an indicatorof

are highestin vapor 1condensate,and reduce down
the evaporator(Wrightand Peterson 1998).Ethanol
contributes significantly to the COD loading in the
effluent leavingthefactory.
The maximum amount of sugar cmtamination

shown in Table 29.2.
At the higher pressures used to achieve very
high thermal efficiencies, a steam transformer may
be used (Magasiner 1996)to isolatethe boiler from
the factory.A system used in a refinery is described
in detail by Vawda (2002). The steam transformer
is a dedicated single stage evaporatorboiling water,
Erom which allexhauststeamcondensed can be safe-

the steamneeded for the factory.The cost penalty is
thecapitalcostof theevaporatorandthefactthat the
exhauststeamis generatedat a pressure higher than
the steam used in process by about 40 kPa (a vapor
saturation temperature higher by 5 to 6 "C).
This
system is recommended for boiler pressures above
40 bar (g) if zero contaminationof condensateis re-
quired, asTable 29.2suggests.
In evaporators and pans, the condensing steam
is at a higher pressure than the liquid being boiled.
Thus if there is a tube leak, condensateor steamwill
leak into the boiling liquid, and €he condensate will
not necessarily be contaminated,unless for instance

a pan is struck and for a short period of time the

29.2.3 Monitoring sugar contamina-
tion in condensate
Various ways of measuring traces of sugar in
condensate online have been reported. They are
generally expensive, complicated and involve an
unacceptable time lag. Methods investigated in-
clude colorimetric methods, online flame photom-
etermeasurementof potassium, measurementof pH
of high temperature reaction products, and a total
organic carbon (TOC) analyzer. None have found
routine application, other than the TOC analyzer,
which is used in three refineries. They can give
good results with measurements accurate down to
1 mg sugar per kg condensate. There is however a
measurement lag, reported as 8 minutes (Simpson
and Carreon 2003) and 7 minutes (TayJield and
Anderson 1983),as well as interferencefrom other
organics such as ethanol.
A fluorescence detector has been used with
somesuccess,but theprinciple of operationremains
unclear because sugar is not fluorescent (Herrara
2001). A more certain way of controlling contami-
nation is through the use of test tanks. Condensate
fillsup a set of tanks and each is tested in the labora-
tory before going forward to boiler feed water. This
is a tedious system but generallyeffective.
In-line measurement of the conductivity of the
condensate stream has been most widely used to
monitor sugar traces. It is an approximate meth-
od, since it does not measure sugar at all, but the
ionic impuritiesin thejuice or syrup with the sugar.
Sometimes spurious high conductivityreadings are
obtained, due to componentsthat have been volatil-
ized and that are not associatedwith physical cany-
over. When used to dump contaminatedcondensates
automatically, it sometimes results in condensate
being dumped unnecessarily; however this is not
Referencesp. 692
29 Water and condensate systems
normally a problem because of the large excess of
condensate over and aboveboiler feed requirements.
Temperature compensation is essential to improve
the reliability.
Conductivity measurements are recommended
as the best optionfor monitoring condensatesonline,
but cannot replace routine laboratory sugar trace
measurements, which are still the primary method
of measurement and control. However conductivity
is generally not useful in refineries where the level
of ash in the liquid streams is much lower.
Regular laboratory checks on all condensates
are essential to keep a check on entrainment, carry-
over or contamination occurring. Samples should be
taken from different parts of the condensate system
so that the cause of any contamination can be identi-
fied. High levels are used to alert the operators to
process problems in the plant that require corrective
action.
The a-naphthol test is most commonly used
and is quick and usually reliable. However it is only
semi-quantitative and the phenol-sulfuric acid or
resorcinol tests must be used for quantitative mea-
surements (SASTA 2005).
29.2.4 Softening
Most mills are equipped with a water soften-
ing plant to provide water for boilers for start-up
and emergency use. Unsoftened water should never
be used for boiler feed. When the boiler pressure
is above 40 bar (g), full demineralization of make
up water is called for. A properly functioning sugar
trace detection and boiler feed management system
should mean that the softening plant is rarely used.
29.2.5 Pressure-dependentquality
parameters
Apart from sugar in feed water, there are other
limits on the quality of feed water, which are tabu-
lated in Table 27.17, and depend on boiler pressure.
The higher the pressure, the more stringent are the
requirements on boiler feed water. Essentially they
require low hardness (and zero above 60 bar (g)), a
low oxygen content, decreasing with boiler pressure,
and a pH value between 8.5 and 9.5 in all cases.
29.2.6 Feed water storage
It is very important that sufficient feed water
storage capacity is provided, to ensure that there
is always sufficient water of good quality available
for periods of unsteady running, for start-up and
shutdown and to cover any problems with the con-
densate systems. Various rules of thumb have been
suggested, but a minimum storage capacity equiva-
lent to four hours steaming at average rate is recom-
mended. This includes storage in the hotwell as well
as in additional tank storage.
29.3 Factory process water re-
quirements
29.3.1 Imbibition
The amount of water used as imbibition varies
widely in different sugar industries, varying from as
little as 15% on cane to over 60 % on cane. The best
water supply to use for imbibition is condensate, and
preferably at as high a temperature as possible. With
diffusers imbibition at about 80 "C is used. Some
milling tandems are also able to use hot condensate,
but most operators of mill tandems opt to use a lower
temperature. The high temperature is alleged to melt
waxes that increase the slip on the rolls and make
target throughputs difficult to achieve. However
Honig (1953) reported that experiments in Java
showed imbibition water at 85 to 95 "C did not ex-
tract any more wax than water at 28 "C. Some mills
have shown that hot imbibition can be used to ad-
vantage to increase extraction, provided that the
mills have suitably rough mill rolls.
If lower imbibition temperatures are required, it
is better to cool the condensate by heating the raw
juice than to add lower quality water to the imbi-
bition supply tank to reduce its temperature. This
improves energy efficiency and does not inflate the
impurity load in raw juice.
29.3.2 Process water usage
Generally all factory process water needs i.e.
water added into the process, should be supplied
29.3.2 Process water usage I 29.4 Servicewater requirements
by surplus condensate. Assuming that all exhaust
condensate from the first effect evaporator is re-

proportion of condensates from other units is
required for boiler feed make up and the rest is
available for process water usage. This quantity is
affected by the amount condensed in the last ef-
fect, which is not availableforprocess usage,i.e. it
is affected by the steam economy of the mill. The
more steam efficient the mill, the more condensate
is available.

29.4 Servicewater require-
ments
Although condenser injection water may be re-
garded as service water, there is usually an overtlow
of water from these cooling systems because of the
direct condensation occuning and they generate a
surplus rather than require additional water input.
Quantitiesinvolved are covered in Section 13.1.5.
29.4.1 Raw water
Most mills have access to a supply of raw water
e.g. from a river, which can be used for wash water
or washing down or at start-up to provide an initial
supply of water. The use of external suppliesshould
be kept to a minimum, becausethey inflatethe quan-
tity to be disposed of ultimately. It is possible for a
mill to exist without an external supply, providing
water circuits in the mill arecarefully managed.
29.4.2 Treatedwater
A mill will oftenhave a water treatmentplant, to
treat raw water to drinking water standards for do-
mestic use. This water or a domestic water supply
is used in preference to raw water in the plant if an
outside source of water is necessary e.g. for soften-
ing water for boiler feed make up.
Referencesp. 692
29 Water and condensatesystems
29.4.3 Service coolingsystems
Cooling water is required for turbine bearings
and oil coolers. Once-through good quality water
is sometimes used for this, but a better solution
makes use of a small dedicated cooling tower sys-
tem. It should not be combined with other cooling
systems which may be contaminated with sugar,
because these cooling systems are vitally impor-
tant and must be free from the potential growth or
buildup of biomass in the system.
Separate cooling systems may also be used for
crystallizer cooling for similar reasons - fouling
of crystallizer elements and particularly corrosion
caused by degradingsugars in the system are high-
ly undesirable. The quantity of cooling water used
is significantbut a closed systemfor this duty has a
negligible effect on the water balance because the
heat load is not high.
Vacuum pump water is usually supplied from
the condenser cooling water circuit, although a
cooling tower for this duty may be installed, par-
ticularly to ensure a cool water supply under all
conditions.
29.4.4 Boiler ash and scrubber water
Boiler ash removal often incorporates sluicing
systems and/or submerged ash conveyors. This
water system is generally integrated with the wet
scrubber system,which incorporates a clarifierand
sometimesa belt filter to dewater the ash and boiler
smuts to produce a lower moisture and more eas-
ily handled cake. Generallya low quality source of
water is used to make up the boiler water scrubber
circuit. This is necessary to replace water evapo-
rated in the scrubber by the hot boiler gases and
the water in the ash and / or smuts dumped from
the system.
29.4.5 Firewatersupply
It is necessary to have a firewater reticulation
system. The water is generally drawn from the
coolingpond or cooling towers as the largestavail-
able source of water. It does not affect average wa-
ter flow rates in the mill.
29.5 Treatment of effluent
29.5.1 Surplus water handlingsystems
All mills will have a surplus of water to dispose
of. Somemills arefortunatein being able to dispose
of the surplus by irrigation onto fields by diluting
with irrigation water, providing runoff is monitored.
Others have ponding systems in which all surplus
water is contained during the crushing season, and
treated during the off-season.This is only an option
for mills with a shortcrushing season.
In all other cases, the surplus has to be treated
before it can either be reused or returned to a wa-
tercourse. In this case, attempts should be made to
reduce the quantity and the concentration of dis-
solved substances in the effluent. In some cases
where other by-products are produced at a mill, the
effluent streams may be combined andlor processed
to produce value-added products.
29.5.2 Quantity of surplus water to be
treated
The most cost-effective way of coping with a
surplus water or effluent disposal problem is to re-
duce the quantity to a minimum. Treatment of ef-
fluent is a pure cost with no added value and it pays
to keep the size of the problem as small as possible.
It is not possible to eliminate a surplus as the water
balance shows. In all cases, if there is a desire to
reduce effluent quantities to a minimum, it is nec-
essary to measure the quantity produced. Because
the effluentoften has suspendedmatter in it, a mag-
netic flow meter or a Parshall flume are the best
flow measurement options. Excessive use of water
for wash-down or cleaning also needs to be curbed.
Purchase (1995) reports that most factories without
cane washing plants produce on averageabout0.2 to
0.3 m3effluent4cane crushed.
All efforts should aim to reduce the intake of
any water other than that in the cane into the fac-
tory system.This requires containment,recycle and
reuse of water, particularly condensates. This also
requires sufficient storage of process water, so that
neither shortages nor surpluses are experienced un-
der unsteady conditions such as start-up and shut-
down. The need to contain rain water from the site

Efforts have been describedby both Wrightand

reducethequantityof effluentto a minimum.Jensen
and Schurnann describework to get to a "zero efflu-
ent" situation, not to be confused with zero surplus

sugar-containing or contaminated streams within a
factoryin suchaway thatthewater surplustothefac-
tory site is "clean" condensateand not effluent. This
is largely achieved by using recycled water rather
than condensate as imbibition. This has two draw-

process,leading to increasedmicrobiologicallosses,

ses as well. Secondly the condensate is not clean,
containing substantial quantities of ethanol, which
has a high COD; so it still needs treatment before
discharge.
Methods by which the quantity of effluent may
be reduced can be summarizedas:
Reduce the amount of fresh water into the fac-
tory;everytonneof waterbrought intothe facto-
ry from an external source (all water other than
that in cane)increasestheeffluentby exactlythe
same amount.
Close all cooling tower systems and stop once-
through cooling.
Use surplus condensate or cooling tower over-
flow for cleaningtwashdown.
Catch spillage in drains and return to the pro-
cess.
If practiced, reduce cane wash to the absolute
minimum.
Use clean condensate as make up in small ser-
vice cooling towers.
Use surplus cooling tower blowdown and con-
densateinthe scrubbersto makeup forevapora-
tion.
Make thefactorylesssteamefficient(notalways
an option).
If leaks and spills are to be recovered and put back
into process, it is important to ensure that microbial
activity in the drains and sumps is minimized. This
requires that drains arekeptempty asfar aspossible,
that the drains are in good repair with smooth sur-
facesto minimize microbialgrowth;furthermorethe
liquidshouldnot be allowed to standin the drains or
sumpsfor any length of time. Bunded areasmust be
separated so that spillages of different qualities can
be kept separate for return to the most appropriate
point Care must be taken to ensure that rain water
doesnot get into the collection areas.

29.5.3 Quality of surpluswater stream
Effluents from a sugar mill are non-toxic and
mainly biodegradable,sincethe dissolved substrates
are mainly organic in nature. This makes effluent
treatment on site a feasible proposition. By defini-
tion, a highly contaminated effluent implies large
losses in the factory.
Thequality of theeffluentstreamis normally as-
sessedfrom a measurementof COD (chemical oxy-
gen demand) or BOD (biological oxygen demand).
Both methods measure the quantity of oxygen re-
quired to oxidizethecompoundsdissolvedin the ef-
fluent, which is expressed in mg oxygen/kg effluent
or mg oxygenll effluent. COD is a quicker analy-
sis, involving boiling for 2-3 h with strong oxidiz-
i
n
g chemicals,usually potassium dichromatewith a
silversulfatecatalyst (SASTA2005). It is oftenused
in preferenceto BOD, an analysis which is not very
reliable and which requires bacterial digestion over
five days. Ln the case of fresh sugar mill effluents,
it is found that the COD is about twice the BOD,
but the ratio increases as decomposable material is
removed.
COD concentration corresponds to the amount
of oxygen that is required for full oxidation of all
organic carbon into carbon dioxide and water. The
COD-equivalent concentration can be calculated
from the stoichiometry of the combustion reactions
of the compoundsinvolved. For sucrose,
This implies that 1 mole of sucrose requires 12
moles of oxygen,or 1.12kg oxygenper kg sucrose.
Other compounds require differentamounts of oxy-
gen. For instance ethanol requires 2.09 kg oxygen
per kg ethanol.
Effluent from a mill can be quite variable, be-
ing much higher following a shut for cleaning, but
generally has a COD in the range of 2000 to 5000
mgkg. The major components in the eflluent are
of course sugars, but include dissolved inorganics
and ethanol and generally some suspended solids,
particularly small pieces of bagasse. Effluent from
ethanol distilleries is much higher in COD, above
30 000 mgkg.
The contribution of ethanol to the total effluent
load can be reduced somewhat by venting vapor 1
and vapor 2 calandrias to the atmosphere and not
into the rest of the evaporator system (Wright and
Peterson 1998).

29.5.5 Biological treatment
As standardsforeffluentsgetmorestringentover
time, it is increasinglynecessary to have to treat ef-
fluent to higher standards. Most environmentalreg-
ulations specify standards for COD (or BOD), pH,
temperatureand suspendedsolids. Of these, meeting
the COD or BOD limit generally dictates the size
and type of biological reactor to be used on sugar
mill effluent. The many options for effluent treat-
ment can be divided into two classes, either aerobic
(in the presence of oxygen) or anaerobic treatment
(excludingoxygen).Developmentsin improvingthe
efficiency of both categories of treatmenthave been
si,pificant as a greater emphasis is placed on meet-
ing increasinglymore severeeffluent standards.
Suspendedsolids are easily removed by screen-
ing. Excessive solids should be removed, or they
settleout in ponds, reducing the effectivevolumeof
the treatmentsystem.
Effluent streams usually have a temperature
in the range of 30 to 70 "C, which is suitable for
biological treatment. The processes are slowed at
the lower temperatures that may be experienced in
cooler winter months.
Aerobictreatment.Thisuses the addition of ox-
ygen to develop a biological culturethat breaks down
the organic contaminants in the effluent. 'I'he most
commontypes of aerobictreatmentprocess are:
Activated sludge: conventional with aerators,
pure oxygeninjection.
Activated sludge:extended aeration, aeration la-
goons.
High rate biofiltration: random media and struc-
turedmedia.
Rotating biologicalcontactors or trickle filters.
The oxygen requirements are roughly 0.5 to 1.5kg
O,/kg BOD, which are supplied in different ways
according to the process employed Generally the
process is quite energy-intensive and may use dis-
solved oxygen (DO) measurements to control the
energy input. The most common systems involve
surface aerators or blowing air into the system. The
purpose of both is to induce mixing and transfer
oxygen.A significantquantity of biomasss (sludge)
is produced, which is separatedfrom the treated liq-
uid and recycled to the reactor. Some of the sludge
has to be regularly wasted and may in itself consti-
tute a disposal problem. A schematic diagram of
the most commonly used activatedsludge systemis
shownin Figure 29.4.
High rate systemssuch as pure oxygen injection
can reduce the size of the aeration tank and mini-
mize the production of sludge. However operating
costs are high. Supplementary oxygen addition can
help if bulking sludge, i.e. sludge which will not
settle, occurs which is generally due to overloading
of the plant and insufficientdissolvedoxygen in the
reactor.

Anaerobic treatment. This takes place in an
environment from which oxygen is excluded. The
simplest form of anaerobic system is a large dam
into which mill effluent is directed. Oxygen in the
effluentis quickly depletedand the systembecomes
anaerobic,the pH drops and off-odorsare produced.
This is due to the production of volatile organic ac-
ids, the first step in anaerobictreatment.With insuf-
ficient microorganismsof the right type in the sys-
tem, very littleimprovementin the removal of COD
occurs. A residence time of at least 25 days in such
a pond system is requiredto get a signi6cantreduc-
tion in COD.
Land shortage and increased public sensitivity
to odor have promoted the need for better design
and the use of more efficientplants.The treatmentis
significantlyimprovedif oneof the various high rate
treatment systems availableis used, the most com-
mon of which are the Up-flow Anaerobic Sludge
Blanket (UASB), the expanded granular sludge bed
(e.g. Biothane), the hybrid reactor design and the
fully mixed reactor. Figure 29.5 shows schematic
diagrams of some of the types of anaerobic reactor
in use.
The key to successfultreatmentlies in maintain-
ing a high enough population of the rnicroorgan-
isms constituting the active biomass required. The
biomass retention time has to be uncoupled from
the hydraulic retention time, by returning separated
biomass to the system or ensuring that there are ad-
equate solid support systemsin the reactors to keep
Figure 29.4: Schematic arrange-
ment of a conventional activated
sludge plant (DOCdissolved oxy-
gen controller)
the biomass attached in the system.In high rate sys-
tems, biomass concentrations can be as high as 20
to 35 kg dried solids/m3,which leads to high volu-
metric treatment capacity. The hydraulic residence
time is much lower than the solids retention time in
the system.
A number of steps take place in an effective an-
aerobic treatmentprocess:
1. Acid formation: Acid-forming bacteria convert
the dissolved substances to volatile fatty acids
and alcohols.
2. Acetogenesis: The products of acid formation
are transformed to acetic acid and hydrogen by
acetogens.
3. Methanogenesis: Acetic acid and methanol
are converted to methane and CO, (biogas) by
methanogens.
The third step is generally rate-limiting and a
healthy population of methanogens is essential. If
the system is overloaded, the methanogens cannot
cope, the acid concentration increases and the pH
drops. This situation is characterized by off-odors
due to the volatile acids, mainly butyric and valeric.
The only action possible is to reduce the load and
give the systemtime to recover.There alsohas to be
sufficientchemicalbuffer capacity in the effluentto
be able to keep the pH between 6.5 and 8.0.Lime is
frequently added to the influent to raise the pH and
provide the buffer capacity.

the nature of the substrateand the finaleffluentqual-

30.1 Generationof electricity
30.1.1 Factory requirements
Because of the availability of bagasse fuel at a
cane sugar mill, this is usually the prime source of
fuelfor generating steamforprocess use. By produc-
ing the steam at a higher pressure and temperature
than that necessary for process use, the excess ener-
gy in the steam can be used to drive turbines, which
can supply mechanical power e.g. to cane prepara-
tion equipment and boiler feed pumps, and which
can drive alternators to provide electrical power for
the mill, and if surplus electricity is available, for
export to irrigation pumping loads, residential areas
and even for sale to a utility supply company.
To optimize mill electricity generation, the fol-
lowing parameters must be considered:
a) Process steam demand;
b) Bagasse availability for fuel;
c) Factory electrical demand;
d) Irrigation power requirements;
e) Electricity sale price;
f ) Cost of supplementary fuel;
g) Emergency power sources.
The availability and cost of plant and funding must
also be considered.
This section will only consider c) Factory elec-
tricity demand, and g) Emergency power sources,
the other considerations being specific to individual
mills.
The electricity demand of a mill depends mainly
on the cane crushing rate, but also on whether me-
chanical drive turbines or electric motors are used
for the larger loads, such as cane knives, shredders,
mill drives, boiler ID fans and feed pumps. Some
mills include in their electrical loads such items as
administration offices, residential villages and other
infrastructure. They may also list "installed" rather
than "absorbed" power. This can make it difficult to
compare the electrical loads of different mills.
Typical Southern African mills have specific
electrical demands of 21 to 22 kwh p a tonne of
cane (kWtc) when using mechanical drive tur-
bines on major cane preparation loads, and 29 to 31
k W t c with all-electric drives. These figures do not
include irrigation loads.
Belotti and Moreau (1995) give a specific electricity
consumption of 28 k W t c with all-electric drives.
Emergency power sources. The emergency power
source other than the sugar mill's own generating
plant, is usually a connection to the external power
supply company. In the event of an unplanned shut-
down of mill generated power, the utility company
supply is switched on, providing power for light-
ing, boiler fans, feed pumps and fuel feeders, to en-
able the mill to be restarted. If the external supply
is unreliable, it may be necessary to install standby
diesel generators. A battery-powered unintermptible
power supply is often also provided to ensure con-
tinuous power to electronic control and monitoring
systems.
30 Electricity
30.1.2 Selectionof voltage
Three voltages are of interest in a sugar mill: a)
the single-phase low voltage (LV) used for lighting
and office equipment, b) the three-phase low volt-
age (LV) of the majority of electric motors driving
pumps, conveyors etc, and c) the three-phase medi-
um voltage (MV) used for main power distribution
and selected large motors.
The single-phase low voltage is 220 or 230 V in
many countries, with 110 V being used in the
USA and some surroundingcountries.
Thethree-phaselowvoltage isoften 380or400 V,
this providing a ready source for 220/230 V sin-
gle phase supplies. 415 V is used in many coun-
tries and 480V is common in the USA. There is
however a tendency towardshighervalues,525V
being used in many South African sugar mills.
Some European variable-speed drives require up
to 690V.
Only relatively small mills, crushing less than
about 100 t/h, would consider a distribution
voltage of 440 V or less. (100 t$ . 30 k W t C
=3 MW; at 440 V, 3-phase and 0.8 power factor,
this would require a total current canying capac-
ity of 4900 A, necessitating over-large conduc-
tors).
The distribution medium volt-
age is mostly 6.6 kV and 11 kV,
with 3.3 kV still being found in
older mills. It is standardpractice
to generate at the higher voltage,
or to install step-up transform-
ers downstream of low voltage
generators. Power is then dis-
tributed at the medium voltage to
load centers located at strategic
points in the mill, where step-
down transformers reduce to
the standard low voltage value.
Large motors, such as shredder
and cane knife drives,are usually
operated at the medium voltage.

30.1.3 Steamturbines
Steam turbines take in steam at relatively high pres-
suresand temperatures,and exhaustthe steameither
to process, or in some cases to a condenser operat-
ing under sub-atmosphericpressure.An example of
a sugarmill installation is shown in Figure 30.1.
For a constant steam flow through the turbine
(i.e. no steam bleeding), the difference in total heat
per unit mass (specificenthalpy, kT/kg) at the steam
inletand the outletof the turbine,representstheener-
gy extractedfrom the steam in the form of mechani-
calwork, used eithertodrivea mechanical load, or to
drive a rotating altemating-currentgenerator.
Mollier diagram. An essential tool in studying
steam turbine operation is the Mollier diagram or
enthalpylentropy diagram, shown in Figure 30.2.
Thisusually has the verticalaxis in specificenthalpy

simplyreferred to as "enthalpy" and "entropy". The
diagram is crossed with lines of constant tempera-
ture (OC) and of constant absolute pressure (kPa or
bar). The inletsteam conditioncan be plotted on the
diagram at the intersectionof the givenpressure and
temperaturelines.Theenthalpy can then be read off

because thelossescausedby fiuidfrictionand eddies

Turbines are less efficient at low loads because
of the throttling losses in the steam control valves
and because the intermediatestagesteam pressures,

be higherunder part-load conditions.In aback-pres-

which requires a steam temperature only slightly
superheated.If the turbine is providing hotter steam
than required, a desuperheater must be used. The
water injected representsa steammass gain.
Desuperheating. The amount of water used for
process steam desuperheating can be important. As
an example: with high pressure steam conditions of
3200kPa and 400 "C,letting down 10tlh to220 kPa
through a pressure reducing station (i.e. no energy
extracted, zero efficiency, horizontal line on Mollier
diagram), will result in an exhaust temperature of
377 "C, compared to the saturation temperature of
123 "C. Reducing the exhaust temperature to close
to the saturation value will require 2.2 t/h of desu-
perheating water at 75 O C ,
i.e. a mass gain of 22 %
(thecalculationof the amountof desuperheatingwa-
ter required is shown in section 27.10.2). A turbine
exhaust temperature will be cooler because of the
mechanical energy extracted, and although it will

The energy extracted from the steam by the

Initial steam conditions.Higher initial steam con-
ditions will permit more energy to be extracted by
a turbine, when the exhaust pressure (and tempera-
ture) is fixed by process requirements.
In the case of a condensingturbine there is an-
other constraint -exhaust steam wetness. When ex-
hausting at low absolute pressures, the steam tends
to condensein the last stages of the turbine, the wa-
ter droplets causing severe blade wear. This condi-
tion is shownon the Mollier diagramby the exhaust
steam condition being below the "saturation line".
Higher initial steam temperaturesand lower turbine
efficiencieshelp to raise the exhaust steamtempera-
ture and reduce exhaust steam wetness. If the initial
steam temperature is not raised enough, it may be
necessaryto limit the efficiency of a condensingtur-
bine to avoid excessivesteamwetness.

Pass-out 1condensing turbines. It is possible
to bleed off some of the steam passing through a
condensing turbine at the appropriate pressure for
process, in which case this is known as a ''pass-out1
condensing" set. Despitethe increasein complexity,
the cost is generally less than having separateback-

combined unit can lead to lowerefficienciesthan for
separate units. This is especially true when the du-
ties differ, e.g. operation as a back-pressureset with
minimum condensing during the crushing season,
and as a pure condensingset during the off-crop.
Impulse and impulse-reaction turbines. Steam
turbines are either "impulse" or "impulse-reaction".
There are no pure reaction turbines. In an impulse
turbine, the steam pressure is caused to drop across
stationary nozzles, generating high steam velocities
with increased kinetic energy. This high velocity
steam impingeson moving blades which extract the
energy by reducingthevelocity.Thereis no pressure
drop across the moving blades. There may be only
one set of fixed nozzles as in a simple mechanical
drive turbine, or multiple stages of fixed nozzles, as
in a"Rateau" turbine. Lnanimpulse-reactionturbine,
which is always multi-stage, there is a steam pres-
sure drop acrossboth the fixed and moving blades.
The impulse turbine is simpler and cheaper be-
cause there is no pressure sealing across the mov-
ing blades. The impulse-reaction turbine is more
efficient because there are more stages of steam
pressure drop, each of which has fewer losses. The
efficiency difference between the two types has de-
creasedin recentyearsbecauseof improved impulse
turbine blade design. It must also be borne in mind
that too high an efficiency with insufficiently high
inlet steam conditions can lead to exhaust steam
wetness,even in back-pressure turbines.
Multi-stage impulse turbines are generally of-
fered with efficiencies of around 78 %, while im-
pulse-reactionunits often haveefficienciesof around
84 %. There is however some overlap, depending
on the complexity and hence the cost of each type.
There are impulse machines with efficiencies of
83 % and impulse-reactionunits with efficienciesof
77 %.
It has been suggested that the higher the effi-
ciency, the less forgiving is the turbine of mal-op-
eration, because of the finer rotor clearances. This
is not borne out in practice, with many other design
and operationalfactors contributingto reliability,or
lack thereof.
