30 Electricity
Geared turbines. For maximum efficiencyin a re-
action turbine, the blade velocity should be close
to 50 % of the steam velocity. Because of the high
steamvelocitiesfrom the nozzles,high blade veloci-
ties and hence high rotational speeds are necessary.
As the maximum rotational speed of a 2-pole syn-
chronousAC generatoris 3000min-I (for50Hz sup-
ply, or 3600 mini for 60 Hz) either a gearbox must
be used to reduce the turbine speed to that of the
generator,or the turbiie must be run at less than op-
timumspeedandbe directlycoupled to a 3000 mini
(or 3600min-I) generator.
Turbines driving such items as boiler induced
draft fans and cane shredders are always coupled
to a gearbox because of the relatively low operating
speeds of such loads. Some boiler feed pumps may
operate at high rotational speeds and can be direct-
coupled to a turbine.
Modern gearboxes are very reliable, and most
mbogenerators now incorporate a speed-reducing
gearbox. When a gearbox is used, it is not neces-
saryto use a 2-pole3000min-I generator,andCpole
1500min-I (or 1800m i d for 60 Hz) generatorsare
popular. In 2-pole generators the winding-end re-
taining rings are highly stressed and vulnerable to
cracking and require careful periodical inspection.
4-pole generatorsare more robust.
Gearboxes may be parallel-shaft or epicyclic.
The latteris morecompactbut more complexandre-
quires more maintenanceskill. In the unlikely event
of a tooth failure, an epicyclic gearbox could suf-
fer major damage and cause damage to the turbine
and alternator.The parallel-shaftgearboxis simpler,
easier to inspect and maintainand more forgivingof
damage. The efficiency of a single-reductionparal-
lel shaft gearbox is typically 99 %, with 94 to 96 %
for an epicyclicgearbox.
30.1.4 Steam usage
The process steam usage of a cane sugar mill
depends on such factors as cane crush rate, number
of evaporator effects; target sucrose extraction and
hence imbibition % fiber and use of downstream
evaporator vapors for pan and juice heating. These
details are covered in section 28.3. The process
steam usage can however be expressed in general
terms as the ratio of the process steam mass flow
rate to the cane crush rate, i.e. tonnes of process
steam per tonne of cane. It is important to specify
process steamand not high pressure steam,because
of the desuperheater mass gain.
Mills with very high thermal efficiencies, such
as are found in Mauritius, have process steamlcane
ratios less than 0.40 i.e. 40 t/100 t cane. Mills with
lower thermal efficienciesmay have process steam1
cane ratios up to about 0.65. Interruptionsto steady
state operation (no-cane stops, mill stops, break-
downs etc.) significantly increase the steamfcane
ratio taken over, say, a week.
An optimum balance must be found between
crush rate, bagasse fuel production, process steam
demand and electrical power demand. A math-
ematicalmodel is necessaryforanythingmore than
rough estimations. More detail is given in Chap-
ter 28.
30.2 Alternators
30.2.1 Size
For sugar mill applications, alternators (i.e. al-
ternating current generators) are presently available
in sizes up to about 25 MW, but larger sizes are pos-
sible. Depending on the electrical load of the mill,
one machine may be abletoprovide allthe electrical
power.
Although one large machine is usually less ex-
pensive than two half-sized units, the decisionis in-
fluenced by the effecton mill operations should one
machine fail. Possible combinations include: one
100% unit; two 50 %; two 75 %, three 50 %.
Alternators employ a rotating magnetic field
(rotor) operating in a stationary armature winding
(stator), in which the electrical power is generated.
The rotor contains an electro-magnet which is en-
ergizedby a DC excitationcurrent.Relativemotion
between the rotating magnetic field and the stator
coils produces the AC output. When the output
current increases due to increasing load, the out-
put voltage tends to reduce because of the internal
30.2.3 Efficiency
impedance of the alternator.In order to maintain a
constant output voltage it is necessary to adjust the
strengthof the rotor magnetic fieldby adjusting the
excitation current. This is carried out by the auto-
matic voltageregulator (AVR).
In olderalternators,the sourceof theDC excita-
tion current is a separate DC generator, mechani-
cally coupledto the alternatorrotor. Theoutputcur-
rent from this commutator generator is fed into the
alternatorrotor via sliprings.
Modern alternator rotors incorporate separate
exciterwindingswhich produce alternatingcurrent,
which is then rectified to the DC excitation current
by diodesrotatingwith therotor, there being no slip
rings. The excitation current is varied by varying
a DC electromagnet which surrounds the exciter
winding on the rotor.
30.2.3 Efficiency
At full load, a typical medium-sized sugar m
i
l
l
alternator would have an overall efficiency of 96.7
% to 97.7 % (electrical power outputlmechanical
power input). Electrical losses which vary with the
load would be about 0.8 % at full load. Fixed losses
(windage, bearing friction and iron losses) would
be about 1.0 % and excitation losses about 0.5 %.
Heat generated by the various electrical losses has
to be removed from the air circulatingthrough the
alternatorby the air cooler.
30.2.4 Controlequipment
Alternator power output is controlled by the
turbine steam flow and the turbine governor is
therefore an integral part of the alternator control
system. If there is only one turbinelalternator unit
("turbo-alternator") supplying an isolated mill
load ("island mode") the frequency of the gener-
ated power is determined by the speed of the tur-
bine, the governor of which is therefore in speed-
control mode. If more than one turbo-alternator
is supplying the isolated mill load, the manner in
which these machines share the load is determined
by their relative size and the matching of the gover-
nor characteristics.
Additionalgovernorcharacteristicsarerequired
if the mill electrical system is operated in parallel
with a nationalgrid (see section 30.6.3)
Thealternatorvoltageandreactivepoweriscon-
trolled by the automatic voltage regulators (AVRs)
which adjust the alternatorexcitationcurrent.
30.2.5 Lubricationand cooling
Alternatorsrequire cooling to dissipate the heat
generated by electrical losses and by cooling air
windagelosses.Coolair is blown overthestatorand
rotor windings by fans mounted on the rotor shaft.
The warmed air then passes over heat-exchanger
pipes in which water or ambient air flows. The
cooled air continues in a closed circuit. The exter-
nal circuitof the air cooler is usually provided with
circulatingwater to removethe heat but ambient air
is sometimesused.
Becausethedustin sugarmillenvironmentscan
cause the ambient air to foul the heat exchangesur-
faces, reducing the effective cooling of the closed
air circuit,water cooling is preferred. Somealterna-
tors have emergency doors which can be opened to
admit ambient air directly to the fans in the case
of failure of the air cooler. This is an undesirable
practice because the dust will find its way into the
windings, causing overheating. Use of air filters is
not satisfactory because of the need for frequent
cleaning and the ingress of dust during the cleaning
process.
Stator winding temperatures and cooling air
and cooling water temperatures must be monitored
and alarms fitted.
Low voltage heaters should be fitted in the sta-
tor casing. These should be switched on automati-
cally when the alternator is shut down, to prevent
condensation taking place on the windings when
moisture-laden ambient air is drawn in as the alter-
nator cools.
Lubrication of the alternator rotor bearings is
usually provided by the turbine and gearbox lu-
brication system. Bearing temperature indicators
with alarm facilitiesshould be provided. Care must
be taken in sealing the rotor bearings to eliminate
oil leakage into the stator windings, a condition
sometimes encouragedby low pressure areas in the
closed cooling air circuit.
30 Electricity
30.2.6 Electrical control
The main electrical control function of an al-
ternator is maintenanceof the specified output volt-
age under conditions of varying power output. This
is the function of the automatic voltage regulator,
which detectsthe output voltage via potential trans-
formers, and adjusts the excitation current accord-
ingly. In a modern alternator the excitation current
is adjusted by varying the stationary field of the
rotating AC exciter which in turn feeds DC to the
main rotating field windings via rotating diodes.
The relatively small DC required for the AC exciter
fieldis often suppliedby a smallpermanentmagnet
generator attached to the common rotor.
The rotating permanent magnet produces AC
in a stator, which is rectified to DC by stationary
diodes. It is this small DC which is varied by the
AVR to cause a variation in the rotor main excita-
tion current.
30.2.7 Protection
Alternatorprotection isa specializedfieldwhich
this sectionwill only addressin general terms. The
following protection relays should be included in
the alternatormain output circuitbreaker:
IDMT (inversedefinite minimum time);
Over-current and earth fault;
Differential current between the alternator star
point and the circuitbreaker;
Reverse power;
Over- and under-voltage;
Synchronizationcheck and diodefailure.
Rotor earth fault and negative phase sequence pro-
tection are also desirable, especially in larger ma-
chines. Over-frequency protection would be pro-
vided by the turbinegovernor.
Rateof changeof frequencyprotection, or a suitable
substitute, will also be needed if cogeneration with
an external grid is to take place (see also section
30.6.2).
Older machines will have the protection in the
form of individual relays, but modern protection is
combined in one or two digital relays, which incor-
porate all the necessary functions. The AVR may
also include some of the protection functions,such
as diode failure and over- and under-voltage.
30.3 Operationof the
power house
30.3.1 Alternatorand turbine
monitoring
Traditionally,discrete gauges and alarm enunci-
atorsprovided information to an operator,either on
a board adjacentto the machine, or in a nearby con-
trol room. The modem tendency is for the informa-
tion to be provided in a control room on a monitor
screen by a SCADA system, usually with graphical
representationof themachine,and mouse1keyboard
control.With this system it is easier for the operator
to assimilatedata from a large number of inputs and
to control the various functions.
Indication and alarm functions should be pro-
vided for: alternator output voltage, current, power,
power factor, output frequency and excitation cur-
rent. Temperatures with an alarm function should
be provided for stator windings, cooling air, cool-
ing water and alternator bearings. Bearing vibration
may also be monitored.
The turbine would have a basic built-in protec-
tion system, such as the automatic shutting of the
steam valves in the event of loss of control of the
oil pressure or on operation of a backup over-speed
trip. A modem governor would incorporate at least
two speed monitoringsystems,with electronicover-
speedtripand automaticrun-up facilities.Additional
turbineprotection would be provided by a program-
mable logic control system, or be incorporated in
the SCADA system.This would includemonitoring
of bearing temperaturesand vibration, oil pressures
and temperatures and cooling water temperature.
Rotor axial position, inlet steam pressure, tempera-
ture and flow and exhaust pressure and temperature
should also be monitored. In the case of a pass-out
/ condensing machine it would be necessary also to
monitor the pass-out steam pressure, temperature
and flow.
30.3.2 Load control
The load (power consumption) is determined
by the consumerof power, not by the power source.
In a sugar mill operating in island mode, the power
30.3.3 Vibration monitoring
output of the alternator(s) is determinedby the total
mill demand.With two or more alternatorsoperating
in parallel,the load can be distributedbetween them,
but thetotalload is thatdemandedby thepower con-
sumers.
When an alternatoris excitedbut running on no-
load with the statorco~ection
open, it only produc-
es an electro-motiveforce (EMF) i.e. volts. If a load
is now applied, a current will be caused to flow by
the voltage. This current will create a back EMF in
the stator windings, which will oppose the rotating
magnetic field of the rotor. In order to maintain the
set frequency, more steam will have to be admitted
to the turbine to producethe necessary torque on the
rotor. In this way thepower outputof the turbo-alter-
natoris increased. Because of the internal staticand
dynamic impedanceof the stator windings, the volt-
age atthe alternatorterminalswill decrease,necessi-
tatinganincreasein excitationcurrent.As theload is
further increased, stillmore steamwill be required.
The total current is that drawn by the load and
this must be supplied by the source if this is one al-
ternator,but it can alsobe proportionedbetween two
or more alternatorsas desired.The conceptof power
factor is described in more detail in section 30.5.3,
whereitis explainedthat the total currentconsistsof
active and reactive components. W
~
t
htwo or more
alternators,the componentsof the actual current can
also be proportioned,one alternator providing more
activeand/orreactivecurrent than the other,i.e,pro-
vidingcurrent with apowerfactor differentfrom the
other.The power factor splitbetween the alternators
is determined by their relativeexcitation.
Additional governor and load control facilities
are required if the turbo-alternators are to operate
in parallel with an external supply grid (see section
30.6.3).
30.3.3 Vibration monitoring
Vibration monitoring is a relatively new and
very useful tool for checking the machine condi-
tion on-line. This facility should be installed on all
but the smallest turbo-alternators. In the simplest
form, vibration transducers aremounted on bearing
housingsand the amplitudesignals displayedon the
machine monitoring system, with suitable trending
and alarm facilities. More complex systems, which
indicate the phase relationshipsbetween the various
probes and shaft displacement, are also used, espe-
cially on larger machines.
The vibration pick-up probes, which are actu-
ally accelerometers, are often fitted on the bearing
cap. The output signal is integrated to provide a
velocity output in units of mm/s. Acceptable values
vary widely depending on the size and speed of the
machine. Typical acceptable values are less than
3 mm/s. Over 1
0mmls would indicate that the ma-
chimeshouldbe taken off linewithout delay.
More advanced systems measure the shaft de-
flection relative to the housing and two probes are
usually installed at right anglesto each other, to pro-
vide information on the shaft "orbit" relative to the
housing.
A simple amplitude measurement and trend-
ing system can give useful indications of increas-
ing bearing wear, misalignmentand imbalance.The
interpretation of the data is a specialized field, but
with the moreadvanced systems,frequencyand har-
monic analysis and phase differences can identify
such problems as increasing bearing wear, simple
unbalance, couple unbalance, misalignment across
couplings,gear teethproblems, alternatorstator and
rotor problems and bearing oil whirl on high speed
machines.
30.3.4 Sale and purchase of power
Becauseof the need forprocesssteamin a sugar
mill, in-house generation of mechanical and electri-
cal power is universally practiced. Conditions can
however arise where additional power is required,
for example for irrigation pumping, especially dur-
ing the off-crop.The cost of purchasing such addi-
tional power is generallyhigh,and somemills resort
to the use of condensingturbo-alternators to reduce
thelevel of power imports. Theimported powermay
beutilizedseparatelyfromthat generatedin themill,
e.g. in a separately-connectedirrigation scheme, or
the systems may be paralleled (see section 30.6 for
more on cogeneration). The economic justification
of a scheme to purchase from, or sell to a utility
company has to be individuallystudied,considering
such factors as purchaselsale price; fuel availability
and price; boiler and turbo-alternatorreliability and
the need for maintenancedowntime.

30.4 Electric motors
30.4.1 Classes
Almost all motors in a modem cane sugar mill
are alternating current (AC) squirrelcage or wound
rotor (slipring) motors.
Squirrel cage motors are the simplest and least
expensive. A squirrelcage motor has no current car-
rying connections to the rotor, which contains built-
in conductor bars running parallel to the rotor axis,
C O M ~ C ~ ~
to short-circuiting rings at each end, i.e.
the arrangementis similar to a squirrelcage.
Slip ring motors have windings in the rotor,
these being connected to slip rings. It is therefore
possible to alter the characteristics of the rotor on-
line,by inserting,via the sliprings,resistancesin the
rotor winding circuits.
The torquelspeed characteristics of squirrel
cage and slip ring motors will be discussed in sec-
tion 30.4.3.
Environmentalprotection.Theenvironmentalpro-
tection of an electric motor can vary from the mini-
mum, which would merely limit the access to live
components for safety reasons, to totally enclosed,
which would exclude water and dust. Explosion-
proof motors are covered by special standards and
are sufficiently robust to prevent ignition of sur-
rounding flammable substances in the event of an
electrical arc inside the motor.
IEC 60529is a standardcommonlyused by mo-
tor manufacturers to define the degree of environ-
mental protection.The letters "IP"(Ingress Protec-
tion) arefollowedby two numbers.
First number:
0 Unprotected;
1 Protected against accidental contact and solid
objectsgreater than 50 rnm;
2 Protected against contact with fingers and solid
objectsgreater than 12rnm;
3 Protected against contact objects greater than
2.5 mm diameter;
4 Protection against contact with fine tools and
solid objects greater than 1mm;
5 Full protection againstcontactand also dust pro-
tected;
6 Completely protected against dust.
Second number (gives the degree of protection
againstharmfulentry of water):
0 Unprotected;
1 Verticallyfalling drops of water;
2 Drippingwater up to 15"from the vertical;
3 Sprayed water up to 60" from the vertical;
4 Sprayed water from any direction;
5 Waterjets from any direction;
6 Water from heavy seas, e.g. on deck of a ship;
I
7 Can withstand specified completeimmersion;
8 Immersion with highest point submerged not
less than 1m.
For most sugar mill environments, where hosing
down may take place, IP 55 would provide adequate
protection. In selected areas where there is negligi-
ble dust andchanceof waterjets, e.g. in anenclosed.
ventilatedirrigationpump house,IP 22 or IP23 may
suffice. The lower the environmental protection, the
less expensive the motor. However when motors of
similarpower and speed areinterchanged,caremust
be taken that motors of lower environmentalprotec-
tion are not used in unsuitableareas.
Another environmental protection description
is TEFC, i.e. Totally Enclosed Fan Cooled. This is
equivalentto IP 55, the motor being totallyenclosed
against water jets and dust, and the external cool-
ing is by a shaft-mounted fan at the non-drive end,
which blows ambientair over axial finson the stator
housing. If this description is used, the IP terminol-
ogy should also be added.

30.4.4 Speedand slip
Definitionof "slip". Unlike an alternator,an induc-
tion motorconnectedto a constantfrequencysupply
will not run at synchronous speed, but at a slightly
lower speed,thedifferencebetween thesynchronous
speed and the actual speed being called "slip".
Slipis necessaryto produce relative motion be-
tween the rotatingmagneticfield in the stator,which
rotates at synchronousspeed, and the conductors in
the rotor, which rotate at lower speed. This relative
Table 30.2: Motor synchronousspeeds and slip
motion produces the motor output power. A typical
full-load slip value is 2 % of synchronousspeed.
Synchronous speed. The synchronous rotational
speed of the stator's magnetic field depends on
the frequency of the supply and on the number of
magnetic pole pairs wound into the stator. The mini-
mum number is one pair of poles, which produces
the highest possible synchronous speed. Increasing
the number of pole pairs reduces the synchronous
speed, and hence increases the output torque, for a
constant outputpower.
The synchronous speed for a given number of
pole pairs is given by:
where n is the synchronousspeed in min-I,f the fre-
quency in Hz and N the number of pole pairs. Typi-
cal speeds are shown in Table30.2.
Slip and efficiency. Efficiency is partly related to
slip. Smaller motors tend to have larger values of
slip and lower efficiencies (80 to 90 %) than larger
motors (efficiency 90to 95 %).
Current and torque vs. slip. When a motor is
startedwith the supply frequency being applied, the
speed is zero and the slip is therefore 100%. When
the motor is running normally at full load, the slip
is around 1% to 3 %, typically 2 %, and the current
drawn is therated full-load value. When the motoris
running under no-load, the speedincreases to nearly
the synchronous value, i.e. slip is nearly zero, and
the current drawn decreases accordingly.

The torque developed versus speed curve is a

For DOL starting of a squirrel cage motor, the
initial current will be approximately 6 times the rat-
ed (nameplate)value,while the availabletorquewill
be about 1.5times the rated value.
Some manufacturers offer special squirrel cage
motors with a higher starting torque (say 2.4 times
rated) and a lower starting current (say 5 times full-
load value) than normal motors. This is achieved by
increasingthe reactance of the built-in squirrel cage
circuit in the rotor
Reduced-voltage starting. In order to reduce the
high DOL starting current, a lower supply voltage
can be used. A convenientsource of lower voltageis
the line-to-neutral ("star") connection of a 3-phase
supply,which will provide ll& i.e. 0.58of theline-
to-line ("delta") voltage. When the motor has accel-
erated sufficiently, the supply can be reconnected
in the normal delta configuration. The connection
changes are provided by a "star-delta" starter which
will reduce the startingcurrent to about2.3 times the
full load value; however the lower voltage causes a
reduction in starting torque to about 0.7 times the
full load value. This can have serious consequences
with a load which has a relatively high torque de-
mand at low speeds,e.g. a boilerhigh-inertia ID fan
or a propeller pump. The motor may not produce
sufficient surplus torque to accelerate the load in
the star connection, and the current drawn after the
change-over to delta connection will be almost as
high aswould be thecasewith the much cheaperand
simplerDOL start.
Star-delta starters can also produce high transient
torques(upto 20 times motorfull-load torque)atthe
moment of changeover, which can damage equip-
ment.
A variation of thestar-deltastarteris the"closed-
transition" star-delta starter, where an additional
contactor and a resistance bank are used to bridge
over the star-delta transition. This eliminates the
torque transientat changeover.

Other means of providing reduced starting
voltages are line resistances and line transformers.
Recently, electronic "soft starters" have been intro-

Startingslipringmotors.Thewound-rotoror "slip
ring" induction motor can typically provide a start-
ing torque of 2 to 2.4 times full load torque, with a
starting current of about 2.4 times the full load val-
ue. The slip rings provide access to the rotor wind-
ings, and by applyingexternalresistances the torque
-and current-speedcharacteristicscan be changed
on-line. The motor is started with a high resistance
in the rotor circuit, andthis is progressively reduced
to zero during the run-up, providing nearly constant
current and torque during the run-up. This type of
motor has been much used for large, high inertial
drives such as cane knives, shredders and boiler ID
fans. Slip ring motors cost more than squirrel cage
motors because of the increased complexity of the
rotor. Switchgearand variable-resistanceequipment
is alsorequired in the rotor circuit in additionto sta-
tor switchgear.Brush gear and slipring maintenance
is also necessary.
Startingsquirrelcagemotorswithvariable-speed
power supplies. A recent development in starting
large motors is to use a variable frequency power

High-slip applications. A common error is the
specification of high efficiency motors for large
variable load drives such as on cane shredders.The
high efficiency implies a low value of full-load slip
and this will result in a motor which produces large
current fluctuationswhen sudden large load swings
occur.
Figure 30.6 is an amplification of the low-slip
end of Figure 30.5, for a typical high efficiency mo-
tor, with 1% slip at full load.The torqueand current
curves are nearly straightlinesin this area.
If the motor is a 6-pole unit (1000 min-I syn-
chronous speed at 50 Hz), with 1 % full load slip,
and the load suddenly increases causing the speed
to drop from 990 to 980 min-I (slip increasingfrom
1% to 2 %), the current will increasefrom 100% to
200 % of the fullload value. If, however the motor
has full-load slip of 5 % (950 min-') and a load in-
crease causes the slipto increaseto 6 % (940min-')
the current will only increasefrom 100% to 120%.
Many shredderdriveslipring motorsarespecifiedto
have between 5 and 7 % full-load slip.
If a high-efficiency low-slip motor has to be
used on a shredder, it is possible to vary the full load
slip by varying the minimum value of the rotor re-
sistance.For example,a motor designedto have 1%
full-load slip can have the full load slip increased
to say 5 % by permanently inserting a resistance
in the rotor circuit via the slip rings. This would
have the beneficial effect of reducing the magnitude
of the current swings caused by a fluctuating load
and would also provide increased full-load torque.
There would be a smallreduction in full-load speed
and efficiency, requiring a small reduction in motor
maximum power output. Inserting a permanent ro-
tor resistance should only be done afterconsultation
with the motor manufacturer.
30.4.5 Direct current @C) motors
The operating characteristics of DC motors
can be readily changed on-line, giving them great
operating flexibility. Good starting torque is avail-
able at reasonable line currents, and as variable
speed is readily achieved, DC motors operate well
in mill drive applications. The disadvantages are
high initial cost, ongoing commutator and brush
gear maintenance,and the need for controlled recti-
fier equipmentto provide variableDC voltagesfrom
the AC systemsuniversally used in mill distribution
schemes.In new installations,the tendency is to use
AC induction motors, powered by variable-frequen-
cy electronic power sources,rather than DC drives.
30.4.6 Variable frequency drives
In an induction motor the torque is a function
of the rotor current and the magnetic flux in the
statorlrotor air gap. The flux is proportional to the
voltage applied to the statorE and inversely propor-
tional tothefrequencyf,i.e. thetorqueis proportion-

al to El$ A modem variablefrequency drive, also re-
ferred to as a variable speeddrive (VSD),establishes
an electronic image of the motor's characteristics,
and by varying the voltage and frequency, can pro-
vide in a squirrel cage motor a starting torque of up
to 150%of thefull-loadrated value. Thistorquecan

Thespeedof themotor can be controlledto clos-

Additional motor cooling by means of a small

30.5 Power distribution and
usage
30.5.1 Transformers
Use of transformers.Transformerstransformelec-
trical power from one supply voltage to another,
with high efficiencies,typically98 to 99 %. In sugar
mills, transformers are mostly used to step down
medium distributionvoltages (6.6 or 11kV) to low
voltages, for powering smaller motors (e.g. at 380
V) and lighting systems.Larger motors may be sup-
plied at the medium voltage.
Transformersmay also be used to match alterna-
tor voltages to distributionvoltages when equipment
is transferredfrom onemill to another. For example,
when a 6.3 kV alternator was moved to a mill with
a 6.6 kV system, it was considered undesirable to
operate the alternator at a continuous5 % over-volt-
age, so a step-up autotransformerwith ratio 6.316.6
kV was successfullyemployed.Similarly,a number
of older 3.3kV alternatorshave been integratedinto
6.6 and 11 kV systems by means of step-up trans-
formers.
Transformers are traditionally supplied with
copper conductor windings but aluminum winding
conductorsarenow also available.
Neutral earthing.There should be only one neutral
(star-point) earth co~ection
on a transmission sup-
ply system,to prevent circulatingearth currents.For
example, where alternators are operated in parallel,
only thelargestshould have the starpoint earthed at
any time, except for brief periods during machine
changeover. Each distribution transformer supplies
its own low voltage distribution system and as such
should have its neutral star point earthed. If trans-
formers are connected in parallel, the star point of
only one should be earthed via a protection relay
arranged to trip both middle voltage (MV) circuit
breakers. Multiple earths in parallel can be accom-
modated but require specialfilteringsystemsor non-
standard transformerwindings.
When a grid supply transformer is operating in
parallel with mill turbo-alternators, either the grid
supply transformer or the largest alternator should
have its star point earthed, depending on which has
the largest power rating. If parallel operationis tak-
ing place with only the grid transformer star point
earthed, and the grid connection is tripped by the
protection, e.g. because of a fault on the grid, the
star point of the largestmill turbo-alternatoron line
shouldbe earthedimmediately, preferably by an au-
tomatic switch.
If a grid supplytransformeris in operationon its
own as may be the case during a mill maintenance
period, or when supplying a separate irrigation
scheme, it should have its star point earthed.

Transformer operation and maintenance. Trans-
formers must be operated within their design limits
as regards current, voltage and operating tempera-
ture. Overheating, voltage surges and moisture in
the oil cause irreversible damage to the insulation,
which can greatly reduce transformer life. Regular
and careful maintenance is important if transform-
ers are to achieve their expected life of about 40
years. Maintenance should include elimination of
oil leaks, maintenanceof breather desiccant, ensur-
ing adequate cooling and most important, regular
oil quality checks followed by oil drying and filter-
ing. Transformers should be located where there is
adequate ventilation and no possibility of excessive
dust deposits.
30.5.2 Cable sizing
Conductors. When considering the data given in
this section,and indeed when dealing with any elec-
trical installation,precedence mustbe given to local
statutory and legal requirements.
Cables have either copper or aluminum con-
ductors. Aluminum is less conductive than copper,
Referencesp. 713
30 Electricity
therefore the cross-sectionalarea has to be larger to
carry the same current.
Because aluminum cable cross-sectionis some-
times stated in terms of the "copper equivalent",
care must be taken to ensure that the correct figures
are used.
It is somewhat easier to make-off copper cable
ends. The decision whether to use copper or alumi-
num is mainly an economic one, tempered by the
availability of the cable types and the installation
and maintenance personnels' familiarity with each
type.
The cost per unit length of a cable is largely de-
termined by the conductor cross-sectional area, al-
though the insulationfor higher voltages also costs
more. Cable installed costsincludethe costsof duct-
ing, trenching or racking, cable end terminations
and installationlabor.These are allhigher forcables
with larger cross-sectionalarea. For the distribution
of large power levels, the use of higher voltages is
essential to limit the current being conducted, and
hence the cable sizerequired.
Insulation.Low voltage cables up to about 1000V
between phases are PVC insulated; MV cables are
insulated with cross-linked polyethylene (XLPE).
Low voltage XLPE-insulated cables are also avail-
able, the higher quality insulationpermitting higher
operatingtemperatures,but the increasedcostmakes
them less attractive. XLPE insulationeliminatesthe
possibility of chlorinefumes in the case of a fire.
Paper-insulated MV cables have given excellent
service for many years, but are now little used for
new installations.
Cablesizing. Cables are sized, i.e. cross-section de-
termined, on three criteria: continuous current, volt-
age drop and fault current. The smallest size which
will satisfy all three criteria can be used.
Continuous current rating. Section 30.1.2 refers

Of importancein cane sugar mills is the orienta-

racking, which should therefore alwaysbe used.

In the case of a single phase circuit, twice the
cable run length must be taken, to provide for the
return path. The resulting figure will be the line-to-
neutral volt drop, and correction to the line-to-line
value will not apply.

30.6.1 Back pressure and condensingturbines
30.6 Cogeneration and export
of power
30.6.1 Back pressure and condensing
turbines
Cogeneration may involve the sale of surplus
electrical power. Back pressure turbines, which are
the norm in cane sugar mills, take in high-pressure
steam and exhaust at the required process pressure,
usually about 200 to 250 kPa. The mill's electri-
cal and mechanical load is generally met without
passing allthe required process steam flow through
the turbine@).The steam not passed through the
turbine(s) is let down to the exhaust pressure via a
pressure reducing valve. The resulting mixture of
turbine exhaust and letdown steam has too much
superheatfor optimumprocess use, and is therefore
passed through a desuperheater, which adds to the
steam mass flow. More information on letdown sta-
tions appearsin Section 27.10.2.
If additional electrical power is required for
export, and if sufficient generating plant and fuel
is available during the crushing season, all the re-
quired process steam can be obtained as turbine
exhaust steam, with no letdown. If there were suffi-
cient high pressuresteamand boiler fuel,even more
electrical power could be obtained by blowing off
to atmospheresurplus exhaust steam, but this is not
usually done as it is wasteful of energy and requires
additional boiler water make-up.
An alternative to blowing off exhaust steam
is to use a condensing turbine, where the exhaust
steam pressure is sub-atmospheric.This results in a
greater enthalpy difference between the high pres-
sure and exhaust steamcondition ("heat drop"), giv-
ing more electrical energy per unit mass of steam.
If the condenser is suitably designed and operated,
the condensate recovered from the condenser will
be suitablefor use as boiler feed water. The amount
of power that can be generated is affected by the
choice of both exhaust steam and condensing tem-
peratures.The lower these temperatures,the greater
the quantity of power that can be generated (Inkson
and Misplon 2005).
A condensing turbine is more expensive than
a back-pressure set because of the extra cost of the
condenser and the necessary cooling water circuit
(pumps,piping and cooling towers or spray ponds).
Because of the greater specific volume of the steam
at sub-atmosphericpressures the finalturbine blades
are also longer and more expensive than for a back-
pressure turbine.
It is possible to combine a back pressure and a
condensingturbine as describedin Section 30.1.3.
Sugar mills generally operate during the winter
months, when the load on the grid is highest. In this
case it couldbe beneficial to both partiesforthe mill
to export during the period of high demand on the
grid. Generationduring the sugar mill non-crushing
season requires stored bagasse or the ability to burn
an alternative fuel. In some countries, notably the
USA, the highest load on the grid occurs during the
summer because of the extensive use of air-condi-
tioning. This can affect the viability of power export
to the grid.
Bagasse is a non-fossil renewablefuel. In some
countries, financial incentivesareprovided for pow-
er generated using such fuels, which can make co-
generationmore financiallyviable.
30.6.2 Safety systems
There is a growing tendency for m
i
l
l
s to export
power to the utility company's grid in order to in-
crease revenue. This may be done with the mill and
grid electrical systems fully paralleled or with one
or more generators separated from the mill system
and connected only to the grid. In either case, close
liaison is necessary with the supply authority, to es-
tablish technical interface and operating conditions
and procedures, includingcommunicationsbetween
the mill and the supply authority and the electrical
protectionrequired on both systems.
A problem often encountered when mill-gener-
ated power is to be exported to the grid, is detection
of loss of synchronismbetween them
i
l
l and thegrid.
The rate-of-change of frequency relay is sometimes
proposed to separate the mill generating plant from
the grid in the event of loss of paralleling. However
this type of relay may not be suitable in the case
where there is a load connectedto the grid between
the mill and a remote circuit breaker.
For example, if the mill is exporting say 3 MW
along a dedicated line, and there is a local grid load
30 Electricity
of approximately 3 MW also connected to that line,
there will be very little power transfer on the far side
of this load. If a grid circuit breaker were to open
on the far side, the rate of change of frequency at
the mill is likely to be too low to operate the relay.
Re-closing of the remote circuit breaker without a
check on synchronism could lead to severe damage
to turbo-alternators and electrical equipment. In this
case interlocks between the remote circuit breaker
and the grid circuit breaker at the mill may be neces-
sary, via dedicated signal lines orradio links.
30.6.3 Control
When generating in parallel with the grid, the
mill load will be met by two sources of power, the
grid, and the mill alternators. The mill will consume
what it requires, and the power exported will be the
difference (positive or negative) between what is
generated and what is consumed.
When generating only for the mill, in island
mode, the turbine governors will operate in speed
control mode, so as to maintain the desired frequen-
cy.
If the turbo-alternators are operating in parallel
with an extensive grid, the frequency of the mill-
generated power will be identical to that of the grid,
and the turbine speed will be fixed.The governor(s)
will therefore have no speed control function. In
order to generate the maximum power under these
conditions, the govemor(s) would normally operate
in "back pressure control" mode, where the steam
flow through the turbine, and hence the power gen-
erated, would be determined by the process steam
pressure, and hence by the process steam demand.
Another option when generating in parallel with the
grid, would be to operate the govemor(s) in a fixed
load mode, with variations in mill demand being ac-
commodated by a varying export level. If the con-
nection to the grid was severed,it would be essential
for the governor(s) to automatically and rapidly re-
vert to speed control mode, in response to a switched
signal from auxiliary contacts on the appropriate cir-
cuit breaker.
Modern electronic governors can accommodate
the above requirements, but may require additional
devices, such as a master load-sharing control.
30.6.4 Power wheeling
If a mill wishes to supply power to a remote
load, usually an irrigation system, it would have to
construct the necessary power lines from the mill
to the remote location. However there may already
be in existence grid-owned power lines close to the
mill, and close to the remote location. It would then
be theoretically possible for the mill to feed power
into the grid and for this power to be withdrawn
at the remote location, using the grid transmission
network. This is known as "power wheeling" and
would require negotiations between the mill and the
grid authorities regarding the apportioning of capital
and maintenance costs, metering the power flow and
allocation of electrical losses.
A further complication arises if the mill is not
exporting exactly the same power as the remote load
is consuming at any given time.
30.6.5 Gasification
In order to maximize cogeneration export power
in a conventional cane sugar mill, increased boiler
steam pressures and temperatures are used. This in-
creases the heat drop from the boiler steam to the
final heat sink, which will be either the process
steam consumers or sub-atmospheric condensers.
The greater heat drop permits more electricity to be
generated per tonne of fuel.
Other process industries which use gaseous or
liquid fuels, achieve higher levels of electricity gen-
eration by the use of combined-cycles employing gas
turbines as well as conventional boilers and steam
turbines. The fuel is burnt in a gas turbine which
drives an electrical generator. The hot exhaust gas
passes to a waste-heat boiler operating at a suitably
high pressure so that the steam generated can flow
through another turbine before passing to process.
This turbine drives a second electrical generator.
The temperature in the gas turbine is higher than the
steam temperature entering a conventional turbine,
so a greater overall heat drop is achieved.
In order to use combined cycle technology in a
cane sugar mill, a means is needed to produce gas-
eous fuel for the gas turbine from bagasse, hence the
term "gasification".

31.1 Filter cake
31.1.1 Quantity and quality of filter
cake
Filter cake represents the material separated
from cane juice in clarification and filtration. It in-
cludes most of the solid material in the raw juice
and solidsprecipitated in the process of heating and
liming thejuice. It alsocontains some fine bagacillo
added to the clarifier mud before the filters to im-
prove filtration.As produced it has a high moisture
content of around 70 g water/100g cake.
The quantity of filter cake varies enormously,
depending on the amount of sand and soil entering
with the cane and the amount of bagacillo added in
the filter station. In most factories the quantity of
filter cake produced is assumed or estimated and is
not known accurately. The quantity is significantly
smaller in factories which have diffusers instead of
mills, as diffusers deliver a much cleaner raw juice.
The quantity of filter cake is normally in the range
of 30 to 80 kg cake/t cane, or 10 to 40 kg/t cane in
a factory with diffusion.A reasonableaveragevalue
is 50 kg/t cane.
The quality also varies substantially.It contains
organic matter precipitated in clarificationand inor-

31.1.4 Extraction of value-added products
31.1.4 Extractionof value-added
products
Filter cake contains some wax originating from
the cane stalk. About 40 % of the cane wax is ex-
tractedintothe raw juice (Paturau 1989)and at vari-
ous times attempts have been made to recover this
wax.Thecarnaubawax in canehas propertieswhich
make it a desirable product. The wax consists of es-
sentially two fractions,fatty lipids and waxy lipids.
Thelatteris thedesirableproduct and the former has
to be separated from it. Roughly half the crude wax
is recovered as refined wax product, representing
about 40 kg wad100 t cane.
The process usually involves extraction with
solventsin either one or two stages.The solventsare
flammable, making it a potentially hazardous pro-
cess. In most cases it does not appear to be an eco-
nomic option and plants which ran commercially for
a number of years have generally closed down.
Most of the protein extracted in raw juice will
end up in the filter cake. Attempts have also been
made at times to recover protein from filter cake,
but the quantities are quite small. Dhamankar et al.
(1988)foundthat protein constituted7.4 dl00 g dry
filter cake.
31.1.5 Animal feed
Filter cake has value as a feed because of the
protein in the cake together with some carbohy-
drate. However variable amounts of sand make it
difficult to use filtercakein a consistent quality ani-
mal feed.
31.2 Bagasse
Themain use forbagasseis as afuelfortheboil-
ers. This enables a sugar mill to be self-sufficientin
terms of all its energy needs, which is a great benefit
to the economics of raw sugar processing. In most
cases the sugar mill can be configured to produce
a surplus of bagasse, which can be used to provide
steam for other by-product activities or to provide a
feedstockfor other activities.Methodsof improving
the steameconomy to produce a bagasse surplus are
outlined in Section 28.4.
The generation and sale of surplus electrical
power may be regardedas a by-productof raw sugar
manufacture. Cogeneration of power in this way is
discussedin Section30.6and gasification of bagasse
to increase the potential for cogenerationis covered
in Section 30.6.5.
The composition of bagasse is covered in Sec-
tion 1.2.4and thephysicalpropertiesin Section 32.5.
Bagasse containsmost of the fibrous materialin the
cane fed to the mill and as produced has a moisture
contentof around 50g water1100 g bagasse. The dry
matteris composedmainly of the threecomponents
of cane fiber, namely cellulose, hemicellulose and
lignin, as well as a small amount of ash and soluble
material, mainly sucrose. Bagasse may be further
processed to produce value-added products from
recovering or reacting one or all of these compo-
nents.
Physically the bagasse is fibrous in nature and
difficult to handle as a solid. Relative quantities of
cellulose,hemicelluloseand lignin may be found by
analysis;the standardprocedurefollows the method
of Kaar and Brink (1991) and the TAPPI method
T 130s-54for lignin. This method involves grinding
the sample to a particle size < 40 mesh, extraction
with an ethanol/benzene mixture and two stages of
hydrolysis with sulfuric acid; the insoluble portion
represents the lignin, the solution glucose content is
used to estimate the cellulose and the dissolved xy-
lose, galactose, arabinose and mannose to estimate
hemicellulose. Cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin
comprise in round numbers 40, 30 and 20 dl00 g
dry matter in bagasse respectively.
31.2.1 Use in pulp and paper
A number of large pulp and paper factories are
based on bagasse as the major raw material. The
products produced from these enterprises include
cormgating medium for boxes, absorbent tissue,
newsprint and high quality printing and writing pa-
pers. By 1990, 1.5 % of the world's pulp produc-
tion was made from bagasse (Atchison 1992). Since
that time the percentage has stayed steady as finan-
cial and environmentalproblems have caused some
mills to close.
Although a number of differenttypes of bagasse
pulp can be produced, the most commonly used
are:
Referencesp. 737
31 By-product utilization
1. High yield bagasse semi-chemical pulp for cor-
rugating medium, in which 50 to 75 % bagasse
pulp is used.
2. Bleached bagasse chemical pulp for writing
and printing paper and for tissueof all types, in
which as much as 90 % bagasse pulp is used.
In terms of quality, bagassepulp is a shortfiberpulp
that has properties similarto those of hardwood pulp
(Atchison 2001). For most grades of paper, bagasse
pulp can be used to supplementorreplacehardwood
pulps almost kilogramfor kilogram. If traded inter-
nationally it can be expected to trackhardwood pulp
prices. The price of pulp traded on the world market
unfortunately fluctuates dramatically, making ratio-
nal investmentdecisionsdifficult.
The viability of a pulp or paper enterprise de-
pends largely on the local cost of production rela-
tive to the pulp and paper prices. Bagasse is often
obtained at a low price, typically not more than its
fuel-equivalent value, but chemicals and either re-
generation or disposal of spent chemicals are often
the biggest cost items in the manufacturing process.
Economies of scale areimportantin paper manufac-
turing and generally only large paper or pulp plants
can be considered.Tbis can be a serious barrier to
investment, particularly in the light of fluctuating
internationalprices. The yield of pulp from the di-
gestersis roughly 65 %forhigh yield pulp and 48 %
for bleached pulp relative to the amountof bone-dry
bagasse fiber supply to the plant (Atchison 1992).
Taking all losses into account, the overall yields of
paper fromfiberfor these two typesof pulp are60 %
and 40 % respectively (Atchison 2001). Morgan et
al. (1974)report a consistent 63 % overallyield for
a millproducing corrugatingmedium.
The use of bagasse has some advantages. Ln
particular it uses less chemicals in the pulping and
bleaching processes. The sequence of operations is
asfollows:
De-pithing and washing of the fiber;
Digesting with chemicals at elevated tempera-
ture and pressure;
Washing to remove chemicals;
Screening;
Bleaching (if required) using oxygen, chlorine
dioxideor peroxide as appropriate;
Washing and neutralizing;
Dewateringand thickening to pulp.
According toAtchison (1989), pulp and paper man-
ufacture from bagasse has been made feasible since
establishing how best to de-pith and store bagasse
and since developing a rapid continuous pulping
system.
De-pithing of the bagasse. The small non-
fibrous particles of cane do not contribute to the
quality of the paper and increase the consumption
of pulping chemicals and de-pithing to remove the
small pith particles is a key process (Section 26.5).
The pith represents up to 40 % of the bagasse and is
returned to the sugar mill where it is burnt as a fuel.
It is alsonecessary to wash the fiber and undertake a
secondarywet de-pithingoperationon thefiberprior
to the pulping stage, particularly if a good quality
pulp is required.
Storage of fiber. The paper mill is usually re-
quired to run all year and most sugar mills operate
for only a part of the year. Quantitiesof bagasse to
be stored are large because of the large size neces-
sary for a paper mill to be profitable - storage of
fiber for a three month off-crop might require the
storageof 60000t bagasse, and the low bulk density
means that a very large storagearea is necessary.
Therearetwo different approachesto storingba-
gasse fiberto preserve the bagasse without degrada-
tion losses or deteriorationin quality:
By drying the bagasse to a moisture content
<20 %;
By storing the bagasse wet and excluding oxy-
gen.
Atchison (1989)reported on theBagatex-20process,
which involves additionof a biochemical catalystto
the bagasse before baling. This reportedly controls
the microbiological action andensures that the bales
dry rapidly to 20 % moisture with no energy usage.
Bagasse can apparently be stored for two years in
this form with no loss of mass. Howeverit has never
been widely used outside of Brazil and is no longer
in use there. However Dawson et al. (1990)showed
that with or without additives,a moisturecontent of
20 % can be achieved between 20 and 30 days in
baled bagasse.
The Ritter system seems to be the most consis-
tently successful and is a widely used method for
storing fiber for pulp and paper. This involves wet
storage of bagasse fiber in large piles on a concrete
slab. Bagasse from the mill is slurried to 3 % sol-
ids, pumped via an elevated flume and distributed
on storage piles. Water is continuously circulated

Newsprint from bagasse. The largest bagasse
newsprint mill in the world is operated in Tamil
Nadu in India (Satyanarayana 1999). The plant
produces 50 000 t/y of newsprint and 40 000 t/y
of writing and printing paper using 70 % of a mix-
ture of mechanical and chemical bleached bagasse
pulp, and 30 % bleached hardwood pulp. Atchison
(1995) reports that successful newsprint produc-
tion is carried out in India, Indonesia and Mexico.
Requirements for success include a high content of
mechanicalpulp,effectivede-pithing and storageof
bagasse and a bleaching system that maximizesthe
increase in brightness with minimal damage to the
mechanical pulp properties.
Water supply and effluent handling. These
are always important issues in any pulp and paper
operation. A source of reasonably priced water is
necessary because the quantitiesused are large.The
cost of effluent treatment can be prohibitive and a
controlled ocean outfallis often required to attain a
financially viable operation.

.
2 Bagasse board
Many attempts at producing board products
of different kinds using bagasse as the main raw
material have been made over the years. A large
number of plants have been built but few of them
havebeen viable overextendedperiods of time and
many have subsequently closed. Whole bagasse
may be used in insulation boards but otherwise
de-pithed bagasse is necessary for good quality
boards.
The simplest board produced is low density in-
sulation board, which is not subjected to pressing
and is formed by adding a binder to the bagasse.
One of the longest running board plants was that
owned by Celotex in New Orleans. It used a low-
cost binder, such as asphalt or starch, and manufac-
tures a fairly soft low density board used as ceiling
panels. Other fiberboards may be formed wet or dry
and pressed to achieve a higher density and greater
strength.They are heated during pressing and may
have some additives mixed in to improve weather-
ing and abrasionresistance.
Particle board resembles that made from wood
chips and uses a resin together with pressing and
heating to form panels used for furniture or hous-
ing. Drying of the bagasseto a low moisture content
(<4 g water1100g bagasse)prior to addition of resin
is usually required. The resin is normally a urea-
formaldehydeor phenol-formaldehyderesin and, at
8-10 % of the board mass, represents a significant
part of the total board manufacturing cost. An iso-
cyanateresin was used in a new boardplant in Loui-
siana,which required only 3 % resin, but this plant
too had a shortlife.
The bagasse is mixed with the binder and then
pressed and heated in a press, to cure the resin. It
is cooled, finished and cut to size. In some cases
the bagasse mat is formed in layers prior to press-
ing,with layersof fine bagasseparticleson theouter
sides to improve the surfacetexture. Often the edg-
es are treated to impart strength to the board and
prevent crumbling of the edges.
Different densities are possible for differentap-
plications. An advantage of bagasse boards is the
abilityto make a light low density board which still
has sufficient strength. Densities between 250 to
1200kg/m3are achievable.The viability of the pro-
cess is mostly determined by the cost of the binder
used together with the bagasse. Materials used in
bagasse board manufacture have included, apart
from resins, concrete,asphalt or pitch.
Some of the reasons for the commercialfailure
of bagasse board plants include:
Inadequate marketing. The board is often pro-
duced in relatively small quantitiesand existing
producers seemto have the abilityto control the
market,making it difficult for new entrants.
Sand in the board. This comes with the bagasse
and is difficulttoremove.Itresultsin high wear
on saw blades and so adds to the cost of manu-
facturingproducts from it.
High cost of the resin. More effective and
cheaper ways of bonding and binding bagasse
could in future make this a more profitable by-
product avenue.
Fermentation of sugars. Residual sugar in the
bagasse can lead to fungal growth in the board.
This can be overcome by the use of fungicides.
31.2.3 Animal feeds
31.2.3 AnimaI feeds
Bagassehas on occasionsbeen made into pellets
and used as an animal feed, particularly to provide
roughage in feed lots. Pelletizing also provides the
opportunity to include additives with the bagasse as
supplements in cattle feeds. Often molasses is used
in combinationwith bagasse. In SouthAfrica a con-
sistently successful feed has involved the mixing of
bagasse pith and molasses, prior to drying and pel-
letizing.
Because the lignin in bagasse is closely associ-
ated with the cellulose, bagasse is not easily digest-
ible. Various forms of pretreatment have been ad-
opted to improve the digestibility, including steam
explosion.
31.2.4 Furfural manufacture
Furfural (or furfuraldehyde) is made from the
pentoses (five carbon sugars) which are obtained
from hydrolyzing the hemicellulose fraction of the
bagasse. This is achieved by a mild acid treatment
using sulfuric acid, which leaves most of the cellu-
lose and lignin untouched.Thus after this treatment,
the remaining solid material can be dewatered and
sent to the sugarmill boilers.
The major problem lies in feeding bagasse into
and out of a continuous reactor which operates un-
der pressure.The pentosesreact to form furfural ac-
cording to the following;
5-Hydroxymethyl-tetrahydro- 2-Furancarboxaldehyde
furan-2,3,4,uiol Furfurylaldehyde.
a-D-Xylose "Furfural"
(31.1)
Furfural has a ring structure with an oxygen atom in
the ring and two double bonds. It is separated after
the reaction by steam stripping and distillation. Pro-
ducersgenerallyprotect the technology used, to pre-
vent new entrants into the market, but some design
informationis given by Nee and H
s
i
e
h (1968).
Since the hemicellulose is roughly 30 % of the
bagasse dry matter, the maximum yield of furfural
per tonne of bagasse dry matter is about 21 %. In
practice the yield is somewhat lower, around 10%
(Paturau 1989). Secondary reactions involving fur-
furalduringthe long time spentin thereactor lead to
a reduction in furfural yield.
Furfural was traditionally supplied by Quaker
Oats,who produced furfuralfromcorncobs.A num-
ber of sugarcompanies have produced furfural over
the years but only two large plants on bagasse re-
main viable, one in the Dominican Republic and the
other in SouthAfrica.
A new process has been developed, which in-
volves volatilizing the furfural as it is made in a
batch reactorunder pressure.The processis claimed
to produce a higher yield, around 80 % of theoreti-
cal, because the secondary reactions are prevented
from occurring (Zeitsch 2000, Arnold and Buzzard
2003). Other claimsforthe processinclude a shorter
reaction time (1 h), lower steam consumption and
very little effluent.A plant to use this technology is
presently (2006) being built in Australia.
The world market is fairly small, about
250 000 tlyear, and in 1989 22 % was estimated to
be produced frombagasse (Paturau1989).It is used
as a solvent in various processes including petro-
leum refining and in the preparation of some small
volume chemicals. Furfural is used to manufacture
furfuryl alcohol for use in resins and in a range of
food flavorings including diacetyl, acetoin and 2,3-
pentanedione.A recently established use for furfu-
ral as a nematicide could promote demand for the
product.
31.2.5 Integratedbiomass processing
Increasing attention is being given to the devel-
opment of a sugarcane biorefinery, in which a slate
of products is produced to augment the revenue
from the factory. Thus chemicals, ethanol and elec-
tric power may be produced in addition to sugar.
Research effortsin the USA are aimed at producing
fermentable sugars from bagasse and CLM (cane
leaf matter) and also at gasifying the material for
use in electrical energy or liquid fuels production.
A biorefinery parallels the conventional refinery in
producing building blocks for further processing to
chemicals. The conventional refinery may produce
ethylene as a building block; a biorefinery may
produce chemicals via biological or chemical con-
versions for use as intermediates.The US National

three major components,cellulose, lignin and hemi-
cellulose, and deriving products with high value
from them. Fractionation of bagasse in this way is
difficult,but activeresearchandrecent technological
improvements are likely to make commercialization

4. Dilute acid hydrolysis (usually dilute sulfuric
acid) releases pentoses from the pentosans con-
stituting the hemicellulose. The treatment must
be carefully controlled to prevent the subse-
quent conversion of pentoses to furfural. Some
acetic acid is also produced during this step.
An autohydrolysis process is possible at tem-
peratures above 160 "C, where the acetic acid
released serves the function of the dilute acid in
hydrolyzing hemicellulose to xylans (Purchase
1995).
5. The pentoses produced are mainly xylose and
arabinose. Purchase (1995) reports that hydro-
lysis with 0.7 % sulfuric acid at 127 "C for 2 h
with a liquid:solid ratio of 5:l leads to the fol-
lowing hydrolysatecomposition:
Xylose 2.14 d l 0 0 g
Arabinose 0.24 dl00 g
Glucose 0.31 dl00 g
Acetic acid 0.44 dl00 g
m a 1 250 mg/L
The sugars need to be separated to use them in
subsequentprocessing.This is most convenient-
ly done by chromatographicseparation.
6. Biotransformation of xylose provides different
routes to new products. Xylitol is convention-
ally produced by hydrogenationof xylose under
pressure. New bio-based routes are being sought
to a lower cost route for xylitol production and
otherproducts.
7. Arabinose chemistry is a relatively neglected
option for adding value to the arabinosefraction
of the pentoses.
8. Alkaline treatment of the solid residue after di-
lute acid hydrolysisremoves the lignin from the
residue. This is essentially a pulping process,
leading to a liquid stream containing the lignin
and a solid cellulose product. Other processes
using organicsolventshave also been proposed.
9. The lignin stream should be produced in a way
that does not degrade the lignin, making it a
more useful by-product than the lignin from pa-
per pulping. Lignin is recovered in a variety of
ways to enable useful products to be recovered.
10. The solid stream from alkaline treatment is
largely cellulose. Suitable treatment should en-
able it to be produced in a pure form for use in
pharmaceuticaland medical applications.
11. Cellulose itself may be hydrolyzed. It is com-
posed of long chains of glucose molecules and
the end-products of the hydrolysis are mainly
the monosaccharide glucose and the disaccha-
ride cellobiose.Cellulosemay be hydrolyzed by
a strong acid treatmentbut the process is expen-
sive and yields intractable effluent problems. A
more appealing approach is enzymatichydroly-
sis, generally using a strain of Trichoderma re-
esei to produce the enzyme. Reducing the cost
of enzyme production is necessary to make this
process viable.
12.The sugars produced from cellulose hydrolysis
are easily fermented to ethanol. This is the goal
of many initiativesunder way to produce sugars
from the enzymatichydrolysisof cellulose.
13. There are otherpotential products of higher val-
ue, which may be produced from the cellulose
hydrolysate, particularly if the hydrolysate may
be easily purified before fermentation.
14.Biotransformation of cellobiose also provides
some opportunitiesfor the production of higher
value products.
31.2.6 Charcoal and activatedcarbon
Charcoal has been made from bagasse follow-
ing the same processes used for making charcoal
from wood.This involves carbonizationof themate-
rial under controlled conditions at temperatures up
to 600 OC. The process was commercializedfirst in
Java in 1939 (Paturari 1989).Following carboniza-
tion, the charcoal was ground and mixed with mo-
lasses to produce briquettes. Paturau states that 10
tomes of mill-run bagasse is required to produce
one tonne of charcoal, and molasses to the extent of
about 12kg/100 kg charcoal is required.
A number of investigationshave been reported
on the manufacture of activated carbon from ba-
gasse, but no commercial production has been re-
ported. Ahmedna et al. (2000) investigated the suit-
ability of bagasse, together with different binding
materials, on its own or mixed with agricultural
wastes. A granular carbon made from bagasse with
corn syrup as a binder was found to be as effective
as commercial carbons made from coal, but had
unsatisfactory physical properties. In particular the
low hardnessmeans that its use must be restricted to
"gentle" applications,excludingits use as a conven-
tionalgranularcarbon.It haspotential as a substitute
for powdered carbon.
31 By-product utilization
31.2.7 Boiler ash, smuts and fly ash
The bagasse ash, partially burnt bagasse par-
ticles, and small pieces of carbon carried over in
the boiler gases, are removed from the boilers and
boiler scrubbers and are almost always handled
wet. Ash on its own has little value, but may be
used as a filler in landfill sitesor in concrete build-
ing blocks.
The fly ash, the fine carbon particles collected
in the scrubbers, has been used in small quantities
as inter alia a carbon source in the production of
cast iron products.
In Mauritius, boiler smuts have been used to
replace bagacillo as a filter aid on rotary vacuum
filters in a sugar mill.
31.3 Cane leaves and tops
Leaves and tops are a potential source of fiber
and fermentable substrates. However, in most in-
stances cane leaves and tops (also called cane leaf
matter or CLM)representa disposalproblem. They
are an undesirablecomponent of the cane and pro-
cessors encourage the delivery of cane with mini-
mum CLM. This means that it should ideally be
left in the field. In some cases CLM left in the field
has value in preserving moisture, restricting weed
growth and improving the organic content of the
soil. However in less tropical regions, extraneous
matter leftin the fieldskeeps the temperatureof the
soil down, delaying germination of the next ratoon
and reducingcane yields.
31.3.1 Collection as additional fuel
Leaves and tops have value in the case of co-
generation or other activities which require that
the maximum amount of steam be generated. De-
pending on the degree of dryness of the leaves, the
calorific value of the CLM can be close to that of
bagasse. In terms of quantity, Section 1.2.2 gives
an average value of CLM as 150kg dry matter per
tonne of fresh clean cane. Since one tome of cane
yields about280kg bagasse/tc,of whichroughly 50
% is moisture, it is clear that combining the CLM
with the cane can virtually double the amount of
bagasse available, a conclusion substantiated by
Schembri et al. (2002). In practice the efficiency
of recovery of CLM from the fieldsvaries between
56 % and 84 % (Hassuani2001). In a study report-
ed by Palmer (2000), the utilization of cane trash
was reported to increase the amount of dry matter
in bagasse by 53 %.
The CLM is preferably not crushed with the
cane, because it contributes to a higher impurity
load in the raw juice and the extra fiber load re-
duces the capacity of the mill. Leaves and tops can
be easily removed from chopperharvested cane by
blowing off the trashy material, with virtually no
loss of billets, in the conveyors leading to the mill
(Schembriet al. 2002, Rein 2005).
Alternatively the CLM has to be removed dur-
ing harvesting and subsequently collected in the
fields, baled and transported to the mill. In both
cases the CLM is best stored in bales, and if kept
for long enough will dry out, making the subse-
quent shredding of CLM very much simpler and
less energy intensive. Brice50 and Torres (2001)
report that there is no evidence of deteriorationin
piles of stored cane trash although there is gener-
ally an increase in temperature in the pile and a
reduction in moisture.
However CLM has a higher ash content and
in particular, the ratio of alkali metals to silica is
high and so will lead to slaggingand fouling in the
boilers if burnt on its own (see Section 27.2.1). It
should therefore be combined with the bagasse, af-
ter drying or dewatering and shredding, and burnt
together with the bagasse.
31.3.2 Recovery of value-added prod-
ucts
Cane leaves and tops may be the source of
chemicals which can be usefully recovered. CLM
is high in aconitic acid, which may be recovered
from juice expressed from it. The juice contains
some fermentable sugar, which can be fermented
to ethanol and then aconitic acid can be recovered
from the stillage.
The juice from CLM also contains antioxi-
dants that could have substantial value. Otherwise
CLM can be included with bagasse in the general
scheme for biomass processing described in Sec-
tion 31.2.5.
31.4 Sugar-based products
31.4 Sugar-basedproducts
Sucrose is not a cheap feedstock for use as either
a raw material for synthesis of other products or for
fermentation use. Thus chemicals made from sucrose
are generally low-volume high-value products. Many
productshave been identifiedin the laboratorybut few
- have commercial significanceat present. Some of the
most promising are:
Dextran is a high molecular mass glucose poly-
saccharide, formed by fermentation of sucrose by
Leuconostoc sp. and not from monosaccharides.
Fructose is produced as a by-product. High qual-
ity pharmaceutical grade dextran as a blood plasma
extenderis made in this way. Quantitiesare small.
Sorbitol and mannitol. These two products are
formed by hydrogenation of sucrose in the pres-
ence of a suitable catalyst in the ratio 3:l. Sorbitol
is mainly used in the production of ascorbic acid.
Both have a slightly sweet taste and may be used
in diabetic foods. Mannitol usually commands a
significantlyhigher price.
Adhesive resin can be made from sucrose
(Sachinvalaand Jakeway 1994) but this approach
has never been commercialized in spite of attrac-
tive looking economics.
Sucrose esters were made for a period of time by
Tate & Lyle and in Japan for use as detergents,sur-
face active agents and food additives, but this has
subsequently been discontinued. Their advantage
was the biodegradability of the detergent. Procter
& Gamble market a liquid fat substitute Olestra
made from sucrose and used as a zero-calorie fry-
ing oil.
Xanthan gums used as lubricants in oil well drill-
ing muds and as viscosity and gelling agents in
foods have been commercially produced in the
UK.
Functional foods can be synthesizedfrom sucrose.
These are sometimes called nutraceuticals,reflect-
ing both their food and pharmaceuticalvalue.They
encourage the growth of beneficial bacteria in the
stomach such as bifidiobacteria while discourag-
ing the growth of pathogenicorganisms (Dayet al.
2001).This has great benefit in chicken and beef
farming. Both gluco-oligosaccharides and fmcto-
oligosaccharideshave these properties,and the lat-
ter are in commercial use and are generally recog-
nized as safe for human consumption.
Sweeteners. Isomaltulose (Palatinose) is pro-
duced from sucrose by an immobilized enzyme
process. Isomalt (Palatinit@)is a derivative of
isomaltulose produced by hydrogenation of iso-
maltulose. Neosugar is a sucrose derived fructo-
olipsaccharide also used as a sweetener. These
sweeteners are less sweet than sucrose and the
market is not large. Sucralose is also produced
from sucrose, but being about 600 times sweeter
than sucrose, the quantities of sucrose used are
very small.
Biodegradable plastics. Work has been done
in Brazil (Leal 2002) and the USA on the fer-
mentation of sugars to polyhydroxy-alkanoates
(PHAs), of which the most common is polyhy-
droxy-butyrate (PHB). The PHAs are used in
the production of plastics, which can be pro-
duced with a wide range of properties, depend-
ing on the use for the plastic. Roughly 3 kg of
fermentable sugar is required to produce 1kg of
plastic. In Brazil, a low grade sugar is used and
in the USA glucose syrup from corn is assumed
to be the most viable feedstock. Polylactic acid
is also a source of biodegradable plastic, but
corn syrup is the preferred feed for this process
as well because of relative costs in the USA.
The market for biodegradable plastics is large
and this is an area which is expected to expand
in future.
Organic sugar may be regarded as a coproduct, made
in small amounts and sometimes with great diffi-
culty. However the price realized in the supermarket
stores is attractive and the market continues to grow.
Sugar fortified with vitamin A is produced on a large
scale in Guatemala.
High test molasses is a sugar-containing product
made in a sugar mill instead of crystalline sugar, and
is an alternative product rather than a by-product. It
is made from evaporator syrup from which no sugar
has been crystallized, rather than from a runoff mo-
lasses as its name suggests. The syrup is diluted and
partially inverted, using acid or preferably invertase,
resulting in a syrup with about two-thirds of the sug-
ar in the form of invert.Alternatively some syrup can
be fully inverted and mixed with uninverted syrup in
the appropriate ratio. It is subsequently concentrated
to about 85 Brix, with the higher content of mono-
saccharides enabling the total sugars content to be
increased, thus minimizing product transport costs
and giving higher microbial stability.

31.5 Molasses
31.5.1 Fermentation products
Products which use sugar for fermentation can
in theory be made from molasses or sugar or high
test molasses. The choice of feedstock depends on
the value of the product made (the price of feedstock
which can be afforded), the cost of recovering the
product from the fermentation process and required
product purity. This is illustrated in Figure 31.5.
Generally a higher valued product will make use of
a higher priced feedstock.
Feedstocks intermediate between sugar and
molasses may be produced from a mill or refinery
to suit the process economics. Typical is high test
molasses made from raw sugar mill syrup or from
a refinery recovery house molasses. Roughly half to
two-thirds of the sucrose is inverted to monosaccha-
rides, either through the use of invertase from yeast
or acid in a diluted syrup. This reduces the purity
to meet particular tariff requirements for import or
export. In addition the greater solubility of invert
sugars enables a higher concentration product to be
produced.
The most common method of adding value to
molasses is through fermentation to ethanol in its
various forms. Rum has been made from molasses
since the 17mcentury and various other more pure
potable products are also made from molasses. Pro-
duction of ethanol for fuel and industrial use has
also been widespread. This is discussed more fully
in section 31.6. Other products produced by fer-
W ~ k d mentation from molasses include yeast, single-cell

acid and lysine. Products which have been produced

31.5.2 Animal feed
Upgradingof molasses.With someof thesefer-
mentations,recovery of the desired product is more
difficult and costly than the fermentation stage. For
this reason, pretreatmentof molasses is sometimes
advisable,realizingbenefits in recoverycostsgreat-
er than the cost of the pretreatment. Most of these
processes aim at reducing the suspended solids
content and/or the calcium levels. Processes which
have been tried are:
Dilution to 40 Brix, heating, addition of floc-
culant, followed by settling in a subsider or
addition of filter aid and filtration (Saska et al.
1993).
Phosphatation,involvingadditionof phosphoric
acid (which promotes precipitation of inversely
soluble calcium salts), heating and flocculant
addition.
Flotation clarification, involving dilution to
50 Brix, heating, aeration, additionof flocculant
and flotationclarification (Rein 1988).
Addition of sodium carbonateto heated (80 OC)
and diluted molasses to precipitate calcium
salts, which are removed by settling, filtration
or centrifuging.
In the case of lysineproduction, it was found bene-
ficial to use a higher grade of molasses and also to
remove ash and particularly calcium before fermen-
tation by ion exchange (Ahmed et al. 2001). In this
process high test molasses from a refinery is used
andionexchangeis conductedat 55Brix and 60 OC.
The reduction in lysine recovery costsjustified the
cost of upgrading the molasses prior to fermenta-
tion. Options for softening molasses are discussed
by Saska et al. (1993).
Food acids. The most importantof the food ac-
ids produced by fermentation are citric, lactic, tar-
taric and gluconicacids.Thesecanalsobeproduced
from glucose and often glucose syrup is a cheaper
and purer option requiring less effort and reduced
lossesin productrecovery andpurification. In citric
acid manufacture, molasses has to be pretreated to
remove trace elements, particularly iron and man-
ganese, to prevent unlimited mycelium growth.
Corn syrup is often used in preference to molasses
because of technical and economic advantages of a
purer raw material.
Amino acids. Until recently lysine was pro-
duced almost exclusively by a single Japanese com-
pany, but this has now changed. Lysine is an impor-
tant ingredientin animal feeds and its price is often
linked to other feed components like soy beans and
varies accordingly.
Another amino acid produced in large quanti-
ties is glutarnic acid (often as monosodium gluta-
mate). This fermentationcan produce lactic acid as
well. Most other amino acids can also be produced
from molasses.
The developments in genetic engineering have
the potential to improve efficiencies and therefore
the economics of production. In particular phenyl-
alanine,tryptophan,asparticacid and threonineare
produced by fermentation.
Alcohols. Glycerolis produced as an adjunct in
ethanolfermentations. Pasteur showedthat roughly
3 % of the sugars used in ethanol fermentation are
converted to glycerol. By increasing the osmotic
pressurethe productionof glycerolcan be increased
at the expense of ethanol. Glycerol is recovered
from stillage by steam distillation.
Yeast. Baker's yeast is commonly produced
from molasses by aerobic fermentation. One kg of
yeast requires roughly 2 kg of fermentable sugars.
Recoveryof yeast from ethanol distilleriesin Brazil
is becoming more widespread. Roughly 15g dried
yeastn ethanol may be obtained in this way with-
out affecting the ethanol yield. Various strains of
Torula and candida yeasts may also be produced
as animal feeds. There are sufficient fermentable
substances in ethanol stillage to permit a yeast fer-
mentation to be feasible.
