.
2 Animal feed
Molasses is a widely used ingredient in cattle
feeds. The compositionof molasses covered in Sec-
tion 21.1 shows significantfood value in the form of
sugarstogetherwith a widerange of traceelements.
Molassesis oftenthe base ingredientof high quality
liquid supplements. It is a source of readily avail-
able carbohydrate for rumen microbes, enhancing
digestibility and microbial protein production. It
also enhances the physical characteristics, en-
abling added nutrients to be distributed uniformly
throughout the ration, reducing ration sorting and
impartingpalatabilityto feed mixtures.Molasses is
a natural carrier for non-protein nitrogen, vitamins
and other additives.
Referencesp. 737
31 By-productutilization
31.5.3 Use as a fertilizer
The ash content is particularlyhigh in molasses.
It contains virtually all the inorganic species in the
cane and is particularly high in potash. It was not
uncommon in days past to return molasses to the
fields because of its fertilizer value but this is not
often practiced nowadays. In fact the response of
cane to molasses is greater than that achieved with
commercially applied fertilizer. Wynne and Meyer
(2002) claim that molasses increasesorganic matter
in the soil, promotes microbial activity, adds some
useful traceelements, improvessoil aggregationand
reduces surfacecrusting in hard-setting soils.
Against this, molasses is hard to handle and ap-
ply uniformly and a big risk is ground water pollu-
tion if incorrectly managed. A mixture of molasses
and filtercakemay be a betteroption.Distillerystill-
age may be even better as a large part of the organic
component has been removed reducing the COD,
but the material is diluted so that the quantity to
handle is much larger.
31.5.4 Recovery of products of value
It may be possible to recover some products of
value from molasses suchas antioxidantsor aconitic
acid. Howeverit may be easierto recover these from
distillery stillage sincea large part of the sugars has
been removed. Commercial production of aconitic
acid from molasses was once carried out in Louisi-
ana.Aconitic acid was precipitated from heated and
pH-adjusted B molasses before addition of calcium
chloride, which precipitates aconitic acid as the cal-
cium magnesium aconitate (Godchaux 1949). The
product was washed and dried and a yield of over
1 kg/t cane was realized,estimatedto be 38 % of the
aconitic acid entering theplant.
31.6 Ethanol production
Various gradesof ethanol may be produced from
molasses. The manufacture of rum is described by
Kampen (1998) and apart from rum, various other
purified cane spirits for potable use are produced.
Industrial ethanol may be produced as rectified spir-
its at 96.5 % by volume or as dehydrated ethanol
mainly for fuel use. The purity of industrial alcohol
depends on the use to which it is put. Ethanol used
asa solventmay have lessdemandingstandardsthan
high quality ethanol used in cosmetics and phar-
maceuticals. In recent years there has been a huge
increase in the production of ethanol for fuel use,
particularly in Brazil, but now universally in many
sugar producing countries. Production of fuel alco-
hol now predominates.
31.6.1 Ethanol yields
The monosaccharides,glucose and fructose, are
fermented to yield ethanol and carbon dioxide. Su-
crose is hydrolyzed to monosaccharidesbefore fer-
mentation and in the process each mole of sucrose
takes up a mole of water as shown below:
C6HI2O4+ 2 C,H,OH + 2 CO, (31.3)
The stoichiometric yield of ethanol from sucrose is
538kg/t sucrose, or 680Ut sucrose, based on a liq-
uid densityof 0.791kg/Lat 20 O
C
. This assumesthat
the sucrosehydrolyzes to invert sugars and then as-
sumes that only ethanol and carbon dioxide are pro-
duced as products.Therelationshipbetween ethanol
and invert sugarsis slightlydifferent,because of the
water uptake in the hydrolysis of sucrose. Thus the
stoichiometricyield frominvertsugaris 511kg/t in-
vert or 646 L/t invert sugar.
In practice a number of other products are also
formed, and Pasteur's classic experiments estab-
lished that the maximum obtainableyield under ide-
al conditionswas 94.5 %of theoreticali.e. a yield of
643 Utonne of sucrose.
Other products formed in ethanol fermentation
apart from CO, are yeast, glycerol, and succinic
acid, with smaller amounts of lactic, pyruvic and
aceticacids and minor amountsof other compounds.
Ethanol yields are difficult to measure accurately
and it is sometimes more useful to measure these
other products. Glycerol concentration is increased
if the osmoticpressure is high, dueto a high concen-
tration of sugars and other components in solution,
and acids may be high if bacterial infection occurs.
Both these can be used to give an indication of the
efficiency of fermentation.
31.6.2 Fermentationsystems
Using conventional analyses, it has been found
in the laboratory that high yields can be obtained
with higher purity feedstocksand the lowest yield is
obtainedon straightfinalmolasses. This isdueto the
fact that some unfermentable reducing substances
are formed during sugar processing which register
as sugars in the traditional chemical analysis pro-
cedures. For this reason chromatographic methods
of analysis using GC or HPLC are desirable. Using
these methods of analyses, laboratoryyields appear
to be independentof the feedstockpurity.
Laboratory yields generally average around
620 Wt TSAS (total sugarsas sucrose).Under prac-
tical plant operating conditions, an annual yield of
95 % of this i.e. 590 L/t TSAS, is considered to be
a reasonable design figure. This represents 86.6 %
of the stoichiometricyield. Higher values have been
reported in Brazil; Finguerut (2005) reported that
yields have risen steadily over the years but have
now plateaued at 91 % of stoichiometric (619L/t
TSAS), but Leal (2002)reported a value of 92 %.
Unfortunately, most of the yield figuresreported
around the world are based on conventional analy-
ses and thereforeare not directlycomparable.In ad-
dition, a large number of reported yield figures are
unreliable, and somevery widely differentvalues of
yield have been reported. The ethanol produced per
tonne of molasses depends very largely on the sug-
ars content in the molasses. Based on a fermentable
sugar content (expressed as sucrose) of 44 g/100 g
molasses and a yield of 590 Ut TSAS, one tonne
of molasses can be expected to produce 260 Ut. In
practice values between 240 and 280 LIt molasses
have been reported.
31.6.2 Fermentationsystems
Molasses has to be diluted prior to fermenta-
tion to keep the alcohol and dissolved solids con-
centrations at levels low enough so that fermenta-
tion is not affected by a high osmotic pressure. It
is desirable to ferment at as high a concentration as
possible to reduce the cost of distillationand mini-
mize the amount of stillage produced. In practice
the ethanol concentration is generally run at about
9 WlOO L fermented liquor (beer). This is taken to
be the optimum in Brazil wherejuice is mixed with
molasses (Finguerut 2005); when lower purity feed
is used, the ethanol content is reduced somewhat.
Some yeast strains can perform at higher ethanol
values but this is not often regarded as a sustain-
able option. Good quality water, either condensate
or filtered, treated and disinfectedwater, is needed
for dilution.
Batch systems.A diagramrepresenting the fer-
mentationsystemis shownin Figure31.6. It showsa
classical batch fermentation system operatingwith-
out yeast recycle. Each batch may be started with
new yeast, or more often some yeast is kept from a
previous batch as seed yeast in a yeast propagation
tank. Each batch is initiated in a pre-fermenter, into
which air is blown fortheaerobicgrowthphase,and

31 By-product utilization
where the pH is regulated and nutrients are added.
The yeast concentration has to be at the right level
beforepassingto oneof the main fermenters.Feed is
added to the fermenters progressively as the sugars
ferment.The rate at which feed is added determines
the sugars concentration. This procedure is often
referred to as a fed-batch system. The fermentation
cycle is about two daysbut can be longer depending
on the yeast concentration and the ethanol concen-
tration in the mash.
Fermentation proceeds under anaerobic condi-
tions and is exothermic,producing about 580 Wkg
monosaccharide consumed and cooling is neces-
sary to remove the heat produced by fermentation.
The temperature should be controlled between 30
and 34 OC, because fermentation at temperatures
outside this range generally result in a lower yield.
At higher temperatures,products other than ethanol
may be formed. At lower temperatures,the fermen-
tation time is extended,providing more opportunity
for bacterial or other organismsto ferment sugars to
unwanted products.
The fermentation section is designed so that
the whole plant, including the interconnecting pipe
work, can be properly drained, cleaned by water
and sterilizedby steam to guard againstinfection.A
commercialyeast is normally used in the fermenta-
tion process, since the yeast adapts and acclimatizes
to the fermentation conditions and gives yields as
good as those obtained from specialyeasts.
The traditionalsystemforfuelethanolpracticed
in Brazil is the Melle-Boinet system, whereby yeast
is continuously separated from the fermented mash
in high-speed disc-type centrifugals and recycled
back tofermentation.This has the significantadvan-
tage that yeast concentrations can be kept high at
about 800 x lo6cells/mL, leading to fast fermenta-
tion rates, and hence lower fermentation volumes;
fermenter volume of 6 8 m3for each m3/dethanol
produced is common (Leal 2002). Fermentation
times are low, less than 12 h and averaging about
8.5 h, because of the high yeast concentration. In
addition less carbohydrate is required to grow the
yeast, and so in theory at least, higher fermentation
yields result. It is necessary to limit bacterial con-
taminationby acid washing of the yeast, and the oc-
casionaladditionof antibioticsis necessary.
In thisprocess ayeastcreamis separatedin disc-
type centrifugals. Attempts have been made to uti-
lize flocculatingyeasts, which can be separated by
sedimentation, eliminating the need for expensive
high speed centrifugals.
Continuous systems. A great deal of attention
has been given to improving the efficiency of fer-
mentation. Some of this has focused on making use
of continuousrather than batch systems.Continuous
systemsinvolve a number of fermentationtanks op-
eratingin series,with a recycleof yeastfrom the last
to the first fermenter. These systems lead to more
efficient use of fermenter volumes and continuous
systems are generally easier to run with less labor.
However fennenters are simple in construction and
fermenter volume is probably the least expensive
part of the ethanol plant. In general continuoussys-
tems have not always been able to match the yields
achieved by batch systems. Contaminationis more
likely in a continuous system and if it occurs, the
losses are high. There has been considerable dif-
ference of opinion as to which is the better system.
Continuous fermentation accounted for a peak of
50 % productionin Brazil but subsequentlydropped
to around 25 %. Batch fermentationis a saferoption,
but in the long termwith better controland measure-
ment systems, continuous fermentation should turn
out to be the better system.
A modified systemintegratingfermentationand
distillation was introduced by Alfa Laval called the
Biostil process. Ethanol produced in the fermenters
is continuously sent to the distillation columns and
part of the stillage is continuously returned to fer-
mentation. Fermentation is no longer controlled by
the ethanol concentration but by the osmotic pres-
sure of the salts in solution. The advantage of this
process is that the quantity of stillage produced is
vastly reduced, at a concentration roughly three
times that from a conventional system. Water re-
quirements are reduced correspondingly and infec-
tion is not an issue with the continual sterilization
of the returning stillage. A sketch of the system is
shown in Figure 31.7.
Vaporscrubbing.The vapor produced from the
vats is scrubbed in packed towers, and the vapors
produced can be sent to a carbon dioxideplant. The
fermentation equations show that one mole of CO,
is produced for each mole of ethanol, so on a mass
basis almost as much CO, as ethanol is produced.
Carbon dioxidecan in somecasesbe a profitable by-
productand in additionthe vapor scrubbingrecovers
31.6.3 Distillation
ethanolvapor that would otherwisebe lost.It is con-
sidered that the recovery of ethanol from the vapor
raises the yield by around 1to 2 %, with the water
used to scrub the gases being returned and used to
dilutethe feed.
31.6.3 Distillation
The ethanol concentration in the fermented li-
quoris normallyabout9L/100Land isrecoveredby
distillation.Ethyl alcohol has a boiling temperature
of 78.3 "Cat atmosphericpressure but water-ethanol
phase relationships are such that ethanol cannot be
recovered as a pure product by conventionaldistilla-
tion. If it is required toproduce ethanolin anhydrous
form for use as fuel extender, there are two major
stepsrequired in the distillationprocess:
a) The stripping and rectification to produce recti-
fied spirits (96.5 % ethanolby volume).
b) Dehydration to produce anhydrous ethanol,
by azeotropic distillation or through the use of
molecular sieves or by extractive distillation.
The three options are compared by Moura and
dxvila (2005).
If good quality rectified spirits (hydrous ethanol) is
produced, the dehydration stage is usually replaced
with a second distillation step, involving washing
with water to improve the purity of the product.
A typical flow sheetforan azeotropicdistillation
system is shown in Figure31.8. Some modifications
on this flow diagram in different plants are evident
but the principles arecommon.The fermentedmash
fed tothestrippingcolumnis firstheatedby themash
column overheads and then by heat exchange with
stillagefrom the strippingcolumn. It entersnear the
top of the strippingcolumn,and alcohol-freestillage
is produced at the bottom. At the top of the column
is a smallde-gasifying section with a smallaldehyde
concentrationcolumn.Vapor fromthe strippingcol-
umn passes to the bottom of one or more rectifica-
tion columns and rectified spirits is produced as the
top product from this stage. This is produced as a
constant boiling ethanol-water azeotropic mixture
containing about 96 % ethanolby volume and is re-
ferred to as rectified spirits.
In order to remove the remaining water, it is
necessary to introducea third phase into the system
called an entrainer,usually benzene or cyclohexane.
This forms an azeotrope with a lower boiling point
than rectified spirit, and hence facilitates the final
removal of water. The separationis done in the de-
hydration column which results in the product etha-
nol being removed as the bottom stream from the
column.
Fuse1oil amounts to about 10to 15kg/t ethanol
and isremoved from the rectifyingcolumn.Both al-
dehydes and the fuse1 oils (mainly amyl, iso-amyl
and butyl alcohols) interfere with the dehydration
step, and so need to be removed. They have little
additionalvalueon their own, and may be sold sepa-
rately or even added back into the product fuel.

31.6.4 Storageandhandling
Solvent extraction using monoethylene glycol
is a more recent development. The solvent has an
affinity forwater and sois addedat thetop of thed e
hydration column to strip the vapor of water.Anhy-
drous ethanol is condensed at the top of the column
and the solvent/water mixture exits at the bottom.
A stripping column is used to recover the solvent
which is recycled.The advantages of theprocess in-
clude smalIer columnsand a lower steam consump-
tion than with azeotropicdistillation.
After distillation, the ethanol is cooled and
pumped to run down tanks and from there to the
product storage tanks. It is produced at a quality
of 99.8 % ethanol, and is denatured before being
pumped to rail tank carsfor transport to the oil com-
pany depots.Distillationefficiencyis normally very
high and a value of 99 % is commonly assumed for
the recovery of ethanol in distillation.
The distillation columns often use sieve plates,
or some variant of sievetrays, rather than the bubble
cap trays which have been conventionally used in
Brazil. Sieve plates have the advantage that they
are able to operateover a wide range of throughput
rates at high efficiency, but are particularlyuseful in
the stripping column, because scaling can be severe
in this column and they are easier to clean. It has
been found in practice that the lower the purity of
the feedstock used, the more serious is the scaling
problem in this column.The distillationplant has to
be taken off-lineroughlyeveryfour weeks when us-
ing a low purity feedstock to clean the column. This
is done by boiling caustic in the columnfollowed if
necessaryby a manual brushing of the plates.
The conventional distillation system is not de-
signedto be particularlyfuelefficient.Variousmod-
ifications of the system are possible, which make
use of double effect distillation or mechanical va-
por recompression to improve the steam economy
of the plant. These generally involve utilizing the
condenserof one column as the reboiler for another
and require therefore that some of the columns do
not operate at atmosphericpressure. This inevitably
increasesthe capital cost of the plant.
Table 31.4gives some idea of possibleimprove-
ments in steam economy and the increased require-
ments in terms of capital and steam pressure. The
steam efficient systems generally operate the strip-
ping column under vacuum. This has the advan-
tage of reducing the extent of scaling occurring.
A scheme utilizing this approach for distillation is
shown in Figure 31.10.

Once anhydrous ethanol has been produced, it

31.6.5 Stillage productionand disposal
In the case of ethanolproduction from corn, the
effluentstreamafterthealcoholhas been distilledoff
has a significantvalue as an animal feed. Becauseof
this it can significantlyimprove the economicsof an
ethanol from corn operation.
By contrast, the effluent product in the ethanol
from a sugarcaneplant is generally the source of a
severe problem. Dependingon the process used, the
quantity of vinasse or stillage produced varies from
about 8 to 15 litersof stillageperliter of ethanolpro-
duced. The solids content of the stillage varies de-

pending on the purity of material used as feedstock
and the ethanol concentration in the mash. In gen-
eral it contains between 5 to 15 g dissolved solids/
100g stillage. The BOD is high, depending on the
purity of the feedstockused, but usually aboutabove
50 000 mg/L with a range of 40 000-90 000mgL.
The COD has a range of 70 000-170 000 mgL,
averaging about 120000 m@. The pH is also low,
below 5, because of the organic acids formed.
The quantity of stillage can be reduced i.e. its
concentrationincreased,by recyclingpart of thestill-
age back to the fermenters.This technique has been
used with no adverseeffect in a number of plants.
The stillage may be centrifuged prior to treat-
ment to recoveryeastforrecycleor foruse in animal
feeds. Various options for effluent handling are as
follows:
Irrigation. This is the simplest and cheapest
method and has substantial value as a source
of potash. However care must be taken not to
overload the soil; ideally the stillage should be
returned to the total area from which the cane
originated, or else the buildup of both organic
and inorganic components to excessively high
levels may occur, resulting in salt accumulation
and a fall-off in the cane yield. Return of still-
age to the fields is the system widely practiced
in Brazil, but the cost of returning stillage to the
fields furthest from the m
i
l
l can be very high.
In general it is accepted that the benefits of re-
turning stillage to the fields outweigh the costs,
particularlybecause of the valueof potash in the
stillage, providingthe applicationis managed to
prevent any runoff.
Evaporation. If more concentrated effluent
can be produced, it may have use as a binder in
animal feeds, or merely reduce the quantity of
material and hence transport costs to outlying
fields. However, the high capital cost of stain-
less steel evaporators, the need to clean with
aggressive chemicals and the additional steam
required generally makes this an unfavorable
option. Integration of stillage evaporation with
distillation can however reduce the steam usage
significantly.
Solar evaporation.The evaporation of stillage
in largeshallowponds has been shown tobe fea-
sible in Malawi.This can be a feasible option in
areaswherethecane growingoperationrelieson
irrigation, and not natural rainfall. In most cane
producing areas, the natural rainfall is so high
that this optionis impractical.
Spraydrying.The systemwas extensively used
in South Africa to produce a concentrated feed
31.6.7 Economicsof ethanol production
for animals.It hasto be preceded by evaporation
to get the solids content to above 50 g/100 g.
Biological treatment. Anaerobic fermenta-
tion producing methane as a by-product has
been shown to be feasible. Sufficientgas can be
produced to supply a significant proportion of
fuel needed for the ethanol plant. However, the
anaerobic reactors are large and cumbersome,
and the effluent from the anaerobic digester
still has a COD too high for disposal or reuse
and requires further treatment. The process re-
moves roughly 65 % of the COD and 85 % of
the BOD.
Incineration. This process has considerable
attraction on paper, particularly because a sig-
nificant amount of the fuel value of the concen-
trated stillage is recovered, and the solid ash
product has considerablefertilizer value. Incin-
eration of concentrated stillagehas been shown
to be possible. However, the process has not yet
been proven successful over a long period of
time, and the capital involvedis high.
Composting. Distillers in India and Pakistan
add stillage to filter cake on large concrete
slabs. The heat generated by the composting
process is sufficientto evaporate the water, and
very good quality compost high in potash is
produced in about 30 days. The disadvantages
arethe very largeareasrequiredfor composting
and the cost of transporting a bulky relatively
low valueproduct to the market.
Recovery of high value products. The still-
age has small quantitiesof componentsof some
value such as glycerol, succinic acid and aco-
nitic acld, which could be recovered and sold.
However the recovery processes involved are
not simpleand thebulk of the stillagestillneeds
to be disposed of.
31.6.6 Carbon dioxide recovery
The quantity of carbon dioxide produced in
fermentation is equimolar with ethanol as equa-
tion (31.2) indicates, so by mass slightly less than
the quantity of ethanol will be produced, in the ratio
of their molecular mass 44:46. Based on Pasteur's
yield, a maximum quantityof 486 kg CO,/t ferment-
ables expressed as sucrose is expected. Depending
on the sugars content of the molasses, and allow-
ing for an 80-85 %recovery, CO, produced is about
180kg/t molasses.
The process of producing liquid CO, involves
adsorption of impurities in a carbon bed and drying
before compressing.A CO, plant can add substan-
tially to the viability of an ethanolproject under the
rightconditions.In somecasesthe CO, plant may be
operated by the consumerof the product.
31.6.7 Economics of ethanol produc-
tion
Ethanolproductionisnot acapital-intensivepro-
cess, unlike most high-volumechemical production
processes. There are no exotic materials required in
theplant and most vessels operateat atmosphericor
close to atmosphericpressure. Capital costs depend
on the country where the plant is sited,but typically
an anhydrous ethanol plant to produce 50 million L
ethanollyear will cost$16million and aplant topro-
duce 500 million Llyear will cost$80 million (2004
prices). This includes fermentation and distillation
and the cost of integrating the ethanol plant into a
sugar mill but excludes stillage treatment. Although
there are some economies of scale inherent in large
production plants, thisis not an overridingissueasis
the casein many chemicalproductionfacilities.Fer-
menters arediscretevesselsand largerplantsusually
just mean additionalvessels.In very largeplants du-
plicate distillationtrains may be used. Capitalcostis
roughly proportionalto capacityto the power 0.7.
An annexeddistillery i.e. oneattachedto a sugar
mill, isusuallythefavoredoption,becauseitcanben-
efit from utilizing the services and utihties provided
by the sugar mill, especially steam. If steam can be
provided "free", the economics are enhanced.
The major cost item is the cost of the feed. For
this reason, crystallizable sugar is seldom a suitable
feed, without significantsubsidy, but molasses gen-
erally is priced low enough for the feedstock cost
to be acceptably low for a viable project. In most
instances, the cost of the feedstockrepresents about
two-thirds of the total cost of production.The level
of technologyin ethanolproductionis similar to that
used in a sugar mill and the two processes of sugar
production and ethanol production integrate easily.
Technologicalrisk is minimal. The deciding factors
in the viabilityof ethanolmanufactureare the cost of
feedstock and the price received for the product.
